text: On Thursday, U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis announced that he had authorized the deployment of additional troops to Afghanistan, marking a significant move by the Trump administration in addressing the ongoing conflict, which is now the longest in U.S. history. Although Mattis refrained from disclosing the number of troops involved, he mentioned that this force would aid in the fight against Taliban militants and other extremist groups. "I have indeed signed orders, but the process is not finalized. In other words, I have approved some of the orders for troops that will be sent, while we are still determining the specifics," Mattis informed journalists. He indicated that further details regarding the number of troops would be shared during his upcoming briefing to Congress next week; however, sources within the U.S. government have indicated to Reuters that President Trump has granted Mattis the ability to deploy approximately 4,000 more personnel to Afghanistan.  "This includes more advisers and enablers, along with fire support, for instance," Mattis elaborated. He clarified that no additional troops had yet been deployed and that the process might take a "couple of days". Following a comprehensive review of his administration's strategy for Afghanistan, Trump last week pledged the U.S. to a prolonged military presence in the nation while vowing to intensify efforts against the Taliban insurgents. According to the Pentagon’s report released on Wednesday, roughly 11,000 American soldiers are currently stationed in Afghanistan, which is significantly more than previously reported figures.  Mattis also remarked that the composition of U.S. forces in Afghanistan would begin to evolve in accordance with Trump's directives. Even with the potential increase of several thousand troops, U.S. military presence in Afghanistan would still be considerably lower than its peak during 2011, which saw over 100,000 troops at a time when there was substantial domestic pressure in Washington to reduce the costs associated with the operation. Some officials in the U.S. have expressed skepticism regarding the effectiveness of sending more troops, suggesting that any number deemed politically acceptable would likely be insufficient to alter the current situation, let alone foster stability and security. Thus far, more than 2,300 American lives have been lost, and over 17,000 have been injured in Afghanistan. The security landscape in Afghanistan has worsened for both the U.S. and the Afghan government over recent years. As of February 20, the U.S. military assessed that the Afghan government controlled or influenced nearly 60 percent of the country's 407 districts, a decline of nearly 11 percentage points when compared to 2016, as reported by the U.S. Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction. Earlier this month, the Taliban addressed Trump in an open letter, asserting that the military situation in Afghanistan was "far worse than you realize" and warned that sending additional troops would be counterproductive. The Taliban has been engaged in an insurgency against the Western-supported Afghan government since their removal from power following the U.S.-led invasion after the September 11 attacks in 2001, which were orchestrated by al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden from a haven in Afghanistan.
source_text: Mattis signs orders to send additional troops to Afghanistan. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis said on Thursday he had signed orders to send additional troops to Afghanistan, the most concrete step yet by President Donald Trump’s administration in tackling America’s longest war. Mattis did not specify the size of the force, which will help combat Taliban insurgents and other armed Islamists.      “Yes, I have signed orders but it is not complete. In other words I have signed some of the (orders for) troops that will go and we are identifying the specific ones,” Mattis told reporters. Mattis said he would not comment on how many additional troops were included in the orders until he briefs Congress next week, but U.S. officials have told Reuters that Trump has given Mattis the authority to send about 4,000 additional troops to Afghanistan.  “It is more advisers, it is more enablers, fire support, for example,” Mattis said. He added that no additional troops had moved in yet and could take a “couple of days.” After a months-long review of his Afghanistan policy, Trump committed the United States last week to an open-ended conflict in the country and promised a stepped-up campaign against Afghan Taliban insurgents. About 11,000 U.S. troops are serving in Afghanistan, the Pentagon said on Wednesday, thousands more than it has previously stated.     Mattis said that the make up of those U.S. forces in Afghanistan would also start changing in line with Trump’s guidance.  Any increase of several thousand troops would leave U.S. forces in Afghanistan well below their peak of more than 100,000 troops in 2011, when Washington was under huge domestic political pressure to draw down the costly operation. Some U.S. officials have told Reuters they questioned the benefit of sending more troops to Afghanistan because any politically palatable number would not be enough to turn the tide, much less create stability and security. To date, more than 2,300 Americans have been killed and over 17,000 wounded in Afghanistan. The security situation in Afghanistan has deteriorated for the United States and Afghan government over the past few years. The Afghan government was assessed by the U.S. military to control or influence almost 60 percent of Afghanistan’s 407 districts as of Feb. 20, a nearly 11 percentage-point decrease from the same time in 2016, according to data released by the U.S. Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction.  Earlier this month, the Taliban told Trump in an open letter that the military situation in Afghanistan was “far worse than you realize”, and sending in more troops would be self-destructive. The Taliban, seeking to restore strict Islamic law, has waged an insurgency against the Western-backed Afghan government since losing power in a U.S.-led invasion after the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001. Those attacks were planned by al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden from a base in Afghanistan.

text: On Thursday, Turkish authorities arrested 136 individuals suspected of connections to the coup attempt that occurred last year, according to the state-run Anadolu news agency. Among those detained were former members of the police force, educators, and military personnel, as part of four distinct operations. The capital city of Ankara was the main focus of one operation, where 60 former security officials were taken into custody, with actions spreading across 30 provinces, Anadolu reported. Another operation, which started on Wednesday and focused on Diyarbakir, led to the detention of 55 soldiers across an additional 26 provinces. Authorities continued to search for one additional suspect. Furthermore, six individuals were apprehended in the northern provinces of Samsun and Karabuk, along with 15 teachers who were detained in Ankara, as per Anadolu's coverage. The suspects reportedly utilized the encrypted messaging application, ByLock, which the government claims was employed by the network associated with Fethullah Gulen, a cleric residing in the United States. Ankara holds Gulen responsible for the failed coup in July 2016, which he has denied and condemned. In the wake of the coup attempt, over 50,000 individuals, including civil servants, military members, and police, have been imprisoned awaiting trial. In addition, approximately 150,000 people faced dismissal or suspension. This extensive crackdown has raised concerns among Turkey's Western allies and human rights organizations, who argue that President Tayyip Erdogan is leveraging the coup as a justification to suppress dissent. The government defends these actions, implemented under the emergency rule established post-coup, as essential to address the security challenges faced by Turkey.
source_text: Turkey detains 136 for suspected ties to coup plotters: agency. ISTANBUL (Reuters) - Turkey detained 136 people, including former police, teachers and soldiers, in four separate operations on Thursday over suspected links to last year s attempted military coup, the state-run Anadolu news agency said. Authorities detained 60 former security officials in the operation centered in the capital Ankara and spread over 30 provinces, Anadolu said. In a separate operation that began on Wednesday and centered on Diyarbakir and spread over 26 other provinces, 55 soldiers were detained, Anadolu said. Officials were still searching for one more suspect. Six others were detained in the northern provinces of Samsun and Karabuk, as well as 15 teachers in Ankara, Anadolu said. The suspects were alleged to be using the encrypted messaging app, ByLock, which the government says was used by the network of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen. Ankara blames Gulen, for orchestrating the failed coup in July 2016. Gulen has denied involvement and denounced the putsch. More than 50,000 people, including police, military personnel and civil servants, have been jailed pending trial in the aftermath of the July 2016 coup. Some 150,000 people were sacked or suspended. The crackdown has alarmed Turkey s Western allies and rights groups, who say President Tayyip Erdogan is using the coup as a pretext to muzzle dissent. The government says the measures, taken under emergency rule that was imposed after the coup, are necessary due to the security threats Turkey faces.

text: A historic agreement was finalized on Wednesday, allowing the United States to provide Israel with $38 billion in military support over the next ten years, marking the largest military assistance package in U.S. history. This deal, which was previously reported by Reuters, will enable Israel, Washington's primary ally in the Middle East, to enhance its fighter aircraft capabilities, boost the mobility of its ground forces, and fortify its missile defense systems, according to a senior official from the U.S. government. While this package represents the highest amount of military aid ever allocated to any nation, it requires certain concessions from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as indicated by officials from both nations. Among these concessions is Israel's commitment to refrain from requesting additional funding from Congress beyond the annual guarantees established in the new package and to gradually discontinue a unique arrangement that has permitted Israel to utilize a portion of its U.S. aid for its own defense industry rather than exclusively on American-made military equipment, as reported by the officials. The prolonged negotiations, which spanned nearly ten months, highlighted ongoing tensions between President Barack Obama and Netanyahu, particularly concerning the nuclear agreement with Iran, Israel's long-time adversary, which Netanyahu opposed. Additionally, the United States and Israel have experienced disagreements over issues related to the Palestinians. However, the right-leaning Netanyahu concluded that it was more advantageous to create a new agreement with Obama, who is set to leave office in January, instead of relying on potentially more favorable terms from the incoming U.S. administration, according to officials from both sides. With this new pact, Netanyahu can avoid uncertainties regarding the next president, whether it be Democrat Hillary Clinton or Republican Donald Trump, allowing Israel’s defense establishment to engage in forward planning. Obama’s advisors sought a new agreement prior to the conclusion of his presidency, viewing it as a crucial aspect of his legacy. Critics from the Republican Party have accused him of not paying sufficient attention to Israel’s security needs, which the White House has firmly rejected, asserting that Obama has maintained a stern approach with Netanyahu. The memorandum of understanding, which is valued at $38 billion, encompasses U.S. fiscal years 2019 to 2028, succeeding the previous $30 billion MOU established in 2007, which is set to expire at the conclusion of fiscal year 2018. In a written statement, Obama expressed, "Prime Minister Netanyahu and I are confident that the new MOU will make a significant contribution to Israel’s security in what remains a dangerous neighborhood." The signing of the agreement took place at the State Department, with U.S. Undersecretary of State Thomas Shannon and Jacob Nagel, the acting head of Netanyahu’s national security council, signing on behalf of their respective governments. A fact sheet released by the White House outlines the details of the agreement, which includes: - annual payments amounting to $3.3 billion in foreign military financing - $500 million allocated each year for Israeli missile defense funding, marking the first time this has been formally incorporated into the aid pact. - The gradual phase-out of a special arrangement that for decades has allowed Israel to allocate 26.3 percent of the U.S. aid toward its own defense industry instead of solely on American-made armaments. - The removal of a longstanding provision that has enabled Israel to utilize about 13 percent of the U.S. aid for military fuel purchases. - The financial support will facilitate Israel in updating "the lion’s share" of its fighter aircraft, which includes the acquisition of additional F-35 Joint Strike Fighters. Israel is expected to receive 33 F-35 aircraft, with the first two scheduled for delivery in December.

text: In eastern Syria, a fatal airstrike struck the Qusur area of Deir al-Zor city, which is under government control, resulting in the deaths of over a dozen individuals, as reported by state television and a war monitoring group on Monday. According to state media, the attack was carried out by aircraft from a U.S.-led coalition targeting Islamic State, claiming that 14 civilians lost their lives and 32 others sustained injuries. However, a representative from the coalition stated on Tuesday that they did not conduct such an operation, noting that their most recent strike in the region occurred in September across the Euphrates River from the city. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a UK-based war monitor, indicated that the identity of the aircraft responsible for the strike remains unclear, but at least 22 fatalities were reported. The Syrian military, with the support of Russia, Iran, and Shiite militia groups, is engaged in combat against Islamic State in Deir al-Zor and other areas nearby. Both Russian and Syrian planes have been conducting operations against Islamic State in this region. Meanwhile, the U.S.-backed coalition has been executing airstrikes on Islamic State forces to assist the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which consist of Kurdish and Arab fighters located to the east of Deir al-Zor, across the Euphrates. Recent months have seen multiple encounters between U.S.-backed forces and the Syrian army as both have sought to displace the jihadists from their positions in eastern Syria. Communication has been established between the U.S. and Russia to mitigate potential clashes between these opposing military efforts.
source_text: Deadly air strike hits Syrian government-held Deir al-Zor: state TV, monitor. BEIRUT (Reuters) - An air raid in the government-held Qusur district of Deir al-Zor city in eastern Syria killed more than a dozen people, Syrian state television and a war monitor said on Monday.  State television said jets from a U.S.-led international coalition battling Islamic State carried out the air strike and that it killed 14 civilians and wounded 32 others.  A spokesman for the coalition said on Tuesday it had not carried out such a raid, and that its only strike in the vicinity in recent weeks took place in September across the Euphrates from the city. The war monitor, the Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, reported that it was not known which aircraft carried out the strike, but that at least 22 people were killed.  The Syrian army, backed by Russia, Iran and Shi ite militias, is fighting Islamic State in the city of Deir al-Zor, as well as in parts of the surrounding countryside. Both Syrian and Russian jets have been hitting Islamic State in that area.  The U.S.-backed coalition has been conducting air strikes against Islamic State in support of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) alliance of Kurdish and Arab militias to the east of Deir al-Zor across the Euphrates.  The rival U.S.-backed and Syrian army offensives against Islamic State have clashed several times over recent months as they have pushed the jihadists from territory in eastern Syria.  The U.S. and Russia have said they communicate with each other to prevent possible points of conflict of violence between the two offensives.

text: The United Kingdom anticipates a rapid consensus on a transitional framework for its exit from the European Union, as stated by a spokesperson for Prime Minister Theresa May on Tuesday. However, notable disagreements regarding the Brexit timeline remain. The UK is aiming for an implementation phase lasting approximately two years following its withdrawal from the EU in March 2019, during which time access to the EU single market would remain largely the same while new arrangements are established. Businesses are eager to obtain details about this agreement to eliminate any uncertainty regarding the trading regulations they will encounter after the UK departs from the bloc. The spokesperson expressed confidence, stating, "In terms of the broad outline of an implementation period, we believe that we can agree that quickly." Nevertheless, the spokesperson did not specify when the UK hopes to finalize such an agreement. He added, "We’re clear that we want to achieve this implementation period, that we believe we can do so, and that our priority is to provide certainty for business." On Monday, May's comments left some businesses perplexed, as she indicated that any implementation phase would not be settled until a deal concerning the UK's future trading relationship with the EU was established. This contradicted expectations that a transitional arrangement would be finalized long before any trade deal. The remarks also underscored a significant divergence between the UK and the EU regarding the timing of the trade agreement. The UK is pursuing a robust trade deal with the EU to replace the current arrangement at the conclusion of the implementation period. Officials believe that their existing close relations with the EU will facilitate reaching an agreement by October 2018. In contrast, Michel Barnier, the EU's chief negotiator, stated that negotiating a trade agreement would require three years, indicating that if discussions commence in December, the deal would be finalized by the end of a transition period extending until December 2020. When asked if the UK maintained that it could still secure a trade agreement by the end of next year, given the two-year exit process, May's spokesperson affirmed, "Yes." An EU official responded to the timeline proposed by the UK, expressing that the bloc aimed to "define a framework for our future relationship" by the same time next year to ensure that a withdrawal treaty could reflect that future under the conditions of the Article 50 legal exit process. However, the official clarified that the EU would only engage in discussions on the specifics of a free trade agreement after the UK officially exits in March 2019, due to legal restrictions that prevent the EU from negotiating trade deals with its own member states. A spokeswoman for May, when questioned about the EU official's position, remarked, "Article 50 states that the withdrawal agreement must consider our future relationship, so by our exit, we will know the terms of our partnership with the EU." However, she added, "As for the details, that’s subject to negotiation, and I can’t pre-empt those."

text: SEOUL/WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The incoming U.S. President Donald Trump has demonstrated awareness of the pressing threat from North Korea's nuclear ambitions, as indicated by South Korea on Tuesday. The South Korean government noted that Trump's recent "clear warning" to North Korea signifies his commitment to maintaining sanctions against the reclusive nation. On Sunday, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un proclaimed that his nation, capable of nuclear strikes, was nearing the launch of an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), which could potentially target parts of the U.S. In response, Trump refuted this assertion via Twitter, stating, "It won’t happen." The Foreign Ministry of South Korea remarked that Trump's statement, marking his first reference to North Korea's nuclear concerns since the November election, could be seen as a significant warning to the regime. "Thanks to our proactive outreach, President-elect Trump and U.S. officials are evidently cognizant of the serious and urgent nature of the North Korean nuclear threat," explained ministry spokesperson Cho June-hyuck during a press conference. He added, "They are holding a firm position on the necessity of sanctions against North Korea and the importance of close cooperation between South Korea and the United States." The U.S. State Department acknowledged that North Korea persists in its quest for nuclear and missile technology. "At this moment, we don’t believe he possesses the capability to equip one of these missiles with a nuclear warhead...but we are aware that he continues to aspire to acquire such capabilities, with his programs advancing in that direction," stated State Department spokesperson John Kirby to the press. Although Trump has not yet detailed a specific North Korea strategy, he hinted during his election campaign that he would be open to dialogue with Kim if the situation allowed. Kellyanne Conway, a spokesperson for Trump, informed ABC’s "Good Morning America" that the president-elect was signaling to North Korea through this tweet and other statements that such an event would not occur. "As the president of the United States, he aims to position himself between them and their missile capabilities, which experts claim could be deployed to reach Seattle very quickly," Conway noted. She further mentioned that Trump has not publicly outlined how he might address North Korea’s nuclear and missile endeavors and that he would refrain from doing so until after his inauguration. "We are aware that sanctions are a potential course of action," Conway remarked. "Their effectiveness has varied. I believe that China must play a significant role in this context as well." Trump's critiques of China regarding this matter have been apparent. On Monday, he asserted that while China has benefited from its economic relationship with the United States, it has failed to use its influence to help manage North Korea. In reaction to this, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Geng Shuang stated that China has been advocating for the denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. "China's contributions in this area are quite evident," Geng remarked during a press briefing. "As a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, we have actively participated in relevant discussions about the North Korean nuclear situation and have collectively passed several resolutions with other nations. This reflects China’s responsible stance." When queried about Trump’s assertion that China is not assisting in curbing North Korea's nuclear aspirations, Kirby from the State Department responded: "We do not concur with that viewpoint." For years, the United States has dismissed North Korean proposals for negotiations, insisting on disarmament as a prerequisite. The U.S. and its ally South Korea have reacted to two nuclear tests and several missile launches conducted by North Korea last year with increasingly stringent sanctions. Following Pyongyang's fifth and most significant nuclear test in September, the U.N. Security Council imposed additional sanctions on North Korea at the end of November. A fully operational North Korean ICBM could pose a threat to the continental United States, situated approximately 9,000 km (5,500 miles) from North Korea. ICBMs typically have a minimum range of around 5,500 km (3,400 miles), although some can exceed that distance.
source_text: Trump recognizes 'urgency' of North Korea nuclear threat: South Korea. SEOUL/WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. President-elect Donald Trump’s “clear warning” to North Korea shows he is aware of the urgency of the threat posed by North Korea’s nuclear program and will not waver from a policy of sanctions against the isolated country, South Korea said on Tuesday. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said on Sunday his nuclear-capable country was close to test-launching an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), raising the prospect of putting parts of the United States in range. Trump dismissed the claim, saying on Twitter: “It won’t happen.” South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said Trump’s comment, his first mention of the North Korean nuclear issue since the U.S. election in November, could be interpreted as a “clear warning” to the North. “Because of our active outreach, President-elect Trump and U.S. officials are clearly aware of the gravity and urgency of the North Korean nuclear threat,” ministry spokesman Cho June-hyuck said at a briefing. “They are maintaining an unwavering stance on the need for sanctions on North Korea and for close cooperation between South Korea and the U.S.”  The U.S. State Department said it recognized that North Korea continued to pursue nuclear and ballistic missile technologies. “We do not believe that at this point in time he has the capability to tip one of these (missiles) with a nuclear warhead ... but we do know that he continues to want to have those capabilities and the programs continue to march in that direction,” State Department spokesman John Kirby told reporters.    Trump has not outlined a policy on North Korea, but during the U.S. election campaign indicated he would be willing to talk to its leader, Kim, given the opportunity. Trump spokeswoman Kellyanne Conway told ABC’s “Good Morning America” program that the president-elect was “putting North Korea on notice through this tweet and through other statements that this won’t happen.” “He as president of the United States wants to stand between them and their missile capabilities, which experts say could be deployed to reach Seattle almost immediately,” Conway said. She said Trump had not publicly stated how he might respond to North Korea’s nuclear weapons and missile programs and “won’t before he’s inaugurated.” “We do know that there are sanctions that are possible,” Conway said. “They haven’t always worked. I think that China would have to have a significant role here as well.”Trump has been critical of China over the issue. On Monday, he said China had benefited from its economic ties with the United States but would not use its influence to help control North Korea. In response, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Geng Shuang said China had been pushing for the denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. “China’s efforts in this regard are perfectly obvious,” Geng told a news briefing. “As a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council we have proactively participated in relevant discussions on the North Korean nuclear issue and have jointly passed several resolutions with other parties.  “This shows China’s responsible attitude.” Asked about Trump’s view that China was not helping to contain North Korea’s nuclear ambitions, the State Department’s Kirby said: “We would not agree with that assessment.” The United States has for years dismissed North Korean calls for talks, insisting it must disarm first.  The United States and ally South Korea have responded to two North Korean nuclear tests and various missile tests last year with ever-more-severe sanctions. The U.N. Security Council imposed new sanctions on North Korea at the end of November after Pyongyang carried out its fifth and largest nuclear test so far in September. A North Korean ICBM, once fully developed, could threaten the continental United States, which is about 9,000 km (5,500 miles) from the North.  ICBMs have a minimum range of about 5,500 km (3,400 miles), but some are designed to travel 10,000 km (6,200 miles) or further.     North Korea worked last year on developing components for an ICBM, saying it was close to a test-launch plausible, international weapons experts said on Monday.

text: A justice official reported that French law enforcement discovered a second cache of explosive substances on Thursday in the vicinity of Paris, following a similar discovery in a nearby neighborhood the previous day. The operation on Thursday targeted a garage leased by one of three individuals detained after the raid on an apartment in Villejuif, located on the southern fringe of the French capital. According to Interior Minister Gerard Collomb, substances used for creating TATP, an explosive commonly utilized by suicide attackers, were located in the apartment, which came to the attention of authorities after a plumber alerted them to suspicious activities. Following Wednesday's operation, two individuals in their 30s and 40s were taken into custody, and Collomb noted that these suspects were being interrogated on the grounds of suspected terrorism, even though they mentioned plans for a bank robbery. A third suspect was apprehended overnight, a source disclosed. The individuals under scrutiny expressed intentions to detonate a bank using the TATP, yet Collomb stated that authorities believe they have connections to terrorism, and this will be the focus of the investigation. This line of inquiry was initiated based on findings from phone communications after the initial raid, he added. Later developments in the day revealed that law enforcement found explosive materials in a garage located in Thiais, southeast of Paris. Over the last three years in France, Islamist-inspired assailants have killed more than 230 individuals, as the nation collaborates with the United States and other nations to conduct bombings against Islamic State positions in Iraq and Syria. TATP, known for its instability, has been employed by extremists in several incidents across western Europe, including attacks in Manchester in May, Brussels in 2016, and Paris in 2015.

text: The U.S. Supreme Court seemed inclined on Wednesday to support property owners challenging the federal government regarding permit requirements under a national water protection statute, in a case centered on plans for a peat mine in Minnesota. During a one-hour argument, the justices considered the balance between property rights and environmental regulations, particularly the significant 1972 U.S. Clean Water Act. A majority of the eight justices indicated they were sympathetic toward Hawkes Co Inc, a North Dakota-based company contesting an Obama administration determination that its land contains wetlands. Under the law, property owners must obtain permits in such cases. For developers and other landowners, clarity on whether a specific area is subject to the law’s jurisdiction holds considerable importance, as such a designation initiates a prolonged and costly permitting procedure. Attorneys representing Hawkes contended that the company should have the opportunity to dispute the necessity of undergoing the permit process altogether. Justices from both liberal and conservative backgrounds voiced concerns regarding the burdens placed on property owners by the existing framework. Chief Justice John Roberts, who is conservative, remarked that applicants who ignore a government finding stating they require a permit operate at "great practical risk." On the liberal side, Ruth Bader Ginsburg described the process as "very arduous and very expensive." Meanwhile, Stephen Breyer, also a liberal, asserted that the government’s determination that Hawkes was obligated to secure a permit was "perfectly suited for review in the courts." Only liberal Elena Kagan showed support for the government’s position, expressing worries about how a ruling favoring property owners might influence actions by other governmental bodies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission. Advocates for property rights noted that the permitting process could extend up to two years and incur costs reaching $270,000, with owners facing fines of up to $37,500 daily for failing to comply. Business organizations, such as the National Association of Home Builders and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, along with 29 states, submitted legal documents opposing the Obama administration in this matter. This case follows a unanimous ruling by the justices in 2012, which allowed property owners facing Clean Water Act enforcement actions to seek judicial intervention before being compelled to comply or face financial penalties. Last year, the Obama administration introduced a new rule clarifying the extent of federal authority over water bodies, but a federal appeals court has stayed the regulation after it was contested by 18 states. Following the February death of Justice Antonin Scalia, only eight justices participated in the deliberations. A decision is expected by the end of June.

text: In a detailed court filing, it was revealed that Paul Manafort, the former campaign manager for President Donald Trump who has been indicted, lavished considerable amounts on luxury items. Over a span of two years, he expended nearly $1 million on eight rugs and more than $1.3 million on clothing purchased from high-end retailers located in Beverly Hills, California, and New York City. The extravagant lifestyle he led, which included residences in Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Hamptons, and Arlington, Virginia, was highlighted in an indictment made public on Monday, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. According to the indictment from Special Counsel Robert Mueller of the Justice Department, Manafort “used his hidden overseas wealth to enjoy a lavish lifestyle in the United States.” Evidence presented by prosecutors indicated that Manafort financed the acquisition of four Range Rovers and a Mercedes-Benz through transactions they alleged were illegally sourced from abroad to evade U.S. income taxes, as detailed in the 31-page court document. They also noted that he purchased a condominium in a renovated red-brick structure in New York’s fashionable Soho district for $2.85 million, with funds frequently traced back to Cyprus. On Monday, both Manafort and his associate Rick Gates entered not guilty pleas to charges of money laundering and other allegations stemming from the investigation into Russian meddling in the 2016 presidential election. During the court session, both men maintained stoic expressions. Greg Andres, a federal prosecutor on Mueller’s team, remarked that his office faced challenges in establishing the net worth of Manafort and Gates, complicating the process of determining suitable bail conditions. Andres specified that Manafort reported a diverse range of net asset values in various financial documents, with figures fluctuating from $20 million to $100 million. Gates reported asset values ranging from as low as $2 million to as high as $30 million. A judge in the federal court ordered both individuals to be placed under house arrest and established a $10 million unsecured bond for Manafort and a $5 million unsecured bond for Gates. Manafort’s lawyer, Kevin Downing, asserted on Monday that there was no proof suggesting his client conspired with the Russian authorities while he was affiliated with the Trump campaign. The indictment did not reference Trump or his campaign. Manafort directed the Trump campaign from June to August of 2016 before stepping down amid allegations that he may have accepted millions in illicit payments from a pro-Russian political faction in Ukraine. The indictment reported that both Manafort and Gates amassed tens of millions of dollars from work in Ukraine and laundered funds through numerous U.S. and foreign entities to obscure payments from American officials. It detailed Manafort's spending of $849,215 at a men's clothing retailer in New York and $520,440 at another store in Beverly Hills. Additionally, he invested $5,434,793 in a residence in Water Mill, New York, located in the Hamptons, which included a landscaping expenditure of $820,240. Aerial imagery of the property reveals gardens, a swimming pool, a tennis court, a basketball court, and a putting green with a sand trap spread across 2.37 acres (0.96 hectare). Furthermore, a seven-bedroom brownstone in Brooklyn, which he purchased for $3 million, was described in a real estate listing as “dripping with detail - perfectly intact crown moldings and medallions, gold leafed carved window detail, 5 marble mantels, and original Lincrusta paper wall covering.”
source_text: Manafort spent millions on homes, rugs, clothes: court filing. text: In Manchester, N.H., a breakfast gathering highlighted a significant hurdle for presidential candidate Bernie Sanders. After achieving a notable victory over Hillary Clinton in the New Hampshire Democratic primary, Sanders shared a meal with Al Sharpton, one of the nation’s leading civil rights figures. This meeting underscores Sanders’ recognition that to sustain a viable campaign against Clinton, he must quickly expand his support base, particularly among African American voters, who have consistently favored Clinton in polling. As the Democratic contest proceeds to South Carolina, where over half of the primary electorate in 2008 identified as African American, the importance of appealing to diverse demographics becomes even more pronounced, especially given that New Hampshire and Iowa, the initial states in the 2016 election cycle, have less diversity. The Vermont senator met Sharpton at the same Harlem establishment where the activist previously convened with Barack Obama during the latter's 2008 campaign for president, a strategic choice intended to symbolize Sanders’ outreach to minority communities. "My concern is that in January of next year for the first time in American history a black family will be moving out of the White House. I do not want black concerns to be moved out with them," Sharpton expressed to journalists following their discussion. The senator and Sharpton tackled topics including a recent surge in police violence against black men and various other critical issues. Sharpton indicated he would withhold his endorsement until he had the opportunity to meet with Clinton. Even before voter exit surveys confirmed Sanders’ triumph in New Hampshire, Clinton’s team was actively emphasizing her substantial lead over Sanders among African American and Latino constituents. "It will be very difficult, if not impossible, for a Democrat to win the nomination without strong levels of support among African American and Hispanic voters," asserted Robby Mook, Clinton’s campaign manager, in a memo directed to the press. Mook anticipated that the Democratic nomination would be decided in March, as the race transitions to 22 states rich in delegates, many of which possess significant urban and minority populations, a scenario that would likely favor Clinton. Clinton has an extensive history of advocating for civil rights and has profited from her husband Bill Clinton’s popularity within the African American community during his presidency, a relationship that became strained during the intense 2008 primary contest with Obama. National polling data from Reuters/Ipsos indicated that as of January, African Americans supported Clinton at a ratio of 3 to 1 over Sanders. Among Hispanic voters, 48 percent preferred Clinton while 32 percent showed support for Sanders. However, as black and Hispanic constituents became increasingly familiar with Sanders through televised debates, his favorability ratings among these groups experienced a slight uptick in recent months, as indicated by polling results. Thus far, Sanders' impressive performance can be attributed largely to the support he has garnered from predominantly young white voters who resonate with his populist anti-Wall Street rhetoric and his advocacy for income equality. However, in the forthcoming nominating contests, Sanders must convey his message to a wider audience, specifically targeting minority voters, who are pivotal in determining the Democratic nominee. According to a Gallup poll conducted in 2013, African Americans and Hispanics make up 35 percent of the Democratic party. To enhance his outreach to black voters, Sanders has ramped up campaign events aimed at African American audiences and has run advertisements on radio stations targeting black listeners. At rallies, rapper Killer Mike occasionally introduces Sanders, while academic Cornel West has also lent his support to the senator's campaign. Sanders frequently denounces the disproportionate targeting of black individuals by police forces and has advocated for greater accountability and transparency within law enforcement. The senator's heightened efforts to engage minority voters follow concerns raised about whether he possesses sufficient support to secure the presidency. Clinton has herself questioned Sanders’ electability both on the campaign trail and during debates. Nevertheless, the race continues.
source_text: A breakfast in Harlem underscores key challenge for White House hopeful Sanders. MANCHESTER, N.H. (Reuters) - Bernie Sanders had breakfast with one of America’s most prominent civil rights activists, Al Sharpton, just hours after trouncing Hillary Clinton in the New Hampshire Democratic presidential nominating contest. The meeting marked a recognition by Sanders that his campaign must swiftly broaden its base of support if he has any chance of mounting a long-term challenge to Clinton, who consistently polls better among African American voters. They will play a crucial role in the Democratic race as it moves to South Carolina - where more than half of the Democratic primary voters in 2008 were African American - and other states more diverse than New Hampshire or Iowa, which held the first contest of the 2016 election. Sanders met Sharpton in the same Harlem restaurant where the activist met with Barack Obama during his 2008 presidential campaign - an obvious bit of symbolism for the Vermont senator trying to connect with minority voters. “My concern is that in January of next year for the first time in American history a black family will be moving out of the White House. I do not want black concerns to be moved out with them,” Sharpton, a Baptist minister and television talk show host, told reporters afterwards. Sharpton discussed a recent spate of police shootings of black males and other issues with the senator. He said he would not endorse a candidate until he met with Clinton. Even before the exit polls showing that Sanders had won New Hampshire, Clinton’s campaign was already trying to highlight  her double-digit lead over Sanders among African American and Latino voters. “It will be very difficult, if not impossible, for a Democrat to win the nomination without strong levels of support among African American and Hispanic voters,” Clinton campaign manager Robby Mook said in a memo sent to reporters. He predicted the Democratic race would be won in March, when it quickly expands to 22 delegate-rich states with some of the largest minority and urban populations — and that Clinton would have the advantage.  Clinton has a long history of support for civil rights, and she has benefited from her husband Bill Clinton’s popularity in the black community during his presidency, although that became strained during the fierce 2008 primary battle with Obama. Reuters/Ipsos polling nationally showed that in January, blacks backed Clinton by a margin of 3 to 1 over Sanders. Among Hispanics, 48 percent supported Clinton and 32 percent backed Sanders. But as black and Hispanic voters became more familiar with Sanders through televised presidential debates, they seemed to like him more, with his favorability ratings rising slightly among those groups over the last few months, the polling showed. So far Sanders’ strong performance has been due to the mostly young white voters who have embraced his populist anti-Wall Street message and call for income equality. But in the upcoming nominating contests, Sanders needs to carry that message to a broader group of voters, particularly minority voters, who will help determine the Democratic nominee. African Americans and Hispanics comprise 35 percent of the Democratic party, according to a 2013 Gallup poll. Sanders already has intensified his efforts to reach black voters with more campaign stops before African-American audiences and ads on black-oriented radio stations. Rapper Killer Mike sometimes introduces Sanders at rallies, and academic Cornel West has also campaigned for him. The senator also frequently condemns the disproportionate rate at which blacks are targeted by police and has called for increased police transparency and accountability. Sanders’ intensified effort to appeal to minority voters follows questions about whether he has broad enough support to take the White House. Clinton herself has raised the issue of Sanders’ electability on the campaign trail and in debates. Even some Sanders supporters have expressed fears that a vote for him could allow Republicans to win the election.  But Sanders’ campaign shrugs off any worries about the road ahead. “We recognize we are moving to a bigger stage, but it’s another opportunity for him to spread his message. People have responded to his message when they hear it,” said Sanders campaign spokesman Michael Briggs. Sanders already has begun airing ads in Nevada and South Carolina, has hired staff in 15 states and is prepared for a national race, Briggs said. On Super Tuesday, Sanders will be looking to do well in several states, including his home state of Vermont, as well as Massachusetts, Colorado and Minnesota, where the grassroots enthusiasm of his supporters could be an advantage. Still Irene Matz, a retiree in Minneapolis, Minnesota, said she was worried about Sanders’ electability and had yet to make a decision on who to vote for. “Hillary has been hit with everything for years, we know what we are getting with her. Now Bernie will get his turn, and they won’t be kind to him,” Matz said. “I’ll vote for Hillary unless I feel Bernie has a good shot,” she said. text: The Europa Building, which serves as the venue for EU summits, will remain closed for another week due to toxic fumes that led to a venue change last week. Investigators are currently working to resolve the issue resulting from the fumes leaking from the drains. This month, the building, also referred to as The Egg, has been evacuated twice, including prior to the EU leaders’ summit held on Thursday and Friday. Opened in January amid contentious discussions regarding its cost of 321 million euros ($378 million), the new facility is now temporarily relocating staff and meetings to the adjacent Justus Lipsius building until the problem is addressed. On October 13, approximately 20 catering personnel required hospitalization, with more individuals treated on Wednesday. An EU representative indicated that both incidents are believed by health and safety agencies in Belgium and the Council to have originated from the same source.
source_text: Toxic fumes keep EU summit venue shut for another week. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - The building that houses EU summits, where toxic fumes forced EU leaders to switch venues last week, will be closed for a further week as investigators seek to resolve the problem. The fumes leaking from the drains have forced the Europa Building, also known as  The Egg , to be evacuated twice this month, including before a summit of EU leaders on Thursday and Friday. The new building was opened in January amid controversy over its 321-million-euro ($378 million) price tag. Staff and meetings will be temporarily transferred to the next door Justus Lipsius building until the issue is resolved. About 20 catering staff had to go to hospital on Oct. 13 and an unspecified number on Wednesday. An EU official said the Council and Belgian health and safety agencies believe the two incidents were due to the same source.

text: As the European Union grapples with concerns regarding democracy in Poland, discussions among member states are set to intensify this month, according to informed sources. This marks a new phase in a process that could lead to an official condemnation of the Polish government as anti-democratic. The Law and Justice party (PiS), which leads the government in Warsaw, has implemented reforms affecting the judiciary and media that critics within the EU argue have undermined democratic principles. In response to these allegations, PiS dismisses the critiques, accusing Brussels of exceeding its authority and asserting that it enjoys significant domestic support for its reforms in Poland, a nation of 38 million people and a prominent economy in the former communist eastern Europe. Following over a year of mounting pressure from the European Commission, the executive body has requested EU's 28 ministers for affairs to convene and address its concerns on September 25, right after Germany's national elections. Frans Timmermans, the Commission's deputy chief, will inform the ministers about his ongoing but unsuccessful attempts to persuade Warsaw to alter its stance, as reported by sources. German Chancellor Angela Merkel has added her voice to the increasing calls for stronger measures against Poland and has had discussions with the chief of the Commission, Jean-Claude Juncker, regarding the situation. Should Warsaw continue to remain unyielding, it faces the possibility of losing substantial EU funds, which are supported by wealthier member states, intensifying the debate within the Union. Currently, the EU's ability to act is somewhat limited. However, it may initiate Article 7 proceedings, which would require the other 27 EU nations to formally acknowledge that the rule of law is at risk in Poland — a move that would be unprecedented in the history of the EU. Timmermans has established a definitive line by indicating that Article 7 proceedings would commence if Warsaw were to dismiss judges from the Supreme Court as part of the judicial reforms. The ongoing dispute illustrates Poland's increasing estrangement within the EU since the eurosceptic PiS came to power in 2015, highlighting a growing divide between eastern and western Europe within the bloc. Initiating Article 7 would be a significant embarrassment for Poland; however, Hungary, a regional ally whose leader Viktor Orban has also clashed with Brussels, has signaled that it would obstruct any sanctions against Poland under this punitive framework. Meanwhile, in the West, frustrations are rising over the escalating conflicts with Warsaw, which also encompass issues related to migration and environmental policies, prompting some to question the wisdom of the EU's 2004 enlargement that brought eight former communist nations into the fold. Polish opposition parties have raised alarms, claiming that PiS is abandoning core EU values and could ultimately jeopardize Poland's EU membership, which has provided the country with billions of euros and secured its position in the western world following decades of communism imposed by Moscow after World War Two. Nevertheless, PiS has largely succeeded in consolidating support among its constituents, portraying its actions as defending Poland's national interests against what it describes as EU overreach, similar to how Orban has framed his own disputes with the bloc to his supporters. The immediate consequence is that Warsaw is losing political influence within the EU and has diminished ability to influence the bloc's policies, despite being the sixth largest nation by population, and fifth largest once Britain exits.
source_text: EU to raise pressure on Poland over democracy concerns: sources. TALLINN (Reuters) - European Union states will this month debate increasing pressure on Poland to uphold the rule of law, sources said, as the next stage in a process that could see its government formally denounced as anti-democratic. The nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government in Warsaw has pushed through reforms to the judiciary and media that critics within the EU say have weakened the democratic order.  PiS rejects the criticism, accuses Brussels of overstepping its mandate and says it has broad backing for its reforms within Poland, a country of 38 million and formerly communist eastern Europe s dominant economy. After more than a year of growing pressure from the European Commission, the executive on Wednesday asked the bloc s 28 EU affairs ministers to discuss its concerns on Sept. 25, the day after national elections in Germany. The Commission s deputy head Frans Timmermans will brief the ministers on his so far futile efforts to persuade Warsaw to shift its position, the sources said. German Chancellor Angela Merkel has joined the growing chorus of those calling for firmer action on Poland and discussed the matter with the Commission s chief, Jean-Claude Juncker. Should Warsaw remain adamant, it eventually risks losing generous EU handouts if it continues to upset its wealthier peers that chip in for the funds, a debate gradually heating up in the bloc. For now, the EU has limited firepower at its disposal.  But it could trigger Article 7 proceedings under which it would ask the other 27 EU states to formally state that the rule of law was under threat in Poland - an action unprecedented in EU history. Timmermans has set a clear red line by saying that Article 7 would be opened should Warsaw start to fire the country s Supreme Court judges under the judicial overhaul. The dispute highlights Warsaw s growing isolation in the EU since the eurosceptic PiS won power there in 2015, but also a growing east-west divide within the bloc. Launching Article 7 would be a major embarrassment for Poland, but its regional ally Hungary - whose leader Viktor Orban also has a track record of crossing swords with Brussels - has made clear it would block any sanctions against it under the punitive procedure. In the west, increasingly frustrated with multiplying feuds with Warsaw that also touch on migration and environmental issues, some express renewed doubts about the 2004 EU enlargement that added eight ex-communist countries to the bloc.  In Poland, opposition parties sound alarm that PiS is reneging on fundamental EU values and could eventually risk sabotaging Poland s EU membership, which gave the country billions of euros and anchored it in the western world after decades of the Moscow-imposed communism after World War Two. But PiS has largely been successful in rallying its supporters around what it presents as standing up for Poland s national interests against the EU dictate, just as Orban has portrayed his own feuds with the bloc to his voters. The more immediate effect is that Warsaw is hemorrhaging political influence in the EU and has less capacity to shape the bloc s policies despite being the sixth largest state by population, and the fifth one after Britain leaves.

text: Following discussions with Republican legislators on Capitol Hill, Mike Pence, the Vice President-elect, addressed the media on Wednesday. He indicated that the GOP's strategy for replacing the Affordable Care Act is set to develop in the upcoming months. This statement aims to counter the Democratic criticism regarding the GOP’s approach to dismantling the health care initiative without providing a substitute. Pence remarked, "The structure of the Obamacare replacement will, as it ought to, come together via the legislative process in the weeks and months ahead."
source_text: Pence: Obamacare replacement to come together in weeks, months ahead. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Vice President-elect Mike Pence said on Wednesday the Republican plan to replace the Affordable Care Act will evolve in the months ahead, seeking to deflect criticism by Democrats over dismantling the health care program without an alternate plan. “The architecture of the replacement of Obamacare will come together, as it should, through the legislative process in the weeks and months ahead,” Pence said at a brief news conference after meetings with Republican lawmakers on Capitol Hill.

text: In an effort to bring stability back to Catalonia, Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy called upon Catalans to participate actively in the upcoming December election. This visit to Barcelona marked Rajoy's first since the Spanish government enacted direct rule over Catalonia and dismissed its separatist leaders. He emphasized that the election on December 21 is crucial for protecting the region's economy and preventing businesses from relocating away from this economically vital area. "We desire a significant voter turnout to initiate a new political era characterized by tranquility, normality, coexistence, and respect," Rajoy stated during his address to the Catalan faction of his conservative party, the People’s Party (PP). "It is imperative that we swiftly restore normalcy to Catalonia to alleviate social tensions and mitigate economic harm." While there is dissent regarding the early election, which was mandated by Madrid to address the ongoing deadlock, the two main pro-independence factions—PDeCAT, led by ousted leader Carles Puigdemont, and the ERC—have confirmed their participation. However, these parties could not reach a consensus to run jointly, which may jeopardize the separatists' prospects of securing a majority in the regional legislature. Additionally, the far-left pro-independence party CUP, which played a significant role in Puigdemont's administration, declared on Sunday its intention to compete in the forthcoming election. The direct rule imposed by Madrid has exacerbated divisions among political entities at both the regional and municipal levels. On Sunday, the faction led by Barcelona's Mayor Ada Colau decided to terminate its coalition with the Catalan Socialist Party (PSC), citing the latter's endorsement of direct governance. A recent survey for the newspaper El Pais indicated that 54 percent of Spaniards view Madrid's management of the Catalan situation positively, while only 28 percent of Catalans share this perspective. Meanwhile, on Saturday, 750,000 individuals demonstrated in Barcelona, advocating for the release of separatist leaders detained prior to trial.
source_text: Spanish PM, in Catalonia, calls for big turnout at December election. BARCELONA - Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy urged Catalans to turn out in force in a December election to  restore normality  to a region buffeted by attempts to split from Spain. In his first visit to Barcelona since Madrid imposed direct rule on Catalonia and sacked its separatist leaders, Rajoy said the Dec. 21 election would safeguard the economy and stop companies moving out of the economically important region.  We want a massive turnout to begin a new political era of tranquillity, normality, coexistence and respect,  Rajoy told the Catalan wing of his conservative People s Party (PP).   We must urgently bring back normality to Catalonia ... to reduce social tension and stop damage to the economy.  Despite opposition to the early election imposed by Madrid as a way to resolve the impasse, the two leading pro-independence parties, PDeCAT of deposed leader Carles Puigdemont, and the ERC, have said they will participate.  However, they failed to agree to run on a united ticket, potentially harming the separatist camp s chances of winning a majority in the regional parliament.  The far-left pro-independence CUP party, whose support was key to Puigdemont s government, decided on Sunday to run in the upcoming election. Madrid s imposition of direct rule on Catalonia has widened a rift between political parties both in regional politics and at the municipal level.  On Sunday, the party of Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau voted to break its pact to govern with the Catalan Socialist Party (PSC), citing the latter s support for the application of direct rule. Some 54 percent of Spaniards evaluate positively Madrid s handling of the Catalan crisis, but only 28 percent of Catalans share this view, according to a poll for newspaper El Pais. On Saturday, 750,000 people marched in Barcelona to call for the release of separatist leaders from pre-trial detention.

text: On Thursday, President Barack Obama emphasized the need for Congress to prioritize action over politics regarding the funding required to address the Zika virus, as financial resources are dwindling. At a Pentagon press event, he stated, "Our experts at the CDC, the folks on the front lines have been doing their best in making due by moving funds from other areas, but now the money we need to fight Zika is rapidly running out." He cautioned that delays in vaccine development could occur if Congress does not allocate additional funds, urging citizens to reach out to their representatives to advocate for the matter. Heightened concern surrounding Zika, a virus linked to a birth defect known as microcephaly that results in reduced head size and severe developmental issues in infants, has emerged following the detection of local transmission in Florida last week within the continental U.S. Six months have passed since Obama requested that the Republican-controlled Congress approve $1.9 billion in emergency funding, yet Zika funding remains in limbo. On Thursday, forty-one Democratic senators sent a correspondence to Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and House Speaker Paul Ryan, requesting that lawmakers be called back from their summer break to vote on the emergency funding necessary to tackle the virus. However, Ryan accused the Democrats of obstructing the funding, asserting that the Obama administration has not effectively utilized the existing funds to curb the spread of the virus carried by mosquitoes. According to congressional records, Congress has interrupted its own recesses at least eight times since 1998, with the most recent instance occurring in 2013 when lawmakers returned early to discuss military action in Syria. The recent exchange of accusations suggested that there is minimal likelihood of legislators cutting short their seven-week summer hiatus to address Zika funding. A compromise package amounting to $1.1 billion failed after House Republicans included provisions that would impose restrictions on abortion and defund parts of the Affordable Care Act, a key achievement of Obama’s administration. Senate Democrats, who had previously blocked the proposal twice before Congress adjourned last month, are insisting that Republicans agree to a new funding proposal that excludes these controversial provisions, which Republicans have dismissed. Ryan articulated in an opinion piece in USA Today, "We need the White House and Senate Democrats to drop politics and put the public’s health first. We hope for a change of heart, and soon." Meanwhile, Don Stewart, a spokesperson for McConnell, encouraged Democrats to permit the current bill to be approved through unanimous consent during a routine session scheduled for Friday.
source_text: Obama, Senate Democrats urge Zika funding vote as reserves run low. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Barack Obama on Thursday said it was time for Congress to lay aside politics and to act to provide additional money to combat the Zika virus before government funding dries up. “Our experts at the CDC, the folks on the front lines have been doing their best in making due by moving funds from other areas, but now the money we need to fight Zika is rapidly running out,” Obama said at a press conference at the Pentagon. He warned that development of a vaccine for the virus could be delayed if Congress does not provide any more money and urged Americans to contact lawmakers to pressure them to take up the issue. Concern over the threat from Zika, which can cause a birth defect called microcephaly marked by small head size that can lead to severe developmental problems in babies, has risen since Florida authorities last week detected the first signs of local transmission in the continental United States. Zika funding remains stalled six months after Obama asked the Republican-led Congress to approve $1.9 billion in emergency funds. Forty-one Democratic U.S. senators on Thursday sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and House of Representatives Speaker Paul Ryan urging them to summon lawmakers back from their summer recess to vote on emergency funding to fight the virus. But, Ryan accused Democrats of obstructing the funding and said the Obama administration has failed to spend existing funds to prevent the spread of the mosquito-borne virus. Congress has interrupted its own recesses at least eight times since 1998, most recently in 2013 when lawmakers returned early to debate the use of military force in Syria, according to congressional records. The latest round of finger-pointing indicated there was little chance lawmakers would cut short their seven-week summer break to vote on Zika funding. A $1.1 billion compromise failed after House Republicans attached language that would place restrictions on abortion and defund part of Obama’s signature 2010 healthcare law. Senate Democrats, who blocked the measure twice before Congress left Washington last month, want Republicans to agree on a new funding measure that drops those provisions, a step Republicans reject. “We need the White House and Senate Democrats to drop politics and put the public’s health first. We hope for a change of heart, and soon,” Ryan wrote in an opinion piece in the USA Today newspaper. McConnell spokesman Don Stewart invited Democrats to allow the current bill to pass by unanimous consent at a perfunctory session on Friday.

text: On Monday, German Chancellor Angela Merkel expressed that she had no intention of resigning following the failure of negotiations for a three-party coalition government. She indicated that her conservative faction would be more unified in the event of new elections. In an interview with German broadcaster ZDF, Merkel, who is prepared to continue her chancellorship for another four years, emphasized the necessity of demonstrating stability for Germany, Europe, and globally. When questioned about the potential for re-establishing a grand coalition with the Social Democrats, she mentioned that she would await their response after discussions with President Frank-Walter Steinmeier scheduled for Wednesday. However, she remarked that any requests for her resignation would not be a constructive way to initiate a new coalition. Merkel expressed her disappointment regarding the pro-business Free Democrats' decision to withdraw from the coalition negotiations, yet she did not foresee a reversal of their stance.
source_text: Merkel sees no reason to resign; focused on building stable government. BERLIN (Reuters) - German Chancellor Angela Merkel on Monday said she saw no reason to resign after the collapse of talks about a three-way coalition government, adding her conservative bloc would enter any new elections more unified than before. Merkel told German broadcaster ZDF she was ready to serve four more years as chancellor, and felt it was important to send a signal of stability for the country and Europe and the world. Asked about the possibility of another  grand coalition  with the Social Democrats, Merkel said she would wait to see the party s response after their talks with President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Wednesday. But she said any demand for her to step down would not be a good way to start a new coalition. She said she was disappointed by the decision of the pro-business Free Democrats to pull out of the coalition talks, but did not expect the party to reverse course.
