source_text: Russian foreign ministry to meet visiting North Korean diplomat - RIA. MOSCOW (Reuters) - Russia s foreign ministry plans to hold talks with a representative of North Korea s foreign ministry who is due to arrive in Moscow on Tuesday, the RIA news agency cited the North s embassy to Russia as saying.

text: Following the tragic Orlando shooting, Donald Trump, the Republican candidate for president, suggested on Sunday that the United States should contemplate implementing more racial profiling. This statement came after he was asked whether he endorsed heightened law enforcement scrutiny of Muslim Americans. Trump expressed on CBS’ “Face the Nation,” "I think profiling is something that we’re going to have to start thinking about as a country." He referenced the successful profiling practices of Israel and other nations, stating, "You look at Israel and you look at others, and they do it and they do it successfully. And you know, I hate the concept of profiling, but we have to start using common sense," when pressed about his support for increased profiling of Muslims within the U.S. This was not the first time Trump had broached the topic; he made similar remarks last December, following the deadly San Bernardino attack where a Muslim American and his spouse killed 14 individuals in California. Trump, who is the presumptive nominee for the Republican presidential election set for November 8, faced backlash from various members of his party for his statements regarding American Muslims in the wake of the Orlando incident, which saw a U.S.-born Muslim man take the lives of 49 people at a gay nightclub. In a Monday address focusing on national security, Trump reaffirmed his call for a temporary halt on Muslims entering the country and suggested putting a suspension on immigration from nations with "a proven history of terrorism." He further asserted that the Muslim community needed to "cooperate with law enforcement and turn in the people who they know are bad." Hillary Clinton, the presumptive Democratic nominee, criticized Trump, asserting that his remarks indicated he is unfit to hold the presidency. The shooter in Florida, identified as Omar Mateen, was born in the U.S. to Afghan parents. During a three-hour standoff at the nightclub, he voiced his support for the Islamic State, although officials believe he had become "self-radicalized." In his Sunday interview, Trump remarked on the "red flags" surrounding Mateen, noting that he had been investigated twice by the FBI yet was ultimately cleared. Trump also reiterated his stance on increasing scrutiny of mosques, comparing it to a contentious surveillance program previously implemented in New York City that has since been dismantled. "If you go to France right now, they’re doing it in France. In fact, in some instances they’re closing down mosques," he noted. This was in reference to actions taken by French authorities after gunmen connected to the Islamic State killed 130 individuals in a series of attacks in Paris on November 13. Paul Ryan, Speaker of the House of Representatives, has expressed his support for Trump, although he maintains that a ban on Muslims is not in the interests of the United States. In a recently released NBC interview excerpt, Ryan, the leading elected Republican official in the U.S., advised party members considering whether to support Trump to act according to their "conscience." Trump dismissed the criticism on Sunday, stating that he would finance his campaign with his own resources if necessary. "It would be nice if the Republicans stuck together," Trump mentioned during an ABC interview. "I can win, one way or another."
source_text: Trump says U.S. should mull more racial profiling after Orlando shooting. (Reuters) - Republican Donald Trump said on Sunday the United States should consider more racial profiling, in response to a question about whether he supported greater law enforcement scrutiny of Muslim Americans after the Orlando mass shooting. “I think profiling is something that we’re going to have to start thinking about as a country,” Trump told CBS’ “Face the Nation.”  “You look at Israel and you look at others, and they do it and they do it successfully. And you know, I hate the concept of profiling, but we have to start using common sense,” he said when asked if he supported increased profiling of Muslims in America. Trump made similar comments last December about profiling, the targeting of specific demographic groups for extra scrutiny, after a Muslim American and his wife killed 14 people in San Bernardino, California. Last week, Trump, the presumptive Republican presidential nominee for the Nov. 8 election, sparked criticism from many in his party for his comments on American Muslims after the Orlando attack on Sunday, in which a U.S.-born Muslim man killed 49 people at a gay nightclub.  In a speech on national security on Monday, Trump stood by his call for a temporary ban on Muslims entering the United States and proposed a suspension of immigration from countries with “a proven history of terrorism.”  He also said the Muslim community had to “cooperate with law enforcement and turn in the people who they know are bad.”  Hillary Clinton, the presumptive Democratic nominee, has said the comments show Trump is unfit to be president. The Florida gunman, Omar Mateen, was born in the United States to Afghan parents. During a three-hour siege at the club, he expressed support for Islamic State, but officials believe he was “self-radicalized.” In his interview on Sunday, Trump said there were “red flags” around Mateen, who had been investigated twice by the FBI but ultimately cleared.  Trump also reiterated his support for more scrutiny of mosques, saying that could resemble a controversial New York City surveillance program that has been shut down.  “If you go to France right now, they’re doing it in France. In fact, in some instances they’re closing down mosques,” he said. Police in France closed some mosques shortly after gunmen aligned with Islamic State militants killed 130 people in Paris in a series of attacks on Nov. 13. House of Representatives Speaker Paul Ryan endorsed Trump but has said a Muslim ban is not in U.S. interests. In excerpts of an NBC interview released on Friday, Ryan, the top elected U.S. Republican, said Republicans weighing whether to vote for Trump should follow their “conscience.” Trump brushed off the criticism on Sunday and said he would put up his own money for his campaign if needed. “It would be nice if the Republicans stuck together,” Trump said in an ABC interview. “I can win, one way or another.”

text: On Thursday, U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry asserted the continued dedication of the Obama administration to the NATO military alliance and the security obligations outlined in the treaty. He emphasized that every administration in the United States, Republican or Democratic, has maintained this commitment since 1949. "I want our NATO partner to be clear where we stand. This administration, like every single administration Republican or Democratic alike since 1949, remains fully committed to the NATO alliance and to our security commitments on the Article 5," Kerry stated during a press briefing. His comments were in reaction to Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump, who mentioned to the New York Times that, if he were to win the election, he might consider withdrawing from NATO’s assurance that all members, including the U.S., would protect one another if attacked.
source_text: Kerry says U.S. remains committed to NATO alliance, security commitments. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Obama administration, like every U.S. administration since 1949, remained committed to the NATO military alliance and  security commitments under the treaty, U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry said on Thursday.  “I want our NATO partner to be clear where we stand. This administration, like every single administration Republican or Democratic alike since 1949, remains fully committed to the NATO alliance and to our security commitments on the Article 5,” Kerry told a news conference. He was responding to comments by Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump, who told the New York Times that if elected he might abandon NATO’s guarantee that any member, including the United States, would defend the others if they were attacked.

text: On Thursday, the U.S. Senate enacted a law that prohibits states from imposing taxes on Internet access permanently, advancing the measure to President Barack Obama for his signature. The Senate approved the bill with a vote tally of 75-20, which also strengthens the enforcement of U.S. tariffs on foreign products and includes the indefinite extension of the "Internet Tax Freedom Act." Furthermore, this legislation will eliminate certain taxes on digital services and products, concluding a series of temporary extensions regarding these tax restrictions. In a statement, Democratic Senator Ron Wyden noted, "Most Americans pay $0 in taxes to connect to the Internet. And thanks to a bill that passed today, you will never have to pay taxes just to get online, or pay more taxes for goods and services just because they’re bought online." However, this legislation does not tackle the ongoing demands for improved enforcement of state sales tax collections linked to online purchases, a concern that has been raised by physical retail businesses for quite some time. According to aides in the Senate, Congress may consider separate legislation to address this issue later this year. While most states in the U.S. have enacted sales taxes on online transactions, the actual enforcement of these taxes remains inconsistent.
source_text: Congress approves permanent Internet access tax ban. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. Senate on Thursday passed legislation placing a permanent ban on states’ taxing Internet access, sending the measure to President Barack Obama for signing into law. By a vote of 75-20, the Senate gave final approval to a bill toughening enforcement of U.S. duties on foreign goods, which contains the permanent extension of the “Internet Tax Freedom Act.” The measure also would ban some taxes on digital goods and services and will put an end to a series of temporary extensions on the tax prohibitions. “Most Americans pay $0 in taxes to connect to the Internet. And thanks to a bill that passed today, you will never have to pay taxes just to get online, or pay more taxes for goods and services just because they’re bought online,” Democratic Senator Ron Wyden said in a statement. The legislation, however, fails to address calls for better enforcement of state sales tax collections related to Internet purchases, something that brick-and-mortar businesses have long sought. Separate legislation on this could be considered by Congress later this year, according to Senate aides. Most U.S. states have imposed sales taxes on online purchases, but the actual collection is spotty.

text: In a significant development, Turkish officials have initiated the issuance of arrest warrants for 25 military personnel throughout Turkey and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, according to security insiders. This action is part of an expanding crackdown that follows the failed military coup attempt from the previous year. The individuals targeted, who are currently serving and hold various ranks within Turkey's armed forces, are being pursued across 13 different provinces as well as in Turkish Cyprus, the insiders revealed. Prosecutors located in the southeastern Mardin province have requested the apprehension of these soldiers due to their alleged involvement in the covert military organization linked to U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, the sources indicated. Gulen, who has been residing in self-imposed exile in the United States since 1999, is accused by Turkish authorities of orchestrating the coup attempt that occurred on July 15. He has firmly denied any participation. Following the coup, over 50,000 individuals have been imprisoned while awaiting trial for their connections to Gulen, and around 150,000 have faced dismissal or suspension from their roles in military, public, and private sectors. Human rights organizations and some of Turkey's allies in the West have expressed alarm over the ongoing crackdown, fearing that the government is exploiting the coup as justification to silence opposition. The authorities assert that only such a purge can eliminate the threat posed by Gulen's network, which they claim has deeply infiltrated various institutions including the military, educational establishments, and judicial bodies.
source_text: Turkey issues arrest warrants for 25 soldiers in post-coup probe - sources. DIYARBAKIR (Reuters) - Turkish authorities have issued arrest warrants for 25 soldiers across Turkey and the breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in northern Cyprus, security sources said, as part of a widening crackdown following last year s failed military coup. The soldiers, on active duty and of varying ranks in Turkey s military, are being sought across 13 provinces and Turkish northern Cyprus, the sources said. Prosecutors in the southeastern province of Mardin ordered the arrest of the soldiers over the  secret military structuring  of the network of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, the sources said.  Gulen, who has lived in self-imposed exile in the United States since 1999, is accused by Ankara of masterminding the July 15 coup attempt. He has denied involvement. Since the coup, more than 50,000 people have been jailed pending trial over links to Gulen, while 150,000 people have been sacked or suspended from jobs in the military, public and private sectors. Rights groups and some of Turkey s Western allies have voiced concern about the crackdown, fearing the government is using the coup as a pretext to quash dissent. The government says only such a purge could neutralize the threat represented by Gulen s network, which it says deeply infiltrated institutions such as the army, schools and courts.

text: On Tuesday, discussions among German political parties aiming to form a coalition government led to an agreement on establishing a compulsory registry for lobbyists. They may also impose a requirement for private companies to report any breaches in their cyber defenses, as outlined in a security draft document reviewed by Reuters. This 3-page proposal reflects a growing alignment among Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservatives, the business-oriented Free Democrats, and the environmentalist Greens regarding certain security matters. However, there are still several unresolved topics, including the addition of police personnel, regulations concerning the storage of personal data, and the future of a contentious hate speech law. Merkel is urging party officials to reach a consensus by Thursday, with the goal of finalizing a comprehensive coalition accord by Christmas. On Tuesday, negotiators made headway in increasing support for families with children, yet they remained divided on issues related to transportation and climate policies, postponing discussions on immigration until Wednesday. Sources indicate that top leaders of the parties will have to confront the most challenging issues on Thursday. Alexander Dobrindt, the Transportation Minister from the CSU, which is the Bavarian sister party to Merkel's conservatives, remarked that after four hours of intensive dialogue, negotiators had not managed to reconcile differences on transportation matters. He noted, "The Greens have a package of demands on the table that cannot be fulfilled,” referring to their push for increased diesel taxes. He stated that his party would reject any measures that might restrict individual mobility or jeopardize the German automotive sector. A mandatory registry for individuals lobbying on behalf of interest groups to the government and parliament was agreed upon, aimed at enhancing transparency. Additionally, it was proposed that government entities should be mandated to inform the BSI federal cyber security agency about any cyber security vulnerabilities that could affect relevant systems or a significant number of citizens. The parties expressed intentions to tackle the risks associated with cyber breaches in private enterprises. The draft suggested that this might involve a disclosure requirement, although further details were not provided. The document indicated that the coalition partners had consented to create 2,000 new positions within the federal and state justice systems and committed to accelerating job additions in federal law enforcement. Nonetheless, they continued to disagree on the precise number of jobs to be added. Furthermore, there was an agreement to enhance oversight of intelligence agencies through a specialized parliamentary board. According to the draft, both the intelligence agencies and the federal government would need to keep parliament apprised of their activities. The parties opted to avoid a disagreement concerning the future of the European Stability Mechanism and decided not to address this particular issue in the document outlining their stance on Europe, as stated by negotiators.
source_text: German parties want lobbyist registry, may mandate hack reports. BERLIN (Reuters) - German parties exploring a coalition government agreed on Tuesday to set up a mandatory registry of lobbyists and may require private firms to disclose breaches of cyber defenses, according to a draft paper on security seen by Reuters. The 3-page document, a blueprint for a new German government s stance on security, showed growing consensus on some issues among Chancellor Angela Merkel s conservatives, the pro-business Free Democrats and the environmental Greens. But several issues remained unresolved, including the number of police jobs to be added, rules on storage of private data, and the future of a controversial hate speech law. Merkel is pressing party leaders to resolve their differences by Thursday, with an eye to completing a detailed coalition agreement by Christmas. Party negotiators made progress on boosting aid to families with children on Tuesday, but remained at odds over transport and climate and put off discussing immigration until Wednesday. Top party leaders will likely have to tackle the most difficult issues on Thursday, sources said. Transportation Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a member of the CSU Bavarian sister party to Merkel s conservatives, said negotiators had been unable to bridge gaps on transportation issues despite four hours of intense discussions.  The Greens have a package of demands on the table that cannot be fulfilled,  he told reporters, citing a push by the Greens for higher taxes on diesel. He said his party would not agree to measures that would limit individual mobility or that could jeopardize the German auto industry. Negotiators did agree to create a mandatory registry of individuals lobbying government and parliament on behalf of interest groups to ensure greater transparency. They also said government agencies should be required to report cyber security gaps that affected relevant systems or a large number of people to the BSI federal cyber security agency.  The parties said they also planned to address dangers posed by cyber breaches of private companies.  This could include a reporting requirement,  the paper said, without elaborating. The paper showed the parties had agreed to create 2,000 new jobs in the federal and state justice systems, and pledged to add jobs federal law enforcement as quickly as possible. But they remained at odds about the exact number of jobs. The parties also agreed to expand control of the intelligence agencies via a special parliamentary board, according to the paper. It said the intelligence agencies and the federal government should be required to keep parliament informed about their work. The parties also agreed to dodge a dispute over the future of the European Stability Mechanism and would not include that specific issue in a paper outlining the parties  stance on Europe, negotiators said.

text: BERNE (Reuters) - Switzerland is willing to step in as a mediator to facilitate the resolution of the crisis in North Korea, according to Swiss President Doris Leuthard on Monday. Leuthard mentioned that Swiss military personnel are stationed in the demilitarized zone separating South Korea from North Korea and highlighted her nation’s longstanding tradition of neutral diplomacy, alongside Sweden. This history includes Switzerland representing U.S. interests in both Iran and Cuba. She remarked that both China and the United States must accept their responsibilities in this situation and cautioned against extreme reactions following North Korea's sixth and most significant nuclear test. Leuthard stated that sanctions have not significantly persuaded Pyongyang to relinquish its weapons programs, even as the North Korean populace suffers. "I believe it is indeed time for dialogue," she expressed during a press conference in Berne. "We are prepared to offer our services as mediators." She added that the upcoming weeks would be crucial, depending on the influence of the U.S. and China in the ongoing crisis. "That’s why I think both Switzerland and Sweden can play an important role behind the scenes," she said. A key aspect of this mediation would involve identifying an appropriate venue for officials, possibly the foreign ministers of the involved nations, to convene, she indicated. "Our responsibility is to explore what options are available. Because, frankly, Twitter is not a suitable tool for this... It must remain very confidential." Leuthard also pointed out that the Communist Party congress in North Korea’s ally China is scheduled for October, suggesting that the timing for such diplomatic initiatives may not be optimal, which could be a part of North Korea’s strategy. The North Korean leader, Kim Jong Un, had spent part of his early life in Berne, studying under a false identity. In 1994, a framework agreement was established between North Korea and the United States during the Clinton administration in Geneva after extensive negotiations. This arrangement required Pyongyang to halt the construction of its nuclear reactors, believed to be associated with its secret weapons program, in return for two light water nuclear reactors. However, this agreement collapsed in 2003. "North Korea presents a troubling situation. We are a small nation. They could potentially gather in Switzerland to seek a political resolution, rather than one involving military force," Leuthard remarked.
source_text: Swiss ready to mediate in North Korea crisis. BERNE (Reuters) - Neutral Switzerland is prepared to act as a mediator to help resolve the North Korea crisis, including by hosting ministerial talks, Swiss President Doris Leuthard said on Monday. Leuthard said Swiss troops were deployed on the demarcation zone between South Korea and North Korea and noted that her country - along with Sweden - had a long history of neutral and discreet diplomacy. This has included Switzerland representing U.S. interests in both Iran and Cuba.  But China and the United States had to take their share of responsibility, she added, warning against  over-reactions  after the North s sixth and largest nuclear test. Sanctions  did not change many things  in terms of convincing Pyongyang to abandon its weapons programs, even though its population had suffered, Leuthard said.  I think it really is time for dialogue,  she told a news conference in Berne.  We are ready to offer our role for good services as a mediator. I think in the upcoming weeks a lot will depend on how the U.S. and China can have an influence in this crisis. That s why I think Switzerland and Sweden can have a role behind the curtain.  Part of the task would be to find a suitable location for officials   perhaps the countries  foreign ministers   to meet, she said.  I think that s our role, to look at what kind of possibilities we find. Because, well, Twitter won t be an adequate instrument... This must be very discreet.  Noting that the Communist Party congress in North Korea s neighbor and ally China was due to take place in October,  Leuthard said the time for such initiatives was not ideal, so  perhaps this was also part of the plan of North Korea.  North Korean leader Kim Jong Un spent part of his youth in Berne studying under an assumed name. A framework agreement between North Korea and the United States, under the Clinton administration, was clinched in 1994 in Geneva after long negotiations. The deal by which Pyongyang was to freeze construction of its nuclear reactors, suspected of being part of its covert weapons program, in exchange for two light water nuclear reactors, unraveled in 2003.  North Korea is a worrying situation. We are a small country. Perhaps they could meet in Switzerland to find a political solution, not one with arms,  Leuthard said.

text: An 18-year-old former beauty queen from Turkey may potentially serve up to one year in prison due to a tweet linked to last year's unsuccessful military coup, as reported by the private news agency Dogan on Thursday. Itir Esen, who had her Miss Turkey title revoked just a day after winning it in September, has been indicted by a prosecutor in Istanbul for allegedly humiliating a portion of society following three formal complaints regarding her tweet. On July 16 of this year, Esen posted: "I had my period on July 15 morning to celebrate the day to commemorate martyrs. As a representation of our martyrs' blood, I am commemorating this day by bleeding." Subsequently, she deleted the tweet and disabled her Twitter account. According to Dogan, the indictment included Esen’s assertion that her tweet was intended ironically to honor those who lost their lives on July 15, 2016, and that she meant no disrespect towards any segment of Turkish society. In the failed coup attempt on July 15, 2016, approximately 250 individuals, mostly non-combatants, lost their lives and over 1,000 were injured. This date was later designated as Democracy and National Unity Day, becoming a public holiday in Turkey. Following the coup attempt, more than 150,000 state workers have faced suspension or termination, with over 50,000 individuals imprisoned while awaiting trial amid a security crackdown. Rights organizations and certain Western allies of NATO-member Turkey have expressed concerns regarding the crackdown, fearing the government is leveraging the coup as an excuse to suppress dissent.
source_text: Ousted Turkish beauty queen may face jail time over tweet. ISTANBUL (Reuters) - A former Turkish beauty pageant winner may face up to a year in prison over a tweet referring to last year s failed military coup that cost her  Miss Turkey  title, the private Dogan news agency said on Thursday. An Istanbul prosecutor has indicted 18-year-old Itir Esen, who in September was stripped of her title after one day, for  publicly humiliating a segment of the society  following three official complaints over her tweet, Dogan reported. On July 16 this year, Esen tweeted:  I had my period on July 15 morning to celebrate the day to commemorate martyrs. As a representation of our martyrs  blood, I am commemorating this day by bleeding.  She later deleted the tweet and deactivated her Twitter account. Dogan said the indictment included a statement by Esen in which she said her tweet was shared in an ironic way to commemorate those who died on July 15, 2016 and there was no intent to insult any part of Turkish society.    Around 250 people, mostly unarmed civilians were killed and over 1,000 wounded in the failed coup bid on July 15, 2016. The day was later declared Democracy and National Unity Day and a public holiday in Turkey. text: In a recent press briefing, Barack Obama’s representative in Brussels cautioned Donald Trump about the irrationality of endorsing a disintegration of the European Union, indicating that Nigel Farage, a prominent figure in the Brexit campaign, might have created a misleading narrative regarding the potential for other nations to exit the bloc alongside Britain. Anthony Gardner, who has overseen U.S. relations with the EU for the past three years, expressed these concerns on Friday during his concluding news conference, just a week prior to Trump's directive for all Obama-era appointees to resign. Gardner criticized this action, labeling it an extraordinary "guillotine exit" that has significantly affected the lives of many public officials. He commented on Trump’s enthusiasm for the decision made by the British populace to leave the EU and noted the considerable influence Farage seems to wield in Trump’s circle. Gardner articulated, "To support Brexit and to promote additional versions of it is sheer madness." Recently, Farage, an EU parliament member and ally of Trump, reached out to Gardner seeking to arrange a meeting. The U.S. envoy expressed that Farage’s perspective starkly contrasts with his own, believing that Farage has provided misleading information to Trump's transition team about the current state of the EU. Gardner detailed how Trump’s aides had made inquiries to EU institutions in recent weeks, stating: "The one question posed was essentially, ‘Which country is next to depart?’. This implies that the union is on the verge of collapse." He remarked that this reflects a widespread misunderstanding, likely propagated by Farage in Washington, describing it as a caricature of reality. According to Gardner, it would be a significant error for the United States to dismiss the EU as "dysfunctional" and to instead concentrate solely on traditional allies such as Germany and Britain. "We must not deviate from decades of foreign policy concerning the EU," he asserted. "We should avoid becoming advocates for Brexit, especially if it seems increasingly probable that Brexit will lead to a tumultuous and disorderly exit." He further warned, "A hard Brexit or the disintegration of the European market would spell disaster for American enterprises." He emphasized that businesses are aware of this reality, asserting, "They’ve recognized it ... and it’s imperative we advocate this viewpoint." Gardner appealed to both Europeans and the incoming U.S. administration to maintain unity regarding sanctions against Russia relating to Ukraine, highlighting Trump’s desire for improved ties with Moscow after assuming office next Friday. Additionally, he urged American diplomats to communicate openly with the new administration, even if doing so might jeopardize their careers. He expressed admiration for Britain’s EU ambassador, who recently resigned amid internal disagreements in London over Brexit. According to him, Ivan Rogers had "paid the price" for conveying uncomfortable truths to political leaders. "It’s crucial," Gardner stated, "that while remaining loyal to the new team ... individuals must speak truth to power."
source_text: Obama's EU envoy says Brexiteer Farage misleading Trump. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Barack Obama’s envoy to Brussels warned Donald Trump against the “lunacy” of backing an EU break-up, saying Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage may have given the incoming U.S. president a false impression that more countries might follow Britain out of the bloc. Anthony Gardner, a banker who has run U.S. relations with the European Union for three years, made the frank comments on Friday in a final news conference a week before Trump has ordered all Obama appointees to quit. Gardner condemned the move as an unprecedented “guillotine exit” that had disrupted public servants’ lives. Referring to Trump’s welcome for the British vote to leave the EU and the apparent influence of Farage in the Trump camp, Gardner said: “For us to be the cheerleaders of Brexit and to be encouraging Brexit Mark 2, Mark 3, is the height of folly.” Gardner said Farage, an EU lawmaker and Trump ally, had written to him recently requesting a meeting. The U.S. envoy said Farage’s views were the “polar opposite” of his own and he thought Farage had misled Trump’s transition team on the state of the EU. Describing calls to EU institutions from Trump’s aides in recent weeks, Gardner said: “That was the one question that was asked - basically, ‘What’s the next country to leave?’. Which is kind of suggesting that the place is about to fall apart.” “It’s just reflective of the general perception, a misperception, a perception that Nigel Farage is presumably disseminating in Washington and it’s a caricature.” He said it would be “fundamentally flawed” for the United States to ignore the EU as “dysfunctional” and instead focus on key allies like Britain and Germany. “We should not depart from 50 years of foreign policy with regard to the EU,” he said. “We should not become the cheerleaders for Brexit, particularly if Brexit appears more likely to be a hard, disorderly unmanaged Brexit.” “A hard Brexit or a fragmentation of the European market would be very bad news for American business,” he added.  “They’ve understood it ... and we need to make the case.” Gardner urged Europeans and the incoming administration not to break ranks on sanctions against Russia over Ukraine - Trump says he wants better relations with Moscow after he takes office next Friday. And he urged U.S. diplomats to speak frankly to the new leadership, even if that carried risks to their careers. He spoke of his “respect” for Britain’s EU ambassador, who resigned this month in a sign of behind-the-scenes arguments in London over Brexit. Ivan Rogers, he said, had “paid the price” for telling political leaders things they did not want to hear. “It’s critically important,” Gardner said, “That while being loyal to the new team ... people speak truth to power.”

text: In Libya, as the crisis deepens, people have begun trading jewelry for medical services. In a square located behind the central bank of Tripoli, armed black market traders transport small plastic bags filled with dollars and larger ones containing dinars to and from various informal exchange booths. These traders purchase food and other imports at the official exchange rates and resell them at unofficial rates, reaping substantial profits. Others generate significant income by smuggling heavily subsidized fuel out of the country. Meanwhile, in the narrow alleyways of the old city, many citizens are forced to sell jewelry or cash they have hidden away as the ongoing turmoil from six years of post-dictatorship instability impacts their lives. Fatima, a 40-year-old from the southern city of Sabha, shared her struggles, stating, "I haven’t received a salary for four months," as she sold three small gold charms to afford diabetes treatment for her sister, Hasina, who remarked, "We’re helpless; there’s nothing else we can do." Signs of increasing poverty are evident, with elderly women begging drivers for money on the streets of Tripoli, and families lining up for charitable food distributions. The United Nations has estimated that approximately 1.3 million people in Libya require humanitarian aid this year. In the last two weeks, the situation deteriorated further as the black market value of the dinar, which had already been at historically low levels, fell again, exacerbating inflation that currently hovers around 25-30 percent. The central bank attributed this decline to the audit bureau and the U.N.-endorsed government, which have limited letters of credit necessary for procuring essential supplies in a fragmented nation where security vacuums and smuggling operations have destabilized the broader region. Officials discovered questionable import requests, including one for tuna worth $120,000, a figure exceeding the annual consumption of the country, as stated by a Libyan businessman who wished to remain anonymous due to fears of retribution from Libya’s influential armed factions. According to this trader, only $2.5 billion of an anticipated $7.4 billion in credit has been allocated, which has contributed to the dinar’s drop from about 8.5 to 9.25 against the dollar in the black market. Since early 2014, its value has plummeted by over 600 percent. The economy ministry could not be reached for immediate comment regarding a complicated credit system that involves commercial banks and where the audit bureau has previously recorded instances of misuse and insufficient oversight. "We are dealing with an extremely dire economic and financial condition," remarked Central Bank Governor Sadiq al-Kabir during a rare press event on Tuesday. "Everyone, whether in legislative or executive positions, shares equal responsibility." Economists and traders point out that political instability is a significant contributor to the currency’s weakness, especially with U.N. negotiations aimed at reconciling opposing factions currently at a standstill. Libya is facing challenges in financing food imports and safeguarding its foreign reserves, which the World Bank predicts will be around $67.5 billion by the end of this year, down from $123.5 billion in 2012. Experts from abroad argue that the only viable solution involves devaluing the dinar from its official exchange rate of 1.37 to the dollar, but reaching consensus on an economic strategy in a nation dominated by rival armed groups and lacking budgets presents considerable difficulties. A small, influential minority benefiting from a thriving underground economy has little incentive to push for reform. The central bank has refrained from commenting on the possibility of devaluation; however, economists and diplomats indicate that the bank is hesitant to proceed without a structured plan to mitigate the subsequent impacts. Libya has managed to increase oil production to approximately 1 million barrels daily this year, yet output remains significantly below pre-2011 uprising levels that led to the ousting of Muammar Gaddafi. Revenues, which typically constitute around 80 percent of gross domestic product, are largely utilized for salary payments, including those for armed groups that were integrated into the state payroll for their involvement in the uprising. Subsidies encompass an annual fuel subsidy exceeding $4 billion, ranking among the most generous worldwide.

TRIPOLI (Reuters) - In a square behind Libya s central bank, black market dealers, some of them armed, carry small plastic bags filled with dollars and larger ones with dinars in and out of one of many informal exchanges. Traders buy food and other goods from abroad at the official rate and sell them at the unofficial one, pocketing vast profits; others make equally large sums by smuggling out heavily subsidized fuel. In the back streets of the old city meanwhile, ordinary people have resorted to selling jewelry or dollars hidden at home as six years of post-dictatorship chaos take their toll.  I haven t been paid for four months,  said Fatima, 40, from the southern city of Sabha as she sold three small gold charms to pay for diabetes treatment for her sister, Hasina, who added:  We re helpless, there s nothing else we can do.  In other signs of rising poverty, elderly women beg motorists for cash on Tripoli s streets and families queue for charity food handouts. The U.N. estimated that about 1.3 million people in Libya need humanitarian assistance this year. Their situation took another turn for the worse in the past two weeks after the black market rate of the dinar, which has long languished at record lows, slid again, fuelling inflation that is already around 25-30 percent. The central bank blamed the audit bureau and the U.N.-backed government for restricting letters of credit that fund basic supplies to a divided country where a security vacuum and smuggling networks have destabilized the wider region. Officials had come across suspect requests - one to import tuna worth $120,000, more than the country consumes in a year, according to a Libyan entrepreneur who declined to be named, fearing retribution from Libya s powerful armed groups. Just $2.5 billion of an expected $7.4 billion of credit has been allocated, the trader said, helping knock the dinar from around 8.5 to 9.25 against the dollar on the black market. Its value has fallen by more than 600 percent since early 2014. The economy ministry was not immediately available for comment on a complex credit system that passes through commercial banks and where the audit bureau had documented earlier abuses and lack of oversight.  We re talking about an extremely bad economic and financial situation,  Central Bank Governor Sadiq al-Kabir said in a rare news conference on Tuesday.  Everyone, whether legislative or executive, holds responsibility equally.  Traders and economists say political uncertainty is a major factor weakening the currency, with U.N. talks to broker a deal between rival factions currently suspended. Libya is struggling to fund food imports and defend its foreign reserves, which the World Bank estimates will stand at $67.5 billion at the end of this year, compared to $123.5 billion in 2012. International experts say the only way to resolve the issue is to devalue the dinar from the official exchange rate of 1.37 to the dollar, but agreeing an economic strategy in a country dominated by armed factions with rival governments and no budgets is no simple task. A powerful or well-connected minority who are profiting from a flourishing shadow economy have little interest in change.      The central bank did not comment on devaluation, but economists and diplomats say the bank is reluctant to devalue without a policy plan in place to deal with the resulting shock. Libya managed this year to lift oil production to about 1 million barrels a day, but output is stuck well below the levels before the 2011 uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi. Revenues that normally account for about 80 percent of gross domestic product are largely used to pay salaries, including those of armed factions added to the state payroll for their role in the uprising. Subsidies include a $4 billion-plus annual fuel subsidy that is among the most generous in the world. Premiums on the official exchange rate and subsidized fuel make Libya  a criminal and terrorist cross-border funding paradise , said Husni Bey, chairman of HB Group, one of Libya s biggest private firms.  Most instability in Libya today is of a criminal nature... due to the lack of equitable exchange rate for the Libyan dinar and the subsidies that must be changed from goods to direct cash contributions.  Last year Libya spent around $26 billion, but earned just $6 billion.  This year we estimate that revenues should increase to around $14 billion, but spending will likely be more than double this,  said Mark Griffiths, Libya Mission Chief for the International Monetary Fund.  This is not sustainable.   The government has sought to reduce the public salary bill by 5 billion dinars annually, clamping down on abuse by removing some 100,000 people who had been claiming several salaries, according to a finance ministry report. Libyans became used to plentiful public jobs and state handouts as Gaddafi sought to buy loyalty like other Middle Eastern oil producers. Migrant workers used to do the manual work, now Libyans without contacts have taken their place. Salman Rashid, a public servant, said he had received just three months-worth of pay in the past year.  It s not enough for basic needs,  he said.  Now I work on construction sites and in buildings maintenance.  Entrepreneurs have withdrawn deposits from banks for fear of employees leaking word of them to kidnappers and others also prefer to keep money at home. In a second shop in the old city, a woman who gave her name as Karima was changing 500 euros.  I need to go to Tunis for surgery and am selling my foreign currency holdings,  she said.  Times are very difficult now.  Shop owner Salahedin Zarti, 52, said up to 10 people come in daily to sell necklaces, bracelets and rings.  In the beginning it was every day, but now I think people are starting to run out of jewelry,  he said.

text: In Boston and Washington, large crowds gathered to express their opposition to the influence of significant financial contributions in United States politics. On Friday, individuals from conservative and independent backgrounds drew inspiration from the presidential campaigns of Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders, throwing imitation donations into Boston Harbor. This action was part of approximately 30 demonstrations occurring across the nation aimed at addressing the issue of money in politics. Meanwhile, in Washington, a total of 142 participants from a more progressive group, Democracy Spring, were taken into custody. This included 12 activists who attached themselves to the Capitol Rotunda in a bid to highlight the sway of special interests and to protest against legislation that complicates the voting process. During the week, nearly 1,000 individuals associated with Democracy Spring have faced arrest in Washington. The ongoing protests in Washington, along with the nationwide demonstrations spearheaded by the group Represent.Us, have resonated with voter dissatisfaction evident during the presidential campaign season. Charlotte Hill, the communications director for Represent.Us, stated, “From super PACs (political action committees) to lucrative job offers and campaign contributions, there are tons of perfectly legal ways to bribe a politician.” Represent.Us, which has been advocating for anti-corruption measures in various American cities, clarified that it does not support or oppose any presidential candidate. Plans for events in 33 cities were announced by Represent.Us. Both Trump, a wealthy Republican, and Sanders, who identifies as a democratic socialist vying for the Democratic nomination, have criticized the substantial impact of large financial contributions on their unexpected presidential campaigns. Dan Krassner, the political director of Represent.Us, remarked, “It doesn’t matter if you’re conservative or progressive. Two hundred and forty-three years after the original Boston Tea Party, Americans of all political stripes are still facing taxation without political representation.” Around 40 activists re-enacted the Boston Tea Party at the historical site where colonists protested British taxes by dumping tea into the harbor. The Represent.Us activists threw a stack of wooden crates into the water, symbolizing campaign contributions. In Washington, Democracy Spring activists secured themselves to scaffolding in the Capitol Rotunda. “We the people demand a democracy free from the corrupting influence of big money and voter suppression,” the demonstrators proclaimed in unison. Capitol Police reported that an additional 130 individuals were arrested for unlawful protests. Hundreds of chanting protesters marched up Capitol Hill holding signs that read “Sweep Big Money out of Politics” and “Corporations are not people.” They also voiced their concerns regarding the burdensome cost of college loans, economic disparity, and fracking. David Cheplowitz, 27, from Rochester, New York, expressed, “We need to get money out of politics and overturn Citizens United (a Supreme Court decision on campaign contributions).”

text: A proposal aimed at aiding Puerto Rico in overcoming its severe financial challenges is moving forward in Congress. On Wednesday, U.S. lawmakers showed their support for this initiative, which seeks to alleviate the island's overwhelming debt while also fostering economic growth. The House Natural Resources Committee approved the proposal with a vote of 29-10, maintaining most of the measures that House Speaker Paul Ryan had previously endorsed. This plan would authorize a federal oversight board tasked with negotiating with creditors and determining the recovery amount for the approximately $70 billion loaned to Puerto Rico. According to a statement from Ryan’s office, the rescue will not utilize taxpayer funds, thereby avoiding a bailout situation. Governor Alejandro Garcia Padilla of Puerto Rico expressed his appreciation for the bill, highlighting its provisions aimed at addressing insolvency, safeguarding essential services, and stimulating economic development. Nevertheless, he reiterated his concerns regarding the extensive powers granted to the oversight board. He remarked, "Puerto Ricans are Americans and our democratic rights need to be protected, just like those of American citizens living on the mainland, and the oversight provisions do not meet that obligation," urging Speaker Ryan to revise the bill prior to its full House vote. The proposed legislation includes a stipulation that would prevent investors from filing lawsuits against Puerto Rico while the oversight board is operational, and it suggests that all of the island's creditors may incur losses, despite recent lobbying efforts from Wall Street factions. In the Republican ranks, a majority of lawmakers supported the rescue initiative, although a notable minority cautioned that it could diminish investor appetite for municipal bonds, compelling issuers to offer higher interest rates. Congressman Tom McClintock from California warned, "Taxpayers across the country will have to pay ... as markets adjust to this new world." The bill, officially titled the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act, was passed with minimal amendments. Separate statements from both Speaker Ryan and Nancy Pelosi, the leading Democrat in the House, highlighted the bipartisan backing for the legislation on Wednesday. If this support remains consistent, the lawmakers may successfully navigate the rescue through the Senate to President Barack Obama before the $1.9 billion debt payment due from Puerto Rico on July 1. While Republicans might seek additional concessions, certain Democrats view the oversight board as excessively harsh. Furthermore, Democrats are calling for assurances that the island’s pension system, which faces a $40 billion shortfall, will be prioritized for protection. With the House and Senate preparing for a week-long Memorial Day recess at the end of this week, the full House's consideration of the bill is not anticipated until June.
source_text: Puerto Rico rescue bill advances to full House vote. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. lawmakers on Wednesday backed a plan to help Puerto Rico escape crippling debt and expand the economy, a move that could put a rescue before the House of Representatives within days. The House Natural Resources Committee endorsed the plan by a 29-10 vote and left intact most provisions endorsed by House Speaker Paul Ryan. The plan would empower a federal oversight board to negotiate with investors and decide what they would recover from the roughly $70 billion they lent the island. Taxpayer money will not be spent in the rescue which would prevent a bailout, Ryan’s office said in a statement on Wednesday. Puerto Rico’s Governor, Alejandro Garcia Padilla praised the bill for elements to help address insolvency, protect essential services and grow the economy. However, he reiterated reservations about the broad power of the oversight board. “Puerto Ricans are Americans and our democratic rights need to be protected, just like those of American citizens living on the mainland, and the oversight provisions do not meet that obligation,” he said in a statement, urging Ryan to amend the bill before it goes to the full House for a vote.     Under the plan, investors may not sue Puerto Rico while the oversight board does its work, and all the island’s creditors could face a loss despite recent lobbying from Wall Street interest groups. Among Republicans who voted on Wednesday, more than half endorsed the rescue plan but a vocal minority warned that it would hurt investor demand for municipal bonds and force issuers to offer higher yields. “Taxpayers across the country will have to pay ... as markets adjust to this new world,” warned Congressman Tom McClintock of California. The bill, called the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act, passed without significant changes. Speaker Ryan and Nancy Pelosi, the top Democrat in the House, in separate statements on Wednesday touted bipartisan support for the bill. If that holds, lawmakers may guide the rescue past the Senate to President Barack Obama before $1.9 billion in Puerto Rico debt is due on July 1. Republicans may demand more concessions while some Democrats find the oversight board too punitive. Democrats also want guarantees that the island’s pension system, which has a shortfall of $40 billion, would be protected first. With the House and Senate set to begin a week-long Memorial Day holiday break at the end of this week, debate of the bill by the full House is not expected until sometime in June.

text: On Friday, U.S. Senator Rob Portman expressed concerns regarding the potential removal of sanctions on Russia by President Donald Trump, stating that such an action, unless prompted by a change in Russian conduct, would convey a "dangerous message" to the global community. As a co-founder and co-chair of the Senate Ukraine Caucus, Portman urged that the sanctions enacted against Russia due to its annexation of Ukraine should be codified into law. The Republican emphasized the necessity of supporting allies in the region, particularly Ukraine, in his remarks.
source_text: Republican senator wants Russia sanctions put into law. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Senator Rob Portman, commenting on the possible lifting of sanctions on Russia by President Donald Trump, said on Friday lifting them for any reason other than a change of Russian behavior would send the world “a dangerous message.” Portman, a founder and co-chairman of the Senate Ukraine Caucus, said the Senate should work to put sanctions imposed on Russia over its annexation of Ukraine into law. “We must stand by our allies in the region, including Ukraine,” the Republican said in a statement.

text: The proposal from the White House includes the revival of the Yucca Mountain nuclear waste facility. According to Reuters, the budget plan for the U.S. Department of Energy for 2018 allocates $120 million towards nuclear waste initiatives, which encompasses the resumption of licensing for Yucca Mountain in Nevada, a project that has faced years of delay due to legal disputes and opposition from local communities. This initiative indicates that President Donald Trump may view solutions for nuclear waste as a means to prolong the operational lifespan of current nuclear power plants in the U.S. and to hasten advancements in next-generation nuclear reactors, which proponents assert are safer than earlier models. The budget will be subject to congressional discussions, and it remains unclear if the allocated funds for waste management will be retained in the final plan. While the Yucca Mountain site is intended for long-term waste storage, the budget allocation will also finance programs for temporary waste storage locations prior to the opening of Yucca. A summary of the budget states, "These investments would accelerate progress on fulfilling the federal government’s obligations to address nuclear waste, enhance national security, and reduce future taxpayer burden." The U.S. government has been investigating Yucca Mountain as a possible repository for the nation’s radioactive waste since the 1970s, with billions of dollars already invested. However, the facility has not been inaugurated due to legal obstacles and significant opposition from local politicians, environmental advocates, and Native American groups. In 2010, former President Barack Obama retracted the license for waste storage at Yucca, influenced by then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, a Democrat representing Nevada. Maria Korsnick, who leads the Nuclear Energy Institute, expressed that the industry feels optimistic about the waste management initiatives but noted that nuclear energy innovators are "nervous" regarding cuts to programs that have facilitated public-private collaborations for developing new nuclear technologies. The budget proposal eliminates financing for the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Energy and a loan guarantee program for innovative technologies, both of which have garnered support from Democrats and numerous Republicans. At his confirmation hearing, Rick Perry, Trump's energy secretary, informed lawmakers that restarting the Yucca Mountain project was a possibility, although he emphasized the need to work with state officials. "I am very aware that this is an issue this country has been flummoxed by for 30 years. We have spent billions of dollars on this issue," Perry stated during the January hearing. "I’ll work closely with you and the members of this committee to find the answers to this issue." The budget proposal from the White House for the Department of Energy indicates an overall reduction of 5.6 percent.
source_text: White House proposes reviving Yucca Mountain nuclear waste site. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The White House’s 2018 budget plan for the U.S. Department of Energy includes $120 million for nuclear waste programs including the restart of licensing for Nevada’s Yucca Mountain, a project stalled for years by lawsuits and local opposition. The move signals that President Donald Trump may consider that nuclear waste solutions could extend the lives of existing U.S. nuclear power plants and speed up innovations in next- generation nuclear plants that backers say are safer than previous reactors.   Congress will debate the budget and it is uncertain whether funds for waste will remain in the plan. While Yucca Mountain would store waste on a practically permanent basis, the budget money would also support programs for storing waste at interim sites before Yucca opens.  “These investments would accelerate progress on fulfilling the federal government’s obligations to address nuclear waste, enhance national security, and reduce future taxpayer burden,” according to a summary of the budget. Yucca has been studied by the U.S. government since the 1970s as a potential repository for the nation’s radioactive waste and billions of dollars have been spent on it. But Yucca has never opened because of legal challenges and widespread opposition from local politicians, environmentalists and Native American groups. In 2010, then-President Barack Obama withdrew the license to store waste at Yucca amid opposition from then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, a fellow Democrat from Nevada. Maria Korsnick, the head of the Nuclear Energy Institute industry group, said the industry was encouraged by the plan for waste projects but that nuclear energy innovators were “nervous” about cuts to programs that have supported public-private partnerships to bring new nuclear technologies to market. The budget eliminates funding for the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Energy and an innovative technology loan guarantee program that have been popular with both Democrats and many Republicans.    Trump’s energy secretary, Rick Perry, told lawmakers at his confirmation hearing that restarting the Yucca Mountain project could not be ruled out, but that he would collaborate with states. “I am very aware that this is an issue this country has been flummoxed by for 30 years. We have spent billions of dollars on this issue,” Perry told the hearing in January. “I’ll work closely with you and the members of this committee to find the answers to this issue.” The White House proposal for the Department of Energy budget calls for an overall cut of 5.6 percent.

text: A federal court ruled on Monday that gerrymandering efforts by Republicans in Wisconsin were unconstitutional. The decision, rendered by the United States District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin with a 2-1 vote, concluded that Act 43, which involved redistricting maps sanctioned by the Republican-controlled legislature in 2012, breached the U.S. Constitution, as indicated by court documents. The ruling articulated, "We find that the discriminatory effect is not explained by the political geography of Wisconsin nor is it justified by a legitimate state interest." This case does not affect Donald Trump’s triumph in the state during the presidential election held on Nov. 8, where he surpassed Democrat Hillary Clinton. Wisconsin’s Attorney General Brad Schimel announced intentions to appeal this decision, which would escalate the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court. A ruling from the Supreme Court concerning gerrymandering, defined as the manipulation of electoral borders for political gain, could set significant precedents nationwide, especially as similar cases are currently in progress in Maryland and North Carolina. Richard Hasen, an elections law specialist at the University of California, Irvine, expressed on his blog, "This is a big victory for those who want to see courts rein in partisan gerrymandering. But it is anybody’s guess what happens to this when it gets to the Supreme Court." Since 2010, the Republican Party has significantly expanded its dominance over state legislatures, now controlling both legislative chambers in an unprecedented 32 states, as reported by the New York Times. Republican Assembly Speaker Robin Vos stated, "Republicans win elections because we have better candidates and a better message that continues to resonate with the voters." In their lawsuit, twelve voters from Wisconsin contended that Republicans manipulated district boundaries in 2011 to fragment Democratic voters, ensuring they did not achieve a majority in many districts, while also clustering Democratic voters into specific districts to ensure they won by large margins, thereby diluting Democratic votes across the state, according to the court's ruling. Despite securing 51 percent of the statewide vote in 2012, Democrats managed to win only 39 out of 99 Assembly seats. In 2014, the Republicans garnered a similar proportion of votes statewide but achieved 63 seats, resulting in a 24-seat differential, as noted by the judges. The Wisconsin case centered around a novel approach to assess the discriminatory impacts of gerrymandering. Utilizing the "efficiency gap" metric, it was determined that the redistricting in Wisconsin led to Democrats wasting more votes in comparison to Republicans. Barry Burden, the director of the Elections Research Center at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, remarked to the New York Times that the measure provides judges with "a clear threshold for deciding what is acceptable."
source_text: Court says Republican gerrymandering in Wisconsin was unconstitutional. MILWAUKEE (Reuters) - Republicans in Wisconsin tilted district maps in their favor in order to hamper Democrats and ultimately win state elections in 2012 and 2014, a federal court said on Monday in a case that could influence future rulings on gerrymandering. The United States District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin decided 2-1 that Act 43, a redrawing of districts approved by the state’s Republican-led legislature in 2012, violated the U.S. Constitution, court documents showed.  “We find that the discriminatory effect is not explained by the political geography of Wisconsin nor is it justified by a legitimate state interest,” the court wrote in its ruling. The case has no bearing on Donald Trump’s victory in Wisconsin in the presidential election on Nov. 8, in which he defeated Democrat Hillary Clinton. Wisconsin Attorney General Brad Schimel said in a statement that he planned to appeal, which would send the case to the U.S. Supreme Court. A ruling there on gerrymandering - the practice of manipulating electoral boundaries for political advantage - could have wide implications across the country as similar cases in Maryland and North Carolina work their way through lower courts.     “This is a big victory for those who want to see courts rein in partisan gerrymandering. But it is anybody’s guess what happens to this when it gets to the Supreme Court,” wrote Richard Hasen, an elections law expert at the University of California, Irvine, on his blog. Since 2010, Republicans have more than doubled their control of state legislatures. They now control both legislative chambers in a record 32 states, the New York Times reported. “Republicans win elections because we have better candidates and a better message that continues to resonate with the voters,” said Republican Assembly Speaker Robin Vos in a statement. Twelve Wisconsin voters argued in their lawsuit that Republicans redrew maps in 2011 to divide Democratic voters so they fall short of a majority in districts and to concentrate Democratic voters into districts so they win by overwhelming margins and dilute votes of Democrats statewide, according to the ruling.   Despite receiving 51 percent of the votes statewide in 2012, Democrats won only 39 of 99 Assembly seats. In 2014, Republicans won roughly the same percentage of votes statewide, but won 63 seats, a 24-seat disparity, judges wrote.  The Wisconsin case hinged on a new way to measure the discriminatory effect of gerrymandering. The “efficiency gap” measure found the redistricting in Wisconsin caused Democrats to waste more votes than Republicans.     The measure gives judges “a clear threshold for deciding what is acceptable”, Barry Burden, the director of the Elections Research Center at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told the New York Times.

text: In a move aimed at rejuvenating his political party ahead of the 2019 elections, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan has urged the resignation of mayors from three significant cities, as reported by Hurriyet newspaper. The high-profile mayor of Ankara, the nation's capital, is included in this call, which marks Erdogan's most direct request yet for a renewal among seasoned politicians, several of whom hold national prominence. This follows a scenario where voters in various cities rejected a referendum in April that sought to grant Erdogan extensive powers. While he narrowly secured a victory in the referendum that would alter the constitution to establish an executive presidency, opposition was voiced in 17 out of Turkey's 30 largest cities against the proposed changes. Since that time, Erdogan has emphasized the necessity for a refresh in local governance and within the ruling AK Party, pointing out signals of ‘metal fatigue’ in existing administrations. He stated, "People do not take these offices as independent candidates but as candidates shown by parties. We cannot regard these posts as chairs which are kept eternally and never abandoned," according to Hurriyet, which cited his remarks made during a flight back from Poland this week. The request for the resignation of the Balikesir mayor from northwest Turkey was also noted by the publication. Erdogan specifically mentioned that similar circumstances applied to Melih Gokcek, the mayor of Ankara, and also to the mayor of Bursa, a city in the northwest. Recently, the mayors of both Istanbul and Duzce city in northwest Turkey have resigned, along with the mayor of Nigde city in central Turkey, who stepped down on Wednesday. Despite being the mayor of Ankara since 1994 and securing five consecutive victories in elections, Gokcek has so far remained in his position, amid widespread speculation regarding his potential resignation. He has refrained from publicly addressing the topic and notably avoided discussion on the matter during an unexpected visit to the presidential palace earlier this month. "I presented to my president all the project details of the museum to be built opposite the (presidential) palace. I also gave various information about ongoing municipal projects... For the public's information," he communicated via Twitter. Gokcek, who is widely recognized as a loyal supporter of Erdogan, is particularly noted in Turkey for engaging in disputes on Twitter with journalists and other prominent AKP figures. In February, he proposed that the U.S.-based cleric, who is accused of masterminding last year’s failed coup, might be scheming with foreign entities to trigger an earthquake to harm the economy.

text: NEW YORK (Reuters) - President Barack Obama expressed his hope on Wednesday that the rifts among Democrats would begin to mend in the weeks ahead, following Hillary Clinton's securing of the party’s nomination for the presidential election scheduled on Nov. 8. “My hope is that over the next couple of weeks we’re able to pull things together,” Obama remarked in his initial public comments since Clinton’s primary victories on Tuesday in California and other states, which led her to triumph over Bernie Sanders after an arduous campaign lasting several months. During a taping of “The Tonight Show” with NBC's late-night host Jimmy Fallon, he noted, “What happens during primaries is you get a little ouchy.” Sanders, who has yet to concede the race, is anticipated to meet with Obama at the White House on Thursday at 11:15 a.m. (1515 GMT). Later, while attending a fundraiser at the Central Park West residence of Kenneth Lerer, a venture capitalist and chairman of BuzzFeed, Obama stated that he was “not too worried” about the “bruised feelings” resulting from the primary. “We just ended - sort of ended - our primary season,” he mentioned, correcting himself as the audience of around 60 Democratic donors, who contributed up to $33,400 to participate, chuckled nervously. Obama added, “I am concerned about us doing the hard nuts-and-bolts work of turning out people to vote, particularly young people, particularly low-income people.” When questioned on whether Sanders, a senator from Vermont, should promptly conclude his campaign, White House spokesperson Josh Earnest responded that the senator had “more than earned the right to make his own decision about the course of his campaign.” The Democratic Party will officially endorse Clinton’s nomination during its convention in Philadelphia at the close of July. Obama informed Fallon that he believed “it was a healthy thing for the Democratic Party to have a contested primary” and commended Sanders for the “enormous energy and new ideas” he contributed to the race. “He pushed the party and challenged them. I thought it made Hillary a better candidate,” Obama remarked. The administration has indicated that Obama, who enjoys significant popularity among Democrats, will assume a role focused on unifying the party during the campaign trail. “The main role I’m going to be playing in this process is to remind the American people that this is a serious job. This is not reality TV,” Obama commented to Fallon, referencing presumptive Republican nominee and real estate tycoon Donald Trump, known for his reality television background.

NEW YORK (Reuters) - President Barack Obama said on Wednesday he hoped that divisions between Democrats would start to heal in coming weeks, now that his former secretary of state, Hillary Clinton, has clinched the party’s nomination for the Nov. 8 presidential election. “My hope is that over the next couple of weeks we’re able to pull things together,” Obama said in his first public remarks since primary election wins on Tuesday in California and elsewhere propelled Clinton to victory over rival Bernie Sanders after a hard-fought, months-long campaign.    “What happens during primaries is you get a little ouchy,” Obama told NBC late-night host Jimmy Fallon during a taping of “The Tonight Show” set to air on Thursday. Later, at a fundraiser in the Central Park West apartment of Kenneth Lerer, a venture capitalist and chairman of the BuzzFeed medial company, Obama said he was “not too worried” about “bruised feelings” left over from the primary. “We just ended - sort of ended - our primary season,” Obama said, catching his mistake as the crowd of about 60 Democratic donors, who paid up to $33,400 to attend, laughed nervously. “I am concerned about us doing the hard nuts-and-bolts work of turning out people to vote, particularly young people, particularly low-income people,” Obama said. Asked whether Obama thought Sanders, a U.S. senator from Vermont, should quickly end his campaign, White House spokesman Josh Earnest said the senator had “more than earned the right to make his own decision about the course of his campaign.” The party will officially vote on Clinton’s nomination at its convention in Philadelphia at the end of July.
