text: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump’s choice to head the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services assured a congressional committee that he opposes Medicare privatization and defended his ethical conduct. During his testimony before the Senate Committee on Finance, one of the two main committees overseeing the health department, Representative Tom Price stated that his views align with those of Trump, who has expressed a desire to maintain funding for the federal health program designed for senior citizens. A Georgia orthopedic surgeon by profession, Price had previously advocated for the privatization of Medicare but clarified to lawmakers that his responsibilities as health secretary would differ significantly from those he held as a congressman, emphasizing that his role would involve implementing Congressional decisions. "I would just like to communicate to the nation's Medicare beneficiaries that they need not worry," he remarked. "We are eager to help them access the care and coverage they require." Senator Ron Wyden, the leading Democrat on the committee, raised concerns regarding Price's stock transactions while serving in Congress, particularly in stocks related to the health sector that could be influenced by legislative changes. "It is difficult to perceive this as anything other than a conflict of interest and an abuse of position," Wyden commented. In response, Price defended his stock investments, asserting, "All my actions were ethical, legitimate, transparent, and above reproach." Meanwhile, Republican legislators initiated the process of dismantling the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare, which was implemented during former President Barack Obama’s administration. Hearings took place on Tuesday across two committees in the House of Representatives, with more sessions planned, aimed at establishing "careful, incremental reforms that provide Americans with increased options, improved access, and higher-quality care at reduced costs," according to Kevin Brady, the chairman of the Ways and Means committee, during his address to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Price avoided directly addressing the effects of an executive order signed by Trump on his inaugural day, which targeted Obamacare, but he affirmed his commitment to implementing "the law of the land." Democrats further interrogated Price regarding his strategies for the Medicaid program, which serves low-income Americans. Kellyanne Conway, a senior adviser to Trump, stated in an NBC "Sunday Today" interview that the administration's proposal to replace Obamacare would entail fixed payments from the government to states for the care of Medicaid patients. These payments, referred to as block grants, differ from the current arrangement where states share the actual costs of Medicaid beneficiaries with the federal government. Conway claimed that transitioning to a block grant framework would guarantee that the program is administered by "those who are closest to the individuals" requiring assistance. While Price has long been a proponent of block grants for Medicaid, he refrained from explicitly reiterating his stance on Tuesday, simply noting that he would strive to ensure "individuals receive better healthcare, not diminished healthcare." The hearing on Tuesday followed a similar session held the previous week by the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, which also has oversight of the health department. Only members of the finance committee will cast votes regarding the nomination.
source_text: Trump health nominee says he does not back Medicare privatization. (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s nominee to run the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services told a congressional panel on Tuesday that he does not support the privatization of Medicare and defended his ethics record. Speaking before the Senate Committee on Finance, one of two committees that oversee the health department, Representative Tom Price said his position was consistent with that of Trump, who has stated he does not want to cut the federal health program for the elderly. Price, a Georgia orthopedic surgeon, previously supported privatization of Medicare. But he told lawmakers his role as health secretary would be very different from his role as a congressman and that his job would be to execute the wishes of Congress. “I would just convey to the Medicare population of this nation, they don’t have reason to be concerned,” he said. “We look forward to assisting them in getting the care and coverage that they need.” Senator Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the committee, questioned Price about his stock trading while a lawmaker, including in health industry stocks that could be affected directly by legislation. “It is hard to see this as anything but a conflict of interest and an abuse of position,” Wyden said. Price defended the stock holdings, saying “everything that I did was ethical, above board, legal and transparent.”  Separately, Republican lawmakers began dismantling former President Barack Obama’s 2010 Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. Two House of Representatives committees held hearings on Tuesday. Others will follow with the goal of putting in place  “thoughtful, step-by-step reforms that offer Americans more choices, greater access, and higher-quality care at lower costs,” the chairman of the Ways and Means committee, Kevin Brady, said in remarks to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Price sidestepped questions about the impact of an executive order Trump signed on his first day in office targeting Obamacare but said he is committed to carrying out “the law of the land.” Democrats also grilled Price on his plans for the Medicaid health program covering poor Americans. A senior Trump adviser, Kellyanne Conway, said in an interview on NBC’s “Sunday Today” show that Trump’s plan to replace Obamacare will include fixed payments from the government to the states to care for Medicaid patients. These payments, known as block grants, contrast with the current system in which states share the actual cost of Medicaid enrollees with the federal government. Conway said converting to a block grant system would ensure that people in charge of administering the program are “those who are closest to the people” who need care. Price has long advocated block grants for Medicaid but declined on Tuesday to overtly re-state his position, saying only that he would work to make sure “people have better healthcare, not less healthcare.” Tuesday’s hearing followed a similar hearing last week by the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, which also oversees the health department. Only the finance committee members will vote on the nomination.

text: FBI Director Christopher Wray stated on Thursday that he has not seen any signs of interference from the White House concerning the ongoing investigation into Russian involvement in the 2016 presidential election. This was Wray's first public statement since his confirmation as the head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. He expressed his trust in Robert Mueller, the special counsel tasked with determining whether President Donald Trump’s campaign colluded with Russia during the election. "I can say very confidently that I have not detected any whiff of interference with that investigation," Wray remarked during a panel at the Intelligence and National Security Summit in Washington. Wray took over the role of FBI director after James Comey was dismissed by Trump in May. Following Comey's termination, Trump revealed in an NBC interview that he had been contemplating "this Russia thing" when he made the decision to fire Comey. Comey later testified before Congress that he felt Trump attempted to persuade him to halt an FBI inquiry into former national security adviser Michael Flynn as part of the larger Russia investigation—a claim that has raised concerns about possible obstruction of justice by Trump. The White House has consistently rejected accusations that the Trump campaign coordinated with Russia during the election. Advisors and supporters of Trump have also scrutinized the independence and credibility of Mueller, pointing out that he has engaged attorneys who have made political contributions to Democrats. Nevertheless, Wray conveyed his "enormous respect" for Mueller, a former FBI director himself. He highlighted that Mueller is leading the investigation while the FBI provides assistance by allocating agents and offering additional support. Furthermore, Wray reaffirmed his faith in a January report produced by U.S. intelligence agencies, which concluded that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election in an attempt to favor Trump—a conclusion that Trump has often questioned. Before his confirmation, Wray had only reviewed a non-classified version of the report. "I have no reason to doubt the conclusions that the hard-working people who put that together came to," Wray stated.
source_text: FBI chief sees no evidence of White House interference in Russia probe. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - FBI Director Christopher Wray said on Thursday he has “not detected any whiff of interference” by the White House into the ongoing investigation into Russian meddling in the 2016 presidential election. Speaking publicly for the first time since being confirmed as head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Wray also expressed confidence in Robert Mueller, the special counsel investigating whether President Donald Trump’s campaign colluded with Russia during the election. “I can say very confidently that I have not detected any whiff of interference with that investigation,” Wray said during a panel discussion at the Intelligence and National Security Summit in Washington.  Wray was installed as FBI director after his predecessor, James Comey, was fired by Trump in May. In an interview with NBC after Comey’s removal, Trump admitted he was thinking about “this Russia thing” when he decided to fire the then-FBI chief. Comey later told Congress he believed Trump had tried to get him to drop an FBI probe into former national security adviser, Michael Flynn, as part of the broader Russia investigation - testimony that has raised questions about whether Trump was potentially trying to obstruct justice. The White House has repeatedly denied the Trump campaign colluded with Russia in the election. Trump’s advisers and allies also have questioned Mueller’s independence and credibility, with some pointing out that he has hired attorneys who have given political donations to Democrats. But Wray said he has “enormous respect” for Mueller, who is also a former FBI director. He stressed that Mueller is running the probe but said the FBI is assisting by dedicating agents and providing other support to the investigation. Wray also reiterated his confidence in a January report compiled by U.S. intelligence agencies which concluded that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election and tried to tilt it in Trump’s favor - a finding Trump has often questioned. Prior to his confirmation as FBI director, Wray had only read a non-classified version of the report. “I have no reason to doubt the conclusions that the hard- working people who put that together came to,” Wray said.

text: Protests in Togo turned violent on Thursday, leading to security forces firing live ammunition and tear gas, resulting in injuries to at least seven individuals. These demonstrations are aimed at opposing the ruling family dynasty that has been in power for 50 years in this West African hub for banking and transport. Since August, activists have voiced their dissent against President Faure Gnassingbe’s lack of a definitive timeline for his departure and the suppression of opposition parties in the only country in the region that has yet to embrace presidential term limits. Witnesses from Reuters observed armed paramilitary gendarmes arrive in trucks, dispersing crowds with volleys of tear gas. In the Be suburb of Lome, surrounded by dilapidated buildings and palm trees, protesters constructed barricades, ignited tires, and hurled stones at the authorities. A physician at the Social Medical Centre in Be reported, "We’ve received seven people wounded by bullets so far," as some of the injured were being treated with bandages. With a population of 8 million, this former French colony hosts several major corporations, such as Ecobank and regional airline ASKY, and has seen significant upgrades to its port facilities as the president aims to establish the resource-deficient nation as a commercial center. However, the ongoing repression and a single family's hold on power—Faure ascended to the presidency in 2005 following the death of his father, Gnassingbe Eyadema, who had governed for 38 years—pose challenges to its stability. Opponents of Gnassingbe argue that the reforms introduced last month, in response to protests in August, will still permit him to lead the West African nation until 2030.
source_text: Togo forces fire on protesters, seven wounded. LOME (Reuters) - Security forces in Togo fired bullets and teargas on Thursday, wounding at least seven people as they sought to break up violent protests against the 50-year ruling family dynasty in the West African banking and transport hub. Activists have been demonstrating since August against President Faure Gnassingbe s refusal to give a clear date for stepping aside and to allow opposition parties to flourish in the region s only country that still does not accept presidential term limits. A Reuters cameraman saw trucks carrying armed paramilitary gendarmes drive into crowds and fire volleys of teargas. Protesters in the Lome suburb of Be, flanked by rundown buildings and palm trees, set up barricades, burned tyres and threw stones at the security forces.  We ve received seven people wounded by bullets so far,  said a doctor at the Social Medical Centre in Be, where some were being wrapped in bandages. The former French colony of 8 million people is home to several large firms, including Ecobank and regional airline ASKY, and has undergone major port upgrades as the president has sought to turn the resource-poor nation into a commercial hub. But a history of repression and the monopoly of power by one family - Faure took power in 2005 upon the death of his father Gnassingbe Eyadema, who had ruled for 38 years - threaten its stability.  Ghassingbe s opponents says reforms announced last month, in response to August s protests, will still allow him to run the West African country until 2030.

text: Next week, the Republican majority in the U.S. House of Representatives will deliberate on the potential impeachment of John Koskinen, the commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service, over accusations from conservative members that he obstructed a congressional inquiry, House leaders announced on Wednesday. Democrats criticized this initiative as a politically driven embarrassment, asserting that it would ultimately be halted in the Senate. Some Republicans also expressed doubts that Koskinen's actions warranted impeachment from his role as IRS commissioner. Conservative Republicans in the House have alleged that Koskinen did not adhere to a congressional investigation concerning whether the IRS had subjected conservative groups to heightened scrutiny when they applied for tax-exempt status from 2010 to 2012. Despite this, House Speaker Paul Ryan and other prominent House Republicans have exhibited minimal enthusiasm for pursuing impeachment. However, Ryan stated on Wednesday that he anticipated action on the House floor due to conservatives submitting a privileged resolution, which can skip regular procedures and take precedence. "We will hold a planning conference on this next week," Ryan remarked at a standard press briefing. He added, "Congress will assert its will on this matter." Harry Reid, the Democratic leader in the Senate, referred to the impeachment process as a "waste, put that in big capital letters" and mentioned that it could be obstructed in the Senate by Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, a Republican. A spokesperson for McConnell refrained from commenting on any potential actions he might take if the House were to vote in favor of Koskinen's impeachment. "I am quite familiar with Koskinen," Finance Chairman Orrin Hatch, a senior Senate Republican, conveyed to Reuters. "Sure, he has made errors, but those errors do not rise to the level of justifying impeachment." Koskinen took over as IRS commissioner in December 2013, following the uproar regarding the agency's handling of tax-exempt status applications. Members of the House Freedom Caucus, known for being the most conservative faction in the chamber, have argued that Koskinen ought to be removed due to his involvement in the aftermath of the scandal. They pointed out that he was in charge when backup tapes containing emails from former IRS official Lois Lerner, who previously led the IRS’ tax-exempt division, were destroyed. Democrats have highlighted that no criminal charges were brought against Lerner by the Justice Department, asserting that the case against Koskinen reflects little more than mismanagement and inaccuracies within the agency.
source_text: U.S. House Republicans to discuss whether to impeach IRS chief. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Members of the Republican majority in the U.S. House of Representatives will discuss next week whether the nation’s top tax collector, John Koskinen, should be impeached over conservative charges he stonewalled a congressional investigation, House leaders said Wednesday. Democrats decried the move as a politically motivated embarrassment that would in any case be stopped in the Senate. Even some Republicans said they did not think Koskinen’s activities justified impeachment from his post as Internal Revenue Service (IRS) commissioner. Conservative Republicans in the House have said Koskinen failed to comply with a congressional investigation into whether the IRS applied extra scrutiny to applications for tax exempt status by conservative groups between 2010 and 2012. House Speaker Paul Ryan and other leading House Republicans have shown little interest in pursuing impeachment. But Ryan indicated Wednesday that he expected floor action because conservatives had filed a privileged resolution, which can bypass regular procedures and take precedence on the House floor. “This is something that we’re going to have a planning conference on next week,” Ryan told a regular press conference. “This is something where Congress is going to work its will.” The Senate’s Democratic leader, Harry Reid, called the process a “waste, put that in big capital letters” and said it could be blocked in the Senate by that chamber’s Majority Leader, Republican  Mitch McConnell. A spokesman for McConnell declined to say what action McConnell might take if the House does vote for Koskinen’s impeachment. “I know Koskinen very well,” another senior Senate Republican, Finance Chairman Orrin Hatch told Reuters. “Yeah, he’s made mistakes but he hasn’t made mistakes that justify an impeachment.” Koskinen became IRS commissioner in December 2013, after the controversy already had exploded over the way the agency had handled the applications for tax exempt status. Members of the House Freedom Caucus, the chamber’s most conservative bloc, have said Koskinen should be pushed out because of his role in the aftermath of the scandal. They noted that he was commissioner when backup tapes were destroyed containing emails from former IRS official Lois Lerner, who had headed the IRS’ tax-exempt division. Democrats have noted that the Justice Department brought no criminal charges against Lerner and say the case against Koskinen shows little more than agency mismanagement and misstatements.

text: In a bid to counter Bernie Sanders, Hillary Clinton, the leading candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination, is preparing to launch a significant critique of Republican rival Donald Trump regarding foreign policy. On Wednesday, Clinton's campaign announced plans for a robust attack on Trump, coinciding with her efforts to fend off challenges from Sanders as they both campaign in California. A major speech is set to be delivered by Clinton in San Diego on Thursday, where she will emphasize the potential dangers to U.S. national security posed by Trump if he were to win the presidency on November 8. Her rhetoric towards Trump has intensified with each passing day. text: Following a deadly typhoon, the opposition in Macau has made modest advancements in the recent legislative elections. Observers interpreted these changes as indications of public discontent towards the pro-Beijing administration after the Asian gambling center was struck by a devastating storm a month prior. The outcomes of the voting held on Sunday, which were revealed on Monday, indicated that the opposition secured five seats in the legislative assembly of 33, marking an increase of one seat from the previous elections held four years ago, as reported by local media. For a long time, the political sphere in Macau has been heavily influenced by pro-establishment groups, pro-Beijing interests, and the casino sector, and any progress made by the opposition is viewed by critics as a significant accomplishment. Among the legislative seats, only 14 are filled through direct elections, a significantly lower percentage compared to neighboring Hong Kong, another former colony of China that has fought harder for greater democratic freedoms and liberties than Macau, which transitioned from Portuguese to Chinese sovereignty in 1999. In addition, twelve seats are filled through indirect elections in smaller constituencies, while seven are appointed by Macau's leader with Beijing's backing, Fernando Chui, making it nearly impossible for the opposition to secure a majority. A notable victor in the elections is Sulu Sou, a 26-year-old pro-democracy advocate and vocal critic of the government, who now holds the title of the youngest lawmaker in Macau's history. Sou played a key role in leading one of Macau’s largest anti-government demonstrations three years ago, where approximately 20,000 citizens protested against a bill that proposed a generous compensation package for departing officials. This proposal was later rescinded by Macau's leader, Chui. After his electoral success, Sou expressed on his Facebook page, "In the past four years, people in Macau have faced various struggles, big and small. Today, the electorate has utilized their votes to signify their desire for change." At the moment, Reuters was unable to get a comment from Sou. Unlike in Hong Kong, where large protests are commonplace, significant public dissent remains relatively subdued in Macau, a former Portuguese territory that reverted to Chinese governance in 1999 under the 'one country, two systems' principle. The elections occurred less than a month after the devastation caused by Typhoon Hato, which resulted in the deaths of ten individuals. The administration's inability to adequately alert residents about the catastrophic storm, coupled with poor preparedness and prolonged interruptions to electricity and water services, stirred public frustration and highlighted the deficiencies in Macau's infrastructure. Despite the opposition's limited progress, critics remarked that the impressive 57 percent voter turnout and Sou's victory should serve as a critical warning to the government. Au Kam-sang, a seasoned pro-democracy legislator who was re-elected, remarked to Reuters, "It’s an ideal result... The public came out in larger numbers to back the opposition. It reflects the incompetence of the Macau government and the repercussions following Typhoon Hato." text: On Thursday, the heads of the U.S. intelligence services urged Congress to prolong the National Security Agency’s surveillance legislation that is poised to expire, cautioning in an unprecedented public announcement that the nation’s security could be compromised if lawmakers allow it to lapse. This appeal from the intelligence leaders aimed to exert influence on legislators, who seemed to have dropped a plan to approve a bill that would have reauthorized the NSA’s warrantless online surveillance initiative for multiple years, set to end on December 31. This proposal faltered late on Wednesday in light of significant pushback from a considerable group of both Republican and Democratic lawmakers advocating for enhanced privacy protections within the program, which primarily focuses on foreign targets but also captures communications from an unspecified number of U.S. citizens. In a different approach, House Republicans introduced a temporary funding bill on Thursday which includes an extension of the surveillance law until January 19. Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act is regarded by U.S. intelligence authorities as crucial for maintaining national security. In a joint statement, Director of National Intelligence Dan Coats, along with Attorney General Jeff Sessions and the leaders of the NSA, FBI, and CIA, asserted, "There is no substitute for Section 702," emphasizing that failing to renew this authority would facilitate foreign adversaries in planning attacks against American citizens and allies without being detected. The NSA is permitted under Section 702 to amass extensive digital communication data from foreign suspects outside the U.S. However, this program inadvertently collects communications from Americans due to various technical factors, including interactions with foreign targets residing abroad. These communications may then be subjected to warrantless searches, including by the FBI. Some legislators from both parties express the desire to eliminate or partially limit the government's capacity to examine the data of American citizens obtained through Section 702 without a warrant. The intelligence leaders also criticized the current strategy to extend the program temporarily, asserting that short extensions "fail to provide certainty and will create needless and wasteful operational complications." Recently, U.S. officials acknowledged that the deadline at the end of the year may not be critical, as it is believed the program can legally persist until April due to the annual certification process. Nevertheless, the intelligence chiefs cautioned that the surveillance initiative would need to start “winding down” well before the April deadline.
source_text: Spy chiefs pressure Congress to renew expiring surveillance law. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The leaders of the U.S. intelligence community on Thursday pressed Congress to renew the National Security Agency’s expiring surveillance law, warning in a rare public statement that national security may be endangered if lawmakers let it lapse. The message from the intelligence chiefs sought to apply pressure on lawmakers who appeared to abandon an effort this week to pass legislation that would have reauthorized for several years the NSA’s warrantless internet spying program, which is due to expire on Dec. 31. That plan cratered late on Wednesday amid objections from a sizable coalition of Republicans and Democrats who want to have more privacy safeguards in the program, which chiefly targets foreigners but also collects communications from an unknown number of Americans. Instead, House Republicans unveiled a stopgap funding measure on Thursday that includes an extension of the surveillance law until Jan. 19. The law, known as Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, is considered by U.S. intelligence agencies to be vital to national security. “There is no substitute for Section 702,” Director of National Intelligence Dan Coats, Attorney General Jeff Sessions, and the directors the NSA, FBI and CIA wrote in the joint statement, adding that failure to renew the authority would make it easier for foreign adversaries to “plan attacks against our citizens and allies without detection.” Section 702 allows the NSA to collect vast amounts of digital communications from foreign suspects living outside the United States. But the program incidentally gathers communications of Americans for a variety of technical reasons, including if they communicate with a foreign target living overseas. Those communications can then be subject to searches without a warrant, including by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Some lawmakers in both parties want to eliminate or partially restrict the U.S. government’s ability to review data of Americans collected under Section 702 without first obtaining a warrant. The intelligence chiefs also criticized the current plan to temporarily extend the program, saying short-term extensions “fail to provide certainty and will create needless and wasteful operational complications.” U.S. officials recently acknowledged the end-year deadline may not matter much because of a belief the program can lawfully continue through April due to the way it is annually certified.  In their statement, however, the intelligence chiefs warned that the surveillance program would need to begin “winding down” well in advance of the April date.

text: Reports indicate that the Revolutionary Guards of Iran have detained over 30 individuals with dual nationality in the last two years, primarily on allegations of espionage. This information has been corroborated by family members, legal representatives, and diplomats, and represents a doubling of previous figures disclosed by both local and international news outlets. The statistics illustrate a significant increase since 2015, which was a year that brought hopes of improved relations with Western nations following an international nuclear agreement. Prior to this timeframe, the number of dual nationals being held was typically in the low single digits. Furthermore, a notable trend has emerged, as 19 of the 30 individuals arrested since then hold European citizenship, contrasting with earlier cases where most detainees were Iranian Americans. According to lawyers and relatives of those detained, the Revolutionary Guards appear to be utilizing these individuals as leverage in international negotiations and as a means to deter European enterprises from engaging in business in Iran subsequent to the government's accord with global powers to alleviate sanctions. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which wields significant power as Iran’s foremost security apparatus, has extensive business interests and has voiced criticism towards the government for awarding contracts to foreign companies. Efforts to obtain comments from the Guards were met with silence, as were several attempts to engage with the Iranian government, which directed inquiries to the judiciary that also did not respond to repeated requests for information. Iranian officials have historically rejected claims that they hold detainees for ransom, arguing instead that Western governments unjustly imprison Iranians on fabricated charges. Relatives of those detained, along with their legal advisors and diplomats from Western nations, have provided information regarding names, arrest dates, and charges, but only under the condition of anonymity to protect against possible repercussions. Iran does not commonly disclose information about arrests or specific charges and does not acknowledge dual citizenship, which limits the rights of these individuals to receive consular assistance as outlined in the U.N. Vienna Convention. Sources assert that none of the detainees engaged in any form of spying and were arrested solely based on their dual nationality. Their decision to share details stems from a feeling of being kept uninformed by both Iranian authorities and Western governments. Numerous governments contend that maintaining a discreet profile serves the best interests of those detained. "This is very much what guides our approach," stated an official from the UK government. Daphne Kerremans, a spokesperson for the Dutch Foreign Ministry, remarked that revealing the identities of detainees could potentially endanger them. Some family members only choose to speak out after their initial hopes have been dashed. For instance, Vida Mehrannia, the spouse of Ahmadreza Djalali, a scientist with ties to Sweden who was taken into custody in 2016 while attending a conference in Tehran, decided to go public in February. "We were all optimistic about his prompt release. He was communicating with us from prison, indicating that he had not received any formal charges. They informed him that he would be set free after answering a few questions," she recounted via a call from Stockholm. "I brought the case to media attention after nine months when he faced threats of a death sentence from a prosecutor and initiated a hunger strike," she continued. Djalali was sentenced to death in October due to espionage allegations. At the time, Swedish Foreign Minister Margot Wallstrom expressed, "We will point out that this will affect the relationship with the EU, and this in a time when Iran and the EU need to cooperate, not least with the nuclear deal we have with Iran." The agreement to lift sanctions in exchange for limiting Iran's nuclear activities was a global undertaking, although significant U.S. restrictions remained in effect. Often, confirmation of new arrests becomes evident through indirect means. A record from a European Parliament session in June 2017 indicated that three Dutch-Iranian nationals were imprisoned in Iran, though only one case has been disclosed. When questioned about the two unidentified cases, spokesperson Kerremans informed Reuters that the individuals were arrested in November 2012 and January 2016, adding that government actions were primarily focused on ensuring honesty.

We were all hopeful that he would be released soon. He was calling us from jail, saying he had not been officially charged. Only two of those cases were known to the public at the time. Contacted for comment, a UK foreign ministry spokesman declined to specify how many British-Iranian dual nationals had been arrested. London raised all cases with Iran at every available opportunity, he said. Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe, an Iranian-British aid worker employed by the Thomson Reuters Foundation, was arrested in April 2016 while on holiday in Iran and later charged with plotting to overthrow Iran s clerical establishment. Johnson had said,  she was simply teaching people journalism.  He subsequently said  the UK government has no doubt that she was on holiday in Iran  and that his comments  could have been clearer .  My point was that I disagreed with the Iranian view that training journalists was a crime, not that I wanted to lend any credence to Iranian allegations that Mrs Zaghari-Ratcliffe had been engaged in such activity,  he said. In 2016, Iran released five U.S. citizens in a prisoner exchange as the nuclear deal was implemented. One remained behind and six American citizens or permanent residents have been arrested since, their lawyers or relatives have told media, of whom one has been freed on bail. A U.S. State Department official confirmed three cases, did not comment on two others and mentioned another detainee, Nizar Zakka, saying he was unjustly held and calling for his release without clarifying his U.S. status. Asked for more details about Zakka and other detained US citizens and legal residents, the official said the safety and security of U.S. citizens abroad was a top priority, adding:  Due to privacy considerations, we have no further comment.  In an October 25 letter to the U.N. Secretary General seen by Reuters, Zakka s lawyer Jason Poblete said his client was a U.S. permanent resident and  is being held as a hostage, as are other innocent persons, to exact political concessions from the United States and other governments , including on sanctions. For its part, Iran says its nationals are detained unjustly in the West. Kazem Gharibabadi, deputy head of Iran s Council for Human Rights, part of the judiciary, has said more than 56 Iranians are imprisoned in the United States and an unspecified number in other countries.  Some of those are detained under baseless charges, including bypassing sanctions,  he was quoted as saying by state media on Sunday. U.S. Department of Justice spokesman Wyn Hornbuckle declined to comment on Gharibabadi s figure, saying the Justice Department does not track prosecutions by nationality and the U.S. government s Bureau of Prisons does not track how many inmates have Iranian nationality. He said inmates in U.S. federal prison  are serving sentences handed down by federal judges after thorough due process of law .

source_text: New York removes misleading nuclear fallout shelter signs. NEW YORK (Reuters) - New York City has quietly begun removing some of the corroding yellow nuclear fallout shelter signs that were appended to thousands of buildings in the 1960s, saying many are misleading Cold War relics that no longer denote functional shelters. The small metal signs are a remnant of the anxieties over the nuclear arms race between the United States and the former Soviet Union, which prompted U.S. President John F. Kennedy to create the shelter program in 1961 in cities across the nation. The signs, with their simple design of three joined triangles inside a circle, became an emblem of the era. While some New Yorkers may barely notice them today, to others they can be an uneasy reminder that the threat may have altered and diminished, but it has not vanished. Although the Cold War era has long ended, North Korea continues working to develop nuclear-tipped missiles capable of hitting the United States amid bellicose rhetoric from Washington and Pyongyang. A nuclear explosion is now seen as even less likely than during the Cold War. But should catastrophe ever strike, the signs, which still linger in their thousands, would be best ignored, city officials and disaster preparedness experts say.  In the aftermath of a nearby nuclear explosion, any survivors counting on the signs to lead them to safety from radioactive fallout after needlessly dashing outside would likely find themselves rattling locked doors or perhaps breaking into what is now a building s laundry room or bike-storage area. Maintenance of the shelter system, which once entailed federal funding to stock shelters with food and water, ended decades ago.  The removal of some of the signs from public school buildings, which has not previously been reported, is intended to partly reduce this potential confusion, according to the city s Department of Education. Michael Aciman, a department spokesman, confirmed that any designated fallout shelters created in the city s schools are no longer active and said that the department is aiming to finish unscrewing the signs from school walls by roughly Jan. 1. Although some of the tens of thousands of fallout shelter signs placed around the city by the federal government s Office of Civil Defense have vanished as old buildings have been renovated or demolished, city officials say this is the first coordinated effort to remove them. The Office of Civil Defense was eventually abolished in the 1970s, subsumed into the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Aciman declined to say whether, given the signs are technically federal property, the U.S. government was consulted. But FEMA said it did not mind anyway.  FEMA does not have a position regarding the signs,  Jenny Burke, a FEMA spokeswoman, wrote in an email on Tuesday. Although the agency does not maintain lists of the old shelter locations, she added,  as a part of an ongoing planning effort, the agency is conducting research to retrieve Office of Civilian Defense records.      The city s removal appeared somewhat haphazard: on one Brooklyn street, a sign on a school photographed by Reuters this month was subsequently removed, while a second school a few blocks away still had its sign attached, albeit with a screw missing. As a history buff, Jeff Schlegelmilch is fond enough of the signs that he stuck a replica on his office door at Columbia University s National Center for Disaster Preparedness, where he is deputy director.  I love seeing the signs, but, as a disaster planner, they have to come down,  he said.  At best, they are ignored, at worst, they re misleading and are going to cost people s lives.  The consensus now, from the federal government downward, was that designated shelters were an outmoded concept, and updated contingency plans have been widely adopted since al Qaeda s attack on the United States on Sept. 11, 2001, Schlegelmilch said.  Were a nuclear explosion ever to happen, those far enough from the blast center to survive would do well to head to the lower interiors of any standard residential or commercial building, ideally a windowless basement, to shelter from radioactive particles outside, which can burn skin and cause serious illness and death. Cars, on the other hand,  are terrible,  Schlegelmilch said: the particles sail right through a vehicle s thin exterior. NYC Emergency Management, the agency that runs the city s disaster preparations, was not involved in the decision but staff there welcomed the signs  removal. Nancy Silvestri, the agency s press secretary, said even once the signs are gone from schools, many would remain on apartment buildings and other structures. City officials are uncertain who has jurisdiction over those, she said.  Eliot Calhoun, the agency s Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, and Explosives Planner, sees the signs as unhelpfully muddying the waters.  He has spent years endlessly finessing a message, designed to flash as an alert on cellphones, that he hopes he will never have to send. In the nerve center of the agency s Brooklyn headquarters,  he called up onto a screen its current form:  Nuclear explosion reported. Shelter in basement/center of building, close windows/doors.   Every single time I look at it I change it a little bit,  he said.  When you only have 90 characters and you re trying to save lives you can really think too much about it.

text: On Friday, Donald Trump identified U.S. Senator Mike Lee as a likely candidate for the Supreme Court, reaching out to a supporter of his former competitor Ted Cruz. This move appears aimed at appealing to conservative Republicans who have expressed skepticism toward Trump’s presidential bid. Lee’s name was part of a newly released list of 21 individuals that Trump would contemplate nominating for the Supreme Court if he wins against Democrat Hillary Clinton in the election scheduled for Nov. 8. In a statement, Trump asserted, "This list is definitive and I will choose only from it in picking future justices of the United States Supreme Court." The timing of this announcement coincided with a day when both candidates had no public engagements and were gearing up for their first presidential debate on Monday. The updated list provided by Trump features 10 new names, alongside 11 conservative jurists carried over from a previous list he had unveiled in May. Notably, Lee’s brother, Thomas Lee, who serves as an associate justice on the Utah Supreme Court, remains on the expanded list after being included in the initial compilation. By naming Mike Lee, Trump appears to be making a conciliatory gesture towards Texas Senator Cruz, a conservative who fiercely opposed Trump during the Republican primaries and has yet to endorse him. Traditional conservative Republicans have shown signs of discomfort due to Trump’s brash style and his proposals that diverge from established conservative principles, including his stance on free trade agreements. In response to the announcement, Mike Lee expressed gratitude for the consideration. He remarked, "Right now I’m focused on my job in the Senate, where I’m in a good position to defend the Constitution by fighting against government overreach. Both lists that I’ve seen from the Trump campaign are fantastic." He humorously noted, "While my brother and I might disagree as to which list is better, they’re both great." The passing of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia on Feb. 13 led to a stalemate on the court, resulting in a four-to-four split between justices leaning to the right and those leaning to the left. Democratic President Barack Obama has put forward Merrick Garland, the chief judge of the U.S. Court of Appeals in Washington, for nomination, but the Republican-controlled Senate has declined to hold a confirmation vote. One of his primary messages during campaign events has been the potential of Republicans losing control of the court to the Democrats. text: MIDWAY ATOLL (Reuters) - On Thursday, President Barack Obama enjoyed snorkeling in the vibrant blue waters surrounding Midway Atoll, a secluded coral reef that highlights contemporary global climate issues and the United States' historical supremacy in the Pacific following its World War Two triumph there. The purpose of this visit was to convey the importance of safeguarding vulnerable species and environments from the adverse effects of climate change. Additionally, the timing coincided with Obama’s upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and other global leaders during his final tour of Asia, as he aimed to redirect U.S. defense and trade strategies towards this region. Naval historian Tom Hone, who has extensively researched the Battle of Midway, remarked, "It’s a signal, it’s a message saying the United States is committed to staying in the Pacific, and not sort of backing away." Navigating the island in an 18-golf-cart motorcade filled with Secret Service agents, aides, and media crews, Obama paused to observe a few endangered green sea turtles leisurely swimming onto the white sandy beach to bask in the sun. "When I grew up, we’d see these turtles all the time. You almost never see them beaching like this, just basking in the sun," stated Obama, who has roots in Hawaii, situated more than 1,100 nautical miles to the southeast. With just five months remaining in his presidency, Obama has endeavored to inspire a greater awareness of climate change among Americans. According to polling data from Reuters/Ipsos taken between July 24 and August 21, fewer than 5 percent of American voters consider the environment the most pressing issue facing the nation, and 35 percent believe that climate change will not influence their voting decisions in the November 8 election for Obama’s successor. This trip to the island complements Obama’s visit to Alaska last year, where he trekked on a retreating glacier. Carol Browner, a former administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency who served as an advisor to Obama on environmental matters during his first term, expressed, "These aren’t ‘photo ops’ - I think these are real opportunities to help the American people understand." Browner added, "He can get a level of attention that nobody else can get." Just last week, Obama expanded the boundaries of Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument fourfold to establish the largest marine monument globally, safeguarding the waters off the coast of Hawaii from commercial fishing and drilling activities. "This is going to be a precious resource for generations to come," Obama noted, loosening his dress shirt an extra button in the sweltering heat. "This is hallowed ground," he declared near a beach where young soldiers took cover in pillboxes, anticipating Japanese fighter planes during the World War Two Battle of Midway, a highly analyzed battle in military studies. "Had it not been for the courage and the bravery of those airmen, we might have not seen the tide turn in the battle of the Pacific," he remarked. In June 1942, U.S. forces, informed by codebreakers about the Japanese navy's plans for an attack, managed to sink four Japanese aircraft carriers and a heavy cruiser in a monumental air and sea confrontation. As Obama’s motorcade traversed a tarmac marked by shrapnel remnants from the historic battle, it passed dilapidated hangars and a “bone yard” filled with scrap metal, broken office chairs, and discarded appliances. Large bags contained some of the 20 tons of plastic debris that wash ashore on the island each year, with 5 tons originating from the stomachs of albatrosses that mistakenly feed the plastic to their chicks, often with fatal consequences. Young tern fledglings curiously examined his group, which increased the island’s typical human population of around 35 threefold. "Watch the burrow!" shouted Miel Corbett, a representative from Fish and Wildlife Services, as a visitor narrowly missed stepping on the underground nest of the bonin petrel. Each night at dusk, approximately one million of these birds emerge from their nests. Remnants of the island’s past existence as a significant naval base still exist, although many have fallen into disrepair. Since 2012, visitors have been prohibited from accessing the island due to budget constraints.

text: The financial struggles of Connecticut have led to the decision to halt pay increases for managers within state agencies, state officials announced on Monday. This move reflects the deteriorating fiscal outlook for the state, which appears to be more severe than earlier assessments indicated. The suspension of these raises marks an initial sign of the negative impact stemming from the ongoing budget crisis. Officials anticipate further cuts as the state grapples with a budget shortfall projected to reach up to $900 million for the upcoming fiscal year. While the total amounts involved are quite publicized, they are primarily symbolic in nature. Approximately 1,950 workers will be affected by this decision, resulting in a total savings of $12.74 million over the next two years. This figure does not encompass the pay freezes occurring within the judicial system. Connecticut has revised its revenue forecasts downward due to a poor stock market negatively influencing tax receipts from capital gains, which are crucial for the budget. Efforts to increase taxes have faced significant opposition. Earlier this year, General Electric relocated its headquarters out of Connecticut. In a letter, Ben Barnes, who serves as secretary for the Office of Policy and Management, expressed, "We have a responsibility to the taxpayers of Connecticut not to move forward with managerial raises at a time when so many state programs will see reductions and while many state jobs are likely to be eliminated." This letter was jointly signed by Brian Durand, the chief of staff for Democratic Governor Dannel Malloy. A recent report from the non-partisan Office of Fiscal Management indicated that the deficit could reach as high as $900 million in the new fiscal year starting on July 1, up from an earlier estimate of $570 million provided by Barnes’ office. Most of the raises, which had been delayed on two previous occasions, were scheduled for approval on Friday but will now be on hold indefinitely.
source_text: Connecticut cancels pay raises for managers as budget woes bite. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Connecticut will cancel pay raises for managers at state agencies after the latest projections suggest the state’s fiscal situation may be much worse than previously thought, top officials said on Monday. The canceled raises are an early indication of the harm done by the state’s fiscal crisis. Many more cuts are expected this year as officials struggle with a budget deficit that could be as high as $900 million in the coming fiscal year. Although high-profile, the amounts involved are largely symbolic. The cancellations will affect 1,950 employees and represent savings of $12.74 million over two years. The figure does not include pay freezes in the judicial branch.  Connecticut has had to slash its revenue forecast because the weak stock market is cutting into capital gains tax receipts, which play a large role in the budget. It also met resistance when it tried to raise taxes. General Electric moved its headquarters out of the state earlier this year.   “We have a responsibility to the taxpayers of Connecticut not to move forward with managerial raises at a time when so many state programs will see reductions and while many state jobs are likely to be eliminated,” wrote Ben Barnes, secretary of the Office of Policy and Management. The letter was co-signed by Brian Durand, chief of staff to Democratic Governor Dannel Malloy. A report last week from the non-partisan Office of Fiscal Management said the deficit could be as high as $900 million in the next fiscal year, which begins on July 1. An earlier estimate from Barnes’ office put the deficit at $570 million.    Most of the raises, which have already been postponed twice, would have been awarded on Friday. They will be suspended indefinitely.

text: On Saturday, the Russian President Vladimir Putin enacted new legislation permitting the government to designate foreign media organizations as foreign agents. This move is a reaction to what Moscow describes as intolerable pressure exerted by the U.S. on Russian media. The new legal framework was expedited through both chambers of the Russian parliament within the past fortnight. This legislation enables Moscow to compel foreign media to label the news they deliver to Russian citizens as originating from foreign agents and to reveal their funding sources. The law was made available in the online legislative database of the Russian government on Saturday, indicating that it became effective immediately upon publication. The action taken against U.S. media forms part of the consequences arising from claims that Russia meddled in the previous year’s U.S. presidential election to benefit Donald Trump. U.S. intelligence officials have accused the Kremlin of employing Russian media outlets it supports to sway American voters, leading to a requirement for the Russian state broadcaster RT to register a U.S.-based affiliate as a foreign agent. The Kremlin has consistently refuted allegations of election interference and contends that the limitations placed on Russian media in the U.S. constitute an assault on freedom of expression. Last week, the Russian Justice Ministry released a list naming nine U.S.-affiliated news organizations that might be impacted by these new regulations. Additionally, it communicated with the U.S. government-sponsored Voice of America (VOA) and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), as well as seven other Russian or local-language news entities operated by RFE/RL.
source_text: Russia's Putin signs 'foreign agents' media law. MOSCOW (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin signed into law on Saturday new measures allowing authorities to list foreign media outlets as  foreign agents  in response to what Moscow says is unacceptable U.S. pressure on Russian media. The new law has been rushed through both Russian houses of parliament in the last two weeks. It will now allow Moscow to force foreign media to brand news they provide to Russians as the work of  foreign agents  and to disclose their funding sources. A copy of the law was published on the Russian government s online legislation database on Saturday, saying it entered into force from the day of its publication. Russia s move against U.S. media is part of the fallout from allegations that Russia interfered in last year s U.S. presidential election in favor of Donald Trump. U.S. intelligence officials have accused the Kremlin of using Russian media organizations it finances to influence U.S. voters, and Washington has since required Russian state broadcaster RT to register a U.S.-based affiliate company as a  foreign agent . The Kremlin has repeatedly denied meddling in the election and said the restrictions on Russian broadcasters in the United States are an attack on free speech.  The Russian Justice Ministry last week published a list of nine U.S.-backed news outlets that it said could be affected by the changes. It said it had written to the U.S. government-sponsored Voice of America (VOA) and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), along with seven separate Russian or local-language news outlets run by RFE/RL.

text: A parliamentary official announced on Friday that a consensus has been reached between Poland's ruling party and the president regarding judicial reforms, marking progress towards resolving a dispute that has persisted for over three months. Since July, discussions have been ongoing between President Andrzej Duda and the government following Duda's unexpected veto of proposed legislation from the ruling Law and Justice (PiS) party aimed at overhauling the Polish judicial system. "We have come to an initial agreement... I'm optimistic that we can address the project in parliament by late November," stated Stanislaw Piotrowicz, a PiS parliamentary deputy involved in the negotiations. The legislation that Duda vetoed would have led to the immediate dismissal of all current Supreme Court judges unless they received approval from the justice minister. Additionally, the parliament would have been granted the authority to appoint most members of the National Council of the Judiciary, which in turn would propose future candidates for the Supreme Court. By enabling parliament to effectively control the appointments and dismissals of senior judges, these proposals raised significant concerns in the European Union, which Poland is a part of. The EU argued that such changes would undermine judicial independence and jeopardize the rule of law. The newly proposed compromise will still allow parliament to appoint members of the National Council of the Judiciary, but this will necessitate a three-fifths majority in the lower house, according to Piotrowicz. Moreover, opposition parties will also have the opportunity to nominate judges. If candidates do not receive the necessary approval, they may still be selected by a simple majority, he added. The PiS maintains that reforming the judicial system is essential due to the courts being perceived as slow, ineffective, and influenced by outdated communist-era ideologies. Duda's veto and his suggested restrictions on authority over the judiciary led to a deadlock that threatened to delay the party's broader reform agenda, which includes changes to the media and electoral system. The compromise revealed today still requires the endorsement of both the president and PiS leadership.
source_text: Poland's president, ruling party reach compromise on court reforms. WARSAW (Reuters) - Poland s president and its ruling party have reached a compromise on judicial reform, a parliamentary deputy said on Friday, bringing them closer to resolving an issue that has kept them at odds for more than three months. The government and President Andrzej Duda have been negotiating since July, when Duda unexpectedly vetoed legislation backed by the ruling Law and Justice (PiS) party to overhaul the Polish court system.  We ve reached a preliminary agreement ... I hope that in late November we could discuss the project in  parliament,  PiS parliamentary deputy and negotiator Stanislaw Piotrowicz said on Friday. The proposals vetoed by Duda would have immediately removed all current Supreme Court judges unless they had the approval of the justice minister. Parliament would have gained the right to name most of the National Council of the Judiciary, which would nominate future candidates to preside over the Supreme Court. By giving parliament effective control over appointing - and sacking - senior judges, the proposals raised alarms in the rest of the European Union, of which Poland is a member. The EU said they undermined the independence of the courts and threatened the rule of law. The proposed compromise would still give parliament the right to name members of the National Council of the Judiciary, but that would require a three-fifths majority in the lower house of parliament, Piotrowicz said. Opposition parties would gain the right to propose judges, too. If candidates failed to gain approval, they could be chosen by a simple majority, he said. The PiS says the judicial system needs to be reformed because the courts are slow, inefficient and steeped in a communist-era mentality.  Duda s veto of parts of the reforms and his proposed limits on its authority over the court system created a stalemate that could have stalled the party s plans to reform not just the courts but the media and the electorate system as well. The compromise announced today still needs to be approved by the president and the leadership of PiS.

text: A series of confidence votes has been called by the Italian Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni's administration in the Senate on Tuesday regarding a new electoral law. The anti-establishment 5-Star Movement, which is expected to be negatively affected by this new legislation, has vowed to demonstrate in the streets. To prevent secret voting in the Senate, where their majority is precarious and at least four members of the ruling Democratic Party have declared they will abstain from voting, the government is resorting to confidence votes. Open ballot voting will commence on Wednesday afternoon, culminating in the final confidence vote on Thursday. Should the government lose this vote, it would be obliged to resign. A centrist faction, which is not officially part of the ruling coalition, has indicated that it could supply up to 10 votes to ensure the law's passage if necessary. Dubbed the Rosatellum, the bill has the backing of the Democratic Party (PD) and mainstream center-right opposition groups. This legislation tends to favor those parties that form alliances prior to the elections. The 5-Star Movement, which has resisted joining any coalition, and left-leaning parties opposed to a partnership with the PD are likely to be disadvantaged by the changes. On Wednesday afternoon, the 5-Star Movement, which frequently leads in opinion polls, will hold a protest in front of the Senate, opposing what they interpret as an effort by traditional rivals to undermine their electoral prospects. They will be joined by the leftist Democratic and Progressive Movement (MDP), which separated from the PD this year, along with various minor left-wing organizations. In addition to the PD, Silvio Berlusconi's center-right Forza Italia (Go Italy!) and the right-wing Northern League are also in favor of the legislation. According to Ettore Rosato, the leader of the PD parliamentary party, the Rosatellum represents the most viable compromise among political opponents. Previous electoral laws have been annulled by the Constitutional Court in two separate decisions, resulting in divergent rules for the upper and lower houses. President Sergio Mattarella has urged parliament to establish a new electoral law that treats both houses uniformly ahead of the national elections scheduled by May of the following year. Efforts to align the regulations have previously failed, most recently in June when dissenting deputies employed a secret vote to overturn portions of the proposed law. Although the current legislation aims to standardize the rules across both chambers, polling indicates that it will not provide a definitive mandate for any coalition or party to govern. The proposed election law plans to allocate nearly two-thirds of parliamentary seats proportionally, while the remaining third will be determined through a first-past-the-post voting system for specific candidates. To gain entry into parliament, coalitions must secure 10 percent of the national vote, whereas individual parties only need to achieve 3 percent. Candidates will be selected by the leaders of the parties.

The confidence votes will be held by open ballot starting on Wednesday afternoon, with the final confidence vote to be held on Thursday. The government is forced to resign if it loses such a vote.  A centrist group that is not formally part of the government s majority has said it will provide up to 10 votes to help pass the law if needed. The proposed election law would distribute almost two-thirds of the seats in parliament on a proportional basis, while a third would be decided in a first-past-the-post vote on specific candidates. Coalitions would need to get 10 percent of the national vote to get into parliament, while parties running alone would need only 3 percent. Candidates would be chosen by party chiefs.

text: On Friday, Canada announced it was imposing sanctions on 30 Russian officials linked to the 2009 prison death of Sergei Magnitsky, an anti-corruption attorney who was imprisoned after exposing a significant tax fraud scheme. These sanctions, which include asset freezes and travel bans to Canada, were enacted under a new law that allows the government to penalize individuals deemed responsible for human rights abuses, according to a statement from the foreign ministry. Among those affected is Alexander Bastrykin, the chief investigator in Russia and a close associate of President Vladimir Putin. The U.S. had previously blacklisted him in January 2017 due to Magnitsky’s demise. "This announcement clearly indicates that Canada is committed to holding accountable those who have benefited from substantial corruption or have participated in serious human rights violations," stated Foreign Minister Chrystia Freeland. Last month, Moscow indicated that it would respond if Canada enacted bans under the new legislation. Following this, the Russian embassy in Ottawa condemned the sanctions, labeling them as "absolutely pointless and reprehensible." Canada has consistently criticized Moscow for its annexation of Crimea in Ukraine in 2014 and has coordinated sanctions with other Western countries. In 2012, the United States implemented a law that froze assets belonging to Russian officials and prosecutors allegedly involved in Magnitsky's detention. In response, Russia imposed a ban on Americans adopting Russian children. Canada’s actions also included sanctions against 19 Venezuelan officials and three individuals from South Sudan.

text: The U.S. State Department is set to restart its news briefings during the week commencing March 6, as announced by a spokesperson on Friday. This announcement ends a period of silence under Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, which had led to unease among American diplomats and created uncertainty abroad regarding U.S. stances on critical matters. Traditionally, these briefings have been broadcast and conducted daily, attracting significant attention from both U.S. allies and adversaries who look for insights into America’s responses to major global crises and events. The briefings had been discontinued since President Donald Trump assumed office on January 20, a situation that is unprecedented when compared to the last three transitions between parties, based on records of past briefing transcripts. The last time a televised briefing took place at the State Department was on January 19, the final day of Barack Obama’s presidency. Reporters utilize these question-and-answer sessions to inquire about the subtleties of U.S. foreign policy and the actions taken by diplomats overseas. Mark Toner, the acting spokesperson for the State Department, stated, "The Department will host press briefings beginning the week of March 6." He added, "We continue to be responsive to media queries and breaking news on an ongoing basis." However, Toner did not clarify whether the briefings would occur daily or if they would all be broadcasted. Earlier in the week, he mentioned that arrangements might be made for reporters outside Washington to access the briefings through remote video. Within the Trump administration, leading figures such as Vice President Mike Pence, United Nations Ambassador Nikki Haley, Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly, Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, and Tillerson have occasionally issued conflicting or varying statements compared to Trump regarding issues like U.S. support for the NATO alliance, the two-state solution in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, the administration's relationship with the media, and the involvement of the U.S. military in immigration operations. These mixed messages have prompted inquiries among foreign officials about who genuinely represents the Trump administration and what policies it intends to implement. Furthermore, the lack of communication from the State Department during the chaotic initial month of Trump’s presidency has sparked concerns among both current and former U.S. diplomats regarding the department's diminishing role and its capability to influence U.S. foreign policy.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. State Department will resume news briefings the week of March 6, a spokesman said on Friday, breaking a silence under Secretary of State Rex Tillerson that had caused consternation among American diplomats and contributed to confusion abroad about U.S. positions on key issues. The briefings, which in the past were televised and held daily, are watched closely by U.S. allies and adversaries for signals on American positions on major international crises and developments around the world. But they have been halted ever since President Donald Trump took office on Jan. 20, a move that is unprecedented in at least the last three inter-party presidential transitions, according to online archives of briefing transcripts. The last televised news briefing at the State Department was held on Jan. 19, the last full day of Barack Obama’s presidency. The question-and-answer sessions allow reporters to press spokespeople on the nuances of U.S. foreign policy and the actions of diplomats abroad. “The Department will host press briefings beginning the week of March 6,” said Mark Toner, the State Department’s acting spokesman. “We continue to be responsive to media queries and breaking news on an ongoing basis.” Toner did not say if the briefings would be held every day, or if they would all be televised. In a statement earlier this week, Toner said the briefings might be made available to reporters outside Washington via remote video. Top officials in the Trump administration - including Vice President Mike Pence, United Nations Ambassador Nikki Haley, Homeland Security chief John Kelly, Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, and Tillerson - have at times made conflicting or diverging statements from Trump himself on issues including U.S. support for the NATO alliance, support for the two-state solution to conflict between Israelis and Palestinians, attitudes toward the news media, and the role of the U.S. military in immigration operations. The diverging messages have raised questions in foreign capitals over who actually speaks for the Trump administration and which policies it will pursue. The silence from the State Department during the tumultuous first month of Trump’s presidency has also raised fears among current and former American diplomats that the department is being sidelined and is less able to help shape U.S. foreign policy.

text: On Monday, U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mary Jo White disregarded requests from Senate Republicans to postpone the implementation of new regulations concerning various financial instruments such as derivatives and mutual funds until after the inauguration of President-elect Donald Trump. In correspondence addressed to the leading Republicans of the Senate Banking Committee, Richard Shelby and Mike Crapo from Idaho, White emphasized the necessity for the SEC to demonstrate a “spirit of firm independence” while executing its regulatory responsibilities “without fear or favor.” The letter, dated December 12, which Reuters had access to, was written in response to a previous appeal made by Shelby and Crapo, urging the SEC to halt rulemaking until Trump could evaluate the agency’s agenda. Throughout Congress, Republicans have been advocating for federal agencies to minimize their rulemaking efforts. Trump has committed to eliminating numerous regulations enacted during the Obama administration, including the Dodd-Frank Wall Street reform legislation. White, who is an independent, is expected to resign from her position when Democratic President Barack Obama’s term concludes in January. Last week, the Senate was unable to confirm Obama’s two nominees for vacant commissioner positions at the SEC before its recess, which means that following White's departure next month, only two commissioners will remain at the SEC—one from the Democratic Party and one from the Republican Party. Even prior to her exit, there is a possibility that she may fail to pass the regulations if she cannot secure agreement from a quorum of commissioners. Although Trump has not yet revealed a nominee for SEC chair, several members of his financial regulatory transition team, including former SEC Commissioner Paul Atkins, have expressed strong criticism of many SEC rules and the Dodd-Frank Act overall. In her letter on Monday, White provided Shelby and Crapo with a comprehensive list of all the rules that are currently prepared for a vote. Included in this list are reforms related to derivatives stipulated by Dodd-Frank, such as capital and margin requirements for swap dealers, alongside a more contentious rule that would restrict how mutual funds and exchange-traded funds utilize derivatives to amplify returns. The letter did not specify when the SEC might conduct a vote on these rules. The agency has the option to hold the vote during an open meeting or in a private session. An SEC spokesperson declined to disclose any information regarding the timing. "I am not oblivious to the concerns raised in your letter and have thoroughly contemplated the potential impact, if any, the election should have on the Commission's ongoing work," White articulated. She also noted that she had verified that the SEC “historically has proceeded with its work during comparable post-election periods.” To bolster her stance, White appended footnotes in her letter referencing earlier comments made by Republican SEC Commissioner Mike Piwowar, who is expected to take on the role of acting chair in January, in which he expressed support for finalizing new derivatives regulations. This situation is not unprecedented; the SEC has previously encountered criticism for attempting to finalize rules before a leadership transition at the agency. For instance, in 2005, a federal appeals court ruled in favor of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in a legal dispute with the SEC over controversial regulations that mandated that a majority of mutual fund board directors must be independent. The court instructed the SEC to reconsider the rule’s costs. Following this, then-SEC Chairman William Donaldson promptly organized a meeting, and the SEC re-adopted the rule just one day before his resignation, asserting that the regulation would not impose excessive costs. Subsequently, the rule was overturned again, with the court admonishing the SEC for not adhering to proper rulemaking protocols. Even if White manages to finalize the rules in the upcoming weeks, Congress might have the ability to negate them once Trump assumes office on January 20. By statute, Congress can vote to reverse regulations within a span of 60 legislative days after they become final—an action that could be simpler to achieve under a Republican-led Congress.

text: HONG KONG (Reuters) - An official stated on Wednesday that Hong Kong intends to introduce legislation that would impose penalties on individuals who boo the Chinese national anthem, a decision critics argue undermines the freedoms and autonomy of the city ruled by China. In recent years, some football fans in Hong Kong have expressed their discontent by booing the national anthem during World Cup qualifiers and other matches, reflecting a more recent protest in the United States where football players kneel during the anthem—a practice condemned by U.S. President Donald Trump. On Tuesday, the Asian Football Confederation issued a warning to the Hong Kong Football Association concerning the behavior of fans who booed the Chinese national anthem during a match in October. In mainland China, a law has been enacted that states disrespecting the anthem could lead to imprisonment. While this law is already in effect in China, it has not yet been applied to Hong Kong. Patrick Nip, the Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs in Hong Kong, remarked that the city has a constitutional duty to follow up on the actions taken by China’s largely ceremonial parliament. The law will be incorporated into the annex of Hong Kong's mini-constitution, known as the Basic Law, and will be presented to the city's 70-member legislature. "We will expedite this process," Nip informed lawmakers, adding that there would be a consultation phase involved. Once a British colony, Hong Kong reverted to Chinese sovereignty in 1997 under a framework referred to as "one country, two systems," which guarantees the city a considerable degree of autonomy, including an independent judiciary. Nevertheless, China's increasing involvement in Hong Kong's affairs has escalated tensions, leading to widespread protests such as the 2014 Occupy movement, which paralyzed significant thoroughfares in the city for 79 days in an effort to pressure China into granting full democratic rights. Nip indicated that no definitive choices regarding prison sentences had been made, but the government would refer to existing legislation related to the desecration of the national flag, which has a maximum penalty of three years. Critics contend that this initiative would further diminish Hong Kong's autonomy and is just another example of China's tightening grip. "If a country (China) wasn’t employing totalitarian and autocratic methods to exert pressure, I believe many more residents of Hong Kong would show respect for the national anthem," asserted Dennis Kwok, a member of the Civic Party. In recent times, Hong Kong fans have booed the national anthem at various football events involving the local team, with a forthcoming Asian Cup qualifier against Lebanon posing another potential flashpoint. "Some inappropriate behavior...must be addressed," Nip stated, without providing further details. Chinese officials have worked to foster increased patriotism within Hong Kong, while simultaneously denouncing a movement among democracy advocates to create distance from Beijing by embracing the city’s cultural identity and core values, with some even pushing for independence from China. Recently, incidents of disrespect towards the national anthem have surfaced in Hong Kong, challenging the fundamental principles...and inciting outrage, said Zhang Rongshun, who heads a legislative affairs commission of the National People’s Congress, China’s parliament, as reported by the official Xinhua news agency. "It is both urgent and essential to implement the National Anthem Law in Hong Kong to prevent and address such offenses."
