text: On Thursday, a coalition of over a dozen Democratic state attorneys general aimed to step in to safeguard a crucial element of the Obamacare healthcare legislation - the subsidy payments provided to insurers - which are currently jeopardized in an ongoing lawsuit. The motion to intervene was submitted by 16 attorneys general, spearheaded by California's Attorney General Xavier Becerra and New York's Attorney General Eric Schneiderman, in a case that is now before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. This lawsuit, which originated during the Obama administration, was initiated by the Republican-controlled House of Representatives against the federal government, seeking to terminate the subsidy payments to insurance providers for the individual plans established under the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare. These subsidy payments assist in covering out-of-pocket medical costs for Americans with low incomes. Maryland Attorney General Brian Frosh, who endorsed the motion, remarked, "The stakes are very high. In Maryland, we have more than 400,000 individuals relying on the Affordable Care Act for essential healthcare. It sounds alarming, but it’s true: lives are at stake." President Trump has consistently threatened to stop these payments to insurers, which total approximately $7 billion for the current year, labeling them as a "bailout." In their legal documents, the attorneys general referenced Trump's statements expressing his intention to allow Obamacare to "explode" as part of their justification for seeking to intervene. According to the filing, Trump has made it clear that he perceives health insurance decisions for millions of Americans "as little more than political bargaining chips." The Democratic representatives asserted the urgency of the situation, as state insurance regulators are making significant decisions that will impact their insurance markets for the upcoming year. Several insurance companies, such as Aetna (AET.N) and Humana (HUM.N), have largely withdrawn from the Obamacare exchanges, citing a patient pool that is sicker than anticipated, resulting in higher costs. Insurers have repeatedly urged the Trump administration to ensure funding for the cost-sharing subsidies. Advocates for Obamacare, including the attorneys general, have indicated that the threats to withhold these payments have already caused turmoil in the marketplaces and are contributing factors to the double-digit rate hikes experienced by some healthcare consumers. The attorneys general have emerged as formidable adversaries to the Trump administration. They played a leading role in successfully blocking Trump's executive orders that restricted travel from specific Muslim-majority nations, and they continue to fight against attempts to undermine environmental regulations. Notably, even the attorney general from Kentucky, a state known for its conservative leanings, has joined this court filing, despite the state's Republican governor's commitment to reversing a Medicaid expansion enabled by Obamacare. Back in May 2016, a federal judge ruled in favor of the Republican side in the subsidies lawsuit, determining that the Obama administration lacked explicit congressional approval for the payments. An appeal was filed by the Obama administration before Trump assumed office, leaving the new administration to consider its options for moving forward. Following the November presidential election, the appeals court agreed to suspend the litigation at the request of the Republican lawmakers from the House. There is no guarantee that the court will grant the motion to intervene. Earlier this year, the same court denied a similar motion from Democratic attorneys general who sought to defend the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in a legal dispute that could potentially weaken the agency. Should Congress enact new healthcare legislation to replace Obamacare, the litigation might become irrelevant. This month, the House passed a bill called the American Health Care Act. Recently, the Senate has begun drafting its own version of the bill, but has cautioned that the process may take several months to complete. Moreover, the Trump administration has taken steps in recent months to undermine Obamacare through the use of its regulatory powers.

text: A total of six individuals, comprising five Moroccans and one Spaniard, have been detained by law enforcement in Spain and Morocco for allegedly being part of an Islamist extremist group that practiced mock beheadings, according to the Spanish interior ministry's announcement on Wednesday. This operation represents the first significant enforcement action following a dual Islamist assault in Catalonia during August that resulted in 16 fatalities, with the majority occurring when a van struck pedestrians in Barcelona. The ministry indicated that the militant cell was operating at a highly developed phase. It did not specify the gender of the individuals in custody. Meetings were reportedly conducted in secrecy during the night, where they strategized for extensive attacks, and they engaged in physical drills simulating the act of severing heads. Among those apprehended, five were Moroccan, including one with residency rights in Spain, while one person of Spanish nationality had Moroccan ancestry. One individual was taken into custody in Melilla, a Spanish enclave in North Africa, while the others were arrested in Morocco. Since 2015, Spanish authorities have arrested 199 individuals linked to extremist organizations after elevating the security alert by one level below the highest tier.
source_text: Spain and Morocco arrest six suspected of practicing beheadings. MADRID (Reuters) - Spanish and Moroccan police have arrested five Moroccans and one Spaniard suspected of belonging to an Islamist militant cell that simulated decapitations, the Spanish interior ministry said on Wednesday. The arrests mark the first big raids since a double Islamist attack in Catalonia in August that killed 16 people, most of whom were mown down by a van in Barcelona. The cell was at an advanced stage of activity, the ministry said. It did not say whether those arrested were men or women. The group held secret night meetings at which they planned large-scale attacks, and carried out physical training sessions in which they simulated cutting off victims  heads, the ministry said. Five of the arrested were Moroccan, one with Spanish residence rights. One was Spanish of Moroccan heritage. One was arrested in the Spanish north African enclave of Melilla, and the rest in Morocco. Spanish police have arrested 199 people in the country accused of connections to militant groups since raising the security alert to one notch below the highest level in 2015.

text: A letter was sent on Thursday by three Democratic legislators to the president of Kushner Companies, raising issues regarding concerns that the real estate firm may have capitalized on Jared Kushner's position as an adviser in the White House to draw investments through a federal immigration initiative. Early this year, Jared Kushner, who is the son-in-law of President Donald Trump and one of his chief aides, resigned from his role as the chief executive officer of the family-owned real estate business. Dated Thursday, the nine-page correspondence was directed to Laurent Morali, the president of Kushner Companies, and was authored by Senator Patrick Leahy along with Representatives John Conyers and Zoe Lofgren. They requested clarification about a controversial promotional event in China that was held in May, during which the developer presented investors with an opportunity to obtain U.S. visas through the EB-5 program in exchange for investment in a New Jersey project known as One Journal Square. The lawmakers also inquired what measures Kushner Companies had implemented to guarantee that its affiliates would not take advantage of Jared Kushner's role in the White House when soliciting investors going forward. A report from Reuters dated May 12 was referenced in their letter, highlighting that a Chinese immigration agency promoting the Kushner Companies venture had leveraged Kushner’s connections to the White House to persuade potential investors that the One Journal Square project was a sound investment and that they would receive green cards. Such assurances are against the regulations of the EB-5 program, which offers a U.S. green card to foreign nationals who invest $500,000 or more in development projects located in areas of the United States with low employment rates. Kushner Companies did not immediately respond to inquiries for comments. In May, Kushner Companies had expressed regret over Nicole Kushner Meyer’s mention of her brother, Jared Kushner, while marketing One Journal Square in China. The letter from the trio of Democrats came on the heels of a request from Chuck Grassley, the Republican chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, for an investigation into "potentially fraudulent statements and misrepresentations" by firms promoting investment in One Journal Square. Leahy, Conyers, and Lofgren, who are members of the House or Senate Judiciary Committees, pointed out in their communication that they have collaborated with Republican committee members since 2015 to strengthen the EB-5 program by implementing stricter anti-fraud regulations. The letter also noted that Jared Kushner had previously been actively engaged with organizations that lobbied against these reform initiatives, including one entity that is currently promoting the One Journal Square project. The Democratic lawmakers’ correspondence sought to determine whether Kushner Companies had participated in any lobbying efforts related to reforms of the EB-5 program or if discussions regarding the program had taken place with Kushner since President Trump assumed office in January.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Three Democratic lawmakers sent a letter to the president of Kushner Companies on Thursday seeking information related to concerns that the real estate firm has exploited Jared Kushner’s role as a White House adviser to attract investment through a federal immigration program.  Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump and one of his top advisers, early this year stepped down as chief executive officer of his family’s real estate company. Senator Patrick Leahy and Representatives John Conyers and Zoe Lofgren, in the nine-page letter dated Thursday and sent to Kushner Companies President Laurent Morali, asked for details about the company’s controversial May road show in China, where the developer offered investors a chance to get U.S. visas under the EB-5 program if they put money in a project in New Jersey, One Journal Square. The letter, which was released publicly, also asked Kushner Companies what steps it has taken to ensure its affiliates do not exploit Jared Kushner’s White House role when wooing investors in the future. The lawmakers cited a May 12 Reuters report that a Chinese immigration agency promoting the Kushner Companies project had touted Kushner’s White House connections to assure potential investors that the One Journal Square project would succeed and investors would receive green cards.   Such guarantees are prohibited by the rules of the EB-5 program, which grants foreigners a U.S. green card in exchange for investing $500,000 or more in development projects in low-employment areas of the United States. Kushner Companies did not immediately return calls for comment. Kushner Companies had apologized for Nicole Kushner Meyer’s reference to her brother, Jared Kushner, when pitching One Journal Square in China in May.  The letter by the three Democrats follows a call by the Republican chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Chuck Grassley, last week for a probe into “potentially fraudulent statements and misrepresentations” made by companies promoting investment in the One Journal Square project. Leahy, Conyers, and Lofgren - all members of the House or Senate Judiciary Committees - noted in their letter that they have worked with Republican committee members since 2015 to improve the EB-5 program by enacting tougher anti-fraud measures. Jared Kushner used to be closely involved with groups that lobbied against those reform efforts, according to the letter, including one firm that is marketing the One Journal Square project. The Democratic lawmakers’ letter asked if Kushner Companies had engaged in any lobbying related to EB-5 program reforms or discussed the program with Kushner since Trump took office in January.

text: NEW YORK (Reuters) - President-elect Donald Trump announced on Wednesday that he will begin constructing a wall along the border with Mexico without waiting for negotiations to conclude. "I could hold off for approximately a year and a half until negotiations with Mexico, which will commence right after we take office, are completed, but I prefer not to wait," Trump stated during a press conference. He mentioned that his vice president-elect, Mike Pence, is "spearheading an initiative to secure final approvals through various agencies and Congress for the wall's commencement." Trump further asserted, "In some capacity, Mexico ... will reimburse us."

NEW YORK (Reuters) - U.S. President-elect Donald Trump said on Wednesday he would not wait for negotiations with Mexico to be completed before starting to build a wall along the two countries’ border. “I could wait about a year and a half until we finish our negotiations with Mexico which will start immediately after we get into office, but I don’t want to wait,” Trump said at a news conference. He said his vice president-elect Mike Pence is “leading an effort to get final approvals through various agencies and through Congress for the wall to begin.” “Mexico in some form ... will reimburse us,” Trump added.

source_text: Cowboys, Cardinals link arms amid anthem protests. PHOENIX (Reuters) - Two National Football League teams largely steered clear of a controversy over national anthem protests that have ensnared U.S. President Donald Trump and threatened to damage the game’s popularity, staging a “moment of unity” on Monday instead. The entire Dallas Cowboys team, including owner Jerry Jones, linked arms and knelt on the playing field for a moment before the game, but then stood respectfully as the “Star-Spangled Banner” was performed by singer Jordin Sparks. “We all agreed that our players wanted to make a statement about unity and we wanted to make a statement about equality,” Jones said after his team beat the Arizona Cardinals 28-17.  Jones has previously expressed pride that no players on his team had taken to one knee as the anthem was played and said he was disappointed to see such protests. Cardinals players joined arms as a giant flag was unfurled on the field but did not kneel. “Prior to the National Anthem, the @DallasCowboys and @AZCardinals shared a moment of unity on the field,” the NFL said in a Twitter post that was retweeted by the Cowboys.  Former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick stirred a polarizing national debate in 2016 after refusing to stand during pre-game renditions of the “Star Spangled Banner” to protest against police violence against African-Americans. Kaepernick was not signed by an NFL team this season but several players have made similar gestures. Trump kicked off his battle with the largest-grossing U.S. professional sports league at a rally on Friday, when he said any protesting player was a “son of a bitch” who should be “fired.”Those remarks touched off protests by dozens of NFL players, coaches and even some owners at games on Sunday, along with criticism from many corners of the sports world. “The childishness, the gratuitous fear-mongering and race baiting has become so consistent that we almost expect it, the bar has been lowered so far,” Gregg Popovich, head coach of the San Antonio Spurs basketball team, told reporters.  The head of the U.S. Olympic Committee (USOC) spoke out in support of the protesters at NFL games. “The athletes you see protesting are protesting because they love their country,” USOC Chief Executive Scott Blackmun told reporters in Park City, Utah. The International Olympic Committee’s charter prohibits “demonstrations of political, religious or racial propaganda” at Olympic venues. Not all players joined in Sunday’s protests. Notably, Pittsburgh Steelers lineman Alejandro Villanueva, a U.S. Army veteran, stood alone at the entrance to the stadium for the anthem on Sunday while his teammates waited in the locker room. Villanueva jerseys and other apparel have outsold those of all other players in the past 24 hours, said a spokesman for online retailer Fanatics, which operates NFLShop.com. Villanueva’s teammate, Ben Roethlisberger, said on Monday he regretted having missed the anthem. “I was unable to sleep last night,” Roethlisberger said in a statement. “I personally don’t believe the Anthem is ever the time to make any type of protest.”      Trump kept up his verbal battle with the players on Monday, saying on Twitter that his objection to the protests had nothing to do with race but was “about respect for our Country, Flag and National Anthem. NFL must respect this!” The president, who has called for a boycott of NFL games, also tweeted: “Tremendous backlash against the NFL and its players for disrespect of our Country.” The demonstrations have become a thorny issue for the league, which has sought to support players’ rights to protest while trying to keep politics from overshadowing games. CBS Corp said overall viewership of games it broadcast on Sunday was up 4 percent from last year and 1 percent from last week. NBC, owned by Comcast Corp, said viewership for its Sunday night game was down compared with the week before. “The protest has nothing to do with respecting the flag. I agree with their message but not doing it during the anthem,” U.S. Air Force veteran Jimmy Phillips, 43, said before Monday’s game in Phoenix. Nike Inc said it supported athletes who had joined the protests. “Nike supports athletes and their right to freedom of expression on issues that are of great importance to our society,” Nike said in a statement. The debate attracted intense attention online, with the hashtag “#TakeAKnee” racking up 2.4 million mentions and “#TakeTheKnee” used 1.2 million times by Monday, while “#BoycottNFL” had 101,500 mentions. Prominent players continued to speak out against Trump on Monday.     New England Patriots quarterback Tom Brady, who has said he considers Trump a friend, said on Monday he disagreed with the president’s remarks. “I thought it was just divisive,” Brady told Boston’s WEEI radio. At the same time as he berated the NFL, Trump praised car-racing league NASCAR, which saw no protests at its Sunday race in New Hampshire. text: BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Following the violent clashes during the independence referendum in Catalonia, the European Union's executive branch has urged Spain to engage in discussions with Catalan separatist groups on Monday. The EU condemned the violence but also emphasized the importance of unity. The European Commission, cautiously addressing a sensitive issue that poses risks for both Spain's stability and the eurozone, released a measured statement. It expressed confidence in Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy's capability to navigate this internal challenge while simultaneously advocating for dialogue and reminding Madrid of the necessity to uphold the basic rights of citizens. The Commission's statement, delivered by chief spokesman Margaritis Schinas, called for all parties involved to quickly shift from confrontation to constructive dialogue, asserting that violence should never be a political tool. This appeal came just as Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont sought EU mediation. When reporters pressed him for specifics, Schinas refrained from directly condemning the actions of the Spanish police, although it was their behavior at the voting stations on Sunday that shocked many in Europe and led to increased public pressure, prompting other nations, including Germany and France, to call for enhanced dialogue. Later on Monday, Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker spoke with Rajoy after having communicated over the weekend; however, the EU spokesperson did not confirm whether the Union would take on a mediating role, which would be an unusual move for Brussels concerning one of its own member countries. According to aides, Juncker clarified the Commission's stance while also adopting a receptive approach. Donald Tusk, who previously served as Poland's prime minister and currently chairs the summits of EU national leaders, stated after his conversation with Rajoy that he understood the Spanish premier's constitutional reasoning. Nonetheless, he urged Rajoy to seek avenues to avert further escalation and the use of force. The Commission's statement also aligned with Madrid's position that the referendum, which Catalan officials claimed produced a significant outcome favoring independence, was unconstitutional under Spain's laws. Historically, Brussels has not provided support to separatist movements within the European Union, whether they be from Catalonia, Scotland, Flanders, or other regions. The statement conveyed that these are times for unity and stability rather than division and fragmentation. It also indicated that any region seeking to break away would need to exit the EU and reapply for membership, with a potential re-entry dependent on an amicable separation. This situation contrasts with Scotland, which conducted a referendum sanctioned by London in 2014, unlike Catalonia, where Spain's Constitutional Court has ruled that secession is prohibited by the 1978 constitution. Despite the hesitance of many Europeans to publicly engage in the dispute, there has been an increasing concern in Brussels regarding the manner in which the conservative administration in Madrid has dealt with the situation, reviving sentiments linked to the civil war and dictatorship of the 20th century. Images of heavily armored Spanish police striking women on the ground left Europe in shock on Sunday, with only a few governments, including Scotland, Slovenia, which emerged from the violent disintegration of Yugoslavia, and Belgium, a nation that has avoided a definitive split between French and Dutch speakers through multiple devolution rounds, speaking out. On Monday, Germany joined the calls for dialogue, cautioning against a potential cycle of escalation. The BDI industrial federation in Germany warned that the separation of the highly industrialized region from Spain would have severe repercussions for both parties.

BRUSSELS (Reuters) - The EU executive urged Spain to talk to Catalan separatists on Monday, condemning violence but also calling for unity, a day after Spanish police beat people trying to vote in an independence referendum in Catalonia. Edging into a minefield it has tried hard to avoid, despite a danger for stability in Spain and the euro zone, the European Commission issued a cautiously balanced statement. It voiced trust in Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy s ability to manage this  internal matter , but also called for dialogue and reminded Madrid of a need to respect citizens  basic rights.  We call on all relevant players to now move very swiftly from confrontation to dialogue. Violence can never be an instrument in politics,  the Commission said in a statement read out by chief spokesman Margaritis Schinas, just before Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont asked for EU mediation. Pressed by reporters, Schinas declined to say specifically that the EU was condemning Spanish police tactics, though it was their actions at polling stations on Sunday which mostly shocked fellow Europeans and generated public pressure that saw other governments including Germany and France call for more dialogue. Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker spoke to Rajoy later on Monday after being in contact over the weekend, though the EU spokesman declined to say whether the Union would mediate, an unusual step for Brussels to take within one of the bloc s own member states. Aides said Juncker spelled out the Commission position and was also  in a listening mode . Donald Tusk, the former Polish prime minister who chairs summits of EU national leaders, said after his own conversation with Rajoy that he shared the Spanish premier s constitutional arguments but also appealed to him to find ways to prevent a further escalation and the use of force. The Commission statement also supported Madrid s line that the vote, which Catalan leaders said recorded a huge result for independence, was  not legal  under Spain s constitution. Brussels has in the past given little or no encouragement to separatist movements inside the European Union, whether those of the Catalans, Scots, Flemings or others.  These are times for unity and stability, not divisiveness and fragmentation,  it said. Any breakaway state would have to leave the EU and re-apply to join, the statement also noted. Even that could only happen if the split were amicable. This distinguishes Scotland, which held a referendum agreed with London in 2014, from Catalonia, where Spain s Constitutional Court has said the 1978 constitution forbids secession. For all the reluctance of other Europeans to be drawn into the dispute in public, there has been growing unease in Brussels about the way the conservative government in Madrid has handled the confrontation with Barcelona, reviving emotions rooted in 20th-century civil war and dictatorship. As pictures of heavily armoured Spanish police clubbing women on the ground stunned Europe on Sunday, the few governments that spoke out included those of Scotland, Slovenia, which emerged from the bloody collapse of Yugoslavia, and Belgium, where repeated rounds of devolution have averted a final split between French- and Dutch-speakers. On Monday, Berlin joined the calls for dialogue, warning against a  spiral of escalation . Germany s BDI industrial federation warned that splitting the highly industrialised region from Spain would be very damaging for both sides.

text: On Monday, Israel sanctioned the construction of 31 homes for settlers in Hebron, situated in the West Bank, according to a spokesperson. This marks the first such authorization in the Israeli-occupied territory in approximately 15 years. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is experiencing heightened demands for the expansion of settlements from the right-wing members of his coalition, although the actual construction is not expected to begin immediately due to the necessary bureaucratic procedures that must be followed. Recently, his administration has made several announcements regarding the development of settlements, which has sparked outrage among Palestinians who aspire for a state on land that Israel seized during the 1967 conflict; however, these actions have not provoked significant criticism from the United States under President Donald Trump. Nonetheless, proponents of settlement expansion argue that even though numerous plans for thousands of homes for settlers in the West Bank have been revealed, only a small percentage may eventually be realized. Hebron, the largest Palestinian urban center in the occupied West Bank, has around 216,000 residents. Approximately 1,000 Israeli settlers inhabit the center of the city, which has long been a site of religious tensions between Jews and Muslims. The organization Peace Now, which opposes settlement activity, outlined the proposed plans in the section of Hebron where settlers reside, and its website displayed an illustration of what the anticipated four-story, stone-clad residential building would resemble. They noted that the last construction of settler homes in this locality occurred in 2002. Hadar Horen, a representative for the Israeli organization managing civil affairs in the West Bank, was unable to verify the information released by Peace Now and stated that the decision from the planning committee would be made public later.

JERUSALEM (Reuters) - Israel on Monday approved building plans for 31 settler homes in Hebron in the West Bank, a spokeswoman said, a first such move in the Israeli-occupied area for some 15 years. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has felt increased pressure for settlement expansion from the rightist flank of his coalition, though construction is not imminent as a bureaucratic process must still run its course. His government has made numerous announcements of settlement building recently, angering Palestinians seeking a state on land Israel captured in a 1967 war but no longer eliciting serious U.S. criticism with President Donald Trump in the White House. Still, settlement advocates say that despite a string of announcements for construction of thousands of settler homes in the West Bank, only a fraction might be built eventually. Hebron is the largest Palestinian city in the occupied West Bank with a population of some 216,000. About 1,000 Israeli settlers live in the heart of the city, which for decades has been a focus of religious friction between Muslims and Jews. Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now detailed the project s plans in an area of Hebron where the settlers live and its web site showed a graphic of what the prospective four-storey, stone-clad apartment block would look like. It said that the last time settler homes were built in this area was in 2002. Hadar Horen, a spokeswoman for the Israeli body that runs civilian affairs in the West Bank, could not confirm the details issued by Peace Now and said the planning committee decision would be published later.

text: The revolutionary group known as FARC in Colombia is making a significant shift by launching its political party during a conference that commenced on Sunday. This marks a pivotal transition for the organization, which has spent over five decades engaged in conflict, as it moves toward becoming a civilian entity and presents its policies to a doubtful electorate. The assembly, which will last for six days in Bogota, includes FARC members who have surrendered upwards of 8,000 weapons to the United Nations as part of their demobilization process. This gathering is anticipated to culminate on Friday with the announcement of a platform that will guide their electoral campaign in the upcoming elections next year. Following the 2016 peace agreement with the government, which aimed to conclude a war responsible for the deaths of over 220,000 individuals, the majority of the fighters in the group formally recognized as the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia were granted amnesty, enabling them to enter the political arena. It remains uncertain whether the FARC will receive support from the Colombian populace, many of whom harbor animosity towards the group. The FARC's somewhat antiquated Marxist rhetoric is perceived by many as a return to its origins from 1964, yet its proposals for reforming complex property laws may resonate with rural constituents who face difficulties as subsistence farmers. The peace agreement, which was initially rejected by a narrow margin of less than 1 percent in a referendum before being revised and enacted, grants the FARC’s political party ten automatic congressional seats until 2026, although the organization may seek to contest additional seats. In a scene that would have seemed impossible only a few years ago, FARC representatives arrived in the capital via bus, accompanied by police on motorcycles. "From this moment, we will evolve into a new, purely political entity that will operate through legal channels," stated FARC leader Rodrigo Londono, known by his alias Timochenko, addressing hundreds of participants at the event venue in Bogota. "Numerous challenges and obstacles lie ahead of us," Londono remarked. "Nothing comes easily in politics." He emphasized that improvements for rural areas would continue to be a priority for the party. Many participants donned conference t-shirts bearing the slogan "A new party for a new country" and carried branded tote bags. A painting depicting figures of historical significance, including Cuban revolutionary leaders Fidel Castro and Ernesto Che Guevara, the late Venezuelan president Hugo Chavez, and Jesus Christ, was showcased. The party will initially retain the title Revolutionary Alternative Force of Colombia, maintaining the FARC initials in Spanish. Legislative and presidential elections are scheduled for 2018, though it is yet unclear in which contests the FARC will field candidates. Catalina Jimenez, a political science professor at Externado University, commented, "I believe the FARC will aim for regional consolidation, utilizing their presence and influence in specific provinces." "At a national level, however, they require a substantial number of votes, which they do not yet possess." The FARC has expressed openness to forming coalitions, as stated by the group this week. Leftist parties have historically faced challenges in conservative-leaning Colombia, often fractured by internal conflicts, despite achieving some successes in urban areas. The numerous corruption scandals are likely to dominate the discourse among the crowded pool of candidates in the 2018 presidential race. Campaigns will probably concentrate on proposals aimed at enhancing the daily lives of Colombians, many of whom express urgent needs for improved security, public education, and healthcare services. The FARC has asserted that the government led by President Juan Manuel Santos, which allocates a regulated amount of funding to each political party, ought to contribute to the conference costs, given that the rebels have surrendered their assets as reparations for war victims. Nevertheless, despite the peace agreement being a cornerstone of Santos' legacy, skepticism surrounds the authenticity of the FARC's reported $324 million asset list, as the government announced the formation of a commission this week to ensure that the FARC has included all potential earnings from extortion, ransoms, and drug trafficking, insisting that the group adhere to the same regulations as any other political party.

Whether the rebels will get backing from Colombians, many of whom revile them, remains to be seen. The FARC s often old-fashioned Marxist rhetoric strikes many as a throwback to their 1964 founding, but proposals for reforms to complicated property laws may get traction with rural voters who struggle as subsistence farmers. At a national level, they need a large amount of votes they still don t have.  The FARC is open to coalitions, the group said this week. Fractured by infighting, leftist parties have long struggled in conservative-leaning Colombia, despite some success in winning urban positions. Widespread corruption scandals will probably be a top issue for the crowded field of 2018 presidential candidates. text: On Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron declared that he would urge European leaders to assist in the evacuation of Africans facing peril in Libya. This announcement follows a global outcry triggered by reports suggesting that African migrants are being sold in the region. Macron stated during an address in Burkina Faso, "I will suggest that Africa and Europe unite to aid those trapped in Libya by providing significant support for the evacuation of individuals in peril," but he did not provide additional specifics.
source_text: Macron touts European initiative to evacuate Africans trapped in Libya. OUAGADOUGOU (Reuters) - French President Emmanuel Macron said on Tuesday he would ask European leaders to help evacuate Africans in danger in Africa after reports appearing to show African migrants being traded there sparked an international outcry.  I will propose that Africa and Europe come to the rescue of the people trapped in Libya, by bringing massive support to the evacuation of people in danger,  Macron said in a speech in Burkina Faso without giving further details.

text: At a confirmation hearing on Tuesday, Democrats expressed strong concerns regarding billionaire Betsy DeVos’ qualifications for the role of U.S. Education Secretary. This scrutiny raises questions about whether President-elect Donald Trump’s nominee will secure approval from the Senate. The choice of DeVos, who is set to lead an agency responsible for overseeing educational policy for both young children and universities, as well as managing a $1 trillion college financial aid program, has sparked outrage among Democrats. They argue that the Michigan Republican's agenda poses a threat to public education. A significant constituency for the Democratic party, teachers unions, have voiced their opposition to DeVos, who has made her fortune as a philanthropist and investor. Independent Senator Bernie Sanders from Vermont, who recently campaigned for the Democratic presidential nomination, posed a pointed question: "Do you think if you were not a multi-billionaire, if your family had not made hundreds of millions of dollars in contributions to the Republican party, that you would be sitting here today?" Over recent days, Democratic Senators have articulated their dissent through letters, speeches, and notably during the hearing itself. The Education Committee is expected to vote next Tuesday in an executive session to advance her nomination to the full Senate. Following that, Democrats may seek to obstruct the nomination on the Senate floor. Since nominations, barring those for the Supreme Court, require only a simple majority, a filibuster will not be an option, necessitating that Democrats persuade some Republicans to oppose the nomination. Former Senator Joe Lieberman, who was the Democratic vice presidential nominee in 2000, provided a complimentary introduction for DeVos during the hearing. However, her critics from within the party had varied responses. Senator Al Franken from Minnesota expressed astonishment that DeVos was not aware of a significant debate in education regarding the assessment of student achievement by either proficiency or growth. Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut was troubled by DeVos’ failure to denounce the presence of firearms in schools. Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren, a proponent of stringent financial regulations, inquired whether DeVos or her children had attended public schools, used student loans, or accessed federal financial aid known as Pell grants. Warren concluded, "You have no experience with financial aid," when DeVos answered "no." Many attendees were disappointed when DeVos refrained from committing to uphold regulations concerning sexual assault, for-profit colleges, and equitable access for students with disabilities, merely stating that she would evaluate the existing policies. Generally, the Democratic Senators probed how DeVos plans to handle her investments and companies related to the education sector, including an online charter school, while serving as a key public figure in this domain. They persistently questioned her intentions regarding the potential redirection of funds to charter schools, which operate autonomously from school districts and are often managed by corporate entities, as well as her stance on the possible detriment to public schools. Washington Senator Patty Murray, the senior Democrat on the committee, articulated her concerns, saying, "I have major concerns with how you have spent your career and fortune fighting to privatize public education and gut investments in public schools." In response, DeVos attempted to allay their concerns, asserting that she endorses taxpayer-funded education. She also claimed her commitment to offering parents choices regarding the schools their children attend, treating all students fairly, and respecting the educational decisions made by states. The hearing, which had been postponed from the previous week due to missing financial disclosures, commenced at 5 p.m. (EST). Committee Chairman Lamar Alexander permitted each member only five minutes for inquiries. Democrats protested, arguing that due to DeVos not having completed necessary ethics documentation, they lack critical information and require additional time. source_text: Democrats blast Trump's pick for Education Secretary.  (Corrects in 6th paragraph to clarify rules) By Lisa Lambert WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Democrats sliced holes in billionaire Betsy DeVos’ credentials to be the next U.S. Education Secretary at a confirmation hearing on Tuesday, raising doubts whether President-elect Donald Trump’s pick will win approval in the full Senate. The nomination of DeVos to head an agency that sets policy for younger children and universities and also administers a college financial aid program of $1 trillion has outraged Democrats who believe the Michigan Republican wants to dismantle public education.  Teachers unions, a major constituency for the party, roundly oppose DeVos, a philanthropist and investor. “Do you think if you were not a multi-billionaire, if your family had not made hundreds of millions of dollars in contributions to the Republican party, that you would be sitting here today?” asked Independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who recently ran to be the Democrats’ presidential nominee.  Democratic Senators have made their opposition clear in recent days in letters, speeches and most notably at the hearing.  Next Tuesday, the Education Committee will likely approve sending her name to the full chamber when it votes in an executive session next Tuesday. Then, Democrats could attempt to block the nomination on the Senate floor. Because nominations other than those for the Supreme Court only require a simple majority vote, they will not be able to use a filibuster and would have to convince Republicans to join them in voting against the nomination. Former Senator Joe Lieberman, Democrats’ candidate for vice president in 2000, gave DeVos a laudatory introduction at the hearing, but other party members were wide-ranging in their  criticism. Minnesota’s Al Franken expressed surprise DeVos was unfamiliar with a hot education debate over measuring student achievement by proficiency or by growth. Connecticut’s Chris Murphy was dismayed when DeVos did not condemn guns in schools.  Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, an advocate of tough financial regulation, asked whether DeVos or her children had attended public schools, borrowed student loans or received federal financial help known as Pell grants. “You have no experience with financial aid,” Warren summed up when DeVos answered “no.” Many were dismayed DeVos would not pledge to carry out rules on sexual assault, for-profit colleges and fair access for students with disabilities, only saying she would review the policies.  Generally, Democrats pressed on how DeVos will manage her investments and companies in the education sector, including an on-line charter school, while serving as the most powerful public figure in the area.  They also asked repeatedly if she intended to divert money to charter schools that operate independently of school districts and are frequently run by corporations and if she would undermine public schools. “I have major concerns with how you have spent your career and fortune fighting to privatize public education and gut investments in public schools,” said Washington’s Patty Murray, the committee’s senior Democrat. DeVos scrambled to reassure them she supports taxpayer-backed education. She also said she will work to give parents choices in the schools their children attend, treat all students equally and respect states’ decisions on education. The hearing, which was delayed from last week over missing financial disclosures, began at 5 p.m. (EST). Committee Chairman Lamar Alexander only allotted each member five minutes for questions. Democrats called foul, saying that because DeVos has not finished requisite ethics paperwork they are in the dark on issues and need more time. Alexander said the Office of Government Ethics will produce by Friday a letter outlining resolutions for her potential conflicts of interest. Committee Republicans universally backed DeVos, applauding her support of vouchers that families may use to pay for private education and of charter schools.  They praised her history with The Potter’s House, which provides “Christ-centered” education, and spoke of her dedication to literacy.

text: On Wednesday, the U.S. House of Representatives approved a measure to allocate $622.1 million toward efforts to mitigate the Zika virus outbreak. This amount falls significantly short of the $1.9 billion requested by President Barack Obama and is also less than what the Senate had proposed. The House, under Republican control, voted 241 to 184, with the majority of members voting along party lines, setting the stage for a potential clash with both the Senate, which has a Republican majority, and the Democratic administration led by Obama. The White House has indicated it may veto the House's version, labeling it as "woefully inadequate." Meanwhile, the Senate is poised to approve a bill providing $1.1 billion to combat the Zika virus, which is transmitted by mosquitoes and has been associated with birth defects. In contrast to the Senate's approach, the House legislation stipulates that the $622.1 million must be matched by cuts in other areas of spending. Many conservative Republicans in the House are unwilling to support additional funding for Zika that would increase federal deficits, whereas some Senate Republicans and Democrats advocate for treating the situation as an emergency that does not require offsetting cuts. Advocates for the House plan contend that, when combined with the $589 million that the Obama administration has already redirected from unutilized Ebola funds, it will be sufficient to address needs until September 30, the conclusion of the fiscal year. How long it will take for the House and Senate to reconcile their respective proposals remains uncertain. Health officials in the U.S. have determined that Zika infections in expectant mothers can lead to microcephaly, a serious birth defect characterized by an unusually small head, potentially resulting in severe developmental issues in infants. The World Health Organization has emphasized that there is substantial scientific agreement indicating that Zika may also lead to Guillain-Barre syndrome, a rare condition causing temporary paralysis in adults. Last year, Brazil reported a surge in microcephaly cases, and the virus has been quickly spreading across the Americas, with fresh cases emerging in warmer regions of southern states, including Florida. The Obama administration asserts that emergency funding is essential for local and state governments to eliminate the mosquitoes transmitting the virus and to advance vaccine development.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill on Wednesday to provide $622.1 million to control the spread of the Zika virus, far below President Barack Obama’s request and lower than Senate legislation. The bill passed the Republican-controlled House 241 to 184, largely along party lines, and sets up a confrontation with both the Republican-majority Senate and the Democratic Obama administration.  The White House has threatened to veto the House bill, saying it was “woefully inadequate.” The Obama administration has requested $1.9 billion. On Tuesday, the Senate cleared the way for expected approval by the chamber on Thursday of $1.1 billion to fight the mosquito-borne Zika virus, which has been linked to birth defects. Unlike the Senate legislation, the House bill requires that the $622.1 million be fully offset with spending cuts elsewhere. Many conservative Republicans in the House refuse to approve Zika funds that would add to federal budget deficits, while Democrats and some Senate Republicans favor treating the problem as an emergency that would not have to be financed with spending cuts. House Republicans argue their bill, when coupled with $589 million the Obama administration already shifted to Zika from unused funds to battle Ebola, would provide enough money through Sept. 30, the end of this fiscal year. It was unclear how long it might take the Senate and House to work out their differences once they pass their respective bills. U.S. health officials have concluded that Zika infections in pregnant women can cause microcephaly, a birth defect marked by small head size that can lead to severe developmental problems in babies. The World Health Organization has said there is strong scientific consensus that Zika can also cause Guillain-Barre, a rare neurological syndrome that causes temporary paralysis in adults. Last year, Brazil began detecting an increase in microcephaly, and the virus has been spreading rapidly in the Americas, with new cases now being reported in warm climates in southern U.S. states including Florida. text: A significant ruling from Colombia's constitutional court confirmed on Tuesday that the special justice tribunals established in a peace agreement with the Marxist FARC rebels are in accordance with the constitution, just before a congressional vote on the matter. Most provisions set forth in the 2016 peace deal regarding these special courts were upheld by the court, which will impose alternative penalties, such as landmine removal, on ex-guerrilla leaders from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) found guilty of war crimes. Currently, Congress is engaged in discussions concerning a law that will endorse these tribunals. Committees in both the upper and lower legislative chambers have expressed support for the bill, which is anticipated to be presented for voting on the floor later this week. Following the court's ruling, President Juan Manuel Santos appeared on television, urging Congress to expedite the passage of the legislation. He stated that guerrilla leaders who are now involved in politics through the FARC's newly formed political party must adhere to the court's sentences, while also acknowledging that many Colombians hold a deep-seated animosity towards the group. Santos emphasized that it is ultimately the voters of Colombia who will determine whether they accept or reject the proposals and ideas presented by the FARC. "It is undoubtedly preferable for the FARC to deliver speeches rather than engage in violence," Santos remarked. Reports from local media indicated that the court implemented various changes to the law, which could permit the extradition of former rebels for offenses committed after the conclusion of the peace process, and that former guerrillas elected to public office might forfeit their positions if they do not comply with the tribunal's procedures.
source_text: Colombia court approves peace tribunals ahead of congressional vote. BOGOTA (Reuters) - Colombia s constitutional court said in a ruling late on Tuesday that special justice tribunals outlined in a peace deal between the government and the Marxist FARC rebels are constitutional, ahead of a congressional vote on the subject. The court upheld most of the provisions agreed in the 2016 peace accord for the special courts, which will mete out alternative sentences like landmine removal for ex-guerrilla leaders from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) who are convicted of war crimes. Congress is holding debates on a law which would approve the tribunals. The bill has been backed by committees in both the upper and lower houses and is expected to be put to floor votes this week. President Juan Manuel Santos, speaking on television after the court s decision, urged congress to pass the law as quickly as possible. Guerrilla leaders participating in politics as part of the FARC s new political party will still have to comply with sentences from the court, he said, while Colombians, many of whom despise the group, must accept that the deal allows them to run for office.  Colombians, with our votes, will decide if we accept their ideas and proposals or if we reject them. Without a doubt it is better to have the FARC giving speeches than shooting bullets,  Santos said.  The court made several modifications to the law, local media reported, opening the possibility that ex-rebels could be extradited for crimes committed after the peace process ends and that former guerrillas elected to public office could lose their seats if they fail to comply with the tribunal process.

text: On Tuesday, U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry expressed significant concerns regarding the rise of authoritarian populism, and he subtly criticized Donald Trump’s extensive use of Twitter, suggesting it allows the president-elect to evade accountability. In his most direct comments about Trump since the presidential election on November 8, Kerry implied that Trump's Cabinet nominees were receiving leniency from Congress for not presenting tax returns and other necessary documentation prior to their Senate confirmation hearings. "Every country in the world better ... start worrying about authoritarian populism and the absence of substance in our dialogue," Kerry remarked during a forum in Washington. He added, "If policies are going to be made in 140 characters on Twitter, and every reasonable measurement of accountability is being bypassed, and people don’t care about it, we have a problem." Kerry pointed out that issues like climate change were largely overlooked during the campaign between Trump and Hillary Clinton, the Democratic nominee. He drew a comparison between his own vetting experience for the position of secretary of state and the lack of scrutiny that Trump’s Cabinet nominees seem to be facing ahead of their confirmation hearings. In December, Bob Corker, the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, stated that the committee had not asked Rex Tillerson, Trump’s pick for secretary of state, to provide his tax returns, which Corker noted followed established precedent. Tillerson, who previously served as chairman and CEO of ExxonMobil Corp (XOM.N), has not submitted his tax returns; however, his financial disclosure forms and ethics agreement have been made available to the public. Kerry, who was a senator and the Democratic presidential nominee in 2004 before assuming the role of Secretary of State under President Barack Obama in 2013, remarked, "It is quite amazing when you think the hoops I had to jump through with respect to papers submitted, documentation submitted and tax returns. ... Suddenly that’s not as important." When questioned about whether he thought Trump’s nominees were being given a "free pass," Kerry laughed and declined to answer directly. Walter Shaub, the director of the federal Office of Government Ethics, expressed in a letter to senators last week his "great concern" regarding the confirmation schedule for Trump nominees who had not completed the ethics review process, stating it would be "cause for alarm if the Senate were to go forward with hearings on nominees whose reports OGE has not certified." With only 10 days remaining before Trump assumes office, Kerry remarked that there had been limited high-level interactions between officials at the State Department and Trump’s transition team. At a forum hosted by the nonpartisan U.S. Institute of Peace, he stated, "It’s going pretty smoothly because there’s not an enormous amount of it." He continued, "There are some people who have been in the building for a period of time, but you know quite candidly, I think there has not been a lot of high-level exchange at this point in time." Kerry noted that he had not yet had a meeting with Tillerson but anticipated that it would happen soon. They had a phone conversation last month, according to the State Department. A spokesperson for the Trump transition team did not provide a comment regarding Kerry’s statements. Tillerson’s confirmation hearing in the Senate is set for Wednesday, and it is expected to attract significant attention, particularly due to concerns surrounding his connections with Russia during his tenure at ExxonMobil. Trump has advocated for improved relations with Russia, while several Republican lawmakers are urging a tougher response to what American intelligence agencies have determined to be Russian interference in the presidential election.

text: In Bali, Indonesia, authorities have detained three foreigners - an Australian, an American, and a Malaysian - for alleged drug offenses, highlighting the strict narcotics laws enforced in the country. The men, who were apprehended in different incidents, were shown to the press during a briefing, wearing orange prison uniforms, their identities obscured by balaclavas, while armed police officers stood beside them. It remains uncertain if any of the individuals, referred to only by their initials, could face capital punishment upon conviction. According to the customs office, the Australian was found with methamphetamine and ecstasy concealed in a plastic bottle and another container in his luggage after arriving on a flight from Bangkok on a Monday. Himawan Indrajono, the chief of Bali Airport customs, stated, "Based on the results of the inspection, our officers found five packages containing clear crystals weighing 19.97 grams and 14 tablets weighing a total of 6.22 grams." The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade in Australia indicated it is providing consular support to the detained Australian citizen, but they opted not to elaborate further on the situation. Meanwhile, the American was taken into custody at a Bali post office on November 30 after authorities discovered a package sent from the United States containing 336.6 grams of e-cigarette liquid infused with THC, the active component in cannabis. The Malaysian individual was apprehended earlier on November 8 after being discovered with 3.03 grams of leaves suspected to be marijuana and 0.65 grams of a white powder believed to be narcotics, as reported by Indrajono. In Indonesia, possession of even small quantities of drugs can lead to significant prison sentences, while larger quantities may result in the death penalty. The execution by firing squad of two Australians in 2015, alongside six other drug offenders from various nations, strained diplomatic ties between Jakarta and Canberra. Indonesia claims to be facing a drug epidemic, with approximately 6.4 million drug users among its population of 250 million, justifying the need for severe penalties to tackle the issue. President Joko Widodo has advocated for a relentless campaign against narcotics and instructed law enforcement to shoot drug traffickers if they resist arrest. This stance mirrors the hardline approach taken by Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte, who has initiated an anti-drug campaign resulting in thousands of fatalities since mid-2016.
source_text: Australian, American, Malaysian arrested in Indonesia's Bali for drugs. DENPASAR, Indonesia (Reuters) - Indonesian police have arrested an Australian, an American and a Malaysian on the holiday island of Bali for drugs offences, the latest foreigners to run afoul of some of the world s strictest laws against narcotics. The three men, who were arrested in separate cases, appeared before the media at a briefing, dressed in orange prison garb, their faces concealed by balaclava, with armed police officers standing guard. It was not immediately clear if any of the three, who were identified only by their initials, would face the death penalty if convicted. Authorities found methamphetamine and the party drug ecstasy hidden in a plastic bottle and another container in the luggage of the Australian after he arrived on a flight from Bangkok on Monday, the customs office said.  Based on the results of the inspection, our officers found five packages containing clear crystals weighing 19.97 grams and 14 tablets weighing a total of 6.22 grams,  Bali Airport customs office chief Himawan Indrajono said in the statement. Australia s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it was  providing consular assistance to an Australian man detained in Bali  in response to emailed questions on the arrest. It declined to comment further.  The U.S. citizen was arrested at a Bali post office on Nov. 30 in connection with a package sent from the United States containing 336.6 grams of e-cigarette liquid containing THC, or tetrahydrocannabinol, the active ingredient in cannabis. The Malaysian was arrested on Nov. 8 after being found with 3.03 grams of leaves thought to be marijuana and 0.65 grams of a white powder suspected to be narcotics, Idrajono said. Possession of small amounts of drugs can incur lengthy jail sentences in Indonesia and larger amounts can result in a death sentence. The execution by firing squad of two Australians in 2015, along with six other drug convicts from several other countries, strained relations between Jakarta and Canberra. Indonesia says it is facing a drug crisis with an estimated  6.4 million drug users in the country of 250 million people, and needs to impose tough punishments to contained the problem. President Joko Widodo has called for a  merciless  crackdown on narcotics, and told law enforcers to shoot drug traffickers if they resisted arrest. That echoes a tough stand taken by Philippine leader Rodrigo Duterte who has ordered a war against drugs in which several thousand people have been killed since mid-2016.

text: BEIJING (Reuters) - The largely symbolic parliament of China is deliberating on implementing prison sentences of up to three years for individuals who show disrespect towards the national flag or anthem in public spaces, as reported by state media on Tuesday. Since Xi Jinping assumed the presidency in 2013, he has introduced new laws aimed at fortifying China against both internal and external threats while overseeing an extensive crackdown on free speech and dissent. A recent law, passed in September, imposes a maximum of 15 days in police custody for those who ridicule the national anthem, March of the Volunteers, which applies to the Chinese regions of Hong Kong and Macau as well. According to Xinhua, the parliament is currently considering an amendment to the Criminal Law of China that would establish criminal consequences for showing disrespect toward the national anthem, including willfully altering the lyrics or melody. The proposed stricter penalties would also extend to acts that desecrate the national flag or emblem, such as burning, defacing, or trampling it publicly, a violation that previously carried a penalty of up to 15 days in detention. A draft amendment has been presented for examination at a bi-monthly session of the parliament's standing committee, which commenced on Monday. Those found guilty of these offenses could face sentences of up to three years in prison, as indicated in the draft. The timeline for the amendment's approval remains unclear, but it may be finalized by the end of the week, coinciding with the conclusion of the current session of the parliament's standing committee. Furthermore, the National Anthem Law, which took effect on October 1, is expected to be included in an annex to Hong Kong's Basic Law, or mini constitution, as reported by Xinhua, although it remains uncertain whether this will entail the introduction of three-year prison terms. The implementation of the national anthem law has raised concerns in Hong Kong, where residents are increasingly anxious about perceived encroachments on the city’s autonomy. This anxiety has grown in the wake of events such as the mysterious disappearances of booksellers who later appeared in custody on the mainland. In an incident from 2015, football fans in Hong Kong were fined by FIFA after booing the Chinese anthem during a World Cup qualifying match. Recent years have seen multiple instances of national anthem disrespect in Hong Kong, which have provoked challenges to the core principle of one country, two systems, along with social morality, inciting outrage among many in China, including a majority of Hong Kong residents. Zhang Rongshun, deputy head of the Legislative Affairs Commission of the parliament, stated that it is critical and urgent to enforce the national anthem law in Hong Kong to prevent and address such violations. On Tuesday, the Asian Football Confederation cautioned the Hong Kong Football Association regarding the behavior of fans during a match against Malaysia on October 10 in Hong Kong, where some attendees booed the national anthem.

text: NEW DELHI (Reuters) - Requests for the commercial release of a genetically modified mustard, developed locally, have been halted by India, as revealed by a document from the environment ministry released on Tuesday. This decision comes amidst significant resistance from national activists and politicians against genetically modified (GM) foods. If approved, this mustard would have marked the first transgenic food crop permitted for commercial farming in the nation. However, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) of the environment ministry has postponed its endorsement, even after a supervisory panel under the ministry provided technical clearance for the GM mustard last year. "Following the receipt of various representations from several stakeholders, matters concerning the environmental release of transgenic mustard are under further review," the GEAC stated in the minutes from a meeting that was made public on the environment ministry's website, which is marked as "confidential and restricted circulation". Currently, cotton remains the only GM crop authorized for sale in the world's second most populous nation, where the amount of arable land is diminishing. Monsanto Co, a company based in the U.S., holds a dominant position in the cotton seed market in India, frequently encountering pushback from local firms regarding its market stance. On July 31, the environment ministry informed parliament that the GEAC had recommended the GM mustard for "consideration for environmental release and cultivation". A spokesperson from the environment ministry referred inquiries to GEAC head Amita Prasad, whose office indicated she was unavailable for comment. Another GEAC representative listed on the ministry's website, Madhumita Biswas, did not reply to requests for comments. The delay in the mustard’s approval is a disappointment for Deepak Pental and his team at Delhi University, who have dedicated years to the development and testing of this variety. Pental, who had previously acknowledged the challenges of obtaining approval for GM food, chose not to comment on the matter on Tuesday. Opposition to GM food in India stems from concerns regarding food safety and biodiversity, raised by activists and political figures alike. Doubts have also been expressed by some experts regarding the productivity claims of GM crops compared to traditional varieties. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, a Hindu nationalist group that serves as the ideological foundation for Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party, also stands against GM food, advocating instead for the promotion of indigenous varieties. Furthermore, a moratorium on GM eggplant was implemented by the prior government, led by the Congress party, in 2010 after an expert panel had cleared it, effectively causing a standstill in the regulatory framework until Modi reinstated it.

text: The path to the White House for Donald Trump could hinge on the backing of Republican evangelicals who are wary of the more progressive aspects of his views as he shares his social opinions. Trump, a businessman from New York with no prior experience in government, has managed to connect with evangelical voters in places like South Carolina. However, as Indiana’s nominating contest approaches on Tuesday, there are indications that his support may be waning in this traditionally conservative Midwestern state, which has favored Republican candidates in nine of the last ten presidential elections. At 69 years old, Trump has adopted positions regarding Planned Parenthood clinics and issues concerning gay and transgender rights that have raised alarms among Christian conservatives, especially in areas like Indiana where these voters constitute a significant demographic. An NBC/Wall Street Journal/Marist survey reveals that Trump currently leads in Indiana with 49 percent of the vote, while U.S. Senator Ted Cruz from Texas trails with 34 percent, and Ohio Governor John Kasich holds 13 percent. Earlier polls from Indiana suggested a more competitive race, showing Trump ahead of Cruz by only a narrow margin. Winning Indiana could be vital for Trump's chances at securing the nomination and may also serve as an indicator of whether he can unify evangelical voters. Cruz, 45, underscores his Christian beliefs throughout his campaign and asserts that Trump lacks authenticity as a Republican. A recent advertisement from Cruz depicts Trump and Democratic frontrunner Hillary Clinton as two sides of the same coin, arguing, "Both support the Obamacare individual mandate. Both support taxpayer funding for Planned Parenthood. Both support letting transgender men go in little girls’ bathrooms." Trump has acknowledged that Planned Parenthood clinics have assisted many women, although he opposes federal funding for its abortion services. He has also expressed support for allowing transgender individuals to utilize the bathroom they choose. If evangelical voters feel disengaged, they might choose to abstain from participating in the general election on November 8, which could result in a victory for either Hillary Clinton, the leading Democratic candidate, or her opponent, U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders. Bob Vander Plaats, a prominent evangelical figure in Iowa, remarked, "The fear is a lot of them are going to stay home. You can’t win without our base." Trump's previous criticisms of North Carolina’s contentious law mandating that transgender individuals use restrooms corresponding to their birth gender have irritated some social conservatives. “The restroom thing is big with a lot of people,” noted Shan Rutherford, a pastor based in Greenwood, Indiana. Although initially attracted to Trump’s platform, he expressed disappointment regarding the candidate's positions on social issues and his offensive behavior during the campaign. Rutherford, who supports Cruz, indicated that he might refrain from voting if the election pits Trump against Clinton. According to the Pew Research Center, 45 percent of registered Republican voters across the nation identify as "born-again" or "evangelical." Additionally, Pew found that only 44 percent of Republicans see Trump as a religious figure, whereas 76 percent hold that view of Cruz. Cruz has criticized Trump for his opinions on the North Carolina restroom law. Trump has stated that incidents involving transgender individuals in bathrooms are rare and argued that the decision should rest with state governments. Cruz contends that permitting adult men in restrooms with young girls could lead to dangerous situations. Recently, Cruz received the endorsement of Indiana Governor Mike Pence, a social conservative who enacted a controversial bill last year that opponents claimed could allow business owners to refuse services to same-sex couples. Trump has expressed his support for measures that prevent businesses from dismissing employees based on sexual orientation, yet he has also criticized the Supreme Court's ruling from last year that legalized same-sex marriage. Cruz has engaged his father, Rafael Cruz, an evangelical minister, to serve as a surrogate in Indiana churches.
source_text: Indiana puts Donald Trump’s evangelical support to test. INDIANAPOLIS (Reuters) - Donald Trump’s success in the race for the White House may well depend on the support of Republican evangelicals suspicious of the front-runner’s more liberal side as he discloses his social views. A New York businessman who has never held public office, Trump has had some success with evangelicals in states such as South Carolina.  But there are signs of slippage on the eve of Tuesday’s nominating contest in Indiana, a conservative Midwestern U.S. state that has voted Republican in nine of the last 10 presidential elections. Trump, 69, has taken stances on Planned Parenthood family clinics and gay and transgender rights that raise Christian conservative concerns, including in such states as Indiana where they make up a high proportion of voters. A new NBC/Wall Street Journal/Marist opinion poll shows Trump with a wide lead in Indiana, 49 percent, to 34 percent for his nearest rival, U.S. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, and 13 percent for Ohio Governor John Kasich.     Most previous Indiana opinion polls showed a tighter race with Trump leading Cruz by only a few points. A Trump win in the state could be crucial to his chances of securing the nomination but may also offer a gauge of whether he can rally evangelicals. Cruz, 45, emphasizes his Christian faith on the campaign trail. Focused on Indiana, he says Trump is not an authentic Republican. A new Cruz advertisement brands Trump and Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton as two sides of the same coin. “Both support the Obamacare individual mandate. Both support taxpayer funding for Planned Parenthood. Both support letting transgender men go in little girls’ bathrooms,” it says.  Trump has praised Planned Parenthood family clinics as having helped millions of women even if he opposes funding its abortion component. He backs letting transgender people use the bathroom “they feel is appropriate.” If evangelicals are unenthusiastic, they could sit out the Nov. 8 general election, potentially handing the White House to former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, the Democratic front-runner, or her rival, U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders. “The fear is a lot of them are going to stay home,” said Bob Vander Plaats, a leading evangelical activist in Iowa. “You can’t win without our base.” Trump rankled some social conservatives by criticizing North Carolina’s controversial law that requires transgender people to use the bathroom of the gender of their birth. “The restroom thing is big with a lot of people,” said Shan Rutherford, a pastor in Greenwood, Indiana. Rutherford said he was initially drawn to Trump’s message, but was put off by his stance on social issues and his insulting demeanor on the campaign trail. Rutherford, who backs Cruz, said if the White House race came down to Trump versus Clinton, he might not vote. The Pew Research Center says 45 percent of registered Republican voters nationwide identify themselves as “born-again” or “evangelical.” Pew also found that only 44 percent of Republicans view Trump as a religious person. By contrast, 76 percent viewed Cruz that way. Cruz has assailed Trump for his stance on the North Carolina bathroom law. Trump has said there have been few problems with transgender people using bathrooms. He also has said the question should be left to states to decide. Cruz charges allowing grown men in bathrooms with little girls is “opening the door for predators.” On Friday, Cruz was endorsed by Indiana Governor Mike Pence, a social conservative who last year signed a bill that critics said could be used by business owners to deny services to same-sex couples. Trump has said he supports prohibiting companies from firing employees based on sexual orientation, although he has criticized last year’s U.S. Supreme Court decision legalizing same-sex marriage. Cruz has deployed his father, Rafael Cruz, an evangelical minister, as a surrogate in churches in Indiana. A Reuters/Ipsos tracking poll showed 19 percent of respondents would not vote in a White House race between Trump and Clinton. But when filtered to those who attend church nearly every week, the number jumped to 28 percent. The party cannot afford a low turnout in November.  Demographic trends in recent years have favored Democrats, with the pool of Republican voters, overwhelmingly white and older, steadily shrinking. Eric Houseman, a paramedic from Indianapolis who attended a Cruz rally in Franklin, Indiana, predicted Trump would lose support through such missteps as inaccurately referring in January to a book of the Bible as “Two Corinthians” rather than Second Corinthians or Corinthians II. “People are beginning to see he’s a lot of talk,” Houseman said. Upstate, Ron Johnson, pastor at the Living Stones Church in Crown Point, votes Republican but was adamant that he would not vote for Trump. Trump does not share his Christian values, Johnson said.     “I am not going to be part of the demise of this country,” he said. But Mark Burns, a South Carolina pastor who has become a leading Trump surrogate in the media, said Trump’s appeal to evangelicals does not stem from the strength of his religious views. “We’re not voting for the next pastor. We’re voting for the next commander-in-chief,” Burns said.
