text: A senior figure from the Reagan era, who has been influential in Republican foreign policy circles, revealed to Reuters that he contributed to Donald Trump's foreign policy address in late April. Richard Burt, a former high-ranking official during the Reagan administration, shared that he was approached to offer insights for Trump’s speech on April 27 at the Center for the National Interest, a think tank located in Washington, D.C. Burt clarified that he is not affiliated with Trump’s campaign. He stated, "I am willing to engage with individuals seeking guidance on international relations matters." Burt is also a managing director at McLarty Associates, a consulting firm in Washington that was co-founded by Thomas "Mack" McLarty, who served as chief of staff and counselor under former President Bill Clinton. Furthermore, Burt expressed that he would be open to providing foreign policy counsel to Hillary Clinton, the leading candidate for the Democratic Party, should she request it, although he remarked, "She’s not going to." Additionally, Burt chairs an independent organization known as Global Zero, which is focused on eliminating nuclear weapons globally. In comments made to The New York Times in April, Trump indicated uncertainty about the implications of Japan possessing nuclear arms, and he has similarly stated that the same could be true for South Korea and Saudi Arabia. Burt mentioned that he emphasized to Trump the importance of adopting a "more realist foreign policy," advocating for a shift away from pursuing "regime change" in other nations, instead prioritizing the protection of U.S. interests and security. Trump, who was officially recognized as the presumptive Republican nominee last month after the departure of his last competitor from the race, reiterated this perspective in a campaign address on Tuesday, celebrating his victories in the final Republican primaries. During his tenure under Reagan, Burt led the Bureau of Political-Military Affairs at the State Department, later overseeing the Bureau of European and Canadian Affairs, and served as the U.S. ambassador to Germany from 1985 to 1989. Some of Burt’s peers from the administrations of Presidents Reagan, George H.W. Bush, and George W. Bush have openly criticized Trump's foreign policy stance or chosen to remain silent. Earlier this year, Trump convened a meeting with 11 foreign policy advisors, with Republican Senator Jeff Sessions from Alabama, a strong proponent of Trump, at the helm. Reuters reached out to various members of Trump's foreign policy team for comments regarding their recent activities, as well as a spokesperson for the campaign. Most did not respond, and the campaign did not provide an immediate reply to a request for input. One anonymous campaign team member stated that while discussions have taken place following Trump’s speech, the candidate still primarily relies on himself for foreign policy guidance.
source_text: Former Reagan aide helped write Trump foreign policy speech. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A former senior official in the Reagan administration and prominent Republican foreign policy insider told Reuters he provided input for the late-April foreign policy speech by Donald Trump, the presumptive Republican presidential nominee. “I was asked to contribute material” for Trump’s April 27 speech at the Center for the National Interest, a Washington, D.C., think tank, said Richard Burt. Burt said he is not part of Trump’s campaign. “But I am happy to talk to people looking for advice on foreign policy issues,” said Burt, a managing director of McLarty Associates, a Washington-based consulting firm co-founded by former President Bill Clinton’s White House chief of staff and counselor Thomas “Mack” McLarty. Burt said he also would be willing to offer foreign policy advice to Hillary Clinton, the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, if she asked for such advice, though he added, “She’s not going to.”Burt is also chairman of Global Zero, an independent group devoted to ridding the world of nuclear weapons. Trump told The New York Times in April that he was not sure it would be “a bad thing” for the United States if Japan had nuclear weapons, and has said the same about South Korea and Saudi Arabia. Burt said the main theme he talked about to Trump was the need for the United States to pursue a “more realist foreign policy,” in which the United States would avoid seeking “regime change” abroad, and instead make protecting the United States and its interests the main policy goal. Trump, who became the Republican’s presumptive nominee last month after the last of his challengers dropped from the party’s race, articulated this theme again in a campaign speech late on Tuesday, as he claimed victory in the last Republican nominating contests. Under Reagan, Burt headed the State Department’s Bureau of Political-Military Affairs and then its European and Canadian Affairs bureau and served as U.S. ambassador to Germany from 1985 to 1989. Some of Burt’s contemporaries from the administrations of Presidents Reagan, George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush, have publicly denounced Trump’s foreign policy views or remained mute. Earlier this year, Trump met with a group of 11 foreign policy advisers, headed by Republican Senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, one of Trump’s most outspoken supporters.  Reuters sought comment on the recent activities of Trump’s foreign policy team from several of its members and from a campaign spokeswoman. Most declined to comment, and the campaign did not immediately reply to a request for comment.  One campaign team member, who asked for anonymity because he is not authorized to comment publicly, said that while the team had held several discussions since Trump’s speech, the candidate remains his own most important foreign policy adviser.

text: On Tuesday morning, a tragic incident occurred involving a member of the Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte's security detail, who was found dead. At the time of the shooting, the president was not in close proximity, as he was reported to be far away, according to the head of his security team who dismissed any suggestions of foul play. The event, which took place in Malacanang Park—the base of the Presidential Security Group (PSG) in Manila—is being viewed as an isolated case, with terrorism being ruled out, stated PSG commander Lope Dagoy. The deceased, a 37-year-old PSG guard, was discovered by his spouse in his quarters at 8:50 a.m. ET, having sustained a single gunshot wound to the chest. Dagoy addressed the media, asserting, "We are ruling out foul play. Certainly no foul play." Prior to Dagoy's comments, Duterte's location had been unconfirmed for several hours. The unpredictable president had not been seen in public on Monday and had spent several days prior in his southern city of Davao. When asked about Duterte's location during a routine press briefing following the shooting, spokesperson Ernesto Abella responded, "We don’t have any information regarding that." Known for his erratic scheduling, Duterte often creates confusion with abrupt changes to his public engagements, which generally begin in the afternoon and may extend up to four hours late due to his lengthy, impromptu speeches. Typically, he spends weekends in Davao City, sometimes leaving as early as Thursday and returning to Manila by Monday or later. He was expected to participate in multiple public events in Manila on Tuesday evening. Malacanang Park is situated near Duterte's residence, Bahay ng Pagbabago, across the Pasig River from the Malacanang palace. Dagoy mentioned that the police were conducting an investigation into the shooting, and the PSG refrained from speculating on the circumstances. He also expressed condolences to the family of the guard on behalf of the unit.
source_text: Philippine presidential guard shot dead, Duterte not nearby. MANILA (Reuters) - A member of Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte s guard unit was shot dead on Tuesday, but the president was far away at the time of the incident and the head of his security team ruled out  foul play. We are ruling out foul play,  Dagoy told reporters.  Certainly no foul play.  Duterte s whereabouts had not been known for several hours prior to Dagoy s remarks. He was due to attend several public events in Manila on Tuesday evening. Malacanang Park is close to Duterte s Bahay ng Pagbabago residence, separated from his Malacanang palace by the Pasig river. text: In the small community of Huautla, Mexico, challenges continue to mount following recent disasters. Yesenia Vergara, a local resident, hurriedly took her two daughters and fled their home last month when swollen river waters rushed through her window, inundating their dwelling with debris, rocks, and mud. Just a fortnight later, the most devastating earthquake Mexico has experienced in a generation struck, delivering another blow to her modest riverside residence, which was built with funds sent from her husband in the United States.  "This is the end of the world, I thought. Now is the time that God has called us to be judged," Vergara recounted, reflecting on the moment the earthquake hit early last Tuesday afternoon.  "The village was just getting back on its feet and now another tragedy has come," she expressed. The epicenter of the 7.1 magnitude quake, which has resulted in nearly 300 fatalities thus far, caused extensive destruction in Mexico City, leading to an urgent search for survivors. The seismic event occurred 70 km (45 miles) from Huautla, a picturesque village surrounded by the verdant mountains of Morelos state.  While eager volunteers flooded the capital in response to the disaster, the nearby villages in Morelos and Puebla states that are close to the epicenter received considerably less help.  On Friday, a growing group of concerned individuals aimed to address this imbalance, traversing the state's backroads and navigating knee-deep streams to bring food, water, and medicine to isolated communities high in the mountains.  This initiative, far surpassing the governmental response, has uplifted a shaken nation. It also sharply contrasts with the increasingly politicized responses to the earthquake, which triggered a competitive race among political factions eager to outdo one another with donations for relief efforts.  "We feel very grateful," Vergara remarked regarding the volunteers' efforts. "But also very disappointed with the government."  Although Huautla did not suffer any building collapses, Mayor Miguel Medina indicated that 10 families from the population of approximately 1,000 were evacuated due to damage to around 100 structures.  By Friday afternoon, Vergara mentioned that no one had come to assess the significant cracks threatening her home, forcing her and her young family to seek refuge at her mother's house.  Among those who traveled from Mexico City to provide assistance in the region was Fortino Garcia, a 48-year-old taxi driver.  While he acknowledged the government's response to the earthquake, he criticized politicians for attempting to exploit the tragedy by affixing their names or party labels to supplies gathered by volunteers.  "Lots of politicians are sadly jumping on this to campaign," he stated in Huautla's central square after delivering items such as diapers, sanitary products, and water.  Residents expressed growing frustration regarding the distribution of aid by local officials, accusing them of selectively choosing higher-quality donations of clothing and food while leaving inferior items for the villagers.  In a warehouse at the village's center, where hundreds of women were queuing for food and water, Medina denied any wrongdoing on his part or that of his staff regarding the aid distribution, asserting that the donations were sourced from around the globe.  "People from other countries have come to give us their little grain of sand," he said. "We’re very surprised and thankful."  Nonetheless, rumors of official misconduct circulated throughout the area.  A shopkeeper, who requested anonymity for safety reasons, mentioned that crime and violence in Huautla had escalated significantly over the past few years. She disclosed that some villagers took up arms last month, establishing a blockade at the town's entrance to deter outsiders.  She also recounted a tragic incident in July, when an elderly woman was killed after she interrupted a burglary in her own home, an occurrence that was previously unheard of in this typically peaceful agricultural community.
source_text: Problems pile up for unlucky village near epicenter of Mexican quake. HUAUTLA, Mexico (Reuters) - Yesenia Vergara grabbed her two daughters and abandoned her home in the isolated Mexican hamlet of Huautla late last month when rain-swollen river waters burst through her window, flooding her house with branches, boulders and mud. Just two weeks later, Mexico s deadliest earthquake in a generation delivered a second blow to her simple riverside home, financed with money sent back by her husband from the United States.  This is the end of the world, I thought. Now is the time that God has called us to be judged,  Vergara said, recalling the moment when the quake struck in the early afternoon last Tuesday.  The village was just getting back on its feet and now another tragedy has come,  she said. The epicenter of the 7.1 magnitude tremor, which has claimed nearly 300 lives so far, leveled dozens of buildings in Mexico City, sparking a desperate search for survivors. The quake struck 70 km (45 miles) from Huautla, a charming settlement nestled amid the lime-green mountains of Morelos state.     While the Mexican capital has been over-run with eager volunteers amid an outpouring of support, the villages of Morelos and Puebla states that lie near the epicenter have received much less attention.     A growing cadre of well-wishers sought to rectify that on Friday, fanning out across the states  backroads, trudging through knee-high streams to deliver food, water and medicine to remote populations high up in the mountains.     Far outpacing the government response, the volunteers  patriotic reaction has cheered a traumatized country. It has also provided a sharp contrast to the increasingly politicized reaction to the tremor, which sparked a virtual arms race between political parties seeking to outdo each other with donations to relief efforts.      We feel very grateful,  Vergara said of the volunteers.  But also very disappointed with the government.  Although the quake didn t destroy any buildings in Huautla, Mayor Miguel Medina said 10 families out of roughly 1,000 people were evacuated because some 100 structures were damaged.     By Friday afternoon, Vergara said nobody had yet come to inspect the thick cracks menacing her home, exiling her and her young family to her mother s house.     Fortino Garcia, a 48-year-old taxi driver from the city of Cuernavaca, was among eight people who had driven from Mexico City to deliver aid to villages in the area.     Although he approved of the government s reaction to the quake, he criticized politicians who he said were trying to capitalize on the tragedy by placing stickers with their name or party on supplies collected by volunteers.      Lots of politicians are sadly jumping on this to campaign,  he said in Huautla s main square, after delivering diapers, sanitary towels and water.     A growing resentment over how the aid was being distributed by village officials was on display as residents accused officials of cherry-picking better quality donations of clothes and food and leaving less desirable ones for the villagers.     In a warehouse in the center of the village where hundreds of women were lining up for food and water, Medina denied he or any of his employees had been profiting from the aid, which he said came from all over the world.      People from other countries have come to give us their little grain of sand,  he said.  We re very surprised and thankful.      Still, rumors of official malfeasance could be found on every corner.     Like much of Mexico, crime and violence in Huautla had risen dramatically over the last few years, according to a shopkeeper who declined to give her name out of fear. She said some villagers took up arms last month and installed themselves at the entrance to the town to ward off outsiders.     In July, she said, an elderly woman was killed when she interrupted a burglary in her home, something previously unheard of in this quiet farming settlement.      Given the impact of the flood, the quake and rising violence, she said she was less optimistic for the future of her teenage daughter, who was listening by her side.      We re scared,  the shopkeeper said.  Things aren t like they used to be.

text: On Thursday, there was a notable increase in demand for Spanish government bonds and equities following a report suggesting that Catalonian President Carles Puigdemont may announce a snap regional election on December 20. This development could potentially alleviate the existing tensions with the central government in Madrid. According to the Barcelona-based publication La Vanguardia, Puigdemont's decision was influenced by a desire to dissuade Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy's administration from imposing direct rule over the autonomous region. The regional government confirmed that Puigdemont is scheduled to address the media at 1330 CET (1130 GMT). ING strategist Martin van Vliet remarked that this news is encouraging for Spain, indicating that Puigdemont appears to be seeking alternatives to declaring independence. He added that it seems Puigdemont is organizing these elections to prevent Madrid from activating Article 155, which would enable the central government to revoke the region's autonomy. Following the announcement, Spain's 10-year government bond yield, which inversely correlates with price, decreased by 6 basis points to 1.58 percent. The IBEX, Spain's main stock index, experienced a rise of as much as 1.9 percent, reaching its highest level in four weeks. Additionally, the difference between Spanish and German 10-year government bond yields, a critical indicator of market sentiment toward Spain, narrowed to its tightest level in a month. Earlier in the month, this spread had widened significantly after Catalonia's residents overwhelmingly voted in favor of independence in an October 1 referendum deemed illegal by Madrid authorities, despite a low turnout.
source_text: Spanish markets rise on report of possible Catalan election. LONDON (Reuters) - Spanish government bonds and stocks were in demand on Thursday after a media report said Catalonian President Carles Puigdemont was set to call a snap regional election for Dec. 20, a move that could ease tensions with Madrid.  Barcelona-based La Vanguardia said Puigdemont had taken the decision in a bid to persuade the government of Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy not to enforce direct rule in the region. Puigdemont will make a statement at 1330 CET (1130 GMT), the regional government said.  This news is positive for Spain because it looks like Puigdemont is looking for ways other than declaring independence,  said ING strategist Martin van Vliet.   It sounds like he is calling these elections so that Madrid does not have to invoke article 155,  that would allow central government to suspend the wealthy region s autonomy. Spain s 10-year government bond yield - which moves inversely to price - fell 6 basis points to 1.58 percent on the news.  Spain s country stock index IBEX rose as much as 1.9 percent to a four-week high.  The gap between Spanish and German 10-year government bond yields   a keenly watched measure of market sentiment towards Spain   moved to its tightest in a month.  The spread between the two widened sharply earlier this month after Catalonia voted overwhelmingly in favor of breaking away from Spain, albeit on a low turnout, in an Oct. 1 referendum declared illegal by authorities in Madrid.

text: Next week, a vote in the Senate may take place regarding a newly revised healthcare bill. On Tuesday, U.S. Senate Republicans announced their intention to bring their healthcare reform initiative to the Senate floor after a prolonged period of internal conflict within the party. However, it was still uncertain whether they had sufficient votes to pass the legislation or what its final form would be. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, known for his strategic prowess, outlined a schedule for the Senate’s consideration of the bill aimed at fulfilling President Donald Trump’s campaign commitment to dismantle the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare, which was enacted in 2010. Diverging from typical Republican views on tax reductions, sources from the Senate indicated that the new legislation will likely retain certain taxes imposed on wealthy individuals under Obamacare. Still, it remains unclear if the updated bill, which is set to be revealed on Thursday morning, can accommodate the demands of both moderate Republicans and hard-line conservatives, who have expressed dissent towards a previous draft that was presented last month for various reasons. With Trump urging the Senate to act prior to the August recess, McConnell extended the Senate’s scheduled break by two weeks to provide additional time for senators to address the measure that seeks to repeal significant aspects of Obamacare while also pursuing other legislative issues. Following McConnell's announcement, stock prices on Wall Street rebounded during afternoon trading after an earlier decline, fueled by optimism that the shortened recess could signify progress on the stalled Republican legislative agenda. Some Republicans, however, were still engulfed in a gloomy atmosphere regarding healthcare, with party leaders seemingly feeling the pressure to resolve the healthcare issue and shift focus to other pressing matters, including the increase of the U.S. debt ceiling. Senator John Thune, a junior member of the Republican leadership, remarked to reporters, "I believe we have narrowed it down to the key decision points, and now we must make those decisions." He noted that leaders were still trying to "determine how we achieve 50" votes. With Republicans holding 52 out of 100 Senate seats, they would require 50 votes to pass the legislation, with Vice President Mike Pence serving as the tie-breaking vote. "I am feeling quite pessimistic" about the chances for the success of Republican healthcare reform, Chuck Grassley, a senior senator, expressed during an interview with Fox News on Tuesday. Another Republican senator, Lindsey Graham, is reportedly developing his own healthcare proposal, which is expected to be introduced this week, according to a Graham aide. McConnell indicated that the intention was to hold a vote on the healthcare proposal next week, expressing hopes to receive a fresh assessment of the bill from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office at the beginning of the week. He did not disclose any specific changes planned for the draft, which had previously been postponed due to insufficient support. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Senate Republicans said Tuesday they will seek to bring their healthcare overhaul to the Senate floor next week after a lengthy intraparty struggle, but it remained unclear whether they had the votes to pass the measure or even what form it would finally take.  With his reputation as a master strategist on the line, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell laid out a timetable for Senate consideration of legislation to fulfill President Donald Trump’s campaign promise to dismantle the 2010 Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. In a departure from Republican orthodoxy on tax-cutting, the legislation likely will retain some of the taxes that were imposed on the wealthy under Obamacare, Senate sources said. But it was unknown whether a revised version of the bill to be announced on Thursday morning can satisfy both moderates and hard-line conservatives in the Republican majority who voiced opposition to a draft unveiled last month on very different grounds. With Trump urging the Senate to act before taking the August break, McConnell pushed back the Senate’s planned August recess by two weeks to allow senators more time to tackle the measure that would repeal key parts of Obamacare, as well as pursue other legislative priorities. McConnell’s announcement drove a turn-around in stock prices in afternoon trading on Wall Street after an earlier sell-off, on hopes that a shortened recess could mean progress on the stalled Republican legislative agenda.  A dark mood lingered among some Republicans over the healthcare subject, with party leaders appearing to act because of the need to dispense with healthcare and turn to other issues, among them increasing the U.S. debt ceiling. “I think we’ve narrowed down now to where we know where the decision points are, and we just have to make those decisions,” Senator John Thune, a junior member of the Republican leadership, told reporters. Leaders were still trying to “figure out how we get to 50” votes, he said. Republicans, who hold 52 seats in the 100-seat Senate, would need 50 votes to pass the bill, with Vice President Mike Pence providing the tie-breaking vote. “I am very pessimistic” about the prospects for Republican healthcare legislation, Chuck Grassley, a senior senator, told Fox News on Tuesday. Another Republican senator, Lindsey Graham, was working on his own healthcare proposal and will unveil it this week, a Graham aide said. McConnell said the plan was to vote on the healthcare bill next week, and said he hoped to have a fresh analysis of the bill from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office at the start of the week. He did not reveal any of the planned changes to the draft, on which he postponed action last month after it failed to gather enough support. But Senate sources said it is likely that two Obamacare taxes on the wealthy will be kept in place - a 3.8 percent net investment tax and a 0.9 percent payroll tax that helps finance Medicare - which would appeal to moderates who have balked at the prospect of cutting taxes for the wealthy while reducing benefits for the poor. “Obviously that’s the direction I think that a lot of our members want to move, is to keep some of those (taxes) in place and be able to use those revenues to put it into other places in the bill,” Thune said, while stressing that no decisions were final. Republicans could also retain Obamacare’s limit on corporate tax deductions for executive pay in the health insurance industry, one Senate source said. It was unclear whether the bill would include a proposal by conservative Republican Ted Cruz that would allow insurers to offer basic low-cost healthcare plans that do not comply with Obamacare regulations. Cruz argues it would help to lower premiums, but critics say it would allow insurers to offer skimpier plans that may not cover essential health benefits while also charging more for more comprehensive, Obamacare-compliant plans. The Senate Republican healthcare bill unveiled last month would phase out the Obamacare expansion of Medicaid health insurance for the poor and disabled, sharply cut federal Medicaid spending beginning in 2025, repeal many of Obamacare’s taxes, end a penalty on individuals who do not obtain insurance and overhaul Obamacare’s subsidies to help people buy insurance with tax credits. Democrats are united in opposition to the bill and at least 10 Republicans have said they oppose the existing draft. The House of Representatives passed its own version in May. Moderate Republicans are uneasy about the millions of people forecast to lose their medical insurance under the draft legislation, and hard-line conservatives say it leaves too much of Obamacare intact. Democrats call the Republican legislation a giveaway to the rich that would hurt the most vulnerable Americans.

source_text: Trump, Nikki Haley to share U.S. spotlight at U.N. gathering. UNITED NATIONS (Reuters) - When President Donald Trump takes the world stage at the United Nations for the first time this week, he will share the spotlight with his envoy Nikki Haley, who has emerged as the surprising public face of U.S. foreign policy. Haley, the 45-year-old former South Carolina governor, has proven to be a high-profile member of Trump’s administration, at times overshadowing Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, the former chief executive of Exxon Mobil Corp, despite her lack of previous foreign policy experience, diplomats say. “For the U.S., Nikki Haley is remarkable. It’s hard to find in the Trump administration. It’s someone who is very approachable and politically very assertive,” said a senior European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity.  “I see her potentially taking over from Tillerson at some point. It’s clear her long-term objective is the presidency,” the diplomat said.  Haley dismisses speculation she could replace Tillerson, the country’s top diplomat, who has at times publicly differed with Trump during the president’s eight months in the White House. On Sunday, she told CNN that Tillerson is “not going anywhere and I continue to work well with him.” Trump’s speech on Tuesday at the U.N. General Assembly will be his highest profile opportunity to explain his foreign policy vision couched in his America First agenda. Haley arrived at the 193-member world body in January pledging to “take names” of allies who did not have Washington’s back. Trump administration officials say the president, happy with her performance, views her as both tough and smart. He speaks regularly with Haley, his fellow Republican, one U.S. administration official said.  Twice in five weeks she persuaded the 15-member U.N. Security Council to unanimously boost sanctions on North Korea. Her blunt language has raised eyebrows among diplomats. At the same time she has been careful not to steal the limelight from Trump, a wealthy businessman and former reality television star. “I personally think he slaps the right people, he hugs the right people, and he comes out with the U.S. being very strong in the end,” Haley told White House reporters on Friday. European Council on Foreign Relations U.N. expert Richard Gowan said Haley’s success could make Trump nervous and that it would be a “bad deal for her” if she was asked to replace Tillerson as secretary of state.   “She would lose the independence she enjoys in New York and (it would) tie her more closely to the president’s agenda. But it is an offer that she could not refuse. It’s an irony that the one way Trump can hurt Haley is to promote her,” he said.  Haley credits Trump with any U.S. achievements at the United Nations. After the Security Council toughened sanctions on North Korea this month, she praised his “strong relationship” with his Chinese counterpart for the result. When he dismissed the Sept. 11 U.N. resolution, which had been weakened by China and Russia, as “just another very small step, not a big deal,” Haley jumped to his defense and dismissed any suggestion they were not on the same page. “If we have to go further, this is going to look small compared to what we do,” she said at the time. Haley has made her mark also by fighting what she describes as U.N. anti-Israel bias, pushing for U.N. reform amid Trump’s call to slash U.S. funding, accusing Iran of meddling in the Middle East and challenging Russia over Ukraine and its support for Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. A senior administration official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that during a National Security Council meeting on Iran this month, Trump specifically asked Haley’s opinion about what strategy to pursue. “She gave her opinion, and he liked her point of view,” the official said. “She wasn’t afraid to speak up.” A senior Iranian official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said, “This lady for some reason is very angry with Iran.” Before her selection as ambassador, Haley made national headlines when as governor she led a successful effort to remove the Confederate battle flag, viewed by many as a racist emblem, from the grounds of the South Carolina state capitol after the killing of nine black churchgoers in her state. During the 2016 presidential campaign Haley sparred with Trump, backing one of his rivals before he became the Republican candidate. The daughter of immigrants from India, Haley took Trump to task over his harsh campaign rhetoric about illegal immigration and for not speaking forcefully enough against white supremacists. When last month Trump inflamed tensions by saying that counter-protesters were also to blame for a deadly rally by white nationalists in Virginia, Haley spoke up, telling U.S. media she had a “personal conversation” with him about it.  Without naming Trump she wrote to staff at the U.S. mission to the United Nations to say that everyone must stand up and condemn hate.

text: On Tuesday, a collective of over 300 eminent scientists expressed their concerns regarding Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump’s intention to withdraw the United States from the Paris climate agreement if he wins in November. In an open letter, 375 members of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, which includes 30 Nobel laureates, indicated that a U.S. exit from the accord would complicate efforts to formulate global initiatives aimed at reducing the effects of climate change. The letter stated, "It is thus very troubling that the Republican presidential nominee has proposed that the U.S. leave the Paris Accord." It further warned that a 'Parexit' would convey a definitive message to the international community: "The United States does not prioritize the global challenge posed by human-induced climate change. You are on your own." Noteworthy signatories of the letter include biologist E.O. Wilson, physicists Stephen Hawking and Claude Canizares, astrophysicist Simon D.M. White, along with Nobel laureates Thomas Steitz, Michael Levitt, and William Daniel Phillips. The National Academy of Sciences serves as a private organization of experts providing counsel to the U.S. on scientific and technological issues. The individuals who endorsed the letter did so in their personal capacities and not representing the Academy or their respective institutions. In December in Paris, nearly 200 nations reached an agreement to significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions and to maintain the increase in global temperatures to "well below" 2 degrees Celsius. This month, both the United States and China, the leading emitters of carbon dioxide, ratified the agreement. On Thursday, Trump is scheduled to address a natural gas industry conference in Pennsylvania. A representative for Trump has not yet replied to a request for a statement. Trump has referred to human-caused climate change as a fabrication created by the Chinese and has pledged to withdraw from the Paris agreement if he is elected. He has also promised to overturn significant portions of the climate change policies established by President Barack Obama, which include regulations aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Additionally, the Republican Party platform raises questions about the legality of Obama’s executive action to ratify the Paris agreement. In contrast, Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton is a vigorous advocate for the Paris accord.

You are on your own.’” Among the signers are biologist E.O. Wilson, physicists Stephen Hawking and Claude Canizares, astrophysicist Simon D.M. White, and Nobel winners Thomas Steitz, Michael Levitt and William Daniel Phillips. The National Academy of Sciences is a private society of scholars who advise the United States on science and  technological matters. The signers of the letter said they did so as individuals and not on behalf of the Academy or their institutions. In Paris last December, almost 200 countries agreed to slash greenhouse gases and keep global temperature rises to “well below” 2 degrees Celsius. text: On Monday, President Vladimir Putin observed significant military exercises in Russia that have caused concern among Western nations. The largest drills in years saw Russian forces simulate repelling an adversary while launching a counter-offensive led by tanks, an operation referred to as Zapad-2017 (West-2017). Although NATO officials claim they are observing the drills with a sense of calm and assurance, many remain apprehensive, perceiving it as an indication of Moscow's capabilities for potential conflict with the West. The Russian government asserts that this exercise is focused solely on defensive tactics. Putin, who serves as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, was situated in a command post alongside his defense minister and the chief of staff. He utilized binoculars to scrutinize the mock battle that was taking place in front of him amidst a chilly drizzle. In previous similar events, the Russian leader has often worn military attire, using such occasions to enhance his image as a strong protector of national interests among the Russian populace. This occasion, however, saw the 64-year-old president in a dark suit, appearing composed as the range in the Leningrad region morphed into a simulated combat zone. The skyline was illuminated by tracer rounds, while battle tanks maneuvered through muddy landscapes, explosions echoed as shells detonated, helicopters launched missiles, and aircraft soared overhead. Hundreds of paratroopers and armored units were descended from the sky to engage the opposition described by the defense ministry as illegal armed groups. The overarching Zapad exercises commenced on September 14 and will conclude on September 20, taking place across western Russia, the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, and Belarus, which shares borders with both Ukraine and NATO member nations Poland, Latvia, and Lithuania. Moscow has announced that nearly 13,000 military personnel from Russia and Belarus are participating, along with approximately 70 aircraft and helicopters involved. The deployment includes nearly 700 units of military equipment, such as about 250 tanks, a fleet of 10 ships, and various artillery and rocket launch systems. However, NATO representatives believe that the number of troops engaged exceeds what Moscow has officially reported, raising concerns over transparency regarding the exercises, a claim that Russia has denied. In conjunction with these maneuvers, on Monday, Russia declared it had successfully conducted a test launch of a ballistic missile designed to carry a nuclear payload, striking a target located approximately 480 km (300 miles) away at a range in Kazakhstan. Moscow contends that it is the West that poses a threat to stability in Eastern Europe, pointing to NATO's establishment of a multinational force consisting of 4,000 troops in the Baltic states and Poland. Additionally, during the Zapad exercises, the U.S. Army has deployed 600 paratroopers to the Baltic region. For safety measures, the United States has temporarily assumed control over the airspace of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, nations that lack sufficient air defense systems and capable air forces.

text: According to a Reuters/Ipsos survey, support for Donald Trump’s proposed tax cuts is less than one-third among Americans. Released on Tuesday, the poll reflects the current political atmosphere as the U.S. President seeks backing from Republican lawmakers on his initiative to reduce tax rates for both individuals and corporations. As the 2018 midterm congressional elections approach, the survey indicates that over two-thirds of registered voters prioritize reducing the U.S. federal budget deficit over tax cuts targeted at wealthy individuals or corporations. Critics, including independent analysts, argue that Trump's plan would increase the deficit and exacerbate the national debt, which currently stands at $20 trillion. However, Republicans contend that the proposed tax reductions would be compensated by economic growth, leading to new tax revenues. Among Republicans responding to the survey, 63 percent expressed that reducing the deficit should take precedence over corporate tax cuts, while 75 percent believed that deficit reduction should be prioritized over tax cuts for the affluent. Democrats have voiced their opposition to Trump’s initiative, which was revealed on September 27, claiming that it disproportionately harms the poor and working-class citizens. The proposal remains in the form of a nine-page "framework," created behind closed doors by the Trump administration along with congressional leaders. Formal legislation is still being crafted. Trump and congressional leaders are actively working to secure support for the plan from rank-and-file Republicans, many of whom were not involved in the initial drafting of the framework. Since taking office in January, Trump has not achieved a significant legislative success and is eager to have his tax plan enacted by the end of the year, although some policy analysts question whether this timeline is feasible. The poll conducted from October 20 to 23 revealed that more than half of the adults surveyed believe that "cutting taxes for the poor is more important than reducing the federal deficit," with 68 percent of Democrats and 47 percent of Republicans agreeing with this sentiment. The survey also indicated that only 15 percent of registered voters think that Republicans in Congress should prioritize tax reform over other pressing matters. Approximately 25 percent of those queried, including 30 percent of Republicans and 23 percent of Democrats, concurred that Congress should focus on advancing a healthcare bill. Among those adults who were aware of the "tax reform plan recently proposed by congressional Republicans," only 28 percent expressed support, while 41 percent opposed it and 31 percent were uncertain. The poll illustrated a stark division in opinions regarding Trump’s plan along party lines, with 56 percent of Republicans in favor and merely 9 percent of Democrats supporting it. Of those respondents who had heard about the plan, 14 percent believed it would lead to tax reductions for them, while 30 percent anticipated an increase. Another 35 percent indicated that their taxes would remain unchanged, and 20 percent were unsure about its potential impact on their tax situation. The Reuters/Ipsos poll was carried out online in English across all 50 states, collecting responses from 1,862 individuals, including 1,079 who acknowledged awareness of the Republican tax plan. The poll's credibility interval, a metric for accuracy, stands at 3 percentage points.

text: On Thursday, prominent individuals from various political backgrounds in Libya expressed their outrage over comments made by Boris Johnson, the British Foreign Secretary, regarding the removal of deceased individuals from Sirte. During a Conservative Party meeting on Tuesday, Johnson mentioned that British investors had a "brilliant vision" for transforming Sirte, a city that was once a stronghold for Islamic State, into a new Dubai, provided that the bodies could be removed. Lawmakers from the House of Representatives (HOR) in Libya, representing the eastern factions, deemed his statements unacceptable. The foreign affairs committee of the HOR released a statement requesting an explanation from the British Prime Minister, along with an apology directed toward the Libyan populace. Similarly, Fayez Seraj, the leader of Libya's U.N.-recognized government based in Tripoli, which has been rejected by the HOR, sought clarification during discussions with the British ambassador in the capital. "Some of what was said in (Johnson's) statement is unacceptable," declared Seraj in his statement. In the wake of Johnson’s remarks, calls for his resignation emerged from political adversaries in Britain. He responded by accusing them of politicizing the issue, asserting on Twitter that he had been referring specifically to the clearing of booby-trapped bodies belonging to Islamic State militants. Local forces in Libya, supported by U.S. airstrikes, spent over six months last year fighting to expel militants from Sirte, which had become their most significant base outside of the Middle East. The city, with a population of approximately 80,000, suffered extensive damage during the military operations and is currently facing challenges in its recovery. Since 2014, the HOR has been operating from eastern Libya following a conflict in Tripoli that resulted in the formation of competing parliaments and governments in both regions. Its collaboration is deemed essential for the success of a new U.N. initiative aimed at stabilizing Libya and resolving the unrest that has persisted since the NATO-backed uprising that overthrew Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

BENGHAZI, Libya (Reuters) - Senior figures from across Libya s political divides protested on Thursday against remarks by British Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson about clearing dead bodies from the city of Sirte. Johnson told members of his Conservative Party on Tuesday that British investors had a  brilliant vision  to turn Sirte, a former stronghold of Islamic State, into the next Dubai if bodies could be cleared away.     Lawmakers from Libya s House of Representatives (HOR), who represent political and military factions based in the east of the country, called the comments unacceptable. The HOR s foreign affairs committee issued a statement demanding  a clarification from the British prime minister and an apology to the Libyan people . The head of Libya s U.N.- and Western-backed government, which is based in Tripoli and has been spurned by the HOR, also asked for clarification during a meeting with the British ambassador in the capital.   Some of what was said in (Johnson s) statement is unacceptable,  said a statement from Fayez Seraj, head of the U.N.-backed government. Johnson s comments led to calls for his resignation from British political opponents. He accused them of playing politics, saying on Twitter that he had been referring to the clearing of booby-trapped bodies of Islamic State militants.  Local Libyan forces backed by U.S. air strikes fought for more than six months last year to oust militants from Sirte, which Islamic State had turned into its most important base outside the Middle East. The coastal city of about 80,000 was badly damaged during the campaign and is struggling to rebuild.  The HOR has been based in eastern Libya since 2014 when a conflict in Tripoli led to the setting up of rival parliaments and governments in the capital and the east. Its cooperation is considered crucial for the progress of a new U.N. plan to stabilize Libya and the ending of turmoil that began after the NATO-backed uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

text: TransCanada Corp, which ranks as Canada’s second-largest pipeline operator, announced on Friday that a final decision regarding the Keystone XL project will be made by December. This statement came as the company revealed a profit that exceeded expectations. The announcement marks the first time TransCanada has publicly established a deadline for the investment decision on the project since President Donald Trump approved Keystone XL in March, reversing a prior decision by Barack Obama. According to Paul Miller, who is the executive vice president and president of liquid pipeline at TransCanada, the forthcoming investment decision will hinge on demand from shippers and the regulatory verdict from Nebraska, the state through which the pipeline will traverse. During a conference call following the quarterly results announcement, Miller remarked, "Our evaluation of these elements will significantly influence our investment decision as we approach the November-December period." Although TransCanada has reported receiving "good support" from current shippers, including those who left after the rejection of Keystone XL in 2015, the company is now aiming to attract new participants and is seeking a "significant" commitment level, although Miller did not disclose specific numbers. On Thursday, TransCanada kicked off an open season to garner additional commitments for Keystone XL. This expansion will enhance the capacity of the existing Keystone system that transports oil from Alberta, Canada’s oil-producing province, to the Gulf of Mexico. Additionally, TransCanada stated on Friday that it plans to allocate approximately C$160 million (equivalent to $129 million) to boost the capacity of its primary Canadian natural gas line, a development that may assist producers who lost an export pathway following the cancellation of the Pacific NorthWest project earlier this week. The Malaysian state-owned enterprise Petroliam Nasional Bhd, known as Petronas, declared the abandonment of its Pacific NorthWest liquefied natural gas terminal in British Columbia, Canada, this week, attributing the decision to low commodity prices. TransCanada, which has invested at least C$500 million in constructing the pipeline that connects gas wells to the terminal, indicated it would receive reimbursement this year for expenses related to the project. The company’s profits on Friday were bolstered by strong performance in its U.S. natural gas and liquids pipeline operations. Revenue from the U.S. natural gas pipelines division more than doubled, reaching C$879 million. For the second quarter ending June 30, net income attributable to shareholders climbed to C$881 million, or C$1.01 per share, compared to C$365 million, or 52 Canadian cents per share, from the previous year. On an adjusted basis, the firm reported earnings of 76 Canadian cents per share, surpassing analysts’ predictions of 69 Canadian cents per share, as noted by Thomson Reuters I/B/E/S. Total revenue increased nearly 17 percent, totaling C$3.22 billion.

text: On Monday, a federal judge affirmed a law in North Carolina that mandates voters present specific forms of photo identification at polling stations, marking a significant success for Republicans in an election year as they assert the necessity of the law to thwart fraud. This case examined a crucial element of extensive voting restrictions enacted following a 2013 U.S. Supreme Court decision that determined North Carolina and other states with histories of discrimination no longer required federal oversight for changes in voting regulations affecting minority populations. In a 485-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Thomas Schroeder in Winston-Salem sided with Republican Governor Pat McCrory and other state officials, dismissing the law's challenges, stating that North Carolina “has provided legitimate state interests for its voter-ID requirement and electoral system.” Judge Schroeder further commented, “In sum, plaintiffs have failed to show that any North Carolinian who wishes to vote faces anything other than the ‘usual burdens of voting.’” The law faced opposition from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and individual voters, supported by the U.S. Justice Department, who contended that the legislation disproportionately affected African-Americans and Hispanics, demographics more likely than whites to lack acceptable identification. Democrats contend that voter ID laws enacted by Republican-led state legislatures aim to disenfranchise voters who typically lean Democratic. Advocates of such laws argue they are essential to prevent electoral fraud. The trial held in Winston-Salem was part of numerous significant voting rights disputes nationwide as the battle for the White House intensifies between Democrats and Republicans ahead of the November elections. In response to the ruling, Governor McCrory, facing a challenging re-election campaign this year, stated: “This ruling further affirms that requiring a photo ID in order to vote is not only common-sense, it’s constitutional.” According to the North Carolina legislation, voters must display accepted forms of identification, such as a driver's license or passport, prior to voting. Those who claim a “reasonable impediment” to acquiring such identification are permitted to vote using a provisional ballot. Additionally, Schroeder maintained provisions that removed a week of early voting, eliminated same-day registration, and barred the counting of ballots cast out of precinct. He pointed out that the plaintiffs did not demonstrate that African-Americans or Hispanics had lesser opportunities than others to engage in the electoral process, highlighting that North Carolina is one of the few states, alongside South Carolina, to offer voters the “reasonable impediment” option. Opponents of the law expressed intentions to file an appeal. William Barber, the president of the North Carolina State Conference of the NAACP, denounced the law's “restrictive provisions” as “an affront to democracy” and pledged to continue opposing “regressive and discriminatory voter suppression tactics.”

(Reuters) - A federal judge upheld a North Carolina law on Monday that requires voters to show certain forms of photo identification at the polls, in a key victory for Republicans in a presidential election year who say the law is needed to prevent fraud. The case tested a central piece of broad voting restrictions passed after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 2013 that North Carolina and other states with a history of discrimination no longer needed federal approval for voting law changes affecting minorities. In siding with Republican Governor Pat McCrory and other state officials in dismissing challenges to the law, U.S. District Judge Thomas Schroeder in Winston-Salem wrote in a 485-page ruling that North Carolina “has provided legitimate state interests for its voter-ID requirement and electoral system.”  “In sum, plaintiffs have failed to show that any North Carolinian who wishes to vote faces anything other than the ‘usual burdens of voting,’” Schroeder wrote. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and individual voters backed by the U.S. Justice Department had argued that the law disproportionately burdened African-Americans and Hispanics, who are more likely than whites to lack the acceptable forms of identification. Democrats argue voter ID laws passed by Republican-led state legislatures target voters who typically support the Democratic party. Proponents of the measures say they are intended to prevent voter fraud. The trial in Winston-Salem was one of a number of closely watched voting rights battles across the country playing out as Democrats and Republicans fight for the White House in November. Governor McCrory, locked in a tough race for re-election this year, said in a statement: “This ruling further affirms that requiring a photo ID in order to vote is not only common-sense, it’s constitutional.” The North Carolina law requires voters to show approved credentials such as a driver’s license or passport before casting a ballot. Voters who cite a “reasonable impediment” to obtaining such identification are allowed to cast a provisional ballot.  Schroeder also upheld provisions that eliminated a week of early voting, same-day registration, and prohibited the counting of out-of-precinct ballots. Schroeder said that the plaintiffs did not establish that blacks or Hispanics had less opportunity than others to participate in the electoral process, and pointed out that North Carolina joins only South Carolina in extending voters the “reasonable impediment” accommodation. Opponents of the law said they would pursue an appeal.  William Barber, president of the North Carolina State Conference of the NAACP, called the “restrictive provisions” in the law “an affront to democracy” and vowed to continue the fight against “regressive and discriminatory voter suppression tactics.”

text: On Thursday, a suspected U.S. drone strike reportedly hit a hideout belonging to the Haqqani militant network in Pakistan, resulting in the deaths of four individuals, according to officials. If this is verified, it would mark the fourth U.S. drone operation within Pakistan since the inauguration of President Donald Trump in January. Local government officials and two intelligence sources from Pakistan indicated that an unmanned aircraft launched two missiles at a compound where militants were located, overseen by a senior commander, Abdur Rasheed Haqqani. Initial reports from villagers described a loud explosion in the Upper Kurram region, with one official stating, "We received information from our informant later that it was a U.S. drone that aimed at the Haqqanis." The identity of the victims, including whether the commander was among those killed, remains unclear, as the sources requested anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the situation. Trump's recent strategy regarding the Afghanistan conflict advocates for a more aggressive approach towards Pakistan concerning militants like the Haqqani network, who are believed to operate from within Pakistani territory. Following the review of U.S. policy on Afghanistan, there has been increased pressure on Islamabad to take substantial measures against the Haqqani militants, notorious for utilizing Pakistani land to orchestrate assaults against American-led NATO forces in Afghanistan. Islamabad has rejected these claims, instead holding Kabul responsible for failing to eliminate militants who launch attacks on Pakistan from Afghan soil. For over a decade, Pakistan has been grappling with severe Islamist violence. Just Wednesday, gunmen targeted a minority Shiite mosque in the capital, Islamabad, leading to the deaths of two individuals. The Sunni extremist group Lashkar-e-Jhangvi al-Alami, linked to the Islamic State, has taken responsibility for this attack.

Two Pakistani intelligence officials and a local government officer said an unmanned aerial vehicle dropped two missiles on a compound housing  militants under the command of a senior network commander, Abdur Rasheed Haqqani.  Villagers initially reported a blast in the Upper Kurram area to authorities, said one of the officials, adding,  We got it from our informant later that it was a U.S. drone strike that targeted Haqqanis.    It was not clear if the commander was among those killed, added the officials, who sought anonymity as the issue is a sensitive one. Trump s new strategy for the Afghanistan war calls for a tougher stance with Pakistan against militants such as the Haqqani network who have bases inside Pakistan. Islamabad denies the allegations, and, instead, blames Kabul for not taking out militants who use Afghan territory as a base for attacks on targets in Pakistan. Lashkar-e-Jhangvi al-Alami, a Sunni sectarian group linked with militant group Islamic State, claimed responsibility for the mosque attack.

text: On Monday, Taiwan communicated to the United States its desire to avoid provoking any issues in the Taiwan Strait. James Soong, the island's representative at a gathering of Asia-Pacific leaders, made this declaration. He shared with journalists in the Vietnamese city of Danang over the weekend that he engaged in productive discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Rex Tillerson during informal intervals of the summit. Soong remarked, "We don’t want to create trouble in the Taiwan Strait, and lead the U.S., China and Japan, and all observers, to think we are a troublemaker. The whole world doesn’t hope for Taiwan to be a troublemaker." He further added that the intention is to resolve pertinent issues through peaceful means. Additionally, Soong noted he had a "natural interaction" with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Relations between Beijing and Taipei have significantly deteriorated since the election of President Tsai Ing-wen last year. China is convinced that she aims for formal independence for Taiwan, which is a crucial point for Beijing. In contrast, Tsai maintains that her goal is to ensure peace with China while defending Taiwan's democracy and security. Since Tsai took office, China has halted a regular dialogue framework with Taiwan and has intensified military activities in the vicinity of the island. Furthermore, it has increased diplomatic pressure by gaining support from two more of Taiwan's diminishing number of allies. Soong, who leads the China-friendly People First Party, highlighted during the summit that Tsai has consistently emphasized the importance of pursuing peaceful relations and stability with China. Earlier this month, Xi conveyed to Trump in Beijing that Taiwan remains the most critical and sensitive matter in Sino-U.S. relations.
source_text: Taiwan tells U.S. it does not want to cause trouble in Taiwan Strait. TAIPEI (Reuters) - Taiwan has assured the United States it has no intention of causing trouble in the Taiwan Strait, the self-ruled island s envoy to a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders said on Monday.  The comments by James Soong came after he told reporters in the Vietnamese city of Danang at the weekend that he had good exchanges with both U.S. President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Rex Tillerson during informal moments between summit events.  We don t want to create trouble in the Taiwan Strait, and lead the U.S., China and Japan, and all observers, to think we are a troublemaker. The whole world doesn t hope for Taiwan to be a troublemaker,  Soong said in response to a question on his interactions with Trump and Tillerson.  We hope to use peaceful means to solve relevant problems.  Soong also said he had a  natural interaction  with Chinese President Xi Jinping.  Relations between Beijing and Taipei have nosedived since President Tsai Ing-wen was elected last year. China believes she wants formal independence for Taiwan, a red line for Beijing. For her part, Tsai says she wants to maintain peace with China but will defend Taiwan s democracy and security. China has suspended a regular dialogue mechanism with Taiwan since Tsai came to power and stepped up military exercises around the island. It has also increased diplomatic pressure by winning over another two of the island s dwindling number of diplomatic allies. Soong, who is chairman of the China-friendly People First Party, emphasized at the summit that Tsai had repeatedly talked about seeking peaceful relations and stability with China. This month, Xi told Trump in Beijing that Taiwan was the most important and sensitive issue in Sino-U.S. ties.

text: On Thursday, a new version of the healthcare bill was unveiled by Republican leaders in the U.S. Senate. This revised draft keeps significant taxes on high earners and permits insurance companies to market plans that do not adhere to the regulations set by Obamacare, which require coverage for specific health services. Additionally, the legislation maintains the limits placed by Obamacare on corporate tax deductions for executive salaries within the health insurance sector. It allocates $45 billion more to address the opioid crisis and provides an extra $70 billion to assist with out-of-pocket medical costs. Furthermore, the Medicaid reforms from the original proposal remain largely untouched, raising concerns among moderate Republicans about the potential loss of insurance for many vulnerable constituents.
source_text: Senate Republican leaders release revised version of healthcare bill. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Senate Republican leaders released a new draft of their healthcare bill on Thursday that retains key taxes on the wealthy and allows insurers to offer plans that do not comply with Obamacare regulations that mandate they cover certain health services.  The bill also keeps Obamacare’s limit on corporate tax deductions for executive pay in the health insurance industry, includes an additional $45 billion for the opioid epidemic and includes an additional $70 billion to help cover out-of-pocket medical expenses. It also left the Medicaid overhaul in the initial bill largely unchanged, which drew opposition from moderate Republicans concerned it would throw many of their most vulnerable residents off their health insurance.

text: A Lebanese taxi operator, previously arrested for substance abuse, has admitted to the murder of a British worker at the British Embassy in Beirut, according to a high-ranking Lebanese security official on Monday. Another security source indicated that initial investigations into the homicide of Rebecca Dykes revealed that the motive was strictly criminal rather than political. The individual, employed by the Uber taxi service, reportedly confessed to the act immediately after its occurrence early on Saturday, as stated by the source. The senior security official disclosed that the suspect is 41 years old and had faced drug-related charges between 2015 and 2017, which may not appear on his official judicial record. The second security source mentioned that the suspect has a criminal history but did not provide further specifics. The suspect was identified by the Lebanese state news agency NNA as Tariq H, noting that he had picked up Dykes in his taxi from the Gemmayzeh area of Beirut on Friday evening before he assaulted and killed her. Uber has refrained from confirming the identity of the suspect or the duration of his employment with the service. This event has intensified concerns regarding the safety of Uber services in various nations worldwide. "We are horrified by this senseless act of violence. Our hearts are with the victim and her family," stated Uber spokesman Harry Porter. "We are collaborating with authorities to support their investigation in every possible way." Porter emphasized that in Lebanon, the company employs taxi drivers with commercial licenses, and the government is responsible for conducting background checks and issuing licenses. He asserted that only those drivers with clean background checks and judicial records are authorized to operate, adding that the suspect's background check did not reveal any convictions; otherwise, he would not have received a license. Authorities tracked the suspect's vehicle using highway surveillance cameras, according to police reports. They mentioned only that a suspect had been apprehended and reiterated that it was not a politically motivated crime. According to a security source on Sunday, Dykes was strangled and her body was discovered alongside a major highway outside Beirut. She served at the British Embassy in the Department for International Development. "The entire embassy is profoundly shocked and saddened by this news," remarked Britain's ambassador to Lebanon, Hugo Shorter, on Sunday. "We are heartbroken by the loss of our dear Rebecca," the family of Dykes expressed in a statement. "We are doing everything possible to understand what transpired." In September, Uber, based in San Francisco, lost its operating license in London due to serious concerns regarding its handling of criminal offense reporting and driver background checks. In India, the firm faced two lawsuits from a woman who was assaulted by an Uber driver in 2014, one for allegedly failing to uphold basic safety standards and another for improperly accessing her medical records. The driver was convicted of the crime and received a life sentence in 2015. Uber resolved the first lawsuit and has consented to settle the second. In Brazil, a policy allowing cash payments for rides made drivers vulnerable to robbery and murder. Following an investigation by Reuters, Uber introduced new safety protocols in February, which included requiring new cash users to register with a social security number. Additionally, a city investigation in Houston, Texas, in 2016 revealed that Uber's background checks were so inadequate that the company had cleared drivers with extensive criminal backgrounds, including murder, assault, and 17 other offenses. Uber is currently grappling with numerous challenges, including allegations of sexual misconduct, breaches of data privacy, and a lawsuit along with a criminal inquiry over suspected trade-secrets theft. The new CEO, Dara Khosrowshahi, who succeeded co-founder Travis Kalanick in August, has been vocal about addressing past shortcomings and intends to usher in a new era of compliance. The company is in the process of a stock sale, during which Softbank Group is set to acquire a stake.

In September, San Francisco-based Uber was stripped of its operating license in London over concerns about its approach to reporting serious criminal offences and background checks on drivers.  In India, the company was sued twice by a woman who was raped in 2014 by an Uber driver, first for failing to maintain basic safety procedures and again alleging executives improperly obtained her medical records. In Brazil, a company policy of accepting cash payments for rides made drivers the target of robbery and murder. text: On Wednesday, former President Barack Obama presented the design concepts for his presidential center in Chicago, aiming to create a hub for nurturing future leaders. The Obama Presidential Center is set to rise in Jackson Park, which spans 500 acres (200 hectares) on the South Side of Chicago. This park was originally established as the location for the World’s Fair in 1893. The project will comprise three distinct structures: a museum, a forum, and a library, all surrounding a central plaza. The museum, standing as the tallest among the trio, will encompass public spaces, offices, classrooms, and exhibition areas, according to a statement from the Obama Foundation.  "Our aspiration is to establish this as the world’s foremost institution dedicated to cultivating young leaders who can effect change within their communities, nations, and globally. This is our vision," Obama expressed during the unveiling event in Chicago. Since departing from the presidency in January, Obama has gradually returned to the public sphere. Last month marked his first significant public engagement since leaving the White House when he moderated an event at the University of Chicago. Obama indicated that the project is expected to take roughly four years to finish, while educational initiatives will kick off this year. Additionally, he announced on Wednesday that he would contribute $2 million to a community summer jobs program. Though Obama was raised in Hawaii and attended college in New York and California, he spent the majority of his pre-presidential political career in Chicago, beginning as a community organizer, then serving as an Illinois state senator, followed by a U.S. senator. Chicago was selected over competing bids from New York City and Hawaii to host the library. Last year, the design firms Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects Partners from New York and Interactive Design Architects from Chicago were chosen to spearhead the project. Residents in the South Side of Chicago, a region characterized by poverty and crime, are hopeful that the library will bring jobs and investment. However, some local businesses fear they might be displaced due to rising rental costs. Obama remarked that this center has the potential to significantly transform the community.

text: In a recent development, President-elect Donald Trump and U.S. intelligence chief James Clapper provided conflicting narratives regarding a phone discussion centered on a dossier containing unverified and scandalous allegations that connect Trump to Russia. Trump, who is set to assume control of the intelligence agencies in a mere eight days, has had a contentious relationship with these agencies, having challenged their assessments for several months. These assessments claim that Russia engaged in hacking and other methods to influence the outcome of the 2016 presidential election in Trump's favor. On Wednesday, Trump conceded this fact but simultaneously ignited a new controversy by reacting to media reports that included unverified claims of compromising situations involving him in Russia. He accused the intelligence community of employing tactics reminiscent of those used by Nazi Germany. In a statement released on Wednesday night, Clapper, who serves as the director of national intelligence, expressed his disappointment regarding the leaks to the press during his conversation with Trump. Clapper maintained that he did not think the leaks originated from U.S. intelligence agencies. Furthermore, Clapper reiterated to Trump that the report had not been generated by U.S. intelligence and emphasized that they had yet to assess the reliability of the information. However, he stopped short of declaring the document false. Conversely, Trump indicated in a tweet on Thursday that Clapper had concurred that the report was incorrect. Trump wrote, "James Clapper called me yesterday to denounce the false and fictitious report that was illegally circulated. Made up, phony facts. Too bad!" Democratic Congressman Adam Schiff, who opposes Trump and is a prominent figure in the Democratic Party, was questioned by CNN on Thursday morning regarding Trump’s interpretation of Clapper’s remarks about the document's validity. Schiff responded, "Sadly, you cannot rely on the president-elect’s tweets or statements about what he’s receiving in intelligence briefings. And that’s a real problem. If people really want to know what Director Clapper had to say to Donald Trump, do not rely on Donald Trump’s tweets, rely on Director Clapper’s statement." In a press conference held prior to his conversation with Clapper, Trump accused U.S. intelligence agencies of leaking the document to the press. According to two U.S. officials, the allegations concerning Trump, which one referred to as "unsubstantiated," were included in a two-page memo that was attached to a report on Russian interference in the 2016 election that was presented to both Trump and President Barack Obama. CNN reported on the memo's existence on Tuesday. BuzzFeed later released a more detailed 35-page document created by a former British foreign intelligence agent that detailed allegations of compromising behavior by Trump and his supposed connections with individuals in Russia. These claims were part of opposition research documents prepared for Trump’s political opponents during the 2016 election campaign.

text: In the coming days, a memo from the White House is anticipated to reach the Pentagon regarding the implementation of a ban on transgender individuals in the armed forces. A U.S. official disclosed on Wednesday that this document outlines how Defense Secretary Jim Mattis might determine if service members should be discharged based on their deployability. The two-and-a-half-page memo gives Mattis a period of six months to carry out the full enactment of the ban, as originally reported by The Wall Street Journal and confirmed by the official. Furthermore, it instructs the Department of Defense to prohibit the enlistment of transgender individuals and halt funding for medical treatment for those who are currently active, according to the Journal, which cited sources within the U.S. government. The primary legal rationale that Mattis is expected to employ for deciding the separation of service members from military service will center around their ability to deploy, which encompasses serving in combat zones, engaging in military exercises, or living aboard a naval vessel for extended periods, as indicated by the Journal. On July 26, President Donald Trump tweeted that the government of the United States “will not accept or allow transgender individuals to serve in any capacity” within the military, marking a significant shift from previous Pentagon policies. This unexpected declaration, which cited the costs associated with healthcare and the potential for disruption within units, resonated with segments of Trump’s conservative base, but it also generated uncertainty for numerous transgender service members, many of whom had come out following the Pentagon's 2016 announcement permitting transgender individuals to serve openly. Earlier this month, five transgender military personnel, including veterans of the Iraq and Afghanistan conflicts, filed a lawsuit against Trump, alleging that the ban was instituted without dialogue with high-ranking military officials. The lawsuit lists Trump, Mattis, and other military leaders, such as Joseph Dunford, who chairs the Joint Chiefs of Staff, as defendants. Following Trump’s tweets, Dunford issued a memo stating that there would be no policy alterations until Mattis received an official directive from the president. Stephen Peters, a representative from the Human Rights Campaign, an organization advocating for LGBTQ rights, reacted on Twitter, asserting: “This proves @realdonaldtrump knows nothing about what it means to be #transgender or to serve in the military. Trans service members already do deploy, proving repeatedly what matters is their ability to accomplish the mission, not gender identity.” In 2016, the Obama administration reversed the transgender ban, allowing currently serving transgender individuals to begin serving openly right away, but set July 1, 2017, as the date for new enlistments of openly transgender individuals.
