text: A U.S. appeals court has permitted attorneys general from Democratic states to defend subsidy payments to insurance companies as outlined in the Obamacare healthcare legislation. This aspect of funding is essential for the law, which President Donald Trump has indicated he might terminate. On Tuesday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit approved a motion from 16 attorneys general, spearheaded by California's Xavier Becerra and New York's Eric Schneiderman. Trump, exasperated by his inability, along with fellow Republicans in Congress, to fulfill promises to repeal and replace Obamacare, has issued threats to cease the so-called cost-sharing subsidy (CSR) payments. A statement from the White House mentioned, "The President is working with his staff and his cabinet to consider the issues raised by the CSR payments." These subsidies assist low-income Americans in managing out-of-pocket medical costs. The litigation, originating during President Barack Obama's administration, was initiated by the Republican-led House of Representatives against the federal government, aiming to halt the subsidy payments to insurers for individual plans established by the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare. The court's ruling now allows Democrats supportive of the law to participate in the legal proceedings, providing them with the capability to obstruct a settlement or challenge any ruling that halts the payments. They are also permitted to submit briefs and have their attorneys engage in oral discussions. Schneiderman remarked in a statement, "The court's decision is good news for the hundreds of thousands of New York families that rely on these subsidies for their health care. It’s disturbingly clear that President Trump and his administration are willing to treat them as political pawns." Becerra stated, "If Donald Trump won’t defend these vital subsidies for American families, then we will." The panel of three judges, all appointed by Obama, stated in their order that the states had demonstrated "a substantial risk that an injunction requiring termination of the payments at issue here ... would lead directly and imminently to an increase in insurance prices, which in turn will increase the number of uninsured individuals for whom the states will have to provide health care." Furthermore, the court order indicated, "In addition, state-funded hospitals will suffer financially when they are unable to recoup costs from uninsured, indigent patients for whom federal law requires them to provide medical care." Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan, commented that this ruling is significant as it complicates the Trump administration's ability to settle the case. He noted, "Allowing the states to intervene will increase the pressure on the administration to keep making the cost-sharing payments," while also acknowledging that the administration could still opt to halt the payments. Trump has consistently warned about withholding these payments to insurers, which are estimated to be around $7 billion this year, referring to them as a "bailout." In their May court filing, the attorneys general pointed to Trump’s own statements where he vowed to let Obamacare “explode” as a basis for their intervention. Currently, the case is on hold due to a request from both parties involved. Initially, it was anticipated that the case would be dismissed since the Republican-controlled Congress was gearing up to repeal the Obamacare law. However, that attempt fell short last week, resulting in the court case gaining renewed significance. State officials mentioned on Tuesday that U.S. health insurer Anthem Inc is withdrawing from 16 out of 19 pricing regions in California where it had provided Obamacare options this year, partly due to uncertainty surrounding the payments.

text: On Monday, a prominent figure in French conservatism, Xavier Bertrand, announced his departure from The Republicans, the nation's primary conservative party. Bertrand's exit follows the overwhelming election of Wauquiez as the new leader just a day prior, during which Wauquiez criticized President Emmanuel Macron for being insufficiently robust on matters of security and immigration. "I don’t recognize my political family, so I decided to leave it," Bertrand expressed during an interview on France 2. His resignation highlights the increasing unease among moderate factions within The Republicans regarding the party's trajectory, especially after a disappointing presidential campaign that saw its candidate unable to progress beyond the initial round. Concerns have been raised that Wauquiez is steering the party too far rightward, in pursuit of support from the National Front, whose leader Marine Le Pen advanced to the second round of the presidential election last May. In response to Bertrand's departure, Wauquiez remarked on TF1, "Xavier Bertrand obviously considers that he has no place (in the party). It’s his choice. I respect it. I move forward, I look to the future and what I want is to make a new generation emerge, this new right that lives to its ideas."

text: On Wednesday, the U.S. Senate officially appointed Rex Tillerson as the secretary of state for President Donald Trump, a significant role in the Republican's national security apparatus, despite worries regarding the former chief executive officer of Exxon Mobil Corp's connections to Russia. This vote, which largely followed party affiliation, marked the narrowest confirmation in at least fifty years. The result showed 56 senators in favor and 43 against. All Republican senators supported Tillerson, along with four Democrats: Senators Heidi Heitkamp, Joe Manchin, Mark Warner, and the independent Angus King. Notably, Democratic Senator Chris Coons abstained from voting. In contrast, Tillerson’s predecessor, John Kerry, received a confirmation vote of 94 to 3, while Condoleezza Rice, the last Republican-nominated secretary of state, was confirmed with an 85-13 vote. Senate Democrats attempted to postpone the confirmation of Tillerson due to Trump's recent executive order that halted immigration from seven predominantly Muslim nations and temporarily ceased the entry of refugees. They expressed a desire to pose additional questions to Tillerson about this executive order, which had led to protests and disarray at airports nationwide, causing confusion and disruption for travelers globally. However, with Republicans holding a 52-seat majority in the 100-member Senate, they have successfully confirmed all six nominees from Trump who have been presented for votes thus far. Concerns regarding Tillerson’s connections to Russia were also raised, stemming from his extended tenure at the oil firm. Critics pointed out that he did not guarantee to recuse himself from any matters related to Exxon Mobil for the entirety of his tenure as secretary of state, but only for the legally mandated one year. At the age of 64, Tillerson retired as the chairman and chief executive of Exxon Mobil at the close of 2016, following a 40-year career with the organization. Supporters of Tillerson, including Republicans, asserted that he would excel as the nation’s leading diplomat, highlighting his experience managing a large corporation across six continents. They also emphasized the necessity of quickly solidifying Trump’s national security team to effectively respond to global challenges and to reassure allies about the new president’s “America First” foreign policy.
source_text: U.S. Senate confirms Tillerson as secretary of state. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. Senate confirmed Rex Tillerson as President Donald Trump’s secretary of state on Wednesday, filling a key spot on the Republican’s national security team despite concerns about the former Exxon Mobil Corp chief executive officer’s ties to Russia. The vote, mostly along party lines, was by far the closest in at least half a century.  Fifty-six senators backed Tillerson, and 43 voted no. Every Republican favored Tillerson, along with four members of the Democratic caucus, Senators Heidi Heitkamp, Joe Manchin and Mark Warner as well as Angus King, an independent. Democratic Senator Chris Coons did not vote. Tillerson’s predecessor in the position, John Kerry, was confirmed by 94 to 3. Condoleezza Rice, the last secretary of state nominated by a Republican, was confirmed by 85-13. Senate Democrats had tried, but failed, to delay the vote on Tillerson because of Trump’s executive order banning immigration from seven mostly Muslim countries and temporarily halting the entry of refugees. They said they wanted to ask Tillerson more questions about the issue after Trump signed the order on Friday, prompting protests and chaos at airports across the country and uncertainty and disruption for travelers around the world. But Republicans hold a majority of 52 seats in the 100-member Senate, and so far have confirmed all of the six Trump nominees who have come up for votes. Senators had also expressed concerns over Tillerson’s ties to Russia after the executive spent years there working for the oil company. Some faulted him for failing to promise to recuse himself from matters related to Exxon Mobil businesses for his entire term as secretary of state rather than only the one year required by law. Tillerson, 64, retired as chairman and chief executive of Exxon Mobil at the end of 2016 after a four-decade career at the company.  Republicans and other Tillerson supporters said they thought he would be a strong leader as the country’s top diplomat, citing his experience running a giant corporation operating on six continents. They also said it was important to finalize Trump’s national security team quickly, to address international crises and reassure allies wondering about the new president’s “America First” foreign policy.

text: On Tuesday, U.S. Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid expressed the need for amendments to a bill addressing Puerto Rico's debt, which Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell indicated would be brought to a vote the following week. Reid informed the press that alterations were necessary regarding the federal oversight board responsible for managing the restructuring of Puerto Rico’s $70 billion debt, although he did not specify if Democrats would be able to implement any modifications. The House of Representatives had approved a bill for Puerto Rico's debt relief on June 9, after extensive discussions. Advocates are optimistic that the Senate will endorse this legislation without any changes before the approaching July 1 deadline, by which Puerto Rico must make a $1.9 billion debt payment. The island, a territory of the United States, is grappling with a poverty rate nearing 45 percent and is facing escalating debt crises. Numerous schools and health facilities are shutting down, prompting thousands of residents to relocate to the mainland U.S., which is further diminishing Puerto Rico’s tax revenues. Reid articulated that he has “some serious concerns” regarding the current legislation, which was arranged by the Obama administration along with House lawmakers, yet he did not indicate his expectations for the success of any amendments in the Senate. A debate in the Senate concerning these amendments may serve primarily to allow Democrats to formally express their reservations about the proposed legislation. “At the very minimum, we need some amendments to make sure that people understand what is not in that bill,” Reid remarked. Democrats across both chambers have raised alarms about possible minimum-wage cuts for young workers included in the House version of the bill. Furthermore, they have expressed doubts regarding whether the federal oversight board, to be designated by Washington, would prioritize Puerto Rico’s best interests. Proponents of the bill contend that it represents the most viable solution that can pass through the Republican-controlled Congress, warning that without intervention, Puerto Rico could descend into disorder.

text: On Thursday, the United States announced it would prolong certain sanctions relief for Iran in accordance with the 2015 nuclear agreement, although a decision on the future of the deal itself remains pending, as stated by the State Department. President Donald Trump, who faces a mid-October deadline that could jeopardize the agreement, accused Iran of breaching the spirit of the 2015 pact which granted sanctions relief in exchange for limitations on its nuclear activities. In a demonstration of his intent to increase pressure on Iran, which refutes the allegation of violating the agreement, the U.S. Treasury unveiled additional cyber-related sanctions along with other penalties targeting seven individuals from Iran, alongside two Iranian organizations and two entities based in Ukraine. "We are not going to stand for what they are doing," Trump expressed to journalists aboard Air Force One. However, he did not clarify whether he would choose to recertify the agreement. In October, Trump needs to make a determination about certifying Iran's compliance with the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). Should he fail to do so, Congress will have a period of 60 days to deliberate on the re-imposition of sanctions that were suspended under the deal. Concerns regarding the potential U.S. withdrawal from the agreement have arisen among several crucial allies involved in its negotiation, particularly as the global community deals with another nuclear challenge presented by North Korea's development of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles. Republican Senator Bob Corker, who leads the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and was instrumental in drafting the legislation that grants Congress authority to review the Iran deal, indicated that he and the White House were preparing for a potential policy shift. He emphasized the importance of collaborating with allies. "I think it’s important that... we take steps that, to the extent we can, we keep all of our allies together," Corker told Reuters. "What you don’t want to do is self-create a crisis for no reason. You want to ensure that you have an outcome that is favorable for the United States and our interests." When asked whether it would be prudent to abandon the Iran nuclear agreement in light of concerns regarding North Korea, Corker remarked, "I don’t think you should prejudge what they’re (the administration) going to do." Meanwhile, U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson contended that the United States must evaluate the comprehensive threat that it attributes to Iran in the Middle East while developing its new strategy concerning Tehran, asserting that Iran has contravened the spirit of the agreement. "We have to consider the totality of Iran’s activities and not let our view be defined solely by the nuclear agreement," he stated at a press conference in London. Referring to the introduction of the 2015 agreement, Tillerson asserted that "in our view, Iran is clearly in default of these expectations." He pointed to Iran's support for Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad, its advancements in ballistic missile technology, and its cyber operations as evidence. The preface of the agreement does not compel Iran to promote global peace but rather indicates that the nations involved expect that full realization of this JCPOA will positively contribute to regional and international peace and security. Heather Nauert, spokesperson for the State Department, informed reporters that the administration had sanctioned waivers for certain measures against Iran to allow for some flexibility as it formulates its Iran policy. However, she did not detail which specific sanctions had been waived. Earlier reports indicated that the United States would continue to renew a waiver for the most stringent sanctions against Iran. Embedded within Section 1245 of the 2012 National Defense Authorization Act, Washington warned that it would impose sanctions on banks of Iran’s primary oil clients if they did not significantly reduce their purchases of Iranian oil. According to this law, these sanctions can be waived for a maximum duration of 120 days, which requires the U.S. government to revisit the issue every four months. While the administration permitted waivers for oil-related sanctions, the Treasury Department declared it had imposed sanctions on 11 entities and individuals for their involvement in supporting designated Iranian actors or engaging in malicious cyber-enabled actions.

text: The following account outlines the history of the Zika virus, detailing its emergence and international proliferation over the past nearly seven decades. In 1947, a research team investigating yellow fever in Uganda's Zika Forest discovered the virus in a rhesus monkey. The next year, a sample of the virus was retrieved from an Aedes africanus mosquito in the same Zika Forest. By 1952, the first human infections were reported in Uganda and Tanzania. In 1954, the virus was identified in Nigeria. Between the 1960s and the 1980s, Zika was detected in various mosquitoes and monkeys throughout equatorial Africa. From 1969 to 1983, the virus spread to equatorial Asia, affecting countries such as India, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Pakistan. In 2007, Zika made its way out of Africa and Asia, resulting in the first significant outbreak on the Pacific island of Yap. In 2012, scientists distinguished two separate strains of the virus: one from Africa and the other from Asia. During 2013 and 2014, outbreaks were recorded in French Polynesia, Easter Island, the Cook Islands, and New Caledonia. A retrospective investigation revealed a potential connection between Zika infections and severe neurological issues and birth defects in infants from French Polynesia. On March 2, 2015, Brazil reported a surge in illnesses characterized by skin rashes in its northeastern regions. By July 17, Brazil had noted the emergence of neurological disorders in newborns linked to a history of Zika infection. On October 5, Cape Verde recorded cases of illness featuring skin rashes. Then, on October 22, Colombia confirmed instances of Zika virus infection. Brazil announced an increase in microcephaly, a condition characterized by abnormally small heads among newborns, on October 30. Subsequently, on November 11, Brazil declared a public health emergency. Between November 2015 and January 2016, numerous cases emerged in Suriname, Panama, El Salvador, Mexico, Guatemala, Paraguay, Venezuela, French Guiana, Martinique, Puerto Rico, Guyana, Ecuador, Barbados, Bolivia, the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua, Curacao, and Jamaica. On February 1, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a public health emergency of international concern. The following day, the first instance of Zika transmission within the United States was reported, with local health officials indicating that it likely occurred through sexual contact rather than a mosquito bite. By February 5, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported that the virus was actively spreading in 30 countries, primarily in the Americas. On February 8, President Barack Obama requested $1.8 billion to combat Zika. On February 12, Brazilian authorities began investigating a possible relationship between Zika infections and 4,314 suspected cases of microcephaly, confirming 462 as microcephaly and linking 41 of those to the virus. On February 17, Brazil continued to research the potential association between Zika and 4,443 suspected cases of microcephaly, confirming 508 cases of microcephaly, most of which were linked to the virus. The WHO requested $56 million for Zika response efforts. On February 18, the CDC added Aruba and Bonaire to the list of countries and territories experiencing active outbreaks, raising the total to 32. On February 23, the CDC investigated 14 cases that suggested possible sexual transmission of Zika, while also including Trinidad and Tobago and the Marshall Islands in the list of affected areas, which brought the total to 34. On February 25, Brazil reported that confirmed cases of microcephaly had exceeded 580, with most linked to maternal Zika infections, while an additional 4,100 suspected cases were under investigation. On February 27, France identified its first case of sexually transmitted Zika. By February 29, the CDC added St. Maarten and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines to the list of regions with active outbreaks, raising the overall total to 36. On March 1, Brazil announced that confirmed microcephaly cases had risen to 641, most of which were related to maternal Zika infections, with 4,222 additional suspected cases under investigation. On March 8, the WHO recommended that pregnant women avoid areas where Zika was spreading and stated that sexual transmission of the virus was "relatively common." On March 9, the CDC included New Caledonia in the list of regions experiencing active outbreaks, increasing the total to 37. On March 15, Cuba reported its first case of Zika contracted within the nation. The next day, March 16, Cape Verde recognized its first instance of microcephaly. Finally, on March 18, the CDC announced that between January 1, 2015, and February 26, 2016, 116 residents in the United States tested positive for recent Zika virus infections based on laboratory results.

text: On Tuesday, Donald Trump unveiled a controversial strategy aimed at compelling Mexico to finance his proposed border wall. The Republican presidential candidate indicated that he would threaten to halt remittances sent by illegal immigrants to their home country, which he characterized as a form of "welfare" that the Mexican government fails to provide to impoverished families. According to a memo from Trump’s campaign, should he win the election scheduled for November, he plans to utilize a U.S. anti-terrorism statute to prevent such financial transfers unless Mexico agrees to make a one-off payment ranging from $5 billion to $10 billion to fund the wall. Trump’s commitment to constructing the barrier has been a prominent feature of his platform aimed at addressing illegal immigration in the U.S., which has significantly contributed to his status as the leading candidate for the Republican nomination ahead of the election on November 8. The total cost of a wall spanning the approximately 2,000-mile (3,200-km) border between the U.S. and Mexico remains uncertain, and Mexico has firmly stated it will not contribute financially. The memo provided further details on an idea Trump proposed in August, suggesting the seizure of all remittances linked to "illegal wages." It stated that a Trump administration would introduce a regulation requiring companies like Western Union Co (WU.N) to verify that customers are legally present in the United States before processing transactions. Should Mexico agree to fund the wall, Trump would withdraw the proposed regulation, according to the memo. His campaign asserted, "It’s an easy decision for Mexico," noting that approximately $24 billion is sent annually in remittances from Mexican nationals living in the United States, the majority of whom are undocumented. "It (remittances) serves as de facto welfare for poor families in Mexico. There is no significant social safety net provided by the state in Mexico," the campaign added. The World Bank Remittances project reported that in 2014, the last complete year with available data, the remittance flows from the U.S. to Mexico were nearly $24 billion, although it is unclear how much of that total comes from individuals living in the U.S. illegally. Democratic President Barack Obama dismissed the idea of blocking remittances as impractical and potentially counterproductive. He remarked to reporters, "The notion that we’re going to track every Western Union bit of money that’s being sent to Mexico, you know, good luck with that." Obama further stated that a collapse of Mexico’s economy would likely lead to an increase in immigration to the United States. Mexican President Enrique Pena Nieto appeared to reject Trump’s proposal, suggesting it was merely campaign rhetoric. "The (Mexican) Presidency has no comment on any opinion made in the heat of the electoral process to choose candidates for the U.S. presidency," the president’s office communicated via text message to Reuters. Any attempt to target payments sent home by individuals living in the United States could have devastating consequences for Mexico, which is the largest recipient of U.S. remittances. Trump's plan could also impact banks and wire transfer companies, including MoneyGram International Inc (MGI.O) and PayPal Holdings Inc’s (PYPL.O) Xoom. These companies did not provide comments when approached for their views. Aside from his wall initiative, Trump has accused Mexico of exporting rapists and drug traffickers to the United States. His remarks have been repeatedly condemned by Democrats and many Republicans as inflammatory; however, they have resonated strongly with his supporters, particularly white working-class voters. The memo, initially reported by The Washington Post, reiterated Trump’s campaign promises regarding visa restrictions. It also referenced imposing tariffs on trade or enforcing existing trade regulations as mechanisms to pressure Mexico into contributing funds. Benjamin Proto, a lawyer from Connecticut and Trump supporter, recognized that the remittance strategy might be unrealistic but commended the candidate for "looking at different ways to do things." This memo surfaced as rival Republican candidate Ted Cruz seemed poised to surpass Trump in Wisconsin’s primary on Tuesday, a victory that would position him as the leading alternative to the New York billionaire.

Trump’s proposal could also affect banks and companies that handle wire transfers, which also include MoneyGram International Inc (MGI.O) and PayPal Holdings Inc’s (PYPL.O) Xoom.  The companies did not respond to requests for comment. In addition to his wall proposal, Trump has accused Mexico of sending rapists and drug runners to the United States. Democrats and many Republicans have repeatedly condemned his comments as inflammatory, but his remarks have been enthusiastically received by his supporters, especially by white working-class voters. In the memo, first reported by The Washington Post, Trump’s campaign repeated its pledge to target visas. It also cited imposing trade tariffs or enforcing existing trade rules as a way of forcing Mexico to pay. Trump supporter Benjamin Proto, a Connecticut lawyer, acknowledged the remittance plan was unrealistic but praised the candidate for “looking at different ways to do things.” The memo emerged as Republican candidate Ted Cruz appeared set to beat Trump in Wisconsin’s primary contest on Tuesday, a win he would hope would mark him as the best alternative to the New York billionaire.

text: This week, the nation of Turkey has been captivated by serious allegations against its political and financial leaders, while many citizens are left craving substantial updates as some newspapers opt to report on courtroom dramas and attire instead. The front page of HaberTurk newspaper read, "Casual chic on the 2nd day," after Reza Zarrab, the key witness, testified in a New York court that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan endorsed a transaction to assist Iran in dodging U.S. sanctions. On the trial's second day, Reza Zarrab appeared not in a prison outfit but rather dressed casually in a white shirt paired with a dark blazer, as reported by HaberTurk. Like several other news outlets, HaberTurk avoided diving into the core issues at hand. Since the failed coup last year, Erdogan has overseen a crackdown affecting various sectors including the judiciary and media, resulting in numerous journalists being incarcerated. Furthermore, he has regularly pursued legal actions against individuals he perceives as having insulted him. Zarrab is working with U.S. prosecutors in the criminal trial concerning a Turkish bank executive accused of facilitating money laundering for Iran, who has declared his innocence. Erdogan, who has led Turkey for nearly 15 years, has yet to address the assertions made in court but previously characterized the case as a politically motivated endeavor aimed at undermining the Turkish administration. He asserts that the U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, blamed by Ankara for the unsuccessful military coup and referred to by Turkish authorities as FETO, is also behind these legal proceedings. The pro-government newspaper Star labeled the trial as "American Theater" on its cover. It described the Zarrab plot trial as a political spectacle orchestrated by FETO in conjunction with judges, prosecutors, and experts identified as Neo-cons and adversaries of Turkey. The limited or skeptical reporting surrounding the case has prompted inquisitive Turks to turn to Twitter, where hashtags like #Zarrabcase and #Zarrabkonusuyor (Zarrab is speaking) emerged as leading trending subjects late on Wednesday and Thursday. Since the trial commenced this week, there have been hundreds of thousands of tweets, retweets, and replies featuring Zarrab-related hashtags on the platform. "You can't see it on televisions or newspapers here. They either cut feeds or ignore it," stated Oguzcan Gundogmus, a 24-year-old doctoral candidate, while enjoying tea in central Ankara. The courtroom proceedings have resonated throughout the streets. One elderly demonstrator urged Zarrab during a women's protest in Istanbul last weekend, "Spill the beans, my son!" However, the primary focus has shifted online. The number of followers for journalists tweeting from inside the courtroom has skyrocketed over the past two days, with some increases exceeding 20 times. One court reporter's tweets are currently being translated into Turkish in real-time, attracting a following of 10,000 thus far. In court, Zarrab disclosed that he bribed various officials in Turkey as part of his operation. "I am astonished that the government hasn’t banned Twitter yet. My friends and I stay up at night following the case there, making popcorn as if it's movie night, and we’ve dubbed the case 'Lord of the Bribes,'" remarked Mehmet Baglar, a 34-year-old engineer.

text: On Thursday, President Donald Trump designated R. Alexander Acosta, a former member of the National Labor Relations Board, as his nominee for the position of U.S. Secretary of Labor. This announcement came just a day after Trump's initial selection withdrew from consideration. Acosta currently holds the position of dean at the Florida International University College of Law located in Miami and marks Trump’s first nominee of Hispanic descent. With a career spanning decades in public service, Acosta has held three positions that required presidential appointment and Senate confirmation, leading many to believe his confirmation process will proceed smoothly. Senator Lamar Alexander, who chairs the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions responsible for reviewing the nomination, expressed optimism, stating, "Mr. Acosta’s nomination is off to a good start because he’s already been confirmed by the Senate three times." Acosta's prior appointments include a role on the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) under former Republican President George W. Bush, who also made him the assistant attorney general for the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. Following that, he served as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where he targeted notable defendants including Jack Abramoff and UBS, which ultimately faced over $750 million in fines due to a tax-evasion scheme. Additionally, Acosta worked as a law clerk for Samuel Alito from 1994 to 1995, during the time Alito served as a judge on the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. In a statement, Acosta expressed gratitude, saying, "I thank the President and his staff for their confidence in me and I am eager to work tirelessly on behalf of the American worker." Throughout his tenure at the NLRB, Acosta authored hundreds of opinions. Individuals familiar with his work describe him as a diligent and prudent public servant, one whose career path indicates he may one day aspire to a federal judgeship. Given that he has already undergone multiple vetting processes by the U.S. Senate, it is improbable that any potential issues in his background will emerge to impede his nomination. The selection of Acosta, a conventional Republican conservative, is interpreted by some analysts as an indication that Trump had to abandon a more aggressive stance on labor matters. Trump’s previous nominee for labor secretary, Andrew Puzder, who was the CEO of CKE Restaurants Inc, had been vocal against issues like minimum wage increases and overtime pay, even suggesting the advantages of robots over human employees. Puzder withdrew his name from consideration on Wednesday due to worries that he might not secure sufficient Senate votes for confirmation. "This is the humbling of Donald Trump," stated Seth Harris, a former Acting Labor Secretary during the Obama era, who remarked that Puzder would have been a "radical disruptor," while Acosta would not take on such a role. Acosta has consistently defended the civil rights of Muslims who experienced discrimination following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the United States. During a congressional hearing in 2011, he commended the Justice Department's actions in response to civil rights violations, asserting that they helped reassure Muslim Americans that "their government would protect their rights." Some progressive organizations have already voiced their discontent regarding Acosta’s appointment, with Allied Progress accusing him of mismanaging the Civil Rights Division while he led it. An internal Justice Department report from 2008 criticized Acosta for not controlling a staff member who engaged in inappropriate politicized hiring. Nevertheless, the response from labor union organizations, which had firmly opposed Puzder, was considerably more measured on Thursday. AFL-CIO President Richard Trumka stated, "Unlike Andy Puzder, Alexander Acosta’s nomination deserves serious consideration." He added, "In one day, we’ve gone from a fast-food CEO who routinely violates labor law to a public servant with experience enforcing it."

text: Concerns about 'hateful rhetoric' among white nationalists were raised by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum on Monday. This reaction followed a meeting of the National Policy Institute, a think tank associated with the alt-right movement that comprises neo-Nazis, white supremacists, and anti-Semites, which took place over the weekend at the federally owned Ronald Reagan Building. A woman posted a photo on Twitter showing herself performing a Nazi salute at the gathering, prompting a restaurant to apologize for accommodating the group. The alt-right movement gained visibility during the U.S. presidential election. President-elect Donald Trump has faced backlash for appointing Steve Bannon, previously the head of a website linked to the alt-right, as his chief strategist in the White House. On Monday, Trump's transition team released a statement asserting that Trump has consistently condemned racism, according to CNN. "President-elect Trump has continued to denounce racism of any kind and he was elected because he will be a leader for every American," said spokesman Bryan Lanza in a statement regarding the transition. The event on Saturday attracted numerous protesters who obstructed traffic in the vicinity to voice their disapproval of the gathering. A video captured by The Atlantic from within the conference depicted Richard Spencer, the leader of the National Policy Institute, exclaiming, "Hail Trump, hail our people, hail victory!" while some attendees raised their arms in a Nazi salute. The Holocaust Memorial Museum released a statement emphasizing, "The Holocaust did not begin with killings: it began with words." They urged all American citizens, religious and civic leaders, and officials from all levels of government to confront racist ideologies and harmful speech. After the nationalist meeting, some participants congregated for a banquet at Maggiano’s Little Italy restaurant located in northwest Washington. This led to protesters gathering at the site, which caused the restaurant to close for the safety of both staff and patrons, as stated by the management in a Facebook apology. The restaurant clarified that the booking was made last-minute under a different name, hence the staff had no knowledge that the National Policy Institute was present and were unaware of the group's affiliations. "After the event, an attendee sent a tweet in which she made a 'Seig Heil salute' in support of Hitler and white supremacy. This expression of support for Hitler is extremely offensive to us, as our restaurant is home to teammates and guests of every race, religion and cultural background," the Facebook post explained. The establishment also apologized to the local community and announced that it would donate Friday's sales, amounting to $10,000, to the Washington office of the Anti-Defamation League, which advocates for Jewish civil rights. The Ronald Reagan Building, the largest structure in the capital of the United States, is owned by the federal government but operated by Trade Center Management Associates, a branch of Drew Co., a real estate development firm based in Boston. The company defended its decision to allow the nationalist group to use the venue, stating that their contract stipulates the building is available for rental unless a security threat is posed by the requesting organization or individual. The agenda outlined for the National Policy Institute’s meeting included a review of the 2016 election and strategies for expanding the alt-right movement. The Southern Poverty Law Center, a nonprofit organization that monitors hate groups, characterized Spencer as an "academic racist" who supports the establishment of an Aryan homeland. Last week, Twitter Inc took action by suspending multiple accounts affiliated with the alt-right, including Spencer's account. This decision followed the social media platform's announcement of enhancements aimed at better addressing cyberbullying.

The alt-right movement came to the fore during the U.S. presidential election. President-elect Donald Trump has drawn criticism for naming Steve Bannon, former head of a website linked to the alt-right, as his chief White House strategist.  Trump’s transition team issued a statement on Monday saying Trump has continued to denounce racism, CNN reported. “President-elect Trump has continued to denounce racism of any kind and he was elected because he will be a leader for every American,” Trump-Pence Transition spokesman Bryan Lanza said in a statement. The restaurant apologized to the surrounding neighborhood and said it was donating the profits from its sales on Friday, $10,000, to the Washington office of the Anti-Defamation League, a Jewish civil rights group. The Ronald Reagan Building, the biggest structure in the U.S. capital city, is federally owned, but run by Trade Center Management Associates, a unit of Drew Co., a Boston real estate development company. The firm defended allowing the nationalist group to use the venue. It said in a statement that its contract mandates that unless there is a security threat by an organization or person who asks for meeting space, the building is available for rental. text: On Tuesday, formal coalition discussions commenced among leaders of three parties from the eight that were elected during Iceland's parliamentary election on October 28, according to state broadcaster RUV. The Independence Party, along with the Left-Green Movement and the center-right Progressive Party, are aiming to establish a government after previous negotiations involving four left-leaning parties collapsed last week. By the week's end, it should be evident if any advancements have been achieved in the negotiations. President Gudni Johannesson has yet to grant any party leaders a formal mandate to attempt forming a government.
source_text: Icelandic parties from left and right begin formal coalition talks. COPENHAGEN (Reuters) - Leaders of three of the eight parties elected in Iceland in an October 28 parliamentary election began formal coalition negotiations on Tuesday, state broadcaster RUV reported. The Independence Party, the Left-Green Movement and the center-right Progressive Party, are seeking to form a government after talks between four leftist parties broke down last week. It should be clear by the end of the week whether talks have made progress. President Gudni Johannesson has not yet given any party leaders a formal mandate to try to form a government.

text: Recent discussions among top Republicans in the U.S. Congress and the Trump administration are approaching crucial determinations regarding a tax reform initiative. A government representative informed Reuters that an agreement on key elements of the tax overhaul plan is anticipated within a few weeks, with legislation expected to emerge in September. Amid mounting pressure from business sectors and rank-and-file party members, Trump officials alongside congressional leaders are still deliberating the extent of tax rate reductions and whether the proposed package would contribute to an increase in the federal budget deficit, as indicated by sources from both the administration and Congress. The fate of the border adjustment tax (BAT) proposal, introduced by House Republicans to enhance exports and diminish imports, is also likely to be resolved in the upcoming two to three weeks, according to the government representative. President Donald Trump has committed to prioritizing tax reform. However, after two decades in power and facing various distractions, he has yet to submit a tax proposal to Congress. The timeline for legislative action has been delayed multiple times, shifting from spring to summer and now to after the U.S. Labor Day holiday. Nevertheless, stock prices have risen since Trump’s electoral victory in November, prompting companies and affluent individuals to prepare for greater income in 2018, anticipating forthcoming tax reductions. On Friday, the leader of the House Freedom Caucus, a coalition of conservative members numbering around thirty-six, urged Republicans to recognize the existing lack of consensus regarding the BAT and to finalize a tax proposal by the end of July. Trump and fellow party members committed during last year's election campaign to address the most significant tax reform since the Reagan administration in 2017. However, this agenda has encountered delays due to internal conflicts over the repeal of Obamacare and inquiries into potential connections between Trump's campaign and alleged Russian interference in the 2016 elections. This week, the Business Roundtable, a significant lobbying organization representing CEOs, reached out to Trump and congressional leaders, advocating for a “transition from discussion to action” regarding tax reform. The unnamed administration official noted that there is widespread consensus among the negotiating parties on the necessity to lower taxes, streamline the tax code, eliminate tax incentives, cease taxing overseas profits of U.S. corporations, and repatriate approximately $2.6 trillion in corporate profits kept abroad. Nonetheless, vital specifics remain unsettled. Further discussions are anticipated among U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, White House economic advisor Gary Cohn, Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, House Speaker Paul Ryan, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Kevin Brady, Senate Finance Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, and their respective teams, as stated by the official. Following their third meeting on Tuesday, officials had not reached a decision concerning the implementation of full expensing for corporations, the administration official revealed. This policy would permit businesses to immediately write off capital investment expenses, such as equipment, allowing them to reinvest the funds into their operations. The objective of these discussions is to finalize a framework by mid-year and to introduce legislation promptly after the lengthy August recess for lawmakers. A significant decision looms regarding the House Republicans’ BAT, aimed at boosting exports while discouraging companies from transferring jobs, profits, and assets offshore. The BAT, which would impose taxes on imports while excluding export revenue from taxation, has faced opposition from various Republicans and has received criticism from the administration. Congressional and administration officials are exploring alternatives to the BAT that might mitigate the erosion of the federal tax base, including potential regulations and a minimum corporate tax. The resolutions concerning BAT, revenue neutrality, and expensing will influence whether Congress can reduce the corporate income tax rate to 15 percent, as Trump desires, or to 20-25 percent, as proposed in the House Republicans’ tax strategy.
source_text: White House, Congress Republicans nearing key tax overhaul decisions. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Trump administration and top Republicans in U.S. Congress are within a few weeks of agreeing on central aspects of a tax overhaul plan that will determine the contours of legislation now expected in September, an administration official told Reuters this week. President Donald Trump has pledged to make a tax overhaul a priority. But after 20 weeks in power and numerous distractions, he has yet to offer a tax bill to Congress. Expectations for legislation have slipped repeatedly, from spring to summer and now after the U.S. Labor Day holiday.   Still, stocks are up since Trump’s November election win and companies and wealthy Americans are positioning themselves to realize more income in 2018, betting lower taxes are coming. The head of the House Freedom Caucus, a bloc of three-dozen conservatives capable of stalling legislation, on Friday called on Republicans to acknowledge a lack of consensus on the BAT and produce a tax proposal by the end of July. More meetings are expected among U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, White House economic adviser Gary Cohn, Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, House Speaker Paul Ryan, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Kevin Brady and Senate Finance Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch and their staff, the official said. After their third meeting on Tuesday, officials had not decided whether to adopt full expensing for corporations, the administration official said. The policy would allow companies to write off the cost of capital investments such as equipment immediately and plow the money back into their businesses.  The official said the aim of the talks is to agree on a framework by mid-year and release legislation soon after lawmakers’ long August recess. A key decision awaits the House Republicans’ export-boosting BAT, intended to help pay for reforms while dissuading companies from moving assets, profits and jobs abroad. The BAT, which would tax imports but exempt export revenues from taxation, has run afoul of many Republicans and drawn criticism from the administration. Officials in Congress and the administration are examining options to the BAT that could reduce erosion of the federal tax base, including rules and a minimum corporate tax. Decisions on BAT, revenue neutrality and expensing will help decide if Congress can cut the corporate income tax to 15 percent, as Trump seeks, or 20-25 percent as envisioned by the House Republicans’ tax plan.

text: During a recent gathering of Asia-Pacific nations in Vietnam, U.S. President Donald Trump delivered a firm statement concerning trade, emphasizing that the United States will no longer accept ongoing trade violations and will advocate for equitable policies. He expressed that the U.S. is prepared to establish bilateral agreements with any nation in the Indo-Pacific, provided they are based on mutual respect and benefits. Speaking at the coastal city of Danang, he stated, "When the United States engages in trade with other countries or peoples, we will now expect our partners to adhere to the rules faithfully." He further articulated expectations for both markets to be equally accessible and asserted that private investment should steer economic growth rather than government planning. This address came just before the summit of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders. Trump’s visit to Vietnam followed his time in China and marked the fourth stage of a twelve-day tour across Asia. A focal point of his administration's 'America First' agenda is recalibrating the trade balance between Asia and the United States, a strategy he claims will safeguard American workers. The contrast between Trump's trade philosophy and that of China was underscored by remarks from Chinese President Xi Jinping, who described globalization as an irreversible trend and endorsed multilateral trade agreements. While China holds the largest trade surplus with the U.S., the Trump administration is also targeting Vietnam as part of its efforts to diminish those surpluses. APEC, which has long supported free trade, has experienced significant upheaval under Trump's leadership. Since the early days of his presidency when he withdrew from the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), the remaining eleven member countries have faced challenges in maintaining the initiative. On Friday, leaders from TPP nations are scheduled to convene after ministers concluded discussions on Thursday that left some uncertainty, with Japan's economy minister indicating they reached a consensus while his Canadian counterpart contradicted that assertion. Trump’s approach has deviated markedly from the previous administration's 'Pivot to Asia' strategy, raising concerns among traditional allies about the potential for a stronger Chinese influence in the region. We want security and stability in the Middle East ... the independence referendum in Iraq s Kurdistan is a sectarian plot by foreign countries and is rejected by Tehran and Ankara,  Rouhani told a joint news conference with Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan.

source_text: Belgian prosecutor says will study Puigdemont arrest warrant. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Belgian authorities have received Spain s arrest warrant for ousted Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont and will examine it before handing it over to a judge, federal prosecutor Eric Van der Sypt said on Friday.  We will study it, we will give it to an investigative judge maybe tomorrow or the day after tomorrow,  Van der Sypt told Reuters.
