text: In the wake of a lengthy tenure, Chancellor Angela Merkel aims to connect with younger generations as she campaigns online to gain their support for the upcoming elections. After serving for 12 years, Merkel is not just seen as Germany's Mutti, a term that translates to Mummy, but is working to engage the youth demographic in a meaningful way ahead of the elections scheduled for September 24. Despite having strong backing from older voters, the 63-year-old leader, who does not maintain a personal Twitter account like some of her Western counterparts, is eager to rally the nearly 3 million first-time voters to support her conservative CDU party. To achieve this, she has engaged with four YouTube content creators, participated in Europe’s largest gaming convention, and established a walk-in campaign hub in the trendy start-up area of Berlin. Diana Kinnert, a 26-year-old who contributed to the CDU’s modernization proposals, emphasized the importance of using modern communication methods to engage young people who may feel alienated by traditional politics. "It would be a shame if it turned out to be just election noise," Kinnert remarked at the campaign center, sporting a baseball cap and tattoos. The CDU, while unlikely to secure an overall majority in parliament, seeks to capture the youth vote to bolster Merkel's position in coalition discussions following the election. Interestingly, the party has created the Twitter hashtag #fedidwgugl, which may seem like a typing error but actually stands for their campaign motto: Fuer ein Deutschland In Dem Wir Gut und Gern Leben, or "For a Germany in which we can live well and gladly." Consequently, the Berlin walk-in center has been dubbed the #fedidwgugl House, where themed spaces illustrate the CDU's policy platform. In the UK, a surge of young voters supported the Labour Party in June, which resulted in the Conservatives losing their parliamentary majority, demonstrating how the youth vote can significantly influence government outcomes, even if they are less numerous. With an aging population in Germany, older citizens continue to dominate the political landscape. There are more than double the number of eligible voters over 60 compared to those under 30. Although the CDU had the largest share of the youth vote in 2013, its support remains heavily weighted towards older voters, with two-fifths of their supporters being over 60 years old and only 5.4 percent under 25. Kinnert, who has shared an Instagram post wearing a T-shirt that says "Keep Calm and Vote for Angie," believes that Merkel is constantly evolving and is focused on the future, despite her long time in office. A key priority for Merkel is advancing the digitization of Germany’s industrial sector. Although she has accounts on Facebook and Instagram, her attempts to engage with social media can sometimes appear awkward. When asked during the YouTube interview about her preferred emoji, Merkel joked that she favors a smiley: "If things are good, even one with a little heart." Her primary opponent, Martin Schulz, the leader of the Social Democratic Party, has also utilized online platforms. Recently, he faced questions on YouTube regarding topics such as the legalization of cannabis, animal welfare, and expanding broadband internet access. While the CDU faced ridicule for the confusion caused by their #fedidwgugl hashtag, the media interest it generated helped draw attention to their agenda. Efforts to utilize new media resonate well with older voters who wish to ensure a better future for their children and grandchildren, according to Stefan Marschall from Heinrich Heine University in Düsseldorf. For many first-time voters, Merkel is the only chancellor they can remember, which enables the CDU to present her as a stabilizing force during a time marked by uncertainty from events like Donald Trump’s presidency and Brexit. A June opinion poll conducted by Forsa indicated that 57 percent of voters aged 18 to 21 support Merkel, compared to 53 percent of the general populace. In contrast, only 21 percent of young voters favored Schulz. According to Manfred Guellner, managing director of Forsa, younger Germans appear to be more conservative than their counterparts in other nations: "Young people here are pragmatists."
source_text: Hashtag politics: Merkel tries to get in with Germany's kids. BERLIN (Reuters) - After 12 years in power, Chancellor Angela Merkel is presenting  herself as more than just Germany s  Mutti , campaigning in cyberspace to get in with younger voters and win their support for long after elections this month. Merkel, whose nickname means  Mummy , appears to be cruising toward a fourth term with strong backing from older Germans. But the 63-year-old, who unlike some Western leaders has no personal Twitter account, wants to mobilize the almost 3 million first-time voters behind her conservative CDU party on Sept. 24. To this end, Merkel has fielded questions from four YouTube video bloggers, attended Europe s biggest computer games convention and set up a walk-in campaign center in Berlin s hip start-up district. Diana Kinnert, a 26-year-old who helped draft proposals to modernize the CDU, said parties should use new communication tools to make young people put off by  sterile  politics more politically engaged in the long term.  It would be a shame if it turned out to be just election noise,  Kinnert, who wears both tattoos and a baseball cap, told Reuters at the walk-in center. The CDU, which is unlikely to win an overall parliamentary majority, needs the youth vote to strengthen Merkel s hand in coalition negotiations that will follow polling day. To some bemusement, the party has created a Twitter hashtag #fedidwgugl. Rather than the result of a malfunctioning computer keyboard, it is an acronym for the CDU campaign slogan:  Fuer ein Deutschland In Dem Wir Gut und Gern Leben  ( For a Germany in which we can live well and gladly ). So the Berlin walk-in center, where themed rooms bring the CDU manifesto to life, is called  #fedidwgugl House .  In Britain, young people turned out in droves in June to vote for the opposition Labour party, stripping the ruling Conservatives of their majority and showing how youth can twist the fate of governments even if they are less numerous. With German society rapidly aging, older people still dominate the country s agenda. There are more than twice as many eligible voters aged over 60 as there are under 30. The CDU secured the highest share of the youth vote in 2013 but its support remains skewed toward pensioners. At the last election two-fifths of its backers were aged over 60 while just 5.4 percent were under 25. Kinnert, who has posted on Instagram wearing a T-shirt reading  Keep Calm and Vote for Angie , says Merkel never stops learning and is future-orientated despite her lengthy tenure. One of Merkel s top priorities is the digitization of German industry. She has Facebook and Instagram accounts and has made efforts to show she is up on social media even if it sometimes comes across as clunky. Asked about her favorite emoji during the YouTube interview, Merkel said it was a smiley:  If things are good, even one with a little heart,  she joked. Merkel s main challenger, Social Democrat leader Martin Schulz, has not shied away from cyberspace either. This week he was grilled on YouTube on topics such as legalizing cannabis, animal welfare and rolling out broadband internet. While the CDU was mocked for causing confusion with the #fedidwgugl hashtag, the media attention drew eyeballs to the CDU s agenda. Efforts to campaign over new media also play well with older voters who want the best for their children and grandchildren, said Stefan Marschall of Duesseldorf s Heinrich Heine University. Merkel is the only chancellor most first-time voters can recall. This helps CDU to portray her as an anchor of stability in the turbulent era of Donald Trump and Brexit. An opinion poll by Forsa in June found 57 percent of 18 to 21-year-olds backed Merkel compared with 53 percent of the wider population. Just 21 percent of the young supported Schulz. Forsa s managing director Manfred Guellner said younger Germans have become more conservative than their peers in other countries:  Young people here are pragmatic; they worry about their pensions.

text: On Friday, the Indian government announced new regulations that will prevent unruly individuals from boarding flights for durations ranging from three months to over two years, depending on the severity of their actions. A no-fly list has been created for such passengers after a member of the legislature confessed to attacking an official from the state-owned airline Air India. These regulations will also extend to international airlines, according to a statement released by the government. Unruly behavior has been classified into three distinct categories: verbal, physical, and life-threatening. The intent of the no-fly policy is to ensure the safety of fellow passengers, the flight crew, and the aircraft, rather than focusing solely on security risks.
source_text: India bars 'unruly' passengers from flying for three months to over two years. NEW DELHI (Reuters) - India has issued new norms barring unruly passengers from flying for a minimum of three months to more than two years depending on the nature of the misdemeanor, the government said on Friday. The federal government has issued a no-fly list of unruly passengers after a lawmaker admitted assaulting an official from state-owned carrier Air India. The new rules will be applicable to foreign carriers as well, the government said in a statement, adding that unruly behavior has been categorized in three levels - verbal, physical and life threatening.  The concept of no-fly is based on safety of other passengers, crew and the aircraft, and not just on the security threat,  the government said.

text: A public showdown in Congress regarding a bill to prevent a government shutdown emerged on Thursday, revealing the deep divisions between parties. Republicans unveiled a temporary funding proposal that was swiftly dismissed by Democrats. The current federal fiscal year concludes on September 30, making it imperative for Congress to enact a spending bill to maintain government operations. In recent times, reaching consensus on a comprehensive federal budget has been rare, leading lawmakers to rely on these temporary measures instead. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, after extensive negotiations, introduced a continuing resolution aimed at financing government departments from October 1 until December 9, with an annual budget exceeding $1 trillion. This proposal allocates $1.1 billion for efforts to address the expanding Zika virus, $500 million designated for flood recovery in states such as Louisiana, and an annual funding rate of $74 billion for U.S. military activities abroad. "I have put forth a clean continuing resolution in response to widespread requests," stated McConnell, a Republican from Kentucky, who characterized the proposal as the outcome of bipartisan discussions. However, Democrats quickly criticized the resolution, labeling it a "Republican-only bill" that fails to provide assistance to Flint, Michigan, regarding its lead-contaminated water crisis, and retains a restriction preventing the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission from mandating public companies to disclose their political expenditures. "We Democrats cannot support that," declared Senator Barbara Mikulski, the leading Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee. White House spokesperson Josh Earnest informed reporters that if Congress does not reach an agreement on funding, plans for an organized government shutdown are already being prepared. Notably, McConnell excluded a clause favored by Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump and his former rival in the Senate, Ted Cruz, which aimed to obstruct the U.S. government from transferring control of the internet's technical management to a global group of stakeholders on October 1. Additionally, a provision that would have allowed the U.S. Export-Import Bank to sanction loans or guarantees exceeding $10 million was also omitted. Both parties sought to incorporate this into the resolution, but the topic became too contentious for the essential funding measure. A senior aide for the Republicans indicated that Senate voting on the funding bill could commence as early as Monday.
source_text: Senate splits over bill to avoid government shutdown. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A behind-the-scenes congressional battle to avoid a U.S. government shutdown broke into public view on Thursday when Republicans produced a stop-gap funding bill that Democrats immediately rejected. The federal fiscal year ends on Sept. 30 and Congress must pass a spending measure by then to keep the government open. In recent years, lawmakers have seldom been able to agree on a full federal budget and instead have relied on stop-gap measures. Senate Majority Mitch McConnell capped weeks of labored negotiations by proposing a continuing resolution that would fund government agencies from Oct. 1 through Dec. 9 at an annual rate of just over $1 trillion.  The measure also includes $1.1 billion to combat the spreading Zika virus, $500 million in flood relief for states including Louisiana and funding for U.S. military operations overseas at an annual rate of $74 billion.  “There have been broad requests for a clean continuing resolution. So that’s what I’ve just offered,” said McConnell, a Kentucky Republican, who described the measure as a product of bipartisan negotiations. Democrats quickly opposed the resolution as “a Republican-only bill” that would not help Flint, Michigan, cope with lead-contaminated water and would leave in place a prohibition against the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission requiring public companies to disclose political spending. “We Democrats cannot vote for that,” said Senator Barbara Mikulski, top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee. White House spokesman Josh Earnest told reporters that plans were already in place for an orderly government shutdown in the event that Congress cannot agree on a funding measure. McConnell left out a provision backed by Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump and his former White House rival, Senator Ted Cruz, that would have stopped the U.S. government from moving oversight of the internet’s technical management to a global community of stakeholders on Oct. 1. Also absent was language that would have enabled the U.S. Export-Import Bank to approve loans or guarantees of more than $10 million. Republicans and Democrats had sought to include a provision, but the issue proved too controversial for the must-pass funding resolution. A senior Republican aide said the Senate would begin voting on the funding legislation as early as Monday.

text: Despite the ongoing funding deadlock in the U.S. Congress, research into Zika virus transmission through sexual contact is set to commence. The duration during which men infected with the Zika virus can transmit the illness sexually remains uncertain and may take several years to ascertain. Health officials have advised couples to avoid unprotected intercourse for a period of six months following a male partner's infection. This unusual guideline stems from a singular report indicating that Zika could persist in semen for 62 days, potentially impacting millions of individuals. The serious dangers linked to Zika, compounded by its possible spread, are propelling U.S. health agencies to advance research efforts, even as funding remains entangled in political stalemate. One critical study focusing on the risk of sexual transmission exemplifies the urgent need for scientific progress that cannot afford to wait for political resolution. The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in the United States has begun recruiting men infected with Zika in Brazil and Colombia, utilizing funds originally allocated for other initiatives, to investigate how long the virus can remain infectious in semen. Although this research may require years to finalize, preliminary findings could aid public health officials in refining their sexual health recommendations. In an interview, Dr. Anthony Fauci, the director of the U.S. institute, expressed the necessity of action: "We are going out on a limb, but we have to. We can’t say we’re going to wait until we get all the money." The transmission adaptability of Zika has raised alarms among public health officials, as it may extend the virus’s reach. Primarily, Zika is transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, similar to the dengue and chikungunya viruses. However, reports from at least ten nations, including the United States and France, have documented Zika infections in individuals who have not traveled to outbreak regions, but whose sexual partners had. This mode of transmission could allow Zika to establish a stronger presence beyond the warmer environments favored by its main vector, the mosquito. To safeguard women who are either pregnant or attempting to conceive, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recommended that couples abstain from unprotected sex for a duration of six months—three times longer than the 62 days noted in a British case study regarding the virus's survival in semen. The World Health Organization has recently issued comparable recommendations. Despite the necessity for such stringent advice, Dr. Anne Schuchat, a deputy director at the CDC, remarked in an interview that this guidance is not entirely satisfactory: "To tell people not to have sex until we get back to you is not a very satisfying recommendation. We would like to have some more understanding of the sexual risk." In Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory where more than 2,100 cases of Zika have been reported this year, health authorities are distributing protection kits that include insect repellent and condoms, accompanied by the advisory. However, the suggestion to avoid unprotected sex has not been well-received, according to Dr. Chris Prue, a behavioral scientist at the CDC who has researched public reactions. "Condoms are not popular in a lot of places," she stated. "There’s religious and personal preferences and lots of personal factors in that." On Tuesday, U.S. lawmakers were at an impasse regarding funding to combat the Zika virus, as Senate Democrats blocked a Republican proposal they criticized for inadequately addressing the challenges posed by the virus and undermining other health priorities. The timeline for Congress to revisit President Barack Obama’s request for $1.9 billion remains unclear. Meanwhile, the White House has reallocated over $500 million intended for other initiatives to support urgent Zika-related projects, including those where critical scientific opportunities risk being lost if not addressed promptly. One such project will monitor children born to mothers infected with Zika to identify any developmental disabilities that may not be apparent at birth. Other essential initiatives include the development of vaccines and efforts to eradicate mosquitoes. Additionally, a study currently in progress will evaluate whether men exhibiting Zika symptoms, such as fever and rash, pose a greater transmission risk compared to asymptomatic individuals.
source_text: Zika sex research begins despite U.S. Congress funding impasse. (Reuters) - It could take years to learn how long men infected with Zika are capable of sexually transmitting the virus, which can cause crippling birth defects and other serious neurological disorders. In the meantime, health officials have warned couples to refrain from unprotected sex for six months after a male partner is infected. The extraordinary recommendation, based on a single report of Zika surviving 62 days in semen, could affect millions. The grave risks associated with Zika, along with its potential reach, are driving U.S. health authorities to pursue research even though funding is mired in Congressional gridlock. A study of sexual transmission risk is one example of science that health officials said can’t wait for politics. Borrowing money earmarked for other programs, the U.S. National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases has started enrolling men infected with Zika in Brazil and Colombia in the study to determine how long the virus remains transmittable in semen. The study could take years to complete, but interim results could help public health officials fine-tune their recommendations on sex. “We are going out on a limb, but we have to,” Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the U.S. institute, said in an interview. “We can’t say we’re going to wait until we get all the money.” Public health officials are alarmed by Zika’s transmission versatility, which has the potential to expand its reach. It is primarily spread by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, as are the dengue and chikungunya viruses. But at least 10 countries, including the United States and France, have reported Zika infections in people who had not traveled to an outbreak area but whose sexual partners had. This ability to spread through sex could help Zika gain a further foothold outside the warm habitats of its most effective agent, the mosquito. To protect women who are pregnant or trying to conceive, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended couples refrain from unprotected sex for six months - triple the 62 days the virus survived in the semen in one British case study. The World Health Organization recently issued similar guidance. But such strict advice is not ideal, Dr. Anne Schuchat, a CDC deputy director, said in an interview. “To tell people not to have sex until we get back to you is not a very satisfying recommendation,” she said. “We would like to have some more understanding of the sexual risk.” In the U.S. territory of Puerto Rico, where more than 2,100 cases of infection have been reported since the start of the year, health officials are passing out Zika protection kits that include bug spray and condoms, along with the recommendation. But the warning against unprotected sex isn’t going over very well, said Dr. Chris Prue, a CDC behavioral scientist who has studied the response. “Condoms are not popular in a lot places,” she said. “There’s religious and personal preferences and lots of personal factors in that.” U.S. lawmakers deadlocked over funding to fight the Zika virus on Tuesday, as Senate Democrats blocked a Republican proposal they said fell short of the challenge posed by the virus and hurt other health priorities. It was unclear when Congress would revisit the request by President Barack Obama for $1.9 billion. In the meantime, the White House has diverted more than $500 million earmarked for other projects for urgent Zika initiatives, including those where scientific opportunities will be lost if not acted upon immediately. One such study will follow children born to women infected with Zika to identify the development of any disabilities not detected at birth. Other projects on the priority list include vaccine development and mosquito eradication.    One study underway will assess whether the risk of transmission is greater from men who experience Zika infection symptoms, such as fever and rash, than from those who don’t. This information is considered vital since most people experience no symptoms. The study of infected men in Brazil and Colombia will test semen from thousands of men over time to determine how long Zika poses a risk to sexual partners. As long the virus can be grown in a laboratory from semen cell samples, infectious disease experts believe it is potentially contagious. Zika typically clears the bloodstream about a week after infection, but it has been detected in urine for at least twice as long. Its persistence in semen in the British case study has caused some researchers to draw comparisons to other viruses. HIV can last in blood and semen indefinitely, and the mosquito-borne West Nile virus can reside in the kidneys and urine for years, researchers said. One patient who survived the deadly Ebola outbreak had evidence of that virus in his semen for 18 months. “We got very surprised by Ebola that it was hanging around for so long,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor College of Medicine. “One of the big questions we have to ask is does Zika also cause a similar type of latency?”

text: On Tuesday, voters in Colorado decided against a ballot initiative aimed at establishing the first universal health insurance program in the country, as reported by the local NBC News outlet, 9News. Known as Amendment 69, the proposal represented one of the most significant transformations of a public healthcare system in U.S. history. Early results indicated a decisive rejection of the amendment on Tuesday night, according to Colorado’s 9News. The initiative, named ColoradoCare, would have primarily relied on a new payroll tax increase of 10 percent, projected to generate $25 billion in its first year, 2019, as per the Colorado Health Institute. ColoradoCare aimed to significantly decrease the number of residents without insurance in the state; however, critics expressed concerns that the tax increase and extensive changes to public policy could adversely affect the state’s economy. An unaffiliated voter, James Merilatt, 43, who supported Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton in the recent election, voiced his opposition to the single-payer healthcare initiative. "It’s way too complicated and would have opened up a Pandora’s Box," Merilatt stated, who is employed in the publishing sector.
source_text: Colorado voters reject measure to create universal healthcare. (Reuters) - Colorado voters rejected a ballot measure on Tuesday to create the nation’s first statewide universal health insurance program, according to local NBC News affiliate 9News. The proposition, called Amendment 69, would have created one of the most dramatic overhauls to a public healthcare system in U.S. history. Colorado’s 9News reported that the amendment was defeated on Tuesday night, after early results showed an overwhelming defeat. Dubbed ColoradoCare, the program would have been funded largely through a new 10 percent payroll tax increase intended to raise $25 billion in 2019, the first year the program could launch, according to the Colorado Health Institute. ColoradoCare was intended to greatly reduce the number of uninsured residents in the state, but opponents feared the tax hike and sweeping changes to public policy would ripple through the state’s economy. James Merilatt, 43, an unaffiliated voter who supported Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton in Tuesday’s election, said he opposed the single-payer healthcare measure. “It’s way too complicated and would have opened up a Pandora’s Box,” said Merilatt, who works in the publishing industry.

text: On Tuesday, the House of Representatives saw U.S. Representative Paul Ryan secure re-election as its speaker, marking the start of a new congressional session led by Republicans. The Wisconsin lawmaker garnered a total of 239 votes in favor against 189 opposed. Ryan stepped into the role of speaker for the first time in October 2015, following the retirement of his predecessor, John Boehner, amid ongoing dissent from House conservatives.
source_text: Ryan wins re-election as speaker of U.S. House of Representatives. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Representative Paul Ryan was re-elected speaker of the House of Representatives on Tuesday as a Republican-led  Congress began a new session. The Wisconsin congressman was elected on a vote of 239-189. Ryan was first elected speaker in October 2015, after his predecessor John Boehner retired following repeated revolts by House conservatives.

text: In the upcoming presidential run-off in Liberia, former soccer player George Weah will be competing against Vice President Joseph Boakai. On Thursday, the electoral commission announced that Weah secured 38.4 percent of the votes in the initial round, leading Boakai by 10 points. This election marks a significant moment for Liberians, as they consider the possibility of having the only African to have won both the FIFA World Player of the Year and the Ballon d'Or take over from Nobel Peace Prize laureate Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. At 51 years old, Weah has been serving as a senator for the Congress for Democratic Change since 2015, after returning to Liberia following his international soccer career to engage in politics. Previously, he lost a presidential bid in 2005 to Johnson Sirleaf, marking his entry into the political arena. The final official results indicated that Boakai, who represents the ruling Unity Party of Johnson Sirleaf, received 28.8 percent of the vote, which comfortably places both candidates ahead of a broad array of lesser-known contenders. Charles Brumskine, a lawyer who claims that the election was unfair despite observers deeming it credible, finished third with 9.6 percent of the votes. Supporters affectionately refer to Weah as 'King George,' and he enjoys significant popularity among younger voters and the impoverished communities, particularly in the struggling coastal city of Monrovia. Many citizens feel excluded from the benefits of Liberia's post-war recovery, a perception that has hindered Boakai's campaign. However, Weah has not yet articulated clear policies and will encounter challenges in fulfilling the high expectations of the electorate, especially amidst an economic landscape plagued by low commodity prices, essential to Liberia's exports. Johnson Sirleaf, who previously held the position of finance minister and worked at Citibank and the World Bank while in exile after escaping a coup, received the Nobel Prize in 2011 for her efforts in fostering peace after a civil war that lasted 15 years and concluded in 2003. Numerous Liberians credit her with establishing the groundwork for this election, which could lead to the first democratic transition of power in seven decades. Nevertheless, she has struggled to effectively combat corruption and improve living conditions for millions in poverty. The economy was further devastated by an Ebola outbreak, and a decline in iron ore prices has exacerbated the situation. Additionally, inadequate road infrastructure continues to isolate many rural areas during the rainy season, and outside the primary cities, few Liberians have access to grid electricity.
source_text: Soccer star Weah to face vice president in Liberian presidential run-off. MONROVIA (Reuters) - Former soccer star George Weah won the first round of Liberia s presidential election with 38.4 percent of the vote, 10 points ahead of Vice President Joseph Boakai who will face him in a run-off next month, the electoral commission said on Thursday. Liberians are slowly waking up to the prospect of the only African ever to win FIFA World Player of the Year and the Ballon d Or replace Nobel Peace Prize winner Ellen Johnson Sirleaf as their leader. Weah, 51, has served as a senator from the opposition Congress for Democratic Change since 2015, after returning home from an international soccer career to immerse himself in politics. As a political novice in 2005 he lost to Johnson Sirleaf in a presidential election.  The official final results showed Boakai, representing Johnson Sirleaf s ruling Unity Party, had won 28.8 percent of the vote, putting the two frontrunners comfortably ahead of a large field of mostly minor candidates. Lawyer Charles Brumskine, who says the vote was rigged despite observers calling it fair, came third with 9.6 percent.  King George , as Weah s supporters call him, is wildly popular among the youth and the disenfranchised, especially in the shanties of the rundown seaside capital Monrovia. Many of them feel they have not benefited from Liberia s post-war recovery, a sentiment that has counted against Boakai.  But Weah has so far been light on policy and will face a tough time meeting high expectations in a difficult economic climate of low prices for the commodities that are Liberia s main exports. Johnson Sirleaf, a former finance minister who worked for Citibank and the World Bank during years in exile after fleeing Liberia during a coup, was awarded the 2011 Nobel for shoring up peace after a 15-year civil war that ended in 2003. Many Liberians credit her with creating the conditions that allow this election to bring Liberia s first democratic transfer of power for seven decades. But she has not managed to effectively tackle corruption or lift millions out of poverty. An Ebola outbreak ravaged the economy and a drop in the price of iron ore only made things worse. Poor roads still leave most of rural Liberia stranded during the rainy season, and few Liberians have grid power outside the main cities.

text: On Friday, a federal appeals court ruled against New Jersey Senator Robert Menendez, denying his attempt to dismiss a corruption indictment. The 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals determined that Menendez's assertion of constitutional immunity from prosecution was unfounded. Prosecutors are permitted to pursue allegations that he received campaign contributions and luxuries, including a stay at a Caribbean villa and private jet travel, from his affluent associate, Florida ophthalmologist Salomon Melgen, in return for using his political influence to advocate for Melgen's interests. "Congress members are not to be seen as 'super-citizens' who are free from criminal accountability," Circuit Judge Thomas Ambro stated, representing a panel of three judges from the Philadelphia-based court. This ruling indicates that the case may proceed to trial and could pose challenges for Democrats aiming to regain control of the U.S. Senate following the upcoming election on November 8. Should Menendez, who is 62 years old and has served since 2006, be compelled to resign, New Jersey law would allow Republican Governor Chris Christie to appoint a temporary successor. While the senator has committed to remaining in office during his defense, he has stepped down from his role as the leading Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Menendez's attorney, Abbe Lowell, expressed that the senator plans to request a review of Friday’s ruling by the full appeals court and, if necessary, will escalate the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court. Lowell remarked, "This is merely another step in the legal journey that will ultimately demonstrate that Senator Menendez has consistently acted within the law." He added, "The Senator is confident of his eventual vindication." A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Justice, Peter Carr, chose not to comment on the matter. In April 2015, an indictment was brought against Menendez, alleging that he accepted bribes from Melgen in exchange for intervening in various issues on his friend's behalf. Prosecutors claimed that these matters included an $8.9 million dispute related to Medicare billing and a contract disagreement with the Dominican Republic, in which Menendez urged the State Department to get involved. Both Menendez and Melgen have pleaded not guilty to the charges outlined in the 22-count indictment. Last September, U.S. District Judge William Walls in Newark, New Jersey, dismissed four bribery charges but kept the majority of the prosecution's case intact. In his appeal, Menendez contended that his actions were protected under the Constitution's "speech or debate" clause, which provides extensive immunity to congressional members against prosecution for their legislative activities. However, Ambro noted that Menendez's actions were essentially lobbying in favor of a specific party, thus falling outside the constitutional "safe harbor." He asserted, "There is sufficient justification for the district court’s conclusion that the main aim of the contested actions was to seek a political resolution for Dr. Melgen’s issues," Ambro elaborated. "It was not intended to engage in genuine legislative oversight or influence broader policy matters." Lowell had contended that Judge Walls should have concentrated on what actually transpired during the meetings in question, asserting that the evidence indicated "high-level policy discussions" were conducted. Ambro indicated that Menendez retains the right to argue that his efforts were aimed at influencing policy, and the prosecution still bears the burden of proof at trial. "The evidence supporting Senator Menendez will undoubtedly channel his position powerfully at trial," the judge commented. This decision arrived a month after the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously annulled the bribery convictions of former Virginia Governor Bob McDonnell, stating that typical political activities like setting up meetings or contacting public officials usually cannot constitute grounds for criminal charges. The 3rd Circuit primarily concentrated on the speech or debate clause and did not reference the McDonnell case. Lowell remarked that this case illustrates the complexities involved.
source_text: U.S. court rejects NJ Senator Menendez's bid to end corruption case. (Reuters) - A federal appeals court on Friday refused to dismiss a corruption indictment against Senator Robert Menendez of New Jersey, rejecting the Democrat’s claim that the U.S. Constitution shielded him from prosecution. The 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said prosecutors could pursue charges that Menendez accepted campaign donations and gifts, including a stay in a Caribbean villa and private jet flights from a wealthy friend, Florida ophthalmologist Salomon Melgen, in exchange for using his office to lobby on his behalf. “Members of Congress are not to be ‘super-citizens’ immune from criminal liability,” Circuit Judge Thomas Ambro wrote for a three-judge panel of the Philadelphia-based appeals court. Friday’s decision means the case could eventually be headed for trial, and could complicate Democrats’ efforts to regain control of the U.S. Senate after the Nov. 8 election. If Menendez, 62, were forced to give up the seat he has held since 2006, Governor Chris Christie, a Republican, could under New Jersey law appoint a temporary replacement. The senator has pledged to stay in office while defending himself, but has given up his post as the ranking Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Abbe Lowell, Menendez’s lawyer, said the senator intends to ask the entire appeals court to review Friday’s decision, and, if necessary, appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. The decision is “another step in the legal process that, at the end of the day, will show that Senator Menendez has always acted in accordance with the law,” Lowell said in a statement. “The Senator remains confident that he will be vindicated.” Peter Carr, a U.S. Department of Justice spokesman, declined to comment. In an indictment unveiled in April 2015, Menendez was accused of accepting bribes from Melgen in exchange for interceding in various matters on his friend’s behalf. Prosecutors said these included an $8.9 million Medicare billing dispute, and a contract dispute with the Dominican Republic in which Menendez encouraged the State Department to intervene. Menendez and Melgen have pleaded not guilty to the respective charges they faced in the 22-count indictment. Last September, U.S. District Judge William Walls in Newark, New Jersey, dismissed four bribery counts but left most of the government’s case intact. In his appeal, Menendez argued that his actions were protected by the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause, which offers broad protection to members of Congress against prosecution for actions they undertake as legislators. Ambro, however, said Menendez’s actions amounted to “essentially lobbying on behalf of a particular party,” and thus outside the “safe harbor” provided in the Constitution. There is “a sufficient basis for the district court’s conclusion that the predominant purpose of the challenged acts was to pursue a political resolution to Dr. Melgen’s disputes,” Ambro wrote. “It was not to engage in true legislative oversight or otherwise influence broad matters of policy.” Lowell had argued that Walls should have focused on what actually went on at the meetings in question, saying the record reflected that “high-level policy discussions” had taken place. Ambro said Menendez remains free to argue that his efforts were directed toward influencing policy, and the government still has the burden at trial of proving otherwise. “The evidence in favor of Senator Menendez will no doubt channel forcefully his position at trial,” the judge wrote. Friday’s decision came one month after the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the bribery convictions of former Virginia Governor Bob McDonnell. That court said routine political activities such as arranging meetings or reaching out to public officials generally could not form a basis for criminal prosecutions. The 3rd Circuit focused mainly on the speech or debate clause, and did not mention McDonnell. Lowell said that case raised “important” issues that need to be addressed. The case is U.S. v. Menendez, 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, No. 15-3459.

text: In Phoenix, Arizona, police intervened using pepper spray to break up demonstrators outside a rally featuring U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday. Officers reported being struck by rocks and bottles during the incident. Although authorities did not provide a specific count of the protesters, several thousand were estimated by local Arizona media. It remains unclear if the pepper spray targeted supporters of Trump, opponents, or both groups. Sergeant Jonathan Howard, a spokesperson for the Phoenix Police Department, stated, "People in the crowd have begun throwing rocks and bottles at police." He further noted, "Police have responded with pepper balls and OC (oleoresin capsicum) spray in an attempt to disperse the crowd and stop the assaults." Phoenix Police Chief Jeri Williams reported that four individuals were taken into custody amid the protest during a press briefing. "We had tens of thousands of people downtown peacefully exercising their first amendment rights," Williams remarked. "What’s unfortunate is that a very small number of individuals chose criminal conduct." Law enforcement urged the crowds to leave the area. While many protesters complied, several officers dressed in riot gear and wielding shields worked to clear out remaining individuals from the downtown vicinity. The Phoenix Fire Department indicated that 56 individuals were treated for dehydration and heat exhaustion at the convention center, with twelve transported to the hospital.
source_text: Police use pepper spray to disperse protesters at Trump's Phoenix rally. PHOENIX (Reuters) - Police fired pepper spray to disperse protesters outside a rally by U.S. President Donald Trump in Phoenix, Arizona, on Tuesday after being pelted with rocks and bottles, police said. Police have not given an estimate of the number of protesters, but Arizona media said there were several thousand. Police did not say whether the pepper spray was used on pro- or anti-Trump protesters, or both. “People in the crowd have begun throwing rocks and bottles at police,” Phoenix Police Department spokesman Sergeant Jonathan Howard said. “Police have responded with pepper balls and OC (oleoresin capsicum) spray in an attempt to disperse the crowd and stop the assaults,” he said. Four people were arrested during the protest, Phoenix Police Chief Jeri Williams said during a news conference.  “We had tens of thousands of people downtown peacefully exercising their first amendment rights,” Williams said. “What’s unfortunate is that a very small number of individuals chose criminal conduct.” Police called on the crowds to disperse. Many of the protesters quit the scene, while dozens of police in riot gear and carrying shields sought to clear remaining protesters from the downtown area. The Phoenix Fire Department said it treated 56 people for heat exhaustion and dehydration at the convention center. Twelve people were taken to the hospital.

text: On Wednesday, the director of the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) defended himself in front of Congress amidst intense Republican criticism regarding various issues, including the agency's management of the Wells Fargo accounts scandal and his personal job performance. Richard Cordray appeared before the House Financial Services Committee, where he was evasive about his plans to complete his term, which is set to end in July 2018. There has been a push from Republican members of the committee, as well as others, for President Trump to remove him from his position. Additionally, Cordray is rumored to be considering a run for governor of Ohio in 2018. Since taking on the role in 2012, when he was appointed by former President Barack Obama, Cordray has not resigned despite President Donald Trump assuming office. He refrained from confirming whether he would serve until the end of his term, which is due to conclude in July 2018, stating, "I have no insights to provide" when asked about his future. According to the Dodd-Frank Act, the president can remove Cordray only "for cause." However, longstanding critics from the Republican party argue that Cordray's regulatory decisions give the president sufficient grounds to dismiss him. House Financial Services Committee Chairman Jeb Hensarling argued, "For all of the harm caused to consumers, Richard Cordray should be dismissed by the president." Hensarling pointed out that the CFPB has not finalized several regulatory initiatives mandated by Congress, such as establishing rules for financial institutions to gather data on credit applications from minority-owned and women-owned businesses. Republicans have contended that the agency failed to address issues at Wells Fargo & Co, instead relying on external investigations and media reports to uncover extensive problems related to improper account openings. Ann Wagner, a Republican from Missouri, exclaimed, "The CFPB was asleep at the wheel!" She noted that the earliest date on record for the committee's examination of Wells Fargo was May 2015, after the bank had alerted the regulator that the Los Angeles City Attorney was already involved in a civil case. Nonetheless, the CFPB was prominently involved in September 2016 when the significant $185 million multi-agency settlement was revealed. Cordray responded to Wagner's comments by asserting that she was "conflating" different issues, adding that the oversight activities "became exponential over time." The CFPB imposed a $100 million penalty on the bank in an enforcement action alongside the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the City and County of Los Angeles. This investigation was initiated following a 2013 investigative report by the Los Angeles Times.
source_text: U.S. consumer financial protection chief defends agency before Congress. (Reuters) - The U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s director defended himself in Congress on Wednesday against a barrage of Republican criticism over everything from the agency’s handling of the Wells Fargo accounts scandal to the way he has personally managed his job. Appearing before the House Financial Services Committee, Richard Cordray, got coy when asked whether he would finish his term, which expires in July 2018. Republicans on the committee and elsewhere have pushed for President Trump to fire him, and Cordray is widely rumored to be a possible Ohio gubernatorial candidate in 2018.  Cordray, who has headed the agency since 2012 when he was  appointed by former President Barack Obama, has declined to step down since President Donald Trump took office. He did not say whether he will serve out the rest of him term, which expires in July 2018. “I have no insights to provide,” he said in response to a related question. Under the Dodd-Frank law creating the agency, the president could only remove Cordray “for cause.” But longtime Republican critics say Cordray’s decisions as a regulator provide ample evidence to fire him. “For all of the harm caused to consumers, Richard Cordray should be dismissed by the president,” said House Financial Services Committee Chairman Jeb Hensarling.  Hensarling noted that the CFPB has failed to finalize regulatory projects mandated by Congress,  such as writing rules directing financial institutions to collect data about credit applications by minority and women-owned businesses. Republicans claimed the agency failed to detect wrongdoing at Wells Fargo & Co, relying on outside investigators and news reports to point out widespread problems with improper account creation. “The CFPB was asleep at the wheel!” said Ann Wagner, a Missouri Republican. The earliest the committee could determine the CFPB began to examine Wells Fargo was in May 2015, after the bank notified the regulator that the Los Angeles City Attorney was already pursuing a civil case, she said. Yet the CFPB was front and center in September 2016 when the high-profile $185 million multi-agency settlement was announced. Cordray said Wagner was “conflating” issues and said the oversight work “became exponential over time.” The CFPB levied a $100 million fine against the bank in an enforcement action with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the City and County of Los Angeles. The probe began after a 2013 Los Angeles Times investigative story.

text: In Greece, severe flash floods have resulted in the deaths of at least 15 individuals and left many others without shelter, as infrastructure was severely damaged. This disaster struck on Wednesday, following a night of intense rainfall that caused torrents to overwhelm two coastal towns west of Athens. Local residents described the devastation as unprecedented, with Nea Peramos and Mandra, situated at the base of a mountain just outside Athens, being particularly affected by the sudden floods. Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras announced a national mourning period, stating, "These are very difficult moments for Greece. We are living a great disaster," during an official address. He pledged that support measures would be swiftly implemented for the households and businesses that have suffered, although he refrained from providing specifics. Residents reported being startled awake on Wednesday morning by the influx of rainwater and mud filling their homes. As the extent of the destruction became evident throughout the day, vast regions were submerged in water and debris. In certain locations, floodwaters reached the first floor of small buildings. Yiannis Kapakis, the head of Greece's civil protection agency, remarked, "There was just an incredible amount of water which caused raging torrents." Such severe rain is rare in Greece, where inadequate infrastructure often leaves citizens exposed to flooding risks. The nation has experienced consistent precipitation for about a week, and the meteorological service issued a fresh severe weather advisory for Thursday. Some residents sought refuge on rooftops and balconies, while vehicles ended up on porches, colliding with tree trunks or overturned on their sides. Mandra Mayor Yianna Krikouki described the event as a "biblical disaster," telling state broadcaster ERT, "Everything is gone." The Attica prefecture, which oversees both towns, announced its intention to request aid from the EU Solidarity Fund designed for natural disaster responses. A state of emergency has been declared for the affected region. Resident Marina Kolia expressed her despair, stating, "The walls collapsed, the cars were carried away and they broke everything here. There is nothing left. Water is everywhere in the house." The population of Mandra and Nea Peramos is approximately 20,000. Many housing developments in Greece do not adhere to town planning regulations. An Athens prosecutor has initiated an urgent preliminary inquiry into the fatalities and destruction, while also looking into potential violations of urban planning laws. The day before, Greece had declared a state of emergency on the eastern island of Symi, located near Turkey, as a storm had hurled vehicles into the sea, damaged residences, and disrupted electricity and water services.
source_text: At least 15 dead in flash floods on Greek coast. MANDRA, Greece (Reuters) - Flash floods killed at least 15 people, made scores homeless and destroyed infrastructure in Greece on Wednesday after a raging torrent inundated two coastal towns west of Athens following a night of heavy rain. Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras declared a period of national mourning.  These are very difficult moments for Greece. We are living a great disaster,  he said in a state address.  Immediately and without delay support measures will be adopted for households and businesses affected,  he said, without going into details. Residents said they were woken on Wednesday morning by rainwater and mud coming through their homes. As the scale of destruction became clearer during the day, large areas were covered in water and mud. In some areas floodwaters rose to the first story of small buildings.  There was just an incredible amount of water which caused raging torrents,  said Yiannis Kapakis, the head of Greece s civil protection service. Torrential rain of this type is uncommon in Greece, where poor infrastructure can leave citizens vulnerable to flooding. It has been raining steadily for about a week, and the country s met office issued a new severe weather warning for Thursday. Some residents were forced onto rooftops and balconies while cars were thrust onto porches of homes, rammed like dodgem vehicles into tree trunks or tipped onto their side.   This is a biblical disaster,  Mandra Mayor Yianna Krikouki told state broadcaster ERT.  Everything is gone.  The Attica prefecture, the administrative district for both towns, said it would seek assistance from the EU Solidarity Fund, set up to respond to natural disasters. A state of emergency was declared in the region.  The walls collapsed, the cars were carried away and they broke everything here. There is nothing left,  resident Marina Kolia said.  Water is everywhere in the house.  Mandra and Nea Peramos have a combined population of about 20,000. Many Greek housing settlements are built without taking into account town planning regulations. An Athens prosecutor ordered an urgent preliminary investigation into the deaths and destruction caused and was also investigating possible urban planning offences. text: U.S. President-elect Donald Trump has postponed an announcement regarding his business operations until January, which was initially scheduled for this week, as stated by his spokesperson on Monday. Trump’s business interests include hotels and golf courses spanning from Panama to Scotland, along with a winery and a modeling agency. Legal analysts indicate that the only means for him to fully eliminate conflicts of interest would be to divest from his international holdings. Last month, Trump mentioned he would conduct a press conference on Thursday to clarify how he would completely distance himself from his global business interests. Trump’s spokesman, Sean Spicer, confirmed that the announcement would occur in January, but did not provide a specific reason for the delay. Since his victory on November 8, the Republican president-elect has not participated in any press conferences. Following Trump's electoral success, the Trump Organization announced it was considering new business frameworks aimed at transferring control to his children—Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump, and Eric Trump—who are involved in the company. In a series of tweets late Monday, Trump asserted he would withdraw from his businesses before assuming office on January 20, in order to concentrate on his presidential duties. He tweeted, "Two of my children, Don and Eric, plus executives, will manage them. No new deals will be done during my term(s) in office." His tweets did not mention Ivanka Trump's involvement in the business management. Trump also indicated that a press conference would be held in the "near future" to cover business issues, his cabinet selections, and other relevant topics. Previously, in tweets from last month, Trump revealed, "Legal documents are being crafted which take me completely out of business operations," but he did not elaborate on the implications for ownership of his enterprises.
source_text: Trump delays announcement on his business until January. (Reuters) - U.S. President-elect Donald Trump has delayed until January an announcement originally set for this week on how he plans to step back from running his business empire to avoid conflicts of interest, his spokesman said on Monday. Among Trump’s holdings are hotels and golf resorts from Panama to Scotland, besides a winery and modeling agency. Legal experts say the only way he could entirely avoid conflicts of interest would be to sell his global holdings. Last month Trump said he would hold a news conference on Thursday to spell out how he would separate himself “in total” from his worldwide business holdings.  “The announcement will be in January,” Trump spokesman Sean Spicer said on Monday, without giving any reason. The Republican president-elect has not held a news conference since winning the Nov. 8 election. After Trump’s victory, his company, the Trump Organization, said it was looking at new business structures with the goal of transferring control to Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump and Eric Trump, three of his children who are involved with the company. In a series of messages on social network Twitter, Trump said he would leave his businesses before taking office on Jan. 20, to focus on the presidency. “Two of my children, Don and Eric, plus executives, will manage them,” Trump tweeted late on Monday. “No new deals will be done during my term(s) in office.” The messages did not mention a role for Ivanka Trump in the businesses. Trump added that he would hold a news conference in the “near future” to discuss business matters, his cabinet picks and other topics.     In a series of tweets last month, Trump said, “Legal documents are being crafted which take me completely out of business operations.” He did not say what the planned change might mean for ownership of his businesses.

text: A recent investigation has revealed that two inmates in France, who were about to be released from prison, are suspected of plotting a terrorist act and allegedly communicating via smartphone with Syria, a stronghold for Islamic State fighters. This incident underscores the concerns that have been repeatedly raised by prison authorities and human rights organizations regarding the potential for crowded prisons to serve as breeding grounds for extremist ideologies, not just in France but elsewhere. This situation has also led to renewed demands for stricter controls on smartphone usage within correctional facilities. These two individuals, who were nearing the completion of their sentences for robberies and other non-terror related crimes, were removed from their cells late last week. Following four days of interrogation, they were officially placed under investigation for potential terrorist activities, according to a judicial representative. A significant factor prompting the authorities' response was the interception of encrypted messages exchanged with contacts in Syria, as noted by Cedric Boyer, a spokesperson for Fresnes prison staff. However, the exact details of the planned actions remain uncertain. Justice Minister Nicole Belloubet communicated the gravity of the situation during an interview with Europe 1 radio, stating that the events of the previous day highlighted the urgency of addressing these threats. Reports from French television station LCI indicated that the pair was allegedly planning attacks targeting prison guards and law enforcement, while an insider connected to the investigation revealed that they had additional targets in mind. Since 2015, attacks in France linked to individuals who have sworn allegiance to or drawn inspiration from Islamic State have resulted in over 240 fatalities. The issue of radicalization within prisons has a long history in France. Guards have expressed concerns about the ease with which inmates can use smartphones to discreetly communicate with the outside world. Boyer, representing the Force Ouvriere labor union for Fresnes prison guards, stated that the government would need to invest resources to tackle this issue. He emphasized the necessity of increasing staff levels and adapting to technological advancements, advocating for the ability to scramble 4G communications instead of relying on outdated technology like the Nokia 33-10, as he told BFM TV.
source_text: Soon-to-go-free jail convicts snared in French attack plot probe. PARIS (Reuters) - Two French prison inmates who were soon to be freed have been  placed under investigation on suspicion of planning a terrorist attack and communicating by smartphone with Syria, stronghold of Islamic State militants. The news highlighted the risk, regularly flagged by rights groups and jail authorities, that crowded prisons offer fertile ground for religious radicalization and conversion to the cause of Islamist fighters, not only in France. It also prompted calls for a crackdown on use of smartphones  inside prisons.  The two, who were nearing the end of jail time for hold-ups and other criminal activity but not terrorist offences, were taken from their cells late last week and interrogated for four days before being placed formally under investigation for suspected terrorist activity, a judiciary official said. One element that prompted the authorities to act was the  interception of encrypted message traffic with Syria, a Fresnes prison staff representative, Cedric Boyer, said. The precise nature of what was being planned was not clear, he added. Conveying the seriousness of the perceived threat that the two constituted, Justice Minister Nicole Belloubet told Europe 1 radio:  What happened yesterday exposed the urgency of the situation.  French TV station LCI said the two were plotting attacks against jail wardens and police forces, while a source close to the investigation said they also had other targets planned. More than 240 people have been killed in France in attacks since the start of 2015 by assailants who pledged allegiance to, or were inspired by, Islamic State. France has a long record of radicalization in its prisons. Prison guards said the ease with which smartphones can be used to communicate secretively with the world outside was an increasing problem.  The government is going to have to put its hand in its pocket,  said Boyer, a representative of the Force Ouvriere labor union and guards at the Fresnes prison.  Extra staffing is needed but it s also a matter of keeping up with technology, being able to scramble 4G communications rather than staying stuck in the age of the Nokia 33-10,  Boyer told BFM TV, referring to latest technology and the days when mobile phones were a rudimentary novelty.

text: On Wednesday, the military in Zimbabwe apprehended Finance Minister Ignatius Chombo, according to a government insider. source_text: Zimbabwe army detains finance minister: government source. HARARE (Reuters) - Zimbabwe s military detained Finance Minister Ignatius Chombo on Wednesday after seizing power in an attempt to root out  criminals  around President Robert Mugabe who it said were causing social and economic suffering, a government source said. Chombo was a leading member of the so-called  G40  faction of the ruling ZANU-PF party, led by Mugabe s wife Grace, that had been vying to succeed the 93-year-old president.

text: The task ahead for German Chancellor Angela Merkel, who has secured her fourth consecutive term, is formidable as she attempts to establish a coalition involving three parties with divergent political ideologies. Although her party garnered the highest number of votes, Merkel's political bloc achieved its poorest performance since 1949, while her coalition partners, the Social Democrats (SPD), announced their intent to join the opposition following a dismal projection of 20.7 percent, marking a record low since World War II. Merkel has suggested that she may have only one viable alternative for governing. The term "Jamaica" refers to a potential coalition between her conservative party, the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP), and the environmentalist Greens, inspired by the colors of the Jamaican flag which represent the three parties: black, yellow, and green. Current projections indicate that Merkel's conservative faction, consisting of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), stands at 33.0 percent, with the FDP at 10.6 percent and the Greens at 8.9 percent, which could provide a functional majority. However, this type of coalition has never been tested at the national level and previously failed in January 2012 in Saarland after just over two years, although it has seen attempts in Schleswig-Holstein since May. On a national scale, this arrangement would need to navigate significant disagreements on issues such as EU reforms, taxation, energy, and immigration. Both the FDP and the Greens have downplayed the chances of forming such a coalition, fearing that compromises could alienate their respective voter bases. Nevertheless, the incentive to participate in the governance of Europe's largest economy could be compelling. They might also feel a responsibility to prevent the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from becoming the leading opposition party, as its anti-immigrant and anti-Islam rhetoric has drawn unsettling parallels to Germany's Nazi history. The AfD capitalized on public discontent regarding Merkel's 2015 decision to allow approximately one million migrants, primarily from conflict-ridden areas in the Middle East, resulting in the party receiving 13 percent of the vote and emerging as the third-largest group in parliament, marking the first time in over fifty years that a far-right party has held such a position. "It will be very difficult, but we all bear a responsibility to our nation. We don’t desire new elections," remarked conservative Interior Minister Thomas de Maiziere, who noted that a new election could potentially bolster the AfD's momentum. A final coalition agreement may hinge more on demonstrating Germany's dedication to democratic principles than on achieving a wide-ranging consensus on policy, especially since the FDP and the Greens, which lean left, stand at opposing ends of the spectrum. Cem Ozdemir, co-leader of the Greens, stated that his party would not engage in "anti-European populism" by joining forces with the conservatives and the FDP. Although the FDP traditionally supports pro-European policies, its young leader, Christian Lindner, has dismissed proposals from French President Emmanuel Macron for deeper integration within the eurozone. source_text: Hurdles high for Merkel in three-way 'Jamaica' tie-up talks. BERLIN (Reuters) - Germany s conservative chancellor Angela Merkel may have won her fourth consecutive national election, but she faces a huge challenge in trying to forge a three-way alliance between parties far apart on the political spectrum. Despite winning most votes, Merkel s bloc slumped to its worst result since 1949 and, just as significant in terms of government building, her current Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners said they would go into opposition after slumping to 20.7 percent in projections, a post-war low. Merkel herself indicated that she had only one other option to govern.  Jamaica  is the name given to a tie-up between her conservative bloc, the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP) and environmentalist Greens, from the fact that island s flag is made up of the black, yellow and green colors of the three parties. Projections put the conservatives, comprising Merkel s Christian Democrats (CDU) and Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) on 33.0 percent, the FDP on 10.6 and the Greens on 8.9 - enough for a workable majority. But such an alliance, untested at a federal level, collapsed in January 2012 in the western state of Saarland after little more than two years, although it has been tried again since May in the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein. On a national level, it would have to overcome deep differences on EU reform, tax, energy and immigration. Both the Greens and FDP, fearing alienating their supporters with the compromises they would have to make, played down the likelihood of such a partnership. The prospect of sharing power in Europe s biggest economy will be a powerful incentive, however. They may also feel a duty to ensure the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose anti-Islam and anti-immigrant rhetoric have for many raised uncomfortable echoes of Germany s Nazi past, does not become the main opposition party. Fueled by voter anger over Merkel s decision in 2015 to admit around a million migrants, mostly fleeing conflict in the Middle East, the AfD won 13 percent of the vote to become the third-biggest bloc, and the first far-right party in the national parliament for over half a century.  It will be very difficult but we all have a responsibility to our country. We don t want new elections,  said conservative Interior Minister Thomas de Maiziere, adding that such a scenario would probably give further momentum to the AfD. An ultimate coalition deal may be more about showing Germany s commitment to democratic values than securing broad agreement on policy, where the pro-business FDP and the left-leaning Greens, in particular, are poles apart. We want to reverse the trend for our country and, if it becomes apparent in talks that these goals can be achieved, then of course we will be available, but if not, it would be our task to go into opposition,  said Lindner. He has also said Russia s annexation of Crimea from Ukraine in 2014 might have to be accepted as a permanent provisional arrangement. It is hard to see how Merkel could swallow that. The Greens emphasize climate policy and want a commitment to phase out coal power by 2030, which would be difficult for the other parties to agree to.  Refugee policy will also be challenging, especially with the FDP and Merkel s Bavarian partners of the CSU taking a much harder line than the Greens on limiting immigration. Berenberg economist Holger Schmieding argued that in the carve-up of ministries under a Jamaica coalition, Wolfgang Schaeuble, conservative finance minister since 2009, may have to yield his post to the FDP.  (That) would tilt the domestic discussion a bit further toward serious income tax cuts,  he said.

text: On Friday, Athens witnessed violent confrontations as police engaged with masked individuals during a march commemorating the 1973 student uprising that contributed to the downfall of Greece's military junta. Over 10,000 demonstrators peacefully proceeded to the United States embassy, with many Greeks blaming the U.S. for its support of the seven-year dictatorship. Approximately 5,000 officers were stationed throughout central Athens to maintain order. Toward the conclusion of the gathering, hooded protesters began throwing stones and Molotov cocktails at the police in the Exarchia neighborhood, a frequent site for such altercations. In response, law enforcement deployed tear gas to disperse the crowd. Earlier that day, floral tributes were placed at the Athens Polytechnic University to remember those who lost their lives during the insurrection. The military regime fell less than a year after the revolt. This yearly demonstration frequently serves as a catalyst for expressing dissent against governmental policies and austerity measures imposed by international creditors in return for financial aid. The economic crisis, which began in 2010, has resulted in widespread unemployment affecting hundreds of thousands. Protesters carried placards stating: "We will live freely" and "No pensioner will be fired!" Greeks maintain hope of escaping lender oversight by August 2018, coinciding with the conclusion of the nation’s third international bailout, while many hold the political elite responsible for the country’s financial ruin.

The annual protest often becomes a focal point for protests against government policies and austerity measures mandated by the country s international lenders in exchange for bailout funds. text: NEW YORK (Reuters) - While traditional Wall Street firms have been deeply concerned about the implications of a significant U.S. regulation on retirement advisory services, their more modern counterparts in Silicon Valley have remained unfazed. The central question revolves around the timing and manner in which the federal government will enforce the "fiduciary rule," which was issued by the U.S. Labor Department in the preceding year. This regulation, designed to safeguard retirees by eliminating conflicts of interest for brokers who provide them with advice, was originally scheduled to take effect in April, but is currently facing opposition from the Trump administration. Presently, the rule is anticipated to be postponed by 180 days, resulting in considerable uncertainty regarding its future. Major wealth management firms and insurance companies that stand to be most impacted by this regulation have expressed approval at the prospect of the new administration possibly retracting it. These firms have vigorously opposed the rule both in legal battles and on Capitol Hill, contending that it would increase compliance and technological expenses while limiting brokers' ability to earn commissions and market certain high-fee products. Detractors of the regulation argue that the heightened costs could lead brokerages to abandon less affluent clients in favor of wealthier ones. Conversely, startups that provide digital wealth management solutions have taken a different stance, asserting that the regulation would benefit retirees and enhance their own business models. The theory is that investors neglected by larger firms might turn to digital providers, which are known for their transparent and cost-effective alternatives. Following President Trump's directive to the Labor Department earlier this month to reassess the rule, executives from "robo-advisers"—firms that utilize algorithms to manage investment funds—downplayed the significance of the regulation on their operations. They noted that while the rule could potentially accelerate the ongoing transition of investor funds toward "robo-advisers," this trend was already gaining traction independently. "An extension of the fiduciary rule could be advantageous for our business, but it does not fundamentally influence our ultimate success," remarked Andy Rachleff, the CEO of Wealthfront, a leading robo-adviser that interacts directly with clients. Meanwhile, Betterment, a rival in the robo-advisory sector, has been urging Democratic lawmakers in recent weeks to combat attempts to postpone or dilute the rule. Nevertheless, Seth Rosenbloom, Betterment’s Associate General Counsel, stated that any alterations to regulation would have minimal effects on the company's growth trajectory. "We regret that it appears the rule might be rescinded, postponed, or weakened," Rosenbloom expressed. "However, we are hopeful that the focus on this matter will lead to better-informed investors over time." Among robo-advisers catering to brokerages, Mike Sha, co-founder and CEO of SigFig, indicated that he did not foresee the rule’s postponement affecting its business or collaborations in any significant way. SigFig’s technology is employed by the wealth divisions of both Wells Fargo & Co and UBS Group AG, which offer its online investment solutions to their clientele. Robo-advisers represent a minor portion of the wealth management sector, overseeing around $200 billion in client assets as of 2016, according to A.T. Kearney, a consulting firm. They project that this figure will dramatically rise to $2.2 trillion by the year 2020. Interruptions to the fiduciary rule could potentially hinder growth for some firms. For instance, LPL Financial Holdings mentioned last week that if the rule encounters delays, it might slow the rollout of certain compliance initiatives, which encompass its robo-adviser and other innovative technologies. However, the movement toward more affordable digital solutions began prior to the formal establishment of the rule, primarily driven by consumer demand for increased digital alternatives. Analysts believe that this trend is unlikely to wane, regardless of the rule's status. "All indications suggest there is extraordinary demand for digital advice and solutions," stated Kendra Thompson, managing director in the financial services division at consultancy Accenture. She emphasized that the rule serves as "an accelerator for digital, not an originator."

Wealthfront competitor Betterment has encouraged Democrats in recent weeks to fight efforts to delay or gut the rule.
