text: On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump asserted that he did not impede the FBI's investigation into purported Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and claimed he has no recordings of his discussions with former FBI director James Comey. Comey was overseeing the inquiry concerning allegations that Russia attempted to influence the election in favor of Trump and whether any associates of Trump collaborated with Moscow, prior to being dismissed by the president on May 9, which ignited significant political controversy. In an interview with Fox News Channel scheduled to air on Friday, Trump stated, "Look there has been no obstruction, there has been no collusion." A partial transcript of this interview was made available by Fox on Thursday. The former FBI head had previously testified before a Senate committee that Trump requested he terminate an investigation into former national security adviser Michael Flynn’s alleged connections to Russia. Earlier that same day, Trump insisted he had neither created nor possessed any recordings of his conversations with Comey, after hinting last month that such tapes might exist which could contradict Comey’s account of the situation. Trump tweeted, "I have no idea whether there are ‘tapes’ or recordings of my conversations with James Comey, but I did not make, and do not have, any such recordings." Lawmakers probing the claims of Russian interference in the U.S. election had sought any recordings from the White House. Shortly after Comey’s termination, Trump brought up the possibility of tapes in a tweet, stating, "James Comey better hope that there are no ‘tapes’ of our conversations before he starts leaking to the press!" on May 12. The accusations of links to Russia have overshadowed Trump's initial five months in office, diverting attention from his fellow Republicans' efforts in Congress to reform the U.S. healthcare and tax systems. According to a source familiar with the matter, Trump has confided in aides that the mere suggestion of tape existence compelled Comey to testify truthfully in his recent appearance. Adam Schiff, who leads the Democrats on the House Intelligence Committee, remarked that Trump still needed to clarify his stance regarding the potential tapes. Schiff stated, "If the president had no tapes, why did he suggest otherwise? Did he seek to mislead the public? Was he trying to intimidate or silence James Comey? And if so, did he take other steps to discourage potential witnesses from speaking out?" CNN reported on Thursday that two senior U.S. intelligence officials informed investigators that Trump had proposed they publicly refute any collusion allegations between his campaign and Russia, although they did not perceive his suggestion as a direct order. According to CNN, Director of National Intelligence Dan Coats and NSA Director Admiral Mike Rogers had separate meetings with investigators from special counsel Robert Mueller and the Senate Intelligence Committee last week. These two officials expressed surprise at Trump’s recommendation and found their interactions with him to be peculiar and uncomfortable, but they opted not to follow through on the president’s requests, as reported by CNN, citing sources familiar with their discussions. Reuters could not authenticate the CNN report. In his Fox interview, Trump voiced concern over what he characterized as a close friendship between Comey and Mueller, who was appointed to continue the investigation after Comey's dismissal. "Well he’s very, very good friends with Comey, which is very bothersome," Trump remarked, according to the Fox transcript. The Kremlin has rejected the conclusions drawn by U.S. intelligence agencies regarding Moscow's attempts to sway the election in Trump's favor, including actions such as hacking into the emails of senior Democrats. Trump has consistently denied any form of collusion.

text: The Austrian government has declared its intention to consult with Italy regarding its proposal to offer citizenship to the German-speaking population in northern Italy. On Tuesday, the new coalition administration in Vienna confirmed that it would pursue plans for dual citizenship for residents of the Alto Adige region, though it vowed to engage with Rome on the matter, which could potentially revive historical tensions. This initiative was included in a substantial coalition agreement, spanning 180 pages, released over the weekend by Chancellor Sebastian Kurz's conservative People’s Party in conjunction with the far-right Freedom Party (FPO). Following World War One, Austria ceded the Alto Adige region to Italy. In the 1920s, the fascist regime of Benito Mussolini attempted to populate the area with thousands of ethnic Italians; nevertheless, the German-speaking community remains predominant, with a ratio of roughly two to one compared to Italians. Within the region, educational institutions are segregated by language, and the local populace tends to patronize different establishments based on their linguistic background. However, the region benefits from considerable autonomy and substantial financial support from the Italian government, which has contributed to reducing separatist sentiments among the local populace. Chancellor Kurz has asserted that the initiative, long advocated for by the FPO, aims solely to foster collaboration among European countries. "We plan to undertake this in close partnership with Italy and the government in Rome," Kurz stated during a joint press briefing with FPO leader and Vice Chancellor Heinz-Christian Strache, following their cabinet's inaugural meeting. Italian political leaders have voiced strong opposition to Austria's proposal, labeling it a move towards nationalism and asserting that it jeopardizes the fragile ethnic equilibrium within Alto Adige, which is also referred to as South Tyrol. On Monday, Italy's foreign minister remarked to the ANSA news agency that discussing the matter would necessitate "a conversation that requires enormous delicacy." In contrast, Kurz downplayed the likelihood of escalating tensions. "We maintain excellent relations with Rome. I am personally acquainted with the head of the Italian government. I am also friends with the foreign minister," Kurz said, referencing his previous role as foreign minister until the new administration was established. He continued, "Our government program reflects a request from the South Tyrolean population, a sentiment shared by all political parties in South Tyrol and explicitly articulated by the provincial government of South Tyrol." Strache pointed out that Italy has already implemented a similar framework for its citizens of Italian descent living in Slovenia and Croatia. The website of the Italian Foreign Ministry outlines the criteria that allow individuals who lost their citizenship when certain territories transitioned to Yugoslavia to apply for an Italian passport. Notably, this topic did not emerge during Austria's parliamentary elections in October, which were won by Kurz's party, which adopted a stringent stance on immigration that frequently aligned with the FPO's views. Austria has accepted a significant number of asylum seekers amid Europe’s migration crisis, and both political factions committed to preventing a similar influx in the future. However, in Austrian Tyrol, where maps often continue to depict the southern region now part of Italy, the issue remains a deeply emotional one. This province, a bastion of support for Kurz's conservatives, is scheduled to conduct local parliament elections in February. Arno Kompatscher, the head of Alto Adige's provincial government, expressed his backing for the proposal, provided it is framed within a European context aimed at unifying nations rather than creating divisions – a possible nod to any objections from Italy. "It has nothing to do with secession or altering borders or any such matters. This is about expressing a personal connection to Austria, and the debate should revolve around this context," he remarked during a news conference. The criteria for granting citizenship remain undetermined and should be a topic of negotiations between Austria and Italy, he added. In recent years, Austria and Italy have experienced tensions over Austria's threats to impose controls at the Brenner Pass, a crucial transport route along their shared border, should there be a sharp increase in migrants arriving from Italy.

text: A vote was held on Thursday by the Social Democrats (SPD) of Germany to initiate discussions with Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservative party regarding the formation of a government. This decision followed a heartfelt appeal from SPD's leader, Martin Schulz, who urged for the opportunity to advocate for a social United States of Europe. This vote paves the way for negotiations aimed at overcoming the deadlock faced by Europe’s leading economy, which has seen both Merkel and the SPD lose support in the recent September elections, complicating the dynamics within the parliament. Schulz encouraged hesitant members of the center-left SPD to consider Merkel's invitations to revitalize the coalition that has been in power for the last four years. He articulated the party’s duty to rejuvenate social democracy within Germany. The best chance for Merkel to prolong her 12-year leadership appears to hinge on forming a new 'grand coalition' with the SPD, especially after her talks with two smaller parties faltered, thereby enhancing the SPD's negotiating power. "The issue at hand is not whether there will be a grand coalition or not," Schulz stated during a speech at his party's biennial congress. "It’s not about opting for a minority government or calling for new elections. Rather, it’s about how we fulfill our responsibilities, particularly towards the younger generation." He emphasized that for the party to recuperate, it must present a distinct vision for both Germany and Europe that benefits its citizens. Schulz called for increased European integration, envisioning a United States of Europe by the year 2025. He expressed concern that Europe frequently serves the interests of large corporations rather than its populace, articulating a populist agenda that extends beyond Merkel’s more limited openness to structural reform and administrative streamlining. Serious discussions between the two parties are anticipated to commence in the upcoming year. A special congress will be necessary where party members will cast their votes on whether to endorse a final agreement, which may not constitute a formal coalition and could potentially involve tolerating a minority government. The prominent premier of Lower Saxony, Stephan Weil, indicated that the SPD would seek to see its priorities reflected in exchange for backing any government. text: Janet Reno, who made history as the first female attorney general in the United States, passed away on Monday at the age of 78. (Reuters) Known for her straightforward communication style, Reno held office for eight years and was responsible for authorizing the controversial raid on the Branch Davidian compound in Texas just weeks after taking on the role. Her goddaughter, Gabrielle D’Alemberte, reported that Reno died in Miami due to complications related to Parkinson’s disease, a condition she had been diagnosed with in 1995. Serving as the nation's chief law enforcement officer during Bill Clinton's presidency from 1993 to 2001, Reno became the longest-serving attorney general of the 20th century. Among her notable actions was the decision in 2000 to seize six-year-old Elian Gonzalez, a Cuban shipwreck survivor, from his relatives in Miami, along with the initiation of a significant antitrust lawsuit against Microsoft Corp in 1998. "Janet Reno was an American original, a public servant whose intellect, integrity and fierce commitment to justice helped shape our nation’s legal landscape," stated President Barack Obama. Clinton reflected on Monday, "Throughout my presidency, Janet served as attorney general for all eight years, tirelessly working to enhance community safety, safeguard the vulnerable, and find the right balance between pursuing justice and preventing abuse of power." Reno, a former prosecutor from Miami, was selected by Clinton after his initial two picks for the position faced difficulties. She was known for her independent nature and direct demeanor, which often caused friction with the White House. Complaints arose regarding her tendency to appoint special prosecutors, particularly in investigations like the Whitewater controversy involving the financial dealings of President Clinton and First Lady Hillary Clinton. Just 38 days after being appointed attorney general, Reno sanctioned the FBI's raid on April 19, 1993, which resulted in the deaths of approximately 80 individuals, many of whom were children, at the Branch Davidian compound located in Waco, Texas. Earlier, federal agents had attempted to serve a warrant to the cult leader, David Koresh, who claimed to be the Messiah, for possessing illegal firearms. A shootout ensued, resulting in the deaths of four agents and six cult members, leading to a tense 51-day standoff. After negotiations reached a deadlock, Reno authorized the raid based on reports of child abuse within the compound. The operation against the heavily armed cult ended tragically in a fire that consumed the site. "I made the decision. I’m accountable. The buck stops with me," Reno solemnly remarked at a subsequent news conference. Taking a personal interest in the highly publicized case of Elian Gonzalez, the young boy whose mother perished while trying to escape Cuba, Reno engaged with both the boy and his Miami relatives, who were fighting to prevent his return to Cuba, as well as his father and grandmothers, who wished to raise him in his native land. Reno contended that Elian should be with his father and acted decisively after the Miami relatives ignored a U.S. government directive to surrender him. In a predawn operation in April 2000, she authorized armed agents to retrieve the boy from his relatives’ residence and reunite him with his father, who subsequently took him back to Cuba. This raid sparked outrage among Miami's Cuban exile community, with critics labeling her a "witch" and a puppet of Cuban leader Fidel Castro. In 1998, Reno's Justice Department initiated a major antitrust lawsuit against Microsoft. Two years later, a federal judge mandated the breakup of the software giant due to its noncompliance with his ruling regarding monopolistic practices. The case reached a settlement in 2001 under President George W. Bush’s administration, which was viewed as favorable for Microsoft. Following the devastating truck bombing of the Oklahoma City federal building in 1995, which claimed the lives of 168 individuals, Reno appeared alongside Clinton, pledging to pursue the death penalty for those responsible. In 2001, Timothy McVeigh, the convicted Oklahoma City bomber, became the first federal inmate executed since 1963.
source_text: Janet Reno, first U.S. woman attorney general, dies at 78. (Reuters) - Blunt-spoken Janet Reno, who served eight years as the first woman U.S. attorney general and authorized the deadly 1993 raid on the Branch Davidian cult compound in Texas just weeks into the job, died on Monday at age 78. Reno died in Miami of Parkinson’s disease complications, according to her goddaughter, Gabrielle D’Alemberte. Reno was diagnosed with the progressive central nervous system disorder in 1995. Reno served as the United States’ top law enforcement official during Democrat Bill Clinton’s presidency from 1993 to 2001, becoming the longest-tenured attorney general of the 20th century. She authorized the seizure by federal agents in 2000 of 6-year-old Cuban shipwreck survivor Elian Gonzalez from relatives in Miami, as well as the government’s huge antitrust case against Microsoft Corp in 1998. “Janet Reno was an American original, a public servant whose intellect, integrity and fierce commitment to justice helped shape our nation’s legal landscape,” President Barack Obama said in a statement. Clinton said on Monday, “As attorney general for all eight years of my presidency, Janet worked tirelessly to make our communities safer, protect the vulnerable, and to strike the right balance between seeking justice and avoiding abuse of power.” The former Miami prosecutor, picked by Clinton only after his first two choices for the job ran into trouble, exhibited an independent streak and a brusque manner that often upset the White House. Reno weathered White House complaints that she was not a team player and that she sought too many special prosecutors to investigate cases, including the Whitewater affair involving the finances of the president and first lady Hillary Clinton.  Reno was only 38 days into the attorney general’s job when she approved the April 19, 1993, FBI raid that led to the deaths of about 80 people, including many children, at the Branch Davidian cult compound in Waco, Texas. Federal agents had earlier tried to serve a warrant on the cult’s leader, David Koresh, who said he was the Messiah, for stockpiling weapons. Four agents and six cult members were killed in an ensuing shootout, leading to a 51-day standoff. With negotiations at an impasse, Reno gave the go-ahead for the raid after hearing reports of child abuse in the compound. The raid on the heavily armed cultists ended in an inferno that engulfed the site. “I made the decision. I’m accountable. The buck stops with me,” a grim-looking Reno told a news conference later. Reno took a personal interest in the political tussle over Elian Gonzalez, the young shipwreck survivor whose mother drowned fleeing Cuba.  Reno met the boy and his Miami relatives, who battled to keep him from returning to communist Cuba, and his father and grandmothers, who wanted to raise Gonzalez in his homeland. Reno argued that Elian belonged with his father and acted after the Miami relatives defied a U.S. government order to hand him over. She authorized armed agents to take the boy from his relatives’ home in a predawn raid in April 2000 and reunite him with his father, who took him back to Cuba. The raid infuriated members of Miami’s Cuban exile community, who called her a “witch” and a lackey of Cuban President Fidel Castro. In 1998, Reno’s Justice Department brought a huge antitrust case against Microsoft. Two years later, a federal judge ordered the breakup of the software giant because it had ignored his ruling that it had used unlawful monopolistic practices. The case was settled in 2001 by the administration of President George W. Bush, Clinton’s Republican successor, in terms seen as favorable to Microsoft. Reno appeared with Clinton after the 1995 truck bombing of  the Oklahoma City federal building that killed 168 people, and vowed to seek the death penalty for the perpetrators. Convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 become the first federal prisoner executed since 1963. McVeigh said he carried out the attack to punish the U.S. government for the Waco cult raid and another raid in Idaho. Some comedians made fun of Reno during her time in office, lampooning her appearance and 6-foot-2 height (1.88-meter), among them Will Ferrell who impersonated her on “Saturday Night Live.”  Shortly after leaving office, she appeared on the show next to Ferrell, both wearing identical outfits, in a sketch called “Janet Reno’s Dance Party.” Reno was in the job longer than anyone except William Wirt, who held it from November 1817 until March 1829. Reno ran for governor in Florida in 2002, but lost in the Democratic primary. Parkinson’s disease caused trembling in her arms. “All it does is shake, and you get used to it shaking after a while,” she told a TV interviewer. Reno was born on July 21, 1938, in Miami to parents who were newspaper reporters. She attended public schools in Miami and earned a chemistry degree at Cornell University in 1960. She received her law degree from Harvard three years later, and worked as a lawyer in Miami.

text: The U.S. envoy in Britain criticized the media for leaking information regarding the inquiry into the suicide bombing that resulted in the deaths of 22 individuals in Manchester, asserting that the U.S. will take measures to find those accountable. Lewis Lukens, who serves as the acting ambassador to the U.K., described these disclosures as 'reprehensible' and 'deeply distressing' during a Thursday interview on BBC radio. He stated, 'An investigation into these leaks is being initiated by the United States government, and we will take suitable action once we uncover the origin of the leaks.' Furthermore, he emphasized the determination to halt these leaks and identify their sources. source_text: Leaks of Manchester bomb probe 'reprehensible,' will stop: U.S. envoy. LONDON (Reuters) - The most senior U.S. diplomat in Britain condemned media leaks of an investigation into a suicide bomb which killed 22 people in Manchester, saying the U.S. government would take action to identify those responsible. “These leaks were reprehensible, deeply distressing. We unequivocally condemn them,” Lewis Lukens, U.S. charge d’affaires in London and acting ambassador to Britain, said on BBC radio on Thursday. “The United States government is launching an investigation into these leaks and will take appropriate action once we identify the source of the leaks,” he said. “We are determined to identify these leaks and to stop them.”   British Prime Minister Theresa May said on Thursday she would tell U.S. President Donald Trump that intelligence shared between their two countries had to remain secure.

text: A tragic incident occurred on Thursday when a train collided with a school bus at a level crossing near Perpignan in southwestern France, resulting in the deaths of four teenagers. Visuals from the accident site revealed the bus torn in half, with numerous emergency vehicles responding to the scene. Additionally, around 20 individuals sustained injuries from the incident, with 11 of those being categorized as serious, as reported by French Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, who promptly arrived at the location. The majority of the injured were students aged between 13 and 17 who were on the bus. Philippe addressed the media, emphasizing that officials were prioritizing the delivery of accurate updates to the victims' families, a task complicated by the challenge of identifying those who perished and some of the injured. A crisis management center was established at the town hall of Millas, situated approximately 850 kilometers (530 miles) from Paris. Local media indicated that the bus was carrying students from Christian Bourquin college in the town. French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his condolences on Twitter, stating, "All my thoughts (are with) the victims and their families." The reasons behind the collision remain unclear as authorities await the outcome of a comprehensive investigation. Both the bus driver and the train operator survived the crash and are set to be interviewed by law enforcement. The train, which was transporting 25 passengers, was operating at a speed of 80 km/h, the designated limit for that particular stretch of track, according to a spokesperson from the national SNCF railway who spoke to Reuters. The interior ministry reported that three passengers on the train incurred relatively minor injuries. Witnesses claimed that the barriers at the crossing were lowered at the time of the impact, as stated by the SNCF spokesperson, who also noted that all initial information is subject to verification by investigators. France has experienced several significant rail accidents in recent years, with one of the most catastrophic occurring in 1988 when a commuter train heading into Paris Gare de Lyon collided with a stationary train, resulting in 56 fatalities due to brake failure.

text: During a rally in Geneva, Ohio, Donald Trump responded to comments made by Vice President Joe Biden with his own sharp remarks. Biden had previously stated that he would like to take Trump "behind the gym" as retribution for Trump's comments in a 2005 video where he claimed to have groped women. In response, Trump demonstrated a gesture, turning to the side and exhaling forcefully, saying, "You know what you do with Biden? You go like this," implying that Biden would fall over. Trump, who is 70, noted that Biden is 73, highlighting their similar tendencies to exaggerate. Biden had expressed during a campaign event for Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton in Pennsylvania that people often inquire if he wished to debate Trump. GENEVA, Ohio (Reuters) - Donald Trump shrugged off tough talk from Vice President Joe Biden with a verbal counter punch of his own. At a rally in Geneva, Ohio, the Republican presidential nominee on Thursday night addressed Biden’s remark last week that he would like to take Trump “behind the gym” to punish him for videotaped remarks in 2005 in which Trump boasted about groping women. “You know what you do with Biden? You go like this,” Trump said, then turned to the side to blow out a puff of air from his mouth. “And he’d fall over.” Trump is 70 years old. Biden is 73. Both have been known to delve into hyperbole. Biden had said at a campaign event for Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton in Pennsylvania that he is frequently asked whether he wished he had been debating Trump. Biden had flirted with running for president this year. “No, I wish we were in high school. I could take him behind the gym. That’s what I wish,” Biden said. Trump said if he had ever made a statement like that about Biden the news media would be outraged. “Can you imagine if I ever made that statement? ‘Donald trump is a bully! He threatened Vice President Biden!’ But everybody said ‘oh, that was a wonderful statement,’” Trump said. “I dream about Biden,” Trump added. “Boy, that would be easy. That would be an easy one.”

text: Tensions regarding detentions continue to simmer even as the United States and Turkey have resumed the issuance of visas. ANKARA (Reuters) - On Monday, the U.S. began to partially reinstate visa services in Turkey after claiming to have received guarantees about the safety of its mission staff following several detentions. The Turkish embassy in Washington quickly responded by stating it would also implement this change, although it refuted the existence of any such assurances. It characterized the U.S. action as a favorable step, highlighting that it came just before Turkish Prime Minister Binali Yildirim's visit to the United States. Despite this development, the U.S. embassy expressed serious concerns regarding the detention of two local employees at its diplomatic facilities in Turkey, as well as the situation of American citizens who have been arrested under a state of emergency that has been in effect since last year's failed coup. A month ago, the arrest of a long-time employee at the U.S. consulate in Istanbul prompted the U.S. to halt all non-immigrant visa services while it evaluated the security of its personnel in Turkey. Following the U.S. announcement on October 8, Turkey declared that it would enact reciprocal measures, and President Tayyip Erdogan later condemned Washington, accusing it of jeopardizing a long-standing alliance with Ankara. 'We have received initial high-level assurances from the government of Turkey that there are no additional local employees of our mission in Turkey under investigation,' the U.S. embassy stated. 'We have also received initial assurances from the government of Turkey that our local staff will not be detained or arrested for performing their official duties.' However, hours later, the Turkish embassy asserted that it had not provided any assurances to the United States, indicating that decisions regarding the legal treatment of U.S. mission personnel would be determined by Turkey's judiciary. The Turkish statement clarified that the personnel in question employed by the U.S. had faced judicial proceedings due to serious charges unrelated to their official duties. Moreover, the Turkish embassy described the U.S. embassy's mention of security conditions as 'odd' and unreflective of the reality on the ground. The news regarding the partial resumption of visa services, which Reuters reported earlier, contributed to an appreciation of the lira, which strengthened to 3.8356 against the dollar from 3.8708 previously. In May, a translator at the U.S. consulate in Adana was arrested, and more recently, a worker from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) was detained in Istanbul. Both individuals are accused of having connections to the coup attempt that occurred last year. The U.S. embassy has firmly stated that these accusations are unfounded. Turkish authorities have indicated that police are seeking to question a third worker based in Istanbul. His wife and daughter were taken into custody due to alleged ties to the network of Fethullah Gulen, a cleric residing in the U.S. whom Ankara blames for orchestrating the coup attempt. They have since been released. Turkey has expressed frustration over what it perceives as the U.S.'s unwillingness to extradite Gulen, who has lived in Pennsylvania since 1999. U.S. officials maintain that there must be substantial evidence for courts to authorize his extradition. Gulen has denied any involvement in the coup attempt. Erdogan has also criticized the United States after former Turkish economy minister and the ex-head of a state-owned bank were charged with conspiring to breach U.S. sanctions against Iran by illegally transferring hundreds of millions of dollars through the U.S. financial system on behalf of Tehran. These charges are part of an ongoing case against Reza Zarrab, a wealthy Turkish-Iranian gold trader who was arrested last year in the U.S. for evading sanctions. Zarrab is scheduled to stand trial this month and has pleaded not guilty. Erdogan has suggested that U.S. prosecutors have 'ulterior motives' in this case, as they have included mentions of him and his wife in court documents. In their statement, the Turkish embassy emphasized that Turkey holds 'serious concerns' regarding legal proceedings involving its citizens in the U.S.

text: According to French Finance Minister Michel Sapin, the negative remarks made by U.S. President-elect Donald Trump only strengthen the unity among Europeans. On Tuesday, he commented on Trump's assertion that German Chancellor Angela Merkel committed a "catastrophic mistake" regarding her migration policy during an interview released by the German publication Bild on Sunday. Sapin stated to journalists, "The more he (Trump) makes this sort of statement, the more Europeans close ranks," emphasizing that such criticism is intolerable. He added, "The attack on the Chancellor is not an argument we can accept as Frenchmen or as Europeans." When questioned about a potential response from Europe if the U.S. imposes a 35 percent tax on imports, Sapin remarked, "We will all have time to see whether there’s a difference between the content of a tweet and the laws that will be passed." Trump, in the same interview with Bild, indicated his intention to apply a 35 percent tariff on cars manufactured in Germany and sold in the U.S., a proposal that has faced strong opposition from Berlin and impacted the stock prices of car manufacturers. He was quoted saying, "I would tell BMW that if you are building a factory in Mexico and plan to sell cars to the USA, without a 35 percent tax, then you can forget that," with the remarks translated into German.
source_text: Trump's criticism only draws Europeans closer, says French minister. PARIS (Reuters) - Criticism of Europe by U.S. President-elect Donald Trump only serves to reinforce European solidarity, French Finance Minister Michel Sapin said on Tuesday. Trump said German Chancellor Angela Merkel had made a “catastrophic mistake” with her open door policy on migration, according to an interview published on Sunday by German newspaper Bild.  “The more he (Trump) makes this sort of statement, the more Europeans close ranks,” Sapin told reporters, adding that such  criticism was unacceptable. “The attack on the Chancellor is not an argument we can accept as Frenchmen or as Europeans.” Asked whether Europe would have to react if the United States decided to slap a 35 percent tax on imports, Sapin said: “We will all have time to see whether there’s a difference between the content of a tweet and the laws that will be passed.” Trump was quoted as telling Bild he would impose a 35 percent levy on German-made cars imported to the U.S. market, a plan that drew sharp rebukes from Berlin and hit automakers’ shares. “I would tell BMW that if you are building a factory in Mexico and plan to sell cars to the USA, without a 35 percent tax, then you can forget that,” Trump said in remarks translated into German.

text: On Friday, the U.S. State Department provided over 1,100 pages of documents to the committee looking into the fatalities of American citizens in Benghazi, Libya, which occurred on September 11, 2012, as stated by the chairman of the House panel. These documents contained communications from senior officials during the tenure of Democratic presidential hopeful Hillary Clinton as secretary of state, according to Trey Gowdy, Chairman of the Select Committee on Benghazi. Gowdy, a member of the Republican Party, expressed in a statement, "It is unacceptable that the committee had to wait more than a year for these documents to be made available, and that our Democratic colleagues did nothing to assist us in obtaining them." text: On Sunday, an agreement was reached by Congress that will ensure health benefits for retired coal miners. The U.S. government, along with coal companies, will be mandated to provide healthcare coverage to these workers, even amidst the financial difficulties facing the coal industry, which is grappling with bankruptcies. This provision for the United Mine Workers’ healthcare was part of a fiscal spending agreement that totals approximately $1 trillion, aimed at preventing a government shutdown that could occur later this week. Approximately 22,600 miners and their families were at risk of losing their healthcare benefits by April 30, which were in jeopardy due to the industry's ongoing struggles and the financial recovery efforts of various companies after bankruptcy. "This permanent fix to secure these benefits represents a triumph for our miners, their families, and their widows," stated Congressman Evan Jenkins, a Republican from West Virginia representing coal-producing areas. Over the past few months, members of the UMWA have traveled to Washington several times to press lawmakers on the importance of safeguarding their benefits, viewing it as a responsibility of the government. The Krug-Lewis agreement, brokered by President Harry Truman in 1946, provided guarantees for health and pension benefits for coal miners. However, the recent agreement does not provide a long-term solution for the miners' pension funds, which are also facing termination. Legislators from both political parties are still optimistic about passing the Miners Protection Act, which would allocate funds from the Abandoned Mine Land fund to the pension plan of the union to avert insolvency. Senator Joe Manchin, a Democrat from West Virginia, has been collaborating with both Democratic and Republican lawmakers, as well as the UMWA, to push this legislation forward. If Congress fails to authorize the fund transfers, the financially troubled Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp, which ensures failed private-sector pension programs, will take on the responsibility for these plans. Manchin emphasized that there exists a "sacred bond between worker and country" and expressed his determination to fully meet the obligation to secure pension benefits for retired miners.

The provision to secure the United Mine Workers’ healthcare benefits was included in a deal that lawmakers reached late on Sunday for around $1 trillion in federal funding that would avert a government shutdown later this week. Around 22,600 coal miners and their families were on the brink of losing on April 30 their healthcare benefits, which were at risk of default as the industry struggled, with companies trying to recover from bankruptcies. “This permanent solution to protect these benefits is a victory for our miners, their families, and their widows,” said Congressman Evan Jenkins, a West Virginia Republican who represents the state’s coal-producing counties. Members of the UMWA have made several visits to Washington over the last few months to urge lawmakers to protect their benefits, which they say is a government obligation. President Harry Truman in 1946 brokered the Krug-Lewis agreement, which guaranteed health and pension benefits for coal miners. Sunday’s agreement did not address a long-term fix for miners’ pension funds, which are also set to be terminated.    Lawmakers from both parties still hope to pass the Miners Protection Act, which would transfer funds from the Abandoned Mine Land fund to the union’s pension plan to prevent its insolvency. Democratic Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia has been working with the UMWA  and Democratic and Republican lawmakers to pass that bill. If Congress cannot transfer those funds, the financially-strained $5 billion federal Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp, an agency that backstops failed private-sector pension programs, would be responsible for covering the plans. Manchin said there is a “sacred bond between worker and country” and that he “is more determined than ever to fulfill our whole obligation and secure retired miners pension benefits as well.”

text: Tourism has nearly vanished in a Balinese town as the threat of an eruption from Mount Agung looms. AMED, Indonesia (Reuters) - Once a vibrant destination for travelers, a town in Bali has seen its visitor numbers plummet following alerts indicating that the nearby volcano could erupt at any moment. This situation highlights the increasing economic toll that the restless volcano is inflicting on Indonesia. Since authorities raised the alert level for Mount Agung to the highest category last month, many hotels, dive shops, and eateries in the vicinity have experienced significant declines in business. An owner of a dive center located in Amed, approximately 15 km (9 miles) from the volcano and just outside the designated danger zone, stated that numerous clients have canceled their reservations. "If (the situation) lasts for nine months or more... then we have no choice but to close down because we will have no money left to operate and pay the staff," remarked Helene Rabate, the Spanish operator of the center. The local cafes and restaurants are mostly vacant, with only a few individuals spotted at the typically packed dive facilities in this coastal area. The last recorded eruption of Agung occurred in 1963, resulting in over 1,000 fatalities. Since that event, tourism has transformed locations like Amed from tranquil fishing and farming communities. Restaurant proprietor Wayan Widarti has reported a severe decline in clientele. "It could be worse than when the Bali bombing happened because there’s uncertainty on when (the eruption) is going to happen and how long we wait," she stated, referencing the 2002 nightclub bombing that resulted in 202 deaths and caused a drop in tourists to the island. Bali, known for its surfing, beaches, and temples, welcomed nearly 5 million visitors last year, representing more than half of all foreign tourists to Indonesia. As a vital element of Bali’s economy, tourism ranks as Indonesia’s fourth-largest source of foreign currency, following natural resources such as coal and palm oil. Officials in Indonesia have been working to stimulate an economy that has seen growth rates stabilize around 5 percent for several years, making any prolonged disruption to tourism especially concerning. While Indonesian authorities assert that Bali remains safe for travelers, cancellations have occurred even in regions farther from the volcano due to fears that ash clouds could interfere with air travel. Some visitors continue to stay in the area, maintaining a safe distance from the volcano. "We plan to... just follow security instructions... and take a fast boat to escape if there is an eruption," said Arlin Shiu, a traveler from Hong Kong accompanying a friend. Disaster management officials have established an exclusion zone extending up to 12 km, leading to the evacuation of over 140,000 residents to nearby villages. Bali's governor I Made Mangku Pastika noted that those residing in secure areas have no reason to evacuate, adding that makeshift shelters are becoming overwhelmed by the influx of thousands of additional evacuees. text: On Monday, four men were executed by Somalia's al Shabaab insurgents after being charged with espionage. This public execution highlighted the group's significant control over regions in the southern part of the country, despite the government preparing for an upcoming military offensive against them. The men had been detained several weeks prior. Following their confessions of spying, a ruling was made by the court, as reported via phone by Mohamed Abu Abdalla, al Shabaab’s governor for the Jubba regions. It was revealed that two individuals were working for the Ethiopian government, while the other two were accused of collaborating with Somali intelligence services. The execution took place in Buale, which serves as the capital of Middle Jubba, a region predominantly under the influence of al Shabaab, located south of Mogadishu, the capital city. Efforts to obtain comments from the government were unsuccessful, as calls went unanswered. Since being expelled from the capital by African Union peacekeepers in 2011, al Shabaab's power has diminished, but it continues to dominate vast areas of the countryside. The group aims to topple the fragile government supported by the U.N. and enforce a severe interpretation of Islamic law. Somalia has been embroiled in civil conflict since 1991, when clan leaders overthrew a dictator and subsequently turned against one another.
source_text: Somalia's Islamist insurgency executes four men accused of spying. (Reuters) - Somalia s Islamist al Shabaab insurgency shot four men accused of spying on Monday in a public execution which underscored the insurgents  control of swathes of the country s southern region even as the government girds up for an offensive against them.   The four men were captured weeks ago. They were publicly executed today after the court ruling and after admitting espionage,  Mohamed Abu Abdalla, al Shabaab s governor for the Jubba regions said by phone.  Two of them were spying for the Ethiopian government and the other two were spying for Somali government intelligence.  The men were shot in Buale, the capital of Middle Jubba, he said, a region mostly controlled by al Shabaab that lies south of the capital of Mogadishu.  The government did not return calls seeking comment.  Al Shabaab s grip on the Horn of African nation has been weakening since it was pushed out of the capital in 2011 by African Union peacekeepers. But it still controls large parts of the countryside.  It is trying to overthrow the weak, U.N.-backed government and impose a strict form of Islamic law. Somalia has been riven by civil war since 1991, when clan warlords overthrew a dictator then turned on each other.

text: The recent decision to host the European Medicines Agency has led to mixed reactions in Amsterdam. Last month, Dutch lawmakers celebrated securing this regulatory body that will relocate from London due to Britain's exit from the EU. However, not everyone is pleased about the anticipated arrival of around 900 highly-paid pharmaceutical professionals. Residents and local media have expressed growing frustration over yet another influx of visitors - this time, white-collar expatriates. The newspaper NRC Handelsblad posed the question, "A Nice Brexit Trophy, But Can The City Handle It?" highlighting concerns about the impact of these new arrivals on the city. While supporters view the EMA’s presence as a significant economic advantage, critics argue that it adds to the woes of rising rents and property costs, as mentioned in a report by national broadcaster NOS, titled "Home Buyers Will Pay The Price For Drugs Agency In Amsterdam." On social media platforms, numerous users lamented what they perceive as the loss of the city’s unique, free-spirited character, which they believe has been compromised by an influx of bureaucratic personnel from the EMA. This transformation of Amsterdam has been ongoing for over a decade. Marketing efforts have spotlighted the city's picturesque canals, the Anne Frank House, and renowned museums showcasing works by Van Gogh and Rembrandt. Legislative measures have contributed to this rebranding by closing a third of the city’s brothels in 2008 and initiating a plan to shut down marijuana cafes near schools in 2011. According to Amsterdam Marketing, overnight visitors nearly doubled between 2011 and 2016, with the city now hosting over 6 million international tourists annually, alongside its population of 850,000 residents. At the same time, the number of affluent expatriates has surged, increasing from 39,000 in 2009 to 77,000 in 2015, as reported by the city's statistics office. Reinier van Dantzig, head of the largest faction in the city council from the D-66 centrist party, remarked on Amsterdam’s historical openness, stating, "Immigrants played a crucial role during the city’s 17th-century golden age and continue to contribute to the current economic prosperity." He expressed difficulty understanding the viewpoint of those who view incoming residents as a threat, asserting that they enhance the community. Van Dantzig indicated that the municipality is developing housing for an additional 70,000 inhabitants, allocating some of this for low and medium-income families. However, for Danielle van Diemen, a fifth-generation resident, these efforts seem insufficient. She criticized the city for being shaped by a blend of Western expatriates who mistakenly believe in Amsterdam's edgy reputation, which, according to her, has diminished. She highlighted the implementation of a squatting ban in 2010, noting that it has exacerbated the divide between wealthy expatriates who do not speak Dutch and long-time locals. "So: expats go home and leave the city to us," she declared. Bert Nap, a resident living near the city center, echoed her sentiments, feeling like a stranger in his own neighborhood. "We have lost all our local bakers and shops to those catering to tourists," he lamented, reflecting common grievances in Europe’s tourist destinations. A survey conducted by apartment-hunting platform Nestpick in April ranked Amsterdam as the top city globally for millennials, praising its open-mindedness, vibrant nightlife, and flourishing startup culture. Jan Rath, a sociology professor at the University of Amsterdam, pointed out that the incoming expatriates possess qualifications and skills, leading to competition for housing and employment with individuals lacking such credentials. "What’s occurring... could be interpreted as a replacement of the population," he commented. Rising real estate prices have created challenges for unskilled workers, impacting both native Dutch individuals and immigrants from Turkey and Morocco. Statistics Netherlands (CBS) reports that 40 percent of young couples leave the city within four years.

Amsterdam s residents and media, already sick of the numbers of tourists searching out stag-do strip joints on their streets, are increasingly vexed about another group of visitors - white-collar, expatriate workers.  A Nice Brexit Trophy, But Can The City Handle It?  newspaper NRC Handelsblad said in a headline, referring to the decision to move the regulatory agency from London to Amsterdam after Britain leaves the EU. The EMA will come with around 900 staff - a wonderful economic boost, according to supporters of the move. Detractors say it s just another group of foreigners with big pay packets driving up rents and property prices.  Home Buyers Will Pay The Price For Drugs Agency In Amsterdam,  said national broadcaster NOS. On social media, many also mourned the death of the city s free-wheeling and edgy spirit, killed off, they said, by the likes of the EMA s army of bureaucrats. The sanitation of Amsterdam has been going on for more than a decade.  Advertising campaigns have focused on the city s canals, the Anne Frank House, the museums packed with Van Gogh and Rembrandt s greatest works.     Legislators have helped the re-branding by shuttering a third of the city s brothels in 2008 and starting a program to close marijuana cafes near schools in 2011. That has all coincided with a surge in the number of well-heeled expatriates - numbers have also doubled to 77,000 in 2015 from 39,000 in 2009, according to the city s statistics office.   Amsterdam has always been an open city,  said Reinier van Dantzig, leader of the largest faction in city parliament from the centrist D-66 party.     Immigrants were an integral part of the city s 17th-Century golden age and were continuing to contribute to the current economic boom, he added.   That s why I have such difficulty with people who say that people from outside who want to become Amsterdammers would be some kind of danger - I think they re an addition.  The city, he said, was building housing for 70,000 more people, with extra space allotted to apartments for low and medium-income families. Too little, too late for Danielle van Diemen, a 5th-generation Amsterdammer.  The city is being defined by a mix of Western foreigners who think that Amsterdam is edgy but that s no longer true,  she said, pointing to a ban on squatting that went into effect in 2010.  The gap between wealthy expats who don t speak Dutch and locals is all but unbridgeable, she added.  So: expats go home and leave the city to us.   I am like a visitor in my own neighborhood,  said Bert Nap, who lives near the center.  We have lost all our bakers and other shops to tourism-orientated shops,  he added, echoing complaints across Europe s holiday hotspots. A survey by apartment-searching website Nestpick in April ranked Amsterdam #1 on its global list of best cities for millennials, citing its tolerance, night life and thriving startup scene.  These people have qualifications, they have skills, they are networked, and so the fact is that they compete for houses and jobs with people who don t have those qualifications,  said Jan Rath, a sociology professor at the University of Amsterdam.  You could argue that what s happening ... is actually a replacement of the population  he said. Real estate prices have soared, leading to a squeeze on unskilled workers, whether they are native Dutch or Turkish and Moroccan immigrants. According to Statistics Netherlands (CBS), 40 percent of young couples leave the city within four years of having their first child, driven out by the lack of affordable housing. Resentment also stems from a policy that allows skilled immigrants to receive 30 percent of their income tax-free. On a salary of 100,000 euros that amounts to 15,000 euros in extra take-home pay for an expat over a Dutch person doing the same job. Property prices rose 13 percent in the third quarter of 2017 from the same period a year earlier, according to the CBS, above their 2008 highs. Listings have dried up. As one real estate agent put it, the market has  boiled dry . Michiel van Hemert, a kitchen assistant, said government priorities were wrong.  Imagine the  economic boom  that would come from retraining 40 and 50-year-olds, which is clearly needed,  he said. He recommended more funding for educators, police, nurses and other public servants.  I speak for myself and two or three generations before me.

text: A mother from eastern France was sentenced to two years in prison after a French court determined she had financed terrorism by sending money to her son, who was killed while fighting in Syria. Nathalie Haddadi, 42, a mother of three who does not practice Islam, insisted that she had no idea her son, Belabbas Bounaga, would utilize the funds to join forces with Islamist militants. However, the presiding judge accused her of dishonesty. "Without your significant assistance, he would not have been able to reach Syria as easily and engage with Islamic State," the judge stated to Haddadi. Bounaga reportedly became radicalized while incarcerated between 2014 and 2015 due to previous convictions related to drug offenses. Following his release, he moved to Algeria to live with his father, staying there for six months before heading to Malaysia. During his time in these countries, Haddadi transferred several thousand euros to Bounaga, including multiple transactions in April 2016 after he received medical treatment in a Malaysian hospital. Shortly after these transfers, he made his way to Syria. In her ruling, the judge opted not to enforce Haddadi's immediate imprisonment, allowing her the possibility of serving less than the full sentence. "What was I meant to do? Just ignore him because of his past mistakes?" Haddadi remarked outside the courthouse, defending the transfers as funds for his medical expenses. In August 2016, she received word from Syria that Bounaga had passed away a martyr at the young age of 21. The two-year sentence imposed on her exceeded the prosecutor's request of 18 months. Additionally, the court found Haddadi’s younger son and his close friend guilty of the same offense. Earlier this month, in an interview with Le Parisien, Haddadi expressed her concerns about her son potentially trying to reach Syria after his release from prison in 2015. She criticized the authorities for not providing adequate help to "save him" during that time. "I firmly denounce terrorism," Haddadi declared following her conviction. Her legal representative announced that they would be appealing the decision. According to France’s interior ministry, as of last month, there are 18,500 French citizens identified as radicalized, marking a 60 percent rise compared to two years earlier. At that time, it was estimated that around 700 individuals were engaged in fighting in Iraq and Syria. Haddadi’s lawyer warned that other parents of children who have been radicalized might face similar judicial challenges. "This struggle is no longer solely Mrs. Haddadi’s but resonates with all parents of young men radicalized in prison who risk being held accountable by prosecutors for their children’s actions," Herve Denis told Reuters.

text: In Germany, discussions are intensifying regarding the potential formation of another grand coalition. On Saturday, a member of the Social Democrats (SPD) executive leadership indicated that if party leaders can deliver a compelling proposal, the members are likely to endorse a renewed partnership with Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservative party. Niels Annen, speaking to the Passauer Neue Presse newspaper, emphasized the need for prompt action in establishing a new German government due to various global crises, suggesting that a grand coalition should remain a viable possibility. On Friday, SPD leader Martin Schulz expressed his willingness to engage in discussions with Merkel about the revival of their previous coalition, although he clarified that no final decisions had been reached and that the party's members would ultimately determine the outcome of any agreement. He implied that participating in governance might enable the SPD to further its political objectives and urged the youth wing of the party, which had opposed another grand coalition during a recent conference, to demonstrate loyalty and work together constructively. Annen insisted that before the SPD commits to another four-year alliance with the conservatives, they must hear from the former chancellor regarding her vision for the future government. After experiencing its worst electoral outcome in seven decades during the September elections, the center-left SPD had pledged to enter opposition; however, they faced substantial pressure, notably from German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, to reconsider their stance and assist in preventing a potentially disruptive repeat election in Europe's largest economy. Schulz stated that party leaders decided to initiate talks out of a sense of duty to Germany and Europe, particularly following Merkel's unsuccessful attempt to assemble a government with two smaller parties that collapsed on Sunday. "Germany needs a stable and dependable government urgently. A grand coalition could be an option and we should not rule it out," Annen stated, further mentioning that the SPD is concentrating on what benefits the nation. He expressed support for the idea of presenting any coalition agreement to the members for their approval and highlighted the importance of continuing the party's restructuring efforts in the aftermath of the September electoral setback. "I am confident that if the SPD leadership puts forth a convincing proposition, it will successfully persuade the membership," he remarked. Annen also pointed out that topics such as citizens' insurance and enhanced protections for renters require negotiation with the conservatives. Ralf Stegner, the SPD's deputy leader, informed the Funke newspaper group that Schulz would maintain his leadership position, asserting that he still enjoys considerable backing within the party. "There is absolutely no doubt that Martin Schulz will be re-elected as party chairman with a good result," he stated.
source_text: Momentum grows for another grand coalition in Germany. BERLIN (Reuters) - Members of Germany s Social Democrats (SPD) will likely approve a renewed coalition with Chancellor Angela Merkel s conservatives if party leaders present a convincing proposal, a member of the party s executive leadership said on Saturday. Niels Annen of the SPD, in an interview with the Passauer Neue Presse newspaper, called for quick action to form a new German government given a range of crises around the world, and said a  grand coalition  was an option that could not be excluded. But he suggested that governing could help the SPD achieve its political aims and told the party s youth wing - which  rejected another grand coalition at a party conference - that he expected their loyalty and  constructive cooperation.  Annen said the SPD needed to hear from  the failed chancellor  about how she envisioned the future government before agreeing to another four-year tie-up with conservatives. The center-left SPD had vowed to go into opposition after suffering its worst result in 70 years in September s election, but came under intense pressure, including by German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, to rethink its position and help avert a disruptive repeat poll in Europe s largest economy. Schulz said party leaders agreed to talks out of a sense of responsibility to Germany and Europe after Merkel s attempt to form a government with two smaller parties collapsed on Sunday.  Germany urgently needs a predictable and reliable government. A grand coalition could be an option and we should not exclude it,  Annen told the newspaper, adding that the SPD was focused on  what is good for the country.  He welcomed plans to take any coalition agreement to members for a vote, and said the party should continue its restructuring efforts after the September election setback.  I m certain, if the SPD leadership makes a convincing proposal, it will be able to convince the membership,  he said. Annen cited citizens  insurance and better protection for renters as issues to hash out with conservatives. SPD deputy leader Ralf Stegner told the Funke newspaper group that Schulz would retain his leadership role, saying he continued to enjoy strong support within the party.  There is absolutely no doubt that Martin Schulz will be re-elected as party chairman with a good result,  he said.

text: On Wednesday, Israeli officials granted permission for a significant increase in a Jewish settler community located within a Palestinian area of East Jerusalem, approving the construction of 176 new residential units. A spokesperson for the Jerusalem municipality indicated that the city's planning committee had sanctioned the development, which was quickly denounced by Palestinian representatives as a breach of international law. The new housing projects will almost triple the existing number of settler residences in the Nof Zion settlement, which currently consists of 91 homes and is encircled by Palestinian residences in the Jabel al-Mukaber district. This region lies within territory captured and annexed by Israel during the 1967 Middle East conflict, which Palestinians claim as part of a future state that would include the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip, with East Jerusalem serving as its capital. "We are unifying Jerusalem through actions on the ground," stated Jerusalem's Mayor Nir Barkat regarding the expansion of the settlement. The international community has largely not acknowledged Israel's assertion of Jerusalem as its capital, and many nations consider the settlements constructed on occupied territory as illegal, viewing them as barriers to a potential land-for-peace agreement. Israel contests this perspective. Wasel Abu Yousif, an official in the Palestine Liberation Organization, referred to the proposed developments in Jabel al-Mukaber as a provocation against the international community's appeals to cease settlement expansion. Just last week, Israel also greenlit plans for the construction of several hundred additional homes for settlers in the West Bank, igniting condemnation from both Palestinians and the European Union. Since 2014, Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations have been stalled, with settlement expansion being a significant factor in their breakdown. Approximately 500,000 Israelis reside in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, areas that host over 2.6 million Palestinians.
source_text: Israel approves 176 new settler homes in East Jerusalem. JERUSALEM (Reuters) - Israeli authorities approved on Wednesday a major expansion of a Jewish settler enclave in the heart of a Palestinian neighborhood of East Jerusalem, issuing building permits  for 176 new housing units. Construction of the new units will nearly triple the number of settler homes in the Nof Zion settlement, which currently has 91 dwellings and is surrounded by Palestinian houses in the Jabel al-Mukaber neighborhood. The area is located in territory that Israel captured and annexed in a 1967 Middle East war and which Palestinians seek as part of a state they want to establish in the occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip, with East Jerusalem as its capital.  We are unifying Jerusalem through actions on the ground,  Jerusalem Mayor Nir Barkat said in a statement about the settlement s expansion. Israel s claim to all of Jerusalem as its capital has not won international recognition, and many countries regard the settlements it has built on occupied land as illegal and obstacles to any future land-for peace deal.
