text: On Sunday, military leaders from the Iraqi army and the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which are supported by the U.S., convened to establish a collaborative military center aimed at safeguarding their shared border area following the expulsion of Islamic State militants. The SDF, an alliance comprised of Kurdish and Arab armed groups, announced this development in a statement. The discussions revolved around strategies for securing the Syrian-Iraqi border near Deir al-Zor province and the ultimate goal of eradicating Daesh fighters in that vicinity. Daesh refers to the Arabic acronym for the Islamic State. According to the SDF, both parties agreed to the formation of this joint coordination hub to ensure border security. Just last week, the SDF proclaimed a successful conclusion to its operations in Deir al-Zor, Syria, which is adjacent to Iraq. This military campaign concentrated on capturing land situated east of the Euphrates River, which divides the oil-rich province. With the assistance of airstrikes and special forces from the U.S.-led coalition, the Kurdish-led SDF has been engaged in combat for several months against the Islamic State (IS). Meanwhile, Iraqi armed forces regained the last segments of territory that were under IS control along the Syrian border on Saturday, securing the western desert. This event marked the conclusion of the conflict against IS, occurring three years after the group had seized approximately one-third of Iraq’s territory. The Iraqi forces that confronted IS included personnel from the army, air force, police, elite counter-terrorism units, as well as Shiite and Sunni paramilitary groups in addition to Kurdish Peshmerga fighters. They benefited from vital air support provided by the global coalition led by the United States. Meanwhile, Syrian government troops and their allies, backed by Russian air forces, have captured the majority of the remaining regions within Deir al-Zor province, primarily located on the western side of the Euphrates, in contrast to the SDF, which operates on the eastern bank. To mitigate the risk of conflict arising from the competing campaigns against IS, Russia and the United States established a communication link. Now, forces opposing the Islamic State in both Iraq and Syria prepare for a potential shift towards guerrilla warfare tactics. Colonel Ryan Dillon, spokesperson for the coalition, indicated that on Sunday, Iraqi security forces and the SDF had successfully connected at their mutual border segment. He tweeted that a secure international border would shield both Iraqis and Syrians from the residual Daesh movement as terrorist fighters and leaders attempt to escape the battlefield.
source_text: U.S.-backed Syrian forces, Iraqi army coordinate at border: SDF. BEIRUT (Reuters) - U.S.-backed militias in Syria said they have formed a joint military center with the Iraqi army to protect their common border region after ousting Islamic State militants. Commanders of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), an alliance of Kurdish and Arab militias, met with Iraqi military leaders on Sunday. They  discussed protecting the Syrian-Iraqi border in the region adjacent to Deir al-Zor province, and how to finally eradicate Daesh mercenaries there,  the SDF said in a statement. Daesh is an Arabic acronym for Islamic State.  The two sides decided to form a joint coordination center to guarantee the security of the border,  it said. Last week, the SDF declared victory in its assault in Syria s Deir al-Zor, which borders Iraq. The offensive focused on seizing territory east of the Euphrates river that bisects the oil-rich province. The Kurdish-led SDF has been battling for months with the help of jets and special forces from the U.S.-led coalition against Islamic State (IS). On the other side, Iraqi forces recaptured the last swathes of territory still under Islamic State control along the frontier with Syria on Saturday and secured the western desert. It marked the end of the war against IS, three years after they overran about a third of Iraq s territory. Iraqi forces who fought IS came from the army, air force, police, elite counter-terrorism forces as well as Shi ite and Sunni paramilitaries and Kurdish Peshmerga fighters. They received key air support from the U.S.-led global coalition. Syrian government forces and their allies, backed by Russian air power, have taken most of the remaining areas of Deir al-Zor province. They are mostly on the western side of the Euphrates, while the SDF is on the eastern bank. Russia and the United States set up a communications channel to reduce the chance of fighting between the two rival campaigns against Islamic State.  Forces arrayed against Islamic State in Iraq and Syria now anticipate a new phase of guerrilla warfare. Colonel Ryan Dillon, spokesman for the coalition, said Iraqi security forces and the SDF had linked up at their shared stretch of the frontier on Sunday.   Secure international border protects Iraqis (and) Syrians from remnant Daesh movement into (and) across the region as terrorist fighters/leaders attempt to flee the battlefield,  he wrote on Twitter.

text: In a daring operation reminiscent of a film heist, thieves in Kenya managed to dig a tunnel into a bank situated directly across from a police station. On Tuesday, law enforcement reported that the robbers, after months of excavation, made off with an amount equivalent to half a million dollars. Authorities have detained two men and a woman in connection with the incident; however, the missing 50 million Kenyan shillings has yet to be retrieved, according to staff at the Kenya Commercial Bank (KCB) branch, who discovered the theft upon arriving for work on Monday. Simba Willy, the sub-county police commander in Thika, located northeast of Nairobi, stated, "We have not recovered the stolen money." He further suggested that the criminals might have rented a nearby shop to facilitate their tunneling operations. The robbers cleverly concealed the dirt they removed during their lengthy digging process, using boxes to avoid raising any alarms, as reported by local vendors. These traders described the two young men who occupied the store as "very hardworking" and "introverts." KCB, the largest bank in the region by assets, confirmed the break-in via a post on Twitter. Meanwhile, Brazilian authorities recently thwarted a similar robbery attempt in Sao Paulo, where a 500-meter underground tunnel equipped with lighting and ventilation was discovered.
source_text: In movie-style heist, Kenya robbers tunnel into bank opposite police station. NAIROBI (Reuters) - In a heist reminiscent of a Hollywood movie, Kenyan robbers spent months tunneling into the bowels of a bank located opposite a police station and stole the equivalent of half a million dollars, police said on Tuesday. Police said they had arrested two men and one woman over the robbery but had not recovered the 50 million Kenyan shillings, reported missing by staff at the branch of Kenya Commercial Bank (KCB) on Monday when they showed up to work.  We have not recovered the stolen money,  said Simba Willy, sub-county police commander in the town of Thika, northeast of Nairobi, where the heist took place.  We suspect the robbers hired one of the shops near the bank (while digging their tunnel),  Willy told Reuters. The robbers were able to remove the earth during their months-long excavations without arousing suspicion by concealing it in boxes, the Daily Nation newspaper quoted local traders as saying. The traders described the two young men who had rented the store as  very hardworking  and  introverts . KCB, which is the region s biggest bank by assets, confirmed the break-in on Twitter.  But the Kenyans have competition for the title of most ingenious robbery. Last month Brazilian police foiled a plot to rob a Sao Paulo bank after discovering a 500-metre underground tunnel kitted out with lighting and ventilation systems.

text: Questions have arisen surrounding President Donald Trump’s commitment to donate profits derived from foreign governments to the U.S. Treasury, as the Trump Organization has declared that it would be "impractical" to mandate that customers from foreign nations disclose their identities. The Trump Organization, which encompasses various businesses owned or managed by Trump, distributed a pamphlet to the general managers of each hotel, golf course, winery, and social club, indicating that donations would only be made from guests who openly state they represent foreign governments. This pamphlet was subsequently provided to the House of Representatives Oversight and Reform Committee in response to a request for insights on how Trump’s organization intends to meet the pledge made by Trump in January. The pamphlet asserts, "Implementing a policy that requires all visitors to identify themselves would infringe on personal privacy and degrade the guest experience associated with our brand." Requests for comments from the Trump Organization, Sheri Dillon, Trump’s attorney, and the White House have gone unanswered. During a press conference in January, Dillon had stated that Trump would voluntarily contribute all profits from foreign government transactions at his properties to the Treasury. Payments received by Trump’s businesses from foreign governments have faced scrutiny from experts in ethics and constitutional law, who argue that such transactions violate the U.S. Constitution's prohibition against the president receiving "emoluments" from foreign entities. In this context, emoluments are generally understood as valuable funds or gifts. On Wednesday, seven Democratic members of the House Judiciary Committee sent a letter to the Republican president, requesting a comprehensive report on “any benefits or rewards, financial or otherwise” received from foreign governments since he assumed office on January 20. Events have already been hosted by the governments of Kuwait and Azerbaijan at the Trump International Hotel located in Washington, D.C. In March, the Government Accountability Office announced plans to investigate whether any payments have been made by Trump to the U.S. Treasury from the profits generated at his hotels. The pamphlet from the Trump Organization mentioned other organizations through which foreign governments might engage, including entities in aerospace, defense, banking, finance, healthcare, and energy, which are state-owned. It noted that these entities "may not be readily identifiable as foreign government bodies, making it difficult to factor them into our profit calculations for donation purposes." Elijah Cummings, the leading Democrat on the congressional committee that received the pamphlet, responded by criticizing the Trump Organization's approach to recognizing payments from foreign governments as inadequate. Cummings pointed out that foreign entities could still provide unconstitutional emoluments to Trump through organizations that are funded and controlled but not explicitly connected to foreign governments. He emphasized, "Those payments would not be tracked in any way and would be hidden from the American public," in his written response.
source_text: Despite vow, Trump Organization not tracking all profits from foreign governments. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s businesses say it would be “impractical” to require customers representing foreign nations to identify themselves, raising questions about how Trump will fulfill a pledge to donate all profits from overseas governments to the U.S. Treasury. The umbrella Trump Organization sent a pamphlet to the general managers at each hotel, golf course, social club, and winery owned or operated by Trump, saying it would only donate profits from guests who declare they represent foreign governments. The pamphlet was sent to the House of Representatives Oversight and Reform Committee in response to a request for information on how the Trump Organization was fulfilling the pledge Trump made in January.  “Putting forth a policy that requires all guests to identify themselves would impede upon personal privacy and diminish the guest experience of our brand,” said the pamphlet. The Trump Organization, Trump’s lawyer, Sheri Dillon, and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.  Dillon announced at a January press conference that Trump would voluntarily donate all profits from foreign government payments made to his properties to the Treasury. Payments from foreign governments to businesses that profit Trump have drawn criticism from constitutional and ethics experts who say they put Trump in violation of the U.S. Constitution’s ban on the president receiving “emoluments” from foreign governments.  Emoluments are typically defined in this context as funds or gifts of value. Seven Democratic lawmakers on the House Judiciary Committee sent the Republican president a letter on Wednesday asking for a detailed account of “any benefits or rewards, financial or otherwise” he received from foreign governments since he took office on Jan. 20.  The Kuwaiti and Azerbaijani governments have already hosted events at the Trump International Hotel in Washington, D.C. In March, the Government Accountability Office said it would check whether Trump has made any payments to the U.S. Treasury from profits at his hotels.  The Trump Organization pamphlet identified other entities through which foreign governments may operate, such as state-owned aerospace, defense, banking, finance, healthcare, and energy business entities. Those entities “may not be reasonably identifiable as foreign government entities, and therefore may not be included in our calculation of profit to be donated,” the pamphlet read. Elijah Cummings, the top Democrat on the congressional committee that received the pamphlet, said in a response to the Trump Organization that its method for identifying foreign government payments was deficient. Cummings said foreign powers would still be able to provide unconstitutional emoluments to Trump through entities that are funded and controlled but not openly affiliated with foreign governments. “Those payments would not be tracked in any way and would be hidden from the American public,” Cummings wrote.

text: On Thursday, Ukrainian Justice Minister Pavlo Petrenko expressed his willingness to revise recent legal reforms that have raised alarms regarding their potential to facilitate corruption and possibly hinder investigations into the deaths of protesters prior to the revolution in 2014. The nation, situated in Eastern Europe and currently engaged in a conflict with Russia over the annexation of Crimea, adopted modifications to the Criminal Procedure Code the previous week. Anti-corruption organizations argue that these modifications significantly restrict the timeframe available for investigators to resolve cases and bring them to trial. Petrenko indicated that he had not yet reviewed the final wording of the extensive reforms but acknowledged awareness of the existing concerns.  "If there are aspects that cause issues for ongoing or future investigations, I will suggest amendments to the parliament and the president," Petrenko stated in an interview with Reuters while he attended a conference for the legal sector in Sydney. The new legislation, however, still awaits approval from President Petro Poroshenko. Last week, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine released a statement indicating that the revised law could compel investigators to submit a case to the court within a six-month window, extendable to twelve months with judicial permission. The law enforcement agency noted that corrupt officials might gain from this due to the intricate nature of investigations that frequently require international cooperation. Concerns have also been raised that this new legislation could obstruct prosecutions related to offenses that occurred during the Euromaidan protests in 2013 and 2014, which resulted in the deaths of over 100 demonstrators advocating for closer ties with Europe. This popular uprising, driven by issues of corruption and Ukraine's connections to Russia, culminated in the ousting of then-president Viktor Yanukovych. More than three years later, Ukraine continues to grapple with serious corruption allegations, with Transparency International ranking the country 131st out of 176 nations in its Corruption Perception Index earlier this year. During the same interview on Thursday, Petrenko affirmed that the nation is committed to reforming its judicial framework, which involves selecting more than 100 judges for the Supreme Court through a competitive process aimed at eradicating corruption. "Are all these individuals perfect? I would say no, as the country itself is not perfect," Petrenko remarked. "You cannot find ideal candidates from Mars or the moon and simply place them in these roles, but these individuals have gone through a fair, transparent, and thoroughly public selection process." Additionally, Ukraine is receiving support for its reform initiatives from the International Monetary Fund.
source_text: Ukraine's controversial law reforms open to revision: Justice Minister. SYDNEY (Reuters) - Ukrainian Justice Minister Pavlo Petrenko said on Thursday he was open to amending law reforms amid concerns they aided corruption and could lead to the end of probes into the shooting of protesters in the run-up up to the 2014 revolution. The eastern European nation, which is in a dispute with Russia over its annexation of Crimea, passed amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code last week that anti-corruption groups say severely limits the time investigators have to solve a crime and present a case in court.  Petrenko said he had yet to go through the final text of the lengthy reforms, but he said that he was aware of the concerns.  If there (are) some positions which make problems for the investigations process for old cases or for new cases I will give proposals to the parliament and president to change these positions,  Petrenko told Reuters in an interview in Sydney, where he was attending a legal industry conference. The legislation still requires the sign-off from President Petro Poroshenko.  The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine said in a statement last week the new legislation could force investigators to present a criminal case before court within six months, or up to 12 months with a court extension. Corrupt officials could benefit, the law enforcement agency said, given the complexity of investigations that can involve international assistance. There are also fears that the legislation could prevent prosecutions for crimes committed during the Euromaidan street demonstrations in 2013 and 2014, where more than 100 protesters, demanding closer European integration, were gunned down. The popular uprising, that focused on corruption concerns and the country s Russian ties, culminated with the removal of the then president Viktor Yanukovych. More than three years on, Ukraine is still dealing with allegations of deep corruption with Transparency International earlier this year ranking it 131st of 176 countries in the World Ranking of Corruption Perception. Petrenko said on Thursday the country was intent on reforming its judicial system, which included the selection of more than 100 Supreme Court judges after a competition-style candidate process designed to root out corruption.     Are all these people ideal? I think no, because the country is not ideal,  Petrenko said.  You cannot find some ideal people from Mars or from the moon and take them and put in these positions, but those people, they went through the objective, transparent and absolutely public competition.  Ukraine is the recipient of an aid-for-reforms program from the International Monetary Fund.

text: At a gala dinner in Manila, President Rodrigo Duterte showcased his singing talent by performing a beloved Filipino love song, responding to a request made by U.S. President Donald Trump. The event, which took place on Sunday, gathered 19 leaders from various Asian nations in the capital of the Philippines, prior to an annual summit. During the event, Duterte took the stage to sing "Ikaw" (You), joining forces with renowned local singer Pilita Corrales. The lyrics of one verse, when translated from Filipino, convey: "You are the light in my world, a half of this heart of mine." Following his performance, Duterte humorously remarked, "Ladies and gentlemen, I sang uninvited, upon the orders of the commander-in-chief of the United States," as reported by the ABS-CBN news channel. Duterte, often referred to as the "Trump of the East" due to his bold personality, is set to engage with the U.S. president in a meeting on the summit's sidelines on Monday. The Philippines and the United States have maintained a strategic partnership since World War Two, being former colonial ties. However, tensions have emerged due to Duterte's outspoken remarks against the U.S. and his eagerness to strengthen relations with China and Russia. Since he assumed office last year, more than 3,900 Filipinos have lost their lives in a controversial anti-drug campaign initiated by Duterte. While his administration claims that police actions are in self-defense, critics argue that extrajudicial killings are occurring without accountability. Recently, Duterte indicated that he would advise the U.S. president to "lay off" if the topic of human rights arose during their discussion. Nonetheless, Trump, who has faced domestic backlash for overlooking human rights concerns in international dealings, commended Duterte in May for his "unbelievable job" in addressing the drug crisis. During the dinner, Trump, along with leaders from the 10-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations, as well as representatives from China, Russia, Japan, Canada, South Korea, India, Australia, and New Zealand, enjoyed performances by various singers and dancers. Attendees, all dressed in cream-colored barongs, a traditional shirt from the Philippines made from pineapple fiber and hand-embroidered, were treated to a four-course meal that blended Filipino and Asian cuisines, meticulously crafted by Chef Jessie Sincioco, who previously designed the menu for Pope Francis' visit to the Philippines in 2015.
source_text: "You are the light" - Philippines' Duterte croons at Trump's request. source_text: Satellite signals not helpful to Argentine submarine search: navy official. MAR DEL PLATA, Argentina (Reuters) - Seven satellite calls that Argentine officials detected recently believed to have come from a navy submarine missing in the South Atlantic have not helped to determine the vessel s location, a navy official said on Sunday.  We analyzed these signals, which as we know were  intermittent and weak,  said Gabriel Galeazzi, a naval commander.  They could not help determine a point on the map to help the search.

text: The Italian Chamber of Deputies has approved a controversial electoral reform, moving the legislation to the Senate for further discussion. On Thursday, a vote saw 375 members in favor and 215 against the bill, which is anticipated to disadvantage the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement in the upcoming elections. The reform, backed by the ruling Democratic Party (PD) and traditional center-right opposition groups, is expected to lead to a fragmented outcome in the elections scheduled for May 2018, as analysts predict that the center-left, center-right, and 5-Star Movement will divide the electorate. This new electoral framework, known as the Rosatellum law, benefits political parties that form coalitions ahead of the election. The 5-Star Movement has refused to align with any other parties, asserting that this change could result in a loss of at least 50 seats in the next parliament, severely limiting its prospects of gaining power. The party, which leads in several opinion polls, has conducted two days of protests against what they consider an orchestrated effort by mainstream political opponents to undermine their electoral chances. "You are manipulating the foundations of our democratic system and rigging the rules before the game starts," declared 5-Star leader Luigi Di Maio in parliament prior to the voting. "We will remind the public of what you are doing today throughout the entire election campaign." Opposition also comes from smaller left-wing and right-wing parties, although the bill has garnered support from the center-right Forza Italia (Go Italy!) and the right-wing Northern League. Ettore Rosato, the parliamentary party leader of the PD who has championed this reform, articulated that it represents the best possible compromise among competing political factions, criticizing both the 5-Star Movement and leftist parties for their unwillingness to engage in dialogue. "You always said no to everything that we proposed," he commented to the members of the Chamber. President Sergio Mattarella has emphasized the need for updated voting regulations, arguing that the significant differences between the systems used by the upper and lower houses could result in conflicting parliamentary majorities. Past efforts to synchronize these rules have failed, including a recent attempt in June where dissenting deputies utilized a secret vote to overturn part of the proposed legislation. The 5-Star Movement and other critics of the new electoral framework were hopeful that a similar outcome would occur during Thursday's final vote in the Chamber, which had already seen the bill approved in three votes of confidence conducted with open ballots. The upper house Senate, where Gentiloni's administration lacks a reliable majority, is expected to begin its discussions and voting on the bill next week.
source_text: Italy lower house passes new electoral law, moves on to Senate. ROME (Reuters) - The Italian Chamber of Deputies on Thursday gave its final approval to a contested electoral law that is likely to penalize the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement in next year s election. The bill, which is supported by the ruling Democratic Party (PD) and mainstream center-right opposition parties, was approved in a secret ballot by 375 votes to 215, and will now move to the upper house Senate for further debate. An election is due by May 2018. Analysts say the new system looks highly unlikely to throw up a clear parliamentary majority, with opinion polls showing the center-left, center-right and 5-Star splitting the vote three ways. The so-called  Rosatellum  law favors parties which group together ahead of the election. The 5-Star refuses to join any alliance and says the reform could cost it at least 50 seats in the next parliament, hobbling its chances of taking power. The party, which tops many opinion polls, has held two days of street protests against what it sees as an attempt by its mainstream rivals to scupper its chances at the election.  You are manipulating the foundations of our democratic system and rigging the rules before the game starts,  5-Star leader Luigi Di Maio told parliament before the vote.   Every single day of the election campaign we will remind people of what you are doing today.  Small left-wing and right-wing parties are also against the bill, which is supported by the center-right Forza Italia (Go Italy!) and the right-wing Northern League. Ettore Rosato, the parliamentary party leader of the PD who has put his name to the reform, said it was the best compromise possible among political adversaries and blamed 5-Star and leftist parties for refusing to join negotiations.  You always said no to everything that we proposed,  he told the Chamber. President Sergio Mattarella has called for new voting rules because he says the current system is too different for the upper and lower houses, meaning it could conceivably throw up conflicting majorities. All previous attempts to harmonize the rules have failed, most recently in June when dissident deputies used a secret vote to up-end part of the proposed legislation. The 5-Star and other opponents of the new rules had hoped that the same would happen in Thursday s final vote in the Chamber, which had already approved the bill in three votes of confidence held with open voting. The package still needs the approval of the upper house Senate, where Gentiloni s government does not have a stable majority. The upper house is expected to begin discussing and voting on the bill next week.

text: The U.S. Congress is set to hold a hearing on October 24 regarding Puerto Rico’s recovery following Hurricane Maria. source_text: House panel to weigh expanding Puerto Rico oversight board powers. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - An Oct. 24 hearing in the U.S. Congress on Puerto Rico’s recovery from Hurricane Maria will assess whether a financial oversight board managing the American territory’s debt should take on the responsibility of overseeing rebuilding efforts. A spokesman for the House of Representatives Natural Resources Committee also said on Tuesday that the panel will probe whether the financial oversight board would need new tools if it oversees hurricane-related actions, including rebuilding Puerto Rico’s aged and badly damaged electric utility. Witnesses for the hearing have not yet been named.

text: In a significant shift from previous policy, NATO allies expressed their support on Tuesday for President Donald Trump's decision to increase troop levels in Afghanistan. This adjustment is part of a fresh U.S. strategy that the President indicated would necessitate greater military assistance and funding from America’s allies. Trump, who campaigned last year advocating for a quick withdrawal from Afghanistan, altered his stance on Monday, vowing to intensify military operations against the Taliban insurgents, stating: "Our troops will fight to win." U.S. officials disclosed that he had approved plans to deploy approximately 4,000 additional U.S. soldiers to supplement the nearly 8,400 already stationed in Afghanistan. However, his address did not outline specific metrics for achieving a resolution to the conflict that commenced with the U.S.-led invasion in 2001, which he recognized had demanded an extraordinary sacrifice of blood and treasure. "We will request our NATO allies and global partners to endorse our new strategy, with supplementary troops and increased funding comparable to our own. We are confident they will," Trump remarked. This statement suggested that he intends to exert further pressure on U.S. allies, who have already felt the impact of his ongoing demands for increased contributions to NATO, alongside his earlier characterization of the alliance as "obsolete" — a view he has since moderated since taking office. Jens Stoltenberg, NATO’s Secretary General, remarked in a statement: "NATO remains fully committed to Afghanistan, and I look forward to discussing our path forward with Secretary of Defense James Mattis and our Allies and international partners." Currently, NATO has 12,000 troops deployed in Afghanistan, and Stoltenberg noted that 15 nations have committed to providing additional forces. The United Kingdom, a prominent member of NATO, described the U.S. troop commitment as "very welcome." In a recent conversation with Secretary Mattis, Defence Secretary Michael Fallon emphasized that despite the difficulties, it is crucial to maintain our efforts in Afghanistan to help strengthen its fragile democracy and mitigate the terrorist threat against the West. Germany, which has faced substantial criticism from Trump regarding its level of defense spending, also endorsed the new U.S. strategy. A spokesperson for the German government stated, "Our ongoing commitment is essential on the path to stabilizing the country." In June, European nations had already signaled their intent to increase troop levels, although they had refrained from disclosing specific numbers as they awaited the Trump administration’s regional strategic outline. Nearly 16 years after the U.S.-led invasion — a reaction to the September 11 attacks that were orchestrated by al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden from Afghanistan — the nation continues to grapple with a weak central government and a persistent Taliban insurgency. Trump acknowledged the American public's shared frustration over prolonged conflict without a decisive victory, but he cautioned that a rapid withdrawal would create a void for groups such as Islamic State and al Qaeda to exploit.

text: On Wednesday, a challenge to an Arizona voting regulation was brought back to the forefront by a U.S. appeals court. This law limited the capacity of advocates to personally gather absentee ballots. Previously, the Arizona law had been supported by a three-judge panel at the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, but now the entire court has opted to reconsider the matter with an 11-judge panel. A dissenting opinion from five conservative judges on the 9th Circuit expressed concern that the decision came too close to Election Day.
source_text: Appeals court revives challenge to Arizona voting law. (Reuters) - A U.S. appeals court on Wednesday agreed to revisit a challenge to an Arizona voting law which restricted the ability of advocates to collect absentee ballots by hand.  A three judge 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had earlier upheld the Arizona law, but the full court on Wednesday voted to rehear the case before an 11-judge panel. Five conservative 9th Circuit judges dissented from the decision to rehear the case, saying it was made too close to Election Day.

text: During a conference in Beverly Hills, U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin asserted on Monday that the nation can achieve an economic growth rate of three percent within the next two years, fueled by substantial tax cuts initiated by the Trump administration. Addressing attendees at the Milken Institute Global Conference, Mnuchin spoke shortly after revealing a proposal to lower tax rates for numerous individuals and corporations to 15 percent. He emphasized that tax reform alongside regulatory relief is essential for fostering economic expansion. His remarks followed the release of government figures indicating a sluggish growth rate of just 0.7 percent over the past three months. Mnuchin referred to the tax initiative as a jobs bill during an interview on stage with journalist Maria Bartoromo. Despite the stock market's favorable response to Trump's election—evidenced by an 11 percent rise in the S&P 500 index since November—some critics have labeled the tax plan as overly ambitious and lacking in specifics. In a moment of humor, Mnuchin joked that many attendees could credit him for the rise in banking stocks that have positively impacted their investment portfolios, prompting laughter from the crowd. Nonetheless, there were apprehensions among some participants regarding the sustainability of the optimistic sentiment, particularly given the absence of detailed information about Trump’s plans and the uncertain timeline. Scott Minerd, global chief investment officer at Guggenheim Partners, expressed his worries, stating, "I’m concerned that if we don’t see tax or healthcare reform by the end of the year, markets will start to doubt the administration’s ability to deliver it." Mnuchin revealed that he is collaborating with congressional leaders to advance tax reform and expressed hope for bipartisan support. Speaking to CNBC on the sidelines of the event, he noted that the tax proposal was intentionally kept vague to allow the administration to engage legislators in crafting a plan that could successfully pass through Congress. The Trump administration has actively sought input from various business leaders in the White House, paying careful attention to their concerns and aspirations regarding tax modifications, he added. David Solomon, who serves as president and co-chief operating officer of Goldman Sachs, commented that the initial wave of optimism during Trump’s presidency may be waning. He remarked, "This quarter it feels like conviction for tax and regulatory reform is more muted." Solomon's predecessor, Gary Cohn, who took on the role of director of the National Economic Council within the Trump administration, has been focused on tax reform as one of his main objectives. A significant concern surrounding the Trump tax plan is the government’s strategy to finance it. However, Mnuchin stated that there are multiple avenues to compensate for the revenue shortfall resulting from reduced tax collections, although he did not provide many specifics. Indeed, numerous attendees at the conference, including investment managers who could significantly benefit from the tax cuts, expressed their enthusiasm for the new administration’s proactive approach, which also includes initiatives to reform healthcare. Several participants noted that global growth prospects seem to be improving. Yet, there were also murmurs of unease regarding whether ambitious initiatives would come to fruition and whether international tensions with other governments might escalate. Mohamed El-Erian, chief economic advisor at Allianz, pointed out that while stock market optimism is exceptionally high, geopolitical challenges remain a genuine source of concern. (Refiled to include Solomon’s co-chief operating officer title.)

text: On Tuesday, U.S. House Republicans introduced a proposal to either delay or suspend multiple taxes implemented under the healthcare law of former President Barack Obama, which includes a tax on medical devices and the controversial "Cadillac" tax that targets lavish health insurance plans. This action signifies another Republican effort to dismantle aspects of the Affordable Care Act, enacted in 2010 and commonly referred to as Obamacare, following several unsuccessful attempts by the majority party in Congress this year to repeal the legislation. In addition, House and Senate Republicans are nearing the conclusion of a tax reform bill, which includes plans to eliminate the individual mandate of Obamacare that imposes a tax penalty on those Americans who fail to secure health insurance coverage. A representative from the House Ways and Means Committee indicated that these proposed healthcare tax reductions will not be included in the overarching tax reform legislation. There is a possibility that the healthcare tax initiatives could be combined with a crucial government funding bill that must be approved by December 22, the deadline for current funding. However, achieving this would require cooperation from Senate Democrats, as Republicans possess only a narrow majority. House Ways and Means Chairman Kevin Brady released a statement announcing five new bills sponsored by Republicans aimed at offering specific relief from Obamacare taxes, expressing his eagerness to "advance legislation in the weeks ahead." One of the proposed bills aims to retroactively abolish Obamacare penalties for employers who have not provided health insurance to their staff over the past three years, extending this relief to the upcoming year as well. Additionally, this legislation would postpone the Cadillac tax on high-cost employer-sponsored insurance for one year, which is set to take effect in 2020. Labor unions have voiced their opposition to this tax, citing concerns that it would lead to increased expenses for their members who often receive more generous healthcare benefits. Another bill included in the package seeks to suspend the medical device tax, which applies to items such as pacemakers and artificial hips, for a duration of five years. This tax was first enacted in January 2013 to help fund Obamacare, which has extended medical coverage to millions of individuals who were previously uninsured. The medical device tax has faced strong opposition from both parties, and manufacturers have heavily lobbied against it. Additional proposals within the package would also suspend a tax on health insurers for two years and grant two years of relief from a tax on over-the-counter medications.
source_text: Republicans propose to delay, pause Obamacare taxes. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. House Republicans proposed on Tuesday to delay or suspend several taxes under former President Barack Obama’s healthcare law, including a tax on medical devices and the so-called “Cadillac” tax on generous health insurance plans. The move represents a new Republican attempt to roll back provisions of the 2010 Affordable Care Act widely known as Obamacare, after repeated failures by Congress’ majority party this year to repeal the law. Republicans in the House and Senate are also in the final stages of reconciling tax overhaul legislation, including a proposal to scrap Obamacare’s individual mandate, which imposes a tax penalty on Americans who do not obtain health insurance.  A spokeswoman for the House Ways and Means Committee said the additional proposed healthcare tax rollbacks would not be part of the broader tax overhaul bill. Republicans could try to merge the healthcare tax proposals with a must-pass government funding bill that is expected to be passed by Dec. 22, when current funding runs out. But to succeed, Republicans in the Senate, who hold a slim majority of seats, would need an assist from Democrats to get past procedural hurdles.  In a statement, House Ways and Means Chairman Kevin Brady announced five new Republican-sponsored bills to provide targeted relief from Obamacare taxes, saying he looked forward to “advancing legislation in the weeks ahead.” One proposed bill would retroactively eliminate Obamacare penalties for employers who did not offer health insurance to their employees over the last three years, as well as for next year. The bill would also delay for one year the Cadillac tax on high-cost employer-sponsored insurance, which is otherwise scheduled to go into effect in 2020. Labor unions oppose this tax because their members often receive more generous healthcare plans, and they fear it would increase their costs. Another bill would suspend for five years the tax on medical devices, such as pacemakers and artificial hips. It was first imposed in January 2013 as a funding mechanism for Obamacare, a law that has brought medical coverage to millions of previously uninsured Americans. The medical device tax has powerful opponents in both parties and manufacturers have lobbied heavily against it. Other proposals in the package would suspend a tax on health insurers for two years, and provide two years of relief from a tax on over-the-counter medications.

text: Confusion reigns among states and insurers over diverging pricing strategies as they grapple with Obamacare changes. NEW YORK (Reuters) - In the past week, President Donald Trump’s abrupt shifts regarding the continuation of Obamacare subsidies to insurers have created uncertainty about the health insurance options available to consumers, as well as their costs, just two weeks before 2018 enrollment begins. Trump indicated last week that his administration would cease disbursing billions in subsidies that support insurers in providing discounts to low-income families, which is part of the broader dismantling of the landmark healthcare legislation established by his Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama. Since that declaration, Trump has both endorsed and rejected a bipartisan initiative from Republican and Democratic senators aimed at restoring the subsidies for two years, while a comprehensive replacement for the 2010 Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare, is being negotiated. "We are concerned that consumers enrolled in (Obamacare) plans will be perplexed by the constant changes and proposed policy alterations, potentially leading them to forgo seeking assistance," remarked Bryna Koch, special projects coordinator at the Arizona Center for Rural Health, an organization assisting consumers in selecting and enrolling in individual health plans under Obamacare. Trump, who during his campaign vowed to repeal and replace Obamacare, which he has labeled a "disaster," has expressed that the subsidies represent a bailout for insurance firms. Legally, health insurance companies are still required to offer discounts on co-pays, deductibles, and other out-of-pocket expenses, even if government reimbursements cease. Insurers assert that they do not gain profit from these subsidies. Anticipating Trump's actions, insurers have proposed increases in monthly premiums for 2018 to recover potential losses. In most states, they submitted two different sets of premium rates: one lower rate assuming the subsidies would remain intact, and a higher rate in the event that funding was withdrawn. As of Thursday, the status of the subsidies remained uncertain. A senior advisor at the White House indicated that Trump would insist on measures aimed at repealing Obamacare in any healthcare bill, casting a shadow over the likelihood of the bipartisan effort to stabilize insurance markets. A California court is scheduled to review on Monday a request by Democratic attorneys general to continue the subsidies until a legal dispute regarding Trump’s decision is resolved. If the funding is not reinstated by the time enrollment for 2018 starts on November 1, a significant number of consumers will face premium rates approximately 20 percent higher than they would have otherwise experienced. Prior to Trump’s decision on the subsidies, the Congressional Budget Office had projected that the Republican president’s initiatives to diminish Obamacare enrollment would result in 4 million fewer individuals obtaining insurance in 2018 than previously anticipated. Nonetheless, the CBO still expects that 11 million individuals will enroll for the upcoming year—an increase from the current enrollment of 10 million. The federal government has already ceased subsidy payments to the insurance sector for October. However, leading insurers remain uncertain whether this marks the final decision. Anthem Inc Chief Executive Officer Joseph Swedish conveyed to Reuters that he cannot yet forecast how the termination or potential reinstatement of the subsidies through "possible congressional action" would influence pricing in the following year. Anthem has submitted premium proposals that reflect the anticipated cut in subsidies. Should the subsidies be reinstated at any time after November 1, insurers might revert to the lower monthly premium rates or provide refunds to consumers. "A midyear adjustment in premiums would be quite rare, but it would be the appropriate course of action," stated Marc Harrison, CEO of Intermountain Healthcare, a hospital chain and health plan based in Utah. "Intermountain Healthcare would seek to implement this." According to Washington state’s insurance regulator, insurers will be permitted to adjust their rates as soon as feasible—even as soon as the following month—if lawmakers restore the funding, a strategy supported by the National Association of.
source_text: Obamacare whiplash leaves states, insurers with dueling price plans. NEW YORK (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s reversals in the past week on maintaining Obamacare subsidies to insurers are sowing new confusion over what kind of health insurance will be available to consumers, and at what price, when enrollment for 2018 begins in two weeks. Trump said last week his administration would stop paying billions of dollars in subsidies that help insurers give discounts to low-income households, one of several moves to dismantle the signature healthcare law of his Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama.  Since then, Trump has alternately supported, and dismissed, an effort by Republican and Democratic senators that would reinstate the subsidies for two years, until a broader replacement to the 2010 Affordable Care Act, commonly known as Obamacare, can be negotiated. “We are worried that consumers on (Obamacare) plans will be confused by all the back and forth and proposed policy changes and that this will cause them to not seek out assistance,” said Bryna Koch, special projects coordinator at the Arizona Center for Rural Health, which helps consumers choose and sign up for individual health plans offered under Obamacare. Trump, who promised during his election campaign to repeal and replace Obamacare, which he has called a “disaster,” has said the subsidies amount to a bailout for insurance companies.  By law, health insurers must still offer the discounts on deductibles, co-pays and other out-of-pocket costs, even if the government stops reimbursing them. Insurers say they do not profit from the subsidies. Anticipating Trump’s move, insurers proposed higher prices on monthly premiums in 2018 to recoup the money. In all but a handful of states, they submitted two sets of premium rates – a lower rate to use if the subsidies remained, and a higher rate to use if the funding was cut.    The fate of the subsidies remained in limbo on Thursday. A senior White House aide said that Trump would demand steps toward repealing Obamacare in any healthcare legislation, comments that cast doubt on the prospects for the bipartisan effort to shore up insurance markets.  A California court is expected to consider on Monday a request by Democratic attorneys general to keep the subsidies flowing until a legal challenge to Trump’s decision is resolved.  If the funding is not restored when 2018 enrollment opens on Nov. 1, many consumers will see premium rates that are on average 20 percent higher than they would have been otherwise. Even before Trump’s decision on the subsidies, the Congressional Budget Office said the Republican president’s  policies to roll back Obamacare enrollment efforts would lead to 4 million fewer people signing up for insurance in 2018 than previously forecast. The CBO still expects 11 million people to sign up for next year - an increase from this year’s enrollment of 10 million. The federal government has already halted a subsidy payment to the insurance industry for October. But leading insurers are not yet sure whether that is the last word. Anthem Inc Chief Executive Officer Joseph Swedish told Reuters he could not yet predict how ending the subsidies or restating them through “potential congressional action” would affect pricing next year. Anthem has submitted premium rates that account for the subsidies being cut.    Should the subsidies be restored at any time after Nov. 1, insurers may be able to revert to the lower monthly premium rates, or provide rebates for consumers. “A midyear change in premiums would be highly unusual, but this would be the right thing to do,” said Marc Harrison, CEO of Intermountain Healthcare, a Utah-based health plan and hospital chain. “Intermountain Healthcare would pursue this.” Washington state’s insurance regulator said it would allow insurers to change rates as soon as practical - even the next month - if lawmakers reinstate the funding, an approach backed by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners. But that could run up against federal government objections. The Affordable Care Act does not allow for changes to premium rates after they have been finalized, an official for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said. At the same time, the administration is working to approve higher rates in several states that did not take into account Trump’s cut in subsidies for 2018.

text: After an extensive hearing lasting nearly nine hours, Bob Corker, the Chairman of the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, expressed his belief on Wednesday that Rex Tillerson, nominated by President-elect Donald Trump for the position of secretary of state, will receive Senate confirmation. Corker made these remarks following a session where senators pressed Tillerson on various topics, including his stance on Russia, sanctions, climate change, and matters related to China. "I feel confident about his confirmation," Corker stated to the media. He also mentioned that Tillerson had effectively addressed the concerns raised by senators regarding his connections with Russia, although he recognized that some questions remained. Corker added that Tillerson was expected to engage with additional senators and respond to further inquiries on Thursday.
source_text: Corker says he expects Senate to confirm Tillerson as secretary of state. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Bob Corker said on Wednesday he expects the Senate will confirm Rex Tillerson, President-elect Donald Trump’s nominee to be secretary of state. Corker’s comments came after the close of an approximately nine-hour hearing in which senators vigorously questioned Tillerson on his views on Russia, sanctions, climate change and other issues, including China. “I feel good about his confirmation,” Corker told reporters. “I’m going to support his confirmation.” Corker said he felt Tillerson had acquitted himself well in addressing senators’ concerns about his relationship with Russia, although Corker acknowledged that members still had questions. He said he expected Tillerson would spend Thursday answering further questions and talking to more senators.

text: PHNOM PENH (Reuters) - A $2 million grant opportunity was announced by the United States on Wednesday, aimed at assisting in the removal of unexploded ordnance in Cambodia. This development follows the recent statement from the government’s mine clearance agency that U.S. financial support had ceased. This year, relations between Cambodia and the United States have deteriorated, with the Cambodian government alleging that Americans were involved in a purported scheme by detained opposition leader Kem Sokha to undermine Prime Minister Hun Sen. These allegations have been dismissed by Washington as unfounded. Just last week, the U.S. indicated it would be reducing aid ahead of the upcoming elections and could implement additional measures following the Supreme Court’s decision to dissolve the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP) at the behest of the government. According to the U.S. embassy, they are now inviting proposals for a one-year grant worth $2 million to conduct surveys and clear unexploded bombs in eastern Cambodia, an area that experienced extensive U.S. bombardment during the Vietnam War. Ambassador William Heidt remarked in a statement that the U.S. has been involved in humanitarian demining efforts in Cambodia for over two decades and remains dedicated to addressing the legacy of its wartime actions. The ambassador expressed a desire to engage the best national and international specialists for this initiative. The value of the contract corresponds to the funding amount that the Cambodian Mine Action Centre indicated had been reduced from U.S. contributions through Norwegian People’s Aid earlier this month. Huy Vannak, an undersecretary of state at the Interior Ministry, expressed appreciation for the commitment to addressing the war's legacy. Following this development, China, which has become Cambodia's closest ally, quickly proposed assistance for the demining efforts. As Cambodia's largest donor and investor, China has increasingly taken on a significant role as Western nations have condemned the government's crackdown on opposition, civil society, and media in the lead-up to next year’s elections. The European Union, while not taking any action, highlighted last week that Cambodia's access to duty-free benefits, crucial for its garment sector, hinges on adherence to human rights standards. On Wednesday, Hun Sen told garment factory workers that they would bear the consequences if such access were revoked, emphasizing that he would not be affected. In 2016, European Union nations represented approximately 40 percent of Cambodia’s exports, predominantly in clothing. Hun Sen cautioned garment workers in Phnom Penh, stating, "You must remember clearly that if there is any cut of buying orders, it’s all the fault of a group of people of the opposition party." He added ominously, "Hun Sen won’t die but workers, you will die." The prime minister accused opposition leaders in exile of attempting to instigate sanctions. Thus far, these leaders have refrained from calling for trade restrictions due to the potential adverse effects on the livelihoods of around 700,000 garment workers. Despite the political unrest, Cambodia's economy has shown resilience. The World Bank reported on Wednesday that it anticipates a 6.9 percent growth in the economy for next year, slightly up from the projected 6.8 percent growth rate for 2017, despite ongoing uncertainties surrounding the election.
source_text: US renews grant for clearing bombs in Cambodia. PHNOM PENH (Reuters) - The United States on Wednesday opened a $2 million tender to help clear unexploded bombs in Cambodia weeks after the government s mine clearance agency said its U.S. funding had been stopped. Relations between Cambodia and the United States have spiraled downwards this year with the government accusing Americans of involvement in a plan by detained opposition leader Kem Sokha to bring down Prime Minister Hun Sen. Washington has rejected the accusations as baseless. Last week, it said it was cutting aid for next year s election and would take further steps after the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP) was dissolved by the Supreme Court at the government s request. The U.S. embassy said it was accepting applications for a $2 million one-year grant to survey and clear unexploded ordnance in eastern Cambodia, which suffered heavy U.S. bombing during the war in neighboring Vietnam.  The United States has supported humanitarian demining in Cambodia for over 20 years and is committed to addressing our war-time legacy,  Ambassador William Heidt said in a statement.  We are looking for the best national and international experts.  The size of the contract matches the amount which the government s Cambodian Mine Action Centre said earlier this month had been cut from funding it received from the United States through Norwegian People s Aid.  We welcome the commitment in taking part in addressing the legacy of the war,  said Huy Vannak, undersecretary of state at the Interior Ministry. China, now Cambodia s closest ally, was quick to step in with an offer of help for demining soon afterwards. China is Cambodia s biggest donor and investor and has played an ever more prominent role as Western countries have criticized a crackdown on the opposition, civil society groups and media ahead of next year s election. Although it has not taken action, the European Union pointed out last week that Cambodia s access to duty free access vital to its garment industry depended on respect for human rights. Hun Sen told garment workers on Wednesday that they would be the ones to suffer - not him - if the access was withdrawn. European Union countries accounted for about 40 percent of Cambodia s exports in 2016. Most of that was clothing.  You must remember clearly that if there is any cut of buying orders, it s all the fault of a group of people of the opposition party,  Hun Sen told garment workers in Phnom Penh.  Hun Sen won t die but workers, you will die,  he said. The prime minister accused exiled opposition leaders of trying to get sanctions imposed. They have so far said they would not call for measures to curb trade because of the impact it could have on the livelihoods of an estimated 700,000 garment workers. Cambodia s economy has proved largely immune to political turbulence. The World Bank said on Wednesday it expected the economy to grow 6.9 percent next year, compared with a projected 6.8 percent pace in 2017, despite risks including uncertainty over the election.

text: On Tuesday, prime ministers from Bulgaria, Greece, and Romania expressed their support for Serbia's aspiration to join the European Union, emphasizing that the integration of the western Balkans would ensure lasting peace and stability in the region. Serbia, which was regarded as an outcast in the Western Balkans during the 1990s due to its significant involvement in the conflicts that erupted after Yugoslavia's disintegration, hopes to finalize its EU membership negotiations by 2019. After a summit held in Varna, a coastal city by the Black Sea, Bulgarian Prime Minister Boyko Borissov remarked, "We all know that the natural place of Serbia is in the European Union," in the presence of Greek Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras, Romanian Prime Minister Mihai Tudose, and Serbian President Alexander Vucic. Borissov indicated that the three EU nations would endeavor to expedite the accession process, benefiting both the Balkans and Europe as a whole. Starting in January, Bulgaria will assume the rotating presidency of the EU for six months, followed by Romania taking over in 2019. Nonetheless, a considerable number of Serbians harbor doubts about joining the EU, perceiving Western European nations as vocal supporters of the NATO bombings in 1999, which aimed to cease the violence and displacement of ethnic Albanians in the former province of Kosovo, where numerous civilians lost their lives. Vucic has accused the EU of applying double standards, citing the rejection of the Catalan independence referendum while largely accepting Kosovo's independence. "We support Spain, it is our friendly country," he stated. "However, the European Commission reacted differently regarding Kosovo, which was against my people and my state." Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, a move recognized by Washington and many EU countries, but opposed by Belgrade and its allies. Vucic noted that Kosovo achieved its independence without any referendum, while Catalonia was denied a similar opportunity. "At times, we Serbs question why we have to endure such double standards," he stated. Serbia's stance on Kosovo continues to be a major obstacle in its pursuit of EU membership. Brussels has indicated that Serbia must enhance its relations with Pristina's authorities and cease efforts to obstruct their aspirations to join international organizations.
source_text: Balkan leaders back Serbia's bid to join European Union. SOFIA (Reuters) - The prime ministers of Bulgaria, Greece and Romania gave their support to their Balkan neighbor Serbia s bid to join the European Union on Tuesday, saying the integration of the western Balkans would guarantee regional peace and stability.  Serbia, which in the 1990s was seen as pariah of Western Balkans for its central role in wars that followed the collapse of Yugoslavia, expects to complete negotiations on EU membership by 2019.  All of us know that the natural place of Serbia is in the European Union,  Bulgarian Prime Minister Boyko Borissov said after a four-party summit in the Black Sea city of Varna with Greek Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras, Romanian Prime Minister Mihai Tudose and Serbian President Alexander Vucic.  Borissov said that the three EU members would work to speed up the process to the advantage of peace and stability in the Balkans and Europe generally. Bulgaria takes over the rotating six-month EU presidency in January while Romania will take over in 2019. Many Serbs, however, remain skeptical about joining the bloc and view Western European countries as outspoken advocates of the 1999 NATO bombing to halt the killing and expulsion of ethnic Albanians in the former province of Kosovo, in which thousands of civilians had been killed. Vucic accused the European Union of using double standards by refusing to accept the Catalan independence referendum while largely welcoming a separate Kosovo.  We support Spain, it is our friendly country,  said Vucic.  But the European Commission responded in a different way (over Kosovo) and it was against my people and my state. Kosovo s declaration of independence from Serbia in 2008 was accepted by Washington and most EU states, but rejected by Belgrade and its allies.  Kosovo gained independence without even holding a referendum but Catalonia ... cannot get anything like that,  Vucic said.  Sometimes, we, the Serbs, are asking ourselves why we should have been the victim of double standards?  Serbia s position on Kosovo has been one of the main stumbling blocks in its own bid to join the European Union. Brussels has said it needs to improve relations with the authorities in Pristina and stop trying to block their efforts to join international bodies.

text: Supporters of Donald Trump appear to heed his requests not to contribute financially to his presidential campaign. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Trump frequently boasts to his backers about his wealth, claiming he doesn’t require external funding for his bid for the presidency. Financial disclosures made public on Sunday indicate that his followers are inclined to respect his wishes. Although the New York entrepreneur has drawn significant crowds in his pursuit of the Republican party nomination, the amount of contributions he has received has been minimal, according to reports submitted to the U.S. Federal Election Commission. In the final quarter of 2015, he secured only $2.6 million from donors. A substantial portion of this revenue, three quarters, originated from merchandise sales, including baseball caps featuring his campaign's slogan, "Make America Great Again." In contrast, merely around $540,000 was contributed by individuals donating over $200. Many of his Republican competitors have amassed considerably greater sums. Senator Ted Cruz, Trump's closest competitor, raised $20.5 million, while former Florida Governor Jeb Bush, previously a leading candidate but who has since declined in polling, accumulated $7 million. Nevertheless, Trump continues to maintain the lead in all national polls as Iowa voters prepare for the upcoming nominating event on Monday. The majority of the funds Trump is utilizing for his campaign stem from $12.6 million in loans he provided to his campaign throughout 2015. A portion of these funds has been redirected back into his enterprises: his largest campaign expense in the last quarter of 2015 was $826,590 paid to TAG Air, Inc., which operates his fleet of private jets, used to transport him between campaign events and his residences in New York and Florida. Following that, his second-largest expenditure was $478,000 to Wizbang Solutions, a design and printing firm, and $411,000 went to a consulting agency that organizes signatures for candidates to appear on state election ballots. Trump stands as the sole billionaire in the race, although several of his rivals are millionaires. Many supporters nationwide express that his financial self-sufficiency is appealing, as they believe he cannot be influenced by special interest groups. Trump's financial disclosures illustrate that his fundraising efforts are not the only aspect where he diverges from his opponents. During the last three months of 2015, he spent $6.9 million. In comparison, his far-off rival for the Republican nomination, retired neurosurgeon Ben Carson, expended $27 million. Cruz disbursed $15.5 million. Marco Rubio, the Florida senator now viewed as the most viable establishment alternative to Trump, spent $14.8 million in the fourth quarter—nearly $2 million more than Trump’s total expenditures for the entire year of 2015. (Reporting By Emily Flitter in New York; Additional reporting by Jonathan Allen in Washington; Editing by Robert Birsel) SAP is the sponsor of this coverage, which is independently produced by the staff of Reuters News Agency.

text: On Sunday, President Donald Trump reignited his conflict with the sports community, once more urging the owners of the National Football League to terminate players who engage in protests during the national anthem of the United States. In a tweet sent out early in the morning, Trump proposed that fans might consider boycotting NFL games to compel teams to take action against the players who demonstrate during the anthem. "If NFL fans refuse to attend games until players cease disrespecting our Flag & Country, change will occur swiftly," Trump tweeted on Sunday. "Fire or suspend!" In a follow-up tweet, he remarked that the "league should support" the fans who feel discontented with the protests. Trump is spending the weekend at his golf course in Bedminster, New Jersey, having held no public engagements on Saturday. On that Saturday, NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell criticized Trump’s initial remarks on the issue, which surfaced during a political rally in Alabama the prior Friday, indicating an "unfortunate lack of respect" for the NFL and its players. At the rally, Trump labeled any football player who protests as a "son of a bitch" and suggested they should be dismissed from their jobs. "Wouldn’t it be great to see an NFL owner, when someone disrespects our flag, say, ‘Get that son of a bitch off the field right now ... He is fired’,” Trump commented during the rally supporting Alabama Senate Republican candidate Luther Strange. Later on Saturday, Trump conveyed through Twitter that if NFL players desired "the privilege" of receiving high salaries, they "should stand for the National Anthem. If not, YOU’RE FIRED. Find something else to do!" The actions of former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick sparked a contentious national conversation in 2016 when he chose not to stand during the pre-game performances of the "Star Spangled Banner". Rather than standing, Kaepernick knelt to protest police brutality against African-Americans. Since then, several players have adopted similar forms of protest prior to games. As the commissioner, Goodell has a responsibility to NFL owners, some of whom have previously supported Trump. Woody Johnson, the owner of the New York Jets and a significant donor to Trump’s presidential campaign, was confirmed last month by the Senate as Trump’s selection for the role of U.S. ambassador to Britain. The union that represents professional football players also dismissed Trump’s remarks, asserting it would uphold their right to freedom of expression. The White House did not provide a comment when requested regarding this issue. Moreover, players from the National Basketball Association responded to the president's comments on Saturday after he had a confrontation with one of the NBA’s leading figures. In an early morning Twitter post on Saturday, Trump revoked an invitation to Stephen Curry, who had expressed his intention to "vote" against the anticipated visit by the NBA champion Golden State Warriors to the White House. "Going to the White House is regarded as a significant honor for a championship team. Stephen Curry is hesitating, therefore the invitation is withdrawn!" Trump tweeted. Curry responded during a press conference in Oakland, California, stating: "It’s beneath the leader of a country to go that route." "It’s not what leaders do," he added. The Golden State Warriors, based in Oakland, released a statement indicating that the team had planned to convene to discuss the possible visit at the earliest opportunity that Saturday morning. "We accept that President Trump has made it clear that we are not invited," the team’s statement read. LeBron James defended Curry, contesting Trump’s claim that visiting the White House was a privilege. "Going to the White House was a great honor until you showed up!" James, a notable supporter of Hillary Clinton during the 2016 presidential race, posted on Twitter. Additionally, singer Stevie Wonder seemed to reference the protests initiated by Kaepernick and other athletes when he kneeled on the stage during a performance at the Global Citizen Festival in New York City on Saturday. "Tonight, I’m taking a knee for America," Wonder announced to the crowd as his son, Kwame Morris, assisted him down. Wonder subsequently lowered his other leg to kneel.

text: On Tuesday, Myanmar's leader Aung San Suu Kyi remarked that trust and understanding have diminished among the communities in Rakhine state. However, she did not mention the significant number of Rohingya Muslims who have fled the area following a military crackdown. "The situation in Rakhine has garnered the world's attention amid the numerous challenges that our government is confronting," Suu Kyi stated during a speech at a ceremony to receive Pope Francis in Naypyitaw, the capital of Myanmar, on the second day of his visit. She noted, "As we tackle persistent issues—social, economic, and political—that have undermined trust and understanding, as well as harmony and collaboration, the support from our citizens and friends who genuinely wish to see us succeed has been crucial." Over the past three months, more than 620,000 Rohingya have departed from northern Rakhine state to escape what Amnesty International has characterized as "crimes against humanity," and they are now gathered in refugee camps at the southern end of Bangladesh. While the United States has labeled Myanmar's actions as "ethnic cleansing" against the Rohingya, China has continued to support the country, and Suu Kyi is scheduled to visit Beijing later this week. A Nobel Peace Prize winner and a pro-democracy advocate, Suu Kyi has faced international backlash for her skepticism regarding reports of human rights violations against the Rohingya as well as her reluctance to denounce the military's actions.
source_text: Myanmar's Suu Kyi says trust has been eroded between Rakhine state communities.
