text: A federal appeals court has declared that New Hampshire's law against taking selfies with ballots on election day is a violation of free speech rights. The ruling, issued on Wednesday, pertains to a statute enacted in 2014 which forbids voters from capturing images of their ballots. This law was introduced in response to concerns that such practices could lead to a resurgence of vote-buying scandals reminiscent of those that plagued various U.S. states during the 19th century. The case originated when three residents of New Hampshire, one of whom humorously submitted his dog's name as a write-in candidate during the 2014 Republican primary for the U.S. Senate, challenged the law, asserting it infringed upon their First Amendment rights. A lower court in New Hampshire had previously ruled in their favor, prompting the state to appeal the decision, which was heard in Boston just a fortnight ago. The appeals court quickly dismissed the state’s rationale. In the opinion authored by Circuit Judge Sandra Lynch, it was stated, "The statute’s purposes cannot justify the restrictions it imposes on speech." Lynch further pointed out that New Hampshire had failed to provide evidence to support its claim that ballot selfies could lead to vote selling or coercion by employers regarding how individuals should vote. She stated, "The legislative history of the bill does not contain any corroborated evidence of vote buying or voter coercion in New Hampshire during the 20th and 21st centuries." Moreover, Lynch remarked that digital photography, alongside the internet and social media, are well-established elements of modern life, having been present during multiple election cycles without contributing to vote buying or voter intimidation. Additionally, she emphasized that several existing federal and state laws in New Hampshire already prohibit vote buying and selling, enabling prosecutors to address election tampering claims even if ballot selfies were allowed. Other states, such as Rhode Island, have enacted legislation explicitly permitting ballot selfies, partially believing that this trend engages younger voters and promotes enthusiasm for participating in the democratic process.
source_text: New Hampshire 'ballot selfie' ban unconstitutional: appeals court. BOSTON (Reuters) - A 2014 New Hampshire law prohibiting voters from taking selfies with their ballots on election day is an unconstitutional infringement on the right to free speech, a federal appeals court ruled on Wednesday. The New England state had banned the practice, which has become a popular way for voters to show support for favored candidates, claiming that it would set the stage for a return of the vote-buying scandals that rocked many U.S. states in the 19th century. Three New Hampshire citizens, including a man who wrote in the name of his dog to express dismay at his choices in the 2014 Republican primary for the U.S. Senate, sued the state that year claiming the measure violated their rights to free expression, as protected by the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. A federal court in New Hampshire sided with them, but the state appealed, making its case in Boston just two weeks ago. The appeals court swiftly rejected its arguments. “The statute’s purposes cannot justify the restrictions it imposes on speech,” Circuit Judge Sandra Lynch wrote in the court’s decision. New Hampshire’s argument that ballot selfies could lead to people selling their votes or being compelled by their employers to vote in a certain way fell short in no small part because the state had no evidence of that actually happening, Lynch wrote. “The legislative history of the bill does not contain any corroborated evidence of vote buying or voter coercion in New Hampshire during the 20th and 21st centuries,” she wrote. “Digital photography, the internet, and social media are not unknown quantities — they have been ubiquitous for several election cycles, without being shown to have the effect of furthering vote buying or voter intimidation.” Lynch also noted that several federal and state laws in effect in New Hampshire already make it illegal to buy or sell a vote, which would allow prosecutors to take on allegations of election tampering even in an environment where selfies were permitted. Other states, including nearby Rhode Island, have passed laws explicitly allowing ballot selfies, partly reasoning that the trend has helped younger voters show their enthusiasm for the democratic process.

text: On Sunday, House Speaker Paul Ryan revealed that U.S. House Republicans are revising their healthcare overhaul legislation to enhance tax credits aimed at older Americans and introduce a work requirement for Medicaid recipients. Ryan indicated that the Republican leadership is still aiming for a vote on the healthcare proposal in the House of Representatives on Thursday. During an appearance on the "Fox News Sunday" show, he mentioned that they are addressing various concerns brought up by regular Republican members regarding the legislation. The healthcare reform remains a contentious issue among Republicans, who are split over President Donald Trump’s initial significant legislative effort. This initiative seeks to fulfill Trump’s campaign promise to dismantle and replace the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare, which was established by his Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama. Democrats argue that the Republican scheme could lead to millions losing health coverage and adversely impact the elderly, low-income individuals, and working families while simultaneously offering tax reductions for affluent individuals. Ryan, the leading Republican figure in Congress, stated, "We think we should be offering even more assistance than the bill currently does" for individuals aged 50 to 64 with lower incomes, referring to the proposed healthcare tax credits. Additionally, Ryan noted that Republicans are considering modifications to allow federal block grants for states pertaining to Medicaid, which would enable states to enforce a work requirement for Medicaid recipients who are capable of working. Trump, during a short discussion with reporters aboard Air Force One, mentioned that he had engaged in discussions regarding healthcare reform over the weekend in Florida and that the efforts to promote the proposal were progressing positively. He has been reaching out to lawmakers in support of the bill and secured the endorsement of a dozen conservative legislators following a meeting in the Oval Office on Friday, where he backed the work requirement and the block-grant approach for Medicaid. On Monday, Trump is scheduled to confer with Ezekiel Emanuel, a health policy adviser under Obama who played a role in crafting the Affordable Care Act, along with Ryan and Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price at the White House. The block grants would allocate a fixed amount of funding to states for the Medicaid program, granting them more discretion in how to spend it. However, future funding is not guaranteed to meet demand. While Ryan expressed feeling "very good" about the potential success of the health bill in the House, a prominent conservative representative, Mark Meadows, revealed on C-Span’s "Newsmakers" that there are currently 40 Republican members opposed to the bill in the House. Although Republicans maintain a majority in the chamber, they cannot tolerate more than 21 defections for the measure to succeed. Meadows, along with fellow Republican critics of the bill, Senators Mike Lee from Utah and Ted Cruz from Texas, convened at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday to "negotiate with the president’s team, trying to fix this bill," according to Cruz’s statement on CBS’ "Face the Nation." Meadows, representing North Carolina, expressed concern that the proposed modifications for the Medicaid program would not be sufficient if they allowed states to decide on implementing a work requirement. Price acknowledged the challenging negotiations, admitting on ABC’s "This Week": "It’s a fine needle that needs to be thread, there’s no doubt about it." Even if the healthcare bill manages to pass the House, it would still encounter considerable obstacles in the Senate. Senator Tom Cotton, a conservative Republican from Arkansas, commented that the bill would not result in lower premiums for individuals in the private insurance market. "It’s fixable, but it’s going to take a lot of work," Cotton said during an appearance on CNN’s "State of the Union." Moderate Republicans have also raised alarms about the legislation, and their concerns often differ from those of conservative members. Republican Senator Susan Collins from Maine expressed her worries on NBC’s "Meet the Press," stating that the bill could negatively affect older Americans.
source_text: Republicans revamp U.S. health bill, boost benefits to older Americans. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. House Republicans are working on changes to their healthcare overhaul bill to provide more generous tax credits for older Americans and add a work requirement for the Medicaid program for the poor, House Speaker Paul Ryan said on Sunday. Ryan said Republican leaders still planned to bring the healthcare bill to a vote on the House of Representatives floor on Thursday. Speaking on the “Fox News Sunday” television program, he said leaders were working to address concerns that had been raised by rank-and-file Republicans to the legislation. Republicans remain deeply divided over the healthcare overhaul, which is President Donald Trump’s first major legislative initiative. It aims to fulfill his campaign pledge to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, popularly known as Obamacare, the signature healthcare program of his Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama. Democrats say the Republican plan could throw millions off health insurance and hurt the elderly, poor and working families while giving tax cuts to the rich. “We think we should be offering even more assistance than the bill currently does” for lower-income people age 50 to 64, Ryan, the top Republican in Congress, said of the tax credits for health insurance that are proposed in the legislation. Ryan also said Republicans were working on changes that would allow federal block grants to states for Medicaid and permit states to impose a work requirement for able-bodied Medicaid recipients. Trump told reporters in a brief conversation aboard Air Force One that he had meetings about healthcare reform in Florida at the weekend and that the effort to sell the proposal was going well. He has been wooing lawmakers to vote for the bill and won the backing of a dozen conservative lawmakers on Friday after an Oval Office meeting in which the president endorsed a work requirement and block-grant option for Medicaid. Trump is set to meet Ezekiel Emanuel, a health policy special adviser under Obama who helped shape the Affordable Care Acton, at the White House on Monday, along with Ryan and Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price. Block grants would give states a set amount of money to cover people on the Medicaid program and provide flexibility in spending decisions. However, there is no guarantee funding would keep up with future demands. While Ryan said he felt “very good” about the health bill’s prospects in the House, a leading conservative lawmaker, Representative Mark Meadows, told the C-Span “Newsmakers” program that there were currently 40 Republican “no” votes in the House. Republicans hold a majority in the chamber but cannot afford to have more than 21 defections for the measure to pass.  Meadows and two other Republican opponents of the bill, Senators Mike Lee of Utah and Ted Cruz of Texas, met at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday “negotiating with the president’s team, trying to fix this bill,” Cruz told CBS’ “Face the Nation.” North Carolina Republican Meadows said the changes being considered for the Medicaid program would not go far enough if they left it up to states to decide whether to put in place a work requirement. Price acknowledged the tough negotiations, telling ABC’s “This Week”: “It’s a fine needle that needs to be thread, there’s no doubt about it.”   The healthcare bill would face significant challenges in the Senate even if it were to pass the House. Senator Tom Cotton, a conservative Arkansas Republican, said the bill would not reduce premiums for people on the private insurance market. “It’s fixable, but it’s going to take a lot of work,” Cotton said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” Moderate Republicans have also expressed concerns about the bill, and their worries are often not the same as that of conservatives. Speaking on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine worried the bill would harm older Americans, and shift Medicaid costs to states - something critics say a block-grant approach would only make worse. Collins said coverage issues must also be dealt with, citing a report from the Congressional Budget Office that said 14 million people would lose health coverage under the House bill over the next year and 24 million over the next decade. Affordability has been one of the bigger concerns that insurers and hospital groups have raised about the legislation. To the extent that a change in tax credits makes healthcare more affordable for some people, insurers and hospitals could stand to benefit. The BlueCross BlueShield Association emphasized the need for the replacement to be affordable when the draft of the healthcare bill was released earlier this month. The association represents BCBS insurers that cover the vast majority of the roughly 10 million people enrolled in 2017 Obamacare plans.

text: On Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron declared that France is prepared to enhance its military presence in the Sahel, collaborating with African forces in the battle against Islamist groups. The French government has aimed to gradually withdraw from the sparsely monitored scrublands of the Sahel region, which borders the Sahara to the north and has evolved into a hub for Islamist militant recruitment and training, with assistance from a newly established regional African military unit. Officially launched in November, the G5 Sahel comprises troops from Mali, Niger, Chad, Burkina Faso, and Mauritania, working alongside 4,000 French soldiers who have been stationed there since their intervention in 2013, which aimed to suppress an uprising in northern Mali. During his visit to Niamey, the capital of Niger, Macron emphasized that the French military would continue to prioritize the Sahel if necessary in the future. "France is not only prepared to sustain its presence but also, if required, to bolster its involvement in the region, as I believe the struggle against terrorism in the Sahel is crucial," he stated during a joint press briefing with Nigerien President Mahamoudou Issoufou. He further noted, "The battle is not concluded today... it is vital to not only maintain but also enhance our operational flexibility on the ground, to innovate further, and to concentrate our efforts on areas identified as most vulnerable." Additionally, Macron revealed during his trip to Niger that France would allocate an extra 10 million euros to promote girls' education, a key initiative championed by President Issoufou to mitigate migration. This new funding is in addition to the 15 million euros that France has already dedicated to educational support in Niger. In mid-December, Paris committed to investing 400 million euros from 2017 to 2021 to assist Niamey.
source_text: Macron: France ready to strengthen force in Sahel fighting Islamists. PARIS (Reuters) - President Emmanuel Macron said on Saturday France stood ready if needed to strengthen its military force fighting alongside African troops against Islamist insurgents in the Sahel.   France has been seeking to eventually withdraw from the poorly policed scrublands of the Sahel region - which abuts the Sahara to the north and has become a recruiting and training ground for Islamist militants - with the help of a new regional African force.  The G5 Sahel, which began official operations in November, is made up of troops from Mali, Niger, Chad, Burkina Faso and Mauritania that will patrol the region in collaboration with 4,000 French troops deployed there since intervening in 2013 to quell an insurgency in northern Mali. But Macron said on a visit to the Niger capital Niamey that the Sahel would remain a focus for the French army, should it be required in the future.   France is ready, not only to maintain, but if necessary to strengthen its engagement in the region because the fight against terrorism in the Sahel is essential, in my opinion,  he said during a joint news conference with his Nigerien counterpart Mahamoudou Issoufou.  The fight is not won today ... it is essential not only to maintain but to further improve our agility on the ground, to innovate more and to focus our priorities on the regions identified as the most vulnerable,  he added. Speaking during his visit to Niger, Macron also announced an additional 10 million euros to help educate girls, one of the priorities promoted by President Issoufou to curb migration. This sum is on top of 15 million euros already invested by France to help education in Niger. Paris pledged in mid-December to spend 400 million euros over 2017-2021 to support Niamey.

text: A delegate for Donald Trump’s presidential campaign has been charged with serious crimes, including the illegal shipment of explosives and the production of child pornography. The U.S. Justice Department announced on Thursday that Caleb Bailey, 30, from Maryland, was indicted by a grand jury on Wednesday in the U.S. District Court located in Greenbelt, Maryland. Bailey, who was elected as a delegate for Trump, the leading Republican nominee, is still recognized as such on the state’s election board website. Joe Cluster, the executive director of the Maryland Republican Party, confirmed the indictment of Bailey and informed Reuters that the party was urging him to step down from the delegation. "I don’t know too much about him beyond what I’ve read," Cluster remarked, opting not to elaborate further. According to a law enforcement source familiar with the inquiry, Bailey had accumulated a vast collection of illegal firearms in a bunker under his garage, which included numerous machine guns, smokeless grenades, and gas canisters, in addition to ready-to-eat meals. On Thursday, attempts to reach Bailey, the Trump campaign, and the Maryland board of elections for comments went unanswered. As the Republican party aims to solidify its unity ahead of the presidential nominating convention in Cleveland scheduled for July, Trump is actively working on this front. Earlier in March, a man from New Hampshire, who co-led Trump’s veterans coalition in that state, was extradited to Nevada to face allegations related to his involvement in the notorious 2014 armed standoff with federal agents at Cliven Bundy’s ranch. The indictment against Bailey consists of four counts, asserting that he engaged a minor to "participate in sexually explicit conduct to produce child pornography" and possessed a machine gun unlawfully. Authorities became aware of Bailey when he attempted to send explosives and ammunition via U.S. mail from Maryland to Wisconsin in February, as stated in an affidavit by a special agent from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The law enforcement official mentioned that some cartridges Bailey was trying to ship to Wisconsin are now deemed too hazardous for military use, making the shipment both illegal and a significant public safety risk. The recipient in Wisconsin is also under investigation, according to the official. In total, Bailey tried to ship five packages, but one of them burst open at the post office, which led to law enforcement being notified, according to the affidavit.
source_text: Trump delegate indicted on weapons, child pornography charges. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A Maryland man who is a delegate for Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump has been indicted for illegally shipping explosives, owning a machine gun and producing child pornography, the U.S. Justice Department said on Thursday. Caleb Bailey, 30, was indicted by a grand jury in U.S. District Court in Greenbelt, Maryland, on Wednesday. He was elected to be a delegate for Trump, the presumptive Republican presidential nominee, and is still listed as one on the state’s board of elections website.  Joe Cluster, executive director of the Maryland Republican Party, confirmed Bailey had been indicted and told Reuters the party was asking Bailey to resign from the delegation. “I don’t know too much about him beyond what I’ve read,” said Cluster, who declined to comment further. Bailey had hundreds of illegal weapons stored in a bunker beneath his garage, including dozens of machine guns, smokeless grenades and gas canisters, along with ready-to-eat meals, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the investigation. Telephone calls and emails seeking comment from Bailey, from the Trump campaign and from the Maryland board of elections were not returned on Thursday. Trump has been working to unify the Republican party going into its presidential nominating convention in Cleveland in July. In March, a New Hampshire man who co-chaired Trump’s veterans coalition in the state was extradited to Nevada to face charges of helping organize the high-profile 2014 armed standoff with federal agents at the ranch of Cliven Bundy. The four-count indictment against Bailey alleges that he used a minor to “engage in sexually explicit conduct to produce child pornography” and illegally owned a machine gun. Authorities became aware of Bailey after he tried to ship explosives and ammunition from Maryland to Wisconsin through the U.S. mail in February, said an affidavit filed by a special agent with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.  Some of the types of cartridges Bailey was sending to Wisconsin are no longer used by the U.S. military because they are too dangerous, the law enforcement official said, so shipping them was “not only illegal, but posed a significant public risk.” The Wisconsin recipient is under investigation as well, according to the official. Bailey attempted to ship five such packages in total, but one broke open at the post office, prompting the facility to call law enforcement, according to the affidavit.

text: On Tuesday, a senior official from the U.S. administration indicated that President Donald Trump has established a cordial connection with Rodrigo Duterte, the President of the Philippines, despite Duterte's frequent use of profane language in his criticisms of the United States. source_text: Trump has 'warm rapport' with Philippines' Duterte: official. text: On Tuesday, the leaders of the Senate Finance Committee in the United States announced that they had come to a consensus regarding the funding of a federal insurance initiative aimed at millions of low-income children and expecting mothers, which was set to expire at the end of the month. Orrin Hatch, a Republican senator and the committee chairman, along with Ron Wyden, the leading Democrat on the panel, shared that this agreement would allocate resources for the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) for a period of five years. While reauthorizing CHIP usually garners bipartisan backing, lobbyists and industry representatives have indicated that healthcare legislation has become more challenging following the Republicans' unsuccessful attempts to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act. “I am optimistic that we can proceed promptly to prevent any interruption in care for our nation’s most vulnerable children,” Hatch expressed in a statement, referring to the agreement as “a good first start.” Wyden also stated that he was eager to see the CHIP extension enacted into law “as soon as possible.”
source_text: Key U.S. senators reach deal on funding children's health program. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Leaders of the U.S. Senate Finance Committee said on Tuesday they reached an agreement to finance a federal insurance program for millions of lower-income children and pregnant women that was due to expire at the end of the month. Republican Senator Orrin Hatch, chairman of the finance committee, and the panel’s top Democrat, Senator Ron Wyden, said in a statement the agreement would provide money for the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) for five years. CHIP reauthorization is not typically contentious as the program receives bipartisan support. But lobbyists and industry officials have said any healthcare-related legislation has become more complicated following the failure of Republicans to repeal and replace Obamacare. “I am hopeful we can move forward swiftly to ensure no lapse in care for our nation’s most vulnerable children,” Hatch said in a statement, calling the agreement “a good first start.” Wyden said in a statement he hoped to get the extension of CHIP into law “as soon as possible.”

text: The trial of over 1,600 individuals accused of connections to Boko Haram is set to commence in Nigeria on Monday, taking place behind closed doors. This marks the largest legal inquiry into the militant Islamist insurgency that has persisted for eight years. During this conflict, more than 20,000 lives have been lost, and around two million people have been displaced in northeastern Nigeria, contributing to what the United Nations has described as one of the most severe humanitarian crises globally. According to Nigeria's ministry of justice, the proceedings for approximately 1,670 detainees from the Kainji detention center were scheduled to begin in central Niger state on Monday, under the oversight of four judges. Attempts to obtain confirmation from a ministry spokesperson regarding the commencement of the trial were unsuccessful. A representative from the military refrained from commenting, suggesting that inquiries should be directed towards the judiciary. The ministry also indicated that once the Kainji trials are concluded, an additional 651 individuals, suspected of being affiliated with Boko Haram and currently incarcerated in Maiduguri, the capital city of the northeastern Borno state, would face trial. Clement Nwankwo, a human rights attorney located in Abuja, asserted that conducting these trials in an open forum would serve as a more effective deterrent. "It is essential for the public to be informed about the ongoing issues related to Boko Haram and to comprehend the severity of the crimes committed," Nwankwo remarked, emphasizing that a lack of transparency could hinder the assessment of trial fairness. He expressed concerns that the Nigerian authorities have not consistently shown diligence in investigating and prosecuting suspects, warning that perceived injustices could foster resentment among victims' families, potentially leading to future radicalization. Meanwhile, Fatima Akilu, who previously led the government's counter-violent extremism initiative under the last administration, argued for the necessity of secrecy in the trials. This, she claimed, would motivate witnesses and judges to participate, as Nigeria lacks a witness protection framework. "Many witnesses were hesitant to come forward," Akilu stated, referencing earlier attempts to conduct trials. She also noted that judges and witnesses had previously faced death threats. "In the absence of witnesses, the evidence available for securing convictions is limited, leaving us with little choice," she added, mentioning that there were no viable alternatives without an amnesty initiative. The manner in which Nigeria has managed the cases of thousands accused of links to Boko Haram has previously drawn critique. This legal process represents a significant increase in the number of cases related to the insurgency that Nigerian officials are addressing. The Ministry of Justice reported that as of September 11, only 13 terrorism-related cases had been resolved, with nine convictions achieved. The initiation of these trials is a direct response to ongoing concerns raised by both local and global human rights organizations regarding the detention of thousands without access to legal counsel or specific charges, as explained by Nnamdi Obasi from the International Crisis Group.
source_text: Nigeria set to start mass trial of Boko Haram suspects behind closed doors. ABUJA (Reuters) - The trial of more than 1,600 people suspected of ties with Boko Haram was expected to begin in Nigeria on Monday behind closed doors, in the biggest legal investigation into the eight-year militant Islamist insurgency. More than 20,000 people have been killed and two million forced from their homes in northeastern Nigeria during the insurgency, contributing to what the United Nations has said is among the world s worst humanitarian crises.  Nigeria s ministry of justice said last month the trial of around 1,670 people held at the Kainji detention facility would begin at the site, in the central Niger state, on Monday and would be presided over by four judges.  A spokesman for the ministry did not respond to requests for confirmation that the trial had begun. A military spokesman declined to comment, saying questions should be addressed to the judiciary.  The ministry has said that after the Kainji trials are completed, a further 651 people suspected of having links to Boko Haram and currently being held at prisons in Maiduguri, the capital of the northeastern state of Borno, would go on trial.   Clement Nwankwo, a human rights lawyer based in the capital, Abuja, said the trials would provide a more effective deterrent if they were open to the media and public.  On the Boko Haram issue, stories need to be told for the public to be made aware what has been going on and understand the nature of the crimes committed,  said Nwankwo, adding that secrecy also made it hard to determine whether trials were fair.   The Nigerian authorities have not been known to be diligent in investigating and properly prosecuting suspects,  he said, warning that a sense of injustice could breed resentment among relatives that could yield future radicalization.  However, Fatima Akilu - who headed the government s counter violent extremism program under the previous administration - said secrecy was needed to encourage witnesses and judges to take part in the trials because Nigeria does not have a witness protection program.  A lot of witnesses were afraid to come forward,  Akilu, who was based in the Office of the National Security Adviser from 2012 to 2015, said of previous efforts to pursue trials.  She said judges and witnesses had previously been subjected to death threats.   If the witnesses don t come forward there is limited evidence in terms of reaching a conviction, so I think there was little choice,  she said, adding that there were no clear alternatives in the absence of an amnesty program. Nigeria s handling of thousands of people accused of ties with Boko Haram insurgents has previously attracted criticism.  The legal process marks a steep escalation in the number of insurgency-related cases being handled by Nigerian authorities. The Ministry of Justice has said that, as of Sept. 11, only 13  terrorism cases  had been concluded and nine convictions had been secured.   The decision to start the trials is a response to persistent complaints by local and international human rights groups over thousands of persons detained without access to lawyers and without any specific charges, said Nnamdi Obasi, of International Crisis Group.

text: On the mountainous border between Pakistan and Afghanistan, two suspected U.S. drone strikes on Tuesday resulted in the deaths of 11 individuals, according to government and militant sources. This follows a previous strike on Monday that claimed the lives of 20 people. The drone attacks occurred shortly after the release of a Canadian-American couple who had been held captive by the Taliban in the same region of northwest Pakistan, marking a rare instance of positive interaction in the often tense U.S.-Pakistan relations. Just days earlier, U.S. drones were observed in the vicinity where American Caitlan Coleman, her Canadian spouse, Joshua Boyle, and their three children, all born while in captivity, were liberated after being abducted by the Haqqani network in Afghanistan during 2012. Baseer Khan Wazir, the highest administrative official in Kurram Agency, which is part of Pakistan's volatile Federally Administered Tribal Areas, informed Reuters that four unmanned aerial vehicles launched six missiles in the attack on Monday, followed by an additional four missiles in two strikes on Tuesday. Over the course of these two days, the drone strikes targeted Taliban hideouts, resulting in a total of at least 31 fatalities, Wazir stated, with every strike occurring on the Afghan side of the border. 'Yesterday, 20 individuals were killed, primarily from the Afghan Taliban, and today, 11 more perished in the attacks,' Wazir confirmed to Reuters. According to Taliban sources, 18 militants affiliated with the Pakistan-based Haqqani network were killed in the strike on Monday, and six more in one of Tuesday's attacks. A member of the Afghan Taliban, speaking on the condition of anonymity, noted that mud-built houses used by the mujahideen (Afghan Taliban fighters) were targeted. While he claimed that no prominent militants were present during the drone strikes, another Taliban source reported that two commanders were among those killed in Monday's operation. Witnesses recounted hearing the drones and noticing smoke rising before observing 20 makeshift coffins being transported from the area. Local residents indicated that the strikes occurred within 300 meters (yards) of the Pakistani border. 'Drones frequently patrol this border area, but it was unusual to see four drones simultaneously,' remarked Kurram resident Gulab Sher.
source_text: Suspected U.S. drone strikes kill 31 on Pakistan-Afghanistan frontier. PARACHINAR/PESHAWAR, Pakistan (Reuters) - Two suspected U.S. drone strikes on Tuesday killed 11 people on the mountainous Pakistan-Afghanistan border, following a strike a day earlier that killed 20, government and militant sources said.  The attacks came days after a Canadian-American couple held hostage by the Taliban were freed from the area in Pakistan s northwest, striking a rare positive note in the country s often-fraught relations with the United States. On Friday, U.S. drones were seen hovering near where American Caitlan Coleman, her Canadian husband, Joshua Boyle, and their three children, all born in captivity, were freed, after having been kidnapped by the Haqqani network while backpacking in Afghanistan in 2012.   Four unmanned drones fired six missiles in Monday s attack, and four more were dropped in two strikes on Tuesday,  Baseer Khan Wazir, the top administrative official in the Kurram Agency, part of Pakistan s restive Federally Administered Tribal Areasm, told Reuters. The drones fired missiles on Taliban hideouts, killing at least 31 people over two days, he added, with all three attacks taking place on the Afghan side.   Twenty people were killed yesterday, mostly from the Afghan Taliban, and 11 more were killed in today s attacks,  Wazir told Reuters.  Taliban sources said 18 members of the Pakistan-based Haqqani militants, allied to the Taliban, were killed in Monday s strike and six in one of Tuesday s attacks.  There were some mud-built houses which were being used by the mujahideen (Afghan Taliban fighters),  said a member of the Afghan Taliban, who asked not to be identified. No prominent militants were in the area when the drones targeted two or three different compounds, he added. Another Taliban source said two commanders were killed in Monday s attack, however.  Witnesses said they heard the drones and saw plumes of smoke before seeing 20 makeshift coffins moved out of the area. Residents of the area said the strikes were no more than 300 meters (yards) from the Pakistan side of the border.   There are always drones hovering over this border area, but this was the first time four drones were noticed at the same time,  said Kurram resident Gulab Sher.

text: Cairo (Reuters) - On Tuesday, the armed forces of Egypt announced that joint military exercises with the United States would recommence this month for the first time since the year 2009. These drills had been previously called off in 2013 due to a crackdown by the Egyptian military on protests. Typically, these joint training sessions occur biannually, but they were also suspended in 2011 following the Arab Spring uprising that led to the ousting of Egypt's long-serving leader, Hosni Mubarak. The announcement concerning the Bright Star exercises came shortly after the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump decided to withhold $95.7 million in aid to Egypt, alongside a delay of $195 million over concerns regarding the country's progress in upholding rights and democratic principles. The exercises are scheduled to be conducted from September 10 to September 20 at the newly established Mohamed Naguib military base located in western Alexandria, as indicated in a statement released on the official Facebook page of the Egyptian military. The Bright Star training is regarded as one of the most significant collaborative military exercises involving Egyptian and American forces, illustrating the strong ties and cooperation between the two nations' armed services, according to the Egyptian military's announcement. A U.S. official, who requested anonymity due to not having the authority to communicate with the media, corroborated the scheduled timing and location of the exercise and mentioned that an official statement from U.S. Central Command is expected soon. Egypt stands as one of Washington's closest allies in the Middle East, and military assistance from the U.S. has historically reinforced its peace agreement with Israel established in 1979. The stability of this populous Arab nation is a key concern for the U.S. However, the strategic partnership experienced a decline during Barack Obama's presidency, where he temporarily halted aid following the military's removal of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's Islamist, democratically elected predecessor in 2013 after significant protests erupted against him. Annually, the U.S. supplies Egypt with $1.3 billion in military assistance along with approximately $250 million in economic support. Trump has sought to re-establish relations with Sisi, offering solid support and committing to collaboration in combating Islamic extremists. U.S. officials have suggested that last month’s aid freeze was intended to maintain security cooperation while also expressing dissatisfaction with Cairo's approach to civil liberties. A recent law concerning non-governmental organizations has been perceived as part of a larger offensive against dissent.
source_text: Egypt says suspended U.S. military exercises to resume. CAIRO (Reuters) - Egypt s armed forces said on Tuesday that joint U.S.-Egyptian military exercises will resume this month for the first time since 2009, after U.S. officials canceled them in 2013 following an Egyptian army crackdown on protests. The announcement on the  Bright Star  exercises came weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump s administration denied Egypt $95.7 million in aid and delayed $195 million because of its failure to progress on respecting rights and democratic norms. The Bright Star training is considered one of the most important joint Egyptian-American armed forces exercises, which reflects the depth of relations and cooperation between the armed forces of both countries,  the Egyptian statement said. A U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to media confirmed the timing and location of the exercise and said U.S. Central Command is due to make an official announcement soon. Egypt is one of Washington s closest Middle East allies, and U.S. military aid has long cemented its historic 1979 peace deal with Israel. Home to the Suez Canal, the stability of the Arab world s most populous state is a U.S. priority. text: As concerns grow about the legislative pace in Washington, financial markets are increasingly apprehensive regarding U.S. President Donald Trump and the Republican Congress. Investors are particularly attentive to the potential repercussions stemming from any delays in Trump's initiative to dismantle Obamacare. During his campaign and following his inauguration, Trump raised considerable expectations not only for the repeal and replacement of Obamacare but also for tax reductions, deregulation of businesses, and enhancements to infrastructure. However, after eight weeks in office, Trump has yet to propose significant legislation or secure approval for any of his favored policies. The Republican healthcare proposal, which he endorses, has encountered opposition from both Democrats and members within his own party, with a vote anticipated in the House of Representatives on Thursday. Market experts had initially projected that Trump and the Republicans would finalize the confirmation of his Supreme Court nominee by early April; repeal Obamacare by mid-May; pass a budget resolution by the end of June; and reform tax legislation by the end of the year. This week, analysts voiced skepticism regarding these timelines. Below are important dates in 2017 that could impact Trump's policy ambitions. March 23: A vote in the House is anticipated on the Republicans' bill to roll back Obamacare. April 3: The Senate Judiciary Committee is expected to cast a ballot regarding Supreme Court nominee Neil Gorsuch, forwarding the nomination to the full Senate. April 7: A two-week congressional recess is set to begin. April 18: An early evaluation of U.S. voter sentiment towards Trump will occur in a special election in Georgia to fill a vacant House position. April 28: The spending authority for the government under the ongoing budget resolution will expire, necessitating action from Congress. May 25: Trump will participate in the NATO summit in Brussels. May 26: Trump is slated to attend the G-7 conference in Italy. Congress will adjourn for a one-week Memorial Day holiday break. June 14: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will meet, with Chair Janet Yellen holding a press briefing. June 20: The runoff for the Georgia special election will take place. text: On Monday, the executive branch of the European Union announced it has received unanimous backing from all 28 member states to conclude discussions regarding a free trade agreement with the United States. This declaration came shortly after Sigmar Gabriel, the economy minister of Germany, the largest economy within the EU, stated that the negotiations had "de facto failed". Gabriel expressed on Sunday that the discussions surrounding the Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership (TTIP) had faltered due to Europe’s refusal to comply with certain U.S. requests. When a European Commission spokesperson was asked for a response to Gabriel’s comments, he stated, "The ball is still rolling" concerning TTIP. Margaritis Schinas, speaking at a press conference, emphasized, "Although trade talks take time, the ball is rolling right now and the Commission is making steady progress in the ongoing TTIP negotiations." The White House also countered Gabriel’s assertion, clarifying that they still hope to finalize a deal by the year’s end. White House spokesman Josh Earnest conveyed to reporters in Washington, "It's going to require the resolution of some pretty thorny negotiations, but the president and his team are committed to doing that." In Berlin, Germany’s top industry groups criticized Gabriel’s statements, urging the German administration to demonstrate a stronger commitment to free trade agreements. Ulrich Grillo, head of the BDI industry association, remarked that it was "astonishing" for Gabriel, who also serves as vice chancellor and leader of the co-governing Social Democrats, to declare the TTIP discussions a failure while negotiations were still ongoing. Leaders from other industry associations, including VDMA and the Auto Industry Association VDA, voiced their opposition to Gabriel’s comments, which underscored the increasing rifts within Chancellor Angela Merkel’s governing coalition in advance of next year's elections. Numerous differences, particularly regarding food and environmental safety, have remained unresolved after three years of discussions. Critics argue that the agreement would grant excessive power to large multinational corporations, potentially harming consumers and workers. Proponents of a comprehensive U.S.-EU free trade agreement argue that it would yield economic benefits for both sides of the Atlantic. EU trade ministers are scheduled to convene on September 22 in Bratislava to deliberate on this matter. Schinas indicated that the Commission is still prepared to finalize the agreement by the year's end, but not at the detriment of "Europe’s safety, health, social and data protection standards, or our cultural diversity." Separately commenting on Gabriel’s remarks, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Linas Linkevicius expressed his belief that reaching an agreement would be advantageous for both the EU and the United States. "It would be better for all sides to agree," he stated. "Of course, not at an expense of our interests. We have to defend our interests, but we also have to negotiate and conclude this agreement. It would be a big boost for economies, jobs, trade." The Brexit vote in June has further complicated the situation, although Schinas reiterated that Brussels continues to negotiate on behalf of all 28 members of the bloc, including London.

text: On Wednesday, a U.S. appeals court deliberated over President Donald Trump’s latest travel ban, which affects individuals from six predominantly Muslim nations. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals session took place in Seattle, just two days after the U.S. Supreme Court permitted the enforcement of Trump’s travel restrictions while legal challenges regarding its constitutionality continue. This travel ban specifically targets citizens from Chad, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Syria, and Yemen attempting to enter the United States. Trump has claimed that such measures are necessary to safeguard the nation from terrorism. However, the state of Hawaii has contested this ban in court, with a federal judge in Honolulu ruling that it exceeds the authority granted to Trump under immigration law. Additionally, the ban includes provisions for individuals from North Korea and select Venezuelan government officials, although earlier court rulings had already permitted those specific aspects to be implemented. The same panel of three judges from the 9th Circuit, who previously restricted an earlier iteration of Trump’s travel ban, reviewed the arguments on Wednesday. Some judges seemed to express greater hesitation regarding the notion of obstructing the president’s directive. Judge Michael Daly Hawkins inquired about whether the most recent proclamation from Trump is more justified compared to previous versions. He noted that the current ban is grounded in particular findings indicating that certain foreign governments fail to provide adequate information for appropriate vetting of immigrants. "Would you put your trust in Kim Jong Un to verify someone’s identity and allow them entry?" Hawkins questioned. Judge Ronald Gould remarked that the court would render a decision "as soon as practicable." Trump’s initial travel ban, directed at several Muslim-majority nations, was implemented in January, leading to significant turmoil at airports and widespread demonstrations. A revised version was issued in March after the original faced legal obstacles. That version expired in September following an extended legal battle and has since been succeeded by the current ban. There are exceptions included; individuals from the targeted nations may still apply for visas for educational, business, or tourism purposes, and any applicant is eligible to request an individual waiver. A different challenge to the ban is scheduled to be heard by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday, with the U.S. Supreme Court anticipated to ultimately resolve the matter in the upcoming months.

SEATTLE/SAN FRANCISCO (Reuters) - A U.S. appeals court on Wednesday wrestled with a bid by President Donald Trump to show that his latest travel ban targeting people from six Muslim-majority countries is legal. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals hearing in Seattle came two days after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed Trump’s travel ban to take effect while litigation over its ultimate validity unfolds.  The ban targets people from Chad, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Syria and Yemen seeking to enter the United States. The Republican president has said the travel ban is needed to protect the United States from terrorism. The state of Hawaii, however, challenged it in court, and a Honolulu federal judge said it exceeded Trump’s powers under immigration law. Trump’s ban also covers people from North Korea and certain government officials from Venezuela, but the lower courts had already allowed those provisions to go into effect. The same three judge 9th Circuit panel which limited a previous version of Trump’s ban heard arguments on Wednesday. Some of the judges appeared more cautious toward the idea of blocking the president’s policy. Judge Michael Daly Hawkins asked Hawaii’s lawyers whether Trump’s latest proclamation is more sound than prior versions. The current one, he said, is based on specific findings that some foreign governments do not share enough information to properly vet immigrants.  “You would trust Kim Jong Un to say this person is this person, you gotta let him in?” Hawkins said. Judge Ronald Gould said the court would issue a ruling “as soon as practicable.” Trump issued his first travel ban targeting several Muslim-majority countries in January, which caused chaos at airports and mass protests.  He issued a revised one in March after the first was blocked by federal courts.  That expired in September after a long court fight, and was replaced with the current version.  The ban has some exceptions. Certain people from each targeted country can still apply for a visa for tourism, business or education purposes, and any applicant can ask for an individual waiver. The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals is set to hear a separate challenge to the ban on Friday, and the U.S. Supreme Court is expected to ultimately decide the issue in the coming months.

text: In a week where Donald Trump intensified his criticism of Democrat Hillary Clinton, the presumptive Republican nominee has taken his campaign strategy to unprecedented levels in the realm of modern U.S. presidential elections. Trump is seeking to bolster his position while countering a significant advantage that Clinton is expected to wield leading up to the presidential election on November 8: a substantial financial backing that she and her supporters plan to utilize for extensive attacks against him. The Republican candidate is employing a tactic similar to the one he frequently used during his fight for the Republican nomination against opponents such as Ted Cruz: making provocative remarks that capture the attention of U.S. television networks, thereby securing hours of complimentary media coverage and placing his rivals on the defensive. Early indications suggest that this approach may be yielding results. Trump's latest barrage of accusations against Clinton has raised eyebrows, transforming historical events into headlines that resonate in the continuous news cycle of online platforms and cable television. Corey Lewandowski, Trump’s campaign manager, expressed support for the strategy, stating, "Clearly, she’s going to have massive amounts of money. The difference is Mr. Trump has funded his campaign. What we’ve been able to do in this campaign cycle is to generate earned media based on Mr. Trump’s ability to be a straight talker, and genuine and authentic, and I think that’s what drives the news cycle." Trump's most recent allegations include a claim of rape against former President Bill Clinton from the 1970s and the 1993 suicide of an aide to the former president, events that Trump’s team connects to Hillary Clinton. An online video published by Trump features numerous women accusing the former president of rape or unwanted sexual advances, with Trump asserting that Clinton aided in silencing these women. The Clintons and their supporters have characterized these accusations as unfounded and politically motivated. Additionally, in a discussion with The Washington Post, Trump insinuated that the Clintons may have had a role in the 1993 death of Vince Foster, a former aide to Bill Clinton and a friend of Hillary Clinton, despite the fact that multiple investigations, including one by Republican special prosecutor Kenneth Starr, determined that Foster's death was a suicide in a Virginia park. Trump was referencing longstanding theories that have circulated in tabloids, on the internet, and in literature produced by the Clintons’ adversaries. On Wednesday, an email mistakenly sent by Trump’s campaign to a Politico reporter unveiled plans to launch future attacks on Clinton regarding the Whitewater real estate controversy that overshadowed Bill Clinton’s administration, despite no proven wrongdoing by the Clintons. These relentless attacks have put Clinton at a disadvantage. Republican pollster Kellyanne Conway noted, "Trump just continues to gobble news cycle after news cycle," highlighting that Clinton is devoting less time to future campaigning and more to explaining her past than she would likely prefer. This onslaught creates a challenging situation for Clinton. To date, she has chosen to overlook Trump’s personal assaults, with her campaign providing only generalized rebuttals. However, Clinton risks the potential fallout from this negative barrage impacting her public perception and damaging her prospects in the general election irreparably. Jim Manley, a Democratic strategist supporting Clinton, remarked, "I played a lot of hardball in my life, but I don’t envy what the Clinton campaign is up against here. Trump himself has totally changed the political dynamic. What they can’t afford to do is get in the gutter with the guy. He has absolutely no morals or scruples. Getting into the gutter with him is an absolute waste of time." Clinton’s campaign, along with the Super PACs that back her, will not find themselves without resources.
source_text: Trump, aiming to offset money disadvantage, escalates Clinton attacks. WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - Donald Trump this week took his use of sordid accusations against Democrat Hillary Clinton to levels unprecedented in modern U.S. presidential campaigns, in the latest example of the Republican’s unorthodox playbook. The presumptive Republican nominee is working to gain stronger footing and offset a big advantage Clinton is likely to have ahead of the Nov. 8 presidential election: a huge campaign war chest that she and her allies intend to use to launch a barrage of attacks against him.  Trump is using the same strategy he used repeatedly during the Republican nomination fight against rivals like Ted Cruz: making incendiary statements that U.S. television networks cannot resist covering, giving him hours of free media and putting his opponents on the defensive.  The strategy may already be working. Trump has raised more than a few eyebrows with his latest round of attacks against Clinton. He has turned history into headlines that play like a virtual reel in the 24-hour news world of cable TV and the internet. Trump’s campaign manager, Corey Lewandowski, said the strategy makes sense. “Clearly, she’s going to have massive amounts of money,” Lewandowski told Reuters. “The difference is Mr. Trump has funded his campaign. What we’ve been able to do in this campaign cycle is to generate earned media based on Mr. Trump’s ability to be a straight talker, and genuine and authentic, and I think that’s what drives the news cycle.” Trump’s latest salvos include a rape accusation against former President Bill Clinton dating to the 1970s and the suicide of an aide to the former president in 1993 - events that the campaign links to Hillary Clinton. An online video released by Trump has various women accusing the former president of rape or unwanted sexual advances. Trump accused Hillary Clinton of helping to silence the women. The Clintons and their supporters have dismissed the charges as baseless and politically motivated. Then, in an interview with The Washington Post, Trump suggested that the Clintons may have been involved in the 1993 death of Vince Foster, a former aide to Bill Clinton and a friend of Hillary Clinton, even though more than five investigations, including one conducted by Republican special prosecutor Kenneth Starr, concluded that Foster committed suicide in a Virginia park. Trump was alluding to theories over the years that have been circulated in tabloid publications, in the depths of the internet and in books by the Clintons’ foes. On Wednesday, Trump’s campaign accidentally sent an email to a reporter at Politico revealing that the Republican plans to next attack Clinton regarding Whitewater, a real estate scandal that plagued Bill Clinton’s administration. No wrongdoing by the Clintons was ever proven. The attacks have put Hillary Clinton on her back foot. Trump “just continues to gobble news cycle after news cycle,” said Republican pollster Kellyanne Conway, who ran the Super PACs that backed Senator Ted Cruz in the primary and aggressively attacked Trump. “Clinton is spending less time campaigning about the future and more time explaining the past than she would probably like.”  The barrage puts Clinton in a bind. So far, she has opted to ignore Trump’s personal attacks and her campaign has offered general pushback. But Clinton risks the negative onslaught dragging down her standing with the public and irreversibly damaging her general election hopes. “I played a lot of hardball in my life, but I don’t envy what the Clinton campaign is up against here. Trump himself has totally changed the political dynamic,” said Jim Manley, a Democratic strategist who supports Clinton. “What they can’t afford to do is get in the gutter with the guy. He has absolutely no morals or scruples. Getting into the gutter with him is an absolute waste of time.” Clinton’s campaign and the Super PACs supporting her will not be without funds to try to combat the attacks and launch her own. At the end of April, she had $30 million in her campaign account, compared with Trump’s $2 million.  And the PAC supporting her, which can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money, had $46 million at the end of April - a total that is likely to grow over the summer. The PAC backing Trump is just getting off the ground. Clinton will also depend on an army of surrogates to try to combat Trump without having to respond to him herself.  Trump has already proven he can dispatch opponents without spending much money by defining them to voters through aggressive appearances on news programs.  Republican rival Jeb Bush had a more than $100 million advantage going into the primary. But Trump painted him as “low energy” and defined him as inept, a characterization Bush’s money was never able to overcome. The PACs backing Republican Senators Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz spent millions assailing Trump. Trump was able to leverage extensive coverage of his campaign by the media to combat their attacks while spending little money on advertising. Trump has been proven an expert at raising attack lines that have already been settled, but insisting that questions remain. He spent years demanding that President Barack Obama produce his birth certificate, despite myriad evidence that Obama was born in Hawaii, including government records of the president’s birth in Honolulu. For Trump, some of the attacks are targeted at young voters - those in their early 20s and 30s were too young to have been immersed in news about the scandals of the Clinton years.   “You have a whole series of the population who either (a) don’t know anything about it, or (b) weren’t paying attention at the time,” Lewandowski said. A Clinton ally said Trump is simply trying to distract attention from his own liabilities - such as refusing to release his tax returns and his own history of problems with women. “The more he raises these outrageous and outlandish charges,” said U.S. Representative Xavier Becerra, of California, a Democratic leader in the House, “the more he keeps you pedaling in a different direction.”

text: The U.S. government has labeled the military actions in Myanmar against the Rohingya community as "ethnic cleansing." On Wednesday, the United States announced potential targeted sanctions against individuals accountable for the alleged "horrendous atrocities." U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson stated, "The situation in northern Rakhine state constitutes ethnic cleansing against the Rohingya," a term he refrained from using during his visit to Myanmar, also referred to as Burma, the previous week. He added that the U.S. would seek accountability under American law, which might include targeted sanctions against those involved in the alleged violations, leading to the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh. The shift in the U.S. position aims to increase pressure on both military and civilian authorities in Myanmar, who have been sharing power for two years under a fragile arrangement following decades of military dominance, to confront the ongoing crisis. Rights organizations have accused the Myanmar military of committing atrocities, such as killings, widespread sexual violence, and arson, against the stateless Rohingya during operations termed as clearance after attacks by Rohingya militants on 30 police stations and an army post on August 25. Since the onset of the crackdown, which was in response to the insurgent assaults, over 600,000 Rohingya Muslims have fled Rakhine state in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar, primarily seeking refuge in Bangladesh. Tillerson remarked, "These abuses by some among the Burmese military, security forces, and local vigilantes have caused tremendous suffering and forced hundreds of thousands of men, women, and children to flee their homes." While the U.S. has condemned the insurgents' attacks, Tillerson noted, "No provocation can justify the horrendous atrocities that have ensued." The government of Myanmar, led by Aung San Suu Kyi, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, has faced severe international backlash regarding its handling of the situation, even though it lacks control over the military leaders with whom it shares authority. A senior U.S. official mentioned during a conference call, "It’s not a situation that is completely under her authority, but certainly we are counting on her to show leadership and also to work through the civilian government with the military to address the crisis." The phrase "ethnic cleansing" does not have a formal definition in either international or U.S. law and does not inherently imply specific repercussions, a second senior U.S. official explained during the call. Murray Hiebert, an analyst focusing on Southeast Asia with the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, indicated that the State Department's application of the term and the threat of sanctions "will likely have limited to no impact on the ground." He further added, "It is likely to create more distrust between the United States and Myanmar’s military and government and push them closer to China, Russia, and its more authoritarian neighbors in Southeast Asia." The announcement by the U.S. coincided with a U.N. tribunal's conviction of former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic for genocide and crimes against humanity, resulting in a life sentence for his involvement in the massacres of Bosnian Muslims and ethnic cleansing campaigns. The second U.S. official stated that Washington was evaluating whether acts of genocide or crimes against humanity had transpired in Myanmar, which would breach international law, but no conclusions have been reached yet and it would require time for assessment. The official noted, "In the end it’s a court that has to decide that, as we’ve just seen with the verdict against Mladic." A senior U.N. official previously characterized the military's actions as a classic example of "ethnic cleansing," but the U.S. had, until Wednesday, avoided using this terminology. Washington has been attempting to balance its desire to support the civilian government in Myanmar, where it is competing with China for influence, with its goal of holding the military accountable for the reported abuses. U.S. officials are also concerned that the treatment of the Rohingya Muslim minority may exacerbate tensions.

Rights group Amnesty International called for a comprehensive arms embargo against Myanmar as well as targeted financial sanctions against senior Myanmar military officials.

text: SEOUL/TOKYO (Reuters) - Following North Korea's recent missile launch over Japan, military exercises involving two supersonic U.S. B-1B bombers took place above and around the Korean peninsula on Thursday, with participation from South Korean and Japanese aircraft. This show of force came just two days after North Korea increased tensions significantly by firing an intermediate-range missile. The operations included four U.S. stealth F-35B jets alongside fighter jets from both South Korea and Japan, marking the conclusion of the annual U.S.-South Korea military drills that primarily focused on computer-based simulations. General Terrence J. O’Shaughnessy, the Pacific Air Forces Commander, who unexpectedly visited Japan, remarked that North Korea’s actions pose a threat to our allies, partners, and homeland, emphasizing that their destabilizing behavior will be met with an appropriate response. He added that this intricate mission is a clear demonstration of solidarity with allies and highlights the expanding cooperation aimed at defending against a shared regional threat. North Korea has been striving to develop a missile capable of carrying a nuclear warhead to reach the United States, and has recently issued threats to launch missiles in proximity to the U.S. territory of Guam. Just this past Monday, North Korea, perceiving the military exercises as a pretext for invasion, escalated tensions with the United States and its allies by launching a missile over Japan. On Thursday, the state-run news agency KCNA condemned these military drills in a typically vigorous manner, labeling them as the reckless action of those startled by the missile test, which it referred to as the first military operation in the Pacific. President Donald Trump reacted to the missile test with anger, stating on Twitter that talking is not the answer to addressing the crisis surrounding North Korea’s weaponry. On Wednesday, U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis quickly emphasized that a diplomatic resolution was still a possibility, but on Thursday he communicated to reporters that he concurred with Trump’s stance that discussions with a nation launching missiles over Japan, an ally, should not occur at this time. During a regular Thursday briefing, White House spokesperson Sarah Sanders reiterated that all options—diplomatic, economic, and military—are available. Japanese Defence Minister Itsunori Onodera held a phone conversation with Mattis, agreeing to continue applying visible pressure on North Korea, as stated by Japan’s defense ministry. text: YANGON (Reuters) - On Friday, human rights organizations urged that international observers be permitted to oversee the anticipated repatriation of Rohingya Muslims, who have fled to Bangladesh over the last three months, as they return to Myanmar. A pact was signed on Thursday by the two nations, outlining the conditions for this repatriation process. The objective is to begin repatriating the Rohingya in two months to alleviate the strain on refugee camps that have significantly expanded in the Cox's Bazar area of Bangladesh. However, human rights advocates are skeptical about Myanmar, also known as Burma, adhering to the agreement and some have called for impartial monitors to be present. Bill Frelick, the refugee rights director at Human Rights Watch, remarked, "The notion that Burma will now embrace them back into their charred villages is absurd." He emphasized that rather than engaging in a public relations effort, the international community needs to assert that returns cannot occur without the presence of international monitors to guarantee safety, the cessation of placing returnees in camps, the restoration of land, and the reconstruction of devastated homes and villages. Over 600,000 Rohingya have sought refuge in Bangladesh after a severe counterinsurgency campaign was initiated by the military in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar, following assaults by Rohingya militants on an army installation and police stations on August 25. The actions of the military have been labeled as ethnic cleansing by both the United Nations and the United States, with rights organizations accusing the security forces of committing atrocities such as mass rapes, arson, and murders. China has provided support to Myanmar throughout this crisis and has obstructed a more robust international response. On Friday, Chinese President Xi Jinping discussed the situation in Beijing with Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar's army chief. Although Aung San Suu Kyi, the civilian leader of Myanmar, has stated that the repatriation of the largely stateless Muslim community would be based on residency and would be "safe and voluntary," concerns persist regarding potential interference from the country's autonomous military. The memorandum of understanding signed by Myanmar and Bangladesh on Thursday stipulated that a collaborative working group would be initiated within three weeks to prepare for the return of refugees. Nonetheless, it provided minimal information about the criteria for return and the role, if any, that the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) might have. According to spokesman Adrian Edwards, the UNHCR believes that the conditions in northern Rakhine are not conducive to enable the safe and sustainable return of the Rohingya, and some refugees are still escaping from Myanmar. He stated, "It is crucial that international standards are upheld, and we are prepared to assist," adding that the UNHCR has not yet reviewed the repatriation agreement signed by the two nations. Edwards further cautioned that it is vital to ensure that individuals do not end up being returned to confinement and ghettos. Human rights monitors indicated that significant issues were not addressed in the statements issued separately by the two governments, including the protection of the Rohingya against additional violence, a pathway to resolving their legal status, and whether they would be allowed to return to their previous homes. A spokesperson for Suu Kyi was not immediately reachable for comments on Friday and had previously declined to address these concerns when approached by Reuters late Thursday. Charmain Mohamed, the director for refugee and migrant rights at Amnesty International, asserted that the United Nations and the global community "have been completely sidelined," and described the discussions of return as "premature," especially while the flow of Rohingya refugees to Bangladesh continues. Meanwhile, China welcomed the agreement, expressing satisfaction with the positive progress made, according to Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Geng Shuang, who told reporters that the situation in Rakhine has "clearly improved." However, humanitarian workers caution that hundreds of Rohingya continue to flee.
