YANGON (Reuters) - Human rights groups called on Friday for international agencies to be allowed to monitor the planned repatriation of hundreds of thousands Rohingya Muslims from Bangladesh to the homes they have fled from in Myanmar over the past three months. The two governments signed a pact on Thursday settling terms for a repatriation process. They aim to start the return of Rohingya in two months in order to reduce pressure in the refugee camps that have mushroomed in the Cox s Bazar region of Bangladesh. But rights groups have expressed doubts about Myanmar, also known as Burma, following through on the agreement, and some have called for independent observers.  The idea that Burma will now welcome them back to their smoldering villages with open arms is laughable,  said Bill Frelick, refugee rights director at Human Rights Watch.  Instead of signing on to a public relations stunt, the international community should make it clear that there can be no returns without international monitors to ensure security, an end to the idea of putting returnees in camps, the return of land and the rebuilding of destroyed homes and villages.   More than 600,000 Rohingya sought sanctuary in Bangladesh after the military in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar launched a brutal counter insurgency across northern parts of Rakhine State following attacks by Rohingya militants on an army base and police posts on Aug. 25. The United Nations and United States have described the military s actions as ethnic cleansing, and rights groups have accused the security forces of atrocities, including mass rape, arson and killings.  China has backed Myanmar over the crisis and blocked a stronger international response, however. Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday discussed the issue in Beijing with Myanmar s army chief, Min Aung Hlaing. While Myanmar s civilian leader, Aung San Suu Kyi, has said repatriation of the largely stateless Muslim minority would be based on residency and would be  safe and voluntary , there were concerns that the country s autonomous military could prove obstructive. The memorandum of understanding signed by Myanmar and Bangladesh on Thursday said a joint working group would be set up within three weeks to prepare for the return of the refugees. But it gave scant details about the criteria of return and of what role, if any, the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, could play. The agency believed conditions in northern Rakhine  are not in place to enable safe and sustainable returns  of Rohingya and some refugees were still fleeing Myanmar, spokesman Adrian Edwards told reporters.  It is important that international standards apply, and we are ready to help,  he said, adding that the UNHCR had still not seen the repatriation agreement signed by the two countries.  It s important that people don t end up being sent back to confinement and ghettos.  Human rights monitors said other important points not addressed in the statements released separately by the two governments included the protection of Rohingya against further violence, a path to resolving their legal status and whether they would be allowed to return to their old homes. Suu Kyi s spokesman was not immediately available for comment on Friday, and had declined to comment on these concerns when contacted by Reuters late on Thursday. Charmain Mohamed, Amnesty International s director for refugee and migrant rights, said the United Nations and the international community  have been completely sidelined  and the talk of return was  premature  while the flow of Rohingya refugees to Bangladesh continued. China welcomed the agreement, saying it  feels gratified at the current positive progress that has been achieved , Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Geng Shuang told reporters, adding that situation in Rakhine  has obviously been alleviated . Humanitarian workers say, however, that hundreds of Rohingya are arriving in Bangladesh daily, driven out of Myanmar predominantly by chaos, starvation and fear. While the violence has mostly ceased, Rohingya say they have largely lost access to sources of livelihood such as their farms, fisheries and markets.   We will go back if they don t harass us and if we can live life like the Buddhists and other ethnic groups. Our educated children should get government jobs like the others,  said Sayer Hussein, 55, who arrived in Bangladesh two months ago.  Thousands of Rohingya, most of them old people, women and children, are stranded on beaches near the border, waiting for a boat to take them to Bangladesh. Some independent estimates suggest there could still be a few hundred thousand Rohingya in Rakhine State. Thirty-six groups, including the International Commission of Jurists and Amnesty International, called for a U.N. Human Rights Council special session on the situation in Myanmar.  Myanmar should  immediately cease all human rights violations, including crimes against humanity , the groups said in an open letter to the U.N. council.

text: BAGHDAD (Reuters) - On Thursday, Iraqi forces declared that they had seized the last bastion of the Islamic State in northern Iraq, forcing the extremist group to retreat towards the Syrian border as its self-declared caliphate continues to diminish. The offensive, which targeted the town of Hawija and its surrounding regions, was conducted by U.S.-supported Iraqi government troops alongside Shiite paramilitary units known as Popular Mobilisation, which are trained and equipped by Iran. Some clashes occurred in the northern and eastern parts of the town where the militants were encircled. Following the capture of Hawija, located near the oil-rich Kurdish city of Kirkuk, the only territory in Iraq still under Islamic State's control is a strip along the western border with Syria, where the group is also facing setbacks. The takeover of Hawija marked a significant gain for the Iraqi administration, which is grappling with a separate crisis in northern Iraq, where the Kurdish population overwhelmingly endorsed independence for their autonomous region in a recent vote. In Hawija, state television broadcasted footage showing Iraqi forces hoisting flags in a town square while Humvees patrolled the deserted streets, which were strewn with vehicle wrecks, houses pockmarked with bullet holes, and shattered storefronts. The 9th armored division of the army, the Federal Police, the Emergency Response division, and Popular Mobilisation played crucial roles in liberating Hawija, according to a statement from the joint operations commander, Lieutenant-General Abdul Ameer Rasheed Yarallah. Dense black smoke billowed from areas surrounding Hawija due to oil wells set ablaze by the militants to avoid aerial detection. The recapture of Hawija places Iraqi forces in direct contact with Kurdish Peshmerga fighters who control Kirkuk, a diverse area claimed by both Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG). Last month, Kirkuk became a potential flashpoint when the KRG included it in the independence referendum for northern Iraq. "We do not desire any hostility or confrontations, but it is essential for federal authority to be established in the disputed areas," stated Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi during a press conference in Paris alongside French President Emmanuel Macron. Macron extended an offer to mediate between the Iraqi government and Kurdish regional authorities, pledging to maintain military presence until the defeat of the Islamic State. Following the independence vote, the Iraqi government enacted sanctions; however, Abadi expressed that he could comprehend the Kurdish aspirations, provided they were articulated in line with the constitution. The results of the referendum have sparked worries both domestically and internationally about the potential for conflict along ethnic lines in Iraq, which could undermine efforts to combat the Islamic State. Turkey, facing its own long-standing strife with Kurdish militants, has emerged as a vocal opponent of the Iraqi Kurds' aspirations for independence. President Tayyip Erdogan intensified his rhetoric regarding the issue, announcing that Turkey would soon close its border with northern Iraq and restrict its air space in reaction to the referendum. He also indicated that a collaborative decision regarding the cessation of oil exports from northern Iraq, a critical revenue source for Iraqi Kurdistan, would be made by Turkey, Iran, and Iraq. In a statement made on Wednesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose nation has significant energy interests in Kurdistan, remarked that it would not benefit anyone to halt oil supplies from the region. Nonetheless, Erdogan asserted that if a resolution on ceasing oil exports is reached, it will be determined by Turkey. The stance taken by Erdogan has received support from Iran. After meeting with Erdogan in Tehran on Wednesday, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei stated that Iran and Turkey should work together to prevent the Iraqi Kurds from pursuing independence. Although relations between predominantly Sunni Turkey and Shiite Iran have been cool, both countries have expressed alarm over the independence vote, fearing the repercussions it may entail.

text: On Tuesday, Israel's Supreme Court annulled a law that allowed Jewish religious seminary students to be exempt from military service, prompting backlash from ultra-Orthodox politicians, who may threaten the stability of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition government. A panel consisting of nine justices determined that certain provisions of the conscription law, which exempted seminary students, were unreasonable and violated constitutional principles. The court has provided the government with a year to address the ruling. For many years, the exemption for seminary students based on religious beliefs has led to tensions within Israeli society, where the majority of Jewish individuals are drafted into military service upon reaching the age of 18. The ultra-Orthodox community argues that their dedication to studying the Torah is essential for the enduring existence of the Jewish people. They also express concerns that young men serving in the military might encounter women and less devout segments of society. Nonetheless, several hundred ultra-Orthodox individuals have volunteered for specialized military units that accommodate their religious observances. In 2014, legislation was passed to establish new guidelines to replace those that had previously lapsed. This move was driven by Yair Lapid's secular and centrist Yesh Atid party, which campaigned on the idea of sharing the national responsibility. Consequently, this law upset ultra-Orthodox parties, who re-entered Netanyahu's government in 2015 when Lapid's party became part of the opposition, ultimately leading to a dilution of the law's provisions. Of the nine justices, eight agreed that the law should be abolished, with Supreme Court President Miriam Naor stating that the latest agreement made to satisfy the ultra-Orthodox parties significantly undermines equality and infringes on the constitutional right to human dignity. Since the establishment of Israel in 1948, ultra-Orthodox representatives have actively opposed the conscription of their community members, who constitute approximately 10 percent of Israel's total population of 9 million. Netanyahu's administration, which holds 67 out of 120 Knesset seats, includes ultra-Orthodox factions, but two other significant political groups resist any further easing of the conscription laws. In response to the court's decision, Interior Minister Aryeh Deri, the head of the ultra-Orthodox Shas party, criticized the justices as being entirely disconnected from the heritage, traditions, and sentiments of the populace. He urged seminary students to persist in their Biblical studies, declaring, "Do not despair, continue to study the Torah, we will stand firm and will do everything to fix this situation." Lapid, who is viewed by opinion polls as a potential rival to Netanyahu in upcoming elections, called a press conference to commend the court's ruling, asserting that it had issued a judgment that would enforce equality among different communities. "This is why we have come to politics. Conscription for everybody, work for everybody. Benjamin Netanyahu can no longer continue to wriggle out all the time. Military conscription is for everybody, not only for the suckers who don't have a party in his coalition," Lapid emphasized.

Initial findings would be released within about 10 days, Darusman said. Myanmar s ambassador Htin Lynn told the Council that Myanmar was making efforts to restore peace, law and order.  Proportionate security measures targeted only on terrorists are being taken to safeguard our state security, and to restore law and order,  he said.  We continue to believe that instituting such a mission is not a helpful course of action in solving the already intricate Rakhine issue with daunting challenges.

text: Fiscal analysts indicated on Wednesday that the tax plan proposed by U.S. President Donald Trump will drive economic growth, but that growth will fall significantly short of compensating for the trillions in revenue losses. They warned that increasing deficits might even negate some of the economic benefits anticipated from the plan. The core tenets of the proposal, which were disclosed on Wednesday, depend largely on a technique known as "dynamic scoring." This budget analysis approach presumes that tax reductions will enhance economic activity, resulting in increased revenues. These assumptions have formed the foundation of Republican tax policy since Ronald Reagan employed them to rationalize extensive tax cuts in 1981, which critics at that time labeled as "voodoo economics." Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin stated on Wednesday that the plan would "pay for itself with growth" and through the elimination of certain deductions and credits. However, Maya MacGuineas, who is the president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB), noted that the plan could lead to an increase in the federal deficit by between $3 trillion and $5 trillion over the course of five years. "No credible dynamic score is going to show that this bill is paid for," MacGuineas asserted. She added that while the growth effects are genuine and significant, they would only contribute fractions of percentage points to overall growth, rather than whole percentage points. According to her group's analysis, for the tax plan to be fully funded, the U.S. economy would need to maintain a growth rate of 4.5 percent each year, a level that has not been achieved consistently since the late 1960s and early 1970s. Mnuchin has predicted that the plan will elevate U.S. growth rates beyond 3 percent; however, CRFB's projections suggest that even reaching this benchmark would necessitate substantial productivity gains, while an aging baby-boom cohort works against high growth rates. Doug Elmendorf, who previously directed the Congressional Budget Office, an agency responsible for providing cost estimates for legislation, expressed skepticism regarding Congress's ability to discover "politically acceptable" offsets to finance the plan. He cautioned that rising borrowing could counteract Trump's objectives. Elmendorf, who is currently the dean of Harvard's John F. Kennedy School of Government, remarked, "The resultant rise in the deficit will dampen economic activity, offsetting at least some of the stimulative impacts of reduced tax rates." He explained that an increased federal debt burden would "crowd out" available capital for private investment, suppressing long-term economic activity. Congressional Republicans aim to exploit budgetary procedural regulations that permit a 51-vote threshold in the Senate to pass tax reforms, which would confine the cuts to a decade. However, should the plan incur deficits in the years following the first ten years, it might violate another procedural rule that could necessitate a 60-vote approval in the Senate. Temporary tax cuts that lapse after a decade could potentially trigger another fiscal emergency similar to the one experienced in 2012, when tax reductions enacted under George W. Bush came to an end. Chris Krueger, a political analyst at Cowen and Co in Washington, conveyed in a client note, "What the Trump Administration has suggested is not a permanent tax reform but a ten-year tax cut that would create an unprecedented fiscal cliff in 2028."
source_text: Trump U.S. tax plan will not manage to pay for itself with growth: experts. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump’s tax-cut plan will generate growth, but not nearly enough to replace trillions of dollars in lost revenues, while rising deficits could even take back some of the economic gains, fiscal experts said on Wednesday. Core principles of the plan, unveiled on Wednesday, rely heavily on so-called “dynamic scoring,” a budget analysis method that assumes tax cuts will boost economic activity, thus generating more revenues. Such assumptions have been at the heart of Republican tax orthodoxy since Ronald Reagan used them to justify massive tax cuts in 1981 that were derided at the time by critics as “voodoo economics.” On Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin said Trump’s plan would “pay for itself with growth” and closing of some deductions and credits.  From the details released so far, Maya MacGuineas, who heads the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB), said the plan could add $3 trillion to more than $5 trillion to the federal deficit over five years. “No credible dynamic score is going to show that this bill is paid for,” MacGuineas said. “The growth effects, which are real and important, add decimals of percentage points to growth, not full percentage points.” Her budget watchdog group estimates that to pay for the plan, U.S. growth would need to be sustained at 4.5 percent annually, a level not seen on a sustained basis since the late 1960s and early 1970s. Mnuchin has said that he expects the plan to boost sustained U.S. growth above 3 percent, but CRFB estimates that even this level would require massive increases in productivity and that a rapidly retiring baby-boom generation is working against high growth rates. Doug Elmendorf, former director of the Congressional Budget Office, one of the agencies that provides cost estimates for legislation, said he sees little chance of Congress finding “politically acceptable” offsets to pay for the plan, and the rise in borrowing could work against Trump’s goals. “The resulting increase of the deficit will have a dampening effect on the economic activity that will offset at least part of the stimulative effects of lower tax rates,” said Elemendorf, now dean of Harvard University’s John F. Kennedy School of Government. The higher federal debt load will “crowd out” capital for private use, dampening economic activity in the long run, Elmendorf said. Republicans in Congress are hoping to use budget procedural rules that allow a 51-vote threshold in the Senate to pass tax reform, which would limit the cuts to 10 years.  But if the plan creates deficits in the years beyond the first decade, it could also run afoul of another procedural rule that could require 60 votes in the Senate.    Tax cuts that expire in a decade could cause another U.S. fiscal crisis like the one in 2012, when tax cuts passed under George W. Bush expired. “What the Trump Administration has proposed is not permanent tax reform, but a ten-year tax cut and the creation of the most phenomenal fiscal cliff ever in 2028,” Chris Krueger, a political analyst at Cowen and Co in Washington, said in a note to clients.

text: A potential U.S. exit could unexpectedly benefit the global climate accord, according to supporters. OSLO (Reuters) - The 2015 international agreement aimed at addressing climate change may actually gain some advantages if U.S. President Donald Trump follows through on his threat to withdraw, indicating a shift from initial pessimism regarding the future of a pact that took two decades to finalize. The Paris Agreement requires that all decisions be made by consensus, so if the United States, which has been resistant, were to withdraw, it could simplify the process for major emitters like China and the European Union to outline the specifics of a trillion-dollar transition away from fossil fuels. Trump has labeled human-induced climate change a fabrication and has yet to fulfill his campaign promise to "cancel" the agreement, asserting that he aims to support the domestic fossil fuel sector. In an effort to roll back environmental regulations established by former President Barack Obama, Trump is set to sign an executive order on Tuesday that seeks to facilitate energy production within the United States. "If the U.S. ultimately decides to withdraw from Paris, there will be some benefits for other countries, but there will also be significant drawbacks," stated Christiana Figueres, a key figure behind the agreement and the U.N.’s climate chief during the Paris negotiations. "It's not simply a black-and-white situation," she noted. Figueres emphasized that the best scenario, for both the U.S. and other countries, would involve Washington remaining in the agreement and implementing substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. She mentioned that investment opportunities in renewable energy sources, particularly solar energy, are more promising than those related to coal. Concerns have persisted that the withdrawal of the world’s leading economy could diminish the motivation of other countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions under an accord endorsed by a diverse range of nations including China, Saudi Arabia, and various African countries. However, a contrasting perspective is emerging that suggests the Paris Agreement could potentially be strengthened. "The fundamental weakness of the Paris Agreement is its reliance on consensus," remarked Johan Rockstrom, director of the Stockholm Resilience Center at Stockholm University. "Having a major detractor in the room complicates decision-making," he added, indicating that his views have shifted in recent weeks towards believing that a U.S. exit might actually yield better outcomes, contrary to his previous opinion that it would signify a "major setback." The Paris Agreement features minimal binding commitments, allowing every nation to establish its own targets for addressing climate change without penalties for failing to comply. Countries have set a 2018 deadline to finalize a rulebook for the Paris Agreement, which will elaborate on how nations should monitor and report their efforts to limit emissions. Thoriq Ibrahim, the Environment Minister of Maldives and chair of the Alliance of Small Island States, whose members are particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels, advocated for continued U.S. involvement in the Paris Agreement. "Upon closer inspection, it becomes evident that the Paris Agreement also offers significant strategic, economic, and security advantages," he stated. Norwegian Prime Minister Erna Solberg expressed her belief that it would be preferable for the United States to remain part of the accord. "Nevertheless, I don’t believe the Paris Agreement would collapse if the United States chooses to exit," she remarked. Oliver Geden, affiliated with the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, argued against this perspective. He asserted that a U.S. withdrawal would severely weaken the Paris Agreement, rendering any decisions largely futile without the participation of the world's largest economy. "The momentum could diminish quite rapidly," he foresaw. Yet, nearly 200 nations agreed following Trump’s election in November that there exists an "urgent duty" to tackle an "alarming and unprecedented" speed of global warming. "The rate and scale of change that is already taking place within the global economy is extraordinary and irreversible," remarked Stephanie Pfeifer, who leads the Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change, a consortium managing assets worth 18 trillion euros ($20 trillion). "Renewable energy sources have already surpassed coal as a global power generation method, and electric vehicles are emerging as a key growth area.
source_text: Threatened U.S. pullout might help, not hobble, global climate pact.  OSLO (Reuters) - A 2015 global pact for fighting climate change will benefit in some ways at least if U.S. President Donald Trump carries out a threat to pull out, backers say, in a shift from gloom about the fate of a deal that took two decades to negotiate.  The Paris Agreement requires consensus for all decisions, meaning the withdrawal of a recalcitrant United States would make it easier for emitters such as China and the European Union to design details of a trillion-dollar shift from fossil fuels.  Trump has called man-made climate change a hoax and made a so-far unfulfilled campaign pledge to “cancel” the agreement, saying he wants to promote the domestic fossil fuel industry.  In a step to undo environmental regulations introduced under former President Barack Obama, Trump will sign an order on Tuesday aimed at making it easier for companies to produce energy in the United States.  “There will be some advantages for other countries and there will also be extraordinary disadvantages,” if the U.S. ends up quitting Paris, said Christiana Figueres, an architect of the agreement who was the U.N.’s climate chief in Paris.  “It’s not a black and white scenario,” she said.  She said the ideal outcome, both for the United States and other nations, was for Washington to stay and make deep cuts in greenhouse gas emissions. There were better investment prospects for renewable energies such as solar power than coal, she added.  The fear has long been that a pullout of the world’s top economy would drain other nations’ willingness to cut greenhouse gas emissions under an agreement ratified by nations as diverse as China, Saudi Arabia and African countries.  But there is an emerging rival view that Paris might be better off.  “The Achilles heel of the Paris Agreement is that it’s built on consensus,” said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Stockholm Resilience Center at Stockholm University.  “It’s very difficult to have a negative giant in the room” able to obstruct all decisions, he said, adding that he had swung in recent weeks to reckon that a U.S. pullout would be better overall from an earlier view that it would be a “big failure”.  The Paris Agreement has few binding obligations. It lets all nations set their own goals for fighting climate change and has no penalties for non-compliance.  Governments have set a 2018 deadline to work out a rule book for the Paris Agreement, filling in details, for instance, of how nations will report and monitor their curbs on emissions.  Maldives Environment Minister Thoriq Ibrahim - chair of the Alliance of Small Island States whose members fear they are at risk from rising sea levels - urged continued U.S. participation in Paris.  “The closer you look at it, the clearer it becomes that it (the Paris Agreement) also promotes important strategic, economic, and security benefits as well,” he said.  Norwegian Prime Minister Erna Solberg also said it would be better for the United States to stay. “But I don’t think that it’s the end of the Paris Agreement if the United States decides to leave,” she said.  Oliver Geden, of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, disagreed. A U.S. withdrawal would badly undermine the Paris Agreement and any decisions would be largely irrelevant without the world’s biggest economy, he said. “The momentum could fade away pretty soon,” he predicted.  Still, almost 200 nations agreed after Trump’s election in November that the world had an “urgent duty” to combat an “alarming and unprecedented” rate of global warming.  “The pace and scale of change already underway in the global economy is remarkable and irreversible,” said Stephanie Pfeifer, head of the Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change, a forum with 18 trillion euros ($20 trillion) in assets under management.  “Renewables have already overtaken coal as a global power source, electric vehicles are the growth segment of the auto industry and jobs are being created very rapidly in clean energy,” she said.  The U.S. target under Paris, set by Obama, is to cut emissions by between 26 and 28 percent below 2005 levels by 2025 as part of global efforts to avert more downpours, droughts, heatwaves and floods.  Trump’s pro-coal policies are likely to make U.S. emissions cuts less ambitious.  By staying in the Paris Agreement, Trump would also undermine a demand in its Article 4 that successive national climate plans have to be ever deeper cuts. A U.S. pullout would make it easier for backers to argue that the principle has not been violated.  The Paris Agreement sets an over-riding goal of limiting global warming to “well below” two degrees Celsius (3.6 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times. The United Nations says that current pledges are insufficient to meet that goal.  ($1 = 0.9179 euros)

text: Late on Thursday, Senate Republicans introduced their "skinny repeal" bill aimed at dismantling certain aspects of the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare. This move came just hours prior to a scheduled vote on the proposed legislation. Numerous Republican senators indicated they were hesitant to endorse the eight-page document until they received guarantees from House Speaker Paul Ryan that a special committee could be established to draft new legislative proposals. According to Senate Republican leaders, the purpose of the bill is to uphold the long-standing commitment to repeal and replace Obamacare, a promise that has been a key part of President Donald Trump's campaign platform. Earlier that week, the Senate was unable to pass two significant bills designed to either repeal or replace the healthcare law after months of deliberation on the proposals. The Affordable Care Act has provided insurance coverage to 20 million Americans who were previously uninsured and is regarded as the hallmark domestic achievement of former President Barack Obama, a Democrat. Critics from the Republican side argue that the law is excessively expensive and represents an inappropriate level of government involvement in healthcare. The "skinny" repeal bill, officially named the Health Care Freedom Act, includes several provisions: it eliminates the penalty imposed on individuals who fail to obtain health insurance under Obamacare. Additionally, it repeals a penalty for employers with over 50 staff who do not offer health insurance for an eight-year period. Furthermore, the legislation abolishes a 2.3 percent excise tax on sales of medical devices, which would remain in effect until December 31, 2020. Should it become law, this repeal would be positively received by companies like Medtronic Inc and Abbott Laboratories Inc. The Senate bill also effectively cuts off funding for Planned Parenthood for one year by barring Medicaid, the health insurance program for low-income and disabled individuals, from reimbursing the organization that provides women's health services. The majority of Planned Parenthood's clientele are Medicaid beneficiaries. In contrast to earlier legislative efforts aimed at repealing or replacing Obamacare, this skinny bill does not terminate the Medicaid expansion or alter the federal health program.
source_text: Factbox: What's in the Senate's 'skinny repeal' healthcare bill. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Senate Republicans released their “skinny bill” that would repeal some of Obamacare late on Thursday, just hours before they were expected to vote on the legislation. Many Republican lawmakers said they did not want the eight-page bill to become law, and held off supporting it until they received assurances from House of Representatives Speaker Paul Ryan that members of both chambers could set up a special committee that would craft new legislation.  Senate Republican leaders said the bill was simply a way to keep alive the seven-year promise to repeal and replace Obamacare, which was also a top campaign promise from President Donald Trump. The Senate failed to pass two major bills earlier in the week that would repeal or replace the healthcare law after spending months on both pieces of legislation.  The Affordable Care Act, known informally as Obamacare, brought insurance to 20 million previously uninsured Americans and was the signature domestic achievement of former Democratic President Barack Obama. Republicans say the law is too costly and represents undue government interference in healthcare.  Here’s what’s in the “skinny” repeal bill, formally called the Health Care Freedom Act:  The bill repeals an Obamacare penalty on individuals who do not purchase health insurance. It also repeals a penalty for eight years on employers with more than 50 employees that do not provide health insurance.  The legislation repeals a 2.3 percent excise tax on medical device sales, until Dec. 31, 2020. If it were to become law, this repeal would be welcome news to manufacturers such as Medtronic Inc and Abbott Laboratories Inc.  The Senate bill effectively defunds Planned Parenthood for one year by prohibiting Medicaid, the government health insurance program for the poor and disabled, from reimbursing the women’s healthcare provider. The majority of Planned Parenthood patients are on Medicaid.  Unlike previous attempts to craft legislation to repeal or replace Obamacare, the skinny bill does not end the law’s Medicaid expansion or make changes to the federal health program.

text: In a display of allegiance, Boris Johnson provided unsolicited guidance to Prime Minister Theresa May regarding Brexit on Tuesday, while subtly probing the boundaries of her diminished authority. As the Conservative Party Conference unfolded in Manchester, Johnson made public declarations of support for May, simultaneously utilizing media interviews and articles to articulate his own vision for a dynamic Brexit. He commended May for her ability in the snap election of June, an election that resulted in a loss of her party's parliamentary majority, before asserting in his keynote address that her senior ministers were completely aligned with every word of her Brexit proposals presented the previous month in Florence. "The entire nation owes her a debt for her determination in advancing Britain, as she will, toward an excellent Brexit agreement, which is grounded in that Florence address, and on whose every word, I assure you, the entire cabinet stands united," Johnson remarked. However, just a few hours later, the figure who spearheaded the prominent leave campaign during the 2016 referendum concerning Britain's EU membership addressed activists at a different gathering, expressing that there was excessive negativity surrounding Brexit. He proceeded to outline his own perspectives on the future of Britain's departure and suggested that the nation might require distinct regulations across various sectors, including data and bioscience. "I ran my campaign with the slogan... Take Back Control.... I believe the prime minister shares this strong conviction as well," Johnson stated to the audience. "If you are going to undertake this, execute it properly. It must be done in a manner that achieves a favorable outcome for the UK," he added. "We seek an arrangement that does not confine us to a rigid rotational orbit around the EU." Johnson, who is often seen in Britain as harboring significant political ambitions beneath a comical façade, has managed to eclipse the party conference that May intended to utilize for regaining some of her lost authority following her electoral miscalculation. Sporting his signature tousled blonde hair and rifling through his suit jacket pocket, Boris energized Conservative Party members while being cautious not to make a direct appeal to succeed May. Prior to Johnson’s address, May had been consistently confronted with inquiries from journalists about whether she would dismiss Johnson, following his apparent undermining of her Brexit strategy with his own articulated vision. She has avoided answering those queries. On the same day, the European Parliament criticized the British government’s management of Brexit negotiations, voting against initiating discussions on future trade and condemning the chaos within May’s administration. A German ally of conservative Chancellor Angela Merkel, Manfred Weber, remarked that the infighting within the British cabinet jeopardized a potential deal and urged May to dismiss Johnson. Nevertheless, Johnson also injected a rare vigor into Manchester, where Conservative ministers lined up to portray the opposing Labour Party as perilous Marxists, while failing to present any notably new policies. "To me, that was true leadership: motivating and inspiring. What defines a good leader? It’s someone who can achieve that," stated Vanessa Churchman, a local government official from the Isle of Wight in southern England. "Everyone leaving here will feel inspired." In earlier party conferences, Boris, as he is commonly referred to in Britain, similarly stole the limelight from then-prime minister David Cameron. However, after the referendum derailed Cameron’s political career, Johnson withdrew from the leadership contest when a colleague breached a pact to support him. Although Johnson enjoys popularity among party members, numerous Conservative lawmakers are frustrated that he has overshadowed May with what they describe as detrimental and disloyal remarks. May, the composed daughter of a clergyman, possesses a presentational style that starkly contrasts with Johnson’s flamboyant persona on stage. She is scheduled to conclude the conference on Wednesday.

text: The White House criticized Russia on Wednesday for its veto that halted a United Nations initiative aimed at extending an investigation into Syria's use of chemical weapons, which had recently determined that Syria killed numerous individuals with such weapons. Eight days prior, Russia exercised its veto power at the United Nations Security Council, obstructing the renewal of a mandate for the Joint Investigative Mechanism (JIM), a collaborative effort between the United Nations and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) tasked with examining chemical weapon incidents in Syria. In a statement, the White House condemned Russia's actions, stating that its efforts to dismantle the JIM reflect a shocking indifference to the pain and fatalities resulting from chemical weapon usage, as well as a profound disrespect for global standards. According to a report submitted to the United Nations Security Council last Thursday, the investigative body concluded that the Syrian administration led by Bashar al-Assad was responsible for a chemical assault on Khan Sheikhoun, an area held by opposition forces, which resulted in the deaths of dozens last April. The White House remarked that this reprehensible incident represents the fourth occasion on which the JIM has confirmed the Assad regime's deployment of chemical weapons, highlighting the extreme cruelty and barbarism of Bashar al-Assad and making Russia's support for him even more outrageous. text: On Wednesday, at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate, an event unfolded that brought together two elderly Holocaust survivors and a younger Israeli vocalist, who performed uplifting songs amidst a backdrop of rising anti-Semitism in Germany. Saul Dreier, a 92-year-old drummer, and Reuwen "Ruby" Sosnowicz, an 89-year-old accordion player, accompanied Gad Elbaz at a location historically significant for its use by Adolf Hitler for promoting anti-Jewish rhetoric. After a day filled with deep emotions, Dreier expressed his feelings to Reuters, stating, "I don’t want to cry. If I can be 92 and be here after what I went through - there are no words." Prior to the performance, he shared with an audience of approximately 80 that he had lost 30 family members during the Holocaust. Dreier also conveyed his distress over recent neo-Nazi demonstrations occurring in both the United States and Germany, which he found to be nauseating and reminiscent of the atrocities committed by the Nazi regime, which resulted in the deaths of 6 million Jews. He remarked, "It’s very frightening. Young people have to make sure it never happens again." Both Dreier and Sosnowicz, residing in Florida, established their "Holocaust Survivors Band" in 2014, and since then, they have performed for enthusiastic crowds in various cities, including Warsaw, Las Vegas, and Washington, D.C. Elbaz emphasized the importance of the Berlin event, stating that it aimed to encourage the younger generation to stay alert to the threats posed by anti-Semitism. "This is about reviving history and showing our generation how important it is not to forget where we came from, what we’ve been through, and that it should never happen again," he articulated. The organizers intend to produce a music video featuring footage from their performance of the song, "Let the Light Shine On." Shani Ramer, a 48-year-old resident of Berlin who was born in Israel, expressed that the concert was a poignant reminder of her family members who had lost their lives. "It touched my heart," she stated, appreciating the concert's hopeful message. "It’s saying we are still here. No one will kill us now." Abida Ali, a Muslim visitor from Pakistan, was among the audience members who danced to the lively tunes. Despite wearing a headscarf, Ali reported that she had encountered no discrimination during her stay in Germany. "It’s only a small percentage of the people who are violent," she noted. "There is hope. Everyone really wants peace." A recent study conducted by Bielefeld University revealed that 78 percent of Jews in Germany feel that anti-Semitism has escalated either to some degree or significantly over the past five years.

text: The European Union is engaged in negotiations regarding the terms of the United Kingdom's departure, and they are doing so in good faith, according to Donald Tusk, the chairman of EU leaders. He stated on Tuesday that there is currently no consideration being given to a scenario in which an agreement is not reached. The UK is eager to begin discussions promptly about the future relationship it will have with the EU, which includes a transitional phase following its exit in March 2019. However, the EU insists that negotiations concerning this future relationship cannot commence until both London and Brussels finalize the details of the separation, which encompass citizens' rights, border concerns in Northern Ireland, and notably, the financial obligations the UK has towards the EU. Tusk remarked in a speech delivered in Brussels that there have been indications from London suggesting the UK government is preparing for a 'no deal' situation. He emphasized that the EU is not pursuing such a scenario. "We are negotiating in good faith, and we still hope that sufficient progress will be achievable by December," he added. Nonetheless, he cautioned that if discussions proceed slowly and sufficient progress is not achieved, then together with the UK, they will need to reflect on the direction of the negotiations.
source_text: EU not working on 'no deal' scenario for Brexit. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - The European Union is negotiating the terms of Britain s exit from the bloc in good faith and is not working on a scenario where there is no agreement on the separation, the chairman of EU leaders Donald Tusk said on Tuesday. Britain is keen to start negotiating as quickly as possible the terms of its future relationship with the EU, including a transition period, after it leaves the bloc in March 2019.  But the EU does not want to start such negotiating until London and Brussels agree the terms of the divorce - citizen s rights, border issues in Northern Ireland and, crucially, how much money Britain owes the EU.  We hear from London that the UK government is preparing for a  no deal  scenario. I would like to say very clearly that the EU is not working on such a scenario,  European Council President Tusk said in a speech in Brussels.  We are negotiating in good faith, and we still hope that the so-called  sufficient progress  will be possible by December. However, if it turns out that the talks continue at a slow pace, and that sufficient progress hasn t been reached, then   together with our UK friends   we will have to think about where we are heading,  he said.

text: NEW YORK (Reuters) - The fiscal overseer of New York City has indicated that the city is likely to face significantly larger budget shortfalls in the upcoming years than those projected by the mayor, and he cautioned state legislators against viewing the city as a mere 'piggy bank.' As the state works to finalize its budget, decisions that will impact New York City are imminent. 'Some legislators from upstate simply don’t understand the situation,' stated New York City Comptroller Scott Stringer during a Wednesday assessment of the city’s financial plan. 'They regard New York City as their personal piggy bank.' Stringer expressed concerns over hasty, late-night budget decisions that might rob the city of vital funds. His remarks illustrate a rising exasperation with state officials who imply that the city possesses excessive funds following a more robust economic recovery compared to other regions in the state. Tensions have existed between New York State Governor Andrew Cuomo and New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio, particularly after Cuomo convinced the fellow Democrat to allocate $2.5 billion for the city’s public transit system, managed by the state agency Metropolitan Transportation Authority, last year. Discussions in the state capital have also hinted at the city needing to contribute more towards healthcare expenses and support for the local university system. Known for their 'vampire' budget sessions, New York State legislators often work into the early hours to meet the budget deadline that coincides with the start of the state’s fiscal year on April 1. Stringer pointed out that while next year’s budget remains in balance, the projected financial gaps leading up to the fiscal year 2020 exceed the mayor’s estimates by $1 billion. 'Budget monitors and rating agencies have commended this administration’s careful financial management and commitment to safeguarding against economic instability – and investors concur,' remarked Amy Spitalnick, a representative for de Blasio. The mayor’s office highlights that Stringer anticipates an extra $900 million in tax revenue for the current and next financial year, which they present as an illustration of their prudent revenue forecasts. Stringer criticized the mayor for factoring in $731 million from taxi medallion sales through 2020, arguing that the taxi industry is currently facing turmoil. Although the city has already lowered its expectations for revenue from taxi medallion transactions, Stringer has advocated for a more aggressive removal of this assumption in future financial forecasts. Additionally, he asserted that certain taxes may be lower than what the mayor predicts, while expenses related to overtime, healthcare, and homeless shelters are likely to be higher.

text: On Wednesday, President Barack Obama announced his nomination of Merrick Garland to the U.S. Supreme Court, aiming to appeal to Senate Republicans who have shown reluctance in the past. The selection of Garland, a centrist judge, has already sparked a significant political battle, likely affecting the race for the U.S. presidential election on November 8. Leaders of the Senate, which is controlled by the Republicans, have declared they will not conduct confirmation hearings or allow an up-or-down vote on any nominee from Obama. Garland, who is 63 years old, will take the place of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia, who passed away on February 13. Like Obama, Garland hails from Chicago and currently serves as the chief judge on the prominent U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. He has a history as a prosecutor and has garnered respect from both political parties. In a bid to push for Senate approval, the administration is sending Garland to meet with Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont, the leading Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, as well as with Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid from Nevada. These discussions are intended to strengthen support for Garland within the Senate and create media attention around the nomination. Senate confirmation is essential for the lifetime appointment to the Supreme Court. Following Obama's announcement, various private organizations reacted quickly, either supporting or opposing the nomination. The United Auto Workers (UAW), representing workers in the automotive, aerospace, and some agricultural sectors, referred to Garland as 'a distinguished, moderate judge with more federal judicial experience than any other Supreme Court nominee in history.' Conversely, Chris Cox, the Executive Director of the National Rifle Association, remarked, 'An analysis of Merrick Garland’s judicial record reveals that he does not respect our fundamental, individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense.' Republican senators, who are looking to see a member of their party win the presidency, are insisting that Obama should leave the Supreme Court seat open and allow the next president, to be inaugurated next January, to make the appointment. Currently, billionaire businessman Donald Trump is the frontrunner among Republican candidates, while Hillary Clinton, Obama’s former Secretary of State, leads the Democratic field. Obama emphasized the necessity for Republican senators to provide Garland a fair hearing, stating that failing to do so 'will not only be an abdication of the Senate’s constitutional duty, it will indicate a process for nominating and confirming judges that is beyond repair.' He further noted that such an action would damage the Supreme Court’s reputation and diminish public faith in the American judicial system. 'Our democracy will ultimately suffer as well,' he added during the introduction of Garland at a ceremony held in the White House Rose Garden. The passing of Scalia has resulted in a Supreme Court that is evenly divided with four liberal and four conservative justices. The nomination of Obama’s candidate could shift the balance to the left for the first time in several decades, influencing decisions on hot-button issues such as abortion, gun rights, the death penalty, and political funding. Obama asserted that the Supreme Court should function independently of political influences and should continue to do so. He remarked that with the current political climate in the United States being so polarized, 'this is precisely the time when we should play it straight, and treat the process of appointing a Supreme Court justice with the seriousness and care it deserves.' In response, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell from Kentucky quickly reiterated that the Senate would not entertain the president’s nomination. A spokesperson for McConnell noted that the senator had a phone conversation with Garland but would not participate in a 'perfunctory meeting' with him. Additionally, John Cornyn of Texas, the second-highest-ranking Republican in the Senate, remarked, 'This person will not be confirmed, so there’s no reason going through some motions and pretending like it will happen, because it’s not going to happen.'
source_text: Obama picks centrist high court nominee; Republicans unmoved. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Barack Obama selected Merrick Garland for the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday, choosing a centrist judge meant to win over recalcitrant Senate Republicans whose leaders wasted no time in spurning the Democratic president. A bruising political fight is brewing over the nomination, which also promises to figure in the already contentious campaign for the Nov. 8 U.S. presidential election. The Republican-led Senate’s leaders have vowed not to hold confirmation hearings or an up-or-down vote on any Obama nominee. Garland, 63, was picked to replace long-serving conservative Justice Antonin Scalia, who died on Feb. 13. A Chicagoan like Obama, he serves as chief judge of the influential U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and is a former prosecutor who in the past has won praise from both Republicans and Democrats. Wasting no time in pressing its case for Senate confirmation, the administration is dispatching Garland to Capitol Hill on Thursday to huddle with Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont, the senior Judiciary Committee Democrat and then with Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid of Nevada. Such meetings are aimed at shoring up Senate support for the nominee and generating media coverage. The lifetime appointment to the high court requires Senate confirmation. Obama’s announcement prompted a flood of reaction from private groups that will work to advance or kill the nomination. The UAW, representing automobile, aerospace and some agricultural workers, call Garland “a distinguished, moderate judge with more federal judicial experience than any other Supreme Court nominee in history.” National Rifle Association Executive Director Chris Cox said, “A basic analysis of Merrick Garland’s judicial record shows that he does not respect our fundamental, individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense.”   Republicans, hoping a candidate from their party wins the presidential election, are demanding that Obama leave the seat vacant and let his successor, to be sworn in next January, make the selection. Billionaire businessman Donald Trump is leading among Republicans for the nomination. Obama’s former secretary of state, Hillary Clinton, is the front-runner for the Democrats. Obama said Republican senators should give Garland a fair hearing. He said that failing to do so “will not only be an abdication of the Senate’s constitutional duty, it will indicate a process for nominating and confirming judges that is beyond repair.” Such a move, he said, would also undermine the reputation of the Supreme Court and faith in the American justice system. “Our democracy will ultimately suffer as well,” Obama added, as he introduced Garland at a White House Rose Garden ceremony. Scalia’s death left the nine-member Supreme Court evenly split with four liberals and four conservative justices. Obama’s nominee could tilt the court to the left for the first time in decades, which could affect rulings on contentious issues including abortion, gun rights, the death penalty and political spending. Obama said the Supreme Court was supposed to be above politics and it should remain so. Obama said that with politics in the United States so polarized, “this is precisely the time when we should play it straight, and treat the process of appointing a Supreme Court justice with the seriousness and care it deserves.” Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky swiftly reiterated that the Senate will not consider the nomination by the president. A McConnell spokesman said the senator had spoken by phone with Garland and would not hold a “perfunctory meeting” with him.  John Cornyn of Texas, the second-ranking Senate Republican, added, “This person will not be confirmed, so there’s no reason going through some motions and pretending like it will happen, because it’s not going to happen.” Some cracks began appearing in McConnell’s strategy of completely shutting out the nominee. A handful of Republican senators including Susan Collins of Maine, Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire, Jeff Flake of Arizona, Mark Kirk of Illinois and Rob Portman of Ohio said they would be willing to meet with Garland. Collins said the Senate Judiciary Committee should hold confirmation hearings. Judiciary Committee member Orrin Hatch, whose past support of Garland was cited by Obama, said the pick does not change his view “at this point” that no Obama nominee should be considered.  Senator Pat Toomey of Pennsylvania, who is in a tough re-election battle, said, “Should Merrick Garland be nominated again by the next president, I would be happy to carefully consider his nomination.” Garland is the oldest Supreme Court nominee since Republican Richard Nixon in 1971 nominated Lewis Powell, who was 64. Presidents tend to pick nominees younger than that so they can serve for decades and extend a president’s legacy. Obama may reason that the choice of an older nominee might also entice Senate Republicans into considering his selection. Garland would become the fourth Jewish member of the nine-member court. There are five Roman Catholics on the court. Obama considered but passed over Garland when he made two prior Supreme Court appointments.  With solid Republican support, the Senate voted in 1997 to confirm Garland to his present job in a bipartisan 76-23 vote after he was nominated by Democratic President Bill Clinton. Garland is widely viewed as a moderate. He is a former prosecutor who served in the Justice Department under Clinton. He oversaw the prosecution in the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing case including securing the death penalty for the lead defendant, anti-government militant Timothy McVeigh. In his current post, he is known for narrow, centrist opinions and rhetoric that is measured rather than inflammatory even when in dissent. Standing in between Obama and Vice President Joe Biden during the Rose Garden ceremony, an emotional Garland referred to the Oklahoma City bombing case, saying, “Once again, I saw the importance of assuring victims and families that the justice system could work.” Obama said he fulfilled his constitutional duty by naming a nominee and said it was time for the Senate to do its job.  “Presidents do not stop working in the final year of their term. Neither should a senator,” Obama said. Obama, in office since 2009, has already named two justices to the Supreme Court: Sonia Sotomayor, who at 55 became the first Hispanic justice in 2009, and Elena Kagan, who was 50 when she became the fourth woman ever to serve on the court in 2010. Democrats praised his latest choice. “If Merrick Garland can’t get bipartisan support no one can,” Democratic Senator Charles Schumer of New York said. Hillary Clinton called Garland “a brilliant legal mind,” urging the Senate to move ahead with the confirmation process. Trump said it was critical for Republicans to take back the White House to avoid Democrats shaping the Supreme Court for decades to come.

text: The U.S. House of Representatives' tax committee is set to conduct public hearings in the upcoming weeks as they prepare to introduce legislation aimed at revamping the nation's tax system, according to congressional aides on Wednesday. This initiative for hearings was discussed during a meeting lasting an hour between Chairman Kevin Brady of the House Ways and Means Committee and 15 Democrats from the panel, as indicated by a Democratic aide from the House. Specifics regarding the timing of the hearings, the particular tax reform topics to be covered, or whether the full Ways and Means Committee would lead the proceedings have not been disclosed. Brady, a Republican from Texas, remarked in a statement following the meeting, "We had a positive and open discussion, and I appreciated the opportunity to engage in a two-way dialogue." On track to present tax reform proposals this spring, the Republican-controlled committee is preparing for a vote on the House floor in the summer. Staff members have been developing legislation based on a blueprint from House Republicans that aims to significantly reduce taxes for both individuals and businesses. On Wednesday, House Speaker Paul Ryan commented that the House, Senate, and White House, all under Republican leadership, "aren’t on the same page yet on tax reform." Earlier this week, Brady announced the bipartisan gathering, emphasizing that the conversation would concentrate on simplifying the U.S. tax code for citizens and preventing U.S. companies from relocating production and research operations abroad—two goals emphasized by Republicans. A Republican aide from the committee noted, "It was clear from this meeting we share the same fundamental goals on tax reform, particularly as it relates to growth and simplicity." Brady reiterated his commitment to including a border adjustment tax provision within the tax reform legislation, as reported by aides. This policy, which would impose a 20 percent tax on imports, has faced division within the business sector and has been criticized by some Republicans in both the House and Senate. The meeting on Wednesday was the first occasion that Brady engaged with the Democratic members of the committee to discuss the House Republican tax reform strategy, according to aides. However, the bipartisan atmosphere was disrupted by the release of a letter from Republican members of the committee to President Donald Trump, advocating for the dismissal of John Koskinen, the Internal Revenue Service commissioner appointed by former Democratic President Barack Obama. The Democratic aide noted that during the meeting, Democrats brought up this letter, highlighting how such partisan actions could impede bipartisanship on other matters, including tax reform.

text: On Monday, Tropical Storm Ophelia wreaked havoc along the southern coastline of Ireland, resulting in the loss of three lives. LAHINCH, Ireland (Reuters) reported that the storm caused extensive damage, felling trees and power lines, and generating waves measuring 10 metres (30 feet). More than 360,000 residences and businesses experienced power outages, with an additional 100,000 expected to lose electricity by the end of the day, according to Ireland's Electricity Supply Board, which labeled the situation an unprecedented event that would impact all regions of the nation for several days. Approximately 170 flights were canceled from Ireland's primary airports, Dublin and Shannon. Two fatalities occurred in unrelated events when trees collapsed onto vehicles – a woman in her 50s in the southeast and a man on the east coast. A third individual in his 30s lost his life while attempting to remove a downed tree using a chainsaw. The storm, which had been downgraded from hurricane status overnight, represented the most severe weather event to strike Ireland in 50 years. It made landfall at 10:40 a.m. (0940 GMT), as reported by the Irish National Meteorological Service, with winds reaching up to 190 kph (110 mph) affecting the southernmost tip of the nation. The risk of coastal flooding was substantial. Sean Hogan, the chairman of Ireland's National Emergency Coordination Group, cautioned through national broadcaster RTE, "This storm is still very active and there are still very dangerous conditions in parts of the country. Do not be lulled into thinking this has passed." In response to the storm's impact, the armed forces were deployed to enhance flood defenses, while public transportation services and hospitals were closed. Schools throughout Ireland and Northern Ireland were also set to remain closed for another day on Tuesday. Hogan noted that numerous roads had been obstructed due to fallen trees. Social media showcased images of roofs being torn off structures, including one at Cork City soccer club's Turner’s Cross stadium, where a stand's roof had collapsed. Prime Minister Leo Varadkar urged the public to remain indoors, while the transport minister indicated that driving conditions were unsafe. The peak of the storm's winds was anticipated between 1600 GMT and 1800 GMT in Dublin and Galway, two of the largest cities in Ireland, with northern areas expected to face severe weather later on Monday. An Amber Weather Warning was issued by Britain’s meteorological service for Northern Ireland, effective from 1400-2100 GMT, highlighting that the storm posed a life-threatening risk and could result in transportation disruptions, power outages, and flying debris. The storm was predicted to move towards western Scotland overnight, with impactful weather anticipated in other western and northern regions of the United Kingdom. British media have drawn parallels between Ophelia and the Great Storm of 1987, which brought hurricane-strength winds to parts of the United Kingdom exactly 30 years ago. According to the Irish government, the storm is likely to be the most severe since Hurricane Debbie, which claimed 11 lives in Ireland in 1961. The storm passed close to a golf course in western Ireland owned by U.S. President Donald Trump, who has been preparing a wall to shield its greens from coastal erosion. Climatologists noted that similar storms in the past have altered the configuration of various segments of the Irish coastline.
source_text: Three dead as Storm Ophelia batters Ireland. LAHINCH, Ireland (Reuters) - Three people died as Tropical Storm Ophelia battered Ireland s southern coast on Monday, knocking down trees and power lines and whipping up 10-metre (30-foot) waves. Over 360,000 homes and businesses were without electricity with another 100,000 outages expected by nightfall, Ireland s Electricity Supply Board said, describing it as an unprecedented event that would effect every part of the country for days. Around 170 flights from Ireland s two main airports at Dublin and Shannon were canceled. Two people were killed in separate incidents when trees fell on their cars   a woman in her 50s in the south east and a man on the east coast. Another man in his 30s died while trying to clear a fallen tree in an incident involving a chainsaw. The storm, downgraded from a hurricane overnight, was the worst to hit Ireland in half a century. It made landfall after 10:40 a.m. (0940 GMT), the Irish National Meteorological Service said, with winds as strong as 190 kph (110 mph) hitting the most southerly tip of the country. Coastal flooding was likely.  This storm is still very active and there are still very dangerous conditions in parts of the country. Do not be lulled into thinking this has passed,  the chairman of Ireland s National Emergency Coordination Group, Sean Hogan, told national broadcaster RTE.  The armed forces were sent to bolster flood defenses, public transport services and hospitals were closed and schools across Ireland and Northern Ireland will remain shut for a second day on Tuesday.  Hundreds of roads were blocked by fallen trees, Hogan said. Photos on social media showed roofs flying off buildings, including at Cork City soccer club s Turner s Cross stadium where the roof of one stand had collapsed. Prime Minister Leo Varadkar advised people to stay indoors. The transport minister said it was not safe to drive. The storm winds were due to peak between 1600 GMT and 1800 GMT in Dublin and Galway, two of Ireland s most populous cities, and later on Monday in northern areas.  Britain s meteorological service put an Amber Weather Warning into effect for Northern Ireland from 1400-2100 GMT, saying the storm posed a danger to life and was likely to cause transport cancellations, power cuts and flying debris. It is expected to move towards western Scotland overnight and  impactful weather  is expected in other western and northern parts of the United Kingdom, it said.   British media are comparing Ophelia to the  Great Storm  of 1987, which subjected parts of the United Kingdom to hurricane strength winds 30 years ago to the day.  The Irish government said the storm was likely to be the worst since Hurricane Debbie, which killed 11 in Ireland in 1961. It passed close to a western Ireland golf course owned by U.S. President Donald Trump, who has been planning a wall to protect its greens from coastal erosion. Similar storms in the past have changed the shape of stretches of the Irish coastline, climatologists said.

text: On Monday, an activist investor associated with Chevron Corp announced that it has submitted a resolution for shareholders that calls for the oil company to evaluate the practicality of ceasing its operations in Myanmar. This move comes amid a widespread denunciation by the United States of the crackdown on the Rohingya Muslim minority, which has been labeled as ethnic cleansing. The resolution, presented last week by Azzad Asset Management, an Islamic finance firm, urges Chevron’s board to explore how the company might mitigate the risks involved with engaging in business with governments that are involved in genocide or crimes against humanity. Previously, Azzad had introduced a similar resolution at the last Chevron shareholder meeting, which received backing from 6 percent of the votes cast. Since late August, over 600,000 Rohingya Muslims have sought refuge in southern Bangladesh, fleeing a military campaign initiated by Myanmar's security forces in response to militant attacks in Rakhine State. The crackdown has drawn condemnation from U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and officials from the United Nations, who have characterized it as a genocidal act. Meanwhile, Myanmar officials have rejected the allegations of committing atrocities against the Rohingya population. Chevron, recognized as the second-largest oil producer based in the U.S., maintains operations in Myanmar through its subsidiary, Unocal Myanmar Offshore Co Ltd. The company’s projects include a minority share in natural gas extraction and a pipeline, as indicated on the company website. In a statement to Reuters on Monday, Chevron's spokesperson Melissa Ritchie emphasized that the company is committed to maintaining dialogue with shareholders regarding the significant issue of violence in Rakhine State, Myanmar. Ritchie added that Chevron intends to collaborate with other U.S. enterprises and government entities to underscore the importance of U.S. investment in Myanmar and the necessity of fostering a business environment that upholds human rights. Chevron has the choice to either accept the proposal or request permission from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to reject it. Should Chevron choose to block the resolution, Azzad would be able to contest this decision with the SEC. The annual meeting for Chevron is scheduled for the upcoming spring. This resolution filing coincides with the recent arrest of two Reuters journalists by Myanmar authorities. The government accuses them of breaching the Officials Secrets Act, a law dating back to the colonial era. Several governments, along with journalists and human rights organizations, have criticized these arrests. Chevron opted not to provide a direct comment regarding the situation involving the journalists.

text: Negotiations are underway for the evacuation of Syrian fighters from a region near the borders of Israel, Syria, and Lebanon, according to rebel representatives. In recent days, government forces have taken control of several strategic positions, effectively trapping the insurgents within the town. Abu Kanaan, a representative of a local rebel faction, mentioned that talks are focused on the exit of the combatants and those who wish to accompany them. He noted that the militias are encouraging them to relocate to Idlib. However, no agreement has yet been finalized, as stated by Ibrahim al-Jebawi, an official from a faction of the Free Syrian Army who is knowledgeable about the ongoing discussions. The Syrian military, along with its allies, has increasingly sought evacuation arrangements for rebel-held areas situated near major cities or other significant sites after enduring long periods of siege and aerial bombardment. The vicinity of Beit Jin holds particular sensitivity due to its proximity to the Golan Heights, which are under Israeli control. Israel has been keen to ensure that Hezbollah, the dominant Iran-supported militia assisting Syrian President Bashar al-Assad against opposition groups, remains distant from its border with Syria. The Israeli military has frequently targeted Syrian military assets close to the border after stray projectiles landed in areas it controls and has also struck Hezbollah convoys and weapon depots within Syria.

text: On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry expressed that it would be beneficial for President-elect Donald Trump’s transition team to obtain advice from the State Department before reaching out to international leaders, although this has not yet occurred. During a session for questions and answers at a think tank event, Kerry stated, "We have not been contacted prior to any of these discussions. No requests have been made for talking points from us." He continued, "I believe there is an advantage in at least having recommendations; whether or not you decide to heed them is a separate matter, but it’s important to consult with those who manage the desk and have considerable experience, to understand the current situation and any pressing issues at hand." Kerry noted, "I find that to be significant, and I would definitely advise it, but, clearly, that hasn’t transpired in several instances." The recent phone call between Trump and Taiwan President Tsai Ing-wen last Friday provoked a diplomatic backlash from China and led to speculation regarding a potential shift in U.S. policy under the Republican president-elect. On Sunday, Vice President-elect Mike Pence characterized the call as merely a "courtesy call." This conversation marked the first instance of a U.S. president-elect or sitting president speaking with a leader from Taiwan since President Jimmy Carter transitioned diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 1979, which acknowledged Taiwan as part of "one China." This diplomatic incident is one of multiple challenges Trump has faced recently, given that he is a real estate mogul without prior experience in public office, foreign affairs, or military matters. Trump, set to assume office on January 20, is still deliberating his selection for secretary of state.

text: Hillary Clinton, a candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination, has urged the pharmaceutical firm Mylan NV to voluntarily decrease the price of its EpiPen, a medication used for severe allergic reactions. Over the last ten years, the cost of this crucial drug has surged by more than 400 percent. "That’s outrageous - and it’s just the latest troubling example of a company taking advantage of its consumers,” Clinton remarked in her statement. She has consistently asserted during the primary campaign that she would challenge pharmaceutical companies, seeking to mitigate the perception that she is overly connected to the insurance sector. Clinton has outlined a strategy aimed at reducing medication costs for consumers. In response to Clinton's comments, Mylan spokeswoman Nina Devlin did not reply to requests for clarification regarding the company's pricing. Mylan obtained the EpiPen in 2007, and the price rose from $100 in 2008 to its current level of $600. Mylan's shares fell by over 5 percent, closing at $43.15 on Nasdaq. "The price of EpiPen is outrageous," stated Robert Weissman, who leads the consumer advocacy organization Public Citizen. "Mylan is endangering lives and ripping off the country." Weissman emphasized that the price of EpiPen in the U.S. ought to be significantly reduced, pointing out that it is accessible in Canada for as little as $112. He also noted that numerous other pharmaceutical companies frequently increase the prices of their prescription medications by 10 percent or more annually, indicating that U.S. legislation is necessary to curb such "price spikes." The White House adopted a more measured approach in addressing rising drug costs, opting not to comment on the actions of specific firms. "I will observe, however, that pharmaceutical companies that often try to portray themselves as the inventors of life-saving medication often do real damage to their reputation by being greedy and jacking up prices in a way that victimizes," said Josh Earnest, a spokesman for the White House, during a news briefing. Clinton’s call aligns with a bipartisan coalition of lawmakers advocating for investigations into the price hike of EpiPens, which are prefilled epinephrine (adrenaline) injections administered during severe allergic reactions that, if untreated, could lead to death. Earlier this week, Republican Senator Chuck Grassley, who chairs the Senate Judiciary Committee, sent a letter to Mylan requesting an explanation for the price increase. Senator Amy Klobuchar, the leading Democrat on the committee’s antitrust subcommittee, demanded an inquiry by the Federal Trade Commission. On Wednesday, Senators Susan Collins, a Republican, and Claire McCaskill, a Democrat, called for Mylan to provide a briefing to the Senate regarding the price changes. Grassley, Klobuchar, and Democratic Senators Patrick Leahy and Richard Blumenthal, along with Republican Senator Ron Johnson, sent a letter to the Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday inquiring about its approval process for alternatives to the EpiPen. "Given the importance of this topic, it is imperative to understand the FDA’s role with respect to EpiPens and its approval of generic equivalents that could help to increase competition and lower prices if introduced," the senators stated in their announcement. "We have reached out to every member of Congress who has sent us a letter, and we look forward to meeting with them and responding to their questions as soon as possible," Devlin stated. In January, Clinton criticized Valeant Pharmaceuticals International Inc for significantly increasing the cost of a heart medication. Following a blog post from her campaign targeting Valeant, the company’s stock prices experienced a decline. In March, she unveiled a campaign advertisement promising to specifically target the company. Additionally, Clinton condemned Turing Pharmaceuticals in the fall of 2015 when public outrage erupted after it decided to hike the price of an antiviral drug commonly prescribed to AIDS patients and pregnant women.
