text: As Italy's national elections approach, the left seems to be sabotaging its own chances, fixating on Matteo Renzi, the leader of the Democratic Party (PD), rather than addressing external threats. The PD suffered a significant setback during a recent regional election in Sicily, where it secured a distant third place behind a coalition of center-right parties and the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement. This election was perceived by many as a precursor to the national election scheduled for May. Despite a recent poll indicating a six-point decline for the PD over the past six months, the party remains entangled in a competitive three-way contest alongside the 5-Star Movement and a center-right coalition that features Silvio Berlusconi's Forza Italia (Go Italy!). With the economy experiencing its most rapid growth in seven years and a notable decrease in migrant arrivals, the ruling PD is hopeful these factors will attract moderate and progressive voters who would typically avoid Berlusconi and are cautious about the relatively new 5-Star Movement. However, a faction of left-leaning lawmakers who broke away from the PD earlier this year accuse Renzi of steering the party too far right and turning it into his personal domain; they continue to resist reconciliation efforts. Former Prime Minister Massimo D'Alema, the architect of the significant split, consistently seizes opportunities to criticize Renzi. Meanwhile, Pietro Grasso, who serves as the Senate president and is a former anti-mafia magistrate, recently departed from the PD, remarking that the party no longer exists. Despite these internal conflicts, the PD and its potential allies could still play a crucial role in the upcoming elections if they can shift their focus from Renzi to their opponents in the months leading up to the ballot. Renzi, a dynamic 42-year-old from Florence, has made his path challenging. In a recent incident, he had a disagreement with the most well-liked member of his party, Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni. Just days before the expiration of Bank of Italy Governor Ignazio Visco’s term, Renzi unexpectedly blindsided Gentiloni with a parliamentary motion suggesting that the premier should not extend the central banker’s tenure for another six years. The PD claimed that Visco failed to act adequately to prevent banking crises that resulted in losses of up to 23 billion euros ($26.8 billion) this year due to government bailouts of struggling banks. To mitigate tensions with President Sergio Mattarella, who is responsible for appointing Bank of Italy leaders and had supported Visco, Gentiloni opted to disregard Renzi’s proposal. A PD lawmaker from Sicily, who requested anonymity, indicated that the Visco situation has exposed a divide within the party. He explained that there are two competing power structures: one inside the current Italian establishment and another outside it, with Renzi positioned outside. A government source and PD member provided a sports analogy, stating that the Visco incident has shown Renzi's growing unpredictability. Three years prior, Renzi was likened to Diego Maradona in Italian politics, the source noted, but now his behavior resembles that of Antonio Cassano, a notoriously temperamental Italian soccer player whose emotional outbursts created complications on the field. The source commented, "He was somewhat difficult to manage, but it was acceptable because the team was winning. Now, however, he resembles Cassano, whose erratic nature undermined his abilities and harmed his team." Under the new electoral regulations, Renzi and other party leaders will have the authority to choose their candidates for the upcoming election. Although many within the PD refrain from speaking out, the dissidents who have separated from the party are openly expressing their views. D'Alema stated last week that reuniting the center-left necessitates alterations in both policy and leadership. Laura Garavini, a PD legislator allied with Renzi, informed Reuters that the internal strife within the party continues. She remarked, "The expectation was that they would vanish after the split, yet they have not." Additionally, Renzi's recent agreement with center-right opponents to enact a proportional electoral law that favors pre-vote alliances has further fueled tensions among the PD splinter faction, which is resistant to participating in such arrangements.
source_text: It's all his fault: Italy's left obsessed with Renzi, not foes. ROME (Reuters) - National elections are looming and Italy s left seems bent on engineering its own defeat as Democratic Party (PD) leader Matteo Renzi continues to come under fire from potential allies.    The PD emerged badly bruised in a Sicilian regional vote last week, coming in a distant third to a center-right coalition and the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement in a contest that many saw as a dry run for a national election due by May.     Though a weekend poll showed the PD has dropped six percentage points in six months, it remains locked in a three-way race with 5-Star and a center-right coalition that includes four-time Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi s Forza Italia (Go Italy!). The economy is growing at its fastest pace in seven years and migrant arrivals have fallen dramatically, two factors the ruling PD hopes will help it win over moderate and progressive voters who would never choose Berlusconi and are wary of the untested 5-Star. But a group of left-wing lawmakers who split from the PD earlier this year accuse Renzi of taking the party too far to the right and turning it into his personal fiefdom; and so far they are refusing to make peace.   Former Prime Minister Massimo D Alema, who orchestrated the dramatic schism, never passes up a chance to attack Renzi. Pietro Grasso, the Senate president and a former anti-mafia magistrate who abruptly left the PD last month, quipped that  the PD doesn t exist any more .     The PD and its potential allies could still be key players after the vote if they can only agree to round on their rivals instead of Renzi in the few months left before the election.   The fast-talking 42-year-old Florentine has not made it easy on himself. Just last month he clashed with the most popular member of his own party - Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni.    Just days before Bank of Italy Governor Ignazio Visco s mandate was to expire, Renzi blindsided Gentiloni with a parliamentary motion inviting the premier not to give the central banker another six-year term.   The PD accused Visco of doing too little to head off banking crises that cost taxpayers up to 23 billion euros ($26.8 billion) this year in salvage operations on sinking lenders.    To defuse a dispute with President Sergio Mattarella, who formally names Bank of Italy chiefs and who backed Visco, Gentiloni ignored Renzi s appeal.     The Visco affair has opened a fault line  in the party, said a PD lawmaker from Sicily who asked not to be named.  Two power systems are squaring off, one outside the current Italian establishment and one inside. Renzi is on the outside.    Using a soccer analogy, a government source and PD member told Reuters the Visco affair revealed Renzi to be increasingly unpredictable.     Three years ago Renzi was the Diego Maradona of Italian politics, the source said, but now he s more like Antonio Cassano, a tantrum-prone Italian soccer star whose volcanic temper caused problems on the field.    Like Maradona, he was a little hard to handle, but it was OK because the team won,  the source said.  But now he s more like Cassano, whose volatile personality offset his talent and hurt his team.    Under the new electoral law, Renzi and other party secretaries will personally pick their candidates for next year s vote. Many inside the PD are not speaking publicly, but the rebels who have split with the party are holding nothing back.  The reunification of the center left requires a change in policy and leadership,  D Alema said last week.  Laura Garavini, a PD lawmaker close to Renzi, told Reuters that tensions within the party persist.     The idea was that after the split they would disappear, but they haven t,  she said.    Another source of tension on the left has been Renzi s agreement with center-right rivals last month to pass a proportional electoral law that favors pre-vote coalitions, angering the PD splinter party that doesn t want to play second fiddle to Renzi.    Senate President Grasso quit the PD hours after the law passed, criticizing Renzi. The PD breakaway party, known as the MDP, is now courting Grasso as their possible leader.   The latest poll had the PD at 24.3 percent, trailing 5-Star that stood at 29.3 percent, while the center-right is pulling 36.5 percent.        If the PD stops its internal bickering... we can win 40 percent,  Renzi said on a TV talk show last week.  That s easier said that done, as the Sicilian lawmaker explains:  In the PD, we re all equally unpleasant to each other. The category of friendship does not exist. Everyone thinks they re smarter than everyone else.

text: The possibility of considering nominees for the Supreme Court from Hillary Clinton, the Democratic presidential candidate, has been acknowledged by Georgia’s two Republican senators, as reported by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution on Sunday. U.S. Senator Johnny Isakson, who is facing re-election on Tuesday, along with U.S. Senator David Perdue, diverged from the stance of some fellow Republicans. This comes after Republican Senators John McCain and Ted Cruz indicated their intention to obstruct any nominations from Clinton. Isakson stated to the Atlanta publication, "As an elected official, you must not evade your duties. You honor your obligations, and I intend to do just that. I will evaluate her nominees when they are presented and make a choice that serves the interests of Georgia’s constituents." A representative for Perdue, who serves on the Senate Judiciary Committee, remarked to the AJC: "His goal is to guarantee the appointment of a Supreme Court justice who respects the Constitution, and he will assess each nominee based on their individual qualifications." The passing of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia in February has resulted in the Supreme Court being short one member, leading to an equal split between liberal and conservative justices. Earlier in March, President Barack Obama put forward Merrick Garland, a judge on the federal appeals court, as Scalia’s replacement. However, the Republican-controlled Senate has opted not to address this nomination, asserting that the next president should select the individual. The Senate’s failure to act on Garland, who is considered a centrist, has transformed the Supreme Court into a significant topic in the electoral race. Should Clinton win, the court, which has historically leaned conservative, could shift to the left for the first time in many years. Isakson expressed his belief that if Clinton were to win, the Senate would likely approve Garland before January. Some Republicans fear that Clinton might appoint a more progressive justice, further tilting the court’s ideological balance to the left.
source_text: Georgia senators will consider Clinton high court nominees: report. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Georgia’s two Republican senators broke with members of their party, saying they would consider Supreme Court nominees put forward by Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton if she wins the presidency, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported on Sunday. The comments from U.S. Senator Johnny Isakson, who is up for re-election on Tuesday, and U.S. Senator David Perdue came after Republican Senators John McCain and Ted Cruz suggested they might block any of Clinton’s potential nominees. “You don’t shirk your responsibility when you’re an elected official. You sanctify your responsibility, and that’s what I’ll do. I’ll consider who she nominates at the time she does and make a decision that’s right for the people of Georgia,” Isakson told the Atlanta newspaper. text: The European Commission asserted on Friday that the 2015 international agreement aimed at limiting Iran's nuclear activities is effective, urging all parties to uphold their obligations. A senior official from the U.S. administration indicated on Thursday that President Donald Trump is likely to declare soon that he will not certify the pivotal accord. Trump is facing a deadline of October 15 to confirm that Iran is adhering to the conditions outlined in the deal. A spokeswoman for the Commission stated during a press briefing in Brussels, "We are monitoring all developments regarding the agreement closely... reminding that it is a non-proliferation accord, which has received approval from the UN Security Council. It is functioning and has been validated eight times by the international atomic energy agency." She emphasized that the agreement represents a long-term, sustainable solution to the Iranian nuclear dilemma, providing essential assurances to all parties, and expressed the expectation that all parties will honor their commitments under the agreement.
source_text: EU Commission says all sides should stick to Iran deal terms. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - The European Commission said on Friday that an international deal to curb Iran s nuclear program struck in 2015 was working and all sides should stick to their commitments. U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to announce soon that he will decertify the landmark agreement, a senior administration official said on Thursday. Trump faces an Oct. 15 deadline for certifying that Iran is complying with the deal s terms.  We are following very closely all the developments on the deal... reminding that it is a non-proliferation deal, which has been endorsed by the UN Security Council, that it s working, delivering as it has been verified eight times by the international agency for atomic energy,  a Commission spokeswoman told a news conference in Brussels.  It is a durable, long-term solution to the Iranian nuclear issue which gives all sides the necessary assurances and we expect all sides to stick to their commitments under the deal,  she added.

text: BRUSSELS (Reuters) - According to a spokesperson for the European Commission, progress in the divorce negotiations regarding Brexit must come from the UK rather than the EU to initiate discussions about the future relationship. Margaritis Schinas stated during a routine briefing that a clear order exists for these discussions, and no resolution has yet been achieved concerning the initial phase, which pertains to the divorce proceedings. "Thus, the UK has the responsibility to move forward for any further developments to take place," he remarked. Schinas also mentioned that the UK could reference last week's debate held in the European Parliament in Strasbourg on this matter. His comments came in anticipation of a speech by British Prime Minister Theresa May, scheduled for later today, in which she is expected to assert that moving forward to the next stage depends on the EU's actions, stating that "the ball is in their (EU) court." This highlights the ongoing complexities in the negotiations as both sides work to define their future relationship.
source_text: EU says 'ball entirely in UK court' for move to next Brexit talks phase. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - It is up to Britain, rather than the European Union, to make progress in divorce negotiations with the European Union to enable the opening of talks on the future relationship, the spokesman for the European Commission said on Monday.  There is a clear sequencing to these talks and there has been so far no solution found on step one, which is the divorce proceedings,  spokesman Margaritis Schinas told a regular briefing.  So the ball is entirely in the UK court for the rest to happen. And the UK can always refer to the debate in the European plenary in Strasbourg on the subject,  he said, referring to last week s debate in the European Parliament. He was responding to excerpts made available of a speech  British Prime Minister Theresa May to Britain s parliament later on Monday in which she will say that  as we look forward to the next stage, the ball is in their (EU) court .

text: TUNIS (Reuters) - Following a dispute over a ban affecting Tunisian women, the Dubai-based airline Emirates announced on Sunday that it would cease operations to Tunisia. This declaration came shortly after officials from the Tunisian government revealed that flights from the Emirati carrier had been prohibited. The ban was announced just two days after it was stated that Tunisian women were not allowed to board or transit through the UAE. No explanations were provided for the actions taken by either party. Emirates confirmed on Twitter that it would halt its Dubai-Tunis route starting Monday, adhering to directives issued by Tunisia. Earlier, the Tunisian transport ministry issued a statement indicating that the suspension of Emirates flights would persist until the UAE airline complied with international laws and agreements. Anwar Gargash, the UAE minister of state for foreign affairs, mentioned on Twitter that discussions between the two nations were ongoing regarding the security measures, but did not provide further details. He also emphasized the UAE's respect for Tunisian women. In Tunisia, frustration has escalated as reports emerged of women being barred from boarding Emirates flights at Tunis airport. Civil groups and political parties in Tunisia urged government intervention.
source_text: Emirates stops flying to Tunisia in row over ban on Tunisian women. TUNIS (Reuters) - Dubai airline Emirates will stop flying to Tunisia, it said on Sunday, after the North African country said it had banned flights from the United Emirates carrier. Emirates said on Twitter it would stop its Dubai-Tunis connection from Monday following instructions from Tunisia. The Tunisian transport ministry said in a statement earlier that Emirates flights would be suspended until the UAE airline found a way to operate according to international law and treaties. Tunisian civil organizations and political parties called on the government to act.

source_text: UK PM May says takes allegations of Russian interference seriously. text: NEW YORK (Reuters) - Hillary Clinton has challenged the harsh judgment from the Federal Bureau of Investigation that labeled her as "extremely careless" regarding classified governmental information, asserting on Friday that she depended on the expertise of her team at the U.S. State Department for classification decisions. After over a year of insisting she did not send or receive classified data via her private email system, she admitted during several interviews on Friday that she might have unintentionally done so, just three days after the FBI determined this occurred at least 110 times. The presumptive Democratic presidential candidate expressed that she "certainly did not believe" she was managing classified information on her email system at that moment, but highlighted that she took cues from her staff on the classification of the information. "I did not have a basis for second-guessing their conclusion," Clinton stated in a CNN interview, expressing her "highest regard" for her former colleagues. "They are skilled diplomats with experience in dealing with classified content," she mentioned in a different PBS Newshour interview. "They were not careless, and the materials they transmitted were not perceived as classified by them." During her four-year leadership at the department, Clinton held the position of the most senior classifying authority but did not respond to the FBI's finding that she had sent information classified as 'top secret', the highest classification level, through a private server located in her basement. "I have acknowledged, and I reiterate, that it was a mistake to utilize personal email, and I regret that decision," she remarked in yet another interview with ABC. Mishandling classified information is a criminal offense, and while FBI Director James Comey noted on Tuesday that evidence existed suggesting Clinton or her aides may have breached these laws, he concluded there was insufficient evidence of criminal intent to pursue prosecution. In an atypical 15-minute statement detailing the FBI's findings, Comey ultimately disappointed both Republicans and Democrats. Clinton's Republican adversaries have expressed outrage over the decision not to pursue criminal charges, while Clinton and her team have contested some of Comey's criticisms that undermine her assertion of possessing better judgment than Donald Trump, the presumptive Republican nominee. Comey characterized her and her team's actions as "extremely careless" and asserted that any "reasonable" government employee should have recognized the necessity of averting such information from email discussions. He added that the security of her server was so inadequate that the FBI could not rule out the possibility of it being hacked by foreign adversaries. When asked if she concurred with the term "extremely careless," Clinton responded to CNN that she did not agree, adding that Comey had "clarified" his statements. However, what specific clarification Clinton was referencing remained ambiguous. In more extensive remarks made before legislators on Thursday, Comey reiterated his points on Clinton's and her team's carelessness and "real sloppiness," remarking that it appeared she lacked sophistication regarding classified information.
source_text: Clinton says she relied on State staff for classification decisions. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Hillary Clinton disputed a scathing assessment by the Federal Bureau of Investigation that she was “extremely careless” with classified government secrets, saying on Friday she relied on the judgment of her subordinates at the U.S. State Department. After maintaining for more than a year that she did not send or receive classified information through her unauthorized private email system, she acknowledged in a string of interviews on Friday she may have at least unwittingly done so, three days after the FBI concluded this happened at least 110 times. Clinton, the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, said she “certainly did not believe” that she was handling classified information on her email system at the time, but emphasized that she followed the lead of her subordinates on whether information was classified. “I did not have a basis for second-guessing their conclusion,” Clinton said in an interview with CNN, saying she had the “highest regard” for her former colleagues. “These are experienced diplomats, they have expertise in handling classified material,” she said in a separate interview with PBS Newshour. “They were not careless and the material that they sent, they did not believe that was classified.” Clinton, who was the department’s most senior classifying authority during her four-year tenure at its helm, did not address the FBI’s conclusion that she herself sent information on topics classified as ‘top secret’, the highest level, through a private server she kept in her basement.  “I have said, and I repeated, that it was a mistake to use personal email and I regret that,” she said in another interview with ABC. It is a crime to mishandle classified information, and while FBI Director James Comey said on Tuesday there was evidence Clinton or her aides may have broken these laws, there was not enough evidence of criminal intent for a prosecution. In an unusual 15-minute announcement explaining the FBI’s findings, Comey ended up dismaying both Republicans and Democrats. While Clinton’s Republican opponents have fumed at the decision not to file criminal charges, Clinton and her staff have disputed some of Comey’s criticisms that undermine her argument that she has better judgment than Donald Trump, the presumptive Republican presidential candidate. Comey called her and her staff “extremely careless” and said that any “reasonable” government employee should have recognized that such information should not be aired in emails. Her server was so poorly secured the FBI could not eliminate the possibility it had not been hacked by the country’s enemies, Comey said. Asked if she agreed that she was “extremely careless”, Clinton told CNN she was not, adding that Comey had “clarified” his remarks. It was unclear what clarification Clinton meant. In lengthier comments before lawmakers on Thursday, Comey again spoke of Clinton’s and her staff’s carelessness and “real sloppiness”, adding that it seemed she was not “particularly sophisticated with respect to classified information.”

text: In an urgent call, leading Democratic figures from the intelligence committees of both the House of Representatives and the Senate urged the White House on Wednesday to contemplate the declassification and public release of any assessments from the intelligence community regarding the breach of the Democratic National Committee's email system. Analysts have linked the intrusion to hackers from Russia. Senator Dianne Feinstein and Representative Adam Schiff conveyed in a letter to President Barack Obama that, "Considering the serious implications of this breach and the possibility that it could be a state-backed effort to interfere with our presidential election, we feel that greater transparency is necessary." In an interview aired by NBC News on Tuesday, Obama remarked that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was looking into the unauthorized release of over 19,000 emails from the DNC, which revealed that the committee had shown a preference for Hillary Clinton over Bernie Sanders in the race for the party's presidential nomination.
source_text: Senior U.S. lawmakers want information on DNC hack declassified. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The top Democrats on the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives intelligence committees called on Wednesday for the White House to consider declassifying and releasing any intelligence community assessments of the hack into the Democratic National Committee email system. Experts have attributed the breach to Russian hackers. “Given the grave nature of this breach and the fact that it may ultimately be found to be a state-sponsored attempt to manipulate our presidential election, we believe a heightened measure of transparency is warranted,” Senator Dianne Feinstein and Representative Adam Schiff wrote in a letter to President Barack Obama. Obama said in an interview broadcast by NBC News on Tuesday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was investigating the leak of more than 19,000 DNC emails, which showed the committee had favored Hillary Clinton over Bernie Sanders for the party’s presidential nomination.

text: A bill designed to curb the surging population of feral hogs in Oklahoma has been approved by the state's legislature. These wild pigs are associated with the spread of diseases and the destruction of crops. This legislation enables individuals to eliminate feral hogs without needing a hunting license. According to research conducted by an agricultural organization, feral hogs are rampant across all 77 counties in Oklahoma, with estimates suggesting their numbers could reach up to 1.6 million, making it one of the states with the largest populations of these animals. The measure, which received approval on Thursday from the Republican-majority legislature, allows hunters to kill hogs either on their own land or with the consent of the property owner on someone else's land. Additionally, the use of night-vision technology for hunting these animals is now permitted. The office of Republican Governor Mary Fallin has not yet indicated whether she will enact this law. Republican state Representative Sean Robert, a co-sponsor of the bill, remarked, "This legislation gives Oklahomans more options to combat the rapidly growing feral hog population." State officials stated that the most effective current method to eradicate wild hogs involves aerial shooting from helicopters. Tom Buchanan, the president of the Oklahoma Farm Bureau, which advocates for the bill, noted, "Feral hogs wreak havoc on Oklahoma’s farms, ranches and ecosystems, and cost farmers, ranchers and landowners." Opponents of the bill expressed concerns that it might lead to an influx of feral hogs being introduced into Oklahoma for the purpose of being hunted. The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service of the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported that damages caused by feral swine nationwide could exceed $2 billion. Dale Nolte, the program manager for the inspection service, stated during an interview, "If you are a farmer, they can clean out your crops overnight. We have farmers tell us they have given up on planting high-dollar crops because of the feral hog problem." According to Nolte, Texas, Oklahoma, and California house the largest populations of feral swine in the United States. He also mentioned that there are operations to remove these animals in 38 states. Kevin Grant, the state director for Oklahoma Wildlife Services at the U.S. Department of Agriculture, explained, "The problem is that feral hogs are so prolific that we have to trap 70 percent of the pig population every year just to maintain the population level we have right now. Out in the wild, feral hogs are an ecological nightmare. There is very little that is beneficial to native wildlife that come from feral swine."
source_text: Oklahoma lawmakers pass bill to reduce feral hog population. OKLAHOMA CITY (Reuters) - Oklahoma’s legislature has passed a bill aimed at reducing the state’s bulging population of feral hogs, blamed for spreading disease and wiping out crops, that would let people kill them without a hunting license. A study by an agricultural research organization found that the animals are running wild in all of Oklahoma’s 77 counties and could number as high as 1.6 million, which would be one of the highest feral hog populations of any state. The measure, passed on Thursday by the Republican-led legislature, would permit hunters to kill hogs without a hunting permit on their property or on someone else’s property with the landowner’s permission. It also would allow use of night-vision equipment to hunt them. Republican Governor Mary Fallin’s office has not said whether she will sign it into law. “This legislation gives Oklahomans more options to combat the rapidly growing feral hog population,” said Republican state Representative Sean Robert, a bill co-sponsor. The most effective method of eradicating the wild hogs currently is aerial shooting from helicopters, state officials said. “Feral hogs wreak havoc on Oklahoma’s farms, ranches and ecosystems, and cost farmers, ranchers and landowners,” said Tom Buchanan, president of the Oklahoma Farm Bureau, an agricultural industry group that supports the legislation. Bill opponents said it could prompt some people to bring even more feral hogs into Oklahoma to be shot by hunters. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said damage caused by feral swine across the United States could top $2 billion. “If you are a farmer, they can clean out your crops overnight,” Dale Nolte, the inspection service’s program manager, said in an interview. “We have farmers tell us they have given up on planting high-dollar crops because of the feral hog problem.” Texas, Oklahoma and California have the highest numbers of feral swine in the country, Nolte said. The inspection service has operations to remove them in 38 states, Nolte added. “The problem is that feral hogs are so prolific that we have to trap 70 percent of the pig population every year just to maintain the population level we have right now,” said Kevin Grant, Oklahoma Wildlife Services state director for the U.S. Department of Agriculture. “Out in the wild, feral hogs are an ecological nightmare. There is very little that is beneficial to native wildlife that come from feral swine,” Grant said.

text: In Washington, a meeting took place on Friday between President Barack Obama and Mohammed bin Salman, the deputy crown prince of Saudi Arabia. The White House disclosed that their discussion revolved around strategies to assist Iraqis in their battle against Islamic State militants, as well as emphasizing the necessity for a political transition in the conflict-ridden nation of Syria. The hour-long conversation occurred in the Oval Office. The deputy crown prince's visit to the U.S. aims to mend strained ties and to advocate for a vision called Vision 2030, which seeks to reduce the kingdom’s reliance on oil exports. According to the White House, "The President expressed appreciation for Saudi Arabia’s contributions to the campaign against ISIL," referring to the Islamic State group. They explored measures to bolster support for Iraqis, which includes increasing Gulf financial aid to address urgent humanitarian and stabilization requirements, as stated by the White House. U.S. officials have conveyed their concerns regarding the Saudi-led military operations against Houthi rebels in Yemen, which have reportedly led to significant civilian casualties according to various human rights organizations and the United Nations. Saudi Arabia has voiced anxiety regarding the growing relationship between the United States and Iran, its primary adversary, particularly following the 2015 nuclear agreement. Obama acknowledged the commitment of Saudi Arabia to find a political resolution to the conflict in Yemen, and also the Gulf Cooperation Council's backing, of which Saudi Arabia is a member, aimed at addressing humanitarian issues and reconstructing the war-torn nation, as reported by the White House. Regarding the situation in Syria, discussions between Obama and the prince highlighted the critical need for a political transition away from the leadership of President Bashar al-Assad, as mentioned by the White House. Currently, the United States is collaborating with global partners on what it designates as a Syrian-led transition process, facilitated by the United Nations; however, progress has been minimal thus far. A memo that was leaked on Thursday, signed by over 50 diplomats at the U.S. State Department, criticized the Obama administration's approach to Syria, urging for targeted military actions against Assad’s regime. In response to inquiries about the memo, Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Adel al-Jubeir, who was also present in Washington, informed reporters that the kingdom has been advocating for "a more robust intervention," which would consist of airstrikes, a no-fly zone, and a no-drive zone since the onset of the five-year civil conflict. White House spokeswoman Jen Friedman articulated that Obama does not envision a military resolution to the Syrian crisis. Both Washington and Riyadh are looking forward to the forthcoming release of classified pages from a U.S. report concerning the September 11, 2001 attacks. Some lawmakers have claimed that the report links Saudi government officials to the attacks. Jubeir asserted that investigations indicate those allegations "are not correct and they don’t hold."
source_text: Obama, Saudi prince focus on Iraq and Syria in Washington meeting. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Barack Obama and the deputy crown prince of Saudi Arabia on Friday discussed ways to support Iraqis in their fight against Islamic State militants and the importance of a political transition in war-torn Syria, the White House said. Obama met with Mohammed bin Salman in the Oval office for about an hour. The deputy crown prince is visiting the United States to repair frayed relations and to promote a plan, known as Vision 2030, to slash the kingdom’s dependence on oil exports. “The President expressed appreciation for Saudi Arabia’s contributions to the campaign against ISIL,” the White House said, using an acronym for the Islamic State group.  The two talked about steps to support Iraqis “including increased Gulf support to fund urgent humanitarian and stabilization needs,” the White House said.  U.S. officials have expressed unease about the Saudi-led campaign against Houthi rebels in Yemen, which according to the United Nations and human rights groups has resulted in large numbers of civilian casualties. Saudi Arabia is worried about closer relations between the United States and Iran, Riyadh’s arch enemy, after a 2015 nuclear deal.   Obama welcomed Saudi Arabia’s commitment to a political settlement of the Yemen conflict and support by the Gulf Cooperation Council, of which the kingdom is a member, to address humanitarian needs and rebuild the country, the White House said. The United States is working with international partners on what it calls a Syrian-led transition process facilitated by the United Nations, but so far there has been little progress.  Over 50 diplomats at the U.S. State Department signed a memo, leaked on Thursday, that was critical of the Obama administration’s Syria policy and called for targeted military strikes against Assad’s government.  Asked about the memo, Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Adel al-Jubeir, also in Washington, told reporters the kingdom had been arguing for a “more robust intervention” including airstrikes, a no-fly zone, and a no-drive zone, from the beginning of the five-year civil war.  Obama does not see a military solution to the crisis in Syria, White House spokeswoman Jen Friedman said.  Both Washington and Riyadh are anticipating the release of classified pages of a U.S. report into the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, that some U.S. lawmakers have alleged link Saudi government officials to the attacks. Jubeir said investigations show that the allegations “are not correct and they don’t hold.”

text: On Monday, the Kremlin confirmed that Ramzan Kadyrov, the prominent leader of the Chechen Republic in Russia, will continue in his position despite his recent remarks about potentially stepping down. source_text: Kremlin says head of Chechnya to remain despite talk of quitting. MOSCOW (Reuters) - The Kremlin said on Monday that Ramzan Kadyrov, the outspoken leader of Russia s republic of Chechnya, would remain in his post despite comments he made about the possibility of standing down. Kadyrov, 41, said in a state interview broadcast late on Sunday that it was  his dream  to one day leave office and that, if asked, he could suggest several candidates capable of taking over his role.  Ramzan continues to remain the current head of the republic,  Dmitry Peskov, a Kremlin spokesman, told reporters on a conference call when asked about Kadyrov s statement.

text: The Turkish Justice Ministry announced on Tuesday that it has called off a planned educational trip to the United States amidst an escalating diplomatic conflict regarding visa issuance. Earlier reports from local news outlets indicated that visa applications submitted by members of the delegation had been denied by U.S. officials. However, the Justice Ministry clarified that it proactively decided to cancel the visit. In a statement, the ministry explained, "Due to the recent visa crisis between the two countries, the visit was canceled by our Ministry," further noting that there were no visa requests that had been rejected. The delegation intended to conduct a study visit in the U.S., invited by American authorities, scheduled for the period between October 29 and November 4, according to the ministry. The pro-government Daily Sabah reported that the group aimed to examine the U.S. criminal justice system and tour American prisons. This month, U.S. missions in Turkey halted the issuance of visas, citing safety issues for their personnel following the detention of two U.S. consular employees, both of whom are Turkish citizens. The ongoing crisis has negatively impacted the value of the lira and raised concerns among investors. On Tuesday, prominent businesses from both Turkey and the U.S. urged authorities to find a resolution to the ongoing dispute. In May, a translator at the U.S. consulate in the southern city of Adana was apprehended, and more recently, a Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) employee was detained in Istanbul. Both individuals are alleged to have connections to last year's unsuccessful coup attempt. The U.S. embassy has dismissed these allegations as unfounded. Turkish law enforcement is also seeking to question a third employee based in Istanbul. His wife and daughter were taken into custody due to suspected ties to the network of Fethullah Gulen, a cleric residing in Pennsylvania since 1999, whom Ankara blames for orchestrating the failed coup. They were subsequently released. Turkey has expressed frustration over what it perceives as the U.S.'s unwillingness to extradite Gulen. U.S. officials have maintained that their judicial system requires substantial evidence before ordering an extradition. Gulen has denied any involvement in the coup attempt. In the aftermath of the uprising, over 150,000 individuals across the police force, civil service, and private sector have faced dismissal or suspension. Approximately 50,000 individuals have been detained. Rights organizations and Western allies of Turkey have voiced concerns regarding the government's alleged use of the coup as a justification for suppressing dissent. However, Ankara insists that these measures are essential due to the significant security threats it confronts. Furthermore, Turkey has been infuriated by the support Washington has extended to the Syrian Kurdish YPG militia in its battle against the Islamic State, as Turkey views the YPG as a branch of the banned Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK).

text: The U.N. has expressed outrage at the 30-year prison term given to a woman in El Salvador under its abortion legislation. On Friday, Liz Throssell, a spokesperson for U.N. human rights, described the ruling as appalling. This past Wednesday, the Second Court of Appeal in San Salvador upheld the conviction of Teodora Vasquez, sentenced in 2008 for aggravated homicide related to the death of her child in 2007. Prosecutors alleged that Vasquez strangled her newborn after delivery. However, her legal representatives contended that she experienced health issues and that the child was stillborn. El Salvador has enforced one of the harshest anti-abortion laws globally since 1997, targeting women suspected of having abortions or assisting others. text: Jerusalem (Reuters) - Concerns are high among Israeli intelligence specialists regarding the potential ramifications of U.S. President Donald Trump’s disclosure of classified information to Russia, which could have endangered an Israeli operative. However, they believe that this incident is unlikely to have lasting effects on collaborative intelligence efforts. Trump confirmed via Twitter that he shared sensitive details during a meeting last week with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the White House. The information was reportedly about a potential airline threat from Islamic State, believed to involve a bomb hidden in a laptop. According to The New York Times, which cited both a current and a former U.S. official, the details shared by Trump originated from an Israeli intelligence source operating within Islamic State-controlled areas in Syria. Israeli officials have refrained from confirming whether they were the source of the leaked information, though they have quickly emphasized that their counter-terrorism collaboration with the U.S. remains robust. On Tuesday, Trump reached out to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to discuss his upcoming visit to Israel next week, but their 20-minute dialogue did not touch on the intelligence breach, as noted by the prime minister’s office. Defence Minister Avigdor Lieberman stated on Twitter, "The security relationship between Israel & our greatest ally the United States is deep, significant & unprecedented in volume," a sentiment echoed by the intelligence minister. Ron Dermer, Israel’s ambassador to Washington, provided a similar reassurance, asserting, "Israel has full confidence in our intelligence-sharing relationship with the United States and looks forward to deepening that relationship in the years ahead under President Trump." Israeli intelligence professionals have not confirmed whether an Israeli asset was indeed the source of the disclosed information. Nevertheless, they indicated that Israel has established a comprehensive network of human and signal intelligence throughout the region, making it feasible that they could have infiltrated Islamic State as part of their ongoing efforts. Aviv Oreg, a former head of the Al Qaeda and global jihad desk within the military intelligence department, who now leads a counter-terrorism consulting firm, stated, "Israeli intelligence agencies have shown that they can have such human sources." He noted the significant challenges involved in placing someone inside ISIS, adding, "If there is an agent, I’m sure it’s the only one. If we have really lost a human source over there, it’s a major loss and it will take years to regenerate another one." Oreg expressed that Israel would be extremely displeased about this potential loss, emphasizing that it could affect how Israel manages its human intelligence operations in general and may deter others from cooperating in the future. Simultaneously, he acknowledged that Trump, as the president and commander-in-chief, possesses the authority to release such information, even if it demonstrates a lack of experience in handling intelligence matters. Kobi Michael, a senior research fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies and the former deputy director of Israel’s ministry of strategic affairs, characterized Trump’s disclosure as "very concerning" due to the risk posed to an Israeli intelligence asset. While there are valid reasons to believe that the compromised source was indeed an operative, he also suggested the possibility that it could have been a well-placed piece of signal intelligence. "In the context of ISIS, they are highly active on social media and digital platforms. So who knows, all options are valid, even if as far as I understand the context, it looks like a human intelligence source." Michael noted that Israel boasts superior intelligence capabilities in the region compared to the United States, making it an essential partner for Washington. Nonetheless, both nations have a mutual interest in maintaining full cooperation regarding intelligence matters. "What occurred is problematic, and it shouldn’t have happened. However, mistakes do happen, not just by the Americans, but sometimes by the Israelis as well," Michael remarked.

text: The recent win by U.S. Republican presidential hopeful Ted Cruz in Iowa could indicate a diminishing sway of the corn industry over political figures, particularly in the heart of America’s agricultural sector. On Monday, Cruz, a conservative senator hailing from Texas and a vocal critic of the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), managed to defeat billionaire Donald Trump during the Iowa caucuses, marking the beginning of the series of state-by-state contests to select party nominees ahead of the election on November 8. Cruz secured 28 percent of the votes, while Trump garnered 24 percent, with Cruz's triumph including a win in Kossuth County, recognized as the state’s leading corn-producing area. This outcome poses challenges for corn producers in the nation’s top ethanol-generating state, who have exerted significant effort to uphold the biofuels policy, which has been in place for over ten years. The RFS mandates the incorporation of ethanol and other biofuels into the country’s fuel supply, aiming to lessen U.S. reliance on foreign oil, promote cleaner domestic energy sources, and enhance rural economies. Cruz’s current stance favors a gradual phasing out of renewable fuel requirements, a shift from his previous call for an immediate repeal in 2013. Nevertheless, Cruz's success in Iowa without support from the corn and ethanol sectors may suggest that candidates can thrive without their endorsement in the long term, potentially undermining a crucial element of the lobby’s influence. Republican strategist and energy lobbyist Michael McKenna commented, "The conversation inside of Congress in the morning will change instantly, as Republicans realize they can be against the mandate and still win,” referring to the implications of Cruz's success. For certain voters, issues like terrorism and healthcare overshadow the significance of the state’s ethanol sector. George David Banks, Executive Vice President of the American Council for Capital Formation, stated, "I think the clear message coming out of Iowa is that whatever political influence ethanol used to have in the state, those days are now over." The RFS has faced increased scrutiny from oil industry representatives who assert that the volumes mandated by Congress are unattainable. Additionally, environmental advocates have raised questions about the advantages of corn-based ethanol, which constitutes the majority of an 18-billion-gallon biofuels market. Efforts to amend or abolish the program have not gained traction. A repeal amendment attached to a Senate energy bill currently under consideration is likely to face rejection if brought to a vote. Leading up to Monday’s caucuses, some equity analysts had minimized the potential effects of the vote on U.S. ethanol producers, emphasizing that it is premature in the election cycle to have significant implications for individual stocks. On Tuesday morning, shares of Green Plains Inc and Pacific Ethanol Inc fell by over 4 percent in low trading volumes, lagging behind the broader stock market. On the same day, BB&T lowered its price target for Green Plains. Archer Daniels Midland reported disappointing earnings due to unfavorable biofuels prices, further highlighting the bleak outlook for ethanol margins, resulting in a nearly 8 percent decrease in its shares, which were priced at $32.73, marking the company’s worst daily performance in four and a half years. Iowa, as the leading ethanol-producing state, continues to be a bastion of support for the RFS, which contributes over $4.9 billion, or 3.5 percent, to the state’s gross domestic product. Ethanol has already integrated into the transportation fuel framework, accounting for about 10 percent of blended gasoline. Some analysts assert that a substantial portion of Iowa voters still back the RFS. Eric Branstad, who leads the pro-RFS organization America’s Renewable Future in Iowa, remarked on Monday evening that despite Cruz’s position potentially harming the state’s economy, "We feel good about our results." He added, "The vast majority of our candidates and the vast majority of caucus-goers realize the economic, national security, and environmental benefits of the RFS."

text: The legal dispute concerning a transgender bathroom law in North Carolina intensified on Monday, as the U.S. government and state officials filed lawsuits against each other, accusing one another of infringing on civil rights and overstepping authority. The Justice Department's lawsuit requested that a federal district court in North Carolina recognize that the state is in violation of the 1964 Civil Rights Act and mandate an end to the enforcement of the bathroom restriction. Earlier that day, North Carolina's Republican governor, Pat McCrory, along with the state’s secretary of public safety, initiated legal action in a separate federal court in North Carolina, claiming that the federal agency is engaging in “baseless and blatant overreach.” Known as HB 2 and enacted in March, the controversial bathroom law restricts individuals from utilizing public restrooms that do not align with their biological sex. This legislation has placed North Carolina at the forefront of a national discourse regarding equality and privacy, potentially leading to an extensive and expensive legal confrontation with the federal government. According to a poll conducted by Reuters/Ipsos, American opinions are split on the restroom usage by transgender individuals, with 44 percent advocating for use according to biological sex while 39 percent support using facilities that correspond to one's identified gender. By enacting this law, North Carolina became the first state to prohibit individuals from accessing multiple-occupancy restrooms or changing rooms in public facilities and educational institutions that do not correspond to the sex listed on their birth certificate. U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch stated on Monday that her department “retains the option” to curb federal funding to North Carolina should the state fail to retract the law. “No one can remain passive when a state decides to legislate identity and demands that individuals act as if they are someone they are not,” Lynch remarked during a press conference, drawing parallels between this law and discriminatory statutes from the Jim Crow era as well as prohibitions on same-sex marriage. Lynch also mentioned that the department is keeping an eye on other states that have enacted or are considering similar legislation, though she refrained from indicating whether actions would be taken against those jurisdictions. White House spokesperson Josh Earnest characterized the North Carolina law as “mean-spirited,” while McCrory defended his position in the lawsuit by describing the legislation as a “common sense privacy policy.” Supporters of the law in North Carolina argue that it prevents men from pretending to be transgender in order to enter women’s restrooms. An analysis from the University of California, Los Angeles Law School suggested that North Carolina could forfeit $4.8 billion in funding, primarily in educational grants, if it does not reverse its stance. The Justice Department's legal action identifies the state of North Carolina, Governor McCrory, the Department of Public Safety, and the University of North Carolina system as defendants. The University of North Carolina system, comprising 17 campuses, emphasized its commitment to federal non-discrimination regulations while also being obligated to comply with state laws such as HB 2. “In such a situation, the University finds itself genuinely in a difficult position,” UNC President Margaret Spellings expressed. McCrory informed the media that the law was a response to an ordinance passed by the Charlotte city council, which permitted transgender individuals to access bathrooms based on their gender identity in both public and private facilities. “We are taking the Obama administration to court. They are bypassing Congress and trying to alter laws and policies for the entire nation, not just North Carolina,” McCrory tweeted. Additionally, the Republican leaders of North Carolina's state legislature initiated their own lawsuit against the U.S. government concerning the law on the same day that McCrory filed his case. Critics, including the American Civil Liberties Union, are also contesting the law in federal district court.

The U.S. Justice Department’s complaint asked a federal district court in North Carolina to declare that the state is violating the 1964 Civil Rights Act and order it to stop enforcing the ban. Hours earlier, North Carolina’s Republican governor, Pat McCrory, and the state’s secretary of public safety sued the agency in a different federal court in North Carolina, accusing it of “baseless and blatant overreach.” The so-called bathroom law, passed in March and known as HB 2, prohibits people from using public restrooms not corresponding to their biological sex. North Carolina stands to lose $4.8 billion in funds, mainly educational grants, if it does not back down, according to an analysis by lawyers at the University of California, Los Angeles Law School. The Justice Department’s complaint named the state of North Carolina, McCrory, the state’s Department of Public Safety and the University of North Carolina system as defendants. The 17-campus University of North Carolina system says it takes federal non-discrimination laws very seriously but must also adhere to state laws like HB 2.     “In these circumstances, the University is truly caught in the middle,” UNC President Margaret Spellings said. McCrory told reporters that North Carolina had been forced to pass the law after the Charlotte city council passed an ordinance that allowed transgender people access to bathrooms based on gender identity in public and private buildings.   “We’re taking the Obama admin to court. That lawsuit came hours after North Carolina Governor Pat McCrory sued the Justice Department, accusing it of overreaching after federal lawyers said the state’s law requiring public bathroom use based on birth gender was a civil rights violation.    In Florida, Marion County Public Schools showed no sign of backing down from a resolution passed in April requiring students to use the bathroom that corresponds with the gender on their birth certificate. “I don’t believe our board will reverse the decision unless it is instructed by the courts,” the school system’s spokesman Kevin Christian said in a telephone interview. Mississippi’s Department of Education said it would comply with the federal guidance. New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio signed an executive order in March allowing a person of any gender to choose whether to use a men’s or women’s toilet or locker room in all municipal properties including public parks, pools, and playgrounds. The order requires city agencies to post the policy in conspicuous locations within three months and to train all employees within two years. New York City’s action came a week after South Dakota Governor Dennis Daugaard vetoed a bill that would have made the state the first to limit transgender students to bathrooms and locker rooms that correspond with their birth gender. In November, Houston voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure known as the “bathroom ordinance” that would have established non-discrimination protections for gay and transgender people. Officials from the organization, which has been a long-standing target for those against its abortion services, view this development as a short-term reprieve rather than the conclusion of ongoing threats to its survival. Leaders within Planned Parenthood expect that Republicans will continue to seek ways to limit its involvement in federally funded public health programs, a crucial source of its financial support. This turn of events represents a significant setback for Republican President Donald Trump, as House leaders decided to pull the healthcare bill after a revolt from both moderate Republicans and the party's most conservative members, resulting in a lack of necessary votes. In response to this situation, Planned Parenthood officials are scheduled to gather in Washington next week to strategize for the forthcoming challenges they anticipate in what they expect to be a prolonged battle. "It’s one good night’s sleep, and then we have to see what they are going to cook up," stated Chris Charbonneau, the chief executive of Planned Parenthood of the Great Northwest and the Hawaiian Islands, during a phone interview. Many Republicans hold opposing views towards the organization, with some citing religious reasons, as its healthcare offerings include abortion services, even though federal law prohibits it from receiving federal funding or reimbursement for abortions. text: In a recent statement, President Donald Trump expressed concerns regarding the treatment of the United States under the Paris Climate Agreement. During an interview with Reuters on Thursday, he indicated that he would reveal his decision about whether to continue U.S. participation in the accord within approximately two weeks. Trump, who took office as a Republican in November, had previously promised to exit the Paris agreement within his first 100 days, a part of his broader agenda to eliminate environmental regulations established by the Obama administration, which he claimed were detrimental to the economy. However, he has now indicated a willingness to remain in the agreement if the U.S. can secure more favorable terms. Numerous large American corporations and several Republican legislators have urged him to remain in the agreement to safeguard U.S. industrial interests abroad. As he approaches the 100-day milestone of his presidency this Saturday, Trump reiterated his position during the interview, remarking, "we want to be treated fairly." He also expressed dissatisfaction that countries like China, India, and Russia were contributing disproportionately less to assist poorer nations in combating climate change through the Green Climate Fund. "It's not a fair situation because they are paying virtually nothing and we are paying massive amounts of money," Trump stated. When prompted for insights into his forthcoming decision, he emphasized, "I can say this, we want to be treated fairly." An administration insider previously informed Reuters that officials from the Trump administration are expected to convene in May to deliberate on the United States’ involvement in the climate agreement, following an initial meeting that took place Thursday at the White House. The advisory group, which includes Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, Energy Secretary Rick Perry, and National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster, aims to reach a conclusion prior to the Group of Seven summit scheduled for May 26, the source disclosed. Tillerson, who formerly led Exxon Mobil Corp, along with Perry, has advocated for the nation to remain within the agreement. According to an external source, McMaster shares this perspective. Conversely, opponents of the deal include Scott Pruitt, head of the Environmental Protection Agency and a former attorney general from oil-rich Oklahoma, as well as Steve Bannon, the chief strategist at the White House. The Paris agreement was established by nearly 200 nations to mitigate climate change by reducing carbon dioxide emissions and investing in renewable energy sources. Many corporations, including BP Plc and Microsoft Corp, have appealed for the United States to uphold its commitment to the agreement to maintain their competitive edge. On Thursday, a collective of nine Republican lawmakers called on Trump to adhere to the agreement while simultaneously advocating for a reduction in the U.S. commitment to decrease greenhouse gas emissions. Congressman Kevin Cramer from North Dakota, an oil-producing state, along with eight other Republican representatives, sent a letter to Trump encouraging him to leverage the United States’ position at the Paris negotiations to advocate for the interests of American businesses, particularly in the manufacturing and fossil fuel industries. In the event that the U.S. decides to remain a part of the 2015 agreement, the letter suggested that Washington should propose a new pledge for emission reductions that would not harm the economy. This letter was penned by Cramer, who provided Trump with counsel on energy and climate issues during the 2016 presidential campaign. Former President Barack Obama, Trump's Democratic predecessor, had committed to a 26 percent to 28 percent reduction in U.S. greenhouse gas emissions from 2005 levels by 2025. The scientific consensus indicates that it is essential to decrease greenhouse gas emissions to mitigate the impacts of climate change, which include rising sea levels, extreme heatwaves, and severe storms and droughts. The Republican legislators also asserted that the U.S. should maintain its involvement with the Green Climate Fund but refrain from making additional financial contributions to it. In 2014, Obama had pledged $3 billion to this fund and contributed $1 billion, with the final $500 million payment occurring during his last days in office.

text: At a conference organized by former Republican nominee Mitt Romney, Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co's CEO Meg Whitman expressed her disapproval of Donald Trump as the party's nominee for president, likening him to historical fascist figures Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini, as reported by media outlets and corroborated by two sources. This statement was made during a Friday event in Park City, Utah, where she confronted U.S. Speaker of the House of Representatives Paul Ryan regarding his support for Trump, as detailed by the Washington Post on Saturday. Two individuals present at the confidential gathering confirmed Whitman’s remarks to Reuters. Attempts to reach Whitman for immediate comment were unsuccessful. A billionaire who initially backed the unsuccessful campaign of New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, Whitman has been actively engaged in efforts to thwart Trump’s nomination, which includes fundraising for an anti-Trump Super PAC. Earlier this year, in February, the technology leader labeled Trump as “unfit” for the presidency. text: The city of Frankfurt is preparing to carry out a massive evacuation as officials work to disarm a large World War Two bomb. Authorities have cautioned that if residents do not comply with evacuation orders, the financial hub of Germany could face significant disruptions on Monday. The operation, which is the largest of its kind since the war, will involve the relocation of around 60,000 individuals starting Sunday to facilitate the bomb defusing at a construction site in Frankfurt's affluent Westend area, known for its wealthy banking community. During a press briefing held on Friday, fire and police leaders stated that they would resort to force and detainment if necessary to ensure that the area is cleared. Frankfurt's fire chief, Reinhard Ries, informed the press that an uncontrolled detonation of the bomb has the potential to devastate an entire city block. He mentioned that the device contains over 1.4 tonnes of explosives, adding that the threat comes not only from flying debris but also from the pressure generated, which could dismantle all structures within a 100-metre (yard) radius. The HC 4000 bomb is believed to have been dropped by the Royal Air Force of Britain during the 1939-45 conflict. Discoveries of such munitions are not uncommon, yet it is rare to encounter unexploded ordnance of this size in such a critical location. The mandatory evacuation zone spans 1.5 km (about a mile) around the bomb and encompasses vital areas, including police headquarters, two hospitals, transportation networks, and Germany's central bank, which stores $70 billion in gold reserves. Authorities urged residents of Frankfurt to vacate the vicinity by 8 a.m. on Sunday, cautioning that the operation could require a minimum of 12 hours. Police indicated that they would only commence the bomb disarming once they confirmed that everyone had evacuated the area. To assist in identifying remaining individuals, they plan to ring doorbells and utilize heat-sensing equipment from helicopters above. Roadways and public transport systems, including sections of the underground, will be closed during the operation and for at least two hours after the bomb is neutralized to ensure safe transportation of patients back to hospitals without traffic delays. Furthermore, air traffic control informed Reuters that flights from Frankfurt airport may be impacted if there is an easterly wind on Sunday. Additionally, the authorities announced that small private aircraft, helicopters, and drones would be prohibited from entering the evacuation zone. Residents of Frankfurt will have the option to spend the day at designated shelters established at the trade fair and the Jahrhunderthalle convention center. Moreover, many museums are offering free admission on Sunday to Frankfurt residents, with some opening earlier than usual, as stated on the city's official website.
