text: In a bid to recover from last year’s presidential loss, Democrats have achieved a series of electoral victories for statehouse positions, testing the waters with a fresh group of candidates and activists who are eager to oppose President Donald Trump’s right-leaning policies. Across the United States, from New Hampshire to Oklahoma, Democrats have successfully transformed eight seats that were previously held by Republicans in special legislative elections, having invested millions in these contests that typically see low voter turnout, primarily focused on local matters. These victories illustrate the determination of Democrats to counter the setbacks faced during the Trump administration, especially after suffering significant losses in statehouses. Nonetheless, the party encounters obstacles in maintaining this momentum as they approach the 2018 midterm elections, where thousands of positions will be contested, as noted by discussions with nearly two dozen Democratic leaders and political experts. "Can we attract sufficient capable candidates, and can we conduct enough contemporary campaigns?" posed Simon Rosenberg, a strategist affiliated with the Democratic Party. He emphasized the necessity of evaluating potential future leaders in real-world scenarios. "Are they prepared? The response is: We are uncertain." November will present an initial gauge of progress. A significant evaluation will occur in Washington state, where Manka Dhingra, a first-time candidate, is contesting for a senate seat in the suburbs of Seattle. A win on November 7 would grant Democrats complete control of the state. Dhingra, who is a prosecutor as well as a parent volunteer in schools, is a Sikh Indian American whose political engagement was sparked by businessman Trump’s unexpected triumph over seasoned politician Hillary Clinton. However, Dhingra intentionally avoids mentioning the president in her appeal to undecided voters. "The reaction to Trump serves to energize volunteers," Dhingra remarked. "Many, including myself, have resolved that we cannot remain passive observers." Approximately 2,000 volunteers have registered through her campaign site, reflecting what the party describes as unprecedented enthusiasm for legislative races. In an August primary, Dhingra outperformed her Republican rival by 10 points, with a turnout that was relatively strong, drawing nearly 6,000 voters who typically abstain from primaries. Conversely, outside of Washington state, a handful of Democratic victories will have minimal impact on the political landscape as the 2018 midterm elections approach. Currently, Republicans maintain control over 26 state governments and two-thirds of the legislative chambers. During President Barack Obama’s two terms, Democrats lost significant influence at the state level as their focus shifted toward national elections. Presently, Democrats regard statehouses as vital for recovery and as a chance to promote legislation that opposes Trump’s efforts to dismantle Democratic healthcare reforms, environmental protections, and stringent immigration policies. The party intends to mobilize hundreds of thousands of volunteers to reach out to over 30 million voters—doubling their engagement efforts in statehouse races compared to the 2016 presidential election cycle. "Due to the stalemate in Washington, individuals are increasingly looking to state governments for protection from Donald Trump," stated Jessica Post, who serves as the executive director of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee. Yet, the numerous inexperienced Democratic candidates must confront seasoned incumbents in the upcoming elections, which are expected to see higher voter turnout. "If Democrats capitalize on every bit of momentum and envision the most favorable scenario, they might shift us from super majorities to mere majorities," explained David Avella, chair of the Republican organization GOPAC. "Nevertheless, we will still hold majorities." In 2017, Democrats flipped legislative seats in states such as Florida, Oklahoma, New Hampshire, and New York. On the other hand, Republicans secured an uncontested seat in Louisiana. In Oklahoma, where Trump garnered 65 percent of the vote during the 2016 general election, Democrats flipped three seats in districts he won. Candidates focused heavily on local concerns, such as a budget crisis that led to four-day school weeks. They had the opportunity to present themselves as relatable individuals rather than merely political figures.
source_text: Democrats rising? Early statehouse wins test new faces. (Reuters) - Democrats desperate to rebuild after losing the White House last year have scored a string of election victories for statehouse seats, testing a new generation of candidates and activists eager to resist President Donald Trump’s conservative agenda. From New Hampshire to Oklahoma, Democrats have flipped eight Republican-held seats in special legislative elections, having spent millions of dollars on low-turnout contests mostly being fought over local issues. The wins showcase how Democrats want to fight back after losing to Trump and hitting historic lows in statehouses. But the party faces challenges carrying this momentum into the 2018 midterm elections when thousands of seats are at stake, interviews with nearly two dozen Democratic leaders, campaigns and other political experts show. “Can we recruit enough capable candidates, and can we run enough modern races?” asked Simon Rosenberg, a Democratic political strategist. He said the party must test its future leaders in real time. “Are they ready? The answer is: We don’t know.” In November, Democrats will get an early read.  One critical test is in Washington state, where first-time candidate Manka Dhingra is running for an up-for-grabs senate seat in Seattle’s suburbs. A victory on Nov. 7 would give Democrats full control of the state.     A prosecutor and school parent volunteer, Dhingra is a Sikh Indian American whose political awakening began with businessman Trump’s surprise election victory over experienced politician Hillary Clinton. Still, Dhingra steers clear of mentioning the president in her pitch to swing voters. “The Trump reaction, the way it works is by invigorating volunteers,” Dhingra said. “There are a lot of people, like myself, who decided we cannot be bystanders.” Nearly 2,000 volunteers have signed up through her campaign website alone, evidence of what the party calls unprecedented interest in legislative contests.  An August primary, where Dhingra finished 10 points ahead of her Republican competitor, had a relatively robust turnout, including nearly 6,000 voters who normally skip primaries. Outside of Washington state, however, a few Democratic wins  will do little to change the political map going into the 2018 midterm elections. Republicans control 26 state governments and two-thirds of legislative chambers. Democrats hemorrhaged power at the state level during President Barack Obama’s eight years in office with their attention on national elections. Now Democrats see the states as critical for rebuilding, and an opportunity to advance legislation pushing back against Trump’s agenda of gutting Democratic health care reforms and environmental protections and cracking down on immigration. The party plans to recruit hundreds of thousands of volunteers to contact more than 30 million voters - double their outreach in statehouse contests in the 2016 presidential cycle.  “Because of the gridlock in Washington, people are turning to statehouses for security from Donald Trump,” said Jessica Post, executive director of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee. But the party’s many inexperienced candidates must beat battle-tested incumbents in elections next year with greater voter turnout.     “If the Democrats have every bit of momentum and the wildest day they could think of, they may take us from super majorities to majorities,” said David Avella, chairman of the Republican group GOPAC. “But we will still have majorities.” Democrats have flipped legislative seats in Florida, Oklahoma, New Hampshire and New York in 2017. Republicans picked up an uncontested seat in Louisiana. In Oklahoma, where Trump won 65 percent of the vote in the 2016 general election, the Democrats flipped three seats in districts he carried. Candidates doubled down on local issues, such as a budget crisis forcing four-day school weeks. They had a chance to “represent themselves as real people that weren’t actually attached to Nancy Pelosi, or Hillary Clinton, or Barack Obama,” said Anna Langthorn, Oklahoma Democratic Party chairwoman. Some of the special elections success reflects startup progressive groups rallying voters. But they have yet to figure out how to expand their scope for 2018. Chris Walsh, a cofounder of Flippable, which is working to win back state governments, went to Florida last month to help Democrat Annette Taddeo beat a Republican former legislator who once competed on Trump’s reality TV show, “The Apprentice.” “There is a lot of knowledge out there that is siloed,” Walsh said, adding the party could help by sharing information such as district voting data with new groups.  This year’s most revealing contests will come in a statewide election in Virginia, where Democrats face a long-shot bid in November to pick up 17 seats and take back the House of Delegates. In a show of enthusiasm to rebuild, the party is fielding a ticket that is more than 50 percent larger than two years ago. Yet fewer than one in four of the mostly women vying for Republican-held seats have raised more money than their competitors, Virginia Public Access Project data showed. Republicans are also ramping up in defense. They anticipate state contests will be central to Democratic efforts in 2018, given their longer odds of reclaiming the Republican-controlled U.S. Congress.     “The Democrats are trying to probe for the weakest link, and they are looking for that at the state level,” said Matt Walter, president of the Republican State Leadership Committee. “It is our job to make sure that doesn’t happen.”

text: In a recent development, Grace Mugabe, the First Lady of Zimbabwe, has refuted allegations that she assaulted South African model Gabriella Engels using an electric cable during an incident at a hotel suite in Johannesburg last month. Mugabe claims that it was Engels, who was reportedly intoxicated and unstable, that attacked her with a knife. This information comes from a deposition dated August 17, which has been exclusively accessed by Reuters, where Mugabe presents herself as the victim after stepping in to help her sons, Chatunga and Robert Junior, who were involved with a drunken young woman. The 52-year-old Grace Mugabe, who is a potential successor to her 93-year-old husband as President of Zimbabwe, is contemplating pursuing attempted murder charges against Engels. A representative group for Engels has dismissed Mugabe’s claims, labeling them as falsehoods. According to Engels, the incident occurred when an enraged Mugabe entered the room where she was with two friends waiting to meet Chatunga on August 13 and began to strike her with an electric cable. Photographic evidence provided by Engels' mother shortly after the event displayed wounds on the model's head, alongside bruises on her thighs. In her statement, Mugabe rejected the narrative put forth by Engels, describing it as malicious and stated that she was attacked while attempting to assist her sons. The deposition indicated that she was concerned for their safety, which prompted her visit to their hotel suite. Upon her arrival, it was alleged that Engels, in a state of intoxication and disarray, assaulted Dr. Grace Mugabe with a knife after being asked to leave the premises. Consequently, security personnel were left with no alternative but to escort Engels out of the hotel suite. Furthermore, the statement insinuated that Engels had engaged in a confrontation with other women at Johannesburg's Taboo nightclub the night before, suggesting that this altercation might have contributed to her injuries. Afriforum, a civil society organization representing Engels, refuted both claims. They stated, "Gabriella never attacked Grace Mugabe in any way and she did not participate in the fight at Taboo." They continued by asserting that Grace Mugabe is attempting to evade accountability for her violent actions by fabricating a narrative that positions the victim as the aggressor. Grace Mugabe was granted diplomatic immunity by South Africa, which enabled her to avoid immediate legal action for the alleged assault. However, Engels and Afriforum have contested this ruling, claiming that Mugabe was not in South Africa for official purposes. They have also asserted that assault constitutes a serious crime that should not fall under the protections of diplomatic immunity. The decision to allow Grace Mugabe to return to Zimbabwe has sparked controversy in South Africa, leading the opposition party, the Democratic Alliance, to pursue legal action to challenge the immunity decision. Documents from Zimbabwean intelligence, reviewed by Reuters, indicated that Robert Mugabe had lobbied his South African counterpart, Jacob Zuma, to resolve the matter amicably and outside of court. Gerrie Nel, an Afriforum attorney recognized for his prosecution of South African athlete Oscar Pistorius concerning the shooting of his girlfriend, indicated last month that Engels had been offered a cash settlement but had declined it. The intelligence document is part of a larger collection of numerous files originating from Zimbabwe's Central Intelligence Organisation (CIO) since 2009. The original author or intended audience of these files remains unverified by Reuters. According to the August 30 report, Mugabe has shifted his stance regarding the situation, now supporting Grace while accusing Engels of misconduct. The report concluded, "Mugabe wants people to stop denigrating his wife and labeling her with derogatory names." Mugabe believes that his wife reacted in a typical angry manner, akin to how any woman might respond in a similar situation.

text: On Tuesday, the United States took steps to impose sanctions on 13 organizations based in China and North Korea, which Washington claims are aiding in circumventing nuclear limitations aimed at Pyongyang and are facilitating trade in commodities such as coal. The U.S. Treasury's announcement came just a day after President Donald Trump reinstated North Korea on the list of state sponsors of terrorism, as noted on its official website. These new restrictions reflect the Trump administration's strategy to disrupt trade between China and North Korea, which is viewed as a crucial element in preventing Pyongyang from achieving its goal of developing a nuclear missile capable of reaching the United States. Treasury Secretary Steven T. Mnuchin stated, "This designation will impose further sanctions and penalties on North Korea and related persons, and supports our maximum pressure campaign to isolate the murderous regime." Among the latest sanctions were the blacklisting of three Chinese firms: Dandong Kehua Economy & Trade Co., Dandong Xianghe Trading Co., and Dandong Hongda Trade Co. The Treasury Department reported that these companies engaged in over $750 million worth of trade with North Korea over a period of nearly five years, concluding on August 31. The firms were involved in trading coal, iron ore, lead, zinc, silver ore, and ferrous products, in addition to notebook computers. Sun Sidong and his company, Dandong Dongyuan Industrial Co., were also included in the sanctions. A report issued in June by the Washington-based think tank C4ADS indicated that this company is part of a complex network of Chinese businesses that significantly contribute to trade with North Korea. U.S. officials have consistently focused on targeting individuals and companies from Dandong, a Chinese city adjacent to North Korea, in an effort to diminish Pyongyang's major revenue streams derived from the sale of natural resources like coal. In response to the U.S. actions, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lu Kang reiterated Beijing's stance against unilateral sanctions imposed by other nations, asserting that China is capable of investigating any violations of its laws or international obligations on its own. Lu mentioned during a daily press briefing on Wednesday, "If other parties wish to have effective cooperation with China on this issue and really have a grasp of certain matters, they can totally share intelligence with China and cooperate with China to appropriately handle the issue." The immediate effects on the sanctioned companies may be minimal, as commerce between China and its reclusive northern neighbor has significantly decreased since the United Nations imposed a ban in September on North Korean exports of various goods, including coal, iron, iron ore, lead, lead ore, and seafood. Additionally, in February, China banned coal imports from North Korea. Anthony Ruggiero, a North Korea specialist at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, noted that financial regulations are not strictly enforced in the Dandong region, which attracts businesses looking to profit from sales to North Korea. The recent sanctions have also targeted several North Korean enterprises that deploy workers to nations such as Russia, Poland, Cambodia, and China. U.S. authorities indicated that they aim to eliminate the revenue North Korea generates from labor exports. In addition to focusing on sources of weapons technology, these restrictions mark the first time that the United States has attempted to directly impact North Korea's everyday consumer trade, according to Peter Harrell, an expert on sanctions at the Center for a New American Security. Harrell stated, "We are sanctioning companies involved in ordinary trade. That’s the logical next step." The objective of the sanctions is to further isolate Pyongyang, as explained by Heather Nauert, a spokeswoman for the State Department, who added that she does not believe that targeting more Chinese companies will hinder Beijing's collaboration regarding the North Korean situation. "I don’t think it jeopardizes anything," she said. "I think the world has come together on this issue. We have a good relationship with China. That’s not going to change."

Besides targeting sources of weapons technology, the curbs were the first time the United States sought to directly attack North Korea s daily consumer trade, said Peter Harrell, a sanctions expert at the Center for a New American Security.   We are sanctioning companies involved in ordinary trade,  Harrell said.  That s the logical next step.  The sanctions aim to further isolate Pyongyang, said Heather Nauert, a State Department spokeswoman, adding that she did not think targeting more Chinese firms would affect Beijing s cooperation on the North Korean issue.  I don t think it jeopardizes anything,  she said.  I think the world has come together on this issue.  We have a good relationship with China. That s not going to change.

text: During a news conference in Canada on Wednesday, U.S. President Barack Obama expressed his frustration with the characterization of Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump as a populist. The Democratic leader, who has openly criticized the wealthy businessman’s language, concluded his remarks with an extensive discussion on the qualities that define an authentic leader eligible for the populist label. text: A lawsuit has been initiated that could potentially revive a segment of U.S. President Barack Obama’s immigration policy aimed at protecting millions from deportation. On Thursday, advocates for immigration rights took the unusual step of filing a legal challenge against the nationwide scope of a judicial ruling that had previously blocked the initiative. The attorneys behind the lawsuit believe that favorable outcomes in court could eventually dismantle the decisions that have prevented the full implementation of Obama’s November 2014 proposal. This initiative was designed to allow as many as four million undocumented individuals to gain work authorization if fully executed. The legal action was submitted in a federal court in New York, representing Martin Batalla Vidal, a 25-year-old immigrant from Mexico who has resided in the U.S. since the age of seven and has previously benefited from the program. Initially granted a three-year work permit, Vidal's authorization was rescinded following a Texas judge’s ruling in February 2015 that halted Obama’s initiative. This ruling was contested by Texas along with 25 other states. However, Vidal remains eligible for a two-year work authorization under an earlier program, which remains unchallenged and not affected by the injunction. Lawyers from the National Immigration Law Center, representing Vidal, argue that a victory could have significant repercussions, potentially reinstating Obama’s program for up to 60 percent of eligible applicants in regions not encompassed by the Texas ruling. The Texas judge’s decision was confirmed upon appeal. On June 23, the Supreme Court reached a 4-4 deadlock regarding the case, which upheld the appellate court's ruling. The court is currently one justice short due to the passing of Justice Antonin Scalia in February, and it is deliberating on whether to revisit the case once it has a complete bench.

With favorable court rulings, the lawyers filing the lawsuit say it has the long-term potential to unravel decisions that blocked Obama’s November 2014 plan nationwide. The White House program, if it had been fully implemented, could have allowed up to four million people with no legal immigration status to obtain work authorization. The lawsuit was filed in federal court in New York on behalf of Martin Batalla Vidal, 25, an immigrant from Mexico who has lived in the United States since he was seven and has benefited from the program.  He initially received a three-year work authorization, which has now been revoked due to a Texas judge’s ruling in February 2015 that blocked Obama’s plan. Texas and 25 other states had challenged it. Vidal would still be eligible for a two-year work authorization under an earlier program, which has not been challenged and was not covered by the injunction. Vidal’s lawyers at the National Immigration Law Center say that if he wins, the ruling could have broad implications because it could help to eventually reinstate Obama’s program for up to 60 percent of potential applicants in parts of the country not covered by the Texas ruling.  The Texas judge’s ruling was upheld on appeal. On June 23, the Supreme Court deadlocked 4-4 on the case, leaving the appeals court decision in place.  The court is currently one justice short following the death of Justice Antonin Scalia in February. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether to rehear the case once it has a full complement of justices.

text: Amid ongoing recovery efforts from Hurricane Maria, President Donald Trump announced on Thursday his intention to collaborate with the U.S. Congress to secure financial assistance for Puerto Rico. The territory has been grappling with significant challenges following the hurricane's devastating impact a month ago. Already facing a precarious financial situation due to prolonged economic downturns, Puerto Rico's damages from the storm have been estimated to reach as much as $95 billion. In light of this, the territory has requested the federal government to allow exceptions to regulations that typically require local and state governments to contribute to recovery costs. Trump did not provide details regarding the potential amounts of aid that may be allocated or lent to the financially strained territory, which is home to 3.4 million American citizens. "I have given my blessing to Congress, and Congress is working with you and your representatives on coming up with a plan and a payment plan and how it’s all going to be funded. Because you are talking about some substantial numbers," Trump conveyed to Puerto Rico Governor Ricardo Rossello during an Oval Office meeting. Last week, Trump and several senior advisors hinted that there could be limitations on the support Puerto Rico might receive from the federal government. However, on Thursday, the president's comments reflected a more supportive stance. The hurricane severely damaged the island’s power infrastructure, leading to the destruction of homes, roads, and other essential facilities. The territory, which is currently bankrupt, continues to face difficulties in providing basic services such as running water. An oversight committee tasked with addressing Puerto Rico’s financial crisis indicated that the island's government would deplete its funds by the end of the month without assistance. Trump reiterated that any federal loans and other storm-related debts incurred by Puerto Rico would need to be repaid before addressing the territory’s existing $72 billion in debt. "Any money that’s put in by people - whether it’s public or private - they’re going to want to come in first position," Trump remarked. "We’re going to come before - far before - any existing debt that’s on the island," he added. When asked whether Puerto Rico would have an easier path to recovery if it were a state rather than a territory, Trump chose not to comment, indicating, "You’ll get me into trouble with that question." While in Washington, Rossello also held discussions with Senate leaders. A vote is anticipated in the Senate within the next few days on a proposed aid package that allocates $18.7 billion to the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which has been instrumental in aiding recovery efforts in Texas, Florida, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands following three massive hurricanes. Some senators have expressed a desire to increase the funding available in that package, Senator John Thune, part of the Republican leadership, stated to reporters. Senator Marco Rubio, a Republican from Florida who has actively participated in the aid negotiations, mentioned earlier on Thursday that he aims to adjust the bill to facilitate faster access to funds for the island. Another aid package is expected to be reviewed by Congress by the end of December; however, Rubio warned that this timeline might be too late for Puerto Rico, which is currently devoid of tax revenue. "I know from experience the further away we get from these hurricanes, the less of a sense of urgency there is," Rubio explained. Rossello has sought the federal government's approval to utilize disaster relief funds for a wide range of expenses. Additionally, he has requested at least $4.6 billion in block grants and various forms of funding from the White House and Congress. "The reality is that we still need to do a lot more for the people of Puerto Rico and that’s why we’re meeting," Rossello asserted. "This is not over, not over by a long shot."

text: The upcoming visit of Benjamin Netanyahu to Washington, his first since the Trump administration began, presents a potential opportunity to heal the strained relationship with U.S. Democrats. However, many within the party express skepticism about any significant reconciliation due to Netanyahu's strong ties with Republican lawmakers. "There’s a lot of mending of fences that has to happen between the Netanyahu government and a lot of Democrats who feel like he unnecessarily politicized the U.S.-Israeli relationship,” remarked Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, who serves on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, during a phone call. The relationship hit a significant low point in March 2015, when Netanyahu chose to bypass the White House and the State Department to deliver a speech to a Congress controlled by Republicans. This speech was aimed at opposing the nuclear deal with Iran that President Barack Obama was negotiating at that time. Over 55 Democratic lawmakers from both the Senate and House, led by the Congressional Black Caucus, boycotted the address, perceiving it as a direct affront to Obama, who was the first African-American president of the United States. Despite nearly seventy years of bipartisan support for Israel within Congress, tensions between Netanyahu and Democratic lawmakers have persisted. Congress has historically utilized its funding authority to ensure Israel remains the largest beneficiary of annual U.S. military assistance. Following Trump’s inauguration last month, Netanyahu publicly praised Trump’s proposal to construct a wall intended to prevent individuals from Mexico from entering the U.S., a move that many Democrats view as an expensive and racially insensitive slight toward a neighboring ally. Additionally, numerous Democrats express concerns regarding Netanyahu's backing of new settlements on territories claimed by Palestinians and are apprehensive about rhetoric from certain members of his administration that opposes the establishment of a Palestinian state. Democrats have criticized their Republican counterparts for leveraging Israel as a divisive issue, even as Democrats have shown strong support for initiatives like the $38 billion military aid package that the Obama administration finalized in September. "It doesn’t look good or feel right when one party says, ‘Well, we’re better on Israel than the other party,’ or if one party is trying to work in lock-step with Israeli officials,” stated Representative Eliot Engel, the leading Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, in an interview with Reuters. Israeli officials conveyed that Netanyahu’s team recognizes the necessity to reestablish a sense of bipartisan cooperation, even while the prime minister attempts to forge a closer relationship with Trump. Requests for comments from aides accompanying Netanyahu were not answered on Tuesday. Nevertheless, prior to his departure for Washington, Netanyahu emphasized his intention to engage with leaders from both parties, indicating a potential shift toward balance. "The alliance between Israel and America has always been extremely strong. It’s about to get even stronger,” Netanyahu asserted to journalists.

text: The Pentagon has announced an indefinite postponement on implementing a ban regarding older types of cluster bombs, a decision officials attributed to insufficient advancements in munitions safety technology. This ban was scheduled to come into effect on January 1, 2019. Cluster bombs, which can be delivered by aircraft or artillery, disperse multiple bomblets over a large area, and they sometimes fail to detonate, making them hazardous remnants that are challenging to locate and remove. Consequently, this poses a risk of civilian casualties long after hostilities have concluded. The military had aimed to move towards cluster munitions that would explode with at least a 99 percent reliability rate, significantly lowering the associated dangers. However, as the deadline for the ban approaches, a spokesperson for the Pentagon informed Reuters that the development of safer alternatives has not progressed sufficiently to replace the current stockpiles. A memo outlining this shift in U.S. policy has been reviewed by Reuters, with confirmation from Pentagon officials regarding its contents. The memo states, "While the Department aims to deploy a new generation of highly reliable munitions, we cannot compromise mission success or invite the risk of increased casualties among military personnel and civilians by abandoning the most effective capabilities available." This document, which is anticipated to be signed by Deputy Defense Secretary Patrick Shanahan on Thursday, referred to cluster munitions as "legitimate weapons with clear military utility." The announcement of the updated policy has drawn sharp rebuke from both Congress and various human rights organizations. Senator Patrick Leahy, a Democrat who has been instrumental in efforts to limit the use of cluster bombs, expressed that the Pentagon is effectively "sustaining the use of an indiscriminate weapon that has been proven to have high failure rates." Senator Dianne Feinstein described the decision as "unbelievable." Human Rights Watch challenged the assertion that the U.S. military requires these weapons, noting that aside from a solitary strike in Yemen in 2009, there has been no use of cluster munitions since 2003 in Iraq. Mary Wareham, the arms division director at Human Rights Watch, stated, "We condemn this decision to reverse the long-standing U.S. commitment not to utilize cluster munitions that fail more than 1 percent of the time, leading to deadly unexploded submunitions." Tom Crosson, a Pentagon spokesperson, conceded that it has been many years since the military engaged in significant use of cluster munitions, and emphasized that the new policy focuses on a future transition to safer options. Nevertheless, it remains uncertain when the Pentagon will be compelled to cease the use of its existing stockpiles, as there must not only be more advanced munitions available, but also adequate quantities of new cluster bombs for U.S. inventories. The updated policy prohibits the Pentagon from acquiring any additional cluster bombs that do not conform to the newly established standards outlined in the memo. Furthermore, the new regulations expand the definition of what types of munitions qualify under the safety requirements beyond the 99 percent detonation success rate. According to the revised policy, the Pentagon deems bombs featuring advanced self-destruct or deactivation capabilities as acceptable for future procurement. Such munitions must fulfill a series of criteria, including a mechanism to render submunitions inoperative within 15 minutes after being armed. Additionally, the Pentagon's policy disallows the purchase of weaponry that is prohibited under the Convention on Cluster Munitions, which outright bans the use of these types of munitions but makes exceptions for certain categories that the Pentagon continues to categorize as cluster munitions.

text: On Monday, Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump alleged that the upcoming Nov. 8 election was manipulated against him, referencing studies that he claimed indicated widespread voter fraud, despite Republican attorneys dismissing his assertions as baseless. Trump, who is a businessman from New York entering the political arena for the first time, has attempted to instill concerns regarding a potentially flawed election as he trails behind Democrat Hillary Clinton in the polls. Speaking to a rally in Green Bay, Wisconsin, Trump stated, "They even want to try to rig the election at the polling place. So many cities are corrupt and voter fraud is very, very common." He pointed to research from Pew Trusts dating back to 2012, which urged updates to the voter registration system, highlighting that approximately 24 million registrations were inaccurate. (bit.ly/1HN4uTF) Additionally, he referenced a 2014 article by two political scientists published in the Washington Post, which suggested that non-citizens voting might have played a role in a few close Democratic wins during the 2008 elections, although the authors admitted their study's sample size was limited. (wapo.st/1pX17Bf) Numerous investigations have established that incidents of voter fraud in United States elections are extremely rare. Republican campaign attorney Chris Ashby remarked that Trump’s allegations could provoke unrest, labeling them as "unfounded" and "dangerous." In an interview, Ashby said, "When you say an election is rigged, you’re telling voters, your supporters, their votes do not matter. I think some of Donald Trump’s comments could cause unrest at the polls." Some members of the Republican Party have encouraged Trump to retract his claims. Early voting and mail-in voting have commenced in various states. Mark Braden, a partner at Baker and Hostetler and a former chief counsel for the Republican National Committee, asserted that any form of election manipulation on a national scale is "just impossible," citing the complex systems in place that would render such an act unfeasible. "Our system is principally a system based upon each side watching the other side," Braden noted during an interview. "Our system is dependent on local volunteer participation. Our system has worked very well because we have people who get involved in the process and perform these functions." Furthermore, Trump seized upon the release of documents from the Federal Bureau of Investigation on Monday, which he claimed revealed "felony corruption." text: The date for Lebanon's first legislative election in almost ten years has been officially set for May 6 of the coming year. BEIRUT (Reuters) - The announcement potentially has significant implications for a nation caught in the rivalry between Saudi Arabia and Iran. A decree was signed on Friday by Interior Minister Nohad Machnouk, thereby allowing the election to finally proceed. This vote has faced delays on three occasions since the last election held in 2009, with officials citing various reasons including security issues, political turmoil, and disagreements regarding the election law. In June, the coalition government led by Prime Minister Saad al-Hariri, which took office a year prior, reached an agreement on the new electoral law, but the formal announcement of the date was delayed as officials debated technical aspects and worked to register Lebanese citizens who reside abroad. Since the previous election, the political climate in Lebanon has changed significantly. The political alliance of Hariri, which has historically been supported by Saudi Arabia and is pro-Western, has fragmented. Over the past year, Hariri has managed a power-sharing government that incorporates the Iran-supported Shiite group Hezbollah, which is viewed unfavorably by Saudi leaders. Last month, Hariri ignited a political crisis by resigning during a visit to Riyadh, where he criticized Hezbollah and Iran. After spending two weeks abroad, he returned and subsequently retracted his resignation the following week. The electoral framework in Lebanon is notably intricate, designed to preserve civil order in a nation that has experienced numerous civil conflicts since gaining independence in 1943. The parliament, consisting of 128 members, is equally divided between 64 Christians from seven denominations and 64 Muslims, comprising equal numbers of Sunnis and Shiites. Districts in the country elect various lawmakers based on strict religious quotas. The president is always a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim, and the parliament speaker a Shiite Muslim, reflecting the three largest factions in parliament. The global community has consistently emphasized the necessity for Lebanon to conduct elections on schedule to rebuild trust in its institutions and ensure stability. Machnouk declared that Lebanese citizens living overseas would be able to participate in the voting process on April 22 and 28.

text: Business leaders were assured by Prime Minister Theresa May that a two-year transition period following Brexit is guaranteed, according to a source who spoke to Reuters. The discussions aimed to gather insights on what businesses expect from the upcoming negotiations concerning the UK's future relationship with the European Union after Brexit. Worries among businesses have intensified due to the sluggish pace of discussions and the looming possibility of the UK departing the trading bloc in 2019 without any new trade agreement. The transitional arrangement is seen by May as essential and non-negotiable, and she urged business leaders to consider the two-year timeframe as guaranteed. This assurance came from a source who relayed May's statements made during the meeting. A spokesperson for May confirmed her reiteration of the government's aim for a seamless and organized exit, ensuring that there would be only one set of changes affecting both businesses and individuals. Concerns over talent access post-Brexit were voiced by nearly all business leaders, with many expressing to May that investment decisions are approaching, particularly at the turn of 2017 and into 2018, as noted by the source. Last week, two insiders informed Reuters that Toyota (7203.T), the Japanese automotive manufacturer, plans to produce the next iteration of its Auris model at its facility in the UK, contingent upon the government securing a transitional Brexit agreement by the year's end. The source indicated that May emphasized the need for clarity for businesses. Meanwhile, the Chancellor remarked that clarity takes precedence over perfection. Business leaders have previously expressed frustration, noting that their concerns have been overshadowed by the internal strife and division within the government, and they have not received the certainty needed to make informed plans and investments. text: Questions have emerged regarding the understanding that President Donald Trump had about his tweets, following his personal attorney's defense of them. Legal experts have expressed skepticism concerning the arguments made by attorney John Dowd related to Trump’s Saturday tweet about former U.S. national security advisor Michael Flynn. In a statement to Reuters on Sunday, Dowd claimed responsibility for the tweet, stating he had "bollixed up" the president’s message, which indicated that Trump dismissed Flynn for lying to the FBI rather than merely misleading U.S. Vice President Mike Pence. Observers have pointed out that this tweet suggested Trump was aware of Flynn's criminal actions and attempted to obstruct justice, including the firing of then FBI director James Comey. Dowd refuted the idea that Trump was aware Flynn had lied to the FBI but also introduced new uncertainties by elaborating on the meetings from January in which former Acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates alerted White House Counsel Don McGahn that Flynn posed a security threat due to his dishonesty regarding conversations with former Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak. Dowd recounted that Yates informed McGahn that Flynn's statements to the FBI mirrored those given to Pence, yet she did not communicate that Flynn faced potential criminal charges. He asserted that McGahn conveyed this information to Trump in that manner. "You may conclude that’s a lie, but the Department of Justice, that had the power to charge, did not," Dowd stated. "The first time the president knows for a fact this guy lies was when he was charged." However, several legal professionals argued that, regardless of whether Yates explicitly indicated Flynn had lied to the FBI, the White House counsel should have recognized the possibility and informed the president accordingly. "It’s not every day that the acting attorney general comes over to the White House with that sort of message," noted Alex Whiting, a former federal prosecutor and current Harvard Law School educator. "It had to have been obvious to McGahn that Flynn probably lied to the FBI whether Yates said it or not." Michael Gerhardt, a law professor at the University of North Carolina, described Dowd’s reasoning as "a stretch" but acknowledged that there might be a "bit of credibility" in the notion that McGahn was waiting for more clarification before updating the president regarding Flynn’s legal troubles. Neither Yates nor McGahn could be reached for comments on Monday. Dowd also turned down requests for additional remarks on the same day. Yates’ testimony in May before a Senate committee, where she mentioned that she did not respond to McGahn’s inquiry about Flynn’s FBI interview, appears to contradict Dowd’s narrative. According to a source close to the situation, Yates never stated that Flynn told FBI agents the same thing he conveyed to Pence. Dowd maintained his version of the events. Last Friday, Flynn pleaded guilty to a charge of lying to the FBI, which was filed by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, who is investigating alleged Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible obstruction of justice by the Trump administration. Russia has denied any involvement in the 2016 U.S. election, and Trump has consistently rejected any allegations of collusion between Russia and his campaign. On Sunday, Dowd further contended that Trump could not commit obstruction of justice because "he’s the chief law enforcement officer of the U.S." Former prosecutor Robert Ray acknowledged that there was some validity to the argument that Trump could not obstruct justice by terminating Comey due to his authority in that regard. Nonetheless, several other attorneys disagreed with Dowd’s assertions, pointing out that President Richard Nixon was impeached for obstruction of justice prior to his resignation linked to the Watergate scandal. "It’s a patently absurd argument," remarked Andrew Wright, a former White House lawyer during President Barack Obama’s administration. "The president as the chief executive sits on top of the org chart, but he has to take care to see that the law is followed."

Neither Yates nor McGahn could be reached for comment on Monday. Dowd also declined requests for further comment on Monday. Yates’ testimony in May before a Senate committee, in which she said she declined to answer McGahn when he asked about Flynn’s FBI interview, appears to conflict with Dowd’s account. text: On November 27, a violent clash in a remote area known for its drug trafficking resulted in the deaths of thirteen individuals, including civilians, according to the ombudsman of Colombia. This confrontation involved combatants from the ELN, a rebel group, and dissidents from the FARC, which has since disbanded. The incident occurred in the southwestern region of Narino, an area notorious for its involvement in the cultivation, processing, and smuggling of coca, the fundamental ingredient for cocaine. Last year, a peace agreement was reached with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), bringing an end to over fifty years of conflict. Nevertheless, a variety of FARC dissidents, ELN fighters, right-wing former paramilitaries, and criminal organizations continue to operate within Colombia, vying for dominance over lucrative illicit mines and drug trafficking routes. Ombudsman Carlos Alfonso Negret reported that during the incident, ELN fighters launched an assault on members of the Rural Resistance, a group comprised of FARC dissidents who opted not to disarm following the peace agreement. Negret communicated to the press that after visiting the scene, his office confirmed the occurrence of gunfire between the Rural Resistance and the ELN. The crossfire resulted in the loss of thirteen lives. The report did not clarify how many of the deceased were civilians. This year, over 11,000 FARC members and their supporters surrendered their arms as part of the peace deal. The organization has retained its name as it transitioned into a political party. However, Negret indicated that approximately 800 former guerrillas chose not to demobilize, while other security experts estimate the number of dissident ex-FARC members to be between 700 and 1,300. The government and the ELN initiated their inaugural bilateral ceasefire in October as part of peace negotiations in Ecuador. This ceasefire is scheduled to last until January 9, with a possibility of extension. Negret indicated that this incident violated the ceasefire agreement, marking the second violent occurrence that has overshadowed the ceasefire, following the ELN's admission of responsibility for the killing of an indigenous leader in the troubled Choco province.
source_text: Shoot-out between Colombia rebels kills 13, government says. BOGOTA (Reuters) - Thirteen people, including civilians, were killed during a confrontation between Colombia s ELN rebels and dissidents from the now-demobilized FARC guerrilla group in a remote area known for drug trafficking, the country s ombudsman said on Tuesday. The incident took place on Nov. 27 in the southwestern Narino region, a place where crime gangs and rebel groups are known to grow, process and smuggle coca, the base ingredient in cocaine. A hard-won peace accord was agreed with the now-disbanded Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebel group last year, ending some five decades of war.  But an array of FARC dissidents, National Liberation Army (ELN) rebels, right-wing ex-paramilitaries and crime gangs are still active in Colombia, competing for control of lucrative illegal mines and drug trafficking routes.  In Narino, fighters from the ELN attacked members of the Rural Resistance, ombudsmen Carlos Alfonso Negret said in a report. The Rural Resistance are FARC dissidents who refused to demobilize following the peace deal.  The ombudsman s office visited the area and was able to determine that there was an exchange of fire between the group that calls itself Rural Resistance and the ELN,  Negret told journalists.  There was crossfire that killed 13 people.  Neither the report nor Negret specified how many of the dead were civilians. More than 11,000 fighters and collaborators from the FARC handed over their weapons this year as part of the peace accord. The group has kept its initials in its reincarnation as a political party. But Negret says some 800 former guerrillas did not demobilize, while other security sources and thinktanks put the number of dissident ex-FARC at between 700 and 1,300. The ELN and the government began their first ever bilateral ceasefire in October, part of peace talks taking place in Ecuador. The ceasefire is set to run through Jan. 9 and may be extended. The incident was a violation of the ceasefire, Negret said. It is the second act of violence which has overshadowed the ceasefire, after the ELN admitted to killing an indigenous leader in restive Choco province.

text: In a recent announcement, Donald Trump shared a list of potential nominees for the Supreme Court, which is made up entirely of conservative figures, some of whom have made controversial statements. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - In a legal argument presented to the U.S. Supreme Court back in 2003, William Pryor, then the attorney general of Alabama and currently a federal appeals court judge, advocated for the upholding of a Texas statute that prohibited homosexual relations. He contended that the U.S. Constitution does not guarantee individuals the right to choose their partners.  Pryor is among the 11 conservative judges that presumptive Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump has indicated he would consider nominating to the Supreme Court if he wins the election.  In a legal document submitted to the Supreme Court, Pryor articulated, “A constitutional right that protects ‘the choice of one’s partner’ and ‘whether and how to connect sexually’ must logically extend to activities like prostitution, adultery, necrophilia, bestiality, possession of child pornography, and even incest and pedophilia.”  With a history of making provocative comments, Pryor is not alone on Trump's list; other nominees share similar backgrounds. However, many of these judges have built solid conservative judicial credentials that would likely resonate with Senate Republicans, who hold the power to confirm Supreme Court appointments and have largely avoided inflammatory language.  On Wednesday, Trump revealed his list, which features judges who have shown support for various conservative initiatives and range in age from 41 to 58 years old, primarily from states governed by conservative or Republican leadership. All 11 nominees are white, with eight men and three women included.  The unveiling of this list appears to have calmed some conservatives who were uncertain whether Trump would select a true conservative for the Supreme Court, especially following the passing of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia in February.  Alabama Republican Jeff Sessions, a prominent supporter of Trump in the Senate, commented, “I’ve heard nothing but positive about this. People in the Senate say this is going to relieve a lot of people.”  The Republican-controlled Senate has declined to consider Democratic President Barack Obama’s nominee, Merrick Garland, arguing that the victor of the Nov. 8 election, which will determine Obama’s successor, should fill the vacancy. The appointment of Scalia’s replacement could influence the ideological dynamics of a court that is currently evenly divided, with four conservative justices and four liberals.  Don Willett, who serves as one of five state supreme court judges on Trump’s list, holds an elected position.  His campaign highlighted a 2012 advertisement stating, “Don Willett helped defend the right of Texas to display the (Bible’s) Ten Commandments and fought the liberals who tried to remove the words ‘under God’ from our pledge” of allegiance.  Prior to his judicial career, Willett was part of the Texas legal team that successfully contested a Supreme Court case allowing the Ten Commandments to be displayed on a monument at the state Capitol, despite objections from opponents who claimed it represented government endorsement of a religion.  During his tenure as Alabama’s attorney general from 1997 to 2004, Pryor referred to the landmark 1973 Supreme Court decision that legalized abortion across the country as “the worst abomination in the history of constitutional law.”  Several judges included on Trump’s list have rendered decisions against abortion and contraceptive rights.  Federal appeals court judges Diane Sykes, Steven Colloton, and Pryor all supported Christian objections concerning the mandate imposed by Obama’s healthcare law that required health insurance to cover birth control for women.  In 2012, federal appeals court judge Raymond Gruender authored a ruling that upheld a South Dakota law mandating doctors to inform patients that women who undergo abortions have a higher likelihood of committing suicide. Colloton, who serves on the same court, concurred with this opinion.  Similar to the debates surrounding abortion and contraception, the U.S. Supreme Court remains closely divided on the interpretation of the individual right to bear arms as articulated in the Second Amendment of the Constitution.  In a case from 2013, Thomas Hardiman, another federal appeals court judge, voiced dissent when the majority of his court upheld a New Jersey law regulating public handgun possession. Hardiman advocated for a broad reading of the right to bear arms.
source_text: Trump's Supreme Court list: all conservative, some provocative. Scroll to the bottom of the page for an interactive graphic.   WASHINGTON (Reuters) - William Pryor, in urging the U.S. Supreme Court in 2003 to uphold a Texas law banning gay sex, argued against the notion that the U.S. Constitution should safeguard a person’s choice of partners.  Pryor, who then was Alabama’s attorney general and now serves on a federal appeals court, was one of 11 conservative jurists who presumptive Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump has named as people he would consider nominating to the Supreme Court, if elected.  “A constitutional right that protects ‘the choice of one’s partner’ and ‘whether and how to connect sexually’ must logically extend to activities like prostitution, adultery, necrophilia, bestiality, possession of child pornography, and even incest and pedophilia,” Pryor said in a legal filing to the Supreme Court.  Pryor has a record of provocative remarks, as do some others on Trump’s list. But many have established solid conservative judicial records that likely would appeal to Republicans in the Senate, which has the power to confirm Supreme Court nominees, and have steered clear of inflammatory rhetoric.  Trump’s list, unveiled on Wednesday, included judges who have indicated support for various conservative causes, range in age from 41 to 58 and hail primarily from conservative and Republican-governed states. The eight men and three women all are white.  The list’s release seems to have reassured some conservatives who may have doubted Trump would name a genuine conservative to the high court, which has a vacancy following the February death of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia.  “I’ve heard nothing but positive about this. People in the Senate say this is going to relieve a lot of people,” said Republican Jeff Sessions of Alabama, a key Trump supporter in the Senate.  The Republican-led Senate has refused to consider Democratic President Barack Obama’s nominee, Merrick Garland, arguing the winner of the Nov. 8 election to determine Obama’s successor should get to fill the post. Scalia’s replacement could tip the ideological balance of the court, now evenly divided with four conservative justices and four liberals.  Don Willett of Texas is one of five state supreme court judges on the list. His job is an elected one.  “Don Willett helped defend the right of Texas to display the (Bible’s) Ten Commandments and fought the liberals who tried to remove the words ‘under God’ from our pledge” of allegiance, his campaign said in a 2012 advertisement.  Before becoming a judge, Willett was part of Texas’ legal team that won a Supreme Court battle to display the Ten Commandments on a monument in the state Capitol despite opponents’ concerns that it amounted to government endorsement of a religion.  During Pryor’s stint as Alabama attorney general from 1997 to 2004, he described the 1973 Supreme Court ruling legalizing abortion nationwide as “the worst abomination in the history of constitutional law.”  Some of the judges on Trump’s list have ruled against abortion and birth control rights.  Federal appeals court judges Diane Sykes, Steven Colloton and Pryor all ruled in favor of Christian objections to the mandate under Obama’s healthcare law that health insurance covers birth control for women.  Federal appeals court judge Raymond Gruender wrote a 2012 ruling upholding a South Dakota law that requires doctors to inform patients that women who have abortions are more likely to commit suicide. Colloton, who sits on the same court, joined the opinion.  As on abortion and contraception, the U.S. Supreme Court is closely divided on the scope of the individual right to bear arms under the Constitution’s Second Amendment.  In a 2013 case, Thomas Hardiman, another federal appeals court judge, dissented when the majority on his court upheld a New Jersey law regulating the possession of handguns in public. Hardiman endorsed a broad reading of Second Amendment gun rights that would protect carrying weapons outside the home for self-defense.  The list also includes David Stras, a member of Minnesota’s Supreme Court. In 2014, that court waded into the contentious subject of when a person who is incapacitated may be taken off life support and allowed to die.  The court ruled, in the case of a 57-year-old man with irreversible brain damage, that a guardian who was given medical-consent power could authorize the removal of life-sustaining treatment when “interested parties” agreed it would be in the incapacitated person’s best interest.  Stras dissented, writing that because the man had already died when the case was heard, the matter was moot and the court should have stayed out of it.

text: A report released on Monday has indicated that South Africa needs to increase its budget for higher education by approximately one-third, aiming for at least 1 percent of the gross domestic product. This recommendation stems from a commission appointed by President Jacob Zuma. The timing of this report coincided with the resignation of a senior Treasury official, who allegedly raised concerns about presidential interference in the budgetary process, and serious liquidity challenges being faced by state-owned utility Eskom. To fund its significant budget and current account deficits, South Africa heavily depends on foreign investment. As crucial credit rating assessments are due this month, investors are becoming increasingly anxious, especially with the ruling African National Congress poised to choose a successor for Zuma as party leader in December. The presidency stated that Zuma would address the findings of the higher education report once they have been reviewed by the ministers. The commission was established early last year in response to protests from university students advocating for free education. Following the announcement of the report, both the rand and benchmark bonds experienced a decline, although they remained relatively stable after the report's actual release. Analysts and currency traders noted that the market was awaiting the presidency’s response to the report, but expressed concerns that its recommendations could pose significant economic risks. "If we continue on this trajectory of escalating budget deficits, we are certainly on a path toward downgrades," warned Nicky Weimar, a senior economist at Nedbank. Last year, South Africa's GDP was around 4.3 trillion rand ($296.6 billion), meaning an increase of 0.25 percent of GDP in government spending on higher education would equate to about $750 million in additional funding. Furthermore, the commission suggested a cost-sharing model to finance all university students, where the government would back income-contingent loans provided by commercial banks. The report proposed that if a student does not achieve a specified income level, the government should take responsibility for repaying the tuition loan. Implementing these measures could complicate Treasury's efforts to manage a projected budget deficit exceeding 4 percent of GDP for the fiscal year 2017/18. However, the proposal could gain popularity among young voters and ANC supporters, many of whom feel that South Africa remains profoundly unequal even after more than two decades since apartheid ended in 1994. The next national election in South Africa is scheduled for 2019, and the ANC has witnessed a decline in its electoral majority during recent elections. Concerns have also risen within South African markets regarding the potential threat to the independence of financial institutions. Local media outlet Fin24 reported on Monday that Treasury Deputy Director-General Michael Sachs had resigned last week after expressing dissatisfaction with Zuma's interference in budget matters. Treasury confirmed the resignation of Sachs, stating only that he wished to contribute to the public sector in a different role. Earlier this year, international ratings agencies downgraded South Africa's debt after Zuma dismissed the well-regarded finance minister Pravin Gordhan in a sudden cabinet reshuffle. S&P Global and Moody's are anticipated to reassess the country's ratings on November 24, with particular attention on whether they will downgrade its local-currency rating to junk status following the disappointing medium-term budget forecasts unveiled by Gordhan's successor, Malusi Gigaba, last month. A downgrade to sub-investment grade could lead to forced sales of South African bonds worth up to $12 billion, adding further strain to the rand, which is currently at a 12-month low against the dollar. On Monday, the cost of insuring South Africa's debt reached a four-month high, indicating an increased probability of ratings downgrades.

text: NEW YORK (Reuters) - Advocates for gun safety are investing substantial amounts of money into initiatives in Maine and Nevada, aiming to enforce background checks on firearm sales. This push comes after numerous unsuccessful attempts to achieve similar reforms at the federal level. With the November 8 vote approaching, the significant financial support for these initiatives could represent a major triumph for gun control advocates, especially following the inability to pass national legislation after the tragic shooting that took the lives of 26 children and educators at a Newtown, Connecticut, elementary school in December 2012. Additionally, voters in California and Washington state will also participate in voting on gun control measures, and current opinion polls suggest favorable outcomes in all four states. Everytown for Gun Safety, an organization founded by billionaire Michael Bloomberg, who previously served as the mayor of New York City, is spearheading these efforts. They are channeling resources into three of the four ballot measures, with an overall budget of $25 million dedicated to this cause nationally. This amount is nearly equivalent to what the influential National Rifle Association has allocated for television ads supporting Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump. The Second Amendment of the U.S. Constitution guarantees the right to bear arms, and any attempts to impose limitations on this right face staunch resistance from gun rights advocates, who hold considerable sway within the Republican Party. If gun control supporters succeed in Maine and Nevada, it would mean that 50% of the U.S. population would reside in states that have adopted expanded background checks, including for private transactions that do not involve licensed dealers. Proponents of gun control argue that achieving this would be a significant symbolic and strategic milestone. Conversely, detractors of the proposed laws argue that they are poorly constructed, ineffective in reducing crime, and would unfairly penalize responsible gun owners. A poll conducted by the University of New Hampshire in late October indicated that 52% of residents in Maine support the measure, while 43% oppose it. In Nevada, two separate polls from late October demonstrated a 16-point and a 25-point lead in favor of the initiative, respectively. These measures emerge in a year where voters nationwide will consider a total of 71 citizen-led ballot initiatives covering various issues, such as marijuana legalization and raising the minimum wage, marking the highest number in a decade according to Ballotpedia.org, a site that monitors voting data. Everytown articulated its approach as part of a strategy to replicate the successful state-by-state campaign that legalized gay marriage across the country, given Congress's reluctance to enact universal background check legislation. "One of the significant benefits of directly appealing to the electorate is the ability to bypass legislative obstacles and create laws," stated Zach Silk, a consultant who has collaborated with Everytown in Nevada and previously oversaw the successful background-check ballot initiative in Washington state in 2014. Nevada has emerged as an especially costly battleground. Bloomberg has contributed nearly $10 million personally to the campaign in that state, while Nevadans for Background Checks had amassed $14.3 million by October 18. This figure is almost three times the $4.8 million collected by the leading opposition group, NRA Nevadans for Freedom, which has received all its funds from the NRA. In Maine, supporters of the background check initiative have outspent their opponents by over five to one, with the Everytown-supported Mainers for Responsible Gun Ownership Fund reporting $5.3 million in contributions as of last week. The NRA did not provide comments regarding its spending on the campaign. Critics have accused Bloomberg of attempting to purchase a victory. "This legislation is complicated and excessively regulatory," remarked David Trahan, the executive director of the Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine and a former state legislator. "It mirrors the mindset of the individual funding this initiative, Michael Bloomberg. His proposed solutions are excessive and verge on social engineering." However, Everytown remains steadfast in its commitment to the cause.

CLEVELAND (Reuters) - The head of the Cleveland police union on Sunday urged Ohio’s governor to declare a state of emergency and to suspend laws allowing the open carrying of firearms during the Republican National Convention, after the shooting of six police officers in Louisiana. “I don’t care what the legal precedent is, I feel strongly that leadership needs to stand up and defend these police officers,” Steve Loomis, the head of the police union, told Reuters in an interview at the union’s headquarters on Sunday. ANKARA (Reuters) - Turkey summoned the U.S ambassador on Monday to protest the treatment of Turkish security officials in the United States during a visit by President Tayyip Erdogan last week, the foreign ministry said. A brawl erupted between protesters and Turkish security personnel outside the Turkish ambassador’s residence during Erdogan’s visit to Washington to meet U.S. President Donald Trump. Turkey blamed the violence on demonstrators linked to the militant Kurdistan Workers Party while Washington’s police chief described the incident as a “brutal attack” on peaceful protesters. The U.S. State Department said in a statement the conduct of Turkish security personnel during the incident was “deeply disturbing.” It confirmed the U.S. ambassador in Ankara had been summoned by the Turkish government to discuss the “violent incidents.”  The Turkish foreign ministry said it summoned the U.S. ambassador to protest “aggressive and unprofessional actions” by U.S. security personnel to the security team of Turkish Foreign Minister Mevlut Cavusoglu. “It has been formally requested that the U.S. authorities conduct a full investigation of this diplomatic incident and provide the necessary explanation,” the foreign ministry said in a statement. It said that lapses of security experienced during Erdogan’s stay in Washington were caused “by the inability of U.S. authorities to take sufficient precautions at every stage of the official program,” adding that incidents would not overshadow what was otherwise a “very successful” visit. Police have said 11 people were injured, including a Washington police officer, and two people were arrested for assault. At least one of those arrested was a protester. Washington said last week it was voicing its strongest possible concern to Turkey over the brawl. U.S. Senator John McCain, one of the leading foreign policy voices in Congress, on Thursday called for the expulsion of Turkey’s U.S. ambassador.

text: According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center, Hurricane Irma is expected to be downgraded to a Category 4 hurricane as it approaches Florida. source_text: Hurricane Irma likely to drop to Category 4 upon landfall in Florida: NHC. (Reuters) - Hurricane Irma is likely to be downgraded to a Category 4 storm by the time it makes landfall in Florida, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said on Thursday.
