text: A major shift is occurring in the Trump administration as U.S. Vice President Mike Pence’s chief of staff, Josh Pitcock, will be stepping down, according to an announcement from Pence’s office on Thursday. Nick Ayers, a veteran Republican political strategist who previously acted as Pence’s chief strategist during the presidential race, will take over the role in August. Pitcock stated that his resignation was a personal choice, expressing that it was time for him to move on to the private sector. Currently, Ayers has been lending his expertise to America First Policies, a political organization that supports President Donald Trump. Recently, this group faced criticism from certain Republican members for airing advertisements that targeted Republican Senator Dean Heller from Nevada over his opposition to the healthcare legislation that is presently being debated in the Senate. In his remarks, Ayers conveyed, "I am honored with the trust the vice president has in me and excited to serve in this capacity." Throughout the administration, Pence has become a vital asset to Trump, acting as the primary connection to Congress amidst challenges to enact healthcare reforms and prepare for tax reform initiatives scheduled for later this year. Ayers has previously provided counsel to former Minnesota Governor Tim Pawlenty and former Georgia Governor Sonny Perdue, who is now the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture, among others.
source_text: VP Pence hires political operative as top aide steps down. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The top aide to U.S. Vice President Mike Pence is leaving the Trump administration and will be replaced by a longtime Republican political operative, Pence’s office said on Thursday. Josh Pitcock, who has served as Pence’s chief of staff, will be succeeded in August by Nick Ayers, who served as Pence’s chief strategist during the presidential campaign. In a statement, Pitcock said his departure was voluntary and that it was time to “transition to the private sector.” Ayers most recently was advising an outside political group, America First Policies, that supports President Donald Trump. The group came under fire from some Republicans for running a series of ads this week that criticized Republican Senator Dean Heller of Nevada for opposing the healthcare bill currently before the Senate. In a statement, Ayers said, “I am honored with the trust the vice president has in me and excited to serve in this capacity.”  Pence has emerged as a crucial member of Trump’s team, serving as his top liaison to Congress as it has struggled to pass healthcare reform and looks to tackle tax-reform legislation later this year. Ayers has advised former Minnesota Governor and Republican presidential candidate Tim Pawlenty and former Georgia Governor Sonny Perdue, now the U.S. secretary of agriculture, among other Republicans.

text: An urgent assembly of the United Nations ceasefire task force in Geneva has been requested by Russia to address the missile attacks by the United States on Syria. A diplomatic source informed RIA news agency about this on Friday. These meetings, which are presided over by U.N. envoy for Syria Staffan de Mistura, were established in early 2016 with the support of both the U.S. and Russia. They serve as a platform for diplomats to discuss violations of the fragile ceasefire in Syria. The Russian government is seeking to convene this meeting in Geneva today at 1500 GMT. The discussion will focus on "the situation on the ground with connection to the U.S. missile strike on Syria’s Shayrat airbase," according to the source. Earlier on Friday, the United States launched cruise missiles at the airbase, which President Donald Trump stated was the origin of a lethal chemical weapons assault. The strikes have drawn strong condemnation from Moscow.
source_text: Russia calls emergency U.N. task force meeting on Syria strikes. MOSCOW (Reuters) - Russia has demanded an emergency meeting of the United Nations ceasefire task force in Geneva to discuss U.S. missile strikes on Syria, the RIA news agency quoted a diplomatic source as saying on Friday. Such meetings are chaired by U.N. Syria envoy Staffan de Mistura and were set up in early 2016 with joint U.S.-Russian backing. They are a forum for diplomats to talk about breaches of Syria’s shaky ceasefire. Moscow wants the meeting to be held in Geneva today at 1500 GMT, the source told RIA, adding that the task force would discuss “the situation on the ground with connection to the U.S. missile strike on Syria’s Shayrat airbase.” The United States fired cruise missiles earlier on Friday at the base from which President Donald Trump said a deadly chemical weapons attack had been launched. Russia has sharply condemned the strikes.

text: Following a conversation between Prime Minister Theresa May and German Chancellor Angela Merkel, it was confirmed by a spokeswoman that Britain and Germany are still dedicated to the nuclear agreement with Iran. This commitment comes in light of a U.S. decision to decertify the deal. The spokeswoman noted in a statement that both nations are resolute in their support for the accord. Additionally, they concurred that the global community must unite to counter Iran's destabilizing activities in the region and to find solutions to address the concerns regarding Iran's ballistic missile program.
source_text: Britain, Germany committed to Iran nuclear deal: May's office. LONDON (Reuters) - Britain and Germany agreed on Sunday they remained committed to the nuclear deal with Iran after a U.S. decision to decertify the agreement, a spokeswoman said after a call between Prime Minister Theresa May and German Chancellor Angela Merkel.  They agreed the UK and Germany both remained firmly committed to the deal,  the spokeswoman said in a statement.  They also agreed the international community needed to continue to come together to push back against Iran s destabilizing regional activity, and to explore ways of addressing concerns about Iran s ballistic missile program.

text: A decision was made by a U.S. District Court judge on Friday to allow former Trump campaign chief Paul Manafort to be freed from house arrest, contingent upon him fulfilling specific requirements. Judge Amy Berman Jackson indicated that she was pleased to confirm the availability of the $10 million he agreed to forfeit, should he ever neglect to show up for court proceedings. In her ruling, she stipulated that, for his release from home confinement, Manafort must sign documents relinquishing four properties, which include two located in New York, one in Alexandria, Virginia, and his residence in Florida. Although he will have to adhere to certain restrictions, such as a curfew and electronic GPS tracking, he will be permitted to travel from his home in Alexandria to his property in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, once he complies with the outlined conditions. Manafort faces charges related to conspiracy to launder money and failing to register as a foreign agent for the former pro-Russia President of Ukraine, Viktor Yanukovych. His prosecution is being handled by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, who is investigating claims of Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and potential collusion between Russia and the Trump campaign. Should the properties not yield the required $10 million, the judge noted that Manafort’s spouse, Kathleen, has placed $5 million into an account, while his daughter, Andrea Manafort Shand, has contributed $2 million to another account to cover any shortfall. Access to these assets will require a court directive. Once in Florida, Manafort must remain in the area unless he is traveling to Washington for court dates or meetings with his legal team, as per the judge’s order. Any other domestic travel will require prior approval, and he is not allowed to leave the country.
source_text: U.S. judge to lift house arrest for former Trump campaign manager Manafort. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A U.S. District Court judge on Friday said she would release former Trump campaign manager Paul Manafort from house arrest once he meets certain conditions, expressing satisfaction that the $10 million he agreed to forfeit would be available if he ever failed to appear for court proceedings. In her order, Judge Amy Berman Jackson said to be released from home confinement, Manafort must execute documents agreeing to forfeit four properties, including two in New York, one in Alexandria, Virginia, and his Florida home.    He will be subject to restrictions including a curfew and electronic GPS monitoring but will be allowed to leave his home in Alexandria for his home in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, once he meets the conditions.  Manafort is charged with conspiring to launder money and failing to register as a foreign agent working on behalf of the government of Ukraine’s former pro-Russia President Viktor Yanukovych.  He is being prosecuted by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, as part of Mueller’s investigation into accusations of Russian meddling in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and possible collusion between Russia and the Trump campaign. In case the forfeited properties do not raise $10 million, the judge said, Manafort’s wife, Kathleen, has deposited $5 million in an account and his daughter Andrea Manafort Shand, $2 million in a separate account, to make up any difference. The assets cannot be touched without a court order. Once in Florida, Manafort must stay within the area, unless he is traveling to Washington for court appearances or meetings with counsel, according to the order. He needs permission for any other domestic travel and cannot leave the country.

source_text: White House welcomes U.S. court ruling on carbon emissions plan. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The White House said on Thursday that it was pleased that a U.S. appellate court had denied a bid by 27 states to block the Obama administration’s Clean Power Plan while litigation challenging the regulation continues. “We are confident that the plan will reduce carbon pollution and deliver better air quality, improved public health, and jobs across the country,” White House spokesman Josh Earnest said in a statement. The rule aims to lower carbon emissions from the country’s power plants to 32 percent below 2005 levels by 2030.

text: The ethics committee of the U.S. House of Representatives has initiated a comprehensive investigation into potential sexual harassment and discrimination amongst its 434 members and their staff. On Friday, the committee requested an extensive array of documents from the congressional office responsible for managing employment disputes. Susan Brooks, the Republican chair of the committee, along with Theodore Deutch, the senior Democrat, sent a letter to the office asking for the immediate sharing of all records related to any claims of sexual harassment, discrimination, retaliation, or other employment practices. This autumn, Capitol Hill has been shaken by revelations of possible sexual misconduct involving lawmakers, coupled with public outrage over the use of taxpayer funds to resolve harassment claims against them. In particular, Representative John Conyers, a Democrat from Michigan, is facing calls for his resignation following allegations of sexual harassment, which Reuters has not confirmed. Reports from U.S. media indicate that Conyers utilized public funds to settle a claim with a woman, and the ethics committee is currently examining whether he misused official resources for personal purposes deemed inappropriate. Conyers has admitted to settling with a former staff member regarding her harassment allegations, but he has denied any wrongdoing. In another instance, Texas Republican Representative Joe Barton chose not to run for re-election after an explicit photo of him surfaced online. The committee refrained from commenting further beyond their initial letter. There is increasing pressure for the ethics committee to enhance its enforcement of congressional regulations. The last disciplinary measure taken by the committee occurred on August 1, when it determined that Representative Ben Ray Lujan had violated a rule concerning campaign communications, yet no penalties were imposed. In addition to resolving conflicts and upholding employment regulations for over 30,000 individuals employed by Congress, the compliance office also allocates public funds for confidential settlements against lawmakers. A bipartisan coalition of legislators is advocating for changes to this practice through new legislation that would mandate timely public disclosure of settlement payments. In correspondence sent to House Administration Committee Chair Gregg Harper on Friday, the compliance office revealed that since 2013, it has disbursed funds for two settlements, which included allegations of sex discrimination and one for sexual harassment. The amount of $84,000 was paid for a sexual harassment case, while $7,000 was allocated for a case involving both sex and religious discrimination. Politico reported that the harassment settlement was arranged on behalf of Texas Republican Blake Farenthold. "While I fully endorse increased transparency regarding claims against Congressional members, I am unable to confirm or deny whether my office was involved in that settlement due to the restrictions imposed by the Congressional Accountability Act," stated Farenthold. In 2014, Farenthold’s former communications director, Lauren Greene, filed a lawsuit against him, alleging a hostile work environment, gender discrimination, and retaliation, according to court records. A mediated settlement was reached between Farenthold and Greene in 2015 to avoid prolonged litigation, but the specifics of the settlement remained confidential, as disclosed in a statement at that time, where Farenthold denied any engagement in wrongdoing.
source_text: House ethics panel launches wide-ranging probe into sexual harassment claims. In a letter to the office, Susan Brooks, the committee’s Republican chair, and Theodore Deutch, its senior Democrat, requested the congressional compliance office promptly share all its records “related to any claims of sexual harassment, discrimination, retaliation or any other employment practice.” Capitol Hill has been rocked this fall by news of possible sexual misconduct by lawmakers, and outrage that public money may have been paid to settle harassment suits against lawmakers. Most notably Representative John Conyers, a Michigan Democrat, is under pressure to resign in light of sexual harassment allegations, which Reuters has not verified. U.S. media have reported Conyers used public funds to settle a claim with a woman, and the ethics committee is currently investigating if he “used official resources for impermissible personal purposes.” Conyers has acknowledged settling with a former staffer over her claims of harassment, but he has denied wrongdoing.  Meanwhile, Texas Republican Representative Joe Barton recently decided not to seek re-election after a nude photo of him appeared on the internet. The committee had no comment beyond the letter. Pressure is mounting for it to ramp up its enforcement of congressional rules. It last took a disciplinary action on Aug. 1, determining Representative Ben Ray Lujan broke a rule on campaign communications but not imposing any sanctions. Along with resolving disputes and enforcing employment laws for more than 30,000 people working for Congress, the compliance office provides public money to confidentially settle claims against lawmakers. A bipartisan group of lawmakers is seeking to change that practice with legislation that would require prompt public disclosure of settlement awards. In a letter sent to House Administration Committee Chair Gregg Harper on Friday, the compliance office said that since 2013 it has paid settlements on two claims including sex discrimination allegations and one alleging sexual harassment.  It paid $84,000 for one sexual harassment claim and $7,000 in one case alleging both sex and religious discrimination.  Politico reported the harassment award was made on behalf of Texas Republican Blake Farenthold.  “While I 100 percent support more transparency with respect to claims against members of Congress, I can neither confirm nor deny that settlement involved my office as the Congressional Accountability Act prohibits me from answering that question,” said Farenthold in a statement.  In 2014 Farenthold’s former communications director Lauren Greene sued him, alleging a hostile work environment, gender discrimination, and retaliation, court documents show. Farenthold and Greene reached a mediated agreement in 2015 to avoid costly litigation, but the settlement’s details were confidential, according to a statement released at the time, where Farenthold denied engaging in any wrongdoing.

source_text: Spain's Rajoy calls on Catalonia leaders to cancel referendum. MADRID (Reuters) - Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy on Wednesday called on Catalonia regional leaders to cancel a planned referendum on splitting from Spain because it goes against the country s laws.  Don t go ahead. Go back to the law and democracy. This referendum is a chimera,  Rajoy said in a televised speech.

text: According to a report, the Trump administration has accused North Korea of being behind the WannaCry cyber attack, which significantly impacted hospitals, banks, and various businesses around the world earlier this year. This attack, which was extensive and incurred costs in the billions, has been attributed directly to North Korea as stated by Tom Bossert, the homeland security adviser to President Donald Trump, in an article released on Monday evening in the Wall Street Journal. Bossert remarked that North Korea has exhibited particularly bad behavior for over a decade without much consequence, and its malicious actions are increasingly becoming more severe. He described WannaCry as being recklessly indiscriminate. A senior administration official indicated that a more formal statement from the White House blaming Pyongyang was anticipated for Tuesday. The U.S. government has concluded, with a very high degree of certainty, that a hacking group known as Lazarus Group, which operates on behalf of the North Korean regime, executed the WannaCry attack, according to the official who requested anonymity to discuss the government's investigative details. Lazarus Group is widely recognized by security experts and U.S. authorities to be the perpetrator of the 2014 cyber breach of Sony Pictures Entertainment, which resulted in data destruction, the leaking of corporate communications online, and the exit of several senior studio executives. Representatives from the North Korean government could not be reached immediately for a response. They have consistently denied any involvement in WannaCry and labeled other cyber attack allegations as a smear campaign. The condemnation from Washington does not include any charges or specify individuals, the administration official noted, asserting that the intent was to hold Pyongyang accountable for its deeds and diminish their capacity to execute further attacks. This accusation emerges amidst escalating concerns regarding North Korea's hacking capabilities, alongside its nuclear weapons program. Numerous security analysts, including the cyber firm Symantec and the British government, have already determined that North Korea was likely behind the WannaCry attack, which rapidly spread globally in May, infecting over 300,000 computers across 150 nations. At the time, the scale of WannaCry was unprecedented, bringing British hospitals offline, leading to thousands of patients having to reschedule appointments, and causing disruptions in infrastructure and businesses worldwide. Initially, the attack appeared to be a ransomware operation, wherein hackers encrypt a targeted system and demand payment for file recovery. However, some experts later suggested that the ransom threat might have served as a diversion, aimed at concealing a more destructive purpose. In June, a different yet similar attack, referred to as NotPetya, struck Ukraine and other countries, resulting in approximately $300 million in damages to the international shipping company FedEx. Some researchers believe that WannaCry may have been unintentionally released by North Korea as their hackers were in the process of developing the code. The senior administration official refrained from commenting on whether U.S. intelligence could ascertain if the attack was intentional. The official stated, "What we see is a continued pattern of North Korea misbehaving, whether through destructive cyber assaults, hacking for financial gain, or targeting global infrastructure." The WannaCry incident was made possible due to a vulnerability in Microsoft’s Windows software, which had been uncovered by the U.S. National Security Agency, and subsequently utilized by the NSA to create a hacking tool for its own purposes. In a significant breach of NSA security, that hacking tool, among others, was leaked online by the Shadow Brokers, a shadowy group known for regularly posting cryptic messages directed at the U.S. government.
source_text: U.S. blames North Korea for 'WannaCry' cyber attack.  (In 13th paragraph of Dec. 18 item, corrects to indicate that a separate attack was launched in June that affected FedEx computers) By Dustin Volz WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Trump administration has publicly blamed North Korea for unleashing the so-called WannaCry cyber attack that crippled hospitals, banks and other companies across the globe earlier this year.  The attack was widespread and cost billions, and North Korea is directly responsible,  Tom Bossert, homeland security adviser to President Donald Trump, wrote in a piece published on Monday night in the Wall Street Journal.  North Korea has acted especially badly, largely unchecked, for more than a decade, and its malicious behavior is growing more egregious,  Bossert wrote.  WannaCry was indiscriminately reckless.  The White House was expected to follow up on Tuesday with a more formal statement blaming Pyongyang, according to a senior administration official. The U.S. government has assessed with a  very high level of confidence  that a hacking entity known as Lazarus Group, which works on behalf of the North Korean government, carried out the WannaCry attack, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the government s investigation. Lazarus Group is widely believed by security researchers and U.S. officials to have been responsible for the 2014 hack of Sony Pictures Entertainment that destroyed files, leaked corporate communications online and led to the departure of several top studio executives. North Korean government representatives could not be immediately reached for comment. The country has repeatedly denied responsibility for WannaCry and called other allegations about cyber attacks a smear campaign.     Washington s public condemnation does not include any indictments or name specific individuals, the administration official said, adding the shaming was designed to hold Pyongyang accountable for its actions and  erode and undercut their ability to launch attacks.  The accusation comes as worries mount about North Korea s hacking capabilities and its nuclear weapons program. Many security researchers, including the cyber firm Symantec , as well as the British government, have already concluded that North Korea was likely behind the WannaCry attack, which quickly unfurled across the globe in May to infect more than 300,000 computers in 150 countries. Considered unprecedented in scale at the time, WannaCry  knocked British hospitals offline, forcing thousands of patients to reschedule appointments and disrupted infrastructure and businesses around the world.  The attack originally looked like a ransomware campaign, where hackers encrypt a targeted computer and demand payment to recover files. Some experts later concluded the ransom threat may have been a distraction intended to disguise a more destructive intent. A separate but similar attack in June, known as NotPetya, hit Ukraine and other nations and caused an estimated $300 million in damages to international shipper FedEx. Some researchers have said they believed WannaCry was deployed accidentally by North Korea as hackers were developing the code. The senior administration official declined to comment about whether U.S. intelligence was able to discern if the attack was deliberate.      What we see is a continued pattern of North Korea misbehaving, whether destructive cyber attacks, hacking for financial gain, or targeting infrastructure around the globe,  the official said. WannaCry was made possible by a flaw in Microsoft s Windows software, which was discovered by the U.S. National Security Agency and then used by the NSA to build a hacking tool for its own use.  In a devastating NSA security breach, that hacking tool and others were published online by the Shadow Brokers, a mysterious group that regularly posts cryptic taunts toward the U.S. government. The fact that WannaCry was made possible by the NSA led to sharp criticism from Microsoft President Brad Smith and others who believe the NSA should disclose vulnerabilities it finds so that they can be fixed, rather then hoarding that knowledge to carry out attacks.  Smith said WannaCry provided  yet another example of why the stockpiling of vulnerabilities by governments is such a problem.  U.S. officials have pushed back on those assertions, saying the administration discloses most computer flaws that government agencies detect. Last month, the White House published its rules for deciding whether to disclose cyber security flaws or keep them secret as part of an effort to be more transparent about the inter-agency process involved in weighing disclosure.

text: On Saturday, German Foreign Minister Sigmar Gabriel refuted a claim suggesting he is contemplating the finance minister role. Reports from the news magazine Der Spiegel indicated that the Social Democrat had recently expressed to prominent figures within his SPD party a desire to take on the finance minister position should the SPD consent to a renewal of the existing grand coalition with Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservatives. "What Spiegel is reporting is utter nonsense," Gabriel stated during an interview with Deutschlandfunk radio. He emphasized that he is part of a caretaker administration and the composition of the future government remains uncertain. Over two months post the national election, Germany has yet to establish a new government, leaving the previous conservative coalition still in power. Following a decline in support to far-right factions in the September elections, Merkel is relying on the SPD to prolong her 12-year leadership after her attempts to forge a challenging three-party alliance with the liberal Free Democrats and the Greens fell apart. If the SPD were to agree to enter another grand coalition—an option the party insists is not guaranteed—and insist on acquiring the finance ministry, it would likely lead to shifts in Germany's European policy, focusing more on spending and investment over austerity measures. Wolfgang Schaeuble, who served as the conservative finance minister until he assumed the presidency in October, gained a negative reputation among struggling eurozone countries during his eight years in that role due to his austerity-focused policies. On Thursday, SPD leader Martin Schulz remarked that Europe could not endure another four years of the type of European policy that Schaeuble had implemented.
source_text: Germany's Gabriel denies report he is eyeing finance minister post. BERLIN (Reuters) - German Foreign Minister Sigmar Gabriel on Saturday denied a report that said the Social Democrat, whose party has agreed to enter talks with Chancellor Angela Merkel s conservatives on forming a coalition, was eyeing the post of finance minister. News magazine Der Spiegel reported that Gabriel had recently told senior members of his SPD party that he was interested in becoming German finance minister if the SPD agreed to a re-run of the current  grand coalition  with Merkel s conservatives.  What Spiegel is writing is sheer nonsense,  Gabriel told Deutschlandfunk radio.  I m in a caretaker government and no one knows what the next government will look like.  More than two months after a national election, Germany has not managed to form a new government, so the conservative coalition from the last legislative period is still in power. Merkel, who lost many supporters to the far-right in September s election, is banking on the SPD to extend her 12-year tenure after attempts to cobble together an awkward three-way alliance with the liberal Free Democrats and environmentalist Greens crumbled. If the SPD were to agree to another  grand coalition  - an option that the SPD says is by no means a foregone conclusion - and demand the finance ministry, it would likely result in changes to Germany s European policy such as more focus on spending and investment rather than austerity. Wolfgang Schaeuble, who was Germany s conservative finance minister until he took on the role of president in October, became unpopular among struggling euro zone states during his eight years in office due to his focus on austerity. SPD leader Martin Schulz said on Thursday that Europe could not afford to undergo another four years of the kind of European policy that Schaeuble had practiced.

text: ANKARA (Reuters) - The planned referendum for independence in northern Iraq has been labeled a matter of national security by Turkish Prime Minister Binali Yildirim, who stated on Saturday that Turkey will undertake any necessary actions. Despite appeals from the United States and other Western nations concerned that the escalating tensions between Erbil and Baghdad could hinder efforts against Islamic State militants still occupying parts of Iraq and Syria, Iraqi Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani asserted on Friday that the vote would proceed as scheduled. Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan expressed in an interview on Friday that Barzani's choice to not delay the referendum was a significant mistake.
source_text: Turkey says northern Iraqi referendum an issue of national security. ANKARA (Reuters) - Turkish Prime Minister Binali Yildirim said on Saturday that the planned independence referendum in northern Iraq is an issue of national security, and Turkey will take any necessary steps. On Friday, Iraqi Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani said the vote would not be delayed, despite requests from the United States and other Western powers worried that tensions between Baghdad and Erbil would distract from the war on Islamic State militants who continue to occupy parts of Iraq and Syria. Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said in an interview on Friday that Barzani s decision not to postpone the referendum was  very wrong .

text: On Wednesday, two journalists from Reuters appeared in court in Myanmar and were ordered to remain in custody for an additional 14 days. YANGON (Reuters) - The two reporters, Wa Lone, aged 31, and Kyaw Soe Oo, aged 27, have been detained for two weeks as authorities investigate allegations that they violated the country's Official Secrets Act. Judge Ohn Myint approved the extension of their detention at the police's request, and following the hearing, the journalists were taken to Insein prison in Yangon. Previously, they had been held at a police facility. During their court appearance at Mingaladon, it was the first time that Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo were permitted to see their families and legal counsel since their arrest. The journalists were involved in reporting for Reuters on the ongoing crisis in Rakhine state, where, according to estimates from the United Nations, around 655,000 Rohingya Muslims have fled due to a severe military crackdown on insurgents. They were taken into custody on December 12 after being invited to a dinner with police officials. The Ministry of Information contends that the pair obtained information unlawfully with the intent of sharing it with international media and have been charged under the British colonial-era Official Secrets Act, which can impose a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison. The journalists reported that they have not faced any mistreatment while in custody. "The situation is okay," Wa Lone remarked following the hearing. "We will face it the best we can because we have never done anything wrong," he expressed. "We have not violated media laws or ethics. We will continue to do our utmost." A spokesperson for Reuters stated that they should be released. "These two journalists are being held for simply doing their jobs and have done nothing wrong. It is time for Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo to be freed," the spokesperson asserted. In the town of Pyay, located 290 km (180 miles) north of Yangon, approximately 100 journalists, lawyers, and farmers gathered to protest for the release of Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo, as reported by one of the demonstrators. Members of the Protection Committee for Myanmar Journalists participated in the demonstration, draped in chains in a public square and inscribing the names of the two detained reporters on their palms, a common symbol of solidarity for imprisoned individuals in Myanmar. Calls for their release have also come from government officials in major countries, including the United States, Britain, and Canada, alongside high-ranking U.N. officials. Outside the courthouse located in a northern district of Yangon, dozens of reporters and cameramen awaited the arrival of the two journalists. They were transported in a white van instead of a police truck, dressed casually and not handcuffed. Their attorney, Than Zaw Aung, who has been engaged by Reuters, asserted that both had merely been executing their duties as journalists. "They are being accused under this charge while doing their work as media," he commented to the press. Lieutenant Colonel Myint Htwe, a senior official from the Yangon Police Division, stated, "We took action because they committed the crime. It needs to be resolved in court." The courtroom was restricted to only their attorney, family members of the two journalists, and police and government lawyers. Later, the families were permitted to ride in the van alongside the journalists as they were taken back to prison. "I believe that he didn't commit any crime," Pan Ei Mon, the wife of Wa Lone, conveyed to Reuters. "I would like to request the government to consider releasing them." Nyo Nyo Aye, sister of Kyaw Soe Oo, mentioned that her brother insisted he had not committed any offense. "I believe that he can come home soon," she stated.

They were brought in a white van, rather than a police truck, dressed in casual clothes and were not handcuffed.  Their lawyer, Than Zaw Aung, who has been retained by Reuters, also said the two had only been doing their job as journalists.  They are being accused under this charge while doing their work as media,  he told reporters. Lieutenant Colonel Myint Htwe, a senior staff officer from the Yangon Police Division, said:  We took action because they committed the crime. It needs to be solved in court.  Only their lawyer and the families of the two journalists,  along with police and government lawyers, were allowed into the courtroom. The families were later allowed to travel in the van as the two journalists were taken to prison.  I believe that he didn t commit any crime,  Pan Ei Mon, Wa Lone s wife, told Reuters.  I would like to request the government to consider releasing them.  Nyo Nyo Aye, a sister of Kyaw Soe Oo, said her brother told her he had not committed any offense.  I believe that he can come home soon,  she said.

text: The global perception of the United States has significantly declined during the presidency of Donald Trump, according to a survey conducted by the Pew Research Center. The study revealed that a substantial number of individuals in various countries lack confidence in Trump's leadership abilities. As Trump entered the fifth month of his presidency, the research, which covered 37 countries, indicated that the favorability rating of the U.S. dropped to 49 percent, a stark decline from 64 percent recorded at the conclusion of Barack Obama’s administration. The downturn was notably pronounced among the U.S.'s closest allies, such as Canada and Mexico, as well as European nations like Germany and Spain. Trump assumed office in January with a commitment to prioritize "America First." Since that time, he has been actively pursuing initiatives including the construction of a border wall with Mexico, announcing the U.S.'s withdrawal from the Paris climate agreement, and accusing nations including Canada, Germany, and China of engaging in unfair trade practices. During his inaugural foreign trip in early June, Trump was warmly received in Saudi Arabia and Israel; however, his European partners greeted him with a much less enthusiastic response, particularly over disagreements related to NATO funding, climate issues, and trade policies. Currently, only 30 percent of Mexicans express a favorable opinion of the United States, a decline from 66 percent at the end of the Obama presidency. Favorability ratings in Canada and Germany fell by 22 points, settling at 43 percent and 35 percent, respectively. In numerous European nations, the favorability ratings were reminiscent of the end of George W. Bush’s presidency, a period marked by significant unpopularity following the 2003 invasion of Iraq. The Pew report highlighted that "the decline in the favorability ratings for the United States is extensive," noting that people from a variety of regions, including Latin America, North America, Europe, Asia, and Africa, have expressed diminished positive views of the U.S. The survey, which gathered responses from 40,447 individuals between February 16 and May 8 of this year, revealed even greater skepticism toward Trump, as only 22 percent of respondents indicated they believed he would act appropriately in global affairs, compared to 64 percent who had confidence in Obama. In terms of confidence ratings, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping fared better than Trump, with their ratings at 27 percent and 28 percent, respectively. The highest confidence rating among the four leaders was given to German Chancellor Angela Merkel, who achieved a score of 42 percent. Those with the least confidence in Trump were in Mexico, where only 5 percent expressed faith in him, and in Spain, where the figure was 7 percent. The only two nations where confidence ratings improved compared to Obama were Russia, where approval for the U.S. president surged to 53 percent from 11 percent, and Israel, which saw an increase of 7 points to 56 percent. Across the globe, 75 percent of participants characterized Trump as "arrogant," while 65 percent labeled him "intolerant" and 62 percent deemed him "dangerous." A majority of 55 percent also viewed him as a "strong leader." The survey indicated widespread discontent with Trump’s hallmark policy proposals, with 76 percent opposing his border wall initiative, 72 percent against his withdrawal from significant trade agreements, and 62 percent opposed to his restrictions on travel to the U.S. from certain majority-Muslim countries. On a more positive note, the survey found that 58 percent of respondents held a favorable view of Americans in general, and in many regions, a majority or plurality of those surveyed anticipated that relations with the United States would remain relatively unchanged despite Trump's presidency.

But the falls were far steeper in some of America’s closest allies, including U.S. neighbors Mexico and Canada, and European partners like Germany and Spain.  Trump took office in January pledging to put “America First”. On his first foreign trip as president in early June, Trump received warm welcomes in Saudi Arabia and Israel, but a cool reception from European partners, with whom he clashed over NATO spending, climate and trade.  Just 30 percent of Mexicans now say they have a favorable view of the United States, down from 66 percent at the end of the Obama era. In Canada and Germany, favorability ratings slid by 22 points, to 43 percent and 35 percent, respectively.  In many European countries, the ratings were comparable to those seen at the end of the presidency of George W. Bush, whose 2003 invasion of Iraq was deeply unpopular.  “The drop in favorability ratings for the United States is widespread,” the Pew report said. “The share of the public with a positive view of the U.S. has plummeted in a diverse set of countries from Latin America, North America, Europe, Asia and Africa”. Globally, 75 percent of respondents described Trump as “arrogant”, 65 percent as “intolerant” and 62 percent as “dangerous”. A majority of 55 percent also described him as a “strong leader”.  The survey showed widespread disapproval of Trump’s signature policy proposals, with 76 percent unhappy with his plan to build the wall on the border with Mexico, 72 percent against his withdrawal from major trade agreements and 62 percent opposed to his plans to restrict travel to the U.S. from some majority-Muslim countries. And in many regions of the world, a majority or plurality of respondents said they expected relations with the United States to stay roughly the same in spite of Trump.

text: In the Philippines, Donald Trump is being hailed by U.S. veterans as he prepares for his upcoming visit. text: A police official reported that two soldiers from Somalia sustained injuries during a clash with fellow military personnel on Monday. This incident raises concerns about internal divisions within a military known for its history of factional issues, particularly as it contends with a resurgence of militant Islamist activity. The al Shabaab group is believed to be responsible for the deadliest civilian attack in the country this month, which resulted in at least 358 fatalities. According to Nur Ali, the police officer, the brief skirmish occurred in the Yaqshid district of Mogadishu and was ignited by a miscommunication involving the district commissioner and the security forces. Ali noted that gunfire erupted between the commissioner’s home guards and the security units, and soldiers temporarily took control of the commissioner’s office. Although the disagreement was settled, two soldiers ended up injured, as stated by Ali. The morale of Somali troops is frequently low due to delayed paychecks, factional disputes, and desertions. Since the overthrow of dictator Siad Barre in the early 1990s, the nation has largely lacked effective governance. While al Shabaab has not claimed responsibility for the dual bombing on October 14 that destroyed numerous buildings, it has regularly targeted security forces while striving to dismantle the western-supported government, often resulting in civilian casualties.

MOGADISHU (Reuters) - Two Somali soldiers were wounded in a gun fight with other troops on Monday, a police officer said, a worrying internal rift for a military with a history of factionalism that is fighting a resurgence by militant Islamists  The al Shabaab group is suspected of being behind the country s single deadliest attack on civilians this month that killed at least 358 people. text: The trial of the alleged mastermind behind the Benghazi attack commenced in Washington. On Monday, federal prosecutors initiated their case against Ahmed Abu Khatallah, asserting that he was the orchestrator of the 2012 assault on a U.S. diplomatic facility in Benghazi, Libya, resulting in the deaths of U.S. Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. Khatallah has been in custody since 2014, following his capture by U.S. military personnel and FBI operatives in Libya, after which he was transported over a 13-day period to the United States aboard a Navy ship. In his opening remarks before the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, prosecutor John Crabb stated that Khatallah harbors a deep-seated hatred for America and played a pivotal role in planning the attack that occurred on September 11, 2012, at the U.S. diplomatic mission in Benghazi. Crabb emphasized that while Khatallah did not engage in direct actions like igniting fires or launching mortars, he bears equal culpability to those who did. Dressed in a white shirt and utilizing headphones for an Arabic translation of the proceedings, Khatallah faces charges that include murder and providing material support to terrorists. His defense attorney, Jeffrey Robinson, contended that Khatallah had no involvement in the attack's planning. He asserted, "The evidence is going to show that Mr. Abu Khatallah did not participate in the attack." The first day of the trial featured distressing testimony from Special Agent Scott Wickland, who recounted his efforts to rescue Stevens and State Department staff member Sean Smith as they crawled on their stomachs through dense, dark smoke while flames consumed the mission. Wickland recalled, "At first, I had my hand on the ambassador, and we were crawling. I was breathing through the last centimeter of air on the ground... and I am yelling to the other guys, 'Come on! We can make it!' And within that 8 meters, they disappeared." Prosecutor Crabb also outlined some of the forthcoming witness testimonies, indicating that some individuals would testify about Khatallah's admissions regarding his role in the attack. One witness, who received $7 million for assisting the U.S. in luring Khatallah to his capture site, is expected to tell the jury that he overheard Khatallah declare he "would have killed all of the Americans that night," according to Crabb. Additionally, Crabb presented grainy video footage from the night of the incident, showcasing images of more than six suspected associates of Khatallah. In one of the videos, Khatallah was seen as armed militia entered a room that contained closely guarded maps and other documents. Robinson insisted that his client visited the mission solely to observe the situation and warned individuals to avoid the gunfire. He also claimed that some of the government’s witnesses "are people who lie." The trial is set to continue on Tuesday and is anticipated to span several weeks.

text: The U.S. Supreme Court's recent decision will not hinder the momentum of the transition to cleaner energy sources in the power sector, according to comments made by state regulators and utility representatives on Wednesday. The high court, in a narrow 5-4 ruling on Tuesday, put a halt to the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) initiative aimed at reducing carbon emissions from coal-fired power plants until the ongoing legal dispute is resolved. Although some states may delay their compliance efforts with the EPA’s Clean Power Plan, many experts remain optimistic that the rule will withstand judicial scrutiny when the D.C. circuit court delivers its verdict this summer. Vicki Arroyo, who is the executive director of the Georgetown Climate Center, remarked, "In a way we are really just postponing the inevitable." Even among the 27 states that initiated legal action to block the rule, there have been ongoing efforts to establish compliance strategies. The majority of states have expressed their commitment to continue reducing carbon emissions from their energy sources. Across the nation, utilities are actively transitioning from coal-based electricity generation to cleaner alternatives, such as natural gas and renewable resources like wind and solar energy. Bill Becker, director of the National Association of Clean Air Agencies, stated, "We fully expect that many of these states will continue their efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions under their own legal authorities." States like California, New York, and Colorado have openly criticized the Supreme Court’s ruling, pledging to advance their clean energy initiatives regardless of the regulatory delays stemming from the EPA decision. Conversely, states such as North Dakota and Montana, which were part of the lawsuit against the EPA, welcomed the additional time the stay provides. However, even these states have acknowledged the need to continue diversifying their energy production. Governor John Hickenlooper of Colorado, a Democrat, emphasized that the state will persist in its compliance efforts to avoid falling behind if the courts ultimately uphold any portion of the Clean Power Plan. Despite the challenges, Colorado initiated a challenge to the EPA's plan, illustrating the conflict within the state's political leadership, as the governor supports the initiative while the state's Republican attorney general questions its legality and potential economic ramifications. On the other hand, Democratic Governor Steve Bullock of Montana opposed the EPA regulations and indicated that the state would pause the work of a task force assigned to develop compliance options. Nevertheless, he affirmed the importance of addressing climate change and advancing Montana’s energy future, stating, "I am committed to ensuring we do so on our own terms." In North Dakota, a state that faced significant reduction targets under the rule, Dave Glatt, the chief of the state health department, asserted that both regulators and utilities would continue their efforts to reduce emissions from power plants. He pointed out that the EPA's plan did not allow sufficient time for the state to devise reasonable solutions and committed to exploring viable paths forward. Overall, the trend has shown a decline in coal-powered electricity across most states. In 2015, operators shut down over 15,000 megawatts of coal capacity, marking the largest reduction in a single year, largely due to low natural gas prices that made coal less economically viable. This decline has rendered it impractical to upgrade older coal facilities to comply with existing federal air quality standards. Ohio regulators expressed uncertainty regarding the state’s forthcoming actions in light of the court's ruling. However, major utility companies in Ohio have already begun moving away from coal. American Electric Power Co Inc (AEP.N) plans to increase its production of energy from natural gas and renewables, as the costs for these alternatives have significantly decreased, according to spokesperson Melissa McHenry. She noted that the five-year extension of federal tax credits for renewable energy has motivated AEP to incorporate more renewable sources into its energy portfolio. "It makes sense that we are sticking to our current plans, and will be positioned to respond to the courts’ ultimate decision on the future of the Clean Power Plan," she stated. Another utility in Ohio, FirstEnergy Corp (FE.N), indicated that it has already begun to adjust its energy generation practices.
source_text: High court emissions ruling won't deter clean energy drive . WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. power sector’s shift toward burning less coal and using more natural gas and renewable energy will not be derailed by the Supreme Court ruling against the Obama administration’s limits on carbon emissions, state regulators and utilities said on Wednesday. The U.S. Supreme Court decided 5-4 on Tuesday to block the Environmental Protection Agency’s carbon emissions crackdown on coal plants until a legal challenge is resolved.  Some states may now slow work on compliance with the EPA’s Clean Power Plan. But some experts said they were confident the rule will survive the legal challenge when the D.C. circuit court makes a decision this summer.  “In a way we are really just postponing the inevitable,” said Vicki Arroyo, executive director of the Georgetown Climate Center. Even in some of the 27 states that sued to block the rule, officials had been working on compliance plans.  Most states said they will continue to decarbonize their energy supply. Utilities across the country have already begun a major shift away from coal-fired electricity toward cleaner burning and cheaper natural gas and renewables like wind and solar. “We fully expect that many of these states will continue their efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions under their own legal authorities,” said Bill Becker, director of the National Association of Clean Air Agencies.  States like California, Colorado and New York criticized the high court’s decision and vowed to pursue their plans to shift to cleaner energy regardless of the delay in the EPA rule. Meanwhile, states like Montana and North Dakota that joined in the lawsuit against the EPA welcomed the “breathing room” the stay provides. But even these opponents of the rule said they will keep diversifying their power supply. Colorado’s Democratic Governor John Hickenlooper said the state will keep working on compliance so it “is not left at a disadvantage if the courts uphold all or part of the Clean Power Plan.” Colorado challenged the EPA plan even though the governor supports it. The state’s Republican attorney general disagrees about the legality of the rule and its economic impact. Montana Governor Steve Bullock, a Democrat, opposed the EPA rule. He said the state would put on hold the work of a group to devise compliance options, but added that it still needs “to address climate change and embrace Montana’s energy future.” He said: “I am committed to ensuring we do so on our own terms.”   For coal-producing North Dakota, which had one of the highest emission reduction targets to meet under the rule, regulators and utilities will keep working on ways to lower power plant emissions, said state health department chief Dave Glatt.  He said the EPA plan did not give the state “a sufficient amount of time to have reasonable solutions.” He pledged to “look at reasonable steps forward.” For most states, coal-fired electricity has been in decline. In 2015, generators shut over 15,000 megawatts of coal-fired power plants, the most in any year, as low gas prices drove down power costs. It became uneconomical to overhaul older coal plants even to meet existing federal clean air rules.  Ohio regulators said Wednesday they were not sure how the state will respond to the court decision, but the state’s major utilities are already shifting away from coal. American Electric Power Co Inc (AEP.N) will continue generating more power with natural gas and renewable energy since prices for those have dropped significantly, said spokeswoman Melissa McHenry. She added that the five-year extension of federal renewable energy tax credits has given AEP an incentive to bring more renewable energy into the mix. “It makes sense that we are sticking to our current plans, and will be positioned to respond to the courts’ ultimate decision on the future of the Clean Power Plan,” she said. Another Ohio utility, FirstEnergy Corp (FE.N), said it already retired a number of older coal plants in 2012. The court decision will have little impact. “The Supreme Court decision does not change the path we are on,” said spokeswoman Jennifer Young. “We think it is the right thing to do – this is a complicated issue and this decision will give the states the appropriate amount of time to develop their compliance plans.”

MADRID (Reuters) - If the ousted Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont fails to appear in court, the normal procedure would be to issue an arrest warrant, the president of Spain s Supreme Court said on Thursday.   When someone doesn t appear after being cited by a judge to testify, in Spain or any other EU country, normally an arrest warrant is issued,  Supreme Court President Carlos Lesmes said. Puigdemont said on Wednesday he would ignore a court order to return to Spain to answer charges over the region s push for independence. He did not turn up at a High Court hearing on Thursday.

However, in the past week, Trump has created some uncertainty regarding his legislative goals. He publicly criticized a crucial aspect of the Republican tax strategy, referred to as the border adjustment tax. Additionally, he appeared to complicate the narrative surrounding his pledge to repeal Obamacare by advocating for healthcare coverage for everyone. While NAM did not express alarm about these developments, they underscore the challenges facing Pence, 57, who will act as Trump’s primary representative to Congress once the businessman is inaugurated as the 45th president of the United States on Friday. Pence, who served for twelve years in Congress starting in 2001, established several personal connections, particularly with conservative members. Although he may not be known on Capitol Hill for his negotiating prowess, lawmakers, aides, and lobbyists characterize him as friendly and an effective communicator, treating both allies and adversaries with respect. Yet, the NAM experience illustrates that Pence might find his greatest challenge in Congress stemming from Trump himself. This is largely due to the uncertainty around whether Pence is communicating Trump’s intentions accurately during negotiations. The differences between Pence and Trump are pronounced. While Trump is known for his confrontational style and eagerness for public attention, Pence, who most recently held the governorship of Indiana, is calm and composed, earning descriptors of being articulate and positive from both Republican and Democratic colleagues. Few vice presidents in recent U.S. history have taken on such a pivotal role in legislative matters as Pence is expected to. Former Vice President Dick Cheney was known for striking deals and persuading lawmakers for President George W. Bush, but Pence’s responsibilities may be even broader. In the first 100 days of Trump’s administration, Pence is set to be at the forefront of numerous congressional initiatives, including the overhaul of Obamacare and tax reform, as noted by senior Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway during a conversation with Reuters. “Pence has the president’s trust and is authorized to proceed with these efforts,” Conway remarked. “He plays a critical role in every significant discussion and decision, particularly regarding the legislative agenda,” she added. Although Pence seems to be situated within Trump’s inner circle, it remains uncertain who among them holds the closest ties to the new president or whether they will align with Pence’s views. Despite the Republican Party controlling both the House and the Senate, Pence will require substantial political skill to unite the party's often fractious members behind Trump’s agenda, which has yet to be fully articulated. The Republican Party continues to be divided, ranging from the conservative Tea Party segment to more moderate members, leading to differing opinions on various issues, including free trade, with some expressing concerns about Trump’s potential willingness to engage in spending that could escalate budget deficits. During the 1990s in Indiana, Pence refined his communication abilities while working as a talk radio host. However, his understated approach sharply contrasted with many of his conservative radio counterparts. He has humorously referred to himself as "Rush Limbaugh on decaf," a nod to the notorious right-wing talk radio figure known for his provocative remarks. source_text: As Trump emissary to Congress, Mike Pence faces potential obstacle - his boss. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Shortly after Donald Trump won the U.S. presidential election in November, Vice President-elect Mike Pence visited the country’s largest manufacturing lobby group, six blocks from the White House, to brainstorm about Trump’s legislative agenda. The conversation at the National Association of Manufacturers was friendly, with a lot of “give and take,” said Aric Newhouse, NAM’s senior vice president of government relations. The business group felt Pence spoke their language and that it would be full-steam ahead on long-sought goals such as simplifying the tax code and repealing Obamacare, President Barack Obama’s signature legislation that aimed to extend health insurance to cover more Americans. But over the past week, Trump has sown confusion about some of his legislative aims. He criticized a key element of his Republican Party’s tax plan, known as the border adjustment tax. He also seemed to muddy the waters on his promise of repealing Obamacare by calling for healthcare insurance for all. While NAM was not unduly alarmed, the episode highlights the challenge facing Pence, 57, who will serve as chief emissary to Capitol Hill for Trump after the New York businessman is sworn in as the 45th U.S. president on Friday. Pence spent a dozen years as a congressman beginning in 2001, forging a number of personal relationships, especially with conservatives. While he does not have a reputation on the Hill as a deal-maker, lawmakers, Hill aides and lobbyists describe him as affable and a good communicator who is respectful in his dealings with both friend and foe.  But the NAM experience shows that Pence’s biggest obstacle in striking deals in Congress may be Trump himself. That’s because people negotiating with Pence may not always know if he speaks for his boss. Pence and Trump are a study in contrasts. Where Trump is combative and chases the limelight, Pence, most recently governor of Indiana, is even-keeled and calm, a man described by Republicans and Democrats as articulate and upbeat. Few vice presidents in modern U.S. history have occupied the central role in legislative affairs that Pence will have. Former Vice President Dick Cheney cut deals and cajoled lawmakers for President George W. Bush, but Pence’s assignment may be broader. In Trump’s first 100 days in office, Pence will be “leading the charge” on a number of initiatives in Congress, such as rewriting Obamacare and overhauling the tax code, senior Trump  adviser Kellyanne Conway told Reuters. “He has the assurance and the green light to do so from President Trump,” Conway said. “He is a major part of every serious conversation and important decision that is made, especially when it comes to the legislative agenda,” she said. While Pence certainly appears to be part of Trump’s inner circle, it’s far from clear who is closest to the new president, or whether they will tend to agree with Pence. Even though Republicans control both chambers of Congress, Pence will need plenty of political finesse to rally the party’s sometimes unruly rank-and-file lawmakers behind Trump’s agenda, once it is more fully fleshed out. From the conservative Tea Party faction to the moderate Republicans, the party remains divided. Many Republicans differ with Trump on issues such as free trade and worry he might be too willing to spend money that could increase budget deficits. In his home state of Indiana during the 1990s, Pence honed his communication skills as a talk radio host. But his low-key style stood in stark contrast to many conservative radio hosts. He has called himself “Rush Limbaugh on decaf,” referring to the influential right-wing talk show host famous for his flame-throwing statements.  Pence, who was raised Catholic and later became an evangelical Christian, would sometimes host Bible studies in his office in the House of Representatives. Texas Representative John Carter attended those meetings and recalled that Pence “had a little setup of a radio station” there in a reminder of his former career. During Republican President George W. Bush’s administration, Pence firmly established himself as a fiscal hawk. He resisted initiatives that he viewed as government overreach, including the 2002 “No Child Left Behind” education reform that emphasized standardized testing as a way of gauging how well schools were doing in raising student performance. Pence’s staunch opposition to big government made him one of the “forerunners” to what later became the Tea Party, said Michael Steel, a former spokesman for House Speaker Paul Ryan’s predecessor, John Boehner. Republican Senator Jeff Flake, who served in the House with Pence during the 2000s, said the two of them fashioned themselves as self-appointed fiscal watchdogs. They kept a close eye on late-night sessions where other lawmakers would seek to get more government spending approved without anyone noticing. “Mike and I would have to wait up all night and rush to the (House) floor and burst through the doors” to object to those measures, Flake recounted in an interview. “Somebody said at one point when we burst through it looked like the saloon doors in ‘Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid,’” Flake said, referring to the 1969 film about the two Wild West outlaws. Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, a leading conservative voice, said Pence has been a role model for other Republicans on how to advance conservative principles without being hard-edged.     “I always remember the line Pence had: ‘I’m a conservative and I’m not mad about it’ ... It’s a line I’ve used many times, saying that Mike Pence always used to say that,” Jordan said. Pence calls Speaker Ryan, who has struggled with staunch conservatives in his caucus, a close friend. Their ties may help to smooth over some of the tensions that arose between Ryan and Trump during the 2016 campaign.  Cultivating Republicans won’t be Pence’s only job. If Republicans in the House of Representatives can rally around Trump’s agenda, Democrats will have few tools to block them. But in the Senate, Democrats can use procedural moves to stop legislation that does not otherwise have support from 60 senators. Republicans control 52 votes in the 100-member chamber. Pence’s smooth demeanor will go only so far given his ideological gulf with congressional Democrats. He has raised the ire of Democrats with his outspoken stance against abortion, his work against gay rights, his opposition to measures aimed at women’s pay equity in the workplace and his determination to repeal Obamacare.  Republican Senator Roy Blunt of Missouri, who was part of the House Republican leadership during the mid-2000s, said he expected Pence would stick to his conservative principles, even if they clashed with Trump’s. “I don’t think he’d be very effective arguing against his own feelings,” Blunt said. “But I think he’d be smart enough to go to the president and say, ‘I can be supportive of this because you are the president and I am the vice president, but I am not going to be a good salesman’” on that particular issue.

text: The investigation into the tragic incident at Grenfell Tower in London continues, with police facing the challenging task of searching through the wreckage for human remains. This residential building was the site of a devastating fire that claimed approximately 80 lives. Located in one of the wealthiest boroughs of London, Grenfell Tower housed a diverse community, many of whom were economically disadvantaged. The fire, which erupted in the early hours of June 14, quickly spread throughout the entire structure, leaving destruction in its wake. This calamity has sparked a nationwide discussion regarding social inequality, the neglect faced by marginalized communities, and the adequacy of fire safety measures in place at the time. Law enforcement officials are currently pursuing a criminal inquiry into the fire, which may result in manslaughter charges, although any potential prosecutions could be delayed for months due to the investigation's intricate nature, as stated by police authorities on Tuesday. Commander Stuart Cundy, who oversees the operations related to Grenfell, expressed that the magnitude of this situation is unprecedented in his experience in policing. Intensive efforts are still underway to recover all human remains from the tower, with officers meticulously searching the devastated apartments and carefully sifting through tons of debris using sieves to locate small pieces of human remains such as teeth, bones, or tissue. Detective Superintendent Fiona McCormack, who leads the search and recovery efforts, described the scene as profoundly distressing. So far, 60 victims have been formally recognized, and Cundy indicated that the ultimate death count would likely be slightly under 80. Due to the building's instability, each room is being individually secured with steel bars to ensure the safety of investigators. As the lifts are non-operational, personnel must transport equipment and supplies up the tower manually. In the wake of this disaster, there has been an outpouring of support, with contributions of money and clothing arriving from across the United Kingdom. Unfortunately, there have also been a few instances of individuals attempting to exploit the situation for personal gain. McCormack reported that one confirmed theft involving a significant amount of cash was being investigated, originating from one of the less damaged units at the base of the tower. Additionally, three other suspected thefts concerning residents' belongings are under scrutiny. These incidents came to light when former inhabitants were granted access to their flats to retrieve cherished items and bid farewell to their homes. Stuart conveyed that the officers involved were taken aback by these occurrences. "We are all here, engaged in the work at Grenfell Tower or related to it, feeling great disappointment that something like this could occur following such a tremendous tragedy," he remarked. In response to these events, additional alarms, cameras, and lighting have been installed, and access protocols to the site have been enhanced. The police are also looking into eight suspected fraud cases involving individuals who feigned being impacted by the fire to claim funds provided by the government for survivors and bereaved families. Two individuals have been charged with fraud, one has been released on police bail, and five others are currently under investigation. The criminal inquiry into the fire encompasses hundreds of officers and is concentrating on four key areas: the construction of Grenfell Tower, the refurbishment processes, its management, and the emergency response during the incident. Detective Chief Inspector Matt Bonner, who heads the criminal investigation, stated, "I am committed to identifying and addressing any offenses that may surface during this investigation." He noted that potential offenses uncovered may include fraud, misconduct, violations of health and safety or fire regulations, as well as manslaughter. Charges could potentially be filed against individuals or entities involved. However, Bonner clarified that this should not be interpreted as an indication that the police have already discovered enough evidence to support such charges. Completed in 1974, Grenfell Tower was owned by the Kensington and Chelsea borough and operated by an organization responsible for managing social housing on behalf of the borough.
source_text: Theft at burned London tower adds to police's grueling work. LONDON (Reuters) - Already facing the grim task of sifting through debris to find human remains at Grenfell Tower, the London social housing block where a fire killed about 80 people, police are now also having to investigate suspected thefts from survivors  apartments. Home to a poor, multi-ethnic community within one of London s richest boroughs, Grenfell Tower was gutted by the blaze which rapidly engulfed the whole building in the middle of the night on June 14. The tragedy has prompted a national debate about social inequalities, neglect of deprived communities and whether fire safety regulations were inadequate or were being ignored. Police are conducting a criminal investigation into the fire that could lead to manslaughter charges, although any prosecutions could be months away due to the scale and complexity of the probe, police chiefs said on Tuesday.  The scale of it is something that I personally have never encountered in policing,  said Commander Stuart Cundy, who has overall control of the Grenfell operations. Efforts to recover all human remains from the tower are still going on, with officers conducting fingertip searches in devastated apartments and sifting through tonnes of debris with sieves to find fragments of teeth, bones or tissue.  It is a really harrowing scene,  said Detective Superintendent Fiona McCormack, who is leading search and recovery operations. Sixty victims have been formally identified, and Cundy said the final death toll would likely be a little below 80. The building is unstable and each room has to be individually secured with steel bars to make it safe for investigators. As there are no functioning lifts, workers have to carry equipment and materials all the way up the tower. The disaster has prompted an outpouring of emotion, with donations of money and clothes pouring in from around Britain, but there have also been a small number of incidents of people trying to profit from the tragedy. McCormack said police were investigating one confirmed theft of  a considerable amount  of money from one of the less damaged apartments at the bottom of the tower, and three other suspected thefts of residents  possessions were also being probed. These came to light when former residents were let into their flats to pick up treasured items and to say goodbye to their homes. Stuart said officers had been shocked.  All of us here, working down on Grenfell Tower or working on it anywhere, are just so disappointed that something like that can happen on the back of such a huge tragedy,  he said. Extra alarms, cameras and lights have now been installed and procedures to access the site have been strengthened. Police are also investigating eight cases of suspected fraud by people who pretended to have been affected by the fire in various ways in order to claim money that the government made available for survivors and bereaved relatives. Two people have been charged with fraud, one is on police bail and five others are under investigation. The criminal probe into the fire itself involves hundreds of officers and is focusing on four strands: the construction of Grenfell Tower, its refurbishment, its management and the emergency response to the fire.  I will seek to identify and deal with whatever offences come to light during that investigation,  said Detective Chief Inspector Matt Bonner, who is in charge of the criminal investigation. He said offences that the police may uncover could include fraud, misconduct, breaches of health and safety or fire regulations, and manslaughter. Charges could be brought against individuals or organizations. However, Bonner said this should not be taken as an indication that police had already found evidence to support any such charges.  Grenfell Tower, which was completed in 1974, was owned by the borough of Kensington and Chelsea and managed by an organization that ran social housing on the borough s behalf. Bonner said police had so far identified 336 companies or organizations that were involved in the construction, refurbishment and management of the tower and officers had obtained 31 million documents from them.

text: On Thursday, a remarkable 19.5 million viewers in the U.S. tuned in to witness former FBI Director James Comey's testimony regarding President Trump. According to the Nielsen ratings agency, this significant viewership indicates strong interest for a daytime broadcast, although it falls short of the 30.6 million who watched Trump’s inauguration back in January. Nielsen’s figures encompass audiences from 10 different broadcast and cable networks in the U.S., but do not account for those who viewed the congressional hearing via streaming on computers or mobile devices. Major networks interrupted their regular programming to provide nearly three hours of live coverage of Comey’s statements concerning his interactions with Trump prior to his dismissal in May. Jeffrey Jones, who directs the Peabody Awards in journalism and teaches at the University of Georgia, noted that such impressive numbers are unusual for daytime events, which typically only attract large audiences during state funerals or royal events. While traveling, Jones observed groups of people watching the hearing around televisions in Atlanta’s airport. He remarked, "Politics is quite often about theater and drama, and this was a classic showdown. People wanted to see it for themselves." The television ratings do not reflect the numerous individuals who tuned in to the much-anticipated hearing at bars, restaurants, or through TV network apps and social media platforms. YouTube, owned by Alphabet Inc., reported a peak of nearly 800,000 concurrent viewers across streams from 20 different news outlets. Additionally, Twitter Inc. indicated that the average minute audience for Bloomberg’s live coverage was 129,000 viewers. The most-watched television event of the year remains the Super Bowl, which drew 111 million viewers in February, while Game Three of the NBA Finals attracted around 20 million during its primetime airing on Wednesday. During his testimony, Comey conveyed to the Senate Intelligence Committee his belief that Trump sought to undermine an FBI investigation into potential collusion between Russia and the 2016 presidential campaign. In response, Trump stated on Friday that Comey’s testimony indicated "no obstruction."
