text: Legislation in Oklahoma is set to address the need for accountability in sex crime cases. Next week, lawmakers in Oklahoma City are expected to introduce a bill to make sure that sexual offenses do not escape punishment when the victims were under the influence or unconscious during the incidents. In a ruling from March, the state's highest criminal court determined that Oklahoma's laws regarding rape do indeed cover situations involving individuals who were incapacitated or intoxicated at the time of the assault. However, the court found that the law regarding forcible sodomy, which also includes oral sex, failed to account for these circumstances. This decision was made in connection with allegations surrounding a case where a teenage boy from Tulsa was accused of sexually assaulting a girl who had lost consciousness after consuming alcohol. A lower court had previously dismissed the case last year. Republican Oklahoma Representative Scott Biggs announced on Friday his intention to propose a bill that would redefine forcible sodomy to explicitly include victims who are unconscious. He indicated that the legislation has garnered considerable support and is anticipated to be reviewed by the state legislature soon. "The judges made a significant mistake, but if they require further clarification, we are willing to assist them by amending the statute," Biggs expressed during an interview. The ruling from the state's top criminal appeals court stated: "Sodomy cannot occur where a victim is so intoxicated as to be completely unconscious at the time of the sexual act of oral copulation." It further noted, "we will not, in order to justify prosecution of a person for an offense, enlarge a statute beyond the fair meaning of its language." Until recently, the March ruling had drawn little attention until it was highlighted by the public interest journalism organization Oklahoma Watch, leading to widespread public backlash. The incident from 2014 involved two high school peers who were using alcohol and marijuana with friends. According to Oklahoma Watch, the young man claimed that the oral sex was consensual, while the female student contended otherwise, with DNA evidence indicating the teen's presence. "Regrettably, legal experts often become entangled in semantics, when the law's intent is clear to most of us," Biggs remarked. "I cannot emphasize enough how deeply sorry I am for the victim and the injustice she experienced," he added.

OKLAHOMA CITY (Reuters) - Oklahoma lawmakers will take up legislation next week aimed at ensuring sex crimes do not go unpunished in the state because the victims were unconscious or intoxicated when they occurred.  In March, Oklahoma’s highest criminal court ruled the state’s rape law addresses sexual assault cases involving people who were either unconscious or intoxicated when they were victims of abuse. But the court ruled that Oklahoma’s forcible sodomy law, which also pertains to oral sex, did not address such cases. The ruling was in response to allegations that a Tulsa teenager sexually assaulted a girl who had passed out after a night of drinking. A lower court judge had dismissed the case last year. Oklahoma Representative Scott Biggs, a Republican, said on Friday he is filing legislation to define forcible sodomy in a way that includes unconscious victims. The bill, which is widely supported, is expected to be heard by the Oklahoma legislature in the coming week, Biggs said. “The judges made a grave error, but if they need more clarification, we are happy to give it to them by fixing the statute,” Biggs said in an interview. The state’s highest criminal appeals court said in its ruling: “Sodomy cannot occur where a victim is so intoxicated as to be completely unconscious at the time of the sexual act of oral copulation.”  It added, “we will not, in order to justify prosecution of a person for an offense, enlarge a statute beyond the fair meaning of its language.” The ruling in March had gone mostly unnoticed until the public interest journalism site Oklahoma Watch reported on it this month, sparking a public outcry. The case from 2014 involved two high school students who were drinking and smoking marijuana with friends. The boy testified the oral sex was consensual but the girl said it was not, according to Oklahoma Watch, which added that the teen’s DNA was found on the girl. “Unfortunately, legal minds often get stuck on questions of semantics, when it is clear to most of us what the intent of the law is,” Biggs said. “I can’t stress enough how sorry I am for the victim and that she was denied justice,” he added.

text: The U.S. State Department expressed its disagreement on Tuesday with the viewpoint of FBI Director James Comey, who suggested that the agency exhibits a more relaxed security culture than other federal entities. State Department spokesperson John Kirby stated during a press conference, "We don’t share the broad assessment made of our institution that there’s a lax culture here when it comes to protecting classified information. We take it very, very seriously.” This statement followed Comey's revelation of findings from the FBI’s extensive investigation into the private email server used by former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton during her time in office. According to Comey, the FBI discovered indications of a widespread indifference toward classified information within the State Department.
source_text: U.S. State Department disputes FBI view that it has lax security culture. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. State Department said on Tuesday it disagreed with FBI Director James Comey’s assessment that the department as a whole has a lax attitude toward security compared to other U.S. government agencies. “We don’t share the broad assessment made of our institution that there’s a lax culture here when it comes to protecting classified information. We take it very, very seriously,” State Department spokesman John Kirby told a news briefing. His comments came after Comey announced some of the results of the FBI’s yearlong investigation into former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton’s use of a private email server while she was in office. Comey said the FBI found evidence of a general lack of care for classified information at the State Department.

text: The leaders of Spain are set to urge their counterparts from France, Italy, and Germany to engage in discussions regarding cross-border counter-terrorism efforts during a summit scheduled in Paris on Monday. This initiative was announced by Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy on Friday, following the recent dual attacks in Catalonia. Despite growing concerns about inadequate communication among various investigative bodies and a prior informal warning from Belgium that did not avert Spain’s deadliest violence in over ten years, Rajoy commended the response of law enforcement. He expressed his desire for European Union allies to evaluate the existing cooperation frameworks and explore ways to enhance and refine them. Last week, a van drove into a crowd in Barcelona, resulting in the deaths of 13 individuals. Additionally, two more fatalities occurred during the driver’s escape and in a separate attack involving a car and a knife in the coastal town of Cambrils. These incidents have raised questions regarding the sharing of intelligence across Europe and within Spain itself, where regional police forces operate alongside national ones. In 2016, Belgian authorities provided a tip-off to Catalan police regarding one of the suspects, Abdelbaki Es Satty, who was part of the group behind the attacks. However, this warning was transmitted through unofficial means. At that point, records from Catalan police did not reveal any connections between Es Satty, a Moroccan-born imam residing in the small town of Ripoll in Catalonia, and Islamist extremism. Investigations are also underway to determine any possible connections to France, as some attackers had traveled to Paris prior to the incidents. Out of the 12 individuals linked to the attacks, six were shot by police, and two died in an explosion before the van incident. Two suspects are currently in custody facing charges of murder and involvement in a terrorist organization, while two others have been released under specific conditions. Rajoy attempted to minimize the divide between his administration and the separatist leaders in Catalonia, who are organizing an independence referendum on October 1, which Madrid deems illegal. "We are more effective in combating terrorism when we put aside our differences... Achieving political unity is crucial," Rajoy remarked. Catalonian leader Carles Puigdemont stated in an interview published on Friday that the Spanish government had intentionally underfunded the police force in the region. "We urged them not to politicize security... Unfortunately, the Spanish government had different priorities," Puigdemont informed the Financial Times. On Saturday, Spain’s King Felipe, along with politicians from both Madrid and Catalonia, is expected to join a demonstration in Barcelona. Residents and local leaders in Cambrils, the location of the second attack last week, were scheduled to march on Friday under the banner "We are all Cambrils."

text: As Thailand readies itself for the extravagant funeral of the beloved King Bhumibol Adulyadej, hotels in the vibrant old town of Bangkok, particularly popular among international travelers, are fully booked, according to the hotel association's statement on Monday. The ceremony honoring King Bhumibol, who passed away on October 13 last year after ruling for seventy years, is set to take place over five days next week, primarily around the Grand Palace and Sanam Luang, a well-known public square in the historical district. text: The situation at an abandoned Australian detention facility has prompted Papua New Guinea to take action against asylum seekers. SYDNEY (Reuters) - Immigration Minister Petrus Thomas announced on Monday that around 450 men still occupying the site would be forcibly removed. For over 13 days, these individuals have barricaded themselves within the Manus Island facility, lacking access to food and clean water. They have resisted efforts from Australia and Papua New Guinea to shut down the center, expressing concerns for their safety if they are relocated to transit centers. "We will be taking steps with relevant authorities to move the residents based on serious exposure to health risk for the food of everyone that is remaining," stated Thomas in a release issued late Sunday. According to several asylum seekers inside the facility who communicated with Reuters via email, as of 5.00 p.m. (0700 GMT) Monday, no actions had yet been taken to remove the men. One individual confined within the center mentioned that water supplies had been depleted after workers from Papua New Guinea came onto the premises and emptied the tanks and garbage bins that collected rainwater. "Immigration came and bored holes in the water tanks where we had been collecting rain water," he remarked, choosing to remain unnamed due to concerns about retaliation from the authorities in Papua New Guinea. "They also demolished the well we built." Two weeks ago, running water and electricity were severed from the center following the withdrawal of Australian security personnel and the facility's closure on October 31. A Papua New Guinea Court had deemed the center illegal. The United Nations has raised alarms about a potential humanitarian crisis developing among the asylum seekers, who predominantly hail from countries like Afghanistan, Iran, Myanmar, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Syria. Australia has utilized this center, along with a facility on the small Pacific island of Nauru, to detain individuals seeking to reach its shores by boat. The Australian government maintains that those arriving by boat will never be allowed to enter the country, even if granted refugee status, as this would incentivize human trafficking in Asia. Under a refugee exchange agreement, the United States has consented to accept up to 1,250 asylum seekers from Manus and Nauru in exchange for Australia taking in refugees from Central America. However, as of now, the United States has only admitted 54 refugees. In addition, New Zealand has proposed resettling 150 asylum seekers, yet Australia has declined this offer. text: A significant overseas military installation has been inaugurated by Turkey in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia. This development took place on Saturday and serves to strengthen Turkey's relationship with the strategically important yet unstable Muslim-majority nation, further establishing its presence in East Africa. As reported by a high-ranking Turkish official, the facility is set to train over 10,000 Somali troops under the guidance of Turkish military personnel. The opening ceremony was marked by attendance from Hulusi Akar, Turkey's military chief of staff. The $50 million installation is a testament to the increasingly close ties between Turkey and Somalia. Historical relations between Turkey and the Horn of Africa trace back to the era of the Ottoman Empire, but in recent times, under President Tayyip Erdogan’s leadership, Turkey has emerged as a key ally of the Somali administration. During the inauguration, Somali Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire expressed gratitude towards the Turkish government for establishing the training academy, emphasizing its role in rebuilding the national military. He articulated the vision of a force that transcends clan affiliations, emphasizing the need for well-prepared military personnel that represent all Somali citizens. Khaire highlighted the significance of the military academy as Turkey's largest base outside its borders. The facility is equipped to train and accommodate 1,000 soldiers simultaneously and features amenities such as sports courts and a running track. Erdogan, whose political background is rooted in Islamism, has emerged as a prominent advocate for Muslims, particularly those in dire humanitarian situations, including Syrian refugees and the Rohingya from Myanmar. Analysts have argued that following the Arab Spring, Turkey's foreign policy initiatives closer to home have struggled, leading Ankara to find a receptive partner in Somalia. According to Sinan Ulgen, a visiting scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Somalia is a nation where Turkey can exert influence without having to compete against other regional or global powers. He noted that Turkey's initial emphasis on providing aid, rather than security support or backing specific political factions, played a crucial role in building trust with the Somali populace. Turkey's extensive aid efforts during the catastrophic famine of 2011 won the hearts of many Somalis, and the nation has continued to provide assistance, largely through contributions from private enterprises. Furthermore, Turkey has invested in developing educational institutions, healthcare facilities, and infrastructure, as well as providing scholarships for Somali students to pursue their studies in Turkey. Erdogan has made two visits to Mogadishu, with his first trip occurring in 2011, when he became the inaugural non-African leader to set foot in the war-torn country in two decades. The burgeoning trade relations between Turkey and Somalia have also been noteworthy. In 2010, the total value of Turkish exports to Somalia was a mere $5.1 million, but by the previous year, this figure had surged to $123 million. Following the failed coup attempt last year, the Somali cabinet swiftly ordered the closure of schools and a hospital in Mogadishu associated with Gulen, whom Erdogan has consistently accused of orchestrating the coup. Gulen, however, has denied any involvement. Somalia's government receives backing from various foreign entities, including the United Nations, the African Union, and the United States, which are assisting in the development of an effective national army capable of combating the militant group al-Shabaab. Although the militants were expelled from Mogadishu in 2010, their violent attacks continue to pose a significant challenge to achieving stability in this tumultuous region of East Africa, which is situated along one of the globe's most critical shipping lanes. The Somali administration has lauded Turkish investment for enhancing the nation's infrastructure, with the information minister particularly acknowledging Turkey's recent commitment to providing security support. "We are quite pleased with the modern facilities being offered for our security forces," he remarked. source_text: Turkey opens military base in Mogadishu to train Somali soldiers. MOGADISHU/ANKARA (Reuters) - Turkey opened its biggest overseas military base on Saturday in Somalia s capital, cementing its ties with the volatile but strategic Muslim nation and building a presence in East Africa. More than 10,000 Somali soldiers will be trained by Turkish officers at the base, a senior Turkish official said ahead of a ceremony in Mogadishu attended by Turkish military chief of staff Hulusi Akar. The opening of the $50 million base signals ever-closer ties between Turkey and Somalia. Turkey s relations with the Horn of Africa date back to the Ottoman Empire, but President Tayyip Erdogan s government has become a close ally of the Somali government in recent years. At the opening ceremony on Saturday, Somali Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire thanked the Turkish government for opening the training school and said it would help the government  reconstruct  its national force    not based on clan...not from a particular place, but well-trained forces that represent the Somali people.  He noted that the military school was Turkey s biggest overseas. The facility can train and house 1,000 soldiers at a time and also has sports courts and a running track. Erdogan, whose roots are in political Islam, is an outspoken defender of Muslims, particularly those in need of humanitarian aid, such as Syrian refugees and Myanmar s Rohingya.  Analysts say that, in the aftermath of the Arab Spring, as Turkey s foreign policy forays close to home have floundered, Ankara has found a willing partner in Somalia.   It s a country where Turkey could make a difference without necessarily having to compete with regional or global powers,  said Sinan Ulgen, a visiting scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Ankara s initial focus on aid, as opposed to security assistance or overt backing of political parties, helped build trust, he added. Turkey s vast aid effort at the height of the 2011 famine endeared it to many Somali people, and it has continued to pour in aid, much of it from private companies. It has built schools, hospitals and infrastructure and provided scholarships for Somalis to study in Turkey. Erdogan has visited Mogadishu twice, and when he made his first trip there in 2011 he became the first non-African leader to visit the war-ravaged nation in 20 years. Rapidly growing trade between the two nations has followed. In 2010, Turkish exports to Somalia totaled just $5.1 million. By last year, they had ballooned to $123 million. In the space of six years Turkey has gone from Somalia s 20th-largest source of imports to its fifth-largest.  Turkey really has won the hearts and minds of Somali people,  Information Minister Abdirahman Omar Osman told Reuters this month.  Somalia s government has also been a vocal backer of the Erdogan government in its bid to quash Muslim cleric Fethullah Gulen s influence abroad. The Somali cabinet immediately ordered schools and a hospital in Mogadishu linked to Gulen to be shut in the aftermath of last year s failed coup, which Erdogan has repeatedly blamed on the cleric. Gulen denies involvement. Somalia s government has a number of foreign backers, including the United Nations, the African Union, and the United States, who are assisting it in building a functional national army capable of taking on the fight against the militant al-Shabaab group. The militants were driven out of Mogadishu in 2010, but their deadly attacks remain one of the main obstacles to stability in the chaotic Horn of Africa country, which lies along one of the world s busiest shipping routes. The Somali government has praised Turkish investment for improving infrastructure in the country, and the information minister singled out Turkey s new move into security support.  We are very happy they are giving us modern facilities for our security forces,  he said.  This is something that Somalia has never seen even though countries like the U.S. and UK are giving us millions. The difference is the camp Turkey built is an institution that will remain for the next 50 or 100 years.  The Turkish official who spoke to Reuters before the opening said the base was in line with Ankara s priority of expanding its weapons sales  to new markets .

text: Supporters of Bernie Sanders reacted with frustration and a sense of validation on Saturday following the release of Hillary Clinton's comments to major financial institutions and corporations, which seemed to corroborate their concerns regarding her stance on international trade and her closeness to Wall Street. Clinton, who relies on Sanders’ base of young and progressive voters to aid her presidential campaign, advocates for open borders and free trade in one of her speeches, while also adopting a conciliatory tone towards Wall Street, both of which she later distanced herself from to align with Sanders’ criticisms of trade agreements and influential banks. The speeches by the former Secretary of State, recorded during private meetings in 2013 and 2014 where attendees were charged for entry, were disclosed online on Friday by WikiLeaks, which attributed them to the email account of John Podesta, Clinton’s campaign chairman. The authenticity of these speech transcripts could not be independently verified by Reuters. Clinton has previously refused to make such transcripts public. "This clearly illustrates why progressives fundamentally distrust Hillary Clinton," remarked Tobita Chow, chair of the People’s Lobby in Chicago, which backed Sanders during the primary elections. "The progressive movement must urge Secretary Clinton to clarify her actual stance on these matters, which must include unequivocal disavowals of the positions revealed in these transcripts," Chow stated. The release of these comments was swiftly overshadowed by the emergence of an 11-year-old tape featuring Donald Trump, the Republican nominee, making inappropriate remarks about women. Clinton has made considerable efforts to cultivate trust among so-called progressives, adopting many of Sanders’ views after defeating him in the primary contest. The senator from Vermont now endorses his former opponent for the general election on November 8 against Trump. Nonetheless, Clinton has faced challenges in gaining the support of young “millennials,” a demographic vital to Sanders’ campaign. Some Democrats voiced concerns that the leaks could deter these supporters from participating in the election. "That is a significant worry, and this absolutely does not help," noted Larry Cohen, chair of the board of Our Revolution, a progressive group formed following Sanders’ presidential run, aimed at promoting his ideas at the grassroots level. "It has implications for turnout, enthusiasm, volunteering, and all those aspects." The Clinton campaign asserted it would not validate the legitimacy of the documents released by WikiLeaks and its founder, Julian Assange. "We will not affirm the authenticity of stolen documents released by Julian Assange, who has openly expressed his intent to harm Hillary Clinton," declared Glen Caplin, a campaign spokesperson. "Guccifer 2.0 has already validated the warnings from top national security officials that documents can be fabricated as part of a sophisticated Russian misinformation initiative," he added, referencing the hacker or hacking group that modified certain data stolen from the Democratic National Committee prior to its public release earlier this year. On Friday, the U.S. government officially accused Russia of conducting a series of cyberattacks against Democratic Party entities leading up to the election. The source of the leaks did not lessen the backlash on social media against Clinton’s speeches from several users. "Bernie was correct about Hillary," commented Facebook user Grace Tilly, "she’s a puppet for Wall Street." "Clinton embodies the archetype of a politician - precisely the Wall Street insider that Bernie depicted," wrote Facebook user Brian Leach. Representatives for Sanders did not reply to requests for comments. NBC News reported a statement from Sanders indicating his intention to promote the Democrats’ policy platform. "Regardless of what Secretary Clinton may or may not have expressed privately regarding Wall Street..."
source_text: Sanders supporters seethe over Clinton's leaked remarks to Wall St.. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Supporters of former Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders on Saturday expressed anger and vindication over leaked comments made by Hillary Clinton to banks and big business that appeared to confirm their fears about her support for global trade and tendency to cozy up to Wall Street. Clinton, who needs Sanders’ coalition of young and left-leaning voters to propel her to the presidency, pushes for open trade and open borders in one of the speeches, and takes a conciliatory approach to Wall Street, both positions she later backed away from in an effort to capture the popular appeal of Sanders’ attacks on trade deals and powerful banks.  The excerpts of remarks by the former secretary of state, made in 2013 and 2014 in closed-door meetings where audiences paid to attend, were published online on Friday by WikiLeaks, which sourced them to the email account of John Podesta, Clinton’s campaign chairman.  Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the speech transcripts. Clinton has previously declined to release any such transcripts. “This is a very clear illustration of why there is a fundamental lack of trust from progressives for Hillary Clinton,” said Tobita Chow, chair of the People’s Lobby in Chicago, which endorsed Sanders in the primary election. “The progressive movement needs to make a call to Secretary Clinton to clarify where she stands really on these issues and that’s got to involve very clear renunciations of the positions that are revealed in these transcripts,” Chow said. The revelations were quickly overshadowed by the release of an 11-year-old recording of Donald Trump, the Republican presidential nominee, making lewd comments about women.  Clinton has worked hard to build trust with so-called progressives, adopting several of Sanders’ positions after she bested him in the primary race. The U.S. senator from Vermont now supports his former rival in the Nov. 8 general election against Trump. Still, Clinton has struggled to win support from young “millennials” who were crucial to Sanders’ success, and some Democrats expressed concern that the leaks would discourage those supporters from showing up to vote.  “That is a big concern and this certainly doesn’t help,” said Larry Cohen, chair of the board of Our Revolution, a progressive organization formed in the wake of Sanders’ bid for the presidency, which aims to keep pushing the former candidate’s ideas at a grassroots level. “It matters in terms of turnout, energy, volunteering, all those things.” The Clinton campaign said it would not confirm the accuracy of the documents released by WikiLeaks and its founder, Julian Assange.  “We are not going to confirm the authenticity of stolen documents released by Julian Assange, who has made no secret of his desire to damage Hillary Clinton,” said Glen Caplin, a campaign spokesman.  “Guccifer 2.0 has already proven the warnings of top national security officials that documents can be faked as part of a sophisticated Russian misinformation campaign,” he said, referring to the hacker or hacking group that altered some data stolen from the Democratic National Committee before making it public earlier this year.  The U.S. government on Friday formally accused Russia of a campaign of cyber attacks against Democratic Party organizations ahead of the election. The origin of the leaks did not dampen social media criticism of the speeches by some. “Bernie was right about Hillary,” wrote Facebook user Grace Tilly, “she’s a tool for Wall Street.” “Clinton is the politicians’ politician - exactly the Wall Street insider Bernie described,” wrote Facebook user Brian Leach. Spokesmen for Sanders did not respond to requests for comment. NBC News quoted a statement from Sanders saying he would work to advance the Democrats’ policy platform. “Whatever Secretary Clinton may or may not have said behind closed doors on Wall Street, I am determined to implement the agenda of the Democratic Party platform which was agreed to by her campaign,” the statement said. Democratic strategist Steve Elmendorf said progressive voters would still choose the former first lady, even with misgivings. “I’d like to meet the Bernie Sanders supporter who is going to say, ‘Well I’m a little worried about her on international trade, so I’m going to vote for Donald Trump’,” he said.

text: The Secretary of Defense of the United States canceled his trip to Afghanistan due to adverse weather conditions, as stated by U.S. President Donald Trump's defense secretary. During his initial visit to the Middle East, he mentioned in Abu Dhabi that he was contemplating future actions in the conflict following talks with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani and the chief U.S. military officer. "We are currently consolidating our thoughts," Defense Secretary Jim Mattis informed journalists. U.S. General John Nicholson, overseeing U.S. and allied forces in Afghanistan, remarked earlier this month that the NATO-led contingent had sufficient personnel for counterterrorism efforts but faced "a shortfall of a few thousand" for its primary task of advising Afghan security forces. Mattis disclosed that he engaged in a lengthy video conference with Nicholson on Sunday but withheld any indication of his stance regarding the deployment of additional U.S. troops. Furthermore, he indicated that he had a detailed conversation with Ghani just before departing Munich, Germany, on Saturday. Thus far, Trump has not provided clear guidance about whether he will authorize an increase in troop levels for Afghanistan, where approximately 8,400 American soldiers remain stationed more than 15 years after the fall of the Taliban regime. "He is waiting for my evaluation and the input from the intelligence sector, and he is receptive to my recommendations on the matter," stated Mattis. "However, I must first determine my position on the issue." Afghan governmental forces currently control no more than two-thirds of the nation’s territory and have encountered significant challenges in managing the Taliban insurgency since the majority of NATO troops departed at the end of 2014. Additionally, the Afghan government is facing challenges from other extremist groups, notably the Islamic State’s faction in Afghanistan. The Islamic State took responsibility for a suicide bombing that resulted in at least 22 fatalities on February 7 near Afghanistan’s Supreme Court. Multiple provincial capitals are under threat from the Taliban, and Afghan military forces have endured substantial losses, with over 5,500 killed during the initial eight months of 2016. "The price paid by Afghan security forces to keep the Taliban at bay has been very steep. Nonetheless, they managed to hold their ground," Mattis commented. "Today, the Taliban finds itself in a more precarious situation, although I do not equate that with success on our part."
source_text: U.S. defense secretary scraps Afghan trip due to weather. ABU DHABI (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump’s defense secretary said bad weather had forced him to scrap a visit to Afghanistan on Sunday but added that he was reviewing the next steps in the war after discussions with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani and the top U.S. commander. “We’re putting our thoughts together now,” Defense Secretary Jim Mattis told reporters in Abu Dhabi during his debut trip to the Middle East. U.S. General John Nicholson, the commander of U.S. and international troops in Afghanistan, said this month the NATO-led force in Afghanistan had enough troops to carry out counterterrorism missions but had “a shortfall of a few thousand” for its major role of advising Afghan security forces. Mattis said he spoke for several hours on Sunday via video-link with Nicholson, but did not disclose whether he was in favor of sending more U.S. forces there. Mattis also said he spoke with Ghani “at length” before leaving Munich, Germany, on Saturday. So far, Trump has offered little clarity about whether he will approve more forces for Afghanistan, where some 8,400 U.S. troops remain more than 15 years after the Islamist Taliban government was toppled.  “He’s waiting for my assessment and the assessment from the intelligence community and he’s open to my advice on it,” Mattis said. “But first of all I’ve got to formulate where I stand.” Afghan government forces control no more than two-thirds of national territory, and have struggled to contain the Taliban insurgency since the bulk of NATO soldiers withdrew at the end of 2014. The government is also struggling with other militants, particularly from Islamic State’s Afghanistan branch. Islamic State claimed responsibility for a suicide attack that killed at least 22 people on Feb. 7 outside Afghanistan’s Supreme Court. A number of provincial capitals have been under pressure from the Taliban and Afghan government forces have been suffering high casualty rates, with more than 5,500 killed in the first eight months of 2016. “The Afghan security forces paid a very heavy price to keep the Taliban on their back foot. But they paid it, they held,” Mattis said. “And the Taliban’s in a worse position today, even though I do not equate that to success on our side.”

text: The trial in Belgium for a significant suspect linked to the November 2015 Islamic State assault in Paris has been rescheduled to February 5. On Monday, the judge granted a request from Saleh Abdeslam's newly appointed attorney for additional time to review the case, thus postponing the proceedings by seven weeks. Abdeslam, who is a French citizen but has lived in Brussels his entire life, returned to Belgium following the attacks in Paris that resulted in the deaths of 130 individuals. He eluded law enforcement for four months before being captured in March of last year. Just four days after his arrest, on March 22, 2016, Brussels experienced twin explosions that claimed 32 lives. Authorities suspect a connection between the assailants of the Paris and Brussels bombings, with Abdeslam being one of the last surviving members of the group; his older brother detonated himself at a café in Paris on November 13, 2015. Abdeslam is currently in custody in France but will first be sent to Belgium to face charges alongside an alleged accomplice for attempted murder due to his evasion during a shootout with police three days prior to his capture. Abdeslam did not appear in court on Monday and had appointed a new lawyer just the previous week.
source_text: Belgian trial of Paris attack suspect postponed to Feb. 5. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - The Belgian trial of a key suspect in the November 2015 Islamic State attack on Paris was postponed on Monday for seven weeks, after Saleh Abdeslam s newly appointed lawyer asked for more time to study the case. Granting the request, the judge set a new trial date of Feb. 5. A French national but a lifelong Brussels resident, Abdeslam fled back to Belgium after the attacks in Paris that killed 130 people, hiding from police for four months before being detained in March last year. Four days later, on March 22, 2016, Brussels was hit by twin bomb attacks that killed 32 people. Investigators believe that those behind the Paris and Brussels suicide attacks were linked and that Abdeslam, whose elder brother blew himself up at a Paris cafe on Nov. 13, 2015, is one of the few surviving participants. Held facing trial in France, he will be transferred to Belgium to first stand trial there, with an alleged accomplice, for attempted murder as Abdeslam evaded capture during a shootout with Brussels police three days before his arrest. Abdeslam, who was not in court on Monday, appointed a new lawyer only last week and his counsel asked for more time to prepare the defense.

text: A recent poll has revealed a dramatic decline in the approval ratings for Michel Temer's presidency in Brazil. The survey, released on Tuesday, indicates that the leader, who is mired in controversy, is facing fresh allegations of corruption while attempting to navigate his economic reform initiatives through the legislature. According to the polling organization MDA, only 3.4 percent of respondents rated the Temer administration as performing a great or good job, a significant drop from 10.3 percent reported in MDA's previous poll conducted in February. Having assumed office a year ago after Dilma Rousseff was impeached, Temer has stated that he prioritizes advancing an austerity package over public approval, aiming to complete this before his term concludes in January 2019. However, his efforts are hindered by serious accusations that include bribery, racketeering, and obstructing justice. These allegations stem from the testimony provided by the owners of JBS SA, the largest meatpacking company globally, who claim that Temer accepted bribes for political favors and plotted to silence a witness who might incriminate him. Temer has consistently denied any allegations of misconduct. The MDA poll, which was conducted between September 13 and 16, involved 2,002 participants across Brazil and has a margin of error of 2.2 percentage points.
source_text: Approval rating for Brazil's Temer plummets: poll. SAO PAULO (Reuters) - Approval for Brazilian President Michel Temer s government has plummeted, according to a poll published on Tuesday, as the scandal-plagued leader faces new corruption charges and struggles to push his economic reform agenda through Congress.  Polling firm MDA said that 3.4 percent of those surveyed thought the Temer government was doing a  great or good  job - down from 10.3 percent in MDA s last such poll in February. Temer took over a year ago from impeached leftist Dilma Rousseff and has said he does not care about popularity and only wants to push through an austerity package before his term ends in Jan. 2019. Yet his ability to do so has been hamstrung by charges of taking bribes, racketeering and obstruction of justice. The charges against Temer are based on the plea-bargain testimony of the owners of the world s largest meatpacker, JBS SA. They accuse Temer of taking bribes in return for political favors and of conspiring to buy the silence of a witness who could implicate the leader.  Temer has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. The MDA poll was commissioned by the national transport lobby CNT and surveyed 2,002 people across Brazil from Sept. 13-16. The poll has a margin of error of 2.2 percentage points.

text: Concerns regarding potential national security risks stemming from reductions in State Department personnel have intensified among congressional members. On Thursday, every Democratic member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee collectively signed a letter requesting a briefing on this issue. They pointed out in their correspondence to Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, "The number of minister counselors in the State Department has decreased by 15 percent, career ministers by 42 percent, and career ambassadors by an astounding 60 percent." The letter emphasized that the departure of skilled professionals from the State Department jeopardizes the institution, posing a threat to American leadership, security, and interests globally. Representative Eliot Engel, who serves as the leading Democrat on the committee, spearheaded this initiative. A bipartisan coalition, including both Democrats and some Republicans who support President Donald Trump, have voiced their opposition to Trump's budget proposal, which seeks to slash the State Department's funding by approximately 30 percent. Tillerson, however, has supported this budget cut, implementing a hiring freeze while he evaluates the agency's operations and deliberates on reorganization strategies. On Tuesday, both the Republican chair and the leading Democrat of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee criticized the agency for its staffing reductions and what they termed a lack of a coherent plan for the proposed restructuring. The following day, Senator John McCain, who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, alongside Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the leading Democrat on a Foreign Relations subcommittee responsible for overseeing the State Department, sent a letter to Tillerson. They requested that he start engaging with lawmakers on matters affecting recruitment, retention, and staffing, as well as lifting the hiring freeze and reinstating promotions. Tillerson has stated that his plan for reorganization is intended to enhance efficiency and reduce expenses, aiming to achieve at least a 10 percent reduction, which translates to around $5 billion, based on fiscal year 2017 figures, over the next five years. A spokesperson for the State Department remarked that all communications from Congress are thoroughly examined and receive suitable responses. "We can affirm that the Secretary has said on many occasions that he will advocate for any resources or reforms America’s diplomats need to do their jobs," the spokesperson noted in an email.
source_text: U.S. House Democrats join growing congressional concern about State Dept. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A chorus of concern in the U.S. Congress over the potential national security threat of State Department staff cuts grew on Thursday when every Democrat on the House of Representatives Foreign Affairs Committee signed a letter asking for a briefing. “The number of minister counselors in the State Department has decreased by 15 percent, career ministers by 42 percent, and career ambassadors by an astounding 60 percent,” they said in the letter to Secretary of State Rex Tillerson. “The amount of talent leaving the State Department endangers the institution and undermines American leadership, security and interests around the world,” said the letter, led by Representative Eliot Engel, the top Democrat on the committee. Many members of Congress, Democrats as well as some of President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans, have rejected Trump’s proposal to cut the State Department budget by about 30 percent. Tillerson has embraced the plan, and imposed a hiring freeze while analyzing the agency’s operations and deciding how to reorganize them. On Tuesday, the Republican chairman and top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee both blasted the agency for cuts in staff and what they described as a failure to have a plan for a proposed organization. On Wednesday, Republican Senator John McCain, the Senate Armed Services Committee chairman, and Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on a Foreign Relations subcommittee overseeing State, delivered a letter to Tillerson asking him to begin consulting with lawmakers on decisions that have an impact on recruiting, retaining and staffing, removing a hiring freeze and resuming promotions. [L1N1NL2AB] Tillerson has said his reorganization plan aimed to increase efficiency and cut costs, with a target of saving at least 10 percent, or about $5 billion, over the next five years from fiscal-year 2017 levels.  A State Department spokesperson said that all congressional correspondence to the department is reviewed and receives an appropriate response. “We can affirm that the Secretary has said on many occasions that he will advocate for any resources or reforms America’s diplomats need to do their jobs,” the spokesperson said in a email.

text: In the village of Hazima, located north of Raqqa, the sound of children learning has returned to bullet-riddled schools that were previously damaged or booby-trapped by the Islamic State. Recently, on a summer day before the new school term commenced, teachers were conducting makeshift alphabet lessons in overcrowded classrooms. Teacher Ahmed al-Ahmed emphasized, "The priority is to ensure children are in school," while standing beside a staircase hole created by a mine explosion that injured a fellow educator. Following its takeover of the region in 2014, three years into Syria’s civil conflict, the ultra-extremist Islamic State had shut down this and numerous other educational institutions in northern Syria, replacing formal education with extremist ideology taught in mosques. However, since the U.S.-supported military coalition, the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), has expelled the group from most of its territory in and around Raqqa, discussions surrounding education have surfaced, highlighting the ethnic tensions anticipated in the aftermath. One major concern is the content of education in areas governed by the SDF, which, despite being comprised of various Arab militias, is chiefly led by the Kurdish YPG. Schools in Raqqa this year will implement a new curriculum derived from former textbooks, but it will remove the Baathist principles associated with President Bashar al-Assad, a change that has gained consensus among both Arab and Kurdish educators. Yet, a representative from the SDF has suggested the prompt implementation of Kurdish language classes in Raqqa schools, a notion that has caused local officials to react negatively. Unlike other regions under SDF jurisdiction where Kurdish has been taught for years, there are currently no plans to introduce the language in predominantly Arab Raqqa. Authorities have indicated that broad agreement would be necessary, suggesting fears that a hurried introduction could lead to unrest. Ahmed noted, "We wouldn’t object to Kurdish being taught. However, if it is forced upon schools, there will be issues." The YPG has maintained control over parts of northeastern Syria since the beginning of the six-year conflict, establishing a self-governing administration that opposes Assad, who retains power in the larger population centers to the west and continues to advance against the Islamic State, along with Turkey, a rival of the YPG that shares a border with Syria. Officials assert that Raqqa is likely to integrate into this administration. All ethnic groups are represented within the local governing bodies managing predominately Arab territories that the SDF captured from IS fighters, yet critics argue that Kurds have a significant influence over decision-making. Interviews conducted by Reuters with SDF officials and local representatives indicate a growing dissatisfaction concerning Kurdish authority, particularly regarding educational policies. A senior adviser and coordinator with the U.S. coalition within the SDF expressed his belief that Kurdish would be taught to Kurdish students in Raqqa this year, in alignment with the educational model established in other SDF-controlled areas. He stated, "No one has contested this ... every ethnic group has the entitlement to receive education in its own language," via an online communication. The Raqqa Civil Council, the newly established local governing authority, expressed surprise at this statement. Ammar Hussein, an official from the education committee, responded from his office in Ain Issa stating, "No, that will not occur without our consultation and the council's agreement." Currently, classes are being conducted in Arabic, with English and French offered as additional languages. Echoing the sentiments of several council members, he asserted that Kurdish instruction would only be provided if there were community requests, a sufficient number of qualified teachers, and approval from the Arab-Kurdish council. Ali Shanna, another official from the education committee, added, "If the local population consents ... there won’t be any objections." Meanwhile, a former Kurdish educator privately criticized Shanna’s perspective, stating, "I despise that viewpoint. It reflects ignorance, akin to the mindset of Daesh (Islamic State)," revealing his past experiences of being imprisoned under Assad's regime for publishing a Kurdish-language journal.

HAZIMA, Syria (Reuters) - The few bullet-marked schools Islamic State did not flatten or booby trap around its former Syrian stronghold of Raqqa are buzzing for the first time in years with the sound of children learning. In the village of Hazima, north of Raqqa, teachers gave ad-hoc alphabet lessons to crammed classrooms on a recent summer s day before the start of term.   Right now, the most important thing is to get children into class,  said teacher Ahmed al-Ahmed, standing next to a hole in the school stairwell left by a mine blast that wounded a colleague. The ultra-hardline Islamic State closed this school and  many others in northern Syria after it seized control of the region in 2014, three years into the country s civil war. Instead it taught children extremist thought in mosques. But now that the group has been ousted from most territory it held in and around Raqqa by a U.S.-backed military alliance, the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), a growing debate over education points to the ethnic tensions expected to follow. What is taught in areas under the control of the SDF, which includes Arab militias but is dominated by the Kurdish YPG, is one of many questions over how predominantly Arab parts of northern Syria will be run as they come into the Kurdish fold. Schools around Raqqa will this year teach a new curriculum that is based on old textbooks but erases the Baathist ideology of President Bashar al-Assad, a decision agreed on by Arab and Kurdish teachers alike. But an official in the SDF has floated the immediate introduction of Kurdish lessons in Raqqa schools, an idea that makes local officials bristle. In contrast with other areas under SDF control that have for years taught Kurdish, there are no plans yet to teach the language in mostly Arab Raqqa.  Officials say it would need broad consensus, hinting at concerns that its introduction too quickly would cause unrest.  We wouldn t object to Kurdish teaching. But if it s imposed on schools then there will be problems,  Ahmed said. The YPG has held areas of northeast Syria since early in the six-year-old war which are now under a self-run administration opposed by Assad, who holds the main population centers in the west and is also advancing against Islamic State, and Turkey, a YPG foe which borders Syria. Raqqa is likely to join the administration, officials say. All ethnic groups are represented in the local bodies that run majority Arab regions captured by the SDF as it ousted IS fighters but critics say Kurds dominate decision-making. Reuters interviews with SDF officials and local authorities suggest resentment over Kurdish power is brewing over education plans. A senior SDF adviser and coordinator with the U.S. coalition said he believed Kurdish would be taught to Kurdish pupils around Raqqa this year, following the model for other schools in SDF territory.  No one has opposed this ... every (ethnic) group has the right to study in its own language,  Amed Sido said via the internet. Officials in the Raqqa Civil Council, the newly-formed local governing body, were taken aback.  No, that won t happen without consultations with us and agreement in the council,  Ammar Hussein, an education committee official, said at its office in the town of Ain Issa.  For now it s in Arabic, with English and French lessons.  Echoing several council members, he said Kurdish would be taught only if families requested it, there were enough qualified teachers and the Arab-Kurdish council approved it.  If the people here agree ... there won t be any objection,  said Ali Shanna, another education committee official.  But the Kurd knows the Kurdish language, why does he need to learn it?   A former Kurdish teacher privately derided Shanna s comments.  I hate that attitude. It s ignorance, it s the same thinking as Daesh (Islamic State),  said the teacher, who had been jailed under Assad for writing a Kurdish-language journal. The sensitivity over language has already caused unrest in Hasaka to the northeast, an area controlled for years by the YPG where a new curriculum is taught in Arabic and Kurdish, both now official languages. In demonstrations reported by a monitoring group, protesters called for Arab children not to have to learn Kurdish. Mostafa Bali, an SDF official, said there was no intention to force Kurdish on Arabs, or to suppress Arabic.  We don t support racism over language. But there are many Kurds who would like to see Arabic teaching banned in Kurdish areas as revenge for the Baath (teaching),  he said. The Baathist curriculum championed Arab nationalism over ethnic identity. Kurdish pupils were punished for speaking their mother tongue in school playgrounds. Now, even in some Arab-majority towns, Kurds are taught Kurdish. Officials in Raqqa are determined to do things their way, regardless of what they say are potential military threats from Assad or neighboring Turkey.  We won t let Turkey or anyone else interfere in our internal affairs. We decide what we ll teach or not teach,  Leila Mostafa, the Kurdish co-president of the Raqqa Civil Council said. At Hazima school, teachers worry about both the legacy left by Islamic State and Assad, and future political upheaval.  One kid turned up singing Islamic State chants,  teacher Ahmed Saoud said.  The teachers say  racist  Baathist modules help fuel Syria s conflict and are anxious to begin the new curriculum.  It s urgent we start teaching. The next phase will be difficult - there ll be a reckoning between factions,  Ahmed al-Ahmed said, without specifying which groups he was referring to.  A reckoning, in general.

text: A bill aimed at providing financial incentives for firms working on Zika virus treatments is anticipated to be signed by U.S. President Barack Obama, according to a spokesperson from the White House. However, the measure that passed the House of Representatives on Tuesday is deemed inadequate to confront the issue effectively. Katie Hill, the spokeswoman, stated, "This legislation is intended to motivate private sector collaborations to tackle the Zika challenge, but it lacks funding and ultimately falls short on its own, as it does not allocate the $1.9 billion that public health experts have indicated is essential at this time to prepare Americans for the impending local transmission of Zika within the nation."
source_text: Obama expected to sign bill on Zika drug development: White House. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. President Barack Obama is expected to sign a bill to provide financial incentives to companies developing treatments for the Zika virus, a White House spokeswoman said, but the bill passed by the House of Representatives on Tuesday is insufficient to meet the challenge. “We hope that this legislation encourages private sector partners to address the challenge of Zika, but it contains no funding and is ultimately insufficient on its own, since it doesn’t provide the $1.9 billion in funding that our public health experts have said is needed right now to prepare Americans for the imminent local transmission of Zika in this country,” spokeswoman Katie Hill said.

text: Reports indicate that a box containing horse waste, wrapped as a gift, was sent to U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin’s residence in an affluent area of Los Angeles. According to local media outlets, police initially suspected that the package, found in a neighbor's driveway in Bel Air on Saturday evening, could be a bomb. The Los Angeles Police Department shared this information with the Los Angeles Times and KNBC, the NBC affiliate in the region. Inside the package, authorities discovered a Christmas card expressing negative sentiments about President Donald Trump and the recent tax legislation he signed into law the previous week. On Sunday, Reuters was unable to obtain comments from LAPD officials regarding the incident. Prior to opening the package, an LAPD bomb squad conducted an X-ray examination and confirmed the presence of horse manure inside, as reported by local media. KNBC aired footage showing officers examining a large, wrapped box and subsequently emptying out a significant quantity of what was determined to be manure while also inspecting the included card. Mnuchin, who had previously served as an executive at Goldman Sachs Group Inc and is known as a Hollywood financier, was reportedly not present at his home at the time the package was found. The road in Bel Air was shut down for approximately two hours, as noted by KNBC. Additionally, the U.S. Secret Service is looking into the matter, according to the TV station.

(Reuters) - A gift-wrapped package addressed to U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin’s home in a posh Los Angeles neighborhood that was suspected of being a bomb was instead filled with horse manure, police told local media. text: On Tuesday, the Pentagon unveiled a defense budget request of $582.7 billion for the year 2017, identifying growing threats posed by Russia, China, and Islamic State militants. However, this proposal has already faced criticism from Republican lawmakers who assert that it fails to adequately support the U.S. military. President Barack Obama’s final budget plan aims to increase spending against Islamic State fighters to $7.5 billion for the fiscal year 2017, marking a significant 50 percent rise from the $5 billion allocated this year. Of that amount, $200 million is earmarked specifically for combating militants in North and West Africa. Additionally, the budget would amplify funding aimed at countering Russian influence in Europe, particularly in light of its annexation of Crimea in Ukraine and recurrent strategic bomber operations near NATO airspace. The allocation for enhancing U.S. military presence and training in Europe would increase to $3.4 billion, a rise from the $800 million set aside this year. This budget proposal signals a strategic transformation as the U.S. shifts focus away from the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan and prepares for a new era of great power competition with nations like Russia and China, as well as addressing challenges from smaller adversaries including Iran and North Korea, according to officials. "This budget signifies a crucial turning point for the Department of Defense," stated Defense Secretary Ash Carter in a formal announcement. "As we engage in current conflicts, we must also brace ourselves for potential challenges in the next 10, 20, or even 30 years." In total, the administration is requesting a base allocation for the Pentagon amounting to $523.9 billion for the fiscal year commencing on October 1, in addition to $58.8 billion dedicated to war efforts and overseas operations. The proposed base budget reflects an increase of about $2.5 billion compared to this year’s allocation, while funding for war remains relatively stable, according to officials. The spending proposal aligns with a budget agreement reached in Congress last year, which outlined funding parameters for the Pentagon for both 2016 and 2017. Nevertheless, Republican lawmakers have voiced objections regarding the war funding component, arguing that the $59 billion figure established in the budget agreement serves as a lower limit rather than a maximum. They contend that the president should have sought additional funds. "This request falls short of what is necessary to address the national security challenges we currently face," expressed Senator John McCain, who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, in a statement. Congressman Mac Thornberry, the head of the House Armed Services Committee, accused the administration of engaging in "budgetary manipulation." McCain emphasized that by pursuing the minimum level of war funding outlined in the budget deal, the president has left the Pentagon short by $17 billion compared to its own estimates for 2017 from the previous year's budget. To bridge the gap in anticipated expenditures, the Pentagon has made cuts exceeding $5 billion by modifying its projections regarding fuel expenses and inflation, as stated by Pentagon Comptroller Mike McCord. Additionally, procurement funding has been reduced to $112.1 billion, representing a 6 percent decrease from this year’s budget. These reductions primarily affect planned aircraft acquisitions, including a decrease of five F-35 Joint Strike Fighters (LMT.N) and a scaling back in various types of Army helicopters, as detailed in budget documents. Despite the cuts in procurement, the Pentagon has proposed a 4 percent increase in research and development spending, raising the total to $71.8 billion, as it aims to innovate new technologies to maintain a military advantage. The department plans to allocate $16.8 billion towards classified military intelligence operations. Furthermore, it has decided to postpone its contentious initiative to retire the A-10 close air support aircraft until 2022; this aircraft is currently utilized in the fight against the Islamic State. The continued operation of the A-10 will incur costs totaling $3.4 billion over the next five years. The budget also includes a continued reduction in the size of the U.S. Army, which is set to decrease to 460,000 soldiers in 2017 from the existing 475,000. On a separate note, the president's budget request allocates $150 million for a new polar icebreaker vessel to ensure that the Coast Guard can access the Arctic throughout the year.

text: On Monday, the United States called on Albania, its ally in NATO, to take decisive action against the leaders of organized crime if the nation intends to progress in its quest for European Union membership. U.S. ambassador Donald Lu emphasized that combating organized crime and corruption represents the most significant and challenging obstacle for the Balkan country, which became an official EU candidate in 2014 and is eager to initiate accession discussions in the near future. Lu warned that unless major crime figures are arrested, prosecuted, and imprisoned, issues like cannabis cultivation will persist, judges will face bribery, and government officials will remain corrupt. He addressed a gathering of judges and future magistrates. According to U.S. assessments, Albania has been characterized as a hub for organized crime, with activities including drug, weapon, and prostitution trafficking. Lu indicated that four primary clans oversee 20 families engaged in a variety of illicit activities. There exists a considerable black market in Albania for smuggled items, mainly including tobacco, jewelry, stolen vehicles, and mobile devices. Lu pointed out that the risk of money laundering remains high due to widespread corruption and an ineffective legal framework. Despite attempts to reform the judiciary under pressure from the EU, an incident involving a police chief and an armored vehicle owned by a powerful businessman in Elbasan last September highlighted that certain groups still act as if they are above the law. Following this event, law enforcement intensified their efforts, seizing 17 luxury armored vehicles. Lu expressed concern regarding the absence of significant drug traffickers being apprehended or prosecuted during 2015 and 2016, coinciding with a marked rise in cannabis cultivation within Albania.
source_text: U.S. urges EU hopeful Albania to get tough with 'big fish' of crime. TIRANA (Reuters) - The United States urged its NATO ally Albania on Monday to start jailing bosses of organized crime if it hopes to make headway in its bid to join the European Union.   U.S. ambassador Donald Lu said fighting organized crime and corruption was  the biggest and most difficult challenge ahead  for the ex-communist Balkan country, which officially became an EU candidate in 2014 and hopes to begin accession talks soon.   Until the big fish are arrested, prosecuted and go to jail, the cannabis will return, judges will be bribed, and government officials will be corrupted,  Lu told a gathering of judges and aspiring magistrates.    Citing U.S. reports, Lu described Albania as  a center of organized crime activity, which includes trafficking in drugs, weapons and prostitution . He said four major clans in Albania controlled 20 families involved in a wide range of criminal activities.  Albania has a substantial black market for smuggled goods, primarily tobacco, jewelry, stolen cars and mobile phones. The country remains at significant risk for money laundering because of rampant corruption and a weak legal system,  Lu said. Despite efforts to clean up the judiciary under EU pressure, a hit-and-run incident involving an armored car belonging to a powerful businessman and a police chief in the central town of Elbasan in September demonstrated again how some groups continue to see themselves as above the law. After the incident, police stepped up their seizure of suspicious luxury cars, confiscating 17 armored cars.  Lu said he was troubled to see no major drug traffickers arrested or prosecuted in 2015 or 2016 when there was a sharp increase in the cultivation of cannabis in Albania.

text: In a report released on Thursday, the U.N. Human Rights Committee stated that Australia needs to amend its migration regulations. The committee, composed of 18 independent specialists tasked with overseeing compliance with an international human rights agreement, emphasized that Australia should cease the rejection of refugees and align its laws with global standards. Additionally, the committee requested that Australia return in one year to account for the actions taken to address their concerns. The nation has faced significant criticism from both the United Nations and human rights organizations for its practice of detaining asylum seekers attempting to reach its borders by boat, even when they have been recognized as refugees, and for housing them in offshore processing facilities located in Nauru and Papua New Guinea. The U.N. has issued warnings about a potential humanitarian disaster brewing in the Manus Island facility in Papua New Guinea. Although it was shut down on October 31, approximately 600 asylum seekers remain, unwilling to depart due to fears of violent reprisals from local residents if they relocate to transit centers while awaiting possible resettlement in the United States. According to Yuval Shany, the vice-chair of the committee, while the recommendations are non-binding, it seems that Australia is not taking its obligations seriously. He stated, "We do not disagree with Australia’s right to adopt a tough policy, for instance on resettlement. What they cannot do is treat asylum seekers as criminals and detain them, and they cannot absolve themselves of their duty not to send them back to danger." Shany noted that it is unusual for a developed nation with a solid human rights record to publicly reject the committee's recommendations repeatedly, as Australia has done. The government could not be immediately reached for a statement. Earlier, Immigration Minister Peter Dutton maintained on 2GB radio that he supported the detention policy, which the government claims is essential to deter asylum seekers from risking dangerous sea journeys to Australia, and he affirmed that the government would not reverse its stance on evictions from Manus. The offshore detention policies enjoy support from both the center-right government and the Labor opposition. The U.N. committee called on Australia to reduce the duration of initial mandatory detention and to limit overall detention periods. Furthermore, it insisted that children should not be detained except as a last resort and for the minimal time necessary. They urged Australia to ensure that the international principle of not returning refugees to danger is enshrined in law and strictly followed. The committee expressed concerns regarding conditions in Manus and Nauru, highlighting serious safety issues and reports of assault, sexual abuse, self-harm, and suspicious fatalities. Additionally, it suggested that Australia should contemplate shutting down the Christmas Island detention facility, citing its remoteness as a factor that compromises the safety of the individuals held there.

The United Nations has warned of a  looming humanitarian crisis  in the Manus island center in Papua New Guinea. It was closed on Oct. 31 but 600 asylum seekers have refused to leave, fearing violent reprisals from islanders if they move to transit centers, pending possible resettlement to the United States. The committee s vice-chair Yuval Shany said although the recommendations were non-binding it did not appear Australia was treating its obligations seriously.  We do not disagree with Australia s right to adopt a tough policy, for instance on resettlement,  he said.  What they cannot do is treat asylum seekers as criminals and detain them, and they cannot absolve themselves of their duty not to send them back to danger.  He said it was exceptional to have such a situation in a developed country with a strong human rights record, and for a country to publicly reject the committee s recommendations one after the other, as Australia had.  The government could not be immediately reached for comment. Immigration Minister Peter Dutton earlier told 2GB radio he stood by the detention policy that the government says is necessary to deter asylum seekers from attempting perilous sea voyages to Australia, and that it would not back down from its evictions from Manus. The offshore detention policies are backed by the center-right government and the Labor opposition.  The U.N. committee said Australia should cut the period of initial mandatory detention and limit detention overall, and ensure that children were not detained except as a measure of last resort and for the shortest time possible. It urged Australia to ensure the international principle of not sending refugees back to danger was secured in law and adhered to.  The committee was concerned about conditions in Manus and in Nauru, citing serious safety concerns and instances of assault, sexual abuse, self-harm and suspicious deaths. text: On Wednesday, an agreement was reached by U.S. lawmakers that sets the stage for the U.S. Senate to vote on a bill aimed at imposing additional sanctions on Russia, with a possible vote occurring within the week. This legislation also seeks to prevent President Donald Trump from lifting sanctions on Russia without obtaining approval from Congress. Earlier that same day, Russia issued a warning indicating it was approaching a point of retaliatory action against Washington after the House of Representatives endorsed new sanctions targeting Moscow. The European Union expressed concerns that these sanctions could impact its energy security and indicated its readiness to respond as well. Senator Bob Corker, who chairs the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee and is a Republican, expressed satisfaction in a statement on Wednesday evening, announcing the agreement that would enable the sanctions bill to move towards the president's desk. He indicated that the Senate would work to approve sanctions on both Russia and Iran, which were initially passed in mid-June, along with sanctions on North Korea that were developed by the House of Representatives and included in a bill that received overwhelming support in the House on Wednesday. Prior to this latest agreement, there were objections from several senators regarding the North Korea sanctions, raising concerns that the already delayed sanctions bill could extend into September without resolution. Should the Senate pass the bill as anticipated, it would subsequently be forwarded to the White House for Trump’s consideration, where he could either sign it into law or veto it. However, it is widely believed that there would be sufficient support to override any potential veto from Trump. The House had voted 419-3 on Tuesday to implement new sanctions against Moscow and to require Trump to secure Congressional approval before easing any punitive actions against Russia. Dmitry Peskov, a spokesperson for the Kremlin, remarked, "This is rather sad news from the point of view of Russia-U.S. ties," describing the actions as an extremely unfriendly act. Peskov noted that it would be up to President Vladimir Putin to determine if and how Moscow would respond once the sanctions were enacted into law. Additionally, Russia’s deputy foreign minister cautioned that this development was steering bilateral relations into unknown territory, effectively extinguishing any hopes for improvement in the near future. WASHINGTON/MOSCOW/BRUSSELS (Reuters) - U.S. lawmakers reached an agreement on Wednesday paving the way for the U.S. Senate to pass a bill as soon as this week to impose new sanctions on Russia and bar President Donald Trump from easing sanctions on Moscow without Congress’ approval. Earlier on Wednesday, Russia warned it was edging closer to retaliation against Washington after the House of Representatives backed new U.S. sanctions on Moscow, while the European Union said the move  might affect its energy security and it stood ready to act too. “I am glad to announce that we have reached an agreement that will allow us to send sanctions legislation to the president’s desk,” Senator Bob Corker, the Republican chairman of the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement on Wednesday evening. He said the Senate would move to approve sanctions on Russia and Iran that it originally passed in mid-June, as well as sanctions on North Korea developed by the House of Representatives and included in a bill the House passed overwhelmingly on Wednesday. Before the latest agreement, some senators had objected to the North Korea measures and it had looked like the sanctions bill, already delayed since mid-June, could languish into September. If the bill passes the Senate as expected, it would be sent to the White House for Trump to sign into law or veto. It is, however, expected to garner enough support to override a Trump veto. The House voted 419-3 on Tuesday to impose new sanctions on Moscow and force Trump to obtain lawmakers’ approval before easing any punitive measures on Russia. “This is rather sad news from the point of view of Russia-U.S. ties,” said Dmitry Peskov, a Kremlin spokesman. “We are talking about an extremely unfriendly act.” He said President Vladimir Putin would decide if and how Moscow would retaliate once the sanctions became law.
