Trump, whose presidency has been embroiled in a distracting dispute over his associates’ alleged ties to Moscow, is on the defensive over accusations Russia helped elect him last year. He has said he wants to mend relations with Russia that are languishing at a post-Cold War low. Trump had denied that there was any collusion between his campaign and Russia. Most White House watchers believe Trump will reluctantly sign off on the new sanctions, given deep support for them among U.S. lawmakers and his desire to avoid being accused of being soft on Moscow. Representative Ed Royce, the Republican chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Trump would have little choice. The Senate passed a version of the legislation, without the North Korea sanctions, on June 15 by 98-2.  “I think the president will sign it,” Royce said on NBC’s Meet the Press Daily on Wednesday. The issue has rattled Russia, which fears that its economy, weakened by 2014 Western sanctions imposed over its role in the Ukraine crisis, will now find it harder to recover and grow. Foreign investors could be scared off. The European Union frets that new U.S. restrictions could pose obstacles to its companies doing business with Russia and threaten the bloc’s energy supply lines. The Kremlin’s alleged interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election is one reason lawmakers have pushed for the new sanctions. Peskov said Moscow would wait until the sanctions became law before fully analyzing them and deciding how to respond.   Moscow had hoped that Trump, who made upbeat statements about Putin before winning the White House, would work to repair the U.S.-Russia relationship. But it has watched with frustration as the vote-meddling allegations killed off hopes of any detente. The Russian Foreign Ministry said this month that too many American spies were operating in Russia under diplomatic cover and it might expel some to retaliate for the expulsion of 35 Russian diplomats last year by then-President Barack Obama’s administration. Many Russian politicians increasingly believe Trump’s political foes and Congress have left the U.S. president with little room for maneuver on Russia and they have nothing to lose by retaliating. In Brussels, European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker said the EU was ready to act “within a matter of days” if it felt the new U.S. sanctions undermined the bloc’s energy security. Brussels fears the new sanctions will damage European firms and oil and gas projects on which the EU is dependent. The Russia section of the bill includes sanctions on a range of industries. Several provisions target Russian energy, with new limits on U.S. investment in Russian companies. U.S. firms also would be barred from participating in energy exploration projects where Russian firms have a stake of 33 percent or higher. The bill includes sanctions on foreign firms investing in or helping Russian energy exploration, although the president could waive those sanctions. The bill would give the Trump administration the option of imposing sanctions on firms helping develop Russian export pipelines, such as the Nord Stream 2 pipeline carrying natural gas to Europe, in which German companies are involved. In a concession to allies, those sanctions are optional, not mandatory. The European Commission said a number of EU concerns had been taken into account in the most recent version of the bill, but said it could lead to sanctions on any company, including European, that worked on Russian energy export pipelines.

text: A military officer with combat experience and a close confidant of President Xi Jinping is anticipated to be elevated to the position of vice chairman of China’s Central Military Commission, according to four sources. This move is part of Xi's efforts to reinforce his authority over the military. Zhang Youxia, aged 67, is among the few high-ranking military officials who have seen combat and is poised to take up one of at least two vice chairman roles within the commission, as disclosed by sources, including three with direct connections to the leadership, to Reuters. The commission, chaired by Xi, oversees the People’s Liberation Army and he also serves as the nation’s president and the general secretary of the Communist Party of China. Zhang is set to succeed Fan Changlong, who is expected to step down during the upcoming 19th Communist Party Congress commencing on Wednesday. Meanwhile, Xu Qiliang, the other vice chairman, is likely to remain, according to the sources. Both Xi and Zhang hail from Shaanxi province in northwestern China and are descendants of former high-ranking officials who fought alongside each other during the civil war in the 1940s. The Defence Ministry of China did not respond to a request sent via fax for further information. Reports indicate that the party is considering a proposal to expand the number of vice chairmen on the military commission from two to four while decreasing the number of other committee members, which currently stands at eight, as per some sources. Since Xi took office in late 2012, there has been significant upheaval within the commission and the military as he seeks to eliminate corruption and streamline the armed forces, which are the largest in the world with a strength of 2 million. Approximately 300,000 troops have been discharged, and the military has developed cutting-edge equipment, including stealth fighters. Despite not engaging in warfare for decades, China has adopted a more assertive stance in the contentious East China Sea and South China Sea, as well as regarding Taiwan, which China claims as its territory. Two outgoing members of the commission are reportedly under investigation for alleged corruption, sources have informed Reuters, although the government has yet to officially verify this information. This is not the first instance of corruption issues within the military. Last year, a previous vice chairman, Guo Boxiong, was sentenced to life imprisonment for graft, and another former vice chairman, Xu Caihou, passed away from cancer in 2015 before he could stand trial for alleged corruption. Currently, Zhang occupies the eighth position out of the 11 members on the military commission. Additionally, he is expected to be appointed to the Communist Party’s 25-member Politburo, which is one of the ruling elite bodies, according to three of the sources. One source connected to the leadership indicated that the fathers of both Xi and Zhang—Xi Zhongxun and Zhang Zongxun—shared a close bond. Their fathers participated together in the civil war that concluded in 1949 with the Communist Party’s victory and the establishment of the People’s Republic of China. Both fathers ascended to significant roles within the government and military. The next generation of these families also maintains a strong relationship, the source noted, referring to Xi and Zhang. Born in Beijing, Zhang Youxia enlisted in the military in 1968 and climbed the ranks, joining the military commission in late 2012. He engaged in combat against Vietnam during a brief border conflict in 1979, which China initiated as retaliation for Vietnam’s invasion of Cambodia the previous year that resulted in the ousting of the Beijing-supported Khmer Rouge regime. At the age of 26, he was deployed to the frontlines to confront the Vietnamese, where he distinguished himself and received quick promotions, according to state media. He also participated in another border skirmish with Vietnam in 1984. Reports from the official China Youth Daily in August highlighted that Zhang Youxia excelled in performance during both offensive and defensive operations, with a piece titled, 'These Chinese generals have killed the enemy on the battlefield.' Another recently promoted officer, Li Zuocheng, who was appointed as chief of the Joint Staff Department of the People’s Liberation Army in August, also fought in the 1979 conflict. It remains uncertain whether he will also join the Politburo, though he is likely to be one of the vice chairmen of the commission.

text: The U.N. Ambassador for China, Liu Jieyi, has called on North Korea to cease its inappropriate actions. During a session of the U.N. Security Council, he emphasized that all involved nations should earnestly reflect on Beijing's suggestion for a mutual halt to North Korea's missile and nuclear activities, as well as military exercises conducted by the United States and South Korea. text: An anti-corruption investigation has led to serious allegations against numerous Saudi princes, officials, and businessmen, according to a Saudi source who spoke with Reuters on Monday. Following a decree from King Salman, which established a new anti-corruption committee under the leadership of his 32-year-old son, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, eleven princes, four ministers, and various former ministers were apprehended late Saturday. The committee has been granted significant authority to probe cases, issue warrants, impose travel bans, and confiscate assets. Among those implicated is billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal, a nephew of the king and the head of the investment firm Kingdom Holding, who faces accusations of money laundering, bribery, and coercing officials. Additionally, Prince Miteb bin Abdullah, who was dismissed from his position as the leader of the influential National Guard, is charged with embezzlement, the employment of fictitious workers, and the awarding of contracts to his own enterprises, including a $10 billion agreement for military communications equipment and protective gear worth billions to Saudi royalty. The former Governor of Riyadh, Prince Turki bin Abdullah, allegedly engaged in corrupt practices regarding the Riyadh Metro initiative, leveraging his influence to secure contracts for his own businesses, as stated by the official. Furthermore, former Finance Minister Ibrahim al-Assaf, who is part of the board for national oil behemoth Saudi Aramco, is accused of embezzlement tied to the expansion of Mecca's Grand Mosque and exploiting his position and insider knowledge to profit from land transactions, the official mentioned. Verification of these claims remains unattainable.

RIYADH (Reuters) - Bribery, embezzlement, money laundering and abuse of power are among the accusations leveled against dozens of Saudi princes, officials and businessmen detained in an anti-corruption probe, a Saudi official told Reuters on Monday. Eleven princes, four ministers and tens of former ministers were detained late on Saturday after King Salman decreed the creation of an anti-corruption committee chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his 32-year-old son who has amassed expansive powers over the past two years. The new body was given broad powers to investigate cases, issue arrest warrants and travel restrictions, and seize assets. The official said billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal, a nephew of the king and owner of investment firm Kingdom Holding, faces allegations of money laundering, bribery and extorting officials. Prince Miteb bin Abdullah, who was removed as head of the powerful National Guard, is accused of embezzlement, hiring ghost employees and awarding contracts to his own companies, including a $10 billion deal for walkie-talkies and bulletproof military gear worth billions of Saudi royals. Former Riyadh Governor Prince Turki bin Abdullah is accused of corruption in the Riyadh Metro project and of taking advantage of his influence to award contracts to his own companies, the official said. Former Finance Minister Ibrahim al-Assaf, a board member of national oil giant Saudi Aramco, is accused of embezzlement related to the expansion of Mecca s Grand Mosque and taking advantage of his position and inside information to benefit from land deals, the official added. The accusations could not be independently verified.

text: Syrian Kurdish leaders indicated that the recent independence vote by Iraqi Kurds could have a positive impact on the Kurdish population in Syria, potentially prompting the Syrian government to engage in discussions regarding autonomy. In a statement to Reuters, prominent Kurdish figure Ilham Ahmed noted that representatives from the Kurdish-led areas in Syria have already held two meetings with the government in Damascus, yet the dialogue facilitated by Russia has not yielded any results. The Syrian government has consistently opposed the autonomy initiatives that have emerged throughout the ongoing six-year conflict in Syria. However, this week, the foreign minister expressed a willingness to enter talks with Kurdish representatives once the battle against the Islamic State militants concludes. Ahmed commented, "The outcomes, if they continue along these lines... will be favorable." She also remarked that the referendum conducted in Iraq could motivate Kurdish authorities there to establish connections with the autonomous regions created by Syrian Kurds and their allies in northern Syria. The Iraqi Kurds executed their referendum despite opposition from their U.S. ally, the Baghdad administration, as well as neighboring Turkey and Iran. The results overwhelmingly confirmed a desire to separate from Iraq, though the vote is not legally binding. In Syria, Kurdish leadership has clarified that they do not aim for secession. Since 2011, the Kurdish YPG militia and its allies have established distinct cantons in northern Syria, having reclaimed extensive territories from the Islamic State with support from the U.S., despite Washington's disapproval of their autonomy ambitions. With the YPG serving as a military backbone, the primary Syrian Kurdish parties now govern nearly 25% of the country, asserting their pursuit of autonomy within a decentralized framework for Syria. Syrian President Bashar al-Assad has vowed to reclaim every part of the nation as his military has regained ground from rebels and militants, aided by Russia and Iran. "We have consistently sent signals... indicating our readiness for negotiations," Ahmed stated. "We have notified the Russians that they should persuade the regime to engage in talks." According to her, during both meetings, the Damascus representatives did not seem sincere in their approach toward discussing the future of the autonomous regions or the call for a federal system in Syria. "Autonomy does not equate to separation." Another notable Kurdish figure, Fawza Youssef, suggested that the recent Iraqi referendum may have influenced the Syrian government's more accommodating stance toward the sizable Kurdish community in Syria. "This represents a positive development. Our efforts over the past six years... along with our military and political successes, are crucial in compelling the Syrian government to consider negotiations," she stated. Although Kurds in northern Syria stand in solidarity with the Iraqi Kurdish's right to self-determination, they do not intend to replicate the actions taken in the recent vote, Youssef asserted. "The circumstances in Syria and Iraq are not identical," she elaborated. Nonetheless, she cautioned, "If there is a continued exclusion of the Kurdish population, stripping them of their political and cultural rights... inevitably, this could lead to a desire for secession over time." Both Youssef and Ahmed hold prominent positions within the Kurdish-led governance of the cantons in northern Syria. While the YPG and the Syrian government have largely avoided direct confrontation during the war, tensions have arisen as both factions, along with their respective allies, race to control the Deir al-Zor province in eastern Syria. The YPG has been engaged in combat against the Islamic State as part of a U.S.-backed coalition known as the Syrian Democratic Forces, which includes Arab fighters and others. Ahmed, who co-chairs the political wing of this force, noted that the territory secured by the SDF in Deir al-Zor has become both a vital agricultural zone and a crucial supply route for Syria. "If Damascus intends to persist with threats, there will be no advantage from that... However, if they recognize that dialogue is the appropriate approach, it would lead to a more favorable situation." She also suggested that the rising tensions in eastern Syria might encourage the government to reconsider its position, as Damascus may be apprehensive about initiating another front in the conflict. Recently, Kurdish-led authorities conducted elections in northern Syria for local community leadership, part of an ongoing development process.

The vote delivered a resounding  yes  to split from Iraq, but is not binding. Across the border in Syria, Kurdish leaders say they do not want secession. The Kurdish YPG militia and its allies have carved out cantons in the north since 2011. They have seized vast territory from Islamic State with U.S. help, although Washington opposes their autonomy plans.   With the YPG as a military backbone, the main Syrian Kurdish parties now hold nearly a quarter of the country, and say they seek autonomy as part of a decentralized Syria.  Syrian President Bashar al-Assad has pledged to take back every inch of the country as his army has captured land from rebels and militants with the help of Russia and Iran.   We have always sent messages... that we are ready for talks,  Ahmed said.  We have informed the Russians that they should convince the regime to negotiate.  At both meetings, Damascus  did not appear serious  about talks over the future of the autonomous regions and the demand for a federal system for Syria, she said.  Autonomy does not mean separation.   Another senior Kurdish politician, Fawza Youssef, said the Iraqi referendum likely had a hand in Damascus adopting a more conciliatory tone toward Syria s large Kurdish population.   This is a positive step. And our struggle in the past six years...our military and political victories  play the major role in pushing the Syrian government to negotiate, she said. Kurds in northern Syria support the Iraqi Kurdish right to decide their own future, but do not look to follow the example of this week s vote, Youssef said.    The reality in Syria and Iraq is not the same,  she said. Still, she added,  if there will be exclusion of the Kurdish people, stripping them of political and cultural rights...of course with time this would lead to secession.   Youssef and Ahmed are both senior members of the Kurdish-led authority running the cantons in northern Syria.  Damascus and the YPG have mostly stayed out of each other s way in the war. But tensions have surfaced as both sides with their allies race to capture Deir al-Zor province in eastern Syria. The YPG has been battling Islamic State under a U.S.-backed alliance known as the Syrian Democratic Forces, which includes Arab and other combatants.  The territory the SDF has captured in Deir al-Zor so far serves as a breadbasket and a route for imports into Syria, said Ahmed, who co-chairs the force s political wing.   So if (Damascus) wants to continue with threats, there will be no benefit from this... But if they understand that dialogue is the right way, that would be the better position.   Tensions in eastern Syria might also fuel a shift in the government stance as Damascus might be wary of opening yet another battlefront, she said.  Kurdish-led authorities held elections in northern Syria last week for local community leaders, part of a process that will culminate with electing a parliament. Syria s Kurdish region borders Turkey and the Kurdish government of northern Iraq, which are both hostile toward the YPG. Ankara views the militia as an extension of the Kurdistan Workers  Party (PKK) that has waged a three-decade insurgency inside Turkey. Youssef and Ahmed said the vote next door could lead to mending ties with Iraq s Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) if Iraqi Kurdistan faces more pressure.  Turkey and Iran have threatened to impose a blockade. They warn the referendum will spark regional chaos, and fear the spread of separatism among their own Kurdish populations.   If they shut the roads, (the KRG) will have to open a route,  fix relations, and possibly trade with northern Syria, Ahmed said.  That would be good of course.

text: Amid a rise in North Korean fishing boats reaching Japan's shores, three members of a North Korean vessel were detained on Saturday by Japanese authorities for allegedly stealing a generator from a remote island hut, according to public broadcaster NHK. TOKYO (Reuters) - Japanese police arrested three crew of a North Korean boat on Saturday for stealing a generator from a hut on an uninhabited island, public broadcaster NHK said, the latest drama amid increasing arrivals of North Korean fishing boats off Japan. The boats, some in distress, some abandoned and some with dead bodies on board, have raised fears about infiltration by spies as tension with North Korea surges over its missile and nuclear programs. North Korea has test-fired two missiles over Japan, a country it has threatened to destroy. Most experts say the wooden boats are just carrying fishermen including soldiers drafted to fish. There has been no suggestion the crew are defectors. A boat, with 10 crew on board, was found moored at the island, off Hokkaido, last month and several crew said they picked up electronic goods from the hut, according to NHK. A spokesman at the Japan coast guard declined to comment. text: On Wednesday, British Prime Minister Theresa May faced renewed attempts to extract concessions regarding her strategy for exiting the European Union, marking the second day of a parliamentary discussion that is intensifying rifts over Brexit. Following a loss of the Conservative Party’s majority in the June elections, May finds herself under pressure from numerous lawmakers, including some from her own party, regarding various aspects of the EU withdrawal legislation that necessitates parliamentary consent. So far, all efforts to modify the bill concerning the disconnection from the EU have been rejected, yet a forthcoming debate next month regarding the specific timing of Britain’s departure, and whether a deadline should even be established, will serve as a significant test of her leadership. May has called on legislators to collaborate ahead of discussions on numerous amendments designed to safeguard EU standards on a broad spectrum of topics, including environmental protections and labor rights.  "We will be leaving the European Union on the 19th of March, 2019, and of course there is a lively debate going on in this place and that’s right and proper, and that’s important," May stated during the regular session of prime minister’s questions.  "We are listening carefully to those who wish to improve the bill and I hope that we can all come together to deliver on the decision that the country took that we should leave the European Union." The discussions are anticipated to extend for several weeks, addressing a bill that May regards as essential for assuring businesses that there will be no significant legal alterations impacting operations when Britain exits the EU in March 2019. On the initial day of the debate, lawmakers exhibited a breakdown of party unity as they turned against one another with shouts, jeers, and accusations of betrayal. Underlying these discussions are the concerns of pro-Brexit legislators who fear that the UK might not exit the EU, alongside pro-EU politicians who are anxious about a potential no-deal exit. "Exit day" has emerged as a focal point for many in parliament, with some legislators asserting that pro-Brexit members desire a definitive date in the bill—11:00 p.m. on March 29, 2019—to restrict flexibility during negotiations with the EU, which are currently stalled primarily over financial issues. May and her cabinet are intensifying their engagement with EU representatives, seeking methods to exert pressure on Brussels negotiators to advance discussions by December, a shift that businesses claim is vital for making investment decisions. On Wednesday, May encountered Manfred Weber, a prominent member of the European Parliament and an associate of German Chancellor Angela Merkel, in London, who expressed optimism that the challenges in the discussions could be resolved. This parliamentary discourse presents yet another challenge for a prime minister who has already lost two ministers due to scandals and is facing demands to dismiss her foreign secretary, Boris Johnson, over comments he made regarding a detained Iranian-British aid worker in Iran. While she has attempted to alleviate tensions by offering some concessions on the bill, she has yet to persuade all her lawmakers, many of whom have declared their intention not to support the government on at least one of the debates, particularly concerning the "exit day."

text: In the heart of Santiago, the candidates vying for the presidency of Chile concluded their campaign efforts on Thursday, just days before a critical election on Sunday. This runoff election holds significant implications for the future political direction of the world's leading copper producer, as it will decide whether the nation will shift toward conservative governance or continue along its center-left path. Voters will have to choose between billionaire conservative Sebastian Pinera and Alejandro Guillier, a senator and journalist representing the center-left. During the first round of voting in November, unexpected gains by candidates from the far left surprised analysts, which led to a decline in market confidence and set the stage for a much closer runoff than previously anticipated. "Everything points to a narrow margin of victory," remarked Guillermo Holzmann, a professor at the University of Valparaiso. He noted the race's unusual nature, citing the challenges in predicting voter behavior. Both Pinera and Guillier are expected to maintain the free-market economic policies that have characterized Latin America’s most developed nation. However, the strong performance of candidates with more radical positions on both sides of the political spectrum in November prompted both contenders to adapt their strategies to attract supporters of eliminated candidates. Former Uruguayan president José "Pepe" Mujica, a leftist figure popular in a region that has largely shifted rightward, publicly endorsed Guillier. "The conservative right has no future in Chile," Guillier declared to his supporters. Pinera, who is 68 years old and previously served as president, emerged as the frontrunner in the first round with 36.6 percent of the total votes. He has promised to stimulate economic growth by decreasing the corporate tax rate while also rolling back tax, labor, and educational reforms introduced by outgoing President Michelle Bachelet, which Guillier intends to enhance. At the Caupolicán theater in Santiago, Pinera assured attendees of a renewed and improved approach towards the middle class, senior citizens, and children. On the other hand, Guillier, who is 64 and hails from northern Chile, received 22.7 percent of the vote in November from constituents eager to sustain the advancements achieved during Bachelet's administration, including reduced university tuition fees and legislation supporting labor unions. Guillier is appealing to leftist voters by suggesting a complete reform of the privatized pension system and a reworking of the constitution. In a bid to attract centrist voters, Pinera has advocated for free vocational education for underprivileged individuals and a public pension alternative. Guillier narrowly surpassed Beatriz Sanchez, the third-place candidate from the leftist Frente Amplio, who garnered support from 20 percent of the electorate with her proposals to tax the "super-rich" to enhance social spending and combat inequality. The votes of Sanchez's 1.3 million backers are deemed crucial for the forthcoming election. In Chile, participation in voting is not mandatory, and there has been a notable rise in abstention rates in recent years. "It ultimately hinges on how many choose to stay home, particularly those on Guillier's side," explained Robert Funk, a professor at the University of Chile.

text: The creation of a global drone registry is being advocated by the United Nations aviation agency, as part of a wider initiative to establish uniform regulations for the operation and monitoring of unmanned aircraft. According to Stephen Creamer, who directs ICAO's air navigation bureau, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) has suggested the establishment of this registry during a symposium held in Montreal this month to ensure that data can be accessed in real-time. This proposed singular registry aims to replace numerous databases with a centralized system, enabling law enforcement to identify and monitor unmanned aircraft, alongside their operators and owners, from a distance. This move comes amidst a surge in drone usage in the United States, Europe, and China, which has led to growing concerns regarding privacy and the risk of collisions with commercial airplanes. "You need to have some commonality so that you are not equipped with five receivers in your police vehicle," Creamer remarked in an interview on Thursday. Although it remains uncertain who will be responsible for managing such a database, ICAO might assume that role. However, there could be resistance from users, especially after hobbyists successfully contested the establishment of a U.S. drone registry by the Federal Aviation Administration in court earlier this year. From September 22 to 23, ICAO will convene the symposium, which will address topics including the registration and tracking of drones, as well as systems similar to geofencing that would restrict their operation in certain areas. Experts and companies, including Google, Rockwell Collins (COL.N), and Amazon.com (AMZN.O), are expected to participate in this event, according to the meeting agenda. The ICAO, headquartered in Montreal, typically sets the standards for international civil aviation that its 191 member countries adopt. They were invited to contribute to the formulation of more consistent domestic regulations for drones, as these remotely piloted aircraft are marketed and operated worldwide. "Drone manufacturers are concerned that Europe may implement one set of standards, the United States another, and China a third. Consequently, they will have to design drones differently for these varying environments," Creamer explained. Parimal Kopardekar, a principal investigator working on Unmanned Aircraft System Traffic Management (UTM) at NASA Ames Research Center in California, expressed his support for the drone industry evolving globally with standardized operating procedures. "I believe it is prudent that ICAO is attempting to create harmony in this regard," he stated via phone. "If a drone is manufactured in one nation, it should be operable in another, and the reverse should also hold true."

source_text: Trump touts tax reform, overlooks White House aide Cohn. SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump made his first major tax reform speech on Wednesday, but in a long list of thank yous he did not mention Gary Cohn, the White House point man on taxes who traveled with Trump to the event. At a manufacturing company in Springfield, Missouri, Trump reiterated his longstanding call for slashing the U.S. corporate tax rate to 15 percent from 35 percent at a time when lawmakers believe they could be lucky to bring it down to 25 percent. When asked about the omission of Cohn’s name, White House spokeswoman Sarah Sanders told reporters on Air Force One, en route to Washington from Missouri, that it was customary for Trump to recognize Cabinet members, but not advisers, in speeches. Cohn traveled with Trump on Air Force One for the Missouri speech, in which Trump called on Democrats to join his tax overhaul effort. He said he would cut taxes and simplify the sprawling U.S. tax code for the middle class. But he offered few specifics, and tax reform will be an uphill task in Congress. “We must reduce the tax rate on American businesses so they keep jobs in America, create jobs in America and compete for workers right here in America,” Trump said in his first presidential speech specifically on tax reform, one of his key 2016 campaign issues. Both congressional Democrats and Republicans say tax reform is needed but the Republican goal of enacting legislation this year faces a battle in Congress, which has already failed to deliver on healthcare reform sought by Trump. During his speech, Trump did single out Cabinet members, including Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross and Small Business Administration head Linda McMahon, as well as members of Congress — more than a dozen people in all. He asked his daughter Ivanka Trump, who is not a Cabinet member but is a staff member, to stand and be recognized in his speech at a manufacturing company in Springfield. “Anybody I forgot?” Trump asked.  Cohn, who stood next to the stage during the speech with Sanders, has worked side-by-side for months with Mnuchin developing Trump’s tax reform strategy. “It’s pretty standard practice for us not to specifically call out staff,” Sanders told reporters afterward. “He regularly mentions Cabinet members but very rarely mentions staff in speeches.” Asked if the oversight of Cohn was significant, Sanders said, “Well, look, Gary is here. The president is here. They’re both working hard and extremely committed to providing tax relief for middle-class America. The president has made very clear this is a top priority for him, for his administration, and Gary is one of the people leading the charge.” Cohn recently criticized Trump for his comments about violence at racially charged protests in Virginia earlier this month. Trump blamed “both sides” for the violence in Charlottesville, in which white supremacists and neo-Nazis battled anti-racism protesters. Trump’s comments drew condemnation from both Republicans and Democrats. Cohn told the Financial Times last week that the Trump administration “can and must do better in consistently and unequivocally condemning” hate groups. The former Goldman Sachs executive, who is Jewish, said he had come under “enormous pressure” to resign over Trump’s remarks. TAX REFORM UNLIKELY BEFORE YEAR-END Independent analysts and lobbyists are increasingly pessimistic that Congress can act by the end of 2017, and some believe final tax legislation could be more like a straight tax cut than a reform. “I don’t want to be disappointed by Congress. Do you understand me?” Trump said to cheers. Trump said business tax cuts would lead to higher wages for workers by boosting economic growth and making American companies more competitive, an argument Democrats dismiss as more of the “trickle-down” economics that they blame for leaving workers behind in recent decades. “If President Trump’s previous tax plans are any indication, the wealthy and big corporations will be the ultimate winner,” Representative Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the tax-writing House Ways and Means Committee, said in a statement.                 There has been no comprehensive overhaul of the tax code since 1986. Trump singled out Missouri’s Democratic Senator Claire McCaskill, telling voters to throw her out of office in the 2018 midterm elections if she does not get on board with tax reform. McCaskill’s office did not respond to queries from Reuters about Trump’s remark.  After more than seven months in power, Trump and Republican leaders who control both the U.S. Senate and the House are still far from agreement on a tax package. Initially expected in the spring, tax reform legislation now may not emerge until as late as November, lobbyists say. Trump will discuss a tax overhaul at a White House meeting next Tuesday with the “Big Six” tax reform negotiators: House Speaker Paul Ryan, Mnuchin, Cohn, Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell and the Republican chairmen of two congressional tax committees.

text: A U.S. official indicated on Tuesday that President Donald Trump is expected to add a stop in China to his Asia itinerary in November, marking his first official trip to the region. This visit occurs against a backdrop of escalating tensions related to North Korea’s nuclear activities. The United States, along with its allies, has emphasized the increasing need for China, the primary ally and trading partner of North Korea, to exert more influence on the isolated nation to compel it to reconsider its nuclear weapons and missile development programs. During their meeting in April in Palm Beach, Florida, Chinese President Xi Jinping extended an invitation for Trump to visit China. Additionally, both leaders engaged in discussions during the G20 summit in July. In November, Trump plans to participate in the U.S.-ASEAN summit and the East Asia summit in the Philippines, in addition to the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Vietnam. A request for comment regarding Trump’s prospective visit was not immediately addressed by China’s foreign ministry. The Japanese public broadcaster NHK reported, citing unidentified diplomatic sources, that Trump might also be contemplating visits to Japan and South Korea on this Asian journey in November. In February, Trump agreed to Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s invitation to visit Japan before the close of the year. A Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesperson mentioned, “The February agreement is still valid. We would definitely like to make it happen sometime within this year. But no specific timing has been fixed yet.” Furthermore, the Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun reported on Wednesday that Japan, the United States, and South Korea are nearing the finalization stage of discussions to organize a trilateral summit during the U.N. General Assembly in New York. According to unnamed government sources cited by the paper, this meeting involving Trump, Abe, and South Korean President Moon Jae-in could occur on September 21 and aims to enhance cooperation in light of provocations from North Korea. Recently, on Monday, the U.N. Security Council unanimously voted to intensify sanctions against North Korea, which now includes a ban on its lucrative textile exports and limits on fuel supplies. After several days of negotiations regarding the resolution, Washington conceded several proposals to gain the backing of Russia and China, such as dropping a push for an oil embargo and the blacklisting of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and the national airline. In Hong Kong, former White House chief strategist Steve Bannon conveyed to the South China Morning Post that the findings of a U.S.-led investigation into allegations of Chinese intellectual property theft will be disclosed prior to the Beijing summit aimed at recalibrating trade relations. Bannon, known for his role in Trump’s 2016 election success, stated at an investor conference arranged by a branch of China’s largest brokerage that the rapport between Trump and Xi could facilitate resolving their differences, according to an attendee of the closed meeting. Although Bannon was dismissed by Trump last month, he revealed during a private lunch gathering in Hong Kong that he continues to “speak with President Donald Trump every two to three days,” as reported by the Wall Street Journal.
source_text: Trump likely to visit China during November Asia trip: U.S. official. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump is likely to make a stop in China in November during his first official visit to Asia, a U.S. official said on Tuesday, a trip that will come amid tensions over North Korea’s nuclear tests. Washington and its allies have said there is a growing urgency for China, North Korea’s top ally and trading partner, to apply more pressure on its already isolated neighbor to get it to back down on its nuclear weapons and missiles programs. Chinese President Xi Jinping had invited Trump to visit China during their meeting in April in Palm Beach, Florida. The two leaders also met on the sidelines on the G20 summit in July. Trump is set to attend the U.S.-ASEAN summit and the East Asia summit in the Philippines in November, as well as the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Vietnam. China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on Trump’s potential visit. Japanese public broadcaster NHK cited unnamed diplomatic sources saying that Trump was also considering visiting Japan and South Korea during his Asian tour in November. In February, Trump accepted Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s invitation to visit Japan by the end of the year. “The February agreement is still valid. We would definitely like to make it happen sometime within this year. But no specific timing has been fixed yet,” a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said. Also, the Japanese daily Yomiuri Shimbun said on Wednesday Japan, the United States and South Korea are in final stages of talks to hold a trilateral summit on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The newspaper, citing unnamed government sources, reported the meeting between Trump, Abe and South Korean President Moon Jae-in could take place on Sept. 21 and would focus on bolstering cooperation in response to North Korean provocation. On Monday, the U.N. Security Council unanimously voted to step up sanctions on North Korea, with its profitable textile exports now banned and fuel supplies capped. After several days of negotiations on the resolution, Washington dropped several measures to win the support of Russia and China, including a bid for an oil embargo and the blacklisting of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and the national airline. In Hong Kong, former White House chief strategist Steve Bannon told the South China Morning Post the results of a U.S.-led investigation into alleged Chinese intellectual property theft would be announced before the Beijing summit to reset bilateral trade. The far-right architect of Trump’s 2016 election victory, Bannon told an investor conference, organized by a unit of China’s largest brokerage, that Trump and Xi had a rapport that should enable them to work out differences, said an attendee at the meeting which was closed to the press. Bannon, who was let go by Trump last month, told a private lunch gathering in Hong Kong that he still “speaks with President Donald Trump every two to three days,” the Wall Street Journal reported.

text: The Supreme Court of South Africa has significantly increased Oscar Pistorius' murder sentence, more than doubling it on Friday. The judges agreed with the prosecution's assertion that the initial six-year prison term for the shooting death of his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp, was excessively lenient. Pistorius, a celebrated athlete and double amputee recognized as the "Blade Runner" due to his carbon-fiber limbs, was absent from the courtroom when the new sentence of 13 years and five months was pronounced. The family of Steenkamp was also not present, but they expressed approval of the increased sentence, which falls short of the mandatory minimum of 15 years for murder, taking into account the time Pistorius has already spent incarcerated. They remarked that this decision indicated that justice could be achieved in South Africa. "This is an emotional thing for them. They just feel that their trust in the justice system has been confirmed this morning," stated Tania Koen, a spokesperson for the family, in comments to Reuters. Advocacy groups in a nation grappling with high rates of violent crime against women have claimed that Pistorius, now 31, received preferential treatment compared to individuals who are non-white or lack his wealth and fame. Barry Steenkamp, the father of the deceased model, conveyed to SABC television that the family can now proceed with their lives. "I always, from the beginning, said justice had not been served; now it has," he remarked. In the same interview, June Steenkamp, Reeva's mother, stated, "We felt that we didn’t have justice for Reeva by that too-lenient sentence, but now we have justice for her." Carl Pistorius, the elder brother of the athlete, expressed his devastation on Twitter, writing, "Shattered. Heartbroken. Gutted." Attempts to reach Pistorius' legal representatives for comment were unsuccessful. The athlete was sentenced to prison in July of the previous year after being found guilty of murdering model and law graduate Steenkamp on Valentine's Day 2013 by firing four shots through a locked bathroom door. The case drew international attention. Initially, he was convicted of manslaughter and received a five-year prison term. However, that verdict was escalated to murder by the Supreme Court in December 2015, and his sentence was extended to six years by trial judge Thokozile Masipa in July of the following year. Masipa articulated in court that while the Steenkamps endured a tremendous loss, Pistorius' life and career as a once-esteemed athlete were also in ruins. She noted that a lengthy prison sentence would not serve justice. During the trial, Pistorius' appearance without his prosthetics elicited gasps from those present in the courtroom. The appeals court delivered a harsh critique, stating that Masipa's decision had improperly deviated from the mandatory minimum sentence of 15 years for murder. Judge Willie Seriti, who announced the unanimous decision of the court, remarked, "The sentence of six years imprisonment is shockingly lenient, to a point where it has the effect of trivializing this serious offence." He expressed, "I am of the view that there are no substantial and compelling circumstances which can justify the departure from the prescribed minimum sentence." Furthermore, Seriti admonished Pistorius, indicating that his apology to the family of the deceased during the hearing did not convey any genuine remorse, and that he does not fully grasp the seriousness of his actions. State prosecutors, led by advocate Andrea Johnson, argued during this month's appeals hearing that there were no mitigating circumstances to warrant Pistorius' six-year sentence. Defense attorney Barry Roux contended that Pistorius did not intentionally kill Steenkamp, urging that the appeal should be dismissed. Roux had previously asserted during the July 2016 trial that Pistorius' disability and mental anguish following the incident should be viewed as factors to lessen his sentence. Pistorius had competed in the semi-finals of the 400 meters at the 2012 London Olympics and secured two gold medals at the Paralympics. He has remained in the news even while incarcerated; in August, he was granted temporary release to attend his grandmother's funeral and was hospitalized for what local media reported was a suspected heart attack. In August 2016, the athlete denied allegations of attempting to take his own life.

text: A significant evacuation is set to take place in Frankfurt, affecting around 60,000 residents in the German financial hub. This action is necessary to secure a large World War Two bomb that was recently found at a construction site, according to police statements. Institutions such as the Bundesbank, Goethe University, and two hospitals will also see evacuations as part of this operation, marking one of the most extensive evacuations in the history of post-war Germany. The 1.4-tonne HC 4000 bomb, which was released by the British air force during World War Two, was discovered on Wismarer Strasse in the affluent Westend area, known for its wealthy banking community. Experts in bomb disposal indicated that the major evacuation could be postponed until the weekend. A representative from the Frankfurt police mentioned on Wednesday, 'We are still working on the modalities of the evacuation plan.'
source_text: Frankfurt to evacuate 60,000 people to defuse British WWII bomb. FRANKFURT (Reuters) - Around 60,000 inhabitants of Germany s financial capital Frankfurt will be ordered to leave their homes on Sunday while a large World War Two bomb discovered at a building site is made safe, the police said. Germany s central bank, the Bundesbank, Frankfurt s Goethe University, and at least two hospitals will also be evacuated, in one of the largest evacuations in German post-war history. The 1.4-tonne HC 4000 bomb dropped by the British air force during World War Two was uncovered on a building site on Wismarer Strasse in Frankfurt s leafy Westend where many wealthy bankers live. Bomb disposal experts who examined it said the massive evacuation could wait until the weekend.  We are still working on the modalities of the evacuation plan,  a spokeswoman for Frankfurt police said on Wednesday.

text: This month, President Donald Trump is set to show his support for Palestinian "self-determination" during his upcoming trip to the Middle East, as indicated by a high-ranking aide on Friday. This implies that Trump may be receptive to the concept of a two-state resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian dispute, even though he has not yet publicly endorsed it. H.R. McMaster, the U.S. national security adviser, made these remarks merely nine days following the visit to the White House by Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, where Trump pledged to work towards an unprecedented peace agreement but did not explicitly recommit to the long-standing objective of Palestinian statehood, which has been a fundamental element of U.S. policy. In previewing Trump’s inaugural foreign excursion, McMaster elaborated that during the initial stop in Saudi Arabia, the president will urge Arab and Muslim allies to take "bold new steps" against those responsible for chaos and violence, including individuals from Iran, Islamic State, al Qaeda, and the regime of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. Trump's journey, commencing late next week, will also encompass visits to Israel and Rome, designed to "broadcast a message of unity" by exploring significant religious sites associated with Christianity, Judaism, and Islam, McMaster informed the press. Observers will closely monitor Trump's discussions with Israeli and Palestinian leaders, which are scheduled to occur separately, to determine if he will begin outlining a cohesive approach to revive the stalled negotiations. Many analysts remain doubtful regarding Trump's ability to facilitate a peace agreement that has eluded previous leaders. In sessions with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Trump aims to "reaffirm America’s unshakeable bond to the Jewish state," while in discussions with Abbas, he plans to "express his desire for dignity and self-determination for the Palestinians," according to McMaster, a highly regarded Army general with considerable expertise in Middle Eastern affairs. It is anticipated that Trump will meet Abbas, the Western-supported leader of the Palestinian Authority, in Bethlehem located in the West Bank, according to sources from Palestine. Disappointment arose among Palestinians when Trump neglected to mention a two-state resolution during a joint appearance with Abbas on May 3. International backlash followed Trump’s comments in February, during a press conference with Netanyahu, where he seemed to distance himself from a longstanding U.S. commitment to Palestinian statehood, stating he would leave the decision to the involved parties. Achieving an independent state is not only the goal of the overwhelming majority of Palestinians, but it has also been the aim of successive U.S. administrations as well as the global community. When questioned about whether Trump would arrange for Netanyahu and Abbas to meet in the same location during the scheduled visit on May 22-23, McMaster replied that such decisions would be at the discretion of the president and the other leaders, adding, "The final plans aren’t set yet."

text: President Michel Temer of Brazil expressed concerns on Friday that the nation's credibility on the international stage could diminish and economic instability could arise if Congress does not approve a proposal aimed at reforming the expensive social security system by early next year. During a press conference, Temer admitted that his declining popularity due to corruption allegations has hindered the progress of the pension reform bill, which is set to be voted on February 19. He also mentioned that his administration would refrain from endorsing any candidate in the 2018 presidential elections who does not support pension reform.
source_text: Temer warns pension reform failure will hurt Brazil's credibility. BRASILIA (Reuters) - Brazil s President Michel Temer warned on Friday the country would face economic volatility and loss of international credibility if a bill overhauling its costly social security system is not passed by Congress early next year. Speaking to reporters, Temer acknowledged that corruption accusations had undermined his popularity and delayed passage of a pension reform bill that is now scheduled to be put to a vote on February 19.  He said his government would not support a candidate in the 2018 presidential elections that does not back pension reform.

text: The campaign for Democratic presidential hopeful Hillary Clinton is seeing a shift as the director responsible for outreach to Asian American and Pacific Islander communities is set to depart. According to a campaign official on Saturday, Lisa Changadveja will take on a new role with the Colorado Democratic Party. Her exit comes just before key Democratic primaries in states featuring significant Asian American populations, such as Washington later this month and California in June. Campaign spokesperson Xochitl Hinojosa noted in an email to Reuters that Changadveja played a vital role in developing the AAPI initiative, stating, "Those efforts will persist with events scheduled in the upcoming weeks." A new Director of AAPI Outreach is anticipated to be announced by the campaign shortly. In an email sent to supporters dated March 18, Changadveja informed them of her new opportunity, expressing “tremendous faith in the campaign’s commitment and ability to continue engaging our community as we move through the rest of the primary and prepare for the general election.” She added, "I will be leaving Hillary for America as I have recently accepted a new job at the Colorado Democratic Party," which was shared with Reuters. Attempts to reach Changadveja for further comment were unsuccessful. The Clinton campaign has relied heavily on minority groups as crucial voting blocs, which have contributed to her successes against Bernie Sanders, the senator from Vermont who represents her primary challenger for the Democratic nomination leading up to the presidential election on November 8. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders make up approximately 6 percent of the total U.S. population, excluding individuals of mixed race. In California, which will hold its nominating event in June, they account for nearly 15 percent, while Washington, hosting its Democratic caucus on March 26, has about 9 percent of its population represented by this demographic. Census data shows that Asian Americans rank among the fastest-growing ethnic groups in the nation, occasionally surpassing Latino growth rates. A study conducted last year by the University of California, Los Angeles projected that the Asian-American electorate could double to 12 million voters by 2040. Changadveja's tenure with the Clinton campaign began in September, as indicated on her LinkedIn profile, where it also noted her previous role as the LGBTQ and AAPI director for Ready for Hillary, a Super PAC that supported Clinton's presidential aspirations.

Changadveja did not immediately return requests for comment.     Minority communities have been key voting blocs for the Clinton campaign, helping her rack up wins over Bernie Sanders, the U.S. senator from Vermont who is her main rival for the Democratic nomination to the Nov. 8 presidential election.  Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders form about 6 percent of the U.S. population, a figure that does not include people of mixed race, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. A study by the University of California, Los Angeles last year found that the Asian-American electorate will double to 12 million voters by 2040.  Changadveja joined the Clinton campaign in September, according to her LinkedIn page. She previously served as the LGBTQ and AAPI director for Ready for Hillary, a Super PAC that supported a Clinton run for the presidency, according to the page.

text: The young woman who disappeared after using the Cabify ride-hailing service has been discovered deceased, Mexican officials announced on Friday. Authorities in Puebla, a central Mexican state, reported that the remains of Mara Fernanda Castilla, 19, were located near a motel in the state's capital, which shares the same name. According to prosecutors, they suspect that the driver, who is known only as Ricardo N., murdered her at the motel following the ride she requested a week earlier, and they intend to file charges against him for her death. Governor Tony Gali took to Twitter to confirm the apprehension of the suspect. A representative from Cabify, a company based in Madrid that competes with Uber in the ride-hailing sector, chose not to comment on the ongoing investigation. However, Cabify did express its sorrow regarding Castilla's passing in an official statement. Incidents of violent crimes associated with ride-hailing services in Mexico have been relatively uncommon. In the previous year, a driver for Uber was arrested on allegations of assaulting a passenger.
source_text: Body of Mexican teenager who vanished after Cabify ride found. MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Mexican authorities said on Friday they had found the body of young woman who went missing after using ride-hailing service Cabify, and had arrested the driver on suspicion of her murder. State prosecutors in the central state of Puebla said the body of Mara Fernanda Castilla, 19, was found near a motel in the state capital, which is also called Puebla. In a statement, prosecutors said they believe the driver, identified only as Ricardo N., killed her at the motel after she had hailed a car with the service a week ago, and that they would be charging the man for Castilla s murder. State governor Tony Gali said on Twitter the suspect had been detained. A spokeswoman for Cabify, a Madrid-based company that competes with Uber for ride-hailing business, declined to comment on the case. In a statement, Cabify expressed its condolences about Castilla s death. There have been few reports of violent crimes involving ride-hailing services in Mexico. Last year authorities arrested a driver for Uber on suspicion of raping a passenger.

source_text: Republican presidential race erupts into four-way battle. CHARLESTON, S.C./SUMTER, S.C. (Reuters) - The Republican race for the party’s 2016 presidential nomination erupted into a four-candidate crossfire on Wednesday over who has the proper experience and is the most conservative, days before South Carolina voters put their stamp on the campaign. In TV interviews and campaign events, front-runner Donald Trump threatened to sue Senator Ted Cruz of Texas over a negative TV ad, while Senator Marco Rubio of Florida accused Cruz of lying about his record, and former Florida Governor Jeb Bush questioned Rubio’s experience to serve as president. Amid the squabbling, South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley endorsed Rubio as the Republicans’ best hope for winning the White House, a boost to Rubio and a blow to Bush, who had lobbied hard for her to pick him. The endorsement gave Rubio, 44, a valuable ally to try to sway voters ahead of Saturday’s South Carolina Republican primary, the third contest after Iowa and New Hampshire to pick a party nominee for the Nov. 8 election to succeed Democratic President Barack Obama. Bush had a tough day, learning of Haley’s endorsement right before a town hall meeting in Summerville, South Carolina, where four members of the audience second-guessed his campaign strategy and offered tips on how to have a greater impact in the state. Much of the debate took place over the television airwaves, as Trump, 69, a billionaire businessman and former reality TV star, lobbed charges at his rivals at an MSNBC town hall, and Rubio and Cruz battled in back-to-back appearances at a CNN town hall in Greenville, South Carolina. Trump fumed about a TV ad put out by the Cruz campaign that brought up Trump’s past position in support of a woman’s right to an abortion. Trump says he has evolved into a conservative and is now against abortion. “You look at a guy like Ted Cruz, he’s a nasty guy,” Trump said. “He doesn’t have one Republican endorsement from the Senate and he works with the Senate. Think of it. Hard to believe.” Cruz dared Trump to sue him over the campaign ad, which featured a 1999 video clip of Trump saying he was “very pro-choice” on abortion. Cruz said Trump sent his campaign a “cease and desist letter” demanding it drop the ad. At the CNN town hall, he said he laughed out loud when he got the letter threatening what he called a “frivolous lawsuit.” “In any defamation case, truth is a complete defense,” Cruz said. Questioners at the town hall pressed Cruz, 45, on charges leveled against him by Trump that he may not be eligible to be president because he was born in Canada, and that none of his U.S. Senate colleagues liked him. Cruz said he met the constitutional requirement that a president must be a “natural born citizen” because his mother was an American. As for his Senate colleagues, Cruz said some may not like him because he serves the interests of his constituents, not fellow senators. The latest national Reuters/Ipsos poll showed Trump taking a more than 20-point lead over Cruz in the Republican race. Trump had 40 percent support in the poll conducted from Saturday to Wednesday, compared with 17 percent for Cruz, 11 percent for Rubio, 10 percent for retired neurosurgeon Ben Carson, and 8 percent for Bush. The results contrasted with those of an NBC News/Wall Street Journal national poll that put Cruz ahead of Trump among Republicans by 28 percent to 26 percent. Rubio, hoping to overtake Cruz for second place in South Carolina, where Trump leads in the polls, accused Cruz of spreading falsehoods with an ad attacking Rubio over his position on immigration. Rubio backed a 2013 Senate immigration reform effort that collapsed. Cruz says Rubio would have supported “amnesty” for illegal immigrants, which his rival denies. “If you say something that isn’t true and you say it over and over and you know it’s not true, it must be a lie,” Rubio said. Bush, running fourth in South Carolina and behind Rubio, questioned Rubio’s level of experience after Rubio said Bush did not have foreign policy experience. Rubio counts his time on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee as valuable experience. “It’s hard for me to be lectured to by a gifted young guy who thinks going to committee hearings means you know something about the world,” Bush said in Summerville. At the event, Bush, 63, the son and brother of former presidents, sounded a note of frustration at frequent criticism of his campaign by TV pundits. “The pundits have made it all – it’s all decided. We don’t have to go vote, I guess. It’s all finished. I should stop campaigning, maybe, huh? It’s all done,” he said. “No,” shouted people in the crowd. text: A recent speech by Donald Trump, the Republican candidate for president, has introduced new elements to his immigration strategies, yet significant legal uncertainties remain. Legal experts contend that while Trump's idea of halting immigration from regions known for terrorism could find some legal justification, his proposal to attach this to a broader prohibition on Muslim immigrants raises constitutional issues. This shift in Trump’s anti-Muslim discourse followed a tragic shooting incident at a Florida nightclub committed by the American-born child of Afghan immigrants over the weekend. During a passionate address on Monday, he elaborated on his earlier suggestion for a temporary ban on Muslim entry into the U.S., pledging that if he were to win the election, he would stop immigration from any locations that have a “proven history of terrorism” aimed at America or its allies. Furthermore, he implicated the Muslim-American community in a widespread conspiracy regarding attacks like the Orlando shooting, which was executed by a shooter who declared allegiance to ISIS, and he warned of severe repercussions for those who do not report suspicious activities among their neighbors. Many scholars in the field of law expressed skepticism, indicating that Trump's religion-focused immigration ban would likely not survive challenges to the U.S. Constitution’s provisions for religious freedom, equal protection, and due process, suggesting that such a measure would probably be invalidated by the judicial system should he attempt to enforce it through executive order. On the other hand, a restriction on immigrants from specific nations does have historical precedent and might withstand legal scrutiny. Some observers have likened this new approach to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which was employed for many years to limit the presence of Chinese workers and is generally viewed as a stain on the history of American immigration policy. However, Trump’s immigration plan appears to extend beyond this, aiming not just at a particular nation or geographic area, but also at a specific religion, a move that no contemporary U.S. president has undertaken. "This is a ludicrous idea aimed at creating a Fortress America by raising the drawbridges," remarked John Bellinger, who served as a legal advisor during the Bush administration. President Barack Obama subtly criticized Trump on Tuesday, asserting that such proposals reflect a "dangerous" perspective. Despite this, U.S. presidents possess considerable authority over immigration issues, and some conservative legal theorists have suggested that the success of any proposed immigration ban would depend on how specifically Trump defines it. They point out that during the 1979 Iran hostage crisis, Democratic President Jimmy Carter prohibited Iranian nationals from entering the United States. "If the Trump administration were to restrict immigration from particular countries instead of targeting religions, it would likely not breach the Constitution," noted John Yoo, a law professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and a former official in the Justice Department who provided guidance to the George W. Bush administration regarding interrogation techniques for terrorism suspects. Herman Schwartz, a law professor at American University in Washington, added that if Trump adhered to his plan for a temporary ban on Muslim immigrants, this raises considerable constitutional dilemmas and "indicates his tenuous grasp of legal principles." In his speech in New Hampshire on Monday, Trump showed no indication of softening his position regarding the prohibition of Muslims entering the U.S., a stance he first proposed in December following a mass shooting linked to ISIS in San Bernardino, California. The discourse surrounding the legality of Trump’s proposals became more complex due to the ambiguous nature of his statements and the uncertainties about the extent of any immigration ban he might impose if he were to be elected. While legal authorities agree that presidents can impose bans on immigrants from certain nations, the current U.S. immigration policy does not include bans from any specific country. Nonetheless, heightened scrutiny is applied to individuals arriving from nations such as Syria and Iran. Depending on the broadest interpretation of Trump’s statements, immigration could potentially be restricted not only from Muslim-majority nations but also from U.S. allied countries across Europe and Asia that have experienced militant assaults.
source_text: Trump adds new twist to immigration proposals, but legal doubts persist. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump’s proposal for suspending immigration from parts of the world with a history of terrorism could have a legal basis, but his assertion that it be part of a broader ban on Muslim immigrants makes it constitutionally untenable, legal scholars say. The new twist in Trump’s anti-Muslim rhetoric came in the aftermath of a weekend shooting massacre at a Florida nightclub by the American-born son of Afghan immigrants. In a fiery speech on Monday, he expanded on his proposed temporary ban on Muslims entering the United States, vowing if elected to halt immigration from any area of the world where there is a “proven history of terrorism” against America or its allies. He also accused the Muslim-American community of broad complicity in attacks such as the Orlando shooting, which was carried out by a gunman pledging allegiance to Islamic State, and threatened “big consequences” for those who fail to inform on their neighbors. Many legal experts said Trump’s proposal for a religion-based ban would be unlikely to pass the test of U.S. constitutional guarantees of religious freedom, due process and equal protection and would likely be struck down by the courts if he tried to implement them by presidential decree. However, a ban on immigrants from certain countries has some precedent and might pass muster.  Some see that new proposal as reminiscent of the congressional Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which was used for years to halt the influx of Chinese laborers and has been widely considered a black mark on America’s immigration record. But Trump’s overall immigration plan would go beyond that, targeting not just a country or a region of the world but also a religion, something that no modern U.S. president has done.  “This is an absurd proposal to build a Fortress America and pull up the drawbridges,” said John Bellinger, former legal adviser to the Bush administration. President Barack Obama took a veiled swipe at Trump on Tuesday, saying such ideas represented a “dangerous” mindset. But U.S. presidents have wide latitude on immigration matters, and some conservative scholars said that the fate of any proposed ban would hinge on how narrowly Trump framed it. They note, for instance, that Democratic President Jimmy Carter barred Iranian nationals from entering the United States during the 1979 Iran hostage crisis. “If a Trump administration cut off immigration from certain countries, rather than certain religions, it would not violate the Constitution,” said John Yoo, a law professor at the University of California Berkeley and former Justice Department official who advised the George W. Bush administration on interrogation methods used on terrorism suspects. Herman Schwartz, a law professor at American University in Washington, said if Trump stuck to his proposal for a temporary prohibition on Muslim immigrants, that raises significant constitutional questions and “shows his shaky command of the legal facts.” In Monday’s speech in New Hampshire, Trump showed little sign of scaling back his call to ban Muslims from entering the United States, which he first laid out in December after an Islamic State-linked deadly mass shooting in San Bernardino, California. Debate over the legality of Trump’s proposals was complicated by the vagueness of his pronouncement and questions on how broadly he would extend any immigration ban if elected. While legal experts say presidents have the power to ban immigrants from specific countries, the United States does not currently ban immigration from any country. Officials do give extra scrutiny to people entering from countries such Syria and Iran. Under the broadest interpretation of Trump’s pronouncement,  immigration could be barred not only from the Muslim world but from U.S.-allied countries in Europe and Asia where militant attacks have taken place. This could include India, the source of many skilled engineers for the U.S. technology sector. Critics say this would be impractical and counterproductive. “Is Mr. Trump proposing to stop issuing visas even for business or tourism or education to nationals of certain countries?” said Bellinger. “Rather than increase economic growth, Mr. Trump’s plan could cost the U.S. economy billions of dollars.” Republican Senator Jeff Sessions, a Trump foreign policy adviser, justified the candidate’s pronouncement, saying “it is perfectly appropriate for the country to refuse admission to those whose presence may be detrimental to the national interest.“ But Orrin Hatch, the longest-serving Republican in the Senate, when asked whether a president has the authority to ban immigrants based on religion, said: “I’m not sure he does.” Legal experts also raised doubts about the legality of Trump’s demand that members of the American Muslim community “cooperate with law enforcement and turn in the people who they know are bad” or else they will be “brought to justice” themselves.” Critics have accused him of anti-Muslim fear-mongering to win votes. “Generally, the idea that knowledge in and of itself comes with criminal liability is antithetical to the way we talk about criminal law in the United States,” said Daniel Richman, a Columbia University law professor and former federal prosecutor. If Trump tried to implement such prosecutions as president, he said, potential defendants could simply invoke their constitutional right against self-incrimination and continue to remain silent.

text: On Thursday, opposition figure Morgan Tsvangirai urged President Robert Mugabe to step down for the sake of the nation following the military's takeover of power. source_text: Zimbabwe's Tsvangirai calls on Mugabe to resign. HARARE (Reuters) - Zimbabwe opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai said on Thursday President Robert Mugabe should resign in the interest of the country after the military seized power. Mugabe is insisting he remains Zimbabwe s only legitimate ruler and has balked at mediation by a Catholic priest to allow the 93-year-old former guerrilla a graceful exit after a military coup, sources said on Thursday.  In the interest of the people, Mr. Robert Mugabe must resign and step down immediately,  Tsvangirai, leader of the Movement for Democratic Change, told a news conference, reading from a statement.

text: In front of an enthusiastic audience at the U.S. Open on Tuesday, Roger Federer, the world’s third-ranked player, managed to overcome a nervous moment in the first round against Frances Tiafoe, eventually securing a 4-6 6-2 6-1 1-6 6-4 triumph over the young American. When Tiafoe’s forehand struck the net on match point, it was clear that Federer felt more relieved than ecstatic, as he kept alive his pursuit of a 20th Grand Slam title. In a post-match interview, Federer remarked, “We had a good fight.” With a chuckle, he added, “It was exciting and this is why I came to New York, to go through these emotions.” The 19-year-old Tiafoe took an early lead, breaking Federer in the very first game and celebrating with a loud “Come on!” after hitting a forehand winner that secured him the initial set. Following a six-month hiatus last year, Federer had previously won both the Australian Open and Wimbledon this year, and he soon found his rhythm by breaking Tiafoe to go ahead 3-1 in the second set, winning nine out of the next ten games. However, a dismal fourth set lasting 23 minutes saw Federer’s serve falter and his one-handed backhand lose its precision. He expressed admiration for Tiafoe, suggesting the young athlete has a promising career in front of him, stating, “He is a great player and has a bright future ahead of him.” Although he emerged victorious, questions lingered regarding the physical condition of the 36-year-old Swiss, who had missed the Cincinnati Masters earlier this month due to back issues. Federer admitted to being apprehensive about his back before the match, but reassured that he felt “much, much better.” He concluded, “This win will give me a lot of confidence.” Owing to inclement weather, the fast-paced 2-hour and 35-minute match unfolded under the closed roof of Arthur Ashe Stadium, which intensified the crowd’s excitement. Next, Federer will face either Slovenia’s Blaz Kavcic or Russia’s Mikhail Youzhny.
