text: This week, the Republican lawmakers found themselves struggling to respond to the rhetoric of their party's figurehead, Donald Trump, in Washington. The efforts to align with Trump appeared particularly awkward as members of Congress sought to evade reporters, ducked into elevators, hurried away, or, in the least favorable cases, attempted to field questions. Just days following the uproar caused by his comments regarding a Mexican-American judge, the presumptive nominee reignited controversy by reiterating his demand for a halt to Muslim immigration after a gunman, who pledged allegiance to Islamic extremists, took the lives of 49 individuals in a Florida nightclub. Additionally, Trump, who gained fame as a reality television personality, delved into two contentious subjects for social conservatives by endorsing the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) community and proposing potential new measures for gun control. For legislators used to polished talking points and predictable inquiries, this week represented a whirlwind of awkward reactions and brief, reticent comments. Senator John Barrasso from Wyoming chose to walk away when questioned about Trump's support for the LGBT community, stating, "I don’t know what the latest is. I haven’t read anything. I haven’t been watching." Florida Senator Marco Rubio, who previously faced off against Trump during the presidential primaries, had to deflect two inquiries related to Trump before he could reveal his consideration for re-election – a choice that could influence whether Republicans maintain control of the Senate in the upcoming election on November 8. Senator Ted Cruz, another opponent from the primaries, avoided giving a direct answer to Trump's speech in which he intensified his stance on Muslims, while Senate Intelligence Chairman Richard Burr described it as "an OK speech" before entering an elevator, subsequently declining to answer further questions. The challenge posed by Trump is clear even to veteran Republicans. "I’m spending my days commenting on everything that Donald Trump says," expressed John McCain, who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee. Orrin Hatch, the longest-serving Republican senator, bounced from dismissing Trump’s remarks concerning Muslims to questioning the legality of his proposed immigration restrictions, expressing confusion regarding the billionaire's reaction to the Orlando tragedy. Furthermore, the controversies surrounding Trump have overshadowed House Speaker Paul Ryan's introduction of a policy agenda, which was intended to align Trump's viewpoints more closely with the mainstream party ideology. When asked on Thursday if he was troubled by the need to address Trump's statements, Ryan characterized Trump as "a different kind of candidate...(in) a different kind of year." When pressed about how often he would need to navigate this situation, Ryan stated, "I don’t know the answer to that question either." In a twist directed at his detractors within the Republican leadership, Trump remarked this week: "Be quiet, just please be quiet. Don’t talk. Please be quiet. Just be quiet." Ryan's reaction was, "...You can’t make this up sometimes," he commented. As a political newcomer with no previous elected office experience, Trump also indicated that he may not require much support from his Republican peers on Capitol Hill. "We have to have our Republicans either stick together or let me just do it by myself. I’ll do very well," he mentioned in a CNN interview. "A lot of people thought I should do that anyway, but I’ll just do it very nicely by myself."

text: During a confirmation hearing on Tuesday, U.S. senators emphasized the importance of trade and business matters when interrogating President Donald Trump's choice for U.S. ambassador to India, expressing significant backing for his appointment to New Delhi. Kenneth Juster, nominated by Trump on September 1, is a 64-year-old economic adviser within the administration and previously held the position of under secretary of Commerce under former Republican President George W. Bush. Recognized as a specialist on India, Juster received commendations from both Trump’s fellow Republicans, who hold a majority in Congress, as well as Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, although they pointed out several challenges affecting bilateral relations. Trump, who ran on an 'America First' agenda, has openly voiced his dissatisfaction regarding the increasing U.S. trade deficit with India. Additionally, he has advocated for changes to the H1B visa system, which has favored Indian technology companies. Indian officials, however, refute claims that Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 'Make in India' initiative is protectionist and have raised concerns about U.S. regulations impacting products like generic medicines and fruits. Senator Bob Corker, who chairs the panel, expressed his irritation at the sluggish pace of economic reforms in India. Republican Senator Rob Portman, a former U.S. Trade Representative, echoed similar sentiments, stating he has 'deep concerns' regarding access to the Indian market for certain U.S. goods and services. 'We must continue to push forward, ensuring India complies with its WTO (World Trade Organization) commitments and addressing a broad array of economic matters,' Portman asserted. Senator Ben Cardin, the leading Democrat on the committee, remarked that India had not been as effective as it could be in enforcing its sanctions regulations. Juster noted he would prioritize business matters in his role in New Delhi, while also pledging to collaborate with Indian officials on issues including North Korea's nuclear ambitions, counterterrorism efforts, and enhancing security in Afghanistan. Last week, U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis engaged in discussions in India, seeking to encourage greater Indian participation in stabilizing Afghanistan amidst the Trump administration's increasing pressure on Pakistan to take action against militants operating from its territory. Democratic Senator Chris Coons inquired about H1B visas, but Juster stated he was not in a position to represent the administration's current stance. The U.S. mission in India handles more visas than any other mission. A vote to confirm Juster has yet to be scheduled. Corker described him as 'extraordinarily well-qualified' and expressed hope for a swift confirmation process. Cardin acknowledged Juster’s 'incredible credentials.'

text: Recent developments indicate that the United States is advising caution to Saudi Arabia, even as both nations express shared concerns regarding Iran. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - While President Donald Trump has consistently voiced strong support for Saudi Arabia, experts suggest that the U.S. is subtly urging Riyadh to adopt a more restrained stance in its ongoing power rivalry with Iran. The Trump administration aligns with Saudi Arabia's perception of Iran as a regional threat and has provided substantial backing to the Kingdom following a thwarted missile strike from Iranian-aligned factions in Yemen that exposed their capability to target the Saudi capital. After a tumultuous relationship with the previous Obama administration, Trump has fostered closer ties with Saudi Arabia, making Riyadh his inaugural destination on his first international tour, and has pledged to confront Iran robustly. However, the U.S., which maintains military personnel in both Syria and Iraq, is conveying a more moderated approach toward the escalating tensions in a region marked by instability. On Thursday, the State Department emphasized the necessity for 'unimpeded access' for humanitarian assistance to Yemen, following Saudi Arabia's implementation of a blockade to restrict the supply of arms to Houthi fighters aligned with Iran. The following day, U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson reaffirmed his recognition of Saad al-Hariri as Lebanon's prime minister, despite Hariri's unexpected resignation announcement on November 4 from Riyadh. During his televised statement, Hariri expressed fears of assassination and accused Iran and its Lebanese ally Hezbollah of inciting discord in the Arab world, positioning Lebanon at the center of the power struggle between Sunni Saudi Arabia and Shiite Iran. Two U.S. officials reported that the Saudis, under Crown Prince Mohammed's leadership, had encouraged Hariri to resign, while Lebanese officials assert that he is being detained in Saudi Arabia, a claim that Riyadh refutes. Hariri has not publicly addressed whether he is free to travel as he wishes. On Saturday, the White House issued a statement rejecting any attempts by militias within Lebanon or foreign forces to undermine Lebanon's stability or use it as a base to threaten other nations in the region. When queried about whether the U.S. was advocating for a more cautious approach from Saudi Arabia, both the White House and the State Department referenced Saturday’s declaration regarding Lebanon. Paul Salem, the senior vice president of the Middle East Institute, a think tank in Washington, noted that Tillerson did not align with the Saudi perspective, which describes the Lebanese state as being under Hezbollah's influence. 'That’s significant,' Salem remarked. He added that Tillerson was signaling to Israeli officials that now is not the appropriate moment to take action against Lebanon, given longstanding Israeli worries about Hezbollah's increasing military capabilities. Ray Takeyh, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, indicated that the Trump administration still aims to assist the Saudis in pursuing their interests against Iran while avoiding further destabilization in the region. 'This is a delicate balancing act,' Takeyh observed. 'It involves supporting allies in a policy that the administration agrees with, while trying to mitigate aspects of it that it sees as overstated.' Tillerson's remarks also called upon all parties, both within Lebanon and externally, to respect the nation's independence, asserting that there is no place for foreign forces in Lebanon. The United States routinely criticizes both Iran and Hezbollah for their involvement in Lebanon. Tillerson’s support for Hariri and the Lebanese government sharply contrasts with Saudi Arabia’s approach, which has categorized Lebanon alongside Hezbollah as adversarial. F. Gregory Gause, chairman of the International Affairs Department at Texas A&M University, characterized Tillerson as an embodiment of traditional American diplomacy, which prioritizes stability in the Middle East. 'I’m not entirely sure that is the position of the chief executive of the United States,' Gause added. The actions taken by Saudi Arabia coincide with these developments.

text: The team transitioning to oversee the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) under U.S. President Donald Trump is largely composed of individuals linked to the oil sector and pro-drilling organizations. According to a Monday email reviewed by Reuters, this newly formed 10-member group is heavily influenced by lobbyists from the energy industry and think-tanks that promote drilling initiatives. The email reveals that at least three individuals previously engaged as researchers in Koch-funded think-tanks are part of this team, along with a former lobbyist from the mining sector. Notably, some members have publicly expressed skepticism about measures aimed at addressing climate change, which was a significant priority for the EPA during Barack Obama’s presidency. The composition of this team has heightened expectations that Trump's administration will act on its commitment to reduce U.S. environmental regulations to facilitate drilling and mining activities. This new group is tasked with preparing the agency for incoming leadership and replaces the original transition team appointed by Trump after the election in November, prior to his inauguration. Currently, Trump’s pick for the EPA, Oklahoma Attorney General Scott Pruitt, is pending Senate confirmation. In the email, it was stated, "We are looking forward to working with the career professionals at the EPA to make this transition work as well as possible, and to carry out the Agency’s mission to protect public health and the environment.” It continued, “While transitions are always hard, straightforward honest communication combined with respect for each other will make the process work much better.” The email identifies Charles Munoz as the White House liaison for the new EPA team. Munoz previously was a key organizer for Trump in Nevada during his presidential campaign and helped establish the state chapter of Americans for Prosperity, a political advocacy organization financed by the Koch brothers. Another individual on the team, David Schnare, possesses credentials as a lawyer and environmental scientist, having dedicated 33 years to the EPA as a staff member. Recently, Schnare served as legal advisor at The Energy & Environment Legal Institute, which has received financial support from the Donors Trust fund associated with the Koch brothers. This institute aims to address “onerous federal and state governmental actions that negatively impact energy and the environment.” Furthermore, Schnare has been affiliated with the Center for Environmental Stewardship at the Thomas Jefferson Institute for Public Policy, which has also received partial funding from the Charles Koch Foundation. George Sugiyama, who was previously part of the initial EPA transition team, is included in the new team. He served as chief counsel for Republican Senator Jim Inhofe of Oklahoma, who is known for his skepticism regarding climate change. Prior to his work with Inhofe, Sugiyama represented the National Mining Association as a lobbyist. David Kreutzer is another member retained from the original team. Kreutzer, who was a senior research fellow at the Heritage Foundation, a group supported by foundations linked to Koch Industries and other energy companies, has characterized Obama’s climate change initiatives as costly and detrimental to specific industries while advocating for increased drilling in the Arctic. Doug Ericksen, a current senator from Washington state, takes on the role of communications director for the new EPA team. He has worked as Trump’s deputy campaign director for the northwestern state and holds a degree in environmental science. Additionally, Ericksen chairs the energy and environment committee in the state senate and opposes the climate policies implemented by Democratic Governor Jay Inslee of Washington, including initiatives aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Budgetary matters within the landing team will be overseen by Holly Greaves, who previously held the position of senior audit manager at KPMG and has experience from her time at Ernst & Young in advisory services. Other members of this team include Justin Schwab, designated as the legal advisor for the EPA, who has a background with the law firm Baker Hostetler. Finally, the team also comprises Washington State Senator Don Benton, a Republican who has managed a county environmental department, along with Patrick Davis, a Republican political consultant.

Several members of the team have also publicly argued against U.S. efforts to combat climate change, a key function of the EPA under former President Barack Obama. Trump’s nominee to run the EPA, Oklahoma Attorney General Scott Pruitt, is awaiting Senate confirmation. “We are looking forward to working with the career professionals at the EPA to make this transition work as well as possible, and to carry out the Agency’s mission to protect public health and the environment,” according to the email. “While transitions are always hard, straight forward honest communication combined with respect for each other will make the process work much better.” Charles Munoz was named in the email as White House liaison on the new EPA team. He was a top organizer for Trump in Nevada during his campaign for the White House and helped set up the state’s chapter of Americans for Prosperity, a political advocacy group funded by the Kochs. Another team member, David Schnare, is a lawyer and environmental scientist who spent 33 years as a staffer at the EPA. More recently Schnare was legal counsel at The Energy & Environment Legal Institute, which has received funding from the Koch brothers-linked Donors Trust fund. He was chief counsel for Republican Senator Jim Inhofe of Oklahoma, a vocal climate change doubter. Before working for Inhofe, Sugiyama lobbied on behalf of the National Mining Association. text: On Friday, Republican presidential hopeful Donald Trump expressed his preference for the United States to negotiate trade agreements with single nations rather than engaging in multilateral pacts such as the Trans-Pacific Partnership. Trump, currently leading the Republican nomination race for the presidency, has made his criticism of trade agreements like the 12-member TPP and the North American Free Trade Agreement central to his campaign as the Nov. 8 election approaches. During a news conference in Palm Beach, Florida, which occurred prior to the state's nominating event on Tuesday, he stated, "To do these deals where they wrap them up and they put 12 countries in one. TPP is an example. I want individual trade deals with individual countries." He remarked, "Some countries treat us better than others. Some are worse." Trump, who has a background in real estate development, added, "China will take advantage of TPP. It’s not in it now but believe me they come through the back door. They are watching it so closely." The agreement was finalized in October. While he supports free trade, Trump emphasized that it should be equitable. He claimed that NAFTA had led to job losses for many Americans and warned that TPP, which requires Congressional approval, would similarly harm the workforce. Currently, the United States has bilateral trade agreements with 20 nations, which include Canada, Israel, Mexico, Peru, Singapore, and South Korea. (Reporting by Eric Beech in Washington; Editing by Howard Goller) This article was funded in part by SAP. It was independently created by the Reuters editorial staff. text: U.S. Senator Rand Paul from Kentucky has announced his return to the Senate on Monday, following an incident that left him with six broken ribs after a neighbor tackled him while he was mowing his lawn. In a Twitter update, Senator Paul, a Republican, expressed that he is still experiencing significant pain but is prepared to resume his duties and advocate for liberty, alongside pushing for tax cuts in the near future. Rene Boucher, 59, the individual accused of the assault, entered a not guilty plea on Thursday to a misdemeanor charge of assault, according to a court representative. Boucher faces a charge of fourth-degree assault that resulted in minor injuries, which could lead to a maximum sentence of one year in jail if found guilty. A pretrial hearing is scheduled for November 30. Furthermore, Boucher’s bond, set at $7,500, includes a stipulation that he must maintain a distance of at least 1,000 feet (305 m) from Paul. The senator, aged 54, reported to law enforcement that Boucher approached him on his property in a gated neighborhood near Bowling Green, tackling him from behind, as detailed in an arrest warrant referenced by the Bowling Green Daily News. On Twitter, Paul previously indicated that the broken ribs were a result of the incident that occurred on November 3, and X-rays had revealed a pleural effusion, which is an accumulation of fluid in the tissues surrounding the lungs and chest. Reports from various media outlets suggest that Boucher, who is also a physician like Paul, had a longstanding feud with the senator. However, in an interview with the Washington Examiner published on Monday, Paul stated that he had no conflict with Boucher and had not interacted with his neighbor for ten years. He claimed ignorance regarding any potential motive for the altercation. When reached for comment by Reuters on Monday, Paul was unavailable. "My first encounter was basically being hit in the back," he recounted. "We’ve never had words over anything, we’ve never had a dispute or discussion or words." The incident is currently under investigation by the Kentucky State Police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, according to statements made by Warren County Attorney Amy Milliken. Fox News reported on Thursday, citing anonymous sources, that federal charges are anticipated in this case. Paul informed the Examiner, "There is going to be a criminal prosecution," but he did not provide further details regarding his statement. An FBI representative in Louisville, David Habich, stated in an email on Monday that there are no new updates concerning the federal charges. The senator’s office opted not to comment on the potential federal charges that day.

Boucher’s $7,500 bond requiring him to keep at least 1,000 feet (305 m) away from Paul remained in effect. Paul, 54, told police that Boucher came on his property in a gated community near Bowling Green and tackled him from behind, the Bowling Green Daily News reported, citing an arrest warrant. Citing unnamed sources, Fox News reported on Thursday that Paul had been told federal charges were expected in the case. “There is going to be a criminal prosecution,” Paul told the Examiner but did not elaborate on what he meant. text: The government of South Sudan and the United Nations declared on Wednesday that the nation requires $1.7 billion in humanitarian assistance for 2018 to support 6 million individuals, which constitutes half of its populace, in managing the repercussions of warfare, hunger, and economic downturn. Following its independence from Sudan, South Sudan descended into civil conflict in late 2013, with a third of its population, totaling 12 million, having been displaced. The strife originated from a rivalry between President Salva Kiir and his former deputy Riek Machar, who is currently detained in South Africa, eventually escalating into ethnic confrontations. Alain Noudehou, the U.N. Humanitarian Coordinator for South Sudan, stated during a press briefing, "We are calling for $1.72 billion to continue providing life-saving assistance and protection for 6 million people most in need in South Sudan." Noudehou emphasized that humanitarian aid is crucial for those afflicted by displacement, food scarcity, malnutrition, violence, and the economic downturn. Since the onset of the conflict, approximately 4 million people have been compelled to leave their residences, with nearly 1.9 million internally displaced and about 2.1 million having sought refuge in neighboring nations, he noted. Furthermore, the ongoing conflict has resulted in a reduction in crude oil output, a vital source of foreign currency, while the resulting instability has obstructed food production. Present at the news conference was Hussein Mar Nyuot, South Sudan’s Humanitarian Affairs Minister, who warned, "I believe if we don’t get the amount ($1.72 billion) and the donors don’t respond to this, more crisis in South Sudan will happen. That means 2018 might be worse than 2017."
source_text: South Sudan needs $1.7 billion humanitarian aid in 2018. JUBA (Reuters) - South Sudan needs $1.7 billion in aid next year to help 6 million people   half of its population   cope with the effects of war, hunger and economic decline, the government and the United Nations announced on Wednesday. South Sudan slid into civil war in late 2013, two years after gaining independence from Sudan and a third of its 12 million population has fled their homes.  The conflict was sparked by a feud between President Salva Kiir and his former deputy Riek Machar, who is being held in South Africa, and eventually led to a fight along ethnic lines.  We are calling for $1.72 billion to continue providing life-saving assistance and protection for 6 million people most in need in South Sudan,  Alain Noudehou, the U.N. Humanitarian Coordinator for South Sudan, told a news conference. Humanitarian assistance was needed for people suffering the effects of displacement, food insecurity, malnutrition, violence and economic decline, Noudehou said. Since the conflict began, about 4 million people have been forced to flee their homes, with nearly 1.9 million people who have internally displaced and about 2.1 million who have fled to neighboring countries, he said. The conflict has also led to a cut in crude oil production, which is a key foreign exchange earner, and the ensuing insecurity has hampered cultivation of food. Also at the news conference was South Sudan s Humanitarian Affairs Minister Hussein Mar Nyuot.   I believe if we don t get the amount ($1.72 billion) and the donors don t respond to this more crisis in South Sudan will happen. That means 2018 might be worse than 2017,  he said.

text: Operations in the Minnesota Senate may be halted as early as December 1 because of a funding disagreement. Senate Majority Leader Paul Gazelka revealed on Wednesday that workers will be furloughed and the chamber will cease operations unless funding previously vetoed by Governor Mark Dayton is restored by the state courts. He expressed concerns that the Senate will exhaust its funds by next month, prompting the chamber to seek specific financial resources from the Legislative Coordinating Committee to maintain operations until January 12. Gazelka stated in a press release, "This decision to suspend operations is not taken lightly – it is a serious matter – but we truly have no other option at this point." The workforce within the chamber consists of numerous lawyers, researchers, analysts, and assistants who support committees and legislative processes. Responsibility for the looming shutdown has been placed on Gazelka by the office of the Democratic governor. Matt Swenson, the assistant chief of staff to Dayton, remarked, "Even with nearly $45 million in available state funding for his operations, he and other legislative leaders are opting to lay off their own employees instead of acknowledging the misleading information they provided to the courts, media, and public regarding their actual financial status." In May, Dayton vetoed funding for the Republican-led legislature from the state's newly established two-year budget to compel lawmakers to amend tax policies that he argued would jeopardize the state's financial health. This action initiated a legal dispute with legislators, who contended that the removal of approximately $130 million in funding was unconstitutional. A judge in Ramsey County District Court sided with the legislature in July, yet on September 8, the state Supreme Court ruled that the governor's veto was constitutional. Nonetheless, the high court expressed concerns about the legislature's ability to function without funding and directed both parties to mediation, which concluded without resolution. Gazelka emphasized the necessity for the court to intervene once again. He stated, "After the beginning of the year, the citizens of Minnesota will effectively have no representation in the legislative branch, not to mention the hardship faced by our employees." In a court document filed in September, the House of Representatives indicated it expected to deplete its funds by February 1.
source_text: Minnesota Senate may halt operations on Dec. 1 due to funding dispute. (Reuters) - The Minnesota Senate will furlough its workers and suspend operations as soon as Dec. 1 due to an ongoing funding dispute with Governor Mark Dayton, the chamber’s Republican leader announced on Wednesday.   Senate Majority Leader Paul Gazelka said his chamber will run out of money by next month unless the state courts restore funding for the legislature that was vetoed by Dayton. He added that the Senate plans to seek certain funds from the Legislative Coordinating Committee which would keep the chamber operating through Jan. 12. “We don’t take the suspension of operations of the Minnesota Senate lightly – this is not a game – but we really have no other choice today,” Gazelka said in a statement. The chamber’s workforce includes dozens of lawyers, analysts, researchers and assistants who work with committees and on legislation. The Democratic governor’s office blamed Gazelka for the impending shutdown. “Despite sitting on nearly $45 million in available state funding for his operations, he and other legislative leaders are choosing to lay off their own employees, rather than admit that they have misled the courts, the press, and the public about their true financial situation,” said Matt Swenson, the governor’s assistant chief of staff.   Dayton in May vetoed funding for the Republican-controlled legislature from the state’s new two-year budget in an effort to pressure lawmakers to revise tax measures that he said will harm the state’s financial stability. The move touched off a legal battle with lawmakers, who claimed the elimination of nearly $130 million in funding was unconstitutional. While a Ramsey County District Court judge sided with the legislature in July, the state Supreme Court on Sept. 8 determined that the governor’s action was constitutional. However, the high court raised concerns over the ability of the legislature to survive without funding and ordered the two sides into mediation, which ended in an impasse. Gazelka said it was imperative for the court to step in again.  “The people of Minnesota will no longer have a voice in the legislative branch after the first of the year, not to mention the pain inflicted on our employees,” he said. In a September court filing, the House of Representatives said it anticipated running out of money on Feb. 1.

text: On Monday, three Democratic senators reached out to high-ranking officials in the administration to inquire about the status of White House counterterrorism adviser Sebastian Gorka regarding a potential criminal investigation. They are particularly interested in whether he failed to disclose his association with a Hungarian neo-Nazi group. In their correspondence, Senators Dick Durbin, Richard Blumenthal, and Benjamin Cardin emphasized the significance of Gorka's role, highlighting that he occupies a position of considerable responsibility and public confidence. They argued that it is crucial for the American public to be informed if a high-ranking official in the White House is subject to criminal scrutiny. This letter serves as a follow-up to a previous inquiry made in March, which requested an examination into allegations that Gorka may have “falsified his naturalization application or otherwise illegally procured American citizenship.” According to the senators, Gorka “reportedly concealed his membership in the Vitezi Rend, a far-right anti-Semitic Hungarian organization with historical ties to the Nazis, when he applied for U.S. citizenship.” No immediate response was provided by the White House to a request for comment. The senators directed their correspondence to Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein and Elaine Duke, the acting secretary of the Department of Homeland Security.
source_text: Democratic senators press on whether White House aide under probe. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Three Democratic U.S. senators wrote to senior administration officials on Monday seeking confirmation on whether White House counterterrorism adviser Sebastian Gorka is under criminal investigation for failing to disclose his membership in a Hungarian neo-Nazi organization. “As a senior counterterrorism advisor, Mr. Gorka is in a position of great importance and public trust. The American people are entitled to know if a senior White House official is under criminal investigation,” Senators Dick Durbin, Richard Blumenthal and Benjamin Cardin said in the letter. They said the letter was a follow-up to a letter they sent in March calling for an investigation of whether Gorka had “falsified his naturalization application or otherwise illegally procured American citizenship.” Gorka “reportedly concealed his membership in the Vitezi Rend, a far-right anti-Semitic Hungarian organization with historical ties to the Nazis, when he applied for U.S. citizenship,” the senators said in Monday’s letter. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The senators’ letter was addressed to Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein and Elaine Duke, acting secretary of the Department of Homeland Security.

text: An unusual underwater signal was detected by an international body responsible for monitoring nuclear test bans near the last known location of an Argentine submarine, as reported on Thursday. The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO), located in Vienna, operates a global network of listening stations that are intended to identify clandestine nuclear detonations. Among these stations, two picked up the peculiar noise, prompting the CTBTO to relay this information to Argentine officials who are managing the search efforts for the ARA San Juan, which had a crew of 44 when it disappeared last week. Earlier on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Argentine navy mentioned that the abnormal sound found near the submarine's last known coordinates in the South Atlantic seemed to align with an explosion; however, the CTBTO was more cautious regarding the interpretation of the signal's origin. "It may correlate with an explosion, but we cannot confirm this with certainty," stated Mario Zampolli, a hydroacoustic engineer for the CTBTO, in comments to Reuters. He concurred with the navy's assessment that the sound was both unusual and brief, emphasizing that it was of a non-natural origin. Additionally, he noted that it is possible to ascertain the timing of the incident at that location, indicating it occurred roughly three and a half hours following the submarine's last reported contact, according to the information available in the media. He also mentioned that the monitoring stations were located in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, highlighting their distance from each other.
source_text: Nuclear test-ban body heard noise near Argentine sub's last position. VIENNA (Reuters) - An international nuclear test-ban body that runs a global network of listening posts designed to check for secret atomic blasts detected an  unusual signal  underwater last week near where an Argentine submarine went missing, it said on Thursday.  The Vienna-based Comprehensive nuclear Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) runs monitoring stations equipped with devices including hydrophones - underwater microphones that scan the oceans for sound waves. Two of its monitoring stations detected the unusual signal, the CTBTO said in a statement, adding that it was passing the information on to the Argentine authorities coordinating the search for the ARA San Juan, which had 44 crew on board when it went missing last week. An Argentine navy spokesman said earlier on Thursday that an abnormal sound detected near the submarine s last known position in the South Atlantic was  consistent with an explosion , but the CTBTO was more guarded on the possible cause.   It could be consistent with an explosion but there is no certainty about this,  CTBTO hydroacoustic engineer Mario Zampolli told Reuters. He agreed with the navy spokesman s description of the signal as unusual and short, adding that the cause was non-natural.  We can also calculate the time when the event happened in that location and that time is about three and a half hours after the last contact that the sub apparently had, according to what s out in the news,  he said. The stations that detected it are far apart, in the Atlantic and Indian oceans, he added.

text: On Sunday, a high-ranking adviser for Ted Cruz, who is running for the Republican presidential nomination, criticized Donald Trump’s campaign for adopting a strategy akin to a "banana republic." Ken Cuccinelli, who managed delegate operations for the Texas senator, made these comments during an appearance on ABC’s "This Week," where he stated that Trump’s team is contesting the process of delegate selection due to their inability to secure victories on the ground. Throughout the Sunday news shows, Cuccinelli, along with Trump’s campaign manager Corey Lewandowski and Ohio Governor John Kasich, exchanged sharp remarks regarding the delegate selection process. Currently, Trump is leading in the race to become the Republican Party’s nominee for the general election in November. However, it remains uncertain if the billionaire will arrive at the party's convention in Cleveland, scheduled for July 18-21, with the required 1,237 delegates to secure the nomination on the first ballot. The upcoming major contest is the primary in New York state on Tuesday, which has 95 delegates available. Polling data indicates that Trump, hailing from New York, is significantly ahead of his competitors, with Kasich and Cruz lagging behind. A recent CBS News poll released on Sunday indicated that Trump holds a commanding lead in New York, capturing 54 percent of respondents, while Cruz garnered 21 percent and Kasich received 19 percent. On the Democratic front, Hillary Clinton, a former U.S. Secretary of State and New York senator, alongside Bernie Sanders, a U.S. Senator from Vermont, will also be engaging with voters in New York on Tuesday. Polls suggest that Clinton is still the preferred candidate, although Sanders, a native of New York City who seeks an upset to maintain his campaign's momentum, has recently closed the gap. Meanwhile, Trump has shown signs of frustration as Cruz’s campaign strategically outmaneuvers him in the intricate process of acquiring delegates, which are not solely determined by popular votes. During a news conference in Staten Island, New York City, on Sunday, he reiterated his claim that the nomination system is "crooked." "You’re essentially purchasing these individuals," he remarked, referring to the delegates at the convention. He further stated, "I could provide them with the finest planes and transport them to the most luxurious destinations globally," but he expressed disinterest in courting delegates in such a manner, labeling it as undemocratic. Different states have unique rules for selecting delegates. Cuccinelli responded to Trump’s complaints by stating that Cruz has been "winning elections. And when we win, Trump complains." He labeled Trump's approach as a "banana republic tactic," asserting that "They have a media strategy. But Ted Cruz has established a grassroots movement." On "Fox News Sunday," Lewandowski, Trump’s campaign manager, pointed to Florida as a state where Trump won the primary decisively. Nevertheless, Trump can only count on 69 out of Florida's 99 delegates because the state Republican Party chairman has the authority to appoint 30 delegates. "Ted Cruz thrives in areas where party leaders determine the rules, and voters are not allowed to participate," Lewandowski stated. Another senior figure in Trump’s campaign, Paul Manafort, who specializes in delegate selection, mentioned on ABC that they intend to contest the outcomes in Missouri and Colorado. However, in various interviews on Sunday, Reince Priebus, the Chairman of the Republican National Committee, consistently refuted the notion that the delegate selection rules are biased against Trump. Kasich ridiculed Trump and his campaign's assertions that the delegate selection regulations are manipulated and that a "dirty trick" enabled Cruz to secure victory in Colorado without a statewide vote. In a CNN interview, Kasich advised Trump to "act like you’re a professional. Be a pro." (This story corrects New York state poll numbers in the 7th paragraph)
source_text: Cruz adviser says Trump campaign taking 'banana republic' approach. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A senior adviser to Republican presidential candidate Ted Cruz on Sunday accused rival Donald Trump’s campaign of taking a “banana republic approach” by complaining that party rules for selecting a nominee are rigged against him. Former Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli, the Texas senator’s delegate operations manager, said on ABC’s “This Week” that the Trump campaign is challenging the delegate selection process “because they’re getting beat on the ground.” Cuccinelli and Trump’s campaign manager, Corey Lewandowski, as well as the third Republican candidate, Ohio Governor John Kasich, traded punches over the delegate selection process on Sunday news shows.  Trump remains the front-runner in the race to be the Republican Party’s candidate in November’s general election. But it remains unclear whether the billionaire businessman will arrive at the party’s July 18-21 convention in Cleveland with the 1,237-delegate majority needed to clinch the nomination on the first ballot. The next big face-off is New York state’s primary on Tuesday, with 95 delegates at stake.  Opinion polls show Trump, a New Yorker, well ahead of his rivals, with Kasich and Cruz trailing behind. The latest CBS News poll, released on Sunday, showed Trump ahead in New York, with 54 percent of those surveyed to 21 percent for Cruz and 19 percent for Kasich. On the Democratic side, Hillary Clinton, a former New York senator and U.S. secretary of state, and U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont will also face New York voters on Tuesday. Polls show Clinton is still favored to win, although Sanders, a New York City native who is hoping for an upset win to ensure the continued viability of his campaign, has managed to narrow the gap in recent days. Trump, meanwhile, has become increasingly agitated as the Cruz campaign outmaneuvers him in the complex art of securing delegates that are not simply allocated by a popular vote.  At a news conference in New York City’s Staten Island borough on Sunday, he repeated his assertion that the system was “crooked.” “You’re basically buying these people,” he said, referring to convention delegates. “I could put them in the best planes and bring them to the best places in the world,” he added. But he said he was not interested in wooing delegates that way, describing it as undemocratic. The party rules for picking delegates vary by state. Cuccinelli said Cruz has been “winning elections. And when we win, Trump whines.” “This is a banana republic approach from the Trump team,” he said. “... They have a media campaign. But Ted Cruz has built a grassroots campaign.” On “Fox News Sunday,” Trump’s Lewandowski pointed to Florida, where the candidate won the primary in a landslide. But Trump can count on the support of only 69 of the state’s 99 delegates because the state Republican Party chairman is allowed to appoint 30. “Ted Cruz does well in places where party bosses get to set those rules and people don’t get to go and vote,” Lewandowski said. Another senior Trump adviser, delegate selection specialist Paul Manafort, told ABC the campaign will protest results in Missouri and Colorado. But in several interviews on Sunday, Republican National Committee Chairman Reince Priebus again denied that the delegate selection rules are rigged against Trump. Kasich ridiculed Trump and his campaign for suggesting the delegate selection rules are fixed and that a “dirty trick” allowed Cruz to win Colorado’s nominating contest without a statewide vote. Kasich, interviewed by CNN, said Trump should “act like you’re a professional. Be a pro.”  (This story corrects New York state poll numbers in 7th paragraph)

text: During a visit to Kuwait, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan announced on Monday that he intends to address the ongoing five-month conflict involving Qatar and its Gulf Arab neighbors. Since June 5, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Egypt have severed diplomatic and transportation connections with Doha, accusing Qatar of backing Iran and Islamist groups, claims that Qatar refutes. Erdogan is expected to arrive in Kuwait on Tuesday, where mediation efforts regarding the Gulf crisis have been made. Following this, he will travel to Qatar on Wednesday, a nation that has received support from Ankara and hosts a Turkish military base.
source_text: Turkey's Erdogan says he will discuss Gulf crisis in Kuwait. ISTANBUL (Reuters) - Turkey s President Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday he will discuss a solution to the five-month dispute between Qatar and its Gulf Arab neighbors during a visit to Kuwait. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Egypt cut diplomatic and transport ties with Doha on June 5, saying Qatar supports regional foe Iran and Islamists, a charge Qatar denies. Erdogan is scheduled on Tuesday to visit Kuwait, which has tried to mediate in the Gulf dispute. On Wednesday he will visit Qatar, which Ankara has supported and where Turkey has a military base.

text: On Thursday, a vote in the United Nations led to escalating tensions between Russia and the United States in the Security Council. British Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson expressed his outrage over Russia's decision to obstruct a U.S.-sponsored resolution aimed at prolonging an international investigation into the accountability for chemical weapons assaults in Syria. He described the veto as shocking. Johnson stated, "It is appalling that the UN Joint Investigative Mechanism has been closed down." He emphasized that the United Kingdom would continue collaborating with global partners to pinpoint and bring to justice those responsible for the use of chemical weapons, despite the termination of the Joint Investigative Mechanism.
source_text: UK's Johnson: Russia veto of chemical weapons inquiry 'appalling'. LONDON (Reuters) - British foreign minister Boris Johnson said on Friday it was  appalling  that Russia had blocked a U.S.-drafted resolution to renew an international inquiry into who is to blame for chemical weapons attacks in Syria.  It is appalling that the UN Joint Investigative Mechanism has been closed down,  Johnson said in a statement.  The United Kingdom will not let the end of the Joint Investigative Mechanism stop work with international partners to identify and hold accountable those responsible for using chemical weapons.  The vote at the United Nations on Thursday sparked a war of words between Russia and the United States in the Security Council.

text: In a recent analysis published on Tuesday, a nonpartisan research organization evaluated a tax proposal from Ted Cruz, a Republican candidate for the presidency. The study indicated that Cruz's plan could reduce federal revenue by approximately $8.6 trillion over the next decade, significantly contributing to the national debt. Introduced in November, Cruz's tax strategy would establish a flat individual income tax rate of 10 percent, which, along with various modifications, would primarily advantage affluent households, according to findings from the Tax Policy Center, located in Washington. Key elements of the proposal include the elimination of the corporate income tax, the removal of payroll taxes associated with Social Security and Medicare, and the abolition of estate and gift taxes. Additionally, it proposes an increase in the standard deduction while mostly discarding other deductions, with exceptions for mortgage interest and charitable contributions, and introduces a broad-based consumption tax at a rate of 16 percent. The Tax Policy Center commented, "The plan would reduce taxes for nearly all income brackets, but the wealthiest households would gain the most while those in poverty would see the least benefit." Furthermore, the value-added tax suggested by Cruz, who is a Senator from Texas and recently secured victory in the Iowa caucuses among Republican contenders, would only cover 70 percent of the costs associated with the tax reductions, as noted by the center. Cruz, a prominent figure within the conservative Tea Party movement, was instrumental in instigating a 16-day government shutdown in September 2013 due to his opposition to a spending bill aimed at undermining the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare. The analysis from the TPC revealed that high-income earners would experience an average tax reduction of roughly $6,100 in 2017, which constitutes about 8.5 percent of their after-tax earnings. Those with yearly incomes exceeding $3.7 million would see an average reduction close to 29 percent, translating to more than $2 million. According to the TPC, households situated in the middle-income range would benefit from an average tax cut of $1,800, representing 3.2 percent of their after-tax income, while taxpayers in the lowest income quintile would obtain an average reduction of $46, or merely 0.4 percent of their after-tax earnings. The proposed changes are expected to enhance motivation for working, saving, and investing; however, the anticipated drop in revenue would necessitate unprecedented reductions in government expenditure to prevent borrowing that could elevate interest rates and hinder private investment, the report stated. The Tax Policy Center operates as a collaborative effort between the Urban Institute and the Brookings Institution, two think tanks based in Washington. It has conducted analyses of other candidates' fiscal proposals. text: In a historic move, Air Force General Lori Robinson is set to be the first woman appointed to lead a U.S. combatant command. According to Defense Secretary Ash Carter on Friday, President Barack Obama is expected to nominate Robinson as the new leader of the military's Northern Command. This role, pending Senate approval, ranks among the highest in the U.S. military and would elevate Robinson, currently in charge of U.S. air operations in the Pacific, to a pivotal position overseeing North America's military activities. "General Robinson, it just so happens, would also be the first ever female combatant commander," Carter remarked while revealing Obama's intentions to put her forward for the nomination. He further emphasized, "That shows yet another thing - which is that we have, coming along now, a lot of female officers who are exceptionally strong. And Lori certainly fits into that category," during an event organized by Politico. Additionally, Carter indicated that Army General Vincent Brooks, who commands U.S. Army Pacific, will also be nominated to take over as the commander of U.S. Forces in South Korea.
source_text: U.S. general Lori Robinson to become first woman to lead combatant command. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Barack Obama will name the first woman to head a U.S. combatant command, selecting Air Force General Lori Robinson as the next head of the military’s Northern Command, Defense Secretary Ash Carter said on Friday. The position, which is subject to Senate confirmation, is one of the most senior in the U.S. military and would make Robinson - who now leads U.S. air forces in the Pacific - the top general overseeing activities in North America. “General Robinson, it just so happens, would also be the first ever female combatant commander,” Carter said, disclosing Obama’s plans to nominate her. “That shows yet another thing - which is that we have, coming along now, a lot of female officers who are exceptionally strong. And Lori certainly fits into that category,” Carter said at an event hosted by Politico. Carter also announced Army General Vincent Brooks, the commanding general of U.S. Army Pacific, would be nominated to become the next commander of U.S. Forces in South Korea.

text: On Wednesday, a contentious debate unfolded among House Republicans in Washington regarding gun control measures. The discussions arose after the mass shooting that occurred in Orlando last month and have raised doubts about House Speaker Paul Ryan's capability to secure the necessary votes for the proposed legislation. While the Democratic Party has criticized the gun control initiative put forth by Republican leaders as inadequate, a significant faction of around 40 conservative Republican representatives also expressed their dissent, arguing that the proposal fails to sufficiently safeguard gun purchasers. In a statement, the conservative Freedom Caucus indicated that the legislation does not adequately address the dangers posed by radical Islamic terrorism. Additionally, they raised concerns about the inclusion of gun control measures that do not sufficiently uphold due process rights. With the Republican proposal facing scrutiny from both sides of the aisle, it remains uncertain whether Ryan can gather the 218 votes required for passage in the House of Representatives. Following the shooting on June 12 at a gay nightclub in Orlando, which resulted in 49 fatalities and 53 injuries, the Senate did not approve any of the various Republican and Democratic gun control proposals that were presented. During this Senate debate, Democratic lawmakers organized a sit-in on the House floor, aiming to apply pressure on Republican leaders to advance legislation that would expand background checks for gun purchases and prohibit sales to individuals on terrorism watch lists. Announced last Friday, the Republican leadership's bill would grant the government three days to persuade a judge to block a gun sale. Ryan stated on Wednesday that he aimed to bring the bill to a vote either this week or next, but acknowledged that many lawmakers were requesting modifications. "We will not rush something to the floor that isn't right," Ryan remarked. Representative Matt Salmon from Arizona, who is a member of the Freedom Caucus, voiced his opposition to Ryan's decision to push the bill forward without allowing it to be examined by the appropriate committees first. Salmon noted that during a closed meeting, Ryan informed House Republicans that he was hastening the legislation to the House floor due to the necessity for certain members to have this vote for political reasons in swing districts that could potentially lean either Republican or Democratic in the elections on November 8. Meanwhile, Democrats continued their push for votes on their broader gun control proposals. Representative John Larson of Connecticut, one of the leaders of the Democratic sit-in, mentioned that his fellow party members intend to support Republican mental health legislation that could potentially prevent some mass shootings. Larson expressed hope that this initiative would be perceived as a gesture of goodwill towards Republicans in striving for progress on gun control. Earlier that morning, numerous gun control supporters gathered outside the House chamber despite the oppressive heat, with 91 individuals wearing orange shirts standing on the steps to demand action. This group symbolized the 91 individuals who, according to government data, lose their lives each day in the United States due to gun violence, many of whom die by suicide.
source_text: U.S. House Republicans battle each other on gun control. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A divided Republican Party on Wednesday fought over gun control legislation that was cobbled together following last month’s mass shooting in Orlando, raising questions over U.S. House Speaker Paul Ryan’s ability to get the measure passed. While Democrats have said the gun control proposal put forward by Republican leaders was too weak, an influential group of approximately 40 conservative House Republicans announced their opposition as well, saying the plan did not do enough to protect gun buyers. The legislation fails “to do enough to address the threat of radical Islamic terrorism,” according to a statement by the conservative Freedom Caucus. The group also complained of “the inclusion of gun control provisions that fail to adequately protect due process.” With the Republican leadership’s legislation under attack from both liberals and conservatives, it was unclear whether Ryan could muster the 218 votes he would need for passage in the House of Representatives. Last month, the Senate failed to approve any of several competing Republican and Democratic gun control proposals offered in the wake of the June 12 shooting at a gay night club in Orlando that killed 49 and injured 53 others. During the Senate debate, Democratic lawmakers staged a sit-in on the House floor to pressure Republican leaders to pass legislation expanding background checks on gun sales and blocking gun purchases by people on terrorism watch lists. The Republican leadership bill, announced last Friday, would give the government three days to convince a judge that a gun sale should be blocked. Ryan said Wednesday that he intended to bring it to the floor for a vote this week or next, but also noted changes were being sought by numerous lawmakers. “The last thing we’re going to do is rush something to the floor that we don’t have right,” Ryan said. Representative Matt Salmon of Arizona, a Freedom Caucus member, said he objected to Ryan pushing the bill without allowing it to be processed by relevant committees first. Salmon said that Ryan told House Republicans in a closed meeting that he was rushing the legislation to the House floor because “there are members that need to have this vote” for political reasons in swing districts that could go either Republican or Democratic in the Nov. 8 elections. Democrats, meanwhile, continued to pressure Ryan for votes on their more sweeping gun control measures. Representative John Larson of Connecticut, a ringleader of the Democrats’ sit-in, said his fellow Democrats plan to support Republican mental health legislation that could help avert some mass shootings. Larson added he hoped it would be seen as an olive branch to Republicans toward progress on gun control. Scores of gun control advocates demonstrated outside the House chamber in sweltering heat on Wednesday morning, as 91 people wearing orange t-shirts stood on the steps leading to the House demanding action. They represented the 91 people who, according to government statistics, die each day in the United States from gun violence. Many of them die as a result of suicide.

text: On Wednesday, the Czech government led by Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka announced its resignation, thereby allowing billionaire Andrej Babis, who emerged victorious in last month’s elections, to assume control before the upcoming EU summit in December. After a routine government meeting, Sobotka informed reporters that the resignation had been approved and would be submitted to the president later today. Sobotka’s coalition, which included the Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats, marked a significant achievement as it was the first in 15 years to successfully complete a full four-year term, overseeing a period of strong economic growth that resulted in the lowest unemployment rate in the EU and wage increases at the highest rate seen in a decade. However, disillusioned voters opted for candidates outside the traditional political framework, leading to a backlash against established parties during the elections. Babis’s party, ANO, capitalized on this trend by promising to combat political corruption and manage the government with a business-oriented approach, despite being part of Sobotka’s outgoing cabinet. Babis has not managed to persuade any of the other eight parties in parliament to join him in a coalition. Instead, he is looking to form a minority government, which President Milos Zeman is anticipated to appoint on December 13, allowing Babis to step into power immediately after. This timing is crucial as it would enable him to participate in the EU leaders' summit on December 14-15, where the focal point will be the ongoing discussions regarding Britain’s exit from the EU. Political parties have distanced themselves from Babis, a businessman valued at $4 billion and recognized by Forbes as the second wealthiest individual in the Czech Republic. This is largely due to police allegations that he improperly obtained a €2 million EU grant for a farm and convention center a decade ago by concealing ownership details. He refutes any claims of misconduct. As a member of parliament, he enjoys immunity from legal action, which the outgoing assembly voted to suspend; however, this immunity will be reinstated with the formation of the new parliament. Some lawmakers, who previously supported his prosecution, have indicated they may maintain his immunity, thereby postponing any legal proceedings for the current parliamentary term. Thus far, only the minor Communist party has expressed a willingness to potentially support Babis’s minority administration, but their 15 votes would not be sufficient to secure a majority in a confidence vote within the 200-seat Chamber of Deputies, where ANO holds 78 seats. Initial voting patterns in the new parliament have shown ANO aligning with the Communists and the far-right, anti-EU, and anti-NATO SPD party, although the latter has stated it will not offer support or tolerance to Babis in a confidence ballot. If appointed as prime minister, Babis would retain his position even if he were to lose a confidence vote while discussions on alternative arrangements take place.
source_text: Czech government resigns, making way for election winner Babis. PRAGUE (Reuters) - The Czech center-left government of Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka stepped down on Wednesday, making way for billionaire Andrej Babis, who won an election last month, to take power in time for an EU summit in December.  The government approved its resignation, the resignation will be delivered to the president today,  Sobotka told reporters after a regular government session.   Sobotka s coalition government was the first in 15 years to complete a full four-year term and presided over robust economic growth that helped cut unemployment to the lowest level in the EU and push up wages at the fastest pace in a decade. However, voters tired of politics as usual opted for anti-establishment candidates, punishing traditional parties at the polls. Babis s ANO party, with pledges to fight political corruption and run the state with a business touch, was the biggest benefactor of this shift despite being part of the outgoing cabinet with Sobotka s Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats. ANO has failed to convince any of the other eight parliamentary parties to join a coalition. Babis has instead sought a minority cabinet, expected to be appointed by President Milos Zeman on Dec. 13 and take power immediately. This would enable Babis to attend the summit of EU leaders on Dec. 14-15, where the main topic will be progress in negotiations with Britain over its departure from the EU. Parties have shunned Babis, a businessman worth $4 billion and ranked by Forbes as the second richest Czech, because of police charges he illegally received a 2 million euro EU subsidy a decade ago for a farm and convention center by hiding ownership. He denies any wrongdoing. As a lawmaker, he has immunity from prosecution, which the outgoing parliament voted to suspend but which comes into effect again with the new parliament. Some lawmakers who voted to allow him to face prosecution in the past have hinted they will uphold his immunity, suspending proceedings for this parliamentary term. Only the small Communist party has said so far that it could consider tolerating Babis s minority government, but its 15 votes are not enough to secure victory in a confidence vote in the 200-seat Chamber of Deputies, where ANO holds 78 seats. Initial votes in the new parliament have shown ANO voting along with the Communists as well as the far-right, anti-EU and anti-NATO SPD party, but the latter has so far said it would not give backing or tolerance to Babis in a confidence vote.     Once appointed prime minister, Babis would remain in the position even if he loses a confidence vote, pending talks on an alternative solution.

text: During an event at Harvard University on Friday, Neil Gorsuch, who was appointed to the U.S. Supreme Court by President Donald Trump, expressed that he does not resonate with the prevalent "cynicism about government and the rule of law". Gorsuch, the latest addition to the highest court in the United States, emphasized the importance of an independent judiciary in his remarks, which also included insights from fellow Justice Stephen Breyer. He noted that the government can face losses in its own legal system and accept those outcomes without military support. According to Gorsuch, 95 percent of cases in the U.S. are settled at the trial court level, suggesting that most litigants feel satisfied with the justice they receive, as only a small fraction advances to higher courts or the Supreme Court. "I know a lot of cynicism about government and the rule of law, but I don’t share it," he stated. Gorsuch’s confirmation to this lifetime position reinstated the conservative majority of the court following the passing of Justice Antonin Scalia in February 2016. He took his seat on the Supreme Court on April 10. Prior to his nomination by Trump in January, Gorsuch served on the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals based in Denver. The opportunity arose for Trump to appoint Gorsuch after Senate Republicans dismissed President Barack Obama’s nominee, Merrick Garland, the previous year. Breyer, appointed by President Bill Clinton in 1994 and part of the court’s liberal faction, highlighted the significance of global values during his speech, stating, "The values you are talking about are very widespread across the world," and mentioned democracy, human rights, and the rule of law.
source_text: U.S. top court's Gorsuch says does not share 'cynicism' about government. CAMBRIDGE, Mass. (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s U.S. Supreme Court appointee Neil Gorsuch said on Friday that he does not share what he acknowledged was currently “a lot of cynicism about government and the rule of law.” Gorsuch, the newest member to the nation’s top court, spoke about the value of an independent judiciary during an evening event at Harvard University that also featured fellow Justice Stephen Breyer. Gorsuch reflected on how the “government can lose in its own courts and accept the judgement of those courts without an army to back it up.” He said 95 percent of all U.S. cases are resolved at the trial court level, with few reaching the appellate level or Supreme Court, a fact that he said indicated that litigants were satisfied that justice had been done. “I know a lot of cynicism about government and the rule of law, but I don’t share it,” he said. Gorsuch, whose confirmation to the lifetime job restored the court’s conservative majority following Justice Antonin Scalia’s death in February 2016, formally joined the Supreme Court on April 10. Gorsuch served on the Denver-based 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals before Trump nominated him in January. Trump was able to fill the vacancy after Senate Republicans last year refused to consider President Barack Obama’s nominee Merrick Garland. Breyer, who was appointed by President Bill Clinton in 1994, and is a member of the liberal wing of the nine-member court, stressed during his comments the value of international values. “The values you are talking about are very widespread across the world,” he said. “Interest in democracy, human rights and so forth and rule of law.”

text: The former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, expressed his willingness to engage with the judicial authorities in Belgium. In an interview that was broadcast by Belgian state media RTBF on Friday, Puigdemont remarked that he believes the Spanish judicial system has become influenced by political motives. He stated, "I will not flee from justice. I will approach the judicial authorities, but those who are truly just." Furthermore, Puigdemont mentioned that he has instructed his attorney to inform Belgian judicial officials of his full readiness to assist, reinforcing his view that the Spanish judiciary has indeed become politicized.
source_text: Ousted Catalan president says stands ready to cooperate with Belgian authorities. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Ousted Catalan president Carles Puigdemont said he stood ready to cooperate with Belgian justice authorities, adding he believed Spanish authorities had become politicized.  I will not run from justice. I will go to the justice authorities, but the real justice authorities,  Puigdemont told Belgian state broadcaster RTBF in an interview aired on Friday.  I have told my lawyer to tell Belgian justice authorities that I am completely ready to cooperate,  he said. Puigdemont added that it was  very clear that the Spanish justice authorities had become politicized .

text: A gathering of black pastors in Chicago decided to boycott the annual Martin Luther King breakfast hosted by Mayor Rahm Emanuel on Friday, expressing dissatisfaction with his management of police-related fatalities. One pastor, however, did attend the breakfast and made his dissent known by chanting protest slogans before being removed by security. Several religious figures joined the demonstrators who obstructed one entrance to the Hyatt Hotel, where the breakfast took place, voicing their demands for Emanuel's resignation. Nonetheless, a significant number of Chicago's African-American leaders were present at the breakfast, which began in the 1980s under the city’s first black mayor, Harold Washington, and is aimed at commemorating the civil rights icon King. Bishop Edgar Mullins, who leads the Grace Family Worship Center and is among those who boycotted, stated, "This boycott is not in opposition to Harold Washington nor Martin Luther King Jr. This boycott stands for the very cause that they stood for, it was through protesting that achievement was made. To sit by and do nothing is to endorse what is going on." Local news outlets captured footage of Rev. Matthew Ross disrupting the breakfast with chants of "16 shots and a cover-up," referring to the 2014 police shooting of Laquan McDonald, before being escorted from the venue by security personnel. The issue of police killings, particularly of men of color, has sparked widespread protests across the United States in the past eighteen months. In Chicago, a surge of protests concerning police violence against primarily young black men has compelled Emanuel to dismiss his police chief and agree to a federal investigation of the police force. Additionally, the city has changed its earlier stance on withholding video evidence of police shootings. On Thursday, authorities released surveillance footage showing the police shooting of Cedric Chatman, a 17-year-old, in January 2013. Family attorneys assert that the video contradicts police assertions claiming that Chatman, who was suspected of carjacking, had pointed a dark object at them. Alderman Anthony Beale, representing the ninth ward, was one of the black leaders who participated in the breakfast on Friday. He remarked that he attended to pay tribute to King’s legacy, which facilitated the possibility of protests. "Either you’re part of the problem or part of the solution. I choose to be part of the solution ... Now is a golden opportunity for us to put real change in this city," he stated.
source_text: Chicago black pastors shun mayor's annual King breakfast. CHICAGO (Reuters) - A group of black pastors boycotted Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s annual Martin Luther King breakfast on Friday, over his handling of police killings, and one pastor attended the event but interrupted it with protest chants before being escorted out. To sit by and do nothing is to endorse what is going on,” said Bishop Edgar Mullins, pastor of Grace Family Worship Center church, one of the boycotters. Local media showed footage of Rev. Matthew Ross interrupting the breakfast and chanting “16 shots and a cover-up,” in reference to the 2014 fatal shooting of Laquan McDonald, before security guards escorted him from the conference room. Police killings, mostly of men of color, have led to protests around the United States in the past year and a half.  A wave of protests over police killings in Chicago, mostly of young black men, has forced Emanuel to fire his police chief and accept a federal probe of the police department. Alderman Anthony Beale of the city’s ninth ward was among black leaders who attended the breakfast on Friday. text: President-elect Donald Trump has made further changes to his transition team, dismissing a national security specialist and lobbyists from his close circle as he approaches the announcement of two loyal supporters from Wall Street for important economic roles. Trump, an outsider in the Republican Party who achieved a surprising electoral victory the previous week, has also resolved a documentation issue that had momentarily hindered his transition after appointing Vice President-elect Mike Pence to oversee the process. "A very organized process is unfolding as I make decisions regarding the Cabinet and various other roles," Trump shared on Twitter following a family dinner at 21 Club, a restaurant located in Manhattan, as his motorcade discreetly exited the scene where reporters were congregated outside his residence. "I am the sole person aware of who the finalists are!" he exclaimed. Leading his selection for major economic roles are campaign finance chair and Wall Street specialist Steve Mnuchin as treasury secretary, alongside longtime supporter and billionaire investor Wilbur Ross for commerce secretary, as noted by Trump ally and activist investor Carl Icahn. Nevertheless, a notable moderate within the Republican Party was removed from the transition planning. Mike Rogers, a former U.S. representative from Michigan who had been speculated as a potential candidate for CIA director, abruptly exited the transition team. Rogers had collaborated with New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, who was unexpectedly replaced by Pence on Friday as the head of the transition team. This reshuffle had stalled discussions about the transition with the White House. Pence was required to sign a memorandum of understanding, which the White House received on Tuesday evening. According to a spokeswoman from the White House, the Trump team is still obligated to submit additional documents before in-depth agency-by-agency briefings can commence. The team must also provide a code of conduct and confirm that members of the transition team have no conflicts of interest. Further modifications are anticipated. Pence and Rick Dearborn, the executive director of the transition team, are "eliminating any lobbyists," an aide from the transition disclosed. "This measure is to ensure that President-elect Trump’s pledge to prohibit lobbyist involvement remains intact at all levels of the transition," the aide remarked. Trump, who had criticized his opponents for their ties to industry interests throughout his campaign, faced backlash from his frequent opponent, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, regarding the inclusion of lobbyists on his transition team. "According to public reports, your transition team and your potential cabinet consist of over twenty Wall Street elites, industry insiders, and lobbyists making decisions that could have significant ramifications for their clients or employers," Warren articulated in a letter. With less than 70 days remaining until his inauguration on January 20, Trump must finalize his Cabinet members and other high-ranking appointments. Ultimately, he will need to fill approximately 4,000 vacant positions. Wall Street is attentively monitoring Trump’s choices for the treasury chief position, as Republicans control majorities in both houses of Congress, granting Trump a more straightforward path to tax and financial regulatory reforms. Although Mnuchin opted not to comment to journalists at Trump Tower regarding Cabinet selections, he did state that the team is "ensuring we enact the largest tax bill, the most significant tax changes since Reagan." A steady stream of advisors was observed entering and exiting Trump’s building on Tuesday, including U.S. Senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who is being considered for the roles of secretary of defense or attorney general. U.S. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, who competed against Trump for the Republican presidential nomination, also visited for discussions, informing reporters that he was "eager to work diligently to fulfill the promises we made" during the election. Bloomberg subsequently reported that Trump is contemplating nominating Cruz as attorney general. Rogers was removed from the team partly due to Trump’s advisors feeling he did not pursue Democratic preside.
source_text: Trump shuffles transition team, eyes loyalists for Cabinet.
