At the top of his list for senior economic positions are  campaign finance chair and Wall Street veteran Steve Mnuchin as treasury secretary, and long-time backer and billionaire investor Wilbur Ross for commerce secretary, according to Trump ally and activist investor Carl Icahn. However, a well-known Republican moderate was pushed out of transition planning. Mike Rogers, a former U.S. representative from Michigan who had been mentioned as a possible pick for CIA director, suddenly left the transition team. Rogers had worked with New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, who on Friday was abruptly replaced by Pence as head of the transition team. That overhaul had put the brakes on transition talks with the White House. Pence needed to sign a memorandum of understanding, which the White House received on Tuesday evening. The Trump team still needs to provide more paperwork before detailed agency-by-agency briefings can take place, a White House spokeswoman said. The team will need to provide a code of conduct and certify that its transition team members do not have conflicts of interest. Additional changes are likely. Pence and Rick Dearborn, the executive director of the transition team, are “removing any lobbyists,” a transition aide said.  “This is to ensure President-elect Trump’s commitment to ban lobbyist involvement is being upheld at all levels of the transition,” the aide said. Trump, who had pilloried opponents for being beholden to industry interests during his campaign, came under fire from his frequent sparring partner, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, for including lobbyists on his transition team. “Based on public reports, your transition team and your potential cabinet include over twenty Wall Street elites, industry insiders, and lobbyists making decisions that could have huge implications for their clients or employers,” Warren wrote in a letter. Trump has fewer than 70 days until his Jan. 20 inauguration  to settle on Cabinet members and other senior appointees. He will eventually need to fill roughly 4,000 open positions. Wall Street is closely watching who Trump picks for treasury chief because Republicans have majorities in both chambers of Congress, giving Trump a clearer shot at tax and financial regulatory reforms. Mnuchin declined to comment to reporters at Trump Tower about Cabinet picks, but said the team was “making sure we get the biggest tax bill passed, the biggest tax changes since Reagan.” A parade of advisers had been seen going in and out of Trump’s building on Tuesday, including U.S. Senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, touted as a possible secretary of defense or attorney general. U.S. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, who ran against Trump for the Republican presidential nomination, also dropped by for a meeting, telling reporters he was “looking forward to fighting hard to actually accomplish and deliver the promises we made” during the election. Bloomberg later reported that Trump was considering nominating Cruz as attorney general. Rogers was pushed off the team in part because Trump’s advisers believed he did not pursue Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton aggressively enough when he headed the House of Representatives Intelligence Committee, a source familiar with the decision said. Rogers led an investigation into the Sept. 11, 2012, attacks by militants on U.S. facilities in Benghazi, Libya. The probe dismissed many of the conspiracy theories that had been circulated by critics of Clinton, who was then secretary of state. Trump’s team viewed the investigation as a whitewash, according to one source familiar with the operation. Some current U.S. intelligence officials worried that Rogers’ departure would mean Trump was leaning toward more confrontational hardliners to lead his foreign policy team. Two national security officials said Trump’s operation had been slow to get up to speed and had not yet engaged deeply with security and intelligence agency personnel who were ready to start helping them. Loyalists such as former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and former U.N. Ambassador John Bolton were being considered for secretary of state, according to sources close to Trump. Giuliani, New York’s mayor at the time of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks by Islamist al Qaeda militants, is known as a hardliner on national security matters. Bolton is also a foreign policy hawk who said last year the United States should bomb Iran to halt its nuclear program. Retired Lieutenant General Mike Flynn, a leading candidate for Trump’s national security adviser, has called for the United States to pull back from protecting long-time allies such as South Korea and Japan. Trump has filled two positions so far. His choice of Republican Party insider Reince Priebus to be White House chief of staff was heralded by Republican leaders as an indication he wanted to work with Congress. Republicans maintained their majority in both the Senate and House in the election, but a number of Republicans in Congress opposed Trump’s candidacy. However, Trump’s appointment of Steve Bannon as chief strategist was criticized by Democrats, civil rights organizations and some Republicans. They denounced the former Breitbart News chief, whose website is a forum for the “alt-right,” a loose grouping of neo-Nazis, white supremacists and anti-Semites.  Neither Priebus nor Bannon need Senate confirmation for their posts, but Cabinet posts do, and some of Trump’s possible picks could face a difficult time winning approval.  Republican U.S. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky said on CNN he could not vote to confirm Bolton unless he repudiated his support for the Iraq war and bombing of Iran. Paul, who also ran for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, said he was concerned by Giuliani’s work on behalf of foreign governments. One loyalist who will not be playing a role in Trump’s Cabinet is retired neurosurgeon Ben Carson, who advised Trump after dropping his own presidential bid earlier this year. “His life has not prepared him to be a Cabinet secretary,” said Armstrong Williams, Carson’s business manager.

text: Amidst their arrival in Tel Aviv, U.S. President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania were greeted with words of encouragement from Sara Netanyahu, the spouse of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. On Monday, shortly after landing at Ben Gurion airport via Air Force One, the couple engaged in a brief conversation with Sara Netanyahu, who stood on the red carpet. She reassured them, stating, "Despite what the media portrays, most people in Israel admire us, and we express to them how wonderful you both are, and they feel the same way about you." Trump responded by saying, "We share a lot in common."  Throughout his presidency, Trump has faced extensive unfavorable press coverage both domestically and globally, especially concerning his dismissal of FBI director James Comey and the ongoing probe into his administration's connections with Russia. This visit to Israel marks the second part of his inaugural overseas journey since taking office, where he plans to engage in discussions with Netanyahu and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas during a brief stop that lasts less than 28 hours. Amidst the noise generated by the presidential aircraft, Sara Netanyahu remarked, "I speak everywhere about your greatness," receiving affirmation from her husband, who said, "I can vouch for that." The Netanyahu couple has had a contentious relationship with the Israeli press, which they have claimed is biased against them. In a statement made in January, Netanyahu characterized the media as "left-wing" and "Bolshevik," asserting that they aim to undermine him. During her testimony in a defamation case the Netanyahus brought against an Israeli reporter, Sara Netanyahu expressed in court: "Everything that is written about me is false, malicious lies that do not reflect my true self... The media exploits me as a means to attempt to oust the prime minister." Their exchange on the red carpet quickly gained traction on social media, alongside another somewhat uncomfortable moment from their arrival. As the couple walked hand in hand, a gesture they frequently display, Trump, who was beside them, attempted to grasp Melania Trump's hand, but footage shared on Twitter appeared to depict her momentarily brushing his hand away.
source_text: Trump, Netanyahu's wife lament negative media coverage. TEL AVIV (Reuters) - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s wife, Sara, offered sympathetic words to visiting U.S. President Donald Trump and his wife Melania on Monday, telling them that people still loved them despite negative media coverage. Standing on the red carpet and chatting minutes after Trump and the First Lady had arrived at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion airport in Air Force One, Sara Netanyahu was caught on camera exchanging a few private words with the visitors. “The majority of the people of Israel, unlike the media, they love us, so we tell them how you are great and they love you,” Sara said to Trump and his wife.  Trump then interjected: “We have something very much in common.” Trump’s presidency has received widespread negative coverage in the U.S. and international media, not least over his firing of FBI director James Comey and amid an investigation into ties between his administration and Russia. In Israel on the second leg of his first overseas trip since entering office, Trump is to hold talks separately with Netanyahu and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas in a stopover lasting barely 28 hours. Speaking over the noise of the president’s jet, Sara Netanyahu added: “I talk every place about how great you are,” she said, and Netanyahu backed her up saying: “I can testify to that.” Netanyahu and his wife have a tense relationship with the Israeli media, which they have both described as biased against them. In January, Netanyahu described the media as “left-wing” and “Bolshevik” and said they were out to bring him down.  Testifying in a libel suit the Netanyahus filed against an Israeli journalist, Sara Netanyahu told the court: “Everything that is published about me, it’s all lies, evil lies that bear no connection with who I really am ... The media uses me as a tool to try and topple the prime minister.” Sara’s red-carpet conversation soon began circulating on social media, along with another awkward arrival moment.  As the Netanyahus strode along holding hands, as they often do, Trump, walking alongside them, reached out to grasp the First Lady’s hand, but video circulated on Twitter appeared to show Melania Trump briefly flicking his hand away.

text: The results of the recent U.S. election, which saw Donald Trump emerge victorious, have sparked a significant surge in the coal industry and a downturn in renewable energy stocks. In the U.S., the expectation of a drastic pivot in environmental policy contributed to a rise in Caterpillar's stock by over 7 percent on Wednesday, driven by hopes that a Trump-led administration would bolster coal mining and infrastructure investment. The Obama administration enacted emissions regulations aimed at discouraging coal-fired energy production, whereas Trump has indicated intentions to rejuvenate the coal sector and reduce regulatory constraints. "There is abundant evidence that free trade, tax reform, infrastructure investment and smart regulation are critically important to manufacturers’ success," Caterpillar remarked in an official statement. However, challenges for coal extend beyond regulation and federal policies. text: On Wednesday, coalition aircraft led by Saudi Arabia targeted a military police facility in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which is under Houthi control, resulting in the deaths of at least 39 individuals and injuring an additional 90, some of whom were prisoners, according to an official and eyewitness accounts. This airstrike is a continuation of the coalition's offensive against the Iran-aligned Houthis, which has intensified following the Houthis' suppression of a recent uprising led by former Yemeni president Ali Abdullah Saleh, who was killed in the turmoil. An official present at the site reported that seven airstrikes were executed by the coalition on the facility located in eastern Sanaa, where approximately 180 detainees were being held. The official further indicated that rescue operations had retrieved 35 bodies from the debris, while the remaining casualties were unaccounted for. This incident marks yet another in a series of air assaults carried out by the coalition on Sanaa and various regions within the country, often resulting in significant civilian casualties. Attempts to reach a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition for comment on the incident were unsuccessful. The coalition maintains that it does not intentionally target civilians. Both the United States and Britain offer political support, as well as military supplies and logistical assistance, to the Saudi-led coalition, which has been engaged in conflict since 2015 to reinstate Yemen's internationally recognized president, Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi.
source_text: At least 39 Yemenis dead in Saudi-led raid on police camp in Sanaa: official. DUBAI (Reuters) - Saudi-led coalition aircraft struck a military police camp in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital Sanaa on Wednesday, killing at least 39 people and wounding 90 more, including some prisoners, an official and witnesses said. The strike is part of an air campaign by the Western-backed coalition on the Iran-allied Houthis that has escalated since the Houthis crushed an uprising last week led by former Yemeni president Ali Abdullah Saleh and killed him. One official in the camp said the coalition aircraft had launched seven raids on the camp, located in the eastern part of Sanaa, where some 180 prisoners were being held. The official said rescue teams had pulled out 35 bodies from the rubble, while the rest were not accounted for. It was the latest in a string of air raids the coalition has conducted on Sanaa and other parts of the country, sometimes causing multiple casualties among civilians. A spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition could not immediately be reached for comment on the report. The coalition denies that it targets civilians. The United States and Britain provide political backing as well as weapons and logistical support for the Saudi-led coalition, which has been fighting since 2015 to restore Yemen s internationally-recognised president, Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi, to power.

text: In light of a recent setback concerning U.S. healthcare legislation, the White House has cautioned disobedient conservative lawmakers that they risk being sidelined on future legislative matters, including tax reform, unless they support President Donald Trump’s initiatives. This warning from Reince Priebus, the chief of staff at the White House, indicated a potential strategy to forge a wide-ranging coalition for tax reform that could involve moderate Democrats. Meanwhile, the Republican chairman of the tax committee in the House of Representatives expressed his intention to advance a tax bill through his committee this spring. Kevin Brady, who heads the House Ways and Means Committee, stated that efforts on tax reform had been ongoing alongside the unsuccessful healthcare reform attempt. "We have never halted our efforts," Brady remarked during an interview on Fox News’ "Sunday Morning Futures with Maria Bartiromo." He added, "We will persist in making enhancements." Brady indicated that the committee is preparing to proceed with the bill in the spring, emphasizing his desire for the House’s outline to serve as the foundation for Trump’s tax reform strategy, rather than having competing proposals from the White House and Treasury. Investors on Wall Street are increasingly concerned that the failure of the healthcare bill could negatively impact tax reform. Following Trump’s election, equities had surged partly based on expectations of tax reductions. Without fiscal stimulus, economic growth is anticipated to be more subdued, leading to a decline of U.S. equity index futures to their lowest point in six weeks as of Sunday. Both Trump and Priebus have criticized hardline conservatives who opposed the legislation supported by the White House to replace the Affordable Care Act of 2010, commonly referred to as Obamacare. On "Fox News Sunday," Priebus indicated the possibility of collaborating with moderate Democrats in addition to Republicans to achieve other elements of Trump’s agenda, including the proposed budget, tax code reform, and renewed efforts at healthcare reform. "If we are able to create a bill that meets the president’s objectives solely with Republicans, we will accept it and proceed with it," Priebus stated. However, he cautioned, "This serves more as a warning that we are open to discussions with anyone. We have always been willing, and I believe that willingness is greater now than it has ever been." In a moment of embarrassment for Trump, who campaigned for the presidency touting his negotiation skills, the healthcare bill was withdrawn from consideration in the House of Representatives on Friday due to insufficient support from within his Republican Party. Resistance from members of both the conservative House Freedom Caucus and moderate Republicans left party leaders lacking the votes necessary for passage, with Democrats remaining united in their opposition. Despite extensive efforts to win over Freedom Caucus lawmakers, Trump was unable to secure their backing. Conservative organizations such as the Club for Growth and Heritage Action for America, which closely align with the Freedom Caucus, vocally opposed the Republican healthcare proposal and urged lawmakers to reject it. In a tweet on Sunday morning, Trump expressed his frustration towards both the Freedom Caucus and the conservative organizations, claiming their actions had resulted in "Democrats smiling in D.C." Priebus expressed disappointment, remarking that it was a "real shame" that conservative lawmakers chose not to support the healthcare initiative. "I think the president feels let down by those he believed were loyal to him who did not stand with him," he noted. With the healthcare bill’s failure, tax reform has risen to the forefront of Trump’s legislative priorities. Priebus affirmed that Trump continues to believe that the tax reform proposal should incorporate a border tax. Additionally, he noted that the initiative would likely feature a tax reduction for the middle class, which he suggested could help garner support from moderate Democrats. In a promising development for Trump as he prepares for tax reform, U.S. Representative Ted Poe, a Republican from Texas, announced his resignation from the Freedom Caucus, suggesting that not all members align with the group’s stance. "To fulfill the conservative agenda we have committed to delivering," Poe stated.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Fresh off a defeat on U.S. healthcare legislation, the White House warned rebellious conservative lawmakers that they should get behind President Donald Trump’s agenda or he may bypass them on future legislative fights, including tax reform. The threat by White House chief of staff Reince Priebus to build a broad coalition on tax reform that could include moderate Democrats came as the Republican head of the tax-writing committee in the House of Representatives said he hoped to move a tax bill through his panel this spring. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Kevin Brady said his committee had been working on tax reform in parallel with the failed healthcare reform push.  “We’ve never stopped working,” Brady told Fox News’ “Sunday Morning Futures with Maria Bartiromo.” “We will continue to make improvements.” Brady said the committee planned to move on the bill in the spring. He said he wanted the House blueprint to be the basis for Trump’s tax reform plan rather than have competing versions from Treasury and the White House. Investors on Wall Street worry the healthcare bill’s defeat bodes poorly for tax reform. Equities have rallied since Trump’s election partly on expectations of tax cuts. Economic growth would be more modest without fiscal stimulus and U.S. equity index futures fell to a six-week low on Sunday. Both Trump and Priebus have scolded hardline conservatives who rejected legislation backed by the White House to replace the 2010 Affordable Care Act, known as Obamacare. Speaking on “Fox News Sunday,” Priebus held out the possibility of working with moderate Democrats as well as Republicans to pass other aspects of Trump’s agenda, such as his proposed budget, the revamp of the tax code and a renewed effort at healthcare reform. “If we can come up with a bill that accomplishes the goals of the president with Republicans alone, we’ll take it and we’ll move forward with it,” Priebus said. But he added: “I think it’s more or less a warning shot that we’re willing to talk to anyone. We always have been and I think more so now than ever.” In an embarrassment for Trump, who had campaigned for the White House on what he said were his skills as a dealmaker, the healthcare bill was pulled from the floor of the House of Representatives on Friday because it failed to draw enough support from within Trump’s Republican Party. Objections from members of the conservative House Freedom Caucus and from moderate Republicans left leaders short of the votes needed for passage, with Democrats unified in opposition. Trump failed to win over the Freedom Caucus lawmakers despite courting them intensively. Outside conservative groups such as the Club for Growth and Heritage Action for America that are closely aligned with the Freedom Caucus had strongly opposed the Republican healthcare bill and urged lawmakers to reject it. In a tweet on Sunday morning, Trump lashed out at both the Freedom Caucus and the conservative groups, saying their actions had left “Democrats smiling in D.C.” Priebus said it was a “real shame” that conservative lawmakers decided not to get behind the healthcare bill. “And I think the president is disappointed in the number of people he thought were loyal to him that weren’t,” he said. MIDDLE-CLASS TAX CUT Trump has put tax reform at the top of his legislative agenda now that the healthcare bill has failed. Priebus said Trump was not backing off his view that the tax reform bill needed a border tax. He also said that the measure would include a middle-class tax cut that he said might help to attract votes from moderate Democrats.     In a sign that not everyone in the Freedom Caucus was in line with its approach and a positive signal for Trump as he looked ahead to tax reform, U.S. Representative Ted Poe, a Texas Republican, said he had resigned from the group. “In order to deliver on the conservative agenda we have promised the American people for eight years, we must come together to find solutions to move this country forward,” Poe said in a brief statement. “Saying no is easy, leading is hard.” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer criticized Trump over his handling of the healthcare bill and said Republicans would face roadblocks from conservatives on other issues. “They’re going to repeat the same mistake they made on Trumpcare with tax reform,” Schumer told ABC’s “This Week.” He urged Trump to go a different path: Reject the Freedom Caucus and work with Democrats.  “If he changes, he could have a different presidency,” Schumer said. “He’s going to have to tell them he can’t work with them and we’ll certainly look at his proposals. But it’s going to be guided on our values.” Republican Representative Mark Meadows, chairman of the Freedom Caucus, said on Sunday he was optimistic on tax reform and that his group could support a plan that is not revenue neutral.  “So, tax reform and lowering taxes, you know, will create and generate more income,” he said. “And so we’re looking at those, where the fine balance is. But does it have to be fully offset?  My personal response is ‘no.’” Another Freedom Caucus congressman, Jim Jordan, rejected fingerpointing over the collapse of the health bill. “Instead of doing the blame game, let’s get to work,” he said on “Fox News Sunday.”

text: COPENHAGEN (Reuters) - On Tuesday, Danish authorities stated that the headless female torso discovered along the seaside in Copenhagen might belong to a Swedish journalist who tragically perished following a submarine excursion with the Danish inventor of the vessel. Ongoing searches by divers in the vicinity are being conducted while they follow up on claims regarding additional body parts that may have been seen in the harbor of Copenhagen. Peter Madsen, the Danish creator of the submarine, faces charges for the murder of Kim Wall, the Swedish journalist. "We are dealing with a torso that has had its arms, legs, and head intentionally severed. The dimensions of the torso do not contradict the possibility of it being Kim Wall, but we still lack confirmation," remarked Jens Moller, a spokesperson for the Copenhagen police, during a video announcement. Madsen had previously informed a court that Kim Wall died accidentally aboard the submarine and that he disposed of her body at sea, contradicting his earlier claim that he had let her off alive in Copenhagen. DNA testing is being undertaken by authorities to ascertain the identity of the torso, which was discovered on Monday by a cyclist passing by, with results expected to be released on Wednesday morning, according to Moller. This unusual case has captivated media outlets in Denmark and Sweden, drawing attention globally. Madsen has been accused of Wall's manslaughter, who has not been seen since he took her out to sea in his 17-meter (56 feet) submarine on August 10. He refutes the allegation. He was rescued the following day after his UC3 Nautilus sank in the narrow waters between Denmark and Sweden, with no other individuals found in the wreckage. Madsen, who is an artist, entrepreneur, submarine designer, and aerospace engineer, attended a preliminary hearing before a judge on Saturday. Authorities indicated that the case remains closed to the public to safeguard ongoing inquiries.

text: On Tuesday, state officials reported that Anthem Inc, a major U.S. health insurance provider, is significantly reducing its offerings of Obamacare plans in California. The company will withdraw from 16 out of the 19 pricing regions where it had previously provided options for Obamacare this year, effective in 2018. Consequently, Anthem will only offer coverage in three pricing areas that encompass 28 counties across California. This adjustment represents just 41 percent of its current enrollment, which translates to approximately 108,000 consumers, leaving around 153,000 individuals without access to Anthem's Obamacare plans, according to state officials. Anthem cited uncertainty regarding the continuation of subsidies by the Trump administration as a contributing factor to this decision, which has created an “increasing overall lack of predictability.” Therefore, the insurer indicated that it is unable to present affordable options for all consumers in California. Brian Ternan, president of Anthem Blue Cross of California, expressed in a statement on the company’s website, “The market for these plans has become unstable. text: On Thursday, U.S. Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke initiated a campaign aimed at decreasing the nation's dependency on imported critical minerals essential for smartphones, military gear, and computers, which he indicated presents both economic and national security challenges. Following a directive issued by President Donald Trump, Zinke is set to collaborate with Defense Secretary Jim Mattis to compile a list within 60 days of non-fuel minerals that are susceptible to supply chain interruptions and are crucial for manufacturing. This initiative will focus on formulating a strategy to diminish U.S. reliance on foreign sources. The policy intends to discover new domestic sources of critical minerals, enhance local exploration, mining, and recycling efforts, provide miners and producers with improved access to mapping and geological information, and simplify the leasing and permitting processes for new mining operations. "The United States cannot continue to depend on foreign nations such as Russia and China for the essential minerals necessary to maintain our economic strength and ensure national safety," Trump remarked. This directive follows the release of a report earlier this week by the Interior Department and the U.S. Geological Survey, which outlined the nation's reliance on foreign competitors for certain minerals. The report identified 23 out of 88 minerals deemed crucial for U.S. national defense and economic stability due to their use in products ranging from military equipment to batteries. Included in the list are rare earth metals, lithium, graphite, and other vital minerals. Although the report did not provide policy suggestions, Zinke mentioned that he would utilize its conclusions to focus research on specific mineral deposit regions located on federal land and to establish policies that encourage mining activities. Of the 23 critical minerals that the United States depends on, 20 are sourced from China. A significant portion of the global lithium supply is produced in Australia and Chile, with the majority of the reserves located in vast salt flats within the lithium triangle encompassing Chile, Bolivia, and Argentina. For instance, lithium exports from Chile were nearly $600 million in 2016, accounting for approximately 40 percent of the global market by volume, as reported by the Chilean development agency Corfo. Prominent lithium producers in the region include SQM, Albemarle, and FMC Lithium.
source_text: U.S. launches effort to reduce reliance on imports or critical minerals. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke on Thursday launched an effort to reduce U.S. dependence on foreign supplies of critical minerals used in smartphones, computers and military equipment, which he said poses a national security and economic risk. Under a directive from President Donald Trump, Zinke will  work with Defense Secretary Jim Mattis to publish in 60 days a list of non-fuel minerals that are vulnerable to supply chain disruptions and necessary for manufacturing and will develop a strategy to lessen U.S. dependence on foreign suppliers. The policy would aim to identify new domestic sources of critical minerals; increase domestic exploration, mining and  recycling; giving miners and producers electronic access to better mapping and geological data; and streamlining leasing and permitting for new mines. “The United States must not remain reliant on foreign competitors like Russia and China for the critical minerals needed to keep our economy strong and our country safe,” Trump said. The order comes after the Interior Department and the U.S. Geological Survey published a report earlier this week that detailed U.S. dependence on foreign competitors for its supply of certain minerals. The report identified 23 out of 88 minerals that are priorities for U.S. national defense and the economy because they are components in products ranging from batteries to military equipment. The list included rare earths metals, lithium, graphite and other minerals.  That report did not offer policy recommendations, but Zinke said he would rely on the findings as he prioritizes research into certain mineral deposit areas on federal land and plans policies to promote mining. Twenty of the 23 critical minerals that the United States relies on are sourced from China. Much of the world’s lithium is produced in Australia and Chile, with the bulk of the world’s reserves straddling huge salt flats in the so-called lithium triangle of Chile, Bolivia and Argentina.  Lithium exports from Chile, for example, approached $600 million in 2016, or roughly 40 percent of the global market by volume, according to Chile development agency Corfo. Lithium producers SQM, Albemarle and FMC Lithium are among the region’s top producers.

text: In an effort to promote a peaceful holiday season, President Rodrigo Duterte of the Philippines has announced a unilateral ceasefire lasting 10 days with communist insurgents. This decision comes two weeks after the official termination of peace negotiations with the rebels. According to presidential spokesperson Harry Roque, Duterte has instructed the military and police forces to halt offensive actions from December 24 until January 2, aiming to alleviate the public's concerns during the Christmas festivities. Roque expressed hope that the Maoists and their political representatives would reciprocate with a similar goodwill gesture. As of now, there has been no response from the communist rebel faction, whose senior leaders and negotiators have been residing in exile in The Netherlands since the late 1980s. The peace process, which had previously stalled, was revived by Duterte when he took office last year, during which he released several communist figures as a sign of goodwill. However, he recently ceased negotiations due to a rise in rebel assaults. He has voiced his anger repeatedly regarding what he perceives as the duplicity of the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) along with its armed faction, the New People’s Army (NPA). Duterte has labeled them as a terrorist organization and has effectively terminated the decades-long peace dialogue. The rebel force, which is estimated to consist of around 3,000 members, has been engaged in a long-running guerrilla conflict for nearly five decades, resulting in over 40,000 fatalities and hindering economic development in resource-rich regions of the Philippines. These insurgents have targeted various industries such as mining, agriculture, construction, and telecommunications, demanding revolutionary taxation to fund their arms acquisitions and recruitment efforts. On Tuesday evening, Duterte stated that he wishes for Filipinos to enjoy a stress-free Christmas. "I do not want to add more strain to what people are now suffering," he remarked to the media.
source_text: Philippine leader declares unilateral ceasefire for Christmas. MANILA (Reuters) - Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has declared a 10-day unilateral ceasefire with communist rebels to allow Filipinos to celebrate a  stress-free  Christmas season, two weeks after peace talks with the insurgents were formally scrapped. Presidential spokesman Harry Roque said Duterte had ordered the army and police to suspend offensive operations from Dec. 24 to Jan. 2  to lessen the apprehension of the public this Christmas season . He said he expected the Maoists and their political leaders to  do a similar gesture of goodwill.  There was no immediate comment from the communist rebel movement, whose top leaders and negotiators have been living in exile in The Netherlands since the late 1980s. Duterte restarted a stalled peace process and freed several communist leaders as a gesture of good faith when he came to office last year but he recently abandoned talks due to escalating rebel attacks.  He has vented his fury on a near-daily basis at what he considers duplicity by the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) and its armed wing, the New People s Army (NPA). He has collectively declared them a  terrorist organization  and has ended the three-decades peace process. The rebel forces, estimated to number around 3,000, have been waging a protracted guerrilla warfare in the countryside for nearly 50 years in a conflict that has killed more than 40,000 people and stifled growth in resource-rich areas of the Philippines. The guerrillas have been targeting mines, plantations, construction and telecommunication companies, demanding  revolutionary taxation  to finance arms purchases and recruitment activities. Duterte on Tuesday night said he only wanted Filipinos to celebrate a  stress-free  Christmas.  I do not want to add more strain to what people are now suffering,  he told reporters.

text: Cyril Ramaphosa's recent election as the leader of the African National Congress (ANC) has not led to a complete takeover of the party from President Jacob Zuma. In Johannesburg, it was reported that while Ramaphosa emerged victorious, he has not managed to fully assert his dominance over South Africa's ruling party, which still holds significant influence from Zuma's faction in the newly formed National Executive Committee (NEC). This ongoing factional struggle was evident during discussions at the conference regarding contentious policies, including land expropriation and nationalization. Ramaphosa's partial triumph may hinder his ability to confront persistent corruption and to implement essential reforms aimed at revitalizing the economy, which were pivotal points in his campaign for the ANC presidency. Additionally, his limited control diminishes the likelihood of removing Zuma from the presidency before his second term concludes in 2019. Such a scenario could lead to disappointment among investors who have placed their hopes on Ramaphosa, a 65-year-old former trade unionist and wealthy entrepreneur, to rejuvenate the continent's most industrialized economy. Since his election, the rand has experienced fluctuations as investors evaluate the extent of his authority. Darias Jonker, the director for Africa at Eurasia Group, noted that Ramaphosa's lack of a robust majority within the NEC and the continued loyalty of Zuma's supporters will impede his ability to pursue his agenda. Zuma's tenure has severely damaged the ANC's reputation both domestically and internationally, coinciding with a slowdown in economic growth to nearly a standstill. He has endured multiple votes of no confidence, and analysts suggest he has solidified his grasp on the ANC through political patronage. The newly announced NEC, revealed in the early hours of Thursday, appears to be evenly divided between the factions supporting Ramaphosa and Zuma. The top six officials of the party, disclosed on Monday, also reflect a similar split. On Thursday, Zuma stated that the election of leaders at the ANC conference did not result in a clear winner or loser. Should Ramaphosa attempt to displace Zuma from his position, he would require the backing of the NEC, which includes his primary competitor in the ANC race, Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma, who is both Zuma's ex-wife and his favored successor. Other influential members of the NEC comprise staunch Zuma allies, such as Finance Minister Malusi Gigaba and Energy Minister David Mahlobo, who are expected to staunchly defend the 75-year-old leader. During the ANC conference on Wednesday, two particularly controversial policy resolutions were adopted, advocating for land expropriation without compensation and the nationalization of the central bank. These initiatives garnered significant support from Dlamini-Zuma. The land expropriation from white farmers in Zimbabwe had dire repercussions on agricultural production, and discussions of nationalization in South Africa tend to alarm investors, especially since left-leaning factions within the ANC have also called for state ownership of mines and banks. According to a senior ANC source who spoke to Reuters, the Ramaphosa faction intends to ensure that the push for complete state ownership of the Reserve Bank does not progress beyond what was resolved at the conference. The Reserve Bank has warned that altering its ownership structure could introduce more uncertainty into the economy and could incur significant costs. Although land expropriation without compensation is unlikely to become standard practice in the near future, the ANC's call for constitutional amendments to facilitate that process could undermine already fragile investor trust. Anne Fruhauf, an analyst at Teneo, remarked that such rhetoric will need to influence Ramaphosa's public addresses and may exacerbate fears regarding property rights at a time when the economy requires the opposite messages. In South Africa, land is a particularly sensitive subject, as the ANC faces pressure to address deep-rooted racial inequalities more than twenty years after the end of white minority rule. On Thursday, the opposition party Democratic Alliance condemned the ANC's proposal for land expropriation, arguing that it overlooks the broader issues concerning property rights for the impoverished population.
source_text: No clean sweep for South Africa's Ramaphosa in ANC race. JOHANNESBURG (Reuters) - Cyril Ramaphosa may have won the race to be leader of the African National Congress, but he failed to decisively wrest control of South Africa s ruling party from President Jacob Zuma. Zuma s faction retains influence in the ANC s incoming National Executive Committee (NEC) and was felt in conference debates on divisive policies such as land expropriation and nationalization. Ramaphosa s incomplete victory could stymie his chances of tackling entrenched corruption and implementing reforms to kickstart economic growth, tasks which he placed at the center of his campaign for the ANC s top job. It also lessens his chances of ousting Zuma from the state presidency before his second term ends in 2019. That could disappoint investors who have bet heavily that Ramaphosa, a 65-year-old former trade union leader and millionaire businessman, will be able to turn around Africa s most industrialized economy. The rand currency has been volatile since Ramaphosa s election, as investors continue to assess how much clout he wields.  Because Ramaphosa does not have a strong majority in the NEC and because of the lingering presence of Zuma loyalists, he will not be able to drive his own agenda,  said Darias Jonker, director for Africa at Eurasia Group. Zuma s decade in power has badly tarnished the ANC s image at home and abroad as growth slowed to a near-standstill. He has survived several votes of no confidence, and analysts say he has cemented his control over the ANC by using political patronage. The ANC s new NEC, announced in the early hours of Thursday, is split roughly 50-50 between the Ramaphosa and Zuma factions. The party s  top six  most powerful officials, announced on Monday, are also split down the middle. Zuma said on Thursday that  there was no winner or loser in the election of leaders  at the ANC conference. Were Ramaphosa to try to force Zuma from office, he would need to secure the support of the NEC, which includes his main rival in the ANC race, former cabinet minister Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma, Zuma s ex-wife and preferred successor. Others on the NEC include prominent Zuma lieutenants Finance Minister Malusi Gigaba and Energy Minister David Mahlobo, who would defend the 75-year-old leader to the bitter end. The two most controversial policy resolutions adopted at the ANC conference on Wednesday called for land expropriation without compensation and nationalization of the central bank. Both those policies were most vociferously backed by Dlamini-Zuma. The expropriation of land from white farmers in neighboring Zimbabwe had a devastating impact on food production and any mention of nationalization in South Africa is enough to spook investors, since left-wing elements of the ANC have also called for mines and banks to be state-owned. A senior ANC source told Reuters the Ramaphosa camp would try to ensure that the shift to full state ownership of the Reserve Bank would go no further than the resolution adopted at the conference.  The Reserve Bank said that changing its ownership structure could raise the level of uncertainty in the economy and would be costly. Land expropriation without compensation is also unlikely to become the norm soon, but the fact that the ANC called for the constitution to be amended as a step in that direction could dent already weak investor confidence.  This kind of rhetoric will now have to inform Ramaphosa s speeches and perpetuate concerns over property rights at a time when the economy needs exactly the opposite signals,  said Anne Fruhauf, an analyst at consultancy Teneo. Land is especially emotive in South Africa, where the ANC is under pressure to address gaping racial inequality more than two decades after the end of white minority rule. The opposition Democratic Alliance on Thursday criticized the ANC s call for land expropriation, saying it failed to address the broader issues of property rights for poor South Africans and government mismanagement of existing land programs. The debate over land was so heated among ANC members on Wednesday that a delegate said a fight broke out, and a party official said it nearly caused the conference to collapse. Jonker at Eurasia Group said ANC policies were always more populist and left-leaning than what was eventually implemented by government.

text: On Monday, the Kremlin announced that discussions were ongoing with the French authorities regarding a potential visit by President Emmanuel Macron to Russia in the upcoming year, although no arrangements have been finalized yet. During a conference call with journalists, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov addressed a story published by the Kommersant newspaper, which claimed that France was open to accepting an invitation for Macron to attend the St Petersburg International Economic Forum scheduled for May. Peskov stated, "The involvement of the French side in the forum aligns with Moscow's interests." He emphasized the significance of France as a key ally to the Russian Federation. Additionally, Peskov reflected on the positive nature of Putin's initial encounter with Macron, which took place at the Palace of Versailles in May of this year. "Given this, we would certainly welcome French companies at the St Petersburg forum... There are ongoing communications about high-level participation, but for the moment, I wouldn’t want to get ahead of myself."
source_text: Kremlin says in touch with France over possible Macron visit to Russia. MOSCOW (Reuters) - The Kremlin said on Monday that it was in touch with the French government over a possible visit to Russia next year by President Emmanuel Macron, but that nothing had yet been confirmed.  Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, on a conference call with reporters, was responding to a report in the Kommersant daily newspaper which said that Paris was ready to accept an invitation for Macron to visit the St Petersburg International Economic Forum in May.  The participation of the French side (in the forum) is in Moscow s interests,  said Peskov.  As you know, France is a very important partner of the Russian Federation.  Peskov said that Putin s first meeting with Macron, at the Palace of Versailles in May this year, had been characterized by  a very positive momentum.   Proceeding from this, we of course would be glad to see  French businesses at the St Petersburg forum ... And there are contacts regarding high-level participation, but I wouldn t run ahead of myself for now.

text: SEOUL (Reuters) - Following Pyongyang's sixth nuclear test the previous day, President Moon Jae-in of South Korea and Prime Minister Shinzo Abe of Japan reached an agreement on Monday to advocate for tougher sanctions from the United Nations against North Korea, as reported by South Korea's presidential spokesperson. The leaders emphasized the importance of close collaboration with one another and the United States, agreeing on the necessity of implementing the strongest possible sanctions and pressure on North Korea, Park Su-hyun, the spokesperson from the Blue House, stated during a press briefing. Additionally, they concurred on the need to aim for more stringent U.N. sanctions, Park mentioned after a 20-minute phone conversation between Moon and Abe. He indicated that the objective of these intensified sanctions was to encourage North Korea to engage in dialogue.
source_text: Moon, Abe agree to pursue strong U.N. sanctions against North Korea: Blue House. SEOUL (Reuters) - South Korea s President Moon Jae-in and Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe agreed on Monday to pursue stronger United Nations sanctions against North Korea after Pyongyang s sixth nuclear test a day earlier, South Korea s presidential spokesman said.  Both heads of state agreed to cooperate closely with each other and the United States and shared the understanding there must be the most powerful sanctions and pressure applied on North Korea,  presidential Blue House spokesman Park Su-hyun told a media briefing.  And as part of that they agreed to push for more powerful U.N. sanctions,  Park said after Moon and Abe spoke for about 20 minutes by phone. The aim of stronger sanctions was to draw North Korea into dialogue, he said.

text: The funeral of Jalal Talabani, the former president of Iraq, took place in his home region of Kurdistan on Friday. Talabani, who represented the revival of Iraq's long-suppressed Kurdish populace following the fall of Saddam Hussein, was honored by tens of thousands of mourners lining the streets as his coffin was transported. The Iraqi Airways flight that carried his remains from Germany, where he passed away on Tuesday at the age of 83, was shown on Iraqi and Kurdish television upon its arrival in Sulaimaniya, his birthplace in northern Iraq. A ceremonial 21-gun salute was rendered for the coffin, which was adorned with the red, white, and green Kurdish flag featuring a golden sun emblem. An Iraqi military band performed the national anthem, 'Mawtini' (my nation), along with Chopin's funeral march during the ceremony. The display of the Kurdish flag on the coffin incited a backlash from media outlets aligned with Shiite political factions supportive of the Iraqi government. Al-Etejah TV halted its transmission, expressing discontent that the coffin was not covered by the Iraqi flag. The aircraft that brought Talabani's body back to Iraq received a special exemption from a recent ban on international flights to the Kurdish area, which had been imposed by the Iraqi government in response to a Kurdish referendum on independence. Talabani, a prominent figure in the Kurdish campaign for self-governance, assumed the presidency of Iraq in 2005, marking the first time a Kurd held this position following the U.S.-led invasion that ousted Saddam Hussein. While the role of the president holds limited power, appointing a member of the Kurdish minority to the position was a significant gesture aimed at fostering unity in Iraq under a constitution designed to distribute power among various ethnic and religious communities. The executive powers are vested in a prime minister from the Shiite Arab majority. After suffering a stroke in 2012, Talabani resigned from the presidency in 2014. His successor, Fuad Musam, who is also a Kurd, oversaw the memorial service at the airport on Friday. Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi, who has called for the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) to annul the results of last week’s independence referendum, was absent from the funeral. Instead, Interior Minister Qasim al-Araji represented the central government. A spokesperson for the government stated that the delegation expressed strong dissatisfaction because the Iraqi flag was absent from Mam Jalal's coffin, despite the national anthem being played. Talabani is affectionately referred to as Mam, which means 'uncle' in Kurdish. Thousands gathered along the road leading to the airport and around the Sulaimaniya Grand Mosque, holding images of Talabani and waving green flags representing his Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) party. The procession, consisting of a dozen SUVs, faced challenges navigating through the dense crowd from the mosque to his burial site on a hill that overlooks Sulaimaniya, near his family residence. The Dabashan hill was packed with attendees as he was interred in the early evening. During the airport ceremony, Kurdish regional government leader Masoud Barzani, who had been Talabani's rival for many years in the quest for autonomy, sat between President Masum and Talabani's widow, Hero. Iranian Foreign Minister Javad Zarif, the highest-ranking foreign representative at the event, reiterated Iran's viewpoint that the independence vote was a 'strategic mistake,' according to Iranian media reports. Talabani had been too unwell to convey his opinions regarding the independence referendum, which his PUK party endorsed only half-heartedly. Unlike Barzani, Talabani maintained amicable relations with Iran and the Iranian-aligned Shiite groups that effectively govern in Baghdad. The Baghdad administration, along with Iran and Turkey, vocally opposed the referendum. Washington, a long-time ally of the Kurdish people, had also discouraged them from proceeding with the vote. There were numerous complaints on Kurdish media and social platforms regarding the flight ban implemented by Baghdad, which they claimed hindered broader international attendance at the funeral. Born in 1933 during a monarchy under British mandate, Talabani pursued legal studies at B.
source_text: Former Iraqi president Talabani buried in Kurdish home region. ERBIL, Iraq (Reuters) - Jalal Talabani, whose presidency of post-Saddam Iraq symbolized the resurgence of the country s long-oppressed Kurdish people, was brought home on Friday and borne to his burial through streets crowded with tens of thousands of mourners.  Iraqi and Kurdish TV showed the Iraqi Airways plane which carried Talabani s coffin from Germany, where he died on Tuesday at the age of 83, landing in Sulaimaniya, his home city in northern Iraq. Although the presidency has few real powers, the decision to give it to a member of the Kurdish minority symbolized unity for Iraq under a constitution intended to share power among ethnic and religious groups. Executive authority lies in the hands of a prime minister from the Shi ite Arab majority. Talabani stepped down as president in 2014 after a long period of treatment following a stroke in 2012. His successor, Fuad Musam, also a Kurd, presided over the ceremony at the airport on Friday. Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi, who is demanding that the autonomous Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) cancels the outcome of last week s independence vote, did not come to the funeral. Interior Minister Qasim al-Araji represented the central government.  The government delegation protested strongly because the Iraqi flag wasn t put on Mam Jalal s coffin, even though the national anthem was played,  said a government spokesman in a statement. Talabani is affectionately known as Mam, the Kurdish for  uncle . Holding pictures of Talabani and waving the green flags of his Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) party, tens of thousands gathered along the airport road and around Sulaimaniya Grand Mosque, where the prayer for the dead was held.  The funeral procession of a dozen SUVs struggled to make its way through the dense crowd from the mosque to his grave on a hill overlooking Sulaimaniya, near the Talabani family home. The Dabashan hill was covered with people as he was laid to rest in early evening.  At the airport ceremony, Kurdish regional government leader Masoud Barzani, Talabani s rival for decades in the movement for self-rule, sat between President Masum and Talabani s widow Hero. Iranian Foreign Minister Javad Zarif, the highest-ranking foreign official in attendance, repeated Tehran s assertion that the independence vote was a  strategic mistake , Iranian media said.  Talabani had been too ill to express his views about the independence referendum. His PUK party gave it only lukewarm support.  Unlike Barzani, Talabani had good ties with Iran and the Iranian-backed Shi ite groups that effectively rule in Baghdad. The Baghdad government, Iran and Turkey all strongly opposed the referendum. Washington, an ally of the Kurds for decades, had also urged them not to hold it. Kurdish media and social media were rife with complaints about the flight ban imposed by Baghdad, which, they said, had prevented larger international participation at the funeral. Born in 1933 in what was then a monarchy ruled under the British mandate, Talabani studied law at Baghdad University, joined the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) in 1946 and by his mid-twenties was a lieutenant to the independence movement s patriarch, Mullah Mustafa Barzani, Masoud Barzani s father. He split from the KDP and formed the PUK in 1974, drawing support from the urban elite and from the small Kurdish Shi ite community. He regarded himself as a modern, socialist, urban alternative to the tribal authority wielded by the elder Barzani. Talabani s harshest lesson came in 1988 when Iraq gassed Kurdish towns near the Iranian border during an Iranian-PUK offensive in the waning days of the Iran-Iraq war. In a brutal campaign, Iraqi forces killed tens of thousands of Kurdish civilians and uprooted many more from their homes. Talabani s PUK has remained the most powerful political force in his home city of Sulaimaniya, while Barzani s KDP dominates the regional capital Erbil. One of Talabani s sons, Qubad, is deputy prime minister of the Kurdish Regional Government.

text: On Wednesday, the French government urged the Spanish administration to handle the ongoing secession crisis in Catalonia according to the stipulations of the Spanish constitution. French government spokesperson Christophe Castaner informed the media, "We advocate for discussions within the framework of the Spanish constitution." He further stated that France should not interfere in Spain's domestic matters. Additionally, French President Emmanuel Macron remarked on the same day that the European Union ought not to step in during Spain's most severe political turmoil since the attempted coup in 1981.
source_text: France calls for Catalonia discussions within Spanish constitution. PARIS (Reuters) - France on Wednesday reiterated a call for the Spanish government to be left to resolve the secession crisis in the northern region of Catalonia within the framework of Spain s constitution.  We call for discussions within the framework of the Spanish constitution,  French government spokesman Christophe Castaner told reporters.  It is not France s place to take a stand on Spain s internal affairs,  he added. French President Emmanuel Macron said on Wednesday that the European Union should not mediate in Spain s worst political crisis since an attempted coup in 1981.

text: On Wednesday, resistance surfaced in Congress regarding President Barack Obama’s initiative aimed at relaxing certain stipulations of a visa regulation that was introduced following the tragic incidents in Paris. The new rule, which became effective in late January, mandates that individuals from 38 nations who were previously permitted to enter the United States for a duration of up to 90 days without a visa must now secure one if they have traveled to Iran, Iraq, Sudan, or Syria since March 1, 2011. Ed Royce, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, expressed a desire on Wednesday to include Libya in the list of nations subject to these restrictions. During a session of the House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee, lawmakers articulated significant apprehensions about exempting certain travelers visiting Iran from the visa limitations, including those engaged in business activities. "This authority is not referenced in the law. In fact, Congress explicitly turned down the waivers that the White House requested," stated Chairman Michael McCaul, a Republican. Fears regarding travelers from primarily European nations in the Visa Waiver Program easily entering the United States, even if they had previously visited regions such as Syria, Iran, or Iraq where militant groups operate, prompted lawmakers to enforce these visa limitations. The attacks on November 13 in Paris heightened these concerns. Several Islamic State attackers involved in the killings of 130 individuals that day held European passports, which would have facilitated their entry into the United States. Representative Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee, voiced similar worries about Obama’s proposal to permit visa exemptions for foreign business individuals traveling to Iran. "I have questions regarding how the Department of Homeland Security would assess the validity of these business-related purposes," he remarked. Conversely, administration representatives argued that they aimed to protect journalists, humanitarian aid workers, and personnel from various international organizations, as well as business professionals supporting economic recovery efforts specifically in Iran and Iraq, from the stricter requirements. To be accepted into the Visa Waiver Program, individuals must undergo background checks against U.S. counter-terrorism and law enforcement databases. Hillary Johnson, a counter-terrorism official from the State Department, informed the committee that regular assessments are conducted for those who gain approval. Gil Kerlikowski, the commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, reported to the committee that roughly 500,000 individuals entering the country under the waiver program have overstayed their visas. He noted uncertainty about how many of these individuals may have previously traveled to Iran, Iraq, Syria, or Sudan. Administration officials raised alarms that if the United States does not relax some of the newly instated restrictions, it could result in foreign governments reducing information sharing or imposing inconvenient new visa conditions on American travelers to their countries.
source_text: Obama plan to ease new U.S. visa limits faces skeptics in Congress. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Barack Obama’s plan to loosen some requirements of a visa law spurred by the deadly attacks in Paris met with open resistance from both Democrats and Republicans in the U.S. Congress on Wednesday. The measure, which went into effect in late January, requires that citizens of 38 countries who previously were able to travel to the United States for up to 90 days without a visa must now obtain one if they have visited Iran, Iraq, Sudan or Syria since March 1, 2011. Ed Royce, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, on Wednesday said he wanted to add Libya to the list of countries covered by the restrictions. At a hearing of the House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee, lawmakers voiced particular concern over exempting from the new visa clamp-down some travelers who visit Iran, including those conducting business.     “Nowhere does the law include this authority. In fact, Congress explicitly rejected the waivers requested by the White House,” Chairman Michael McCaul, a Republican, said. Lawmakers enacted the visa restrictions on fears that travelers from the mainly European countries in the Visa Waiver Program could easily travel to the United States even if they have, for example, visited countries like Syria, Iran or Iraq, where militants are active. The Nov. 13 attacks in Paris stirred fears about such travel. Some of the Islamic State attackers who killed 130 people that day held European passports that would have allowed them easy entry to the United States. Representative Bennie Thompson, the Homeland Security Committee’s top Democrat, echoed Republican concerns about Obama’s announced plan to allow visa waivers for foreign business people who travel to Iran. “I have some questions about how the (Department of Homeland Security) would go about determining the legitimacy of the business-related purposes,” he said. Administration officials countered that they wanted to shield journalists, humanitarian aid workers and employees of other international organizations, as well as business people helping economic reconstruction efforts in Iran and Iraq in particular, from the tougher requirements. Individuals must qualify for the Visa Waiver Program, with background checks against U.S. counter-terrorism and law enforcement databases. State Department counter-terrorism official Hillary Johnson told the committee there are regular reviews of those who are approved. Gil Kerlikowski, U.S. Customs and Border Protection commissioner, told the committee an estimated 500,000 people who come into the country under the waiver program have overstayed their visas. He said he did not know how many of them might have traveled to Iran, Iraq, Syria or Sudan. Administration officials expressed concern that if the United States fails to loosen some of the new restrictions, foreign governments might cut back on information sharing, or impose awkward new visa requirements on Americans who travel to their countries.

text: On Monday, Turkey called on the United States to reconsider its suspension of visa services following the detention of an employee from the U.S. consulate, which escalated tensions between the two NATO partners and negatively affected the value of Turkey's currency and stock market. Ongoing disagreements have characterized the relationship between Ankara and Washington, particularly concerning U.S. backing for Kurdish forces in Syria, Turkey's demands for the extradition of a cleric residing in the U.S., and the indictment of a former Turkish minister by a U.S. court. However, the recent detention of a Turkish worker at the U.S. consulate in Istanbul represents a new low in these relations. Turkey accused the employee of having connections to Fethullah Gulen, a U.S.-based cleric whom Ankara holds responsible for the attempted military coup in July 2016. Gulen has refuted any involvement with the coup. The U.S. embassy in Ankara denounced the allegations from Turkey as unfounded, and announced on Sunday evening that it would pause all non-immigrant visa services in Turkey while it evaluated the Turkish government's dedication to the safety of its missions and personnel. Shortly thereafter, the Turkish government declared that it would implement similar restrictions on U.S. citizens applying for visas to Turkey. The U.S. ambassador indicated that the length of the visa service suspension would rely on discussions between both governments regarding the rationale behind the detention of local personnel in Turkey. In a written communication on Monday, Ambassador John Bass stated that the duration of the suspension would also be contingent upon Turkey's commitment to safeguarding U.S. facilities and staff within the country. He emphasized that this action was not a total visa ban for Turkish citizens, as existing visas remained valid and visa applications could still be submitted from outside Turkey. Bass further noted that the embassy had been unable to ascertain the reasons behind the arrest of its Turkish worker last week or the evidence against that employee, expressing frustration over the lack of access to the employee's legal representative. Justice Minister Abdulhamit Gul remarked that if Washington harbored legitimate security concerns regarding its operations in Turkey, measures would be taken to address those issues. However, he also stated, "If it’s a matter concerning the detention of the consulate employee, then this is a judgment made by the Turkish judiciary. It is our right to try a Turkish national for an offense committed in Turkey." The Turkish foreign ministry summoned a U.S. diplomat to urge the United States to lift the suspension of visa services, arguing that it was creating unnecessary friction. President Tayyip Erdogan also criticized the decision made by the U.S. government. He stated during a press conference while visiting Ukraine, "It is disheartening for the (U.S.) embassy in Ankara to make and enforce such a decision." Additionally, the state-run Anadolu news agency reported that another employee of the U.S. consulate had been called to provide testimony regarding the suspected connections of his wife and daughter to Gulen, which surfaced during the interrogation of Metin Topuz, the individual detained the previous week. This diplomatic dispute unsettled investors, causing the lira to plummet by 3.4 percent to 3.7385 against the dollar after it had reached a level of 3.9223 overnight. The main stock index, BIST 100, experienced a decline of up to 4.7 percent, ultimately closing down 2.73 percent at 101,298 points. The airline industry felt significant impacts, with Turkish Airlines shares dropping by 9 percent. The central bank indicated that it was closely monitoring the situation. Timothy Ash, a strategist at Blue Bay Asset Management, remarked, "This appears to be a very serious situation," and suggested that the central bank would need to act swiftly to alleviate market anxieties, possibly even raising interest rates—an action that Erdogan has been reluctant to endorse. TUSIAD, Turkey's prominent business association, cautioned that the ongoing dispute could negatively affect economic, social, and cultural relations between the two nations, advocating for a calm resolution to the disagreements. The ongoing conflict with the United States also coincides with heightened tensions in Turkey's relations with Germany, another crucial ally, as well as ongoing military operations conducted by Turkey.

ANKARA (Reuters) - Turkey urged the United States on Monday to review its suspension of visa services after the arrest of a U.S. consulate employee sharply escalated tension between the two NATO allies and drove Turkey s currency and stocks lower. Relations between Ankara and Washington have been plagued by disputes over U.S. support for Kurdish fighters in Syria, Turkey s calls for the extradition of a U.S.-based cleric and the indictment of a Turkish former minister in a U.S. court. But last week s arrest of a Turkish employee of the U.S. consulate in Istanbul marked a fresh low. Turkey said the employee had links to U.S.-based Muslim cleric Fethullah Gulen, blamed by Ankara for a failed military coup in July 2016. Gulen denies any connection with the coup. The U.S. embassy in Ankara condemned Ankara s charges as baseless and announced on Sunday night it was halting all non-immigrant visa services in Turkey while it reassessed Turkey s commitment to the security of its missions and staff. Within hours, Ankara announced it was taking the same measures against U.S. citizens seeking visas for Turkey. The U.S. ambassador said the duration of the visa services  suspension would depend on talks between the two governments about the reasons for the detention of local staff in Turkey. In a written statement late on Monday, Ambassador John Bass said the length of the suspension would also depend on  the Turkish government s commitment to protecting our facilities and personnel here in Turkey . He noted that the move was not a visa ban on Turkish citizens, that valid visas could still be used and visa applications could be made outside of Turkey. The U.S. Embassy had been unable to learn the reasons for the arrest of its Turkish staff member last week or what evidence exists against the employee, Bass said, adding that he had not been allowed sufficient access to the employee s lawyer. Justice Minister Abdulhamit Gul said that if Washington had serious security concerns about its missions in Turkey, steps would be taken to address them.  But if it s an issue regarding the arrest of the consulate employee, then this is a decision the Turkish judiciary has made,  Gul told A Haber television.  Trying a Turkish citizen for a crime committed in Turkey is our right.  The Turkish foreign ministry summoned a U.S. diplomat to urge the United States to lift the visa services suspension, saying it was causing  unnecessary tensions , and President Tayyip Erdogan also criticized the U.S. move.  For the (U.S.) embassy in Ankara to take such a decision and implement it, it is upsetting,  Erdogan told a news conference during a visit to Ukraine. State-run Anadolu news agency said another U.S. consulate worker had been summoned to testify over his wife and daughter s suspected links to Gulen - which it said had emerged during the questioning of Metin Topuz, the employee arrested last week. The diplomatic spat spooked investors. The lira dropped 3.4 percent and stood at 3.7385 against the dollar after being quoted overnight as touching a level of 3.9223. The main BIST 100 stock index fell as much as 4.7 percent, closing the day down 2.73 percent at 101,298 points. Airline shares were particularly hard hit, with flag carrier Turkish Airlines falling 9 percent. The central bank said it was following developments closely.  This looks like a really serious situation,  said Blue Bay Asset Management strategist Timothy Ash. He added that the central bank would need to move quickly to calm market nerves and possibly hike interest rates - something Erdogan has resisted. Turkey s leading business association, TUSIAD, warned that the dispute would harm bilateral economic, social and cultural ties, and called for disagreements to be settled calmly. The row with the United States coincides with deep strains in Turkey s relations with Germany, another key ally, and with Turkish military activity at the Syrian and Iraqi borders, though their market impact has so far been limited. U.S.-Turkish tensions have risen in recent months over U.S. military support for Kurdish YPG fighters in Syria, considered by Ankara to be an extension of the banned PKK which has waged an insurgency for three decades in southeast Turkey. Turkey has also pressed, so far in vain, for the United States to extradite Gulen, viewed in Ankara as the mastermind behind the failed coup in which more than 240 people were killed.  Friction with the United States has also arisen from the indictment last month by a U.S. court of Turkey s former economy minister Zafer Caglayan on charges of conspiring to violate U.S. sanctions on Iran. Sinan Ulgen, an analyst and former Turkish diplomat, said those underlying disputes had created a crisis of confidence which made this latest fall-out particularly bitter.  This harshness is a result of a build-up,  he said.  We should not consider this as solely a reaction to the detentions of consulate employees .

text: On Friday, Republican President-elect Donald Trump revealed his choices for key security and legal positions in his administration, including the directors of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the national security adviser, and the attorney general. A member of Trump’s transition team informed Reuters that Trump had appointed retired General Michael Flynn as national security adviser, U.S. Senator Jeff Sessions as attorney general, and U.S. Representative Mike Pompeo to head the CIA. The official confirmed that all three had accepted their roles.  Here are specifics regarding his appointments: At 69 years old, Sessions was the first U.S. Senator to back Trump’s presidential campaign and has remained a staunch ally. Representing Alabama, he is in his fourth term and serves on the Senate Judiciary Committee, which oversees federal courts, immigration laws, crime, and terrorism. Coming from a family of country-store proprietors, he is a former captain in the Army Reserve and held the position of U.S. Attorney for Alabama’s Southern District during Ronald Reagan’s presidency, later becoming Alabama’s Attorney General. Although he received Senate confirmation for his U.S. Attorney role in 1981, he faced rejection for a federal judgeship in 1986 when a Senate committee did not advance his nomination due to allegations of racially charged comments, which he has denied. To take over the Justice Department as attorney general, Sessions needs to gain approval from the U.S. Senate, but only a simple majority is required, given that the chamber is under Republican control. Sessions has consistently advocated for stringent immigration policies and has opposed any pathway to citizenship for those undocumented. During George W. Bush’s presidency, he criticized a bipartisan initiative aimed at establishing a guest-worker program for undocumented immigrants endorsed by Bush. NATIONAL SECURITY ADVISER: RETIRED LIEUTENANT GENERAL MICHAEL FLYNN Flynn, aged 57, was an early advocate for Trump and currently holds the position of vice chairman on the transition team. Previously, he was the director of the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) and began his military career in the U.S. Army in 1981, with deployments in both Afghanistan and Iraq. He also served in the Office of the Director of Intelligence.  Once registered as a Democrat, Flynn became the head of the DIA in 2012 under President Barack Obama but retired earlier than anticipated, according to media sources, becoming a vocal critic of Obama’s foreign policy. Following his retirement, he founded a consulting company that has faced scrutiny for its connections to a Turkish businessman. He indicated to the Wall Street Journal on Thursday that he would dissolve his ties with the firm in order to serve Trump. Flynn has expressed that the U.S. should enhance collaboration with Russia on global security matters. In an interview with the Washington Post in August, he defended a compensated speech he delivered for Russian state-run television. Pompeo, 52, is a congressman from Kansas currently serving his third term, participating in the U.S. House Select Intelligence Committee, which oversees the CIA, National Security Agency (NSA), and cyber security initiatives. Pompeo was also part of the House Select Committee on Benghazi that investigated the 2012 assault on a U.S. compound in Libya. Originally from California, he graduated at the top of his class from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point and served as a platoon leader in the U.S. Army before transitioning to civilian life as a captain to pursue a law degree at Harvard. In 1996, he relocated to Kansas to establish an aircraft parts business. His decision to open a factory in Mexico was criticized when he later sought public office. Pompeo defended his actions, arguing that the company had generated jobs within the state. His association with Koch Industries, owned by billionaire conservative financiers Charles and David Koch, has also attracted attention. According to unofficial election results from Kansas, he secured re-election in the November 8 election with 61 percent of the vote.
