text: During the 2016 presidential election campaign, capturing the essence of the event often required photographers to divert their focus from the main speaker. According to Brian Snyder, a Reuters photographer with over two decades of experience, both the audience and the candidates hold equal significance. He remarked, "The voters need the candidates and the candidates need the voters. Any way you can show that visually is a good campaign picture as far as I’m concerned."  An instance of his work includes a shot featuring a group of youthful Bernie Sanders supporters at Bronx Community College in New York, energetically waving to the Vermont senator. Sanders garnered considerable enthusiasm from younger demographics during his challenging battle against the presumptive Democratic nominee, Hillary Clinton. Another noteworthy moment captured by Snyder was a tree adorned with umbrellas that were drying outside a rainy Sanders rally in Buffalo, New York, after the Secret Service had restricted supporters from bringing them inside. Snyder humorously noted, "I’m sure one person did it, and then the other person thought it was a good idea, and then the next thing you know, there are 30 umbrellas. It was just one of those funny things."  Veteran Reuters photographer Mike Segar characterized his experience covering the presidential campaign as "strangely fun." Over his 23-year career at Reuters, Segar has documented five presidential elections, though he indicated that this particular one stands out, especially with New York businessman Donald Trump emerging as the presumptive Republican nominee. Segar commented, "The tone of the Trump campaign makes everything different for everybody." He also mentioned that the increased security measures surrounding Trump influenced how photographers depict the campaign.  While at a Clinton rally, Segar snapped a photo of his meal: hamburger meat resting on a bed of undressed spinach in a tinfoil container. He shared with a chuckle, "I was trying to give viewers a little bit of a different taste of what we see on a day to day basis. Your photos don’t necessarily have to capture the most earth-shattering moments of the campaign, but they have to capture people’s interest." Lucas Jackson, another Reuters photographer, expressed his desire to find unique perspectives at rallies. One of his images portrays young reporters engrossed in their MacBook screens at a Sanders rally in Pennsylvania. Jackson observed, "Usually cameras are pointed at the candidate. I’m always looking to add context."

text: As the campaign for a national election intensifies in Italy, tensions within the right-wing coalition have become evident. On Thursday, Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right Northern League, announced that he would halt communications with his primary political partner, former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi. This decision stems from a disagreement regarding the level of severity with which the judicial system should treat murderers and rapists. The public dispute over judicial matters has provided a boost to opponents of the right-wing coalition just as the election race heats up, with voting anticipated to take place in early March. Luigi Di Maio, representing the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement and vying for the prime ministerial position, remarked, "I always said the (right) as a coalition didn’t exist. We are getting ever closer to government." Currently, the right bloc, which consists of Berlusconi’s Forza Italia! (Go Italy), leads in opinion polls, while the 5-Star Movement stands in second position. Analysts foresee that no single party will attain a decisive majority, which could lead to political turmoil in the euro zone’s third-largest economy. Salvini has often clashed with Berlusconi, but this week, his frustrations escalated following Forza Italia lawmakers’ rejection of proposals aimed at stopping courts from issuing sentence reductions for serious crimes like murder and rape. "We are receiving hundreds of calls and emails from men and women angry and disappointed by Forza Italia’s astonishing decision to protect rapists and murderers," Salvini stated, as reported by AGI news agency. He further declared, "As far as we are concerned, we are suspending all our contacts and discussions with Forza Italia and Berlusconi until there is an official clarification." Berlusconi assured that he would reach out to Salvini soon, expressing confusion over why his party members had opposed the proposed reforms. Support for the right bloc has been increasing steadily in recent months, particularly after Berlusconi’s return to active politics following years embroiled in scandals related to sex and finance. Nevertheless, he has struggled to mend the rifts between himself and Salvini, who has positioned the Northern League further to the right on the European political spectrum, aligning with Marine Le Pen’s National Front in France. While the right aims to present a united front during the upcoming election, the ruling centre-left Democratic Party (PD) has distanced itself from its traditional leftist allies, who have declined to create any electoral partnerships. Matteo Renzi, the leader of the PD, commented on Facebook, "(The right) will argue before, during and, above all, after the election, but on the day itself they will pretend to be united to scrape together a few more seats. This is pure hypocrisy because everyone knows the truth but pretends not to see."

text: In a rally held in Toledo, Ohio, U.S. Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump launched a critique against Democrat Hillary Clinton on her approach to trade, asserting that her management of trade agreements could be so detrimental that the nation should simply "cancel the election" and declare him the winner. Trump, addressing his supporters, pointed out that the North American Free Trade Agreement, which was enacted during the presidency of Clinton's husband, Bill Clinton, resulted in the loss of numerous jobs in Ohio to Mexico. He pledged to halt this trend if he were to be elected on November 8. "We should just cancel the election and just give it to Trump, right?" he remarked. "What are we even having it for? Her policies are so bad." Trump expressed his opinion that Clinton would advocate for the approval of the 12-nation Trans Pacific Partnership, a trade agreement championed by President Barack Obama, which she currently opposes. His statements were made as the New York businessman attempted to stabilize his fluctuating poll numbers amidst various controversies and self-created difficulties. Handling the aftermath of a 2005 "Access Hollywood" video that revealed the then-reality television star conversing on an open microphone about groping women and pursuing a married woman had proven challenging for him. This video was recorded just months after Trump wed his third spouse, Melania. Trump claimed on Thursday that it was "certainly illegal" for NBC to air the footage and hinted at the possibility of pursuing legal action against the network once the election concludes. Following the video's release, several women have accused Trump of groping them or kissing them without their consent, which he has labeled as "absolutely false." The most recent average from RealClearPolitics indicated that Clinton had a nearly 6-point lead nationally over Trump, bolstered by a drop in support from women for his campaign. Without substantiation, Trump has attributed his declining poll figures to a rigged electoral process, alleging that the media manipulated opinion polls to enhance Clinton's ratings. Research has consistently shown that voter fraud is exceedingly rare in U.S. elections, and numerous prominent Republicans have publicly criticized Trump's assertion that the electoral system is flawed. While campaigning in Ohio, a plane carrying his running mate, Indiana Governor Mike Pence, skidded off the runway upon landing at LaGuardia Airport in New York City on Thursday night; however, the Pence campaign confirmed that there were no injuries. Trump has called the allegations “absolutely false.” The latest RealClearPolitics poll average showed Clinton with a nearly 6-point national lead over Trump, fueled by declining support among women for his candidacy. There were no injuries, the Pence campaign said. Clinton on Thursday made her first joint campaign appearance with one of her most powerful supporters, first lady Michelle Obama, at a North Carolina rally to urge young people and women to vote. Clinton, a former first lady who lost the 2008 Democratic nomination to then-U.S. Senator Barack Obama before becoming his secretary of state, praised Michelle Obama for standing up for the rights of girls and women worldwide, drawing a sharp contrast with her Republican rival. “I wish I didn’t have to say this. ... But indeed, dignity and respect for women and girls is also on the ballot in this election,” Clinton told a crowd of about 11,000. “And I want to thank our first lady for her eloquent, powerful defense of that basic value.” Michelle Obama’s stinging denunciation of Trump after a leaked 2005 video showed him making lewd remarks and bragging about groping women was seen by many as one of the campaign’s most striking condemnations of the New York businessman. Without naming Trump, Obama took him to task again in North Carolina, asking the crowd which candidate they wanted to represent their daughters from the White House. “We want a president who takes this job seriously, and has the temperament and maturity to do it well. Someone who is steady. Someone who we can trust with the nuclear codes,” Obama said.  “I would not be here lying to you: I believe with all of my heart that Hillary Clinton will be that president,” she said. Although Michelle Obama was critical of Clinton during the hard-fought 2008 Democratic nominating race, any trace of bitterness appeared long behind them. The two women showed an easy rapport. They embraced and smiled. Obama called Clinton “my girl” and made a point of telling the crowd they were tight. “If people wonder: Yes, Hillary Clinton is my friend,” she said. Clinton promised to take good care of Obama’s White House vegetable garden if she won and wistfully praised the athletic first lady’s dancing skills. “One could only hope,” Clinton said. text: On Monday, an uproar in Uganda's parliament erupted over a proposed amendment to the constitution, which aims to permit President Yoweri Museveni to remain in power beyond the age of 75. KAMPALA (Reuters) - This legislative initiative led to chaotic scenes, resulting in the ejection of six members of parliament from the assembly. Museveni, aged 73, has been at the helm of the East African nation for over three decades. If the current age limit remains unchanged, the constitution would prevent him from running for presidency again in 2021. The legislative body commenced discussions regarding a bill introduced by one of Museveni's supporters, which seeks to eliminate the restriction on presidential candidates being older than 75 years. Opposition activists and human rights organizations contend that this change paves the way for Museveni to establish a lifelong presidency. The proposed bill has faced criticism from religious figures and even some members of Museveni’s National Resistance Movement (NRM) party, and it requires a two-thirds majority from all voting members of the house to be approved. However, the NRM is anticipated to secure sufficient votes to pass the measure. Demonstrations against the amendment have been met with force, including arrests, the use of teargas, and live ammunition, resulting in at least two fatalities in October. During the parliamentary debate on Monday, a significant presence of police and military forces was observed around the premises. Tensions escalated in the chamber, leading to jeers and heckling, which prompted the suspension of the six legislators for one session; they were ordered to leave for undermining the speaker's authority and disrupting decorum, as reported by parliament spokesman Chris Obore. The dismissed MPs had heckled speaker Rebecca Kadaga and disregarded her directives to take their seats, Obore stated. Following their removal, proceedings in the house were postponed for several hours before resuming in the afternoon to review a report from a parliamentary committee that had conducted public hearings on the proposed bill. The majority of committee members endorsed the recommendation to abolish the age limit and suggested extending the presidential term from five to seven years. Some legislators, however, disagreed and authored a dissenting report. "In our opinion, the proposal...merely aims to facilitate life presidency and undermine contemporary constitutional practices," stated MP Monicah Amoding, who presented the minority report. The debate was highly contentious, with legislators frequently attempting to drown each other out with shouts and interruptions. Opposition MPs, who were the majority in the discussion, attempted to delay the proceedings but were unsuccessful. The speaker later postponed the session to Tuesday, citing technical difficulties with the microphones in the chamber. In late September, physical altercations broke out in parliament over two consecutive days as MPs opposing the bill attempted to stall it, but they were ultimately outvoted. At least 25 members opposed to the constitutional amendment aimed at extending Museveni’s presidency were forcibly removed from the chamber on the speaker's orders due to their participation in the brawls. Initially, Museveni garnered significant international support for adopting market-driven economic policies and restoring political stability following years of chaos in the country. However, in recent times, he has faced increasing scrutiny over various human rights abuses, corruption issues, and reluctance to relinquish power. Advocates for democracy have expressed concern about the resurgence of a trend among regional leaders to amend laws, delay elections, or employ other methods to prolong their terms. In Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo, similar actions have led to instability.

But the NRM is expected to easily muster enough votes. Protests against the move have been put down with detentions, teargas and live bullets, leaving at least two dead in October. text: Following North Korea's sixth nuclear test in September, a tunnel at the nation’s test site reportedly collapsed, potentially resulting in the deaths of over 200 individuals, according to Japanese news outlet TV Asahi on Tuesday, which referenced anonymous sources knowledgeable about the incident. The report has yet to be confirmed by Reuters. Around 100 personnel at the Punggye-ri nuclear facility were impacted by the initial collapse, which allegedly occurred on or about September 10, the broadcaster indicated. A subsequent collapse during rescue efforts raised concerns that the casualty figure might surpass 200, it noted. Analysts have posited that a sequence of tremors and landslides in the vicinity of the nuclear test facility likely indicates that the country's largest explosion on September 3 has compromised the area's stability, suggesting that the Punggye-ri site may no longer be viable for conducting nuclear tests.
source_text: Tunnel collapse may have killed 200 after North Korea nuclear test: Japanese broadcaster. TOKYO (Reuters) - A tunnel at North Korea s nuclear test site collapsed after Pyongyang s sixth atomic test in September, possibly killing more than 200 people, Japanese broadcaster TV Asahi said on Tuesday, citing unnamed sources familiar with the situation. Reuters has not been able to verify the report. About 100 workers at the Punggye-ri nuclear site were affected by the initial collapse, which took place around Sept. 10, the broadcaster said. A second collapse during a rescue operation meant it was possible the death toll could have exceeded 200, it added. Experts have said a series of tremors and landslides near the nuclear test base probably mean the country s sixth and largest blast on Sept. 3 has destabilized the region, and the Punggye-ri nuclear site may not be used for much longer to test nuclear weapons.

text: Approval ratings for New Jersey Governor Chris Christie have decreased following his endorsement of Republican frontrunner Donald Trump, based on a statewide survey. Released on Wednesday, a poll from Fairleigh Dickinson University revealed that Christie’s approval rating has dropped from 33 percent to 27 percent since the endorsement. This decline is particularly pronounced among individuals without party affiliation, whose approval fell from 34 percent to 18 percent. Only 29 percent of respondents believe that New Jersey is moving in the right direction, while 59 percent disagree. According to Fairleigh Dickinson, this represents the lowest approval rating recorded during Christie’s time in office. Criticism has arisen regarding Christie’s frequent absences from the state while he campaigned for the Republican presidential nomination. Although he was anticipated to reengage with New Jersey politics after exiting the race, his endorsement of Trump has placed him back on the campaign trail. The latest survey conducted by Fairleigh Dickinson’s PublicMind took place from February 24 to February 28, utilizing telephone interviews with a randomly chosen sample of 694 registered voters in New Jersey. (Reporting by Edward Krudy; Editing by Lisa Von Ahn) This piece was partially funded by SAP, but was independently produced by Reuters' editorial team, with no input from SAP in its creation.
source_text: New Jersey Governor Chris Christie's ratings slide in state poll. NEW YORK (Reuters) - New Jersey Governor Chris Christie’s approval ratings have fallen after the one-time presidential hopeful endorsed Republican front-runner Donald Trump, according to a statewide opinion poll. The poll by Fairleigh Dickinson University, released on Wednesday, showed that Christie’s approval rating fell to 27 percent from 33 percent before the endorsement.  The drop was greater among those without party affiliation, with approval falling to 18 percent from 34 percent among that group. Only 29 percent said New Jersey was headed in the right direction, with 59 percent saying it was not. Fairleigh Dickinson said the rating was the lowest it had recorded during Christie’s tenure. Christie has drawn fire for spending much of his time out of the state while campaigning for the Republican presidential nomination. He was expected to return to New Jersey politics after he dropped out of the running, but endorsing Trump has put him back on the campaign trail. The most recent survey by Fairleigh Dickinson’s PublicMind was conducted Feb. 24-28 by telephone. It had a randomly selected sample of 694 self-identified registered voters in New Jersey. text: The Congressional Budget Office has indicated that by 2047, the public debt of the United States is projected to surge to 150 percent of the nation's economic output unless there are changes in tax and spending regulations. This estimate, reported on Thursday, significantly surpasses the historical peak observed shortly after World War II. The updated forecasts illustrate a more pronounced escalation in debt over the next three decades compared to the previous year's long-term outlook from the non-partisan budget analysis organization. This situation could complicate the ability of certain congressional members to endorse a tax reform initiative that relies partially on increased deficits for funding. According to last year’s assessment, the CBO had predicted that public debt would rise to 141 percent of gross domestic product by 2046, while the highest recorded figure was 106 percent of GDP in 1946, which is projected to be reached by 2035. In the current projections, the CBO anticipates that in 2017, public debt will constitute around 77 percent of GDP, with forecasts suggesting growth to 89 percent by 2027 and 113 percent by 2037. These new estimates are based on the assumption that the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare, will remain intact for the foreseeable future, following the unsuccessful effort by House Republicans to repeal it last week. The anticipated increase in debt is attributed to various factors, including the rising costs associated with an aging population, interest expenses, and expectations of slower economic growth due to revised predictions regarding productivity improvements. For the period from 2038 to 2047, average annual deficits are projected to be 8.6 percent of GDP, in contrast to the 2.9 percent anticipated for 2017 and 4.0 percent expected during the 2018 to 2027 timeframe. CBO's long-term projections build on assumptions established in its January 10-year budget forecast, which indicated declining deficits for the initial two years, followed by an upward trend. By 2047, net interest expenses are predicted to account for 6.2 percent of GDP, compared to 1.4 percent in 2017 and approximately 1.2 percent in 1967, according to the CBO. A significant uncertainty in the CBO's 30-year outlook is the behavior of real interest rates. It is assumed that real yields on 10-year Treasury bonds will average 1.5 percent across the 30 years, increasing to 2.3 percent by 2047. The CBO noted that considerably higher interest rates, in conjunction with altered assumptions about productivity and healthcare expenditure growth, could lead to vastly different financial scenarios.
source_text: U.S. debt to reach 150 percent of GDP in 30 years: CBO. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. debt held by the public will balloon to 150 percent of economic output by 2047 unless tax and spending laws are changed, the Congressional Budget Office said on Thursday, far exceeding the record level just after World War II. The new projections show steeper 30-year debt growth than last year’s long-term forecast by the non-partisan budget analysis agency, and could make it harder for some members of Congress to support a tax reform plan that is partly financed with higher deficits. Last year, the CBO estimated U.S. public debt would grow to 141 percent of gross domestic product by 2046, while the record was 106 percent of GDP in 1946. That level would be reached in 2035, the CBO said. Under this year’s projection, CBO predicts public debt for 2017 to be about 77 percent of GDP, growing to 89 percent in 2027, and 113 percent in 2037. The new forecasts assume that the Affordable Care Act, the healthcare law known as Obamacare that House Republicans failed to replace last week, stays in place for the long term. The projected debt growth reflects CBO’s estimates of the rising costs of caring for a growing population of people over 65, growth in interest costs, and assumptions of slower economic growth due to reduced assumptions about productivity gains. Annual deficits are expected to average 8.6 percent of GDP in the 2038-2047 period versus 2.9 percent expected for 2017 and 4.0 percent for the 2018-2027 period. The long-term projections extend CBO’s assumptions made in its 10-year budget outlook in January, which showed falling deficits for the next two years, but growth thereafter. Net interest costs in 2047 are expected to be 6.2 percent of GDP, compared with 1.4 percent in 2017 and about 1.2 percent in 1967, the CBO said.   But the wild card in the CBO 30-year projections are real interest rates. Real interest yields on 10-year Treasury notes are assumed to average 1.5 percent over 30 years, rising to 2.3 percent in 2047. Much higher interest rates, coupled with different assumptions in productivity and healthcare cost growth, could  produce significantly different outcomes, CBO said.  The CBO said that its debt-to-GDP ratio could range from 85 percent with low rates and strong growth, to 244 percent with weaker growth and higher rates.

text: An investigation has been initiated into allegations of sexual harassment against a British minister. LONDON (Reuters) - Following a report, British Prime Minister Theresa May has mandated an inquiry regarding a junior minister who reportedly requested a female secretary to purchase sex toys for him, as part of her efforts to combat sexual harassment within the political sphere. The Mail on Sunday stated that Mark Garnier, who serves as a junior international trade minister, had asked secretary Caroline Edmondson to acquire two sex toys and referred to her as "sugar tits." In comments to the newspaper, Garnier claimed that the remark was made during a light-hearted conversation about a TV show, asserting that his request for the toys was merely "good humored high jinks." However, Edmondson challenged Garnier's version of events, including his claim that the interactions were just "high jinks." This report follows a separate analysis published on Friday by another British newspaper, the Sun, which highlighted a pervasive culture of sexual harassment among parliamentarians and their aides. Garnier was not reachable for immediate comments through his constituency or parliamentary offices, as reported by Reuters. Following the Sun's publication, May's spokesperson stated on Friday that any form of unwanted sexual behavior was "completely unacceptable" and that any minister found to have acted inappropriately would face significant consequences. Health Minister Jeremy Hunt indicated on Sunday that May had instructed officials to examine whether Garnier, who operates outside the immediate cabinet surrounding May, had breached the government ministers' code of conduct. "If these accounts are accurate, they are undoubtedly completely unacceptable," Hunt remarked during an appearance on BBC television. "The Cabinet Office will be investigating whether there has been a violation of the ministerial code in this specific instance, but as you are aware, the facts are contested." In a letter made public to the media, May also reached out to John Bercow, the Speaker of the House of Commons, on Sunday, seeking his guidance on how to address the prevailing culture within the institution. "I believe it is crucial that individuals working in the House of Commons are treated appropriately and fairly, as one would expect in any contemporary workplace," May expressed in her correspondence. She argued that existing measures, including a disciplinary process proposed by the Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority and a voluntary code of conduct extended by the Conservative Party to its members, were insufficient. "It is essential that we establish a House-wide mediation service, supplemented by a binding grievance procedure that is accessible to all MPs, regardless of their party affiliation," she added in the letter. "It is imperative that both staff and the public maintain trust in parliament, and addressing this employment irregularity across party lines can significantly contribute to that goal." Reports of inappropriate conduct in British politics, as well as in various other sectors, have surged in light of numerous allegations made against Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein. Weinstein has denied engaging in any non-consensual sexual acts. Meanwhile, Michael Gove, the environment minister in the UK, issued an apology on Saturday after he compared being interviewed by a BBC radio host to entering Weinstein's bedroom. This analogy drew widespread criticism, prompting Gove, a cabinet member, to apologize for what he characterized as a "clumsy attempt at humor." The Sun newspaper reported on Friday that women in Westminster politics had formed a WhatsApp group to share their experiences of harassment and to alert others about potential offenders. "The Prime Minister was unequivocal in our response to the reports regarding Harvey Weinstein in recent weeks, stating that any unwanted sexual behavior is entirely unacceptable, and this standard applies to all facets of life, including politics," May's spokesperson stated on Friday.

text: On Friday, during a speech to a business gathering in Washington, Britain's Brexit minister expressed optimism regarding ongoing negotiations to exit the European Union. David Davis acknowledged that talks had become somewhat tense but maintained his belief that a favorable agreement could be achieved for both parties involved. Having just returned from Brussels the previous day, he noted that EU officials had indicated that the current level of progress in discussions had not met expectations necessary to advance to talks about their future relationship. "I am a determined optimist," Davis stated while addressing the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. He emphasized his conviction that an advantageous deal serves the interests of the UK, the EU, and indeed the entire developed world. The head of international affairs at the U.S. Chamber, Myron Brilliant, pressed Davis for a definitive outline regarding Brexit, particularly for the 7,500 American firms operating in Britain. He urged the need for a framework that includes predictable transition periods to reduce disruptions for businesses. Discussions thus far have revolved around Britain's financial commitments to the EU, with the bloc insisting that any financial settlement must be resolved before moving forward to negotiations on other areas, such as international trade. When asked about the possibility of the UK paying for access to the single market during any transitional phase post-Brexit, Davis refrained from providing a clear answer and mentioned that London was meticulously reviewing the bill related to its EU exit. "It is getting a bit tense. I rule nothing in, nothing out," he remarked. Davis also indicated that once the transition period with the EU concludes, the UK anticipates concluding a free-trade agreement with the United States. He, however, cautioned that negotiating a deal between two significant economies like the UK and the U.S. would likely be "quite complex." He seemed to distinguish British aspirations for global free-trade agreements from the protectionist approach adopted by U.S. President Donald Trump, who has advocated for trade tariffs and has even suggested withdrawing from the North American Free Trade Area to bolster domestic industry. Davis stated that Britain would advocate for enhanced liberalization of services and would engage with international organizations such as the World Trade Organization. In response to Trump's assertion that the United States might disregard WTO decisions, Davis maintained that Britain is keen on establishing strong trade relations. As the UK prepares to exit the EU, it has been actively seeking to strengthen ties with the United States. Prime Minister Theresa May made history as the first foreign leader to meet with Trump following his inauguration in January. During that meeting, she urged Trump to revive the long-standing "special relationship" between the two nations, expressing optimism that a trade agreement could be reached shortly after Brexit, demonstrating that Britain could thrive independently of the EU. However, she has faced criticism from opposition figures for her attempts to align closely with Trump, whose erratic stances on trade and international commitments have raised concerns regarding America's reliability in upholding global agreements.

I am a determined optimist,  Davis told the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Davis came under pressure from the U.S. Chamber s head of international affairs, Myron Brilliant, to lay out a clear path for Brexit for the 7,500 U.S. companies with operations in Britain - one that had  predictable transition periods  that minimized business disruption. text: BEIJING (Reuters) - A warning has been issued by China's propaganda chief on Friday regarding the allure of values presented by Western nations. He expressed concerns that these countries are attempting to impose their cultural and political ideologies on others, enticing them to forsake their own traditions. Since taking office five years ago, Chinese President Xi Jinping has directed a comprehensive crackdown on civil society, tightening the reins on media, society, and the internet. Xi has committed to advancing what the ruling Communist Party defines as core socialist values, emphasizing patriotism, traditional Chinese culture, rule of law, harmony, and prosperity, among other principles. Huang Kunming, who was appointed to his position following last month's pivotal party congress—during which Xi further solidified his authority—asserted in the official People’s Daily that there is a growing surge and clash of values globally. He noted that certain Western nations leverage their technological superiority and established dominance in discourse to promote what they term 'universal values.' Although Huang did not specify which countries he referred to, he indicated that these nations are attempting to entice individuals to glorify the West while also encouraging compliance, thereby undermining or even relinquishing their ties to their own spiritual heritage. Huang emphasized that China's unique cultural traditions, distinct historical trajectory, and specific national circumstances necessitate the safeguarding of its values grounded in its culture. He asserted that only by championing core socialist values can the Chinese populace maintain its stature among the global community. China has consistently criticized those perceived to be imposing Western ideals, such as competitive multi-party democracy and the principle of separation of powers, insisting that the Communist Party will not tolerate any challenge to its authority. Prior to the party congress, the state-run news agency Xinhua condemned Western democracy as divisive and confrontational. The constitution of China enshrines the party's enduring leadership role in governance, although it permits the existence of various political parties under what is termed a multi-party cooperation system. Nevertheless, all such parties are subordinate to the Communist Party. Activists advocating for pluralism frequently face imprisonment, and dissent regarding China's authoritarian regime is routinely suppressed.
source_text: China minister warns against seduction of values by Western nations. PARIS (Reuters) - France will provide 15 million euros ($17.65 million) in aid for areas liberated by the U.S.-led coalition from Islamic State in Syria, its foreign minister said on Friday.  I have decided to allocate additional funds of 15 million euros up to the end of the year for food, de-mining, displaced people, water and health,  Jean-Yves Le Drian said in a statement, without saying who would manage the funds. text: On Monday, President Donald Trump expressed his belief that Cuba is behind a number of incidents that the U.S. claims have harmed at least 22 diplomats over several months while in Cuba, leading to a reduction of American personnel in the country. During an unscheduled press conference in the White House Rose Garden, Trump stated, "I do believe Cuba is responsible. I do believe that. And it’s a very unusual attack, as you know. But I do believe Cuba is responsible." While the United States has yet to officially determine that Cuba executed the attacks, which included strange high-pitched noises, it has indicated that Havana bears the duty of ensuring the safety of U.S. diplomatic staff and has fallen short in this responsibility. The unexplained incidents have impacted at least 22 diplomatic personnel, resulting in symptoms such as hearing loss, dizziness, fatigue, and cognitive problems. Additionally, some private American travelers have also reported being affected.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Monday that he believes Havana is responsible for a series of incidents that Washington thinks hurt at least 22 U.S. diplomats over a period of months in Cuba, prompting Washington to scale back its presence there. “I do believe Cuba is responsible,” Trump told reporters at an impromptu news conference in the White House Rose Garden. “I do believe that. And it’s a very unusual attack, as you know. But I do believe Cuba is responsible.” The United States has not formally concluded Cuba carried out the attacks, some of which involved high-pitched sounds, but it has said Havana is responsible for ensuring the safety and security of U.S. diplomatic personnel and failed to do so. At least 22 diplomatic personnel were affected by the unexplained incidents, which have caused hearing loss, dizziness, fatigue and cognitive issues. Some private U.S. travelers also have been affected.

text: The repercussions of the Harvey Weinstein scandal reached Austria on Saturday, as a prominent political figure announced his decision to resign from parliament following a sexual assault allegation. Peter Pilz, a 63-year-old veteran lawmaker known for his leftist views, has been a significant presence in Austrian politics for several decades. He gained recognition for opposing arms agreements with nations accused of human rights violations and spearheading investigations into corruption, including one this year related to the procurement of fighter jets in Austria. Recently, he made headlines by leaving the Greens to establish his own political party, Pilz List, which not only surpassed the Greens in the parliamentary elections held last month but also successfully crossed the 4 percent threshold required to enter parliament, a mark the Greens narrowly missed. According to a report from the weekly publication Falter, Pilz allegedly groped a female staff member from the center-right European People’s Party during a conference in the Alps four years prior. The article included her account of the incident, where she described Pilz as being "relatively drunk" at that time. Pilz, known for his outspoken nature and a penchant for performing rock songs like "Wild Thing" at political gatherings, claimed he could not recall the events in question. "Not remembering is no excuse," Pilz stated during a press conference, noting that he had been assured by Falter's editor in chief that the article was thoroughly investigated. He expressed that he takes these allegations very seriously, saying, "Because of these accusations, which I take extremely seriously, even though I do not remember, I will not take up my mandate in the coming parliament. I will not be at the swearing-in ceremony on Thursday." Following the Weinstein scandal and the subsequent resignations related to inappropriate conduct, including that of British Defence Minister Michael Fallon earlier this week, Austrian media outlets began questioning whether there may be previously unreported instances of sexual harassment involving influential individuals in Austria. The U.S. film producer Weinstein has faced accusations from numerous women, alleging sexual harassment or assault dating back to the 1980s, with three women claiming they were raped. Weinstein has denied any non-consensual sexual encounters. Pilz mentioned his intention to uncover all the facts regarding the allegations against him. However, he also refuted separate claims made by a former colleague, who accused him of sexual harassment on multiple occasions. This particular allegation was first reported by Austrian media on Friday. Pilz indicated that he would continue to support his party's efforts in parliament "from the outside," although he did not explicitly confirm that he was resigning as party leader. A spokesperson for Pilz was not immediately reachable for comments.
source_text: Austrian party leader quits parliament over accusation of sexual assault. text: DUBLIN (Reuters) - Gerry Adams, who became synonymous with the Irish Republican Army during its violent campaigns and later transitioned into a peacemaker and respected political figure, has played a pivotal role in Northern Ireland's 50-year journey towards relative stability from sectarian strife. On Saturday, Adams revealed his decision to resign as leader of the Sinn Fein party, which advocates for Irish nationalism, while his aspiration for a united Ireland remains unfulfilled. However, the party he departs from stands as the leading Irish nationalist entity in the British-controlled region and holds significant potential to influence governance across the border in the Irish Republic. Throughout the 1970s and 80s, during the peak of the IRA's bombing efforts aimed at ending British authority over Northern Ireland, Sinn Fein functioned as the political arm of the IRA. Adams, who took on the leadership role in 1983, became, for many in Northern Ireland and Britain, the IRA's most recognized figure. Consequently, he faced intense animosity from pro-British unionists and the British government, while simultaneously being celebrated by Irish nationalists. Nevertheless, when opportunities for political advancement emerged, he demonstrated a willingness to find common ground, collaborating with the late Martin McGuinness, a former IRA commander, to garner support from the IRA and the province's Catholic minority for the 1998 agreement with the pro-British Protestant majority. The Good Friday agreement facilitated a power-sharing arrangement for the province's Catholics and effectively brought an end to a conflict that resulted in approximately 3,600 fatalities, many of whom were victims of Irish republican factions like the IRA, as well as pro-British unionist paramilitaries and British security forces. Since that pivotal moment, Adams has contributed to the establishment of Sinn Fein as the preeminent Irish nationalist party within Northern Ireland, overseeing its 2007 agreement to collaborate with its longtime adversary, the Democratic Unionist Party, and in recent months, advocating for the restoration of power-sharing that collapsed earlier this year in January. On Saturday, Adams further declared that he would not pursue re-election to the Dublin parliament, where he has served since 2011, helping to elevate Sinn Fein from the margins to the position of the third-largest party in the Irish Republic and its primary left-wing force. Adams was born into a family in Belfast deeply rooted in revolutionary politics, with several relatives having participated in armed republican activities. At the age of 20, he left his job as a bartender to defend fellow Catholics against what they perceived as an antagonistic British government and to advocate for Northern Ireland's separation from the United Kingdom in favor of unification with the Irish Republic. Adams was interned without trial, like his father, on suspicions of being a senior figure in the IRA. He has consistently denied any affiliation with the IRA, although throughout his career, he has faced allegations from former IRA members regarding his involvement in its violent actions. From 1988 to 1994, British broadcasting restrictions prevented Adams from addressing the public directly; his distinctive glasses and red-tinged beard made him recognizable, but his voice was not heard as actors voiced his speeches. John Major, a former British conservative prime minister and one of the key architects of the peace process in Northern Ireland, once remarked that the idea of negotiating with Adams had "turned my stomach." During this tumultuous period, Adams navigated a precarious political landscape, balancing the demands of IRA hardliners who believed that violence was the only means to expel Britain from the island against those advocating for negotiations as the pathway to a unified Ireland. In October 1997, he emerged from political isolation when he met with newly elected Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair, marking a significant moment in his career. At that time, Sinn Fein had garnered 17 percent of the vote in Northern Ireland's elections, which allowed Adams to secure a position in the British parliament, although he chose not to take his seat. Within a year of that pivotal meeting, Adams and McGuinness played vital roles in negotiating a peace agreement that significantly curtailed violence in the province. Since then, his stature as a statesman has grown, resulting in several visits to international leaders.
source_text: Gerry Adams: Face of IRA who helped cement Northern Ireland peace. DUBLIN (Reuters) - As the public face of the Irish Republican Army during its bombing campaigns, then peacemaker and mainstream politician, Gerry Adams has been a defining figure of Northern Ireland s 50-year journey from sectarian torment to relative stability. Adams announced his intention to step down as leader of the Irish nationalist Sinn Fein party on Saturday with his ultimate goal of a united Ireland still elusive. But the party he leaves is not only the dominant Irish nationalist force in the British-ruled province, but also strong enough across the border in the Irish Republic to have a chance of entering government there, too. During the 1970s and 80s, at the height of an IRA bombing campaign to end British rule over Northern Ireland, Sinn Fein operated as the IRA s political wing. As its leader from 1983 onwards, Adams thus became, for many in Britain and Northern Ireland, the face of the IRA. As a result, he was loathed by pro-British unionists and the British government, but lionized in equal measure by Irish nationalists. Yet when the prospect of political progress arose, he showed himself ready to compromise, working with late former IRA commander Martin McGuinness to swing the IRA and the province s Roman Catholic minority behind a 1998 deal with the pro-British Protestant majority. The Good Friday agreement gave the province s Catholics a share of power and largely ended a conflict in which some 3,600 people had been killed, many at the hands of Irish republican groups such as the IRA, and others by pro-British unionist paramilitaries and British security forces.  Since then, Adams has helped to build Sinn Fein into the dominant Irish nationalist party in Northern Ireland, overseeing its agreement in 2007 to share power with its bitter rival, the Democratic Unionist Party and, in recent months, its efforts to restore power-sharing after it collapsed in January.  Adams also announced on Saturday that he would not stand for re-election to the Dublin parliament, where he has sat since 2011, moving Sinn Fein from the fringes to become the Irish Republic s third party and its main left-wing force.  Adams was born into a Belfast family steeped in revolutionary politics, several of his relatives having been involved in armed republicanism. At 20, he left his job as a barman to help defend fellow Catholics from what they saw as a hostile British state, and to fight for Northern Ireland to split from the United Kingdom and unite with the Irish Republic.   Like his father, Adams was interned - held without trial - on suspicion of being a senior IRA commander.  He has always denied membership of the IRA, although accusations from former IRA fighters that he was involved in its campaign of killings have dogged him throughout his career.  Between 1988 and 1994, Adams was banned from speaking on British airwaves. While his oversized glasses and red-tinged beard were instantly recognizable, his voice was unknown as broadcasters had actors dub his words. Former British conservative prime minister John Major, one of the architects of peace in Northern Ireland, once said the thought of sitting down to talk with Adams had  turned my stomach .  But Adams was at the time walking a political tightrope - between IRA  hawks  who argued that only a continuation of violence would chase Britain from the island, and  doves  who said that negotiations were the route to a united Ireland. He emerged from the political cold in October 1997 when he shook hands with the new Labour prime minister, Tony Blair, at their first meeting. Sinn Fein had polled 17 percent in Northern Ireland s elections and returned Adams to the British parliament, although he refused to take his seat.  Within a year, Adams and McGuinness had helped to broker a peace deal that largely ended the violence in the province. Since that deal, his role as statesman has grown, and he has made several visits to the White House.  He was arrested in 2014 as part of an investigation into one of the province s most controversial murders, but no charges were brought. Latterly he has used social media to create a grandfatherly image in the Irish Republic, with posts about his dog and his taste in cartoons.

text: On Thursday, U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry criticized Carnival Corp for prohibiting Cuban-Americans from participating in its upcoming cruises to Cuba. He urged the Cuban government to revise its policies to permit these individuals to travel. "Carnival must not engage in discriminatory practices," Kerry stated during an interview with CNN en Espanol and the Miami Herald. According to reports from the Miami Herald, individuals born in Cuba are restricted from visiting the island by sea due to a law established during the Cold War, which prevents them from boarding Carnival’s voyages to the destination. However, those born in Cuba are still allowed to fly to the island. "Cuban Americans, as American citizens, possess the right to travel, and we should not find ourselves in a situation where the Cuban government imposes its discriminatory regulations on us," Kerry expressed. He added, "Thus, we urge the Cuban government to amend this policy and to acknowledge that if they seek a complete and normal relationship with the United States, they must adhere to international law rather than solely their own rules," during his visit to Miami. Carnival representatives did not provide an immediate response to a request for a statement. Nonetheless, the company informed the Miami Herald that it was compelled to uphold the regulation when selling tickets for its newly launched Miami-to-Havana service. The company indicated that it has reached out to the Cuban government to request a waiver of the rule before the inaugural ship departs on May 1. A spokesperson from the State Department remarked, "Secretary Kerry in no way intended to imply that Carnival endorses policies that discriminate against Cuban American travelers." Miami serves as the hub for the U.S. Cuban-American population, with many residents having fled Cuba following the Communist revolution. A significant number of these individuals are strongly against President Barack Obama’s initiatives aimed at fostering improved relations with Havana. Detractors of this policy assert that the U.S. should not relax over fifty years of travel and trade restrictions until Cuba implements free elections and enhances its human rights record. Kerry, who conducted two interviews with local news outlets, engaged with business leaders and spoke to college students, noted that Cuba could hasten its efforts to enhance its human rights practices. Nevertheless, he expressed confidence that a more open relationship with the United States would lead to beneficial changes. "I believe that more could occur more rapidly. More should take place sooner. Yet, I am not taken aback. No one anticipated this. It has been over fifty years of the same situation... however, positive changes are underway," Kerry remarked.
source_text: John Kerry: Carnival should not bar Cuban-Americans from cruises to Cuba. MIAMI (Reuters) - U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry condemned Carnival Corp  on Thursday for barring Cuban-Americans from its planned cruises to Cuba and called on the Cuban government to change its policies to allow them. “Carnival needs to not discriminate,” Kerry said in an interview with CNN en Espanol and the Miami Herald. Cuban-born Americans cannot visit the island by sea, due to a Cuban law that dates to the Cold War era, and therefore are barred from joining in Carnival’s sailings to the island, the Miami Herald has reported. People born in Cuba can, however, travel to the island on an airplane. “American citizens, Cuban Americans have a right to travel, and we should not be in a situation where the Cuban government is forcing its discrimination policy on us,” Kerry said. “So we call on the government of Cuba to change that policy and to recognize that if they want a full relationship, a normal relationship, with the United States, they have to live by international law and not exclusively by their own,” he said during a trip to Miami. Carnival officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the company has told the Miami Herald it had no choice but to enforce the rule when booking tickets for its new Miami-to-Havana route. It said it has asked the Cuban government to waive the rule before the first ship sails on May 1. A State Department official said, “Secretary Kerry in no way meant to convey that Carnival is supporting policies that are discriminating against Cuban American travelers.” Miami is the center of the U.S. Cuban-American community, and many of its residents from the island nation, who fled Cuba after its Communist revolution, are vehemently opposed to President Barack Obama’s moves toward more normal relations with Havana. Critics of the policy say Washington should not ease a half century of restrictions on travel and trade until Cuba has free elections and its human rights record improves.  Kerry, who gave two interviews to local media, met with business leaders and addressed college students, said Cuba could move more quickly to improve its rights record. But he said he was sure a more open relationship with the United States would yield positive changes. “I think more could happen faster. More should happen faster. But I’m not surprised. Nobody expected that. This has been 50-plus years of the status quo ... but there are changes that are in place for the positive,” Kerry said.

text: On Friday, the Kremlin expressed its comprehension regarding the intention of the Russian lower house of parliament to deliberate on the prohibition of U.S. media entities. This move is seen as a response to what the Russian government characterizes as the unjust treatment of Russian media by the United States. According to RIA news agency, lawmakers are set to examine a proposal that would prevent U.S. media from entering the State Duma, the parliament's lower chamber. During a conference call with journalists, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov articulated that officials grasped the motivation behind the lawmakers' desire to retaliate against the U.S. for its hostile actions towards Russian media. Peskov remarked that media from Russia has faced severe assaults in the United States, which he claimed infringed upon freedom of expression.
source_text: Kremlin says understands why Russian parliament wants to ban U.S. media. MOSCOW (Reuters) - The Kremlin said on Friday it fully understood why the Russian lower house of parliament planned to discuss banning representatives of U.S. media organizations in retaliation for what it says is U.S. mistreatment of Russian media. Russian lawmakers are to discuss a proposal to bar U.S. media from accessing the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, the RIA news agency quoted the chair of one of the chamber s committees as saying earlier on Friday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a conference call with reporters that the Kremlin understood why lawmakers wanted to hit back against the United States for its mistreatment of Russian media. Peskov said Russian media had been subjected to  outrageous  attacks in the United States which violated freedom of speech.

text: After hearing gunfire outside his residence for four hours, Abu Riwar hurriedly gathered his wife and six children into their vehicle and fled to a distant village located 120 km (75 miles) away. "We left with the clothes on our back and nothing else," he recounted. Abu Riwar, who serves in the Kurdish security forces, hails from the ethnically diverse town of Tuz Khurmato, which was overtaken last month by Iraqi military forces and Shiite paramilitary groups backed by Iran. He feared that if the militias discovered he was Peshmerga, he would have been killed. Instead, his neighbors informed him that his home was set ablaze, and they captured the incident on video. Tuz Khurmato was previously part of a disputed area, situated outside the Kurdish region in northern Iraq, but was under the control of Kurdish Peshmerga forces until the central government reclaimed it last month in a rapid military operation aimed at punishing the Kurds for holding an independence referendum that Baghdad deemed illegal. Approximately 50,000 Kurds, making up near half of the city’s mixed population, fled the offensive to reach villages and towns under Kurdish control in the surrounding countryside, according to Mayor Shalal Abdul. The mayor himself escaped to Zinana, located 120 km east of Tuz Khurmato, where he shared details with Reuters. Most of the displaced individuals do not intend to return, citing ongoing reports of violence. "We can’t cope if it continues like this," lamented the chief of police in Zinana, indicating that both the government and humanitarian organizations have been unacceptably slow in their response. Families have occupied school buildings, homes, and even the local hospital, yet the police chief emphasized, "we can’t turn them out onto the streets." The United Nations reported that more than 180,000 individuals were uprooted due to the Iraqi government’s offensive in disputed regions last month. Aid organizations noted that the majority of the displaced individuals are Kurds, although some Sunni Arabs and Turkmen from Tuz Khurmato also fled. Prior to Baghdad’s military action, Tuz Khurmato had been jointly governed by Kurdish forces, local police, and the Iran-aligned Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) paramilitaries, who were allied with the Shiite Turkmen residents of the town. While the Kurds and Turkmen collaborated to expel Islamic State militants in 2014, their fragile coalition eventually disintegrated, leading to open conflict. Tensions escalated between these communities in the lead-up to the Kurdish independence referendum. In Zinana, displaced Kurdish individuals recounted to Reuters their experiences of mistreatment at the hands of the Shiite paramilitaries who took control of Tuz. One individual shared a video he had recorded showing the body of a relative who had been crushed. Family members claimed that the victim was shot while in his vehicle, forcibly pulled out alive by paramilitaries, and subsequently run over by a tank. "He was crushed to death in front of me, by those monsters," stated Abu Alan, the relative who documented the scene. The video circulating online, apparently depicting the same occurrence, features a tank rolling over a body while armed paramilitaries observe. The paramilitaries, however, refute any allegations of wrongdoing. According to Ali al-Hussaini, a spokesperson for the PMF in northern Iraq and a commander of the Badr Organisation, joint patrols by the PMF and government forces are in place to ensure the safety of Tuz and protect against potential attacks on Kurds. "It’s our responsibility to maintain security in Tuz for all communities," he asserted. The mayor, who is gathering testimonies and evidence of abuses, reported that during the town's capture, seven individuals were killed, including the man who was run over by the tank and three other civilians. He also mentioned being aware of three women and one man who had reportedly been raped. Reuters was unable to verify these claims. The mayor indicated that over 1,000 businesses and 2,000 homes were either looted, set ablaze, or destroyed, showing Reuters images of properties in Kurdish areas that had been blown up and charred, with belongings being removed by men dressed in military uniforms. Additional photographs depicted paramilitaries stationed in the mayor's office.
source_text: Kurds displaced by Iraq advance fear reprisals if they return. ZINANA, Iraq (Reuters) - Four hours after first hearing gunfire outside his home, Abu Riwar bundled his wife and six children into his car and drove to a remote village 120 km (75 miles) away.  We left with the clothes on our back and nothing else,  said Abu Riwar, a member of the Kurdish security forces from the ethnically mixed town of Tuz Khurmato, seized last month by Iraqi troops and Iran-backed Shi ite paramilitaries.  If the militias found out I was Peshmerga, they d have slaughtered me.  They burned his home to the ground instead, his neighbors, who captured it on camera, told him. Tuz Khurmato was part of disputed territory, outside the Kurdish region of northern Iraq but held by Kurdish forces known as Peshmerga, until last month, when the central government recaptured it in a lightning advance to punish the Kurds for staging an independence referendum that Baghdad called illegal. The majority of Tuz Khurmato s 50,000 Kurds   around half of the population of the ethnically mixed city   fled the Iraqi advance to Kurdish-held villages and towns in nearby countryside, said Mayor Shalal Abdul. The mayor himself fled to the village of Zinana, 120 km east of Tuz Khurmato, where he spoke to Reuters. Most residents have no plans to return home, citing reports of continuing attacks.  We can t cope if it continues like this,  said the chief of police in Zinana, adding that the government and aid groups had been too slow to respond.  Families have taken over school buildings, houses and the hospital, but we can t turn them out on the streets.  According to the United Nations, more than 180,000 people were displaced by the Iraqi government offensive on disputed territories last month. Aid agencies say most of those displaced are Kurds, though members of other minorities, including some of Tuz Khurmato s Sunni Arabs and Turkmen, also fled. Until Baghdad s offensive, Tuz Khurmato had been jointly administered by Kurdish forces, local police and the Iran-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) paramilitaries, allied with the town s Shi ite Turkmen population.  Though the Turkmen and the Kurds had worked together to push Islamic State militants out in 2014, the town s fragile coalition soon fell apart and led to open hostilities. In the run-up to the Kurdish independence referendum, tension escalated between the communities. In Zinana, displaced Kurds told Reuters stories of abuse at the hands of the Shi ite paramilitaries who captured Tuz. One man showed a video he had filmed depicting the crushed body of a relative. Family members said the victim had been shot in his car, dragged out alive by paramilitaries and run over by a tank.  He was crushed to death in front of me, by those monsters,  said Abu Alan, the relative who filmed the body.  He was a good man from a good family.  A video circulated on the internet, apparently of the same incident, shows a tank running over a body while uniformed paramilitaries stand by. The paramilitaries deny carrying out any abuse.  Joint patrols by the PMF and government forces are securing the town, to prevent any attacks against Kurds,  said Ali al-Hussaini, a spokesman for the PMF in northern Iraq and a commander of the largest of the armed groups, the Badr Organisation.  It s our job to keep Tuz safe for all sects.  The mayor, who is collecting stories and evidence of abuse, said seven people were killed when the town was captured, including the man who was crushed by the tank and three other civilians. He said he also knew of three women and one man who had been raped. Reuters could not verify those accusations. More than 1,000 businesses and 2,000 homes were looted, burned down or demolished, the mayor said.  He showed Reuters images of houses and shopfronts in Kurdish areas, blown up and scorched, their residents  belongings being carted away by men in military fatigues. Other pictures showed paramilitaries sitting in the mayor s own office, feet propped up on his desk and on his Kurdish flag.  Dozens of people were detained, and some say they were tortured, like Thiaa, a 20-year-old Sunni Turkman from the countryside who had gone to Tuz Khurmato the day after the offensive to check on his sister who was married to a Kurd.  They detained me because I don t speak Arabic, so they thought I was a Kurd,  Thiaa said.  They kept me filthy, hungry and blindfolded in a dark room with three Kurds. They beat us with cables all day long.  One night, fighters put a gun in Thiaa s mouth and threatened to kill him, only to burst out laughing at his panicked tears, he said. He was released after seven days and is now recovering at home from his injuries. The Kurds held with him  had no such luck,  he said. More than five are still missing.

text: The humanitarian chief of the United Nations made a request on Friday for the complete removal of the blockade imposed on Yemen by the Saudi-led military coalition, noting that as many as eight million individuals are teetering on the edge of famine. This week, the coalition had taken steps to partially relax the blockade, allowing aid to reach the ports of Hodeidah and Salif, as well as enabling U.N. flights to land in Sanaa. However, the amount of aid being delivered is merely a small portion of what is necessary for Yemen, as the country relies heavily on imports for nearly all its food, fuel, and medical supplies. The coalition, which receives support from the United States and other nations, instituted the blockade on November 6 after Saudi Arabia intercepted a missile that was launched from Yemen towards its capital, Riyadh. Another missile was destroyed by defense forces on Thursday. According to U.N. humanitarian chief Mark Lowcock, while the blockade has seen some reduction, it has not been eliminated completely. He emphasized that it must be entirely lifted to prevent a devastating humanitarian disaster that could result in the loss of millions of lives, an atrocity not witnessed in decades. "Yemen has a population of 25 million people, with around 20 million requiring assistance. Approximately seven or eight million are currently on the verge of famine," Lowcock stated as he initiated the U.N.'s appeal for humanitarian aid for 2018. When asked by reporters if the Saudi-led blockade constituted a breach of international law, Lowcock refrained from giving a direct answer but reiterated that the United Nations has consistently urged all parties involved in the conflict to adhere to their responsibilities. "I am not a legal expert, but it is evident that international humanitarian law mandates the facilitation of unimpeded access for aid organizations, and that is what I have been striving to ensure through both my public statements and private discussions," he commented. U.N. officials are often reluctant to openly criticize conflict parties due to the potential risks of losing access or financial support. However, Saudi Arabia has been a significant contributor to humanitarian initiatives for Yemen. In contrast, others have been more forthright in their opinions. Jan Egeland, a former U.N. aid chief, labeled the blockade as "illegal collective punishment," while Alfredo Zamudio, the director at the Nansen Center for Peace and Dialogue based in Norway, asserted to Reuters that he believed the International Criminal Court should probe whether it constitutes a war crime. At the event held in Geneva on Friday, Helle Thorning-Schmidt, the leader of Save the Children International, remarked, "The situation in Yemen reflects a blatant violation of humanitarian rules, and it is evident that the obstruction of aid has been weaponized in this conflict." The military coalition entered the Yemeni conflict in 2015 after the Iran-aligned Houthi faction and its allies compelled President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi to seek refuge in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh perceives the Houthis as an Iranian proxy, its primary adversary in the region. The ongoing conflict has resulted in over 10,000 fatalities, displaced more than 2 million individuals, triggered a cholera outbreak, and brought the nation to the brink of famine.

text: President Donald Trump may face significant political and legal repercussions if he intensifies his criticisms of Attorney General Jeff Sessions into a move to purge U.S. law enforcement officials, according to lawmakers and legal analysts on Tuesday. Trump has been vocally attacking Sessions in response to an inquiry into potential connections between his 2016 campaign and Russia, leading to conjecture that he intends to remove Sessions from his position. If the special counsel overseeing the Russia probe, Robert Mueller, becomes Trump's primary target and he attempts to dismiss Mueller, it could lead to a major legal and political confrontation. Independent Senator Angus King from Maine expressed to CNN on Tuesday that he believes his colleagues will not stand for any attempts by Trump to replace Sessions with someone loyal to him, particularly if it seems aimed at sabotaging Mueller’s investigation. King noted, “The senators are going to be very skeptical about this.” He typically votes alongside Democrats and added, “My expectation is you’d see a special prosecutor pass by veto-proof majorities in both houses. And the investigation would continue.” At a press conference on Tuesday, Trump was questioned about Sessions and remarked, “Time will tell. Time will tell.” These comments followed a series of tweets in which he labeled Sessions as “weak” and “beleaguered.” Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell stated to reporters in a Capitol corridor on Tuesday that Sessions is “doing a fine job.” Republican Senator Richard Shelby mentioned to reporters that Sessions, who previously served as his colleague from Alabama, is “not the president’s lawyer; he is the attorney general of the United States.” The fundamental laws regarding the removal of Justice Department officials, including Mueller, who was appointed by Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein due to Sessions’ recusal from the Russia investigation, are as follows. What justifications could exist for firing Mueller? According to Justice Department guidelines, a special counsel can only be dismissed for “misconduct, dereliction of duty, incapacity, conflict of interest, or for any other good cause.” Do Trump’s assertions that Mueller is engaged in a “witch hunt” and that he is conflicted qualify as “good cause?” Likely not. No court has ever defined “good cause” within this context. However, Andrew Wright, who served as associate counsel in the Obama administration and teaches at Savannah Law School, remarked that Mueller enjoys a stellar reputation and there is no evidence suggesting he has overstepped the boundaries of his assignment. Wright further stated that contributions from members of Mueller’s team to Democratic candidates do not create a conflict of interest. Is it possible for Trump to directly terminate Mueller? Probably not. The rules of the Department of Justice stipulate that only the attorney general or the acting attorney general can terminate the special counsel. Trump has criticized Rosenstein for appointing Mueller and, due to Sessions’ recusal, Rosenstein possesses the exclusive authority to dismiss Mueller. Nevertheless, a few legal scholars have indicated that Trump might legally fire Mueller himself. Saikrishna Prakash, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law, stated that the regulations concerning special counsels might clash with the president’s expansive constitutional right to remove officials in the executive branch. “I don’t know if that regulation is constitutional,” he remarked. If Trump were to dismiss Sessions or if Sessions were to resign, would Trump be able to select an attorney general who would terminate Mueller? Typically, the president nominates someone for attorney general, who then requires Senate confirmation. If Trump were to pursue this route, it’s likely that the Senate would scrutinize any nominee regarding their potential stance on firing Mueller, according to Prakash. “The Senate is going to want promises that this person will be independent of the White House and not be a toady,” he explained. How else might Trump appoint an attorney general who he believes would act favorably toward his interests?
