And the investigation would continue.” Trump, who dismissed James Comey as director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation as it was looking into possible Russian connections, was asked about Sessions at a news conference on Tuesday and said, “Time will tell. Time will tell.” These remarks followed Twitter messages by Trump in which he described Sessions as “weak” and “beleaguered.” Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell told reporters in a Capitol hallway on Tuesday that Sessions is “doing a fine job.” Republican Richard Shelby told reporters Sessions, formerly his fellow senator from Alabama, is “not the president’s lawyer; he is the attorney general of the United States.” Here are basics on the law covering dismissal of Justice Department officials, including Mueller, who was appointed by Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein because Sessions is recused from matters dealing with the Russia investigation. On what grounds could Mueller be fired? Justice Department regulations say a special counsel can only be removed for “misconduct, dereliction of duty, incapacity, conflict of interest, or for any other good cause.” Do Trump’s claims that Mueller is on a “witch hunt” and that he is conflicted constitute “good cause?”   Probably not. No court has ever interpreted the meaning of “good cause” in this context. But Mueller has a sterling reputation and there is no indication he has exceeded the scope of his mandate, said Andrew Wright, former associate counsel in the Obama White House and professor at Savannah Law School. Campaign donations from members of Mueller’s team to Democrats do not pose a conflict of interest, Wright said. Could Trump directly fire Mueller?     Probably not. Department of Justice rules say the special counsel can only be fired by the attorney general or the acting attorney general. Trump has criticized Rosenstein for appointing Mueller and due to Session’s recusal, Rosenstein has sole authority to fire Mueller. But a few constitutional lawyers have said that Trump might be able to lawfully fire Mueller directly. Saikrishna Prakash of the University of Virginia Law School said the special counsel regulations may interfere with the president’s broad power under the Constitution to remove executive branch officials. “I don’t know if that regulation is constitutional,” he said. If Trump fires Sessions or Sessions quits, could Trump handpick an attorney general who would fire Mueller? Normally, the president nominates an attorney general who must win Senate confirmation. If Trump followed this course, the Senate would likely press any nominee on his or her intentions on terminating Mueller, Prakash said.  “The Senate is going to want promises that this person will be independent of the White House and not be a toady,” he said.  How else could Trump name an attorney general who he believes would fire Mueller? Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act of 1998, Trump could appoint an interim attorney general, but only someone previously confirmed by the Senate. The law can only be invoked to replace officials who die, resign or are “otherwise unable” to do their job. If Trump invoked the Federal Vacancies Reform Act to replace Sessions, a court may rule that Trump overstepped, Josh Chafetz, a professor of constitutional law at Cornell Law School, said. What about a recess appointment?  Trump could try replacing Sessions while the Senate is on summer recess, expected to begin Aug. 11. The constitution grants the president such authority, said Stephen Vladeck, constitutional law professor at the University of Texas School of Law.      The Supreme Court ruled in 2014 the president cannot make a recess appointment during recesses of less than 10 days. The Senate calendar is controlled by Trump’s fellow Republicans.      Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said on Tuesday that Democrats would use every tool at their disposal to block a recess appointment of a Sessions replacement. If Mueller were fired, could he mount a court challenge? Unclear. Vladeck said the special counsel regulations do not address this question. If he brought a lawsuit, Mueller likely would argue the rules would be pointless if there was no way to enforce them, Vladeck said.

text: On Monday, the administration of President Donald Trump took a stand against permitting the entry of grandparents from six Muslim-majority nations, asserting in a legal document that its interpretation of the temporary travel ban aligns with U.S. immigration legislation. The U.S. Supreme Court, in a decision made the previous Monday, reinstated portions of Trump’s executive order issued on March 6, which prohibits entry for individuals from Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen for a duration of 90 days, an order that had faced legal challenges from lower courts. The Supreme Court allowed the travel ban to proceed but with restrictions, clarifying that it cannot be enforced against individuals who possess a credible “bona fide relationship” with someone in the United States. President Trump contended that the ban is essential for thwarting potential terrorist activities. However, numerous opponents, including various states and organizations advocating for refugees, filed lawsuits to challenge the ban, questioning its security justification and alleging that it is discriminatory towards Muslims. Following the Supreme Court's decision, the government clarified that a “bona fide relationship” only includes immediate family members: parents, spouses, siblings, and children. This means that grandparents, grandchildren, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and cousins from the six designated nations would still be prohibited from entering the country. The lawyers for the Department of Justice maintained in their court documents on Monday that the government’s interpretation closely aligns with the definitions established by Congress in the Immigration and Nationality Act. The government’s legal submission followed Hawaii’s initiative last week to seek clarification from U.S. District Judge Derrick Watson in Honolulu, who had initially issued a ruling to block the travel ban, arguing that the government’s interpretation of “bona fide relationship” was overly restrictive. In its response, the government stated that Hawaii, along with the refugee organizations that submitted a “friend of the court” brief supporting the state, were attempting to impose “broader, free-hand rules.” The organizations had contended that their efforts to assist in resettling refugees, a complex process that may take years in collaboration with the U.S. government, constitute a “bona fide” relationship with a U.S. entity. According to the Supreme Court ruling, any refugees having such a relationship should be exempt from the three-month ban on refugees outlined in the executive order. However, the government argued that individuals with job offers from U.S. companies and international students differ significantly from refugees receiving assistance from U.S. resettlement agencies. The government stated in its brief, “A refugee’s relationship with the agency flows from the government, not from an independent relationship between the refugee and the resettlement agency.” It added that typically, resettlement agencies do not engage directly with the refugees they assist prior to their arrival in the U.S. The government claimed that adhering to the organization’s interpretation would render the refugee provisions within the executive order “largely meaningless.” According to information provided by the State Department, U.S. refugee resettlement processes will proceed as usual until July 6, around the time when the cap of 50,000 for the fiscal year, established by Trump’s executive order, is expected to be reached. Just before the ban was set to take effect on Thursday, the government amended its stance regarding fiancés, stating that they too could qualify for exemptions. The court documents detailed a frantic 72-hour effort to “coordinate among multiple government agencies, and issue detailed guidance” on executing the Supreme Court’s decision. The implementation of the revised version of the ban was notably more subdued on Friday compared to January, when Trump’s initial, more expansive order incited protests and turmoil at airports nationwide and globally.
source_text: Trump administration defends interpretation of travel ban ruling. NEW YORK (Reuters) - The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump opposed opening the door to grandparents from six Muslim-majority countries on Monday, arguing in a court filing that the government’s interpretation of how to implement its temporary travel ban is based on U.S. immigration law. The U.S. Supreme Court in a ruling last Monday revived parts of Trump’s March 6 executive order that banned people from Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen for 90 days, which had been blocked by lower courts. The highest court let the ban go forward with a limited scope, saying that it cannot apply to anyone with credible “bona fide relationship” with a U.S. person or entity. Trump said the measure was necessary to prevent terrorist attacks. But opponents, including states and refugee advocacy groups, sued to stop it, disputing its security rationale and saying it discriminates against Muslims. After the Supreme Court ruling, the government said that a “bona fide relationship” means close family members only: parents, spouses, siblings and children. Grandparents, grandchildren, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews and cousins from the six countries would still be banned.  The government’s definition, “hews closely to the categorical determinations articulated by Congress in the Immigration and Nationality Act,” Department of Justice lawyers argued in court papers on Monday.   The government’s filing came after the State of Hawaii last week went to U.S. District Judge Derrick Watson in Honolulu, who originally ruled to block the ban, to seek clarification of the Supreme Court’s ruling, arguing the government’s definition of “bona fide relationship” was too narrow. The government said Hawaii, and refugee organizations that filed a “friend of the court” brief in support of the state, were seeking to apply “broader, free-hand rules.” The refugee organizations had argued that their work to resettle refugees, a process that can take years of work in coordination with the U.S. government, qualifies as a “bona fide” relationship with a U.S. entity. Any refugees with such a relationship should be exempt from the three-month ban on refugees included in the executive order, according to the Supreme Court ruling.  But the government said workers with offers of employment with a U.S. company and international students are fundamentally different than refugees receiving help from U.S. resettlement agencies. “A refugee’s relationship with the agency flows from the government, not from an independent relationship between the refugee and the resettlement agency,” the government said in its brief. “Indeed, resettlement agencies typically do not have any direct contact with the refugees they assure before their arrival in the United States.”  Using the organization’s interpretation would make the refugee provisions in the executive order “largely meaningless,” the government said.  U.S. refugee resettlement is continuing as normal until July 6, the State Department has said, around when the 50,000 cap for the fiscal year set by Trump’s executive order is likely to be reached.  Late on Thursday, before the ban went into effect, the government reversed its position on fiancés, saying they could also qualify for exceptions. The court filing described a 72-hour scramble to “coordinate among multiple government agencies, and issue detailed guidance” on how to implement the Supreme Court’s ruling.  The roll out of the narrowed version of the ban was more subdued on Friday compared to in January when Trump first signed a more expansive version of the order, sparking protests and chaos at airports around the country and the world.

text: A recent analysis from a nonpartisan congressional office indicated that a bipartisan initiative in the Senate aimed at stabilizing the Obamacare insurance exchanges could lead to a reduction in the U.S. deficit by $3.8 billion over the upcoming ten years. This proposal, introduced last week by Senator Lamar Alexander, a Republican, alongside Democratic Senator Patty Murray, intends to reinstate subsidies for private insurers for a period of two years, aimed at assisting low-income individuals in purchasing health insurance. Earlier this month, President Donald Trump discontinued these subsidies. Furthermore, the legislation would grant states increased flexibility to modify certain regulations established by the 2010 Affordable Care Act, which stands as the major legislative accomplishment of Trump's Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama. The Congressional Budget Office had previously assessed that various Republican initiatives to eliminate and replace Obamacare would result in over 20 million individuals losing their health insurance. However, the CBO stated on Wednesday that the reinstatement of subsidies as proposed in the Alexander-Murray legislation would not significantly change the number of insured individuals. Additionally, the CBO projected that the adjustments would not affect health insurance premiums for 2018, since those rates have already been finalized. Insurers reported an average increase of 20 percent in premiums to compensate for the absence of federal subsidies. According to the CBO, it anticipates that premiums for health insurance in 2019 would be lower if the payments to insurers are reinstated compared to if they are not. Although the Alexander-Murray plan is expected to decrease the federal deficit, the CBO had earlier determined that eliminating the cost-sharing reductions would lead to an increase in the federal deficit by $194 billion over the span of a decade. In the absence of these subsidies, premiums would escalate, necessitating greater government expenditure on financial aid for low-income citizens. Approximately 20 million Americans enrolled in insurance through Obamacare, which contributed to lowering the uninsured rate in the U.S. to a historic low. Nevertheless, Republicans have characterized it as an undue governmental interference in a healthcare system that constitutes one-fifth of the U.S. economy. The future of the Alexander-Murray bill in Congress remains uncertain. Trump has provided inconsistent messages regarding it, having initially expressed support last week only to later voice opposition. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has stated that he will not advance the bill without Trump’s endorsement. Trump has criticized the payments to insurers, labeling them a "bailout," and has expressed intentions to allow Obamacare to "implode." On the Senate floor, Alexander remarked on Wednesday, "It does not bail out insurance companies; it benefits consumers and taxpayers, amounting to $3.8 billion." Insurers contend that they do not profit from the subsidies; rather, they directly pass the benefits to consumers, thereby lowering deductibles, co-payments, and other out-of-pocket medical costs for those with lower incomes. Trump, who campaigned on the promise of dismantling Obamacare, has shown frustration over the inability of Congress, even with his party in control, to pass a repeal and replacement bill, and he has resorted to measures that circumvent legislative action to undermine the law. House Speaker Paul Ryan has conveyed his disapproval and indicated on Wednesday that the House would not revisit the issue or attempt again to enact broader Republican legislation aimed at repealing and replacing Obamacare this year. With substantial Democratic support and backing from a dozen Republican senators, the Alexander-Murray proposal possesses enough votes to surpass the 60 votes required for approval in the 100-member Senate, provided McConnell permits it to proceed to a vote. On Tuesday, two influential Republicans from the House and Senate unveiled an alternative Obamacare solution that is more conservative and seemingly addresses many concerns raised by the Trump administration regarding the Alexander-Murray initiative. This alternative proposal is being led by Republican Senator Orrin Hatch, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, alongside Republican Representative Kevin Brady, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A bipartisan Senate proposal to shore up Obamacare insurance marketplaces would cut the U.S. deficit by $3.8 billion over the next decade and would not substantially change the number of Americans with health insurance, a nonpartisan arm of Congress said on Wednesday. Legislation introduced last week by Republican Senator Lamar Alexander and Democratic Senator Patty Murray would restore for two years subsidies to private insurers to help lower-income people buy insurance. President Donald Trump this month cut off those subsidies. The bill also would provide states more flexibility to change some rules in the 2010 Affordable Care Act, the signature legislative achievement of the Republican Trump’s Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office previously estimated that various Republican proposals to repeal and replace Obamacare would cause more than 20 million people to lose health insurance. In contrast, the CBO on Wednesday said reinstating the subsidies, as called for in the Alexander-Murray bill, would not substantially alter the number of insured. The CBO also estimated that the fix would not impact 2018 health insurance rates because they are already set. Health insurers said they raised premiums on average 20 percent to make up for the lost federal subsidies. The CBO said it expected 2019 health insurance premiums to be lower with the insurer payments than without them. While the Alexander-Murray legislation would reduce the federal deficit, the CBO previously found that eliminating the subsidies, called cost sharing reductions, would raise the federal deficit by $194 billion over a decade. Because premiums would rise in the absence of the subsidies, the government would be compelled to spend more on financial assistance to low-income Americans. About 20 million Americans obtained insurance through Obamacare and the law helped drive the U.S. uninsured rate to a record low, but Republicans have called it an unwarranted government intrusion in a healthcare system that represents a fifth of the U.S. economy. It is unclear whether the Alexander-Murray bill will ever come to a vote in Congress. Trump has sent mixed signals about it, initially supporting it last week and then opposing it. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell said he would not bring it up without Trump’s support. Trump has derided the insurer payments as a “bailout” and has vowed to let Obamacare “implode.”  “It does not bail out insurance companies, it does benefit consumers, it does benefit taxpayers to the tune of $3.8 billion,” Alexander said on Wednesday on the Senate floor. Insurers say they do not profit from the subsidies, but pass them on directly to consumers to reduce deductibles, co-payments and other out-of-pocket medical expenses for low-income people.     Trump, who as a candidate promised to get rid of Obamacare, has been frustrated by the inability of a Congress led by his own party to pass a bill to repeal and replace it, and has taken steps that bypass lawmakers to chip away at the law. House of Representatives Speaker Paul Ryan has signaled his opposition and on Wednesday said his chamber would not take up the matter or try again to pass broader Republican legislation to repeal and replace Obamacare this year. With broad Democratic backing and the support of a dozen Republican senators, the Alexander-Murray bill has sufficient backing to exceed the 60 votes needed for passage in the 100-seat Senate, if McConnell allows it to come to a vote. Two prominent Republicans in the House and Senate on Tuesday announced a competing Obamacare fix that is more conservative and appears to address many of the Trump administration’s objections to the Alexander-Murray proposal.  The proposal by Republican Senator Orrin Hatch, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, and Republican Representative Kevin Brady, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, includes provisions to suspend requirements for individuals and employers to buy health coverage under Obamacare. Ryan told Reuters in an interview he favored the Hatch-Brady proposal.

text: On Thursday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin announced that financial institutions engaging with North Korea would be prohibited from conducting operations within the United States. This measure is part of a new sanctions initiative aimed at disrupting the nuclear and missile development efforts of Pyongyang. Mnuchin remarked that no bank should facilitate the harmful actions of Kim Jong Un, the leader of North Korea. He indicated that foreign banks are now informed that they must choose between operating with the United States or North Korea, but not both. Furthermore, Mnuchin stated that any sanctions enacted under the recent executive order signed by U.S. President Donald Trump would be prospective and would not apply to previous conduct.
source_text: Banks won't be allowed to do business with both U.S. and North Korea: Mnuchin. NEW YORK (Reuters) - U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin said on Thursday that banks doing business in North Korea would not be allowed to also operate in the United States under a new sanctions order aimed at thwarting Pyongyang s nuclear and missiles program.  No bank in any country should be used to facilitate Kim Jong Un s destructive behavior,  Mnuchin told reporters, referring to North Korea s leader.  Foreign financial institutions are now on notice that going forward they can choose to do business with the United States or with North Korea, but not both.  Mnuchin said any sanctions issued under the new executive order signed by U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday would be forward-looking and not target past behavior.

source_text: China's Xi says BRICS countries should deepen coordination, quicken reform of global economic governance. XIAMEN, China (Reuters) - BRICS countries should deepen coordination on important global matters and quicken global economic governance reform, Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Tuesday.  Speaking at the BRICS summit in the southeastern Chinese city Xiamen, Xi also said BRICS countries have made smooth progress on anti-terrorism and internet security cooperation.

As the Republican National Convention approaches, U.S. television networks are ramping up their coverage significantly, driven by robust advertising sales. Executives indicated that compared to the previous election cycle, viewers can expect additional hours of programming this week. Donald Trump, the presumptive nominee, may be new to the political scene, but his background as the former host of the reality series "The Apprentice" gives him an edge in the world of television. He has promised to reinvent the conventional format of the event, aiming for a more entertainment-driven atmosphere. Meanwhile, uncertainties loom with protests anticipated outside the convention center in Cleveland and potential disagreements among delegates. CNN's Washington bureau chief, Sam Feist, remarked, "It’s safe to say that there are going to be surprises."

The stakes for both broadcast and cable networks are considerable. Analysts in the media sector predict that the audience for Trump's acceptance speech might exceed the 38 million viewers who tuned in to see Barack Obama at the Democratic convention in 2008. This possibility of unexpected developments during what is typically a carefully orchestrated event is fueling considerable interest from advertisers, according to network officials. Reports suggest that CNN is securing between $40,000 and $100,000 for 30-second commercial slots, a significant increase from the usual primetime ad costs, which hover around $7,000. Katrina Cukaj, who serves as executive vice president of portfolio sales and client partnerships at Turner Broadcasting, which owns CNN, mentioned, "We are 100 percent sold on primetime and about 95 percent sold on other slots," although she refrained from discussing specific rates. Cukaj also noted that quick-service restaurants and movie production companies are buying more advertising space than in previous conventions. "The advertisers are a lot more diverse than I have ever seen," she added.

CBS, another major broadcaster, has reported strong advertising sales for both conventions, securing spots from various sectors including entertainment, packaged goods, and travel, according to a source within the network. In 2012, advertisers allocated $5.8 million for both conventions, a rise from $7.8 million in 2008, as per Kantar Media data. Coverage will be extensive, with cable networks offering programming throughout the day and into the night. Broadcast networks have scheduled one hour of primetime coverage for each of the four nights, along with online updates. In contrast, during the 2012 conventions, networks only aired an hour of coverage for the last three evenings. CNN plans to deploy hundreds of staff members onsite, marking a record for any prior convention, Feist noted. The network will anchor its broadcasts from Cleveland continuously until noon on Friday.

Competition is expected to be fierce. Fox News Channel, owned by 21st Century Fox, commenced its coverage from Cleveland on Thursday, beginning four days earlier than in previous years, as opposed to the usual Sunday start. The network has also increased its personnel to report on protests occurring outside the venue. According to Kyle Roberts, president and CEO of Smart Media Group, a firm that collaborates with Republican candidates, Trump’s acceptance speech might draw in over 40 million viewers. However, not all brands are eager to participate in the convention, as Barry Lowenthal, president of The Media Kitchen, a media buying agency, cautioned, "It’s just dangerous territory. It’s very unpredictable content. I’m not sure that convention is going to enhance any brand’s image. Why go there if you can go elsewhere?"

This year, media organizations are planning to depend more on social media and live streaming than in the past. MSNBC correspondent Jacob Soboroff expressed his intention to broadcast live for most of the week, utilizing platforms like Snapchat, Twitter, and possibly Facebook Live when he is not on television. "This is going to be a different kind of convention," Soboroff stated. "It doesn’t feel like business as usual because there is a lot of energy around that feels uncertain." ABC News, owned by Walt Disney Co., will offer as many as six live streams at once on its website and applications. CBS will provide live coverage on Twitter and its 24-hour CBSN mobile app, preparing for an engaging and dynamic convention experience.

text: In the ongoing conflict in Syria, the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), a coalition comprising Kurdish and Arab fighters, announced on Friday that they had secured the final neighborhoods of the old city of Raqqa from the Islamic State. However, the U.S.-led coalition, which provides support to the SDF, was unable to verify this assertion. "We declare to our people the liberation of the old city of Raqqa," stated the SDF in their official communication. Since June, the SDF has been engaged in a campaign to seize control of Raqqa, the former capital of the Islamic State's self-proclaimed caliphate, with assistance from U.S. airpower and special operations forces. The historic walled area is situated in the center of Raqqa, yet the jihadist group still retains control over significant sections in the western part of the city. According to the SDF, they currently occupy 65 percent of Raqqa overall. Meanwhile, the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a monitoring group based in Britain, disputed the claim that the SDF had completely taken the old city but acknowledged that they controlled more than 90 percent of that region. The coalition confirmed they had not yet received confirmation of the reports, remarked Colonel Ryan Dillon, a spokesperson for the coalition.
source_text: U.S.-backed forces in Syria's Raqqa say they take old city. BEIRUT (Reuters) - The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), an alliance of Kurdish and Arab militias, said on Friday it had taken the last districts in the old city of Raqqa from Islamic State, but the U.S.-led coalition which backs it could not confirm the report.  We declare to our people the liberation of the old city of Raqqa,  the SDF said in a statement.  The SDF has been battling to capture the former de facto capital of Islamic State s self-declared caliphate since June with backing from U.S.-led jets and special forces.  The walled old city lies in the heart of Raqqa but the jihadist group still holds important districts in the west of the city. The SDF said it now held 65 percent of Raqqa in total. A war monitor, the Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, said it was not true that the SDF had fully captured the old city, but added that it did hold more than 90 percent of that area.  The coalition said it was not yet able to confirm the news.  We have not received confirmation of that through our channels,  coalition spokesman Colonel Ryan Dillon said.

text: On Tuesday, Democrats celebrated significant victories in statehouses, marking a historic achievement in Virginia and ousting Republicans from various state and local positions nationwide. This marked the party's first substantial success since Donald Trump, a Republican, assumed the presidency a year prior. The Democrats now face the challenge of leveraging this momentum as they prepare for the elections in November 2018, where control of the U.S. Congress and numerous state legislatures will be contested. Across the country, Democratic wins reflected a grassroots backlash against Trump, energizing the party's supporters, while independent and conservative voters seemed dissatisfied with the current Republican administration in Washington. In the gubernatorial races, Democrats triumphed in both Virginia and New Jersey, but the outcomes of legislative and local elections across the nation may have provided deeper insights into the party's standing one year into Trump's presidency. The unexpected and significant Democratic gains in Virginia's state legislature astonished even the most hopeful party members in a state that has leaned Democratic lately yet remains a prime target for both major parties in national elections. "To be honest, this is beyond what we ever expected," remarked Catherine Vaughan, co-founder of Flippable, one of several emerging progressive organizations revitalizing the party from the grassroots level. With several electoral outcomes still pending, Democrats were on the verge of taking control or at least splitting the Virginia House of Delegates, which would eliminate a previously established two-to-one Republican dominance. In what had appeared to be a competitive race, Democratic Lieutenant Governor Ralph Northam defeated Republican Ed Gillespie by nearly nine percentage points in the contest for Virginia's governorship, following a year when Democrat Hillary Clinton secured the state by five points in the presidential election. The campaign tactics utilized by the losing candidate mirrored those of Trump, emphasizing polarizing topics like immigration, although Trump did not campaign alongside him. In New Jersey, a Democratic stronghold, voters opted for a Democrat to succeed a two-term Republican governor, thereby bolstering the party's majorities in the state legislature. Additional victories for Democrats included a Senate race in Washington, which granted the party complete control of the state government, as well as gaining three seats in special state legislative elections in Republican-leaning Georgia. "This represented the first opportunity for voters to send a message to Donald Trump, and they seized it," stated John Feehery, a Republican strategist in Washington, during a phone interview. These gains hinted to some election analysts that Democrats might reclaim the U.S. House of Representatives in the upcoming year. Currently, Republicans maintain control over both the House and Senate, as well as the presidency. Dave Wasserman, who assesses U.S. House and state legislative races for the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, described the Virginia results as a "tidal wave." Despite the successes on Tuesday, Democrats remain entirely excluded from power in 26 state governments. Republicans dominate two-thirds of the legislative chambers throughout the United States. Aiming to rebuild, national Democrats have expressed renewed interest in legislative contests and elections further down the ballot this year. The Democratic National Committee effectively invested in mayoral races across various locations, from St. Petersburg, Florida, to Manchester, New Hampshire. "A key takeaway from yesterday is the necessity for us to compete everywhere, because victories are possible for Democrats," remarked DNC Chairman Tom Perez during a media conference call. Jessica Post, executive director of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, emphasized that national party leaders must keep their focus on local elections, even during a congressional election year. "Our lack of attention to state-level races has contributed to our current situation," she noted. "However, when we do prioritize them, we achieve success."

text: Last week, amidst the relentless monsoon rains in Mumbai, Mohammad Altaf stepped outside his residence for a cigarette. He was taken aback by a deafening crash followed by a massive cloud of dust. The six-storey Husainee building, which he had called home for just a month, had collapsed, trapping nearly 50 individuals inside. Tragically, thirty-four people lost their lives in the disaster, including a newborn baby. "It was shocking. I had come down for a smoke, and within two minutes the building was no more," recalled Altaf, who was unaware that housing authorities had declared the apartment structure unsafe six years prior in India’s financial capital. In the bustling city of 20 million, countless families continue to inhabit dilapidated buildings that have been officially deemed uninhabitable, and most residents are aware of this fact. Housing officials indicate that lax regulations prevent them from forcibly evicting residents. This year, the municipal corporation of the city identified 791 buildings as irreparable and hazardous for habitation; however, nearly 500 of these remain occupied, according to a municipal authority representative. While regulations differ from one country to another and even between states, most jurisdictions have greater authority to mandate evacuations. In his mid-thirties, Altaf, who is single, was residing with two co-workers in an apartment located in Bhendi Bazar, one of the oldest areas in the metropolis. His flatmates managed to escape with minor injuries to their knees and shoulders after leaping from their third-floor apartment. Authorities are still investigating the reasons behind the collapse, which occurred following prolonged heavy rainfall. The 117-year-old structure in Bhendi Bazar, a densely populated area characterized by narrow streets, shops, and tenements, was marked as unsafe by the Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Authority (MHADA) in 2011. Nevertheless, it continued to provide shelter for Altaf and his roommates, as well as five additional families, a warehouse for a sweet shop, and even a nursery located on the ground floor. The building’s owner, Hakimmudin Bootwala, noted that seven families had vacated by 2014, yet others declined to leave despite his repeated requests. One of these tenants had sub-leased the apartment to Altaf and his colleagues. "The people were my friends and neighbors first, and tenants later," stated the 73-year-old Bootwala. "I sincerely advised them to move out. The building had lots of problems, leakages. The roof was fine, but the walls had become really weak and porous." An official from MHADA explained that a law exists to compel residents to evacuate unsafe buildings, but enforcement is nearly impossible due to loopholes and legal obstacles. Evicting families with children and senior citizens, for example, could lead to complications, said the housing official, who requested anonymity as he was not authorized to communicate with the media. "We cut off the water and electricity supply to buildings identified as dangerous for living, but people find ways to obtain water and electricity from nearby structures," the official remarked. According to MHADA, which conducts routine assessments of buildings over 30 years old, more than 14,000 structures in the city have been identified as needing repairs, based on its latest inventory. Out of these, 9,000 — housing approximately 250,000 families — require redevelopment. The housing official further noted that the remaining 5,000 buildings are relatively safe due to regular maintenance performed by property owners in collaboration with the housing authority. Once regulators determine a building is in need of redevelopment, they must appoint a developer to either renovate or rebuild the structure for public housing or instruct private owners to engage one. The developer, in turn, is obligated to provide residents with alternative lodging until the renovation is completed, as mandated by state law in Mumbai. However, residents often express dissatisfaction, claiming that the alternative housing offered is too small, in poor condition, or located too far away. Seventy percent of tenants in both privately- and publicly-owned properties must consent to the redevelopment of their building.
source_text: Defying warnings, residents refuse to leave Mumbai's crumbling buildings. MUMBAI (Reuters) - On a sunny morning last week in Mumbai after two days of incessant monsoon rain, Mohammad Altaf had come out of his home for a cigarette when he heard a terrifying crash, followed by a huge swirl of dust. The six-storey Husainee building where he had lived for the last month had collapsed, trapping nearly 50 people. Thirty-four of them were killed, including a newborn baby.  It was shocking. I had come down for a smoke, and within two minutes the building was no more,  said Altaf, who says he was unaware the apartment block was declared unsafe by housing authorities in India s financial hub six years ago. Across the teeming city of 20 million people, thousands of families live in crumbling buildings that have been officially declared uninhabitable - and most of them know it. Housing officials say they cannot be forced out because of lax laws. This year, the city s municipal corporation classified 791 buildings as beyond repair and too dangerous to live in, but close to 500 of these continue to be occupied, a municipal authority official said. Although regulations vary from country to country and also from state to state, authorities in most places have more powers to order evacuations. Altaf, in his mid-thirties, is a bachelor and was living with two co-workers in the apartment in the Bhendi Bazar locality, one of the oldest in the metropolis. His two flatmates survived, with minor knee and shoulder injuries, after jumping out of their apartment on the third floor. Police say they have yet to determine the cause of the collapse, which came after days of intense rain.  The 117-year-old apartment block in Bhendi Bazar, a packed neighborhood of narrow streets, shops and tenements, was declared unsafe in 2011 by the regulator, the Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Authority (MHADA). Yet it continued to house Altaf and his flatmates, along with five other families, a sweet shop warehouse and even a nursery on the first floor.  The owner of the building, Hakimmudin Bootwala, said seven families moved out by 2014, but other tenants refused despite his urging. One of them had sub-let the apartment to Altaf and his colleagues.  The people were my friends and neighbors first, and tenants later,  said the 73-year-old.  I sincerely advised them to move out. The building had lots of problems, leakages. The roof was fine, but the walls had become really weak and porous.  An official at MHADA said there was a law to force residents to evacuate dangerous buildings but enforcing it was impossible because of loopholes and legal challenges. For instance, evicting children and senior citizens could cause trouble, said the housing official, who declined to be identified because he was not authorized to speak to the press.  We cut water and electricity supply of buildings that are identified as dangerous for living, but people manage to get water and electricity from nearby buildings,  said the  official. MHADA, which does a routine check of buildings that are older than 30 years, has identified more than 14,000 buildings in the city that need repair, according to its latest list.  Nine thousand of these, home to nearly 250,000 families, need to be redeveloped, the housing official said, adding that the other 5,000 were relatively safe due to regular maintenance work done by landowners in consultation with the housing body. Once regulators decide a building needs to redeveloped, they have to appoint a developer to renovate or rebuild the structure in the case of public housing, or order private owners to hire one. The developer, in turn, must offer residents alternative accommodation until the work is completed, according to state law in Mumbai.  But residents often complain the housing they are offered is too small, shabby or too far away.  Seventy percent of tenants of both privately- and publicly-owned buildings must agree to redevelop their building according to state rules, or no redevelopment work can commence. Building owners say residents are often unrealistic, refusing to leave even if the alternative housing is adequate. Some worry they could lose their tenancy if they move. The MHADA official said the agency does everything it can to get residents and developers to clinch an agreement, but that the process often gets mired in legal challenges.  The problems of the Husainee building were typical. A neighborhood body, the Saifee Burhani Upliftment Trust, had been selected by its owner in 2009 to redevelop the building along with other buildings in the neighborhood, even before the Husainee had been declared unsafe by MHADA. A trust official told Reuters it offered alternative housing to the residents in a place around 2.5 km (1.5 miles) from the building. The official said the trust repeated the offer in 2011 after MHADA declared the building unsafe.  A Reuters team visited the complex where the Husainee families who had agreed to move had been relocated, a gated high-rise complex with guards and a playground for kids. Residents said they were happy with their new apartments, although they complained about the distance to work.  But other Husainee families refused to move. MHADA officials said the trust was in charge of ensuring relocation and redevelopment and MHADA could not force the Husainee families to leave.  The trust has said it has repeatedly tried to evict families from Husainee but some residents refused to move.      This incident should be a wake-up call for the city, and a policy needs to be actioned to evict non-cooperating tenants who continue to live in dilapidated buildings,  the trust said in a  written reply to Reuters queries. Building owner Bootwala says the residents who refused to leave argued they did not want to upend their lives by moving to a new neighborhood. Also, they did not know how long it would take to renovate the building. Reuters was unable to talk to other residents from Husainee, but neighbors in Bhendi Bazar told similar stories. Despite knowing their buildings were unsafe, many of them did not want to leave.  A man in his 50s in the neighborhood, who refused to give his name, said he was living in a more than 100-year old building that had been deemed unsafe. The developer offered him temporary housing 13 km (8 miles) away, but he said that was too far.  I spent my entire life here. I know every lane in this area,  the man said.  My children s college, my workplace, everything is closer from here.

text: Later this month, the emergency manager of Detroit Public Schools, Darnell Earley, will resign, as confirmed by Michigan Governor Rick Snyder on Tuesday. Earley has faced backlash from the teachers union and African American state legislators regarding the deteriorating condition of the schools in the city. He is set to depart from his role on February 29, according to a statement released by the governor. Since January 2015, Earley has been overseeing the Detroit school system, having previously managed the city of Flint, which has been grappling with a lead-contaminated water crisis. The Detroit school district is burdened with an overwhelming debt of $3.5 billion, which includes $1.7 billion in bonds that are secured by property taxes. The district is experiencing a decline in student enrollment. Significant pension and debt responsibilities are putting the district at risk of running out of funds by April. The governor indicated that should the state Senate approve legislation aimed at reforming the school system and addressing the debt soon, local control might be restored to the district. Without measures to tackle the debt, Snyder warned that the school system would face a state of "virtually insolvency" by April. A report released in November by Earley suggested that if Detroit's school system were to declare bankruptcy, the liabilities for pensions and bonds could shift to both state and local governments. The governor, who must give his approval for bankruptcy proceedings, is not expected to support such an action. On Tuesday, Snyder praised Earley for doing a "very good job under some very difficult circumstances," highlighting efforts to restructure the school system, reduce expenses, and work towards stabilizing student enrollment. Before the month concludes, the governor plans to appoint a transitional leader to implement a strategy for restructuring the district’s academic and financial situations. Last week, the Michigan black legislative caucus urged Snyder to dismiss Earley from his position. Additionally, the union representing Detroit public school teachers filed a lawsuit against the district, seeking Earley’s immediate removal and the reinstatement of local control, along with a plan to repair the district’s failing infrastructure. Ivy Bailey, who is the interim president of the Detroit Federation of Teachers, referred to Earley’s exit as a "step in the right direction." During Earley’s management in Flint, the city changed its water source from Detroit to the Flint River in April 2014, but reverted back last October after discovering elevated lead levels in blood tests of children from Flint. Lead is known to be a neurotoxin that can harm brain function and lead to other health issues. Earley has claimed that he should not be held responsible for this situation, as the decision was made prior to his appointment.
source_text: Detroit school system's manager to step down this month. DETROIT (Reuters) - Detroit Public Schools’ emergency manager Darnell Earley is stepping down later this month, Michigan Governor Rick Snyder said on Tuesday. Earley, who has drawn criticism from the teachers union and black state lawmakers for the crumbling state of the city’s schools, will leave the school district on Feb. 29, the governor said in a statement.  Earley, who had formerly presided over the city of Flint and its now lead-contaminated water system, has served as manager of the Detroit schools since January 2015. The school system is drowning under $3.5 billion of debt, including $1.7 billion of bonds backed by property taxes. Detroit Public Schools is suffering from declining enrollment. Heavy pension and debt obligations have left the district in danger of running out of cash in April. The governor said if the state Senate passes legislation  reorganizing the school and tackling the debt soon, the school system could revert to some form of local control. If the debt is not addressed, the system will be “virtually insolvent” by April, Snyder said. A November report by Earley said a bankruptcy by Detroit’s school system could shift liabilities for pensions and bonds to the state and local governments. The governor, whose approval is needed for the system to file for bankruptcy, is unlikely to support such a move. Snyder said on Tuesday that Earley has done a “very good job under some very difficult circumstances,” restructuring the school system, cutting costs and working to stabilize student enrollment.    The governor said he will appoint a transition leader before the end of the month to set in place his plan to restructure the system to address the district’s academics and finances.     The Michigan black legislative caucus last week asked Snyder to fire Earley. Also last week, the union for Detroit public school teachers sued the district, demanding Earley’s immediate removal and a return of local control with a plan to repair the district’s crumbling buildings. Ivy Bailey, interim president of the Detroit Federation of Teachers, called Earley’s departure a “step in the right direction.” Under Earley’s leadership as emergency manager of Flint, the city switched its water supply from Detroit to the Flint River in April 2014. It switched back last October after tests found high lead levels in blood samples from Flint children. Lead is a neurotoxin that can damage the brain and cause other health problems. Earley has said he is not to blame for the problem since the decision was made before his tenure.

text: A Chinese official stated on Wednesday that the unsuccessful bid for independence by Catalonia serves as evidence that Taiwan's aspirations for independence are also destined to fail, emphasizing that national unity is essential for every nation. China has consistently expressed its opposition to independence or secessionist movements globally, while it maintains a stance of non-interference in the domestic affairs of other countries. Beijing has reiterated its disapproval of any attempts to disintegrate Spain. Following a failed referendum, Madrid took control over Catalonia last month after the Spanish prime minister dismissed the region's secessionist leadership, which had declared independence from Spain. This matter holds particular significance for China due to the situation of Taiwan, a self-governing and democratic region that China claims as its own territory, although many residents desire to declare formal independence, which Beijing views as a critical boundary. Ma Xiaoguang, the spokesperson for China's Taiwan Affairs Office, remarked that the collapse of Catalonia's independence movement is a positive development. He stated during a routine press briefing, "The failure of the Catalonia referendum fully shows that protecting national sovereignty and territorial integrity is a paramount national interest for east or west. So Taiwan independence is doomed to failure." Relations between Beijing and Taipei have deteriorated significantly since Tsai Ing-wen was elected president of Taiwan last year. China perceives her as advocating for formal independence for Taiwan. In contrast, Tsai asserts that her goal is to maintain peaceful relations with China, while also safeguarding Taiwan's democracy and security. Consequently, China has halted a regular dialogue mechanism with Taiwan, increased military exercises in the vicinity of the island, and has attempted to limit Taiwan's international presence by diminishing its remaining diplomatic allies. Recently, Taiwan announced that its environmental minister was barred from participating in a U.N. climate conference in Germany, despite having credentials as a non-governmental attendee, due to Chinese pressure. Ma indicated that Taiwan should accept responsibility for the strained relations and its exclusion from events like the climate summit. He emphasized that the Taiwan side shouldn't shift blame onto others when they themselves are at fault and should sincerely contemplate their actions.
source_text: China says Catalonia situation shows Taiwan independence effort doomed to fail. BEIJING (Reuters) - The failure of Catalonia s effort to declare independence shows that Taiwan independence is also doomed to fail as national unity is paramount for all countries, a Chinese official said on Wednesday. China takes a dim view of independence or secessionist movements around the world, while saying it adheres to a policy of non-interference in other nations  internal affairs. Beijing has said it opposes any actions to split Spain. Last month Madrid assumed direct rule over Catalonia after the Spanish prime minister sacked the region s secessionist government which had declared independence from Spain following an attempted referendum. The issue is particularly sensitive for China because of the status of self-ruled and democratic Taiwan, claimed by China as its inherent territory, but where many people would like to proclaim formal independence, a red line for Beijing. The failure of Catalonia s independence bid was a good thing, said Ma Xiaoguang, the spokesman of China s policy-making Taiwan Affairs Office.  The failure of the Catalonia referendum fully shows that protecting national sovereignty and territorial integrity is a paramount national interest for east or west,  Ma told a regular news briefing.  So Taiwan independence is doomed to failure.  Relations between Beijing and Taipei have nosedived since the island elected Tsai Ing-wen as president last year. China believes she wants formal independence for Taiwan. Tsai says she wants to maintain peace with China, but will defend Taiwan s democracy and security. China has suspended a regular dialogue mechanism with Taiwan, stepped up military drills around the island and sought to squeeze its international space by siphoning off Taiwan s remaining diplomatic allies. This week, Taiwan said its environment minister had been prevented from attending an annual U.N. climate meeting in Germany, despite credentials as a non-governmental participant, due to pressure from China. Ma said Taiwan had itself to blame for the poor state of ties and its inability to participate in events such as the climate talks.  The Taiwan side shouldn t put blame on others while they themselves are to blame, and should earnestly reflect on things,  he added.

text: During a statement made in New York on Saturday, Hillary Clinton, the Democratic presidential hopeful, expressed her regret over her previous remark that categorized "half" of Donald Trump’s supporters as belonging in a "basket of deplorables." text: The foreign ministry of North Korea has declared that the latest sanctions imposed by the United Nations are equivalent to an act of war. On Sunday, the ministry articulated that these measures represent a total economic blockade against the nation, threatening retaliation against those who endorsed the sanctions. The U.N. Security Council reached a unanimous decision on Friday to implement new sanctions following North Korea's recent test of an intercontinental ballistic missile. The aim of these sanctions is to restrict North Korea's access to refined petroleum products and crude oil, as well as to limit its foreign workers' earnings. The resolution from the U.N. seeks to reduce refined petroleum exports to North Korea by nearly 90 percent, setting a cap at 500,000 barrels per year. Additionally, in a last-minute modification, the resolution now requires the repatriation of North Korean laborers abroad within a period of 24 months, as opposed to the initially proposed 12-month timeline. Crude oil supplies to North Korea are also capped at 4 million barrels annually, with the Council pledging further reductions should the nation conduct another nuclear test or launch another ICBM. In a statement released via the official KCNA news outlet, North Korea's foreign ministry accused the United States of being increasingly frantic due to its nuclear capabilities, resulting in a push to impose the severest sanctions on the country. The ministry characterized the new resolution as a complete economic blockade of North Korea. They described the sanctions resolution orchestrated by the U.S. and its allies as a serious violation of the sovereignty of the Republic, branding it an act of war that disrupts peace and stability in both the Korean peninsula and the surrounding region, and firmly rejected the resolution. The foreign ministry warned that there is no greater error than the misjudgment that the U.S. and its allies could halt the triumphant progress of North Korea, which has successfully completed the historic task of establishing a state nuclear force through outdated sanctions. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un announced the completion of the nuclear force on November 29 following the largest ICBM test conducted by the nation, which they claimed can reach all parts of the United States. During a meeting with the ruling Workers' Party members on Friday, Kim asserted that despite facing significant shortages and difficulties due to the despicable actions of adversaries, the country had successfully achieved the historic objective of completing its state nuclear force. North Korea's official title is the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK). In response, South Korea's foreign ministry acknowledged the North Korean statement regarding the new sanctions, reiterating its stance that these actions serve as a serious warning from the international community. They maintained that the region must immediately halt reckless provocations and pursue dialogue aimed at denuclearization and peace. The North Korean foreign ministry defended its nuclear arsenal, claiming it serves as a self-defensive deterrent and does not contravene international law. They expressed commitment to further strengthen their nuclear deterrence, aiming to eliminate U.S. nuclear threats, blackmail, and hostile actions by achieving a practical balance of military power with the U.S. The ministry emphasized that the U.S. must not forget, even for a moment, the existence of the DPRK, which has quickly evolved into a strategic state capable of posing a significant nuclear threat to the U.S. mainland. North Korea warned that nations that voted in favor of the sanctions would suffer consequences. Those countries that supported this sanctions resolution will be held fully accountable for all outcomes resulting from it, and North Korea pledged to ensure that they would face severe repercussions for their actions. Both China and Russia, longstanding allies of North Korea, expressed their support for the latest U.N. sanctions. Tensions have escalated in light of North Korea's ongoing nuclear and missile initiatives, which it continues to pursue in defiance of years of U.N. resolutions.
source_text: North Korea says new U.N. sanctions an act of war. BEIJING/SEOUL (Reuters) - The latest U.N. sanctions against North Korea are an act of war and tantamount to a complete economic blockade against it, North Korea s foreign ministry said on Sunday, threatening to punish those who supported the measure. The U.N. Security Council unanimously imposed new sanctions on North Korea on Friday for its recent intercontinental ballistic missile test, seeking to limit its access to refined petroleum products and crude oil and its earnings from workers abroad. The U.N. resolution seeks to ban nearly 90 percent of refined petroleum exports to North Korea by capping them at 500,000 barrels a year and, in a last-minute change, demands the repatriation of North Koreans working abroad within 24 months, instead of 12 months as first proposed. The U.S.-drafted resolution also caps crude oil supplies to North Korea at 4 million barrels a year and commits the Council to further reductions if it were to conduct another nuclear test or launch another ICBM. In a statement carried by the official KCNA news agency, North Korea s foreign ministry said the United States was terrified by its nuclear force and was getting  more and more frenzied in the moves to impose the harshest-ever sanctions and pressure on our country . The new resolution was tantamount to a complete economic blockade of North Korea, the ministry said.  We define this  sanctions resolution  rigged up by the U.S. and its followers as a grave infringement upon the sovereignty of our Republic, as an act of war violating peace and stability in the Korean peninsula and the region and categorically reject the  resolution ,  it said.  There is no more fatal blunder than the miscalculation that the U.S. and its followers could check by already worn-out  sanctions  the victorious advance of our people who have brilliantly accomplished the great historic cause of completing the state nuclear force , the ministry said. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on Nov. 29 declared the nuclear force complete after the test of North Korea s largest-ever ICBM test, which the country said puts all of the United States within range.  Kim told a meeting of members of the ruling Workers  Party on Friday that the country  successfully realized the historic cause of completing the state nuclear force  despite  short supply in everything and manifold difficulties and ordeals owing to the despicable anti-DPRK moves of the enemies . North Korea s official name is the Democratic People s Republic of Korea (DPRK). South Korea s foreign ministry told Reuters it is aware of the North Korean statement on the new sanctions, again highlighting its position that they are a  grave warning by the international community that the region has no option but to immediately cease reckless provocations, and take the path of dialogue for denuclearization and peace . The North Korean foreign ministry said its nuclear weapons were a self-defensive deterrence not in contradiction of international law.  We will further consolidate our self-defensive nuclear deterrence aimed at fundamentally eradicating the U.S. nuclear threats, blackmail and hostile moves by establishing the practical balance of force with the U.S,  it said.  The U.S. should not forget even a second the entity of the DPRK which rapidly emerged as a strategic state capable of posing a substantial nuclear threat to the U.S. mainland,  it added. North Korea said those who voted for the sanctions would face its wrath.  Those countries that raised their hands in favor of this  sanctions resolution  shall be held completely responsible for all the consequences to be caused by the  resolution  and we will make sure for ever and ever that they pay heavy price for what they have done.  The North s old allies China and Russia both supported the latest U.N. sanctions. Tension has been rising over North Korea s nuclear and missile programs, which it pursues in defiance of years of U.N. Security Council resolutions, with bellicose rhetoric coming from both Pyongyang and the White House. In November, North Korea demanded a halt to what it called  brutal sanctions , saying a round imposed after its sixth and most powerful nuclear test on Sept. 3 constituted genocide. U.S. diplomats have made clear they are seeking a diplomatic solution but proposed the new, tougher sanctions resolution to ratchet up pressure on North Korea s leader. China, with which North Korea does some 90 percent of its trade, has repeatedly called for calm and restraint from all sides.  China said on Saturday the new resolution also reiterated the need for a peaceful resolution via talks and that all sides needed to take steps to reduce tensions. Chinese state-run tabloid the Global Times said on Saturday  the tougher resolution was aimed at preventing war. It suggested the United States had wanted an even harsher resolution, and noted there was no indication in the resolution that the United Nations could grant the United States permission for military action.  The difference between the new resolution and the original U.S. proposal reflects the will of China and Russia to prevent war and chaos on the Korean Peninsula. If the U.S. proposals were accepted, only war is foreseeable,  it said in an editorial.

text: BANGKOK (Reuters) - As officials donned traditional garments and black attire, drums and music filled the air during Saturday's rehearsal for the elaborate funeral procession of the late King Bhumibol Adulyadej of Thailand. The cremation, set to occur next week, is anticipated to draw a crowd of 250,000 mourners. A replica of a golden urn, historically used to hold the remains of deceased kings, was held by some participants. Currently, the king's body rests in a coffin, yet the urn continues to symbolize the monarch's remains. The rehearsal for the procession, which was projected to last around five hours, moved past numerous mourners dressed in black within Bangkok's historic district. Some attendees appeared visibly touched, while others clutched gold-framed images of the late monarch. The military government has allocated 3 billion baht (approximately $90 million) for the extravagant funeral. Nearly a year was spent on preparations, with thousands of artisans engaged in constructing an intricate display of gold-tipped Thai pavilions in a square located in front of the magnificent Grand Palace. King Bhumibol, who passed away on October 13 last year at the age of 87, reigned over Thailand for seven decades and is regarded by many as having restored the monarchy's prestige. A resurgence in the monarchy's popularity was bolstered by a powerful public relations campaign; the evening news in Thailand features a daily segment about the royals, and the late king frequently appeared in his youth, traveling across the nation to connect with the impoverished and marginalized. This public relations effort played a significant role in elevating the king's status to that of a demi-god among his 68 million subjects. The five-day funeral is expected to include numerous heads of state, including Bhutan's King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck and Japan's Prince Akishino and Princess Kiko, among others. Analysts suggest that the period following the funeral may bring uncertainty for many Thais, highlighting the king's historical role as a moral guide and mediator during times of political turmoil. Last year, King Maha Vajiralongkorn, the late king's only son, officially took the throne, although his coronation will occur after his father's funeral. The cremation is scheduled for October 26. This day has been declared a national holiday, leading many businesses to announce their plans to either close for the entire day or shut down by midday. Throughout the nation, over 10,000 7-Eleven convenience stores, a common choice for many Thais, will be closed on that day.

text: As the investigation into contacts between Donald Trump’s election campaign and Russia unfolds, former national security adviser Michael Flynn may play a pivotal role, according to sources familiar with the inquiry. On Friday, it was reported that Flynn's legal team has ceased communication with Trump’s attorneys, a development that could be significant for the ongoing probe. Robert Kelner, Flynn’s attorney, reportedly informed Trump’s private lawyer, John Dowd, on Wednesday that discussions between the two sides could no longer continue, as per two individuals acquainted with the conversation. This information was first disclosed by The New York Times. Flynn, a retired Army general, is a crucial participant in the federal investigation spearheaded by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, which is examining the possibility of collusion between Trump associates and alleged Russian efforts to influence the 2016 presidential election. It remains uncertain whether Kelner's call was prompted by a plea agreement that allows Flynn to cooperate with Mueller or whether Flynn has opted to engage directly with the Special Counsel, according to two other sources. Jay Sekulow, another attorney representing Trump, stated on Thursday, "No one should draw the conclusion that this means anything about General Flynn cooperating against the president." On Friday, Dowd chose not to comment on the situation, nor did Peter Carr, who serves as Mueller’s spokesperson. Kelner also refrained from making any statements. Officials from the White House declined to provide any remarks as well. Flynn's cooperation would represent a significant advantage for Mueller’s investigation, given that he served as a senior campaign adviser before his appointment as Trump’s national security adviser in the White House. Back in March, while attempting to secure immunity for his client to testify before congressional inquiries about the matter, Kelner remarked, "Mr. Flynn certainly has a story to tell, and he certainly wants to tell it, should the circumstances permit." Two individuals familiar with Mueller's investigation indicated that Flynn might offer valuable information regarding three primary areas of focus. These areas include any potential collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia during the 2016 election, the possibility of money laundering and other financial crimes involving Trump associates, and whether Trump attempted to obstruct justice when he dismissed former FBI Director James Comey in May, as Comey was investigating the Trump campaign’s interactions with Russia. Russia has consistently denied any interference in the elections, while Trump has repeatedly asserted that there was no collusion between his campaign and Russia, labeling the inquiry as a witch hunt. According to two congressional officials engaged in distinct investigations into the Trump campaign’s Russia connections, a significant line of inquiry is whether Flynn or other Trump advisers ever proposed that U.S. economic sanctions against Russia could be lifted in exchange for advantageous business arrangements. Potential arrangements could involve a planned commercial nuclear power project that Flynn has actively promoted in recent years to potential clients in the Middle East, as reported by sources knowledgeable about the project. One of the congressional officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, noted, "At this point, there is no evidence of an effort to negotiate that kind of deal, but Flynn is near the top of the list of people who probably would know if there was any such effort." Trump terminated Flynn's employment on February 13, following revelations that Flynn had discussed U.S. sanctions with then-Russian Ambassador Sergei Kislyak in December, prior to Trump's inauguration, and subsequently misled Vice President Mike Pence regarding those discussions. Flynn has acknowledged having interactions with Kislyak dating back to 2013, but has not disclosed the specifics of their conversations that occurred during Trump’s campaign and after his election, merely stating that their discussions encompassed various topics. According to sources knowledgeable about the investigation, Flynn has been under scrutiny by the special counsel in multiple respects. Mueller has been probing whether Flynn knowingly made false statements.

It was not clear whether Kelner made the call because he had negotiated a plea agreement with Mueller for Flynn to cooperate in the probe, or because Flynn had decided to engage with Mueller, said two other sources. “No one should draw the conclusion that this means anything about General Flynn cooperating against the president,” Jay Sekulow, another attorney for Trump, said on Thursday.     Dowd on Friday declined to comment on the matter, as did Peter Carr, Mueller’s spokesman. Kelner also declined to comment. White House officials also have declined to comment. In March, as he unsuccessfully sought immunity for his client to testify to House and Senate investigations into the issue, Kelner said, “Mr. Flynn certainly has a story to tell, and he certainly wants to tell it, should the circumstances permit.”  Two sources familiar with Mueller’s investigation said Flynn may be able to provide insight into three major areas of inquiry. Flynn also has come under scrutiny for work on behalf of Russian clients, and over whether his work for a businessman with ties to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan was lawful.  Mueller has been investigating Flynn’s son, Michael Flynn, Jr.’s, involvement in some of his father’s business dealings in Russia, Turkey, and elsewhere, the sources said, and that could provide a potent additional incentive for Flynn to cooperate. text: After a contentious battle for a U.S. Senate seat, Doug Jones, a Democrat from Alabama, urged his Republican opponent to accept the results and assist in mending the state’s divisions. On Thursday, Jones made his appeal following a hard-fought election week. His rival, Roy Moore, a conservative Christian Republican, had his campaign overshadowed by allegations of inappropriate conduct with teenage girls during his 30s. On Wednesday night, Moore issued a second statement but did not acknowledge defeat. With a narrow lead of 1.5 percentage points, Jones, a former federal prosecutor, is poised to be the first Democrat in a Senate seat in Alabama in 25 years, which reduces the Republican majority in the Senate to 51 out of 100 seats. This shift could complicate the GOP's efforts to advance President Donald Trump’s initiatives. As of now, 99 percent of the votes have been counted, and Alabama's Republican secretary of state indicated that the outstanding ballots from Tuesday's election are unlikely to alter the margin sufficiently to necessitate a recount. In an NBC interview, Jones expressed confidence about the election results. He stated, "It’s time to move on. The people of Alabama have now spoken ... Let’s get this behind us so the people of Alabama can get someone in there and start working for them.” When asked if Moore should concede, White House spokesperson Sarah Sanders remarked to the press, "I’m surprised. It sounds like it ... should have already taken place.” On Wednesday, Jones mentioned that he had received congratulatory calls from Trump, who previously endorsed Moore, along with Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. Sanders noted, "The president’s already called and congratulated Doug Jones and expressed his willingness to work with him and meet with him when he arrives.”
source_text: Alabama Senate race winner urges Republican rival to 'move on'. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Alabama Democrat Doug Jones, who won a bitter fight for a U.S. Senate seat this week, on Thursday called on his Republican opponent to concede the race and help heal the Southern state after a deeply divisive contest. Roy Moore, the conservative Christian Republican whose campaign was tainted by accusations that he pursued teenaged girls while in his 30s, made a second statement on Wednesday night in which he did not concede the election. Jones, a former federal prosecutor, will be the first Democrat to hold a Senate seat in Alabama in a quarter-century, narrowing Republicans’ majority in the Senate to 51 of 100 seats and potentially making it more difficult for them to pursue President Donald Trump’s agenda. With 99 percent of the vote counted, Jones had a lead of 1.5 percentage points over Moore, a former Alabama Supreme Court Justice. Alabama’s secretary of state, a Republican, has said the remaining ballots from Tuesday’s election were unlikely to shrink the victory to the half a percentage point margin required to trigger a recount. Jones said in an interview with NBC that he was confident of the outcome. “It’s time to move on,” he said. “The people of Alabama have now spoken ... Let’s get this behind us so the people of Alabama can get someone in there and start working for them.” Asked whether Moore should concede, White House spokeswoman Sarah Sanders told reporters, “I’m surprised. It sounds like it ... should have already taken place.” Jones on Wednesday said he had received congratulatory phone calls from Trump, who had endorsed Moore, as well as Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. “The president’s already called and congratulated Doug Jones and expressed his willingness to work with him and meet with him when he arrives,” Sanders said.

text: Next month, a summit will take place between South Korean President Moon Jae-in and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing to improve relations that have been strained due to a year-long dispute over the placement of a U.S. missile defense system in South Korea, according to an announcement from Seoul's foreign ministry on Thursday. source_text: South Korea, China to hold summit next month to mend ties. (Reuters) - South Korean President Moon Jae-in will visit Beijing next month for a summit with China s Xi Jinping as the two countries seek to mend ties frayed by a year-long spat over the deployment of a U.S. anti-missile system in South Korea, Seoul s foreign ministry said on Thursday. text: CARACAS (Reuters) - In a rerun of the October election, Omar Prieto, representing Venezuela's ruling Socialist Party, secured the governorship of Zulia state by receiving 57 percent of the votes, according to election officials on Sunday. source_text: Venezuela socialists win Zulia state governorship. CARACAS (Reuters) - The candidate for Venezuela s ruling Socialist Party, Omar Prieto, won the governorship of western Zulia state with 57 percent of the ballots in a rerun of an October vote, election authorities said on Sunday. Turnout for nationwide mayoral elections, also being held on Sunday, was 47 percent, the national election board said.
