text: The U.S. Justice Department announced a review on Thursday concerning the Federal Bureau of Investigation's choice to disclose an investigation into Hillary Clinton’s emails right before the presidential election in November, a decision Clinton claims contributed to her loss. According to a statement from the Office of Inspector General, the inquiry will examine the circumstances surrounding public statements made by FBI Director James Comey about the Clinton case, and whether those statements were influenced by "improper considerations." The issue centers on Clinton's use of a private email server for her official communications while she served as Secretary of State under President Barack Obama, which included messages later found to have classified content.  Inspector General Michael Horowitz's office indicated that the decision to initiate this review stemmed from requests made by various congressional oversight committee leaders, organizations, and members of the public. Although the FBI ultimately chose not to recommend charges against Clinton, Democrats argued that Comey’s announcement negatively impacted her campaign right before the election, leading to accusations that his actions were politically motivated. Typically, law enforcement entities, including the FBI, refrain from revealing details about investigations that do not result in criminal charges. Should the review uncover evidence of wrongdoing, officials implicated may face disciplinary measures. Comey expressed his intent to fully cooperate with the investigation and thanked Horowitz for conducting the review. He remarked, "He is professional and independent and ... I hope very much he is able to share his conclusions and observations with the public because everyone will benefit from thoughtful evaluation and transparency regarding this matter." Brian Fallon, who is Clinton’s spokesperson, stated to MSNBC on Thursday that Comey’s actions warranted an independent examination. Senator Dick Durbin, the second-ranking Democrat in the U.S. Senate, criticized Comey’s comments, claiming they were neither "fair, professional nor in accordance with the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s policies." President-elect Donald Trump, set to take office on January 20, does not have the authority to terminate the investigation. However, federal law allows U.S. presidents to remove inspectors general from federal agencies, provided they furnish Congress with a written rationale for the dismissal at least 30 days prior. During the campaign, Trump frequently led crowds in chants of "lock her up!" and repeatedly accused Clinton of wrongdoing regarding her emails. In a debate held in October, he claimed she would "be in jail" if he were to assume the presidency; however, he later stated that he would not seek to prosecute her.  Comey made two public declarations regarding the FBI’s investigation into Clinton’s emails in 2016. In July, he conducted a press conference and testified before Congress to clarify why the FBI opted not to recommend prosecution of Clinton, asserting that she was "extremely careless" yet should not be charged with gross negligence or any other federal crime. Then, in October, just under two weeks before the election on November 8, Comey sent a letter to Congress members indicating that the FBI was reopening the investigation due to new emails discovered on the computer of former Representative Anthony Weiner, who is married to one of Clinton’s senior aides. U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch had previously informed Comey the day before he dispatched the letter that doing so would conflict with official Justice Department guidelines, which advise employees to "never select the timing of investigative steps ... for the purpose of affecting any election." Comey inquired whether he was being explicitly instructed not to send the letter, and Lynch never explicitly ordered him not to do so, as reported by a senior government official to Reuters.
source_text: FBI investigated over pre-election decisions on Clinton email. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. Justice Department on Thursday said it would probe a Federal Bureau of Investigation decision to announce an inquiry into Hillary Clinton’s emails shortly before the November presidential election, a move she has blamed as a factor in her defeat. The Justice Department’s Office of Inspector General said in a statement that its investigation would focus in part on decisions leading up to public statements by FBI Director James Comey regarding the Clinton investigation and whether they may have been based on “improper considerations.” The controversy involved Clinton’s use of a private email server for official correspondence when she was secretary of state under President Barack Obama, including for messages that were later determined to contain classified information.      The office of Inspector General Michael Horowitz said it decided to open the review “in response to requests from numerous chairmen and ranking members of congressional oversight committees, various organizations and members of the public.” Although the FBI ultimately decided not to refer Clinton’s case for prosecution, Democrats said Comey’s announcement damaged her with voters right before the election, and he faced complaints that his moves were politically motivated. Law enforcement authorities, including the FBI, by custom do not disclose information about investigations that do not end in criminal charges.   If the review finds evidence of misconduct, any officials involved would be referred for disciplinary action.  In a statement, Comey said the FBI would cooperate fully and he was “grateful” to Horowitz for the probe.  “He is professional and independent and ... I hope very much he is able to share his conclusions and observations with the public because everyone will benefit from thoughtful evaluation and transparency regarding this matter.” Brian Fallon, Clinton’s spokesman, told MSNBC on Thursday that Comey’s actions “cried out for an independent review.” Senator Dick Durbin, the No. 2 Democrat in the U.S. Senate said Comey’s statements were not “fair, professional or consistent with the policies of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.”   President-elect Donald Trump, who will be sworn in Jan. 20, will not have the power to dismiss the probe. But federal law permits U.S. presidents to dismiss inspectors general for federal agencies, as long as the president provides Congress a written justification for the removal 30 days in advance.  Often leading crowds in chants of “lock her up!” during the election campaign, Trump as a candidate repeatedly accused Clinton of illegal conduct over the emails. In a debate in October, he vowed she would “be in jail” over the matter if he became president, but he has since said he would not pursue prosecution. PRE-ELECTION ANNOUNCEMENT  Comey publicly announced the status of the agency’s investigation into Clinton’s emails two times in 2016.  In July, Comey held a press conference and testified before Congress to explain why the FBI had decided not to refer Clinton for prosecution, explaining that she was “extremely careless” but should not be charged with gross negligence or any other federal crime.  In October, less than two weeks before the Nov. 8 election, Comey sent members of Congress a letter saying the FBI was resuming the investigation because of new emails found on the computer of disgraced former Representative Anthony Weiner, the husband of one of Clinton’s top aides. U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch had informed Comey the day before he sent the letter that doing so would conflict with official Justice Department guidance that instructs employees to “never select the timing of investigative steps ... for the purpose of affecting any election.” Comey asked whether he was being explicitly directed not to send the letter, and Lynch never gave Comey the order not to do so, a senior government official told Reuters at the time. On Nov. 6, Comey said the investigation into Weiner’s computer produced no new evidence that would incriminate Clinton.     Republican Senator Chuck Grassley, who chairs the Senate Judiciary Committee, on Thursday commended Horowitz for opening the probe.  “Conspicuously absent, though, is any specific reference to the attorney general’s failure to recuse herself from the probe, particularly after her meeting with former President (Bill) Clinton,” said Grassley in a statement. That half-hour meeting, which took place in June on board Lynch’s plane while it was parked on the tarmac in Phoenix, drew criticism that Lynch was politically biased and unfit to oversee the investigation into Hillary Clinton’s email server. Critics of Comey’s decisions also said he could be in violation of the Hatch Act, a 1939 law that bars government employees from interfering with U.S. elections.

text: A tragic mass shooting in Orlando, Florida has presented Donald Trump with an opportunity to address an issue he has often leveraged for political gain—the perceived threat from Islamist extremists and his proposal to restrict Muslim immigration to the United States. This situation could serve as a pivotal moment to rejuvenate his struggling presidential campaign. However, while grassroots voters may respond favorably to Trump’s renewed advocacy for a ban on certain Muslim immigrants, his initial response to this horrific event has not resonated positively with established Republican foreign-policy leaders who have distanced themselves from the New York businessman. Peter Feaver, a former high-ranking National Security Council aide under George W. Bush, remarked, "It’s a missed opportunity to present a different image. He has doubled down on policies I oppose and that aren’t going to solve the problem." In a speech delivered in New Hampshire on Monday, Trump proposed halting immigration from nations that have a documented history of terrorism against the United States. He claimed that radical Muslim immigrants are "trying to take over our children and convince them how wonderful ISIS (Islamic State) is." Following the tragic mass murder in the U.S., which left 50 individuals dead, Trump quickly adjusted his speech, shifting from a general critique of Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton to a grave warning about the dangers posed by Islamist militants. Although the Islamic State has asserted responsibility for the attack, U.S. officials have indicated that Omar Mateen’s motivations remain unclear and that he had no established direct connections to the group based in Syria. They suggested that Mateen was possibly radicalized online. Just a week earlier, the presumptive Republican nominee faced significant challenges; he was under fire from fellow Republicans for his remarks regarding a federal judge's Hispanic heritage, and polls showed Clinton gaining ground. A renewed emphasis on national security might provide Trump the opportunity to broaden his appeal to undecided voters and to the Republican foreign-policy establishment. While Trump occasionally appears to take pleasure in opposing the establishment, the dissatisfaction among the party’s hawkish members is more than mere frustration. This discord suggests that should Trump ascend to the presidency, attracting skilled and seasoned advisers could prove challenging. Max Boot, a prominent conservative figure at the Council on Foreign Relations, noted that the Orlando tragedy "could have provided an opening for Trump to rally Republicans against terrorism." Yet Boot criticized Trump for being "partisan and petty." He condemned Trump’s insinuation on Monday that President Barack Obama may have sympathies for radicalized Muslims, as well as his revival of the proposed Muslim ban. "His performance has been in character," Boot remarked, "which is to say appalling." Mainstream Republicans have been unsettled by Trump's promises to dismantle international trade agreements, his insistence that Mexico finance a border wall, and his skepticism regarding foundational U.S. foreign policy commitments like security assurances to NATO and allies in Asia. In contrast, Clinton delivered a markedly different address on Monday, advocating for "statesmanship, not partisanship" and emphasizing the need for "clear, rational discussion" on safeguarding the nation from terrorist threats. Eliot Cohen, a senior State Department official during the Bush administration, characterized Trump’s response to the shooting as "opportunistic and shallow" and not reflective of what Americans expect from a president. Lanhee Chen, a former senior aide to Mitt Romney's 2012 presidential campaign, expressed doubt about Trump’s ability to reshape his public persona. "While it would be true in most cases that a significant speech like this could reset the decks, I think the challenge with Donald Trump is always who he is at his core," Chen commented. Nevertheless, voters represent a different story. Trump's rapid ascendance within the Republican Party was, in part, fueled by the aggressive rhetoric he employed regarding immigrants and refugees.
source_text: Trump's post-Orlando message falls flat with Republican establishment. WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - The mass shooting in Orlando, Florida has allowed Donald Trump to seize upon a familiar issue he has used to great advantage -the threat of Islamist militants and his plan to limit Muslim immigration to the United States, offering him what could be a crucial moment to re-boot his sputtering presidential campaign.  But while rank-and-file voters might respond positively to Trump’s renewed call for a ban on some Muslims entering the country, his reaction to the massacre showed few initial signs of winning over Republican foreign-policy figures who have spurned the New York mogul. “It’s a missed opportunity to present a different image,” said Peter Feaver, a top National Security Council aide in the George W. Bush White House. “He has doubled down on policies I oppose and that aren’t going to solve the problem.” Trump said in a speech Monday in New Hampshire he would suspend immigration from countries “where there is a proven history of terrorism” against the United States. He said radical Muslim immigrants were “trying to take over our children and convince them how wonderful ISIS (Islamic State) is.” After the worst mass murder in modern U.S. history on Sunday left 50 dead, Trump’s speech was hastily refashioned from a broad critique of Democratic rival Hillary Clinton to a dire warning of the threat from Islamist militants. Although Islamic State has claimed responsibility for the attack, U.S. officials have maintained that Omar Mateen’s motives were unclear and that he had no known direct links with the Syria-based group. Mateen, they said, was likely radicalized over the Internet. A week ago, the presumptive Republican presidential nominee’s bid was taking on water. He was being battered by fellow Republicans for his comments about the Hispanic heritage of a federal judge, and Clinton was pulling away in the polls. A renewed focus on national security could provide Trump with the chance to expand his appeal both to undecided voters and to the Republican foreign-policy establishment. While Trump at times seems to relish being at odds with the establishment, the unhappiness among the party’s hawks isn’t just a matter of hand-wringing. It means if Trump does reach the White House, he could have a difficult time recruiting talented, experienced advisers.  Max Boot, an influential conservative at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the Orlando tragedy “could have provided an opening for Trump to rally Republicans against terrorism.” But instead, Boot said, Trump has been “partisan and petty.” Boot criticized Trump for suggesting on Monday that President Barack Obama may sympathize with radicalized Muslims and for reviving the proposed Muslim ban. “His performance has been in character,” Boot said, “which is to say appalling.” Trump has alarmed some mainstream Republicans with vows to shred international trade deals, his demands that Mexico pay for a border wall and his questioning of U.S. foreign policy pillars such as its security commitments to NATO and Asian allies.  Clinton struck a very different tone in a speech on Monday, urging “statesmanship, not partisanship” and “clear, rational discussion” on how to protect the United States from terrorist threats. Eliot Cohen, a top-ranking State Department official during the Bush administration, called Trump’s reaction to the shootings “opportunistic and shallow” and “not what Americans expect from a president.”   Lanhee Chen, a top aide to Mitt Romney during his 2012 presidential campaign, suggested Trump will not be able to refine his image. “While it would be true in most cases a big speech like this could reset the decks, I think the challenge with Donald Trump is always who he is at his core,” Chen said. But voters are another matter. Trump’s swift rise within the Republican Party was at least partly due to the strident tone he has taken toward immigrants and refugees. When Trump responded to last year’s terror attacks in Paris and California with a call for banning Muslims from entering the country, he surged in the Reuters/Ipsos poll in the weeks that followed, opening up a 30-point lead over his Republican primary rivals.  Republicans continue to be strongly supportive of Trump’s approach to handling terrorism. This month, two-thirds of Republicans said they agreed with Trump’s proposal to temporarily ban Muslims from entering the country.  Overall, 42 percent of Americans said they agreed with a Muslim ban while 50 percent said they disagreed, with another 8 percent not sure, according to another Reuters/Ipsos poll from May 17 to June 6. The poll of more than 6,000 people has a credibility interval, a measure of accuracy, of about 1.5 percentage points. Combating Islamist extremism was on the mind of Texas billionaire Doug Deason, a major Republican donor who told Reuters he will meet with Trump later in the week to discuss his support.  Nothing Trump has said since the Orlando shooting has caused him to re-think backing him, Deason said.  Peter King, a U.S. congressman from New York, said his party’s foreign-policy establishment will eventually have to get on board with Trump. “As one of the two major candidates for president, he will have to get advice or consultation with top national-security people,” King said.

source_text: Obama wants Pacific trade deal to pass this year: White House. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. President Barack Obama wants Congress to approve the Trans-Pacific Partnership deal this year to help write the rules on global trade while keeping a competitive edge, the White House said on Friday. “This will be something that Congress has to contend with. text: In response to rising violence, a congressional committee in the U.S. is set to discuss the threats posed by militant groups. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A hearing on violent extremism, which will include domestic militant threats, is scheduled for next month by a U.S. congressional panel after a deadly rally by white supremacists in Charlottesville, Virginia. Republican Michael McCaul, who chairs the U.S. House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee, informed the committee’s leading Democrat, Bennie Thompson, about the hearing planned for September 12. Annually, the committee conducts a hearing around the anniversary of the September 11, 2001, attacks to review global threats. According to a committee staff member, the decision to expand the hearing to encompass domestic militant threats was influenced by the events in Charlottesville. However, Thompson expressed that this approach was “not adequate or appropriate” to fulfill his demand for a hearing focused specifically on the dangers posed by neo-Nazi and white supremacist organizations. “The hearing on September 12 concerning global threats had already been scheduled prior to the domestic violence this past weekend,” Thompson remarked. “It will not sufficiently delve into the extensive and complex nature of the threats from domestic terrorism linked to white supremacist and neo-Nazi organizations.” McCaul indicated that leaders from the Department of Homeland Security, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the National Counterterrorism Center would be invited to participate. “It is essential that we unite and denounce racism, bigotry, and prejudice, including the hateful ideologies espoused by neo-Nazis, the KKK, and all other white supremacist entities,” McCaul stated in his reply to the Democrats' call for a hearing. A tragic incident occurred on Saturday in Charlottesville, resulting in the death of a 32-year-old woman when a vehicle barreled into a counter-protest against white supremacist rally attendees. A 20-year-old man from Ohio, who is believed to have Nazi sympathies, has been charged with murder. On Tuesday, President Donald Trump remarked that both factions were responsible for the violence, which led to criticism from Republicans and Democrats alike for not specifically condemning the white nationalists.
source_text: Violence prompts U.S. Congress to discuss militant threats. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A U.S. congressional panel next month will hold a hearing on violent extremism, including threats from domestic militants, following a white supremacist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, that turned deadly. The chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee, Republican Michael McCaul, announced the Sept. 12 hearing in a letter to the panel’s top Democrat, Bennie Thompson. The committee holds a hearing once a year, around the anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, to discuss worldwide threats. A committee aide said the Charlottesville protests had  prompted the decision to broaden the hearing to include threats from domestic militants. But Thompson said the move was “not adequate or appropriate” to address his request for a hearing on threats from white supremacists and neo-Nazi groups. “The September 12 hearing to cover worldwide threats is an annual hearing that was already scheduled prior to the domestic attacks this weekend,” Thompson said. “It will not allow us to go into the depth necessary to address the far-ranging and multifaceted aspects of the threat posed by domestic terrorist threats from white supremacist and neo-Nazi groups.” The Homeland Security Committee will invite leaders of the Homeland Security Department, the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the National Counterterrorism Center, McCaul said. “We must stand together and reject racism, bigotry, and prejudice, including the hateful ideologies promoted by neo-Nazis, the KKK, and all other white supremacy groups,” McCaul wrote in his response to Democrats’ request for a hearing. A 32-year-old woman was killed on Saturday in Charlottesville when a car plowed into a rival protest to white supremacist demonstrators. A 20-year-old Ohio man said to have harbored Nazi sympathies has been charged with murder.  President Donald Trump on Tuesday said both sides were to blame for the violence, drawing condemnation from both fellow Republicans and Democrats for failing to single out the white nationalists.

text: ROME (Reuters) - The United Nations is set to enhance its security measures by sending 150-250 guards to Libya, primarily from Nepal, to safeguard its facility in the capital as part of a strategy to reinstate its operations in the region, officials from the U.N. revealed on Friday. Supported by governments from the West, the U.N. aims to mend divisions among Libya's competing factions to bring stability and address issues related to militant activities and human trafficking from the northern coastline of Libya. Since 2014, the mission has operated from Tunis due to conflicts among various Libyan brigades that led to the evacuation of most foreign diplomatic personnel; however, it has been progressively augmenting its footprint in Libya and has been preparing for a more comprehensive return for several months. Jean-Pierre Lacroix, who serves as the U.N. Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, stated during a news conference in Geneva that the security contingent is expected to comprise around 150 guards, primarily from Nepal. "To ensure the safety of our colleagues as they move into Tripoli, there will be a unit of military personnel from the U.N. coming from Nepal," Lacroix emphasized. text: The White House expressed that Israel's decision to decline a summit meeting with President Barack Obama was not a significant issue, although it could have been communicated more appropriately. On Tuesday, spokesperson Josh Earnest remarked that it would have been courteous for Israel to inform the U.S. directly rather than through media channels. However, he emphasized that there was "no offense taken" regarding Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's choice, which he attributed to a preference to avoid the ongoing U.S. presidential campaign. This incident marks the continuing strain in the relationship between the right-leaning Israeli leader and the Democratic president, which has yet to mend following profound disagreements over last year's nuclear agreement involving Israel's adversary, Iran. The day also bore witness to a tragic event in Tel Aviv, where an American tourist was killed in a stabbing incident, highlighting the stagnation in peace negotiations that Obama attempted to rejuvenate early in his administration. This attack was one of several Palestinian assaults occurring on the same day. Coincidentally, the stabbing took place just as U.S. Vice President Joe Biden commenced a two-day visit to Israel. During his trip, Biden was scheduled to meet with former Israeli president Shimon Peres and hold discussions with Netanyahu in Jerusalem and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas in the West Bank the following day. Given the ongoing wave of Palestinian violence that has persisted for five months, U.S. officials did not anticipate any significant advancements toward peace during Biden's stay. Biden's previous visit in 2010 was overshadowed by tensions related to an Israeli settlement announcement made while he was present. The White House revealed on Monday that it was "surprised" to first find out via Israeli media about Netanyahu's decision to skip the AIPAC conference in Washington on March 20, noting that some reports suggested Obama's unavailability was part of the reasoning. It was indicated that Netanyahu had been extended an invitation for a meeting with Obama on March 18, prior to the president's historic trip to Cuba on March 21 and 22. When questioned about whether the Netanyahu administration should have reached out to the Obama administration before informing the media, Earnest replied, "I think it's just good manners." In contrast, Zeev Elkin, a minister in Netanyahu's cabinet, argued that Israeli ambassador Ron Dermer had provided advance notice to the White House about the possibility that the trip would not occur. Netanyahu's office cited the U.S. election campaign as a reason for his decision not to attend the AIPAC event, while expressing gratitude for Obama's offer to host him. Back in 2012, Netanyahu welcomed Republican candidate Mitt Romney to Israel, which many Democrats interpreted as an effort to undermine Obama's quest for a second term. Claims of interference were denied by Israel. As both Republican and Democratic contenders for the presidential nomination strive to demonstrate their support for Israel, it is noteworthy that Obama is not seeking re-election in November, having already served the maximum of two terms. Earnest clarified that Biden's visit was not intended to address discussions related to a memorandum of understanding on U.S. military aid to Israel, stating that those negotiations were taking place through a different channel.

On Friday, Puerto Rico announced it will default on $779 million in senior debt, which is constitutionally backed, fulfilling warnings that it would prioritize essential services for its residents over its commitments to creditors. Payments exceeding $2 billion were due on the same day. Governor Alejandro Garcia Padilla informed the media that the U.S. commonwealth territory would not fulfill $911 million of its liabilities. A U.S. federal oversight board will soon take charge of the territory's finances, following the signing of a bill by U.S. President Barack Obama on Thursday that allows the island to undergo a debt restructuring process and puts a halt to litigation related to any defaults on its debt, which totals $70 billion. "Today, Puerto Rico is shielded from creditor actions," Garcia Padilla stated. The General Obligation (GO) debt, which carries a GO guarantee, is a type of debt that has not seen any defaults from U.S. states in many years. Puerto Rico lacks coverage under Chapter 9 of the U.S. bankruptcy code, which is applicable to municipalities. The Government Development Bank (GDB) for Puerto Rico indicated that the island would only have $95 million in cash available by the end of the year, even after the defaults declared on Friday. The benchmark 2035 GO bond for Puerto Rico increased in price by 0.25 points to 67.50 points, resulting in a yield decrease to 12.519 percent. On Thursday, Garcia Padilla authorized Puerto Rico to delay some of the $2 billion in payments due on Friday, under a locally established debt moratorium law. The events of Friday mark the lowest point in a ten-year struggle by Puerto Rico to stave off economic disaster. The island is burdened by a significant emigration rate and a staggering 45 percent poverty rate. 

The GDB emphasized in a statement on Friday that even if the Commonwealth dedicated every last cent in its accounts to debt obligations on July 1, it would still owe public debt holders hundreds of millions of dollars. Certain debts expected to be defaulted on, such as PBA (Public Building Authority) ex-series L bonds, are likely to be mostly safeguarded by reserve funds held by the trustee bank. Similarly, nearly all payments due on the Puerto Rico Infrastructure Financing Authority (PRIFA) Bond Anticipation Notes (BANs) will also be secured by reserve funds. In cases where some debts are backed by insurance policies, certain creditors might receive a portion of their owed payments. The GDB, which serves as Puerto Rico’s primary fiscal agent, revealed that the island holds only $200 million in its operating account, along with an additional $150 million in revenue that has been redirected from other debt obligations in recent months. 

Despite the continuation of emergency measures such as delaying vendor payments and withholding contributions to a pension fund that is already insolvent, the GDB reported that the operating account will still face depletion of cash within 30 to 60 days. "We anticipated this day would arrive, that they would default, and it has come. It was beneficial that they enacted PROMESA, even at the last possible moment," commented Ted Hampton, a senior credit officer at Moody’s Investors Service, referring to the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management and Economic Stability Act (PROMESA). Late Thursday, the legislature of the island ratified an $8.9 billion budget for fiscal year 2017, which is now pending Garcia Padilla’s approval. In the early hours of Friday, Puerto Rico disclosed long-awaited audited financial results for the fiscal year 2014, arriving more than a year later than expected. The statements, which were audited by KPMG, revealed that Puerto Rico’s largest public pension has depleted its assets and is now insolvent. The funding gaps for Puerto Rico’s pensions rank among the largest in U.S. history. "When I took office, Puerto Rico was under the control of Wall Street," Garcia Padilla remarked, adding: "Today, there is a consensus that we have been truthful about Puerto Rico’s financial situation."

text: On Monday, the U.S. Department of the Interior announced the withdrawal of a regulation established during the Obama administration concerning the valuation of coal, oil, and gas sales from federal and tribal lands. This decision was made to alleviate what was described as "confusion and uncertainty" affecting energy companies. Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke indicated that the newly formed royalty policy committee would seek alternatives to this rule and emphasized the commitment to ensure that all dues are collected. In a statement, Zinke remarked, "The removal of the valuation regulation establishes a fresh start for developing effective valuation guidelines." Former Interior Secretary Sally Jewell had introduced the valuation rule the previous year to address a loophole that allowed companies to evade royalty payments while extracting resources from public lands owned by taxpayers. The rule mandated that energy firms pay royalties based on sales to the first unrelated buyer, referred to as arm's-length transactions, as the resources progressed to market. A 2012 investigation by Reuters revealed that coal companies utilized affiliated brokers to negotiate royalty payments for exports to Asia at rates significantly lower than domestic prices. Zinke noted that the valuation regulation had raised expenses for companies in the coal, oil, and gas sectors, affecting production on federal properties and increasing dependence on foreign oil and gas imports. Several industry representatives and trade organizations initiated three lawsuits against the Obama-era regulation. Additionally, the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a group monitoring taxpayer interests, reported that nearly $30 billion in revenue was lost to taxpayers over a thirty-year period due to the loophole. The repeal of the valuation regulation was recorded in the Federal Register on August 7 and will take effect on September 6.
source_text: U.S. Interior Department rescinds coal valuation rule. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. Department of the Interior said on Monday it has rescinded an Obama-era rule that reformed how energy companies value sales of oil, gas and coal extracted from federal and tribal land to protect taxpayers because it caused “confusion and uncertainty” for energy companies. Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke said the department’s newly formed royalty policy committee would propose alternatives to the rule and “remain committed to collecting every dollar due.” “Repealing the valuation rule provides a clean slate to create workable valuation regulations,” Zinke said in a statement.  The valuation rule was proposed by former Interior Secretary Sally Jewell last year to close a loophole that enabled companies to dodge royalty payments when mining on taxpayer-owned public land. It required energy companies to pay royalties on sales to the first unaffiliated customer, known as an arm’s-length sale, as the fuel moves to market. A Reuters investigation found in 2012 that coal companies were using affiliated brokers to settle royalty payments on exports to Asia at much lower domestic prices. Zinke said the valuation rule had increased costs for coal, oil and gas companies, which hampered production on federal lands, “making us rely more and more on foreign imports of oil and gas.”  Industry stakeholders and trade associations filed three lawsuits challenging the Obama-era rule. Meanwhile, the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a taxpayer watchdog group, found that taxpayers missed out on nearly $30 billion in revenues over three decades because of the loophole. The repeal of the valuation Rule was published in the Federal Register on Aug. 7 and will become effective on Sept. 6.

On Thursday, Puerto Rico’s governor, Alejandro Garcia Padilla, authorized the suspension of payments on the territory’s general obligation debt, mere moments after U.S. President Barack Obama enacted a law that establishes a federal oversight board empowered to negotiate the restructuring of the island’s staggering $70 billion debt. This executive order comes just one day prior to a significant deadline for Puerto Rico, which was set to make $1.9 billion in debt payments on July 1, inclusive of approximately $780 million in constitutionally guaranteed general obligation bonds. It is uncertain if Puerto Rico will proceed with any payments toward the GO debt or the non-GO obligations. In a statement, Garcia Padilla’s administration indicated, "These executive orders safeguard the limited resources available to the entities mentioned in these orders and ensure that creditors cannot seize them, thereby preventing Puerto Ricans from losing essential services." 

This rapid sequence of actions marks the lowest point in a prolonged struggle that has persisted for a decade, as Puerto Rico, home to around 3.5 million U.S. citizens, battles to avoid economic disaster, counteract a 45 percent poverty rate, and curb the significant outflow of residents that worsens the economic downturn. Under a previously passed local debt moratorium law, Garcia Padilla has enacted the suspension of general obligation payments, although this law is already facing a creditor lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Manhattan. Furthermore, Garcia Padilla has declared states of emergency for the island's largest public pension system - the Commonwealth’s Employee Retirement System - which is over 99 percent underfunded, alongside the University of Puerto Rico and other governmental bodies. 

The benchmark 2035 General Obligation bond for Puerto Rico saw an increase of 0.44 points in value, reaching 67.19 points, which resulted in a yield reduction to 12.578 percent. Meanwhile, in Washington, Obama signed the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management and Economic Stability Act, known as PROMESA, in the Oval Office on Thursday. This legislation is one of the rare bipartisan measures to be sent to his desk. Before affixing his signature, Obama addressed reporters, stating, "I want to let the people of Puerto Rico know that although there are still some tough work that we’re going to have to do to dig Puerto Rico out of the hole that it’s in, this indicates how committed my administration is to making sure that they get the help they need." 

This new law allows the island to engage in a debt restructuring process that resembles bankruptcy, yet it places its financial management under the jurisdiction of an appointed federal board — a stipulation that has caused discontent among many Puerto Ricans, including Garcia Padilla. text: On Monday morning, thousands of Rohingya refugees crossed into Bangladesh from Myanmar, escaping violence and starvation, according to witnesses from Reuters. These individuals, impoverished, fearful, and hungry, navigated through waist-deep water, with children secured to their sides. They reported to Reuters that their journey involved traversing dense underbrush and swollen streams during monsoon conditions for several days. A continuous stream of refugees arrived in Bangladesh close to the Palongkhali village. Many of them sustained injuries; the elderly were transported on improvised stretchers, while women carried essential items like rice sacks, cookware, and clothing atop their heads. "We couldn’t leave our home for an entire month because the military was robbing people," stated Mohammad Shoaib, 29, who donned a yellow vest and balanced food-filled jute bags along with aluminum pots on a bamboo pole. "They began firing into the village. Consequently, we fled to another area. Each day, conditions deteriorated, prompting us to head toward Bangladesh. Before departing, I returned to my village to check on my home, and I found that the entire village had been reduced to ashes," Shoaib recounted. They joined approximately 536,000 Rohingya Muslims who have fled Myanmar since August 25, when coordinated assaults by Rohingya insurgents ignited a brutal military retaliation, with those escaping accusing security forces of setting fires, committing murders, and perpetrating sexual violence. Myanmar has dismissed the claims of ethnic cleansing and labeled the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, the group behind the attacks, as terrorists, asserting that they have killed civilians and torched villages. On Monday, the European Union announced that it would halt invitations to Myanmar's army commander-in-chief and other senior military officials due to the disproportionate force used by security personnel. Following a meeting of EU foreign ministers, a statement also demanded a comprehensive investigation into credible claims of severe human rights violations and abuses. Tragically, not everyone managed to reach Bangladesh safely on that Monday. A few kilometers south of Palongkhali, a boat overloaded with refugees capsized at dawn, resulting in at least 12 fatalities and leaving 35 individuals unaccounted for. According to Bangladeshi authorities, there were 21 survivors. Police official Moinuddin Khan stated, "So far, 12 bodies, including six children and four women, have been recovered." The border guards of Bangladesh informed Reuters that the boat sank due to an excess of refugees onboard, who pay high fees to navigate the Naf River, which serves as a natural boundary with Myanmar in the Cox's Bazar region of Bangladesh. This disaster occurred roughly a week after another vessel sank in the river estuary, which has become a burial ground for numerous Muslim refugees. Survivors of the treacherous journey indicated that they were compelled to flee due to food scarcity, as markets in the western Rakhine State of Myanmar have been closed and aid deliveries have been limited. They also reported assaults by military forces and Rakhine Buddhist mobs. The influx of refugees is expected to exacerbate the unprecedented humanitarian crisis currently unfolding in Cox's Bazar, where aid workers are struggling to provide food, clean water, and shelter to those in need. On that Monday, the Red Cross inaugurated a field hospital covering an area equivalent to two football fields, featuring 60 beds, three wards, an operating room, a delivery suite with a maternity ward, and a psychosocial support unit. Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya had previously sought refuge in Bangladesh after escaping earlier waves of violence in Myanmar, where they have been systematically denied citizenship and have faced restrictions on their movement and access to fundamental services. The EU's recent decision to avoid further interactions with Myanmar's military leadership follows reports indicating that both the European bloc and the United States are contemplating targeted sanctions against military officials. Although the actions announced by Brussels are primarily symbolic, the EU mentioned it may consider additional measures.
source_text: Thousands of new Rohingya refugees flee violence, hunger in Myanmar for Bangladesh. Wading through waist-deep water with children strapped to their sides, the refugees told Reuters they had walked through bushes and forded monsoon-swollen streams for days. A seemingly never-ending flow entered Bangladesh near the village of Palongkhali. Many were injured, with the elderly carried on makeshift stretchers, while women balanced household items, such as pots, rice sacks and clothing, on their heads.  We couldn t step out of the house for the last month because the military were looting people,  said Mohammad Shoaib, 29, who wore a yellow vest and balanced jute bags of food and aluminum pots on a bamboo pole.  They started firing on the village. So we escaped into another.  Day by day, things kept getting worse, so we started moving towards Bangladesh. Before we left, I went back near my village to see my house, and the entire village was burnt down,  Shoaib added. They joined about 536,000 Rohingya Muslims who have fled Myanmar since Aug. 25, when coordinated Rohingya insurgent attacks sparked a ferocious military response, with the fleeing people accusing security forces of arson, killings and rape. Myanmar rejects accusations of ethnic cleansing and has labeled the militants from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army who launched the attacks as terrorists, who have killed civilians and burnt villages. The European Union said on Monday it would suspend invitations to Myanmar s army commander-in-chief and other senior generals  in the light of the disproportionate use of force carried out by the security forces . A statement issued after a meeting of EU foreign ministers also called for thorough investigation of  credible allegations of serious human rights violations and abuses . Not everyone made it to Bangladesh alive on Monday. Several kilometers (miles) to the south of Palongkhali, a boat carrying scores of refugees sank at dawn, killing at least 12 and leaving 35 missing. There were 21 survivors, Bangladesh authorities said.  So far 12 bodies, including six children and four women, have been recovered,  said police official Moinuddin Khan. Bangladesh border guards told Reuters the boat sank because it was overloaded with refugees, who pay exorbitant fees to cross the Naf River, a natural border with Myanmar in the Cox s Bazar region of Bangladesh. The sinking came about a week after another boat capsized in the estuary on the river, which has become a graveyard for dozens of Muslim refugees. Refugees who survived the perilous journey said they were driven out by hunger because food markets in Myanmar s western Rakhine State have been shut and aid deliveries restricted. They also reported attacks by the military and Rakhine Buddhist mobs. The influx will worsen the unprecedented humanitarian emergency unfolding in Cox s Bazar, where aid workers are battling to provide refugees with food, clean water and shelter.   On Monday, the Red Cross opened a field hospital as big as two football fields, with 60 beds, three wards, an operating theater, a delivery suite with maternity ward and a psychosocial support unit. Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya had already been in Bangladesh after fleeing previous spasms of violence in Myanmar, where they have long been denied citizenship and faced curbs on their movements and access to basic services. Monday s EU move to shun further contacts with Myanmar s army top brass comes after officials told Reuters the European bloc and the United States were considering targeted sanctions against military leaders.  The action announced by Brussels is largely symbolic, though the EU said it may consider further measures. Western governments, who have invested politically in Myanmar s democratic transition, are wary of doing anything that would hurt the wider economy or destabilize already tense ties between civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi and the military. The powerful army chief, Min Aung Hlaing, told the United States ambassador in Myanmar last week that the exodus of Rohingya, whom he called non-native  Bengalis , was exaggerated. But despite Myanmar s denials and assurances that aid was on its way to the north of violence-torn Rakhine State, thousands more starving people were desperate to leave.  We fled from our home because we had nothing to eat in my village,  said Jarhni Ahlong, a 28-year-old Rohingya man from the southern region of Buthidaung, who had been stranded on the Myanmar side of the Naf for a week, waiting to cross. From the thousands gathered there awaiting an opportunity to escape, about 400 paid roughly $50 each to flee on nine or 10 boats on Monday morning, he added.  I think if we go to Bangladesh we can get food,  he said.

text: The investigation into the Trump team's connections with Russia has brought Representative Mike Conaway into the limelight, previously a less visible member of Congress. The 68-year-old Texas lawmaker has been appointed to lead the House Intelligence Committee’s inquiry, a role that has made him a central figure in one of the most divisive matters currently facing the nation. Both parties, Republicans and Democrats, have expressed approval of his appointment. Conaway’s previous experience as chairman of the House Ethics Committee from 2013 to 2015 has provided him with the necessary administrative skills to tackle such sensitive issues. "I like him. I hope he can get us back on track,” Representative Eric Swalwell, a Democratic member of the committee, remarked during a short conversation outside the U.S. House of Representatives. While he has established connections with mainstream Republicans and has a long-standing relationship with the Bush political dynasty, Conaway was a fervent supporter of Trump throughout the 2016 election campaign. His backing of Trump in 2016 was influenced by the choice of Mike Pence for vice president, Trump's commitment to appoint conservative justices to the Supreme Court, and Conaway's strong opposition to Hillary Clinton, the Democratic candidate. However, unlike Devin Nunes, who recently resigned from leading the investigation into the alleged Russian interference in the presidential election and potential collusion with Trump associates, Conaway was not part of the transition team for the incoming president. Russia has rejected these allegations. Compared to other Republican members on the committee, such as Trey Gowdy, who chaired the House Select Committee that examined the 2012 attacks on the U.S. diplomatic mission in Benghazi, Libya, Conaway is viewed as having a less partisan approach. Gowdy has faced accusations from Democrats of conducting a partisan investigation aimed at undermining Clinton's 2016 presidential bid. In his announcement of stepping down, Nunes indicated that Gowdy and another Republican member, Tom Rooney, would also take on leadership roles within the Russia investigation. According to Fox News, Nunes reached out to Conaway on Wednesday evening. Nonetheless, some of Conaway’s statements regarding the Russia investigation have garnered attention. During a committee hearing on March 20, he inquired of FBI Director James Comey if reporters from the Washington Post had assisted intelligence agencies in formulating their evaluation that Moscow aimed to support Trump’s election. Furthermore, in a January discussion with the Dallas Morning News, he appeared to trivialize the alleged Russian interference, equating it to the Democrats’ use of Mexican entertainers to engage their supporters, describing both instances as examples of "foreign interference." Although he also holds the position of chairman for the House Agriculture Committee, Conaway has maintained a relatively modest public presence and is more widely recognized for his connections to the Bush family than for media attention. Elected to the House for the first time in 2004 and re-elected six consecutive times, he ranks second among Republicans on the intelligence panel. On Thursday, House Speaker Paul Ryan expressed his confidence in Conaway's ability to conduct a thorough investigation. "I am confident that he will oversee a professional investigation into Russia’s actions and follow the facts wherever they may lead,” Ryan stated.

text: Concerns have been raised by Republican lawmakers regarding discussions that the U.S. government may permit Iran to conduct transactions in dollars. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Thursday, several Republican representatives expressed significant unease about the possibility suggested by reports that the Obama administration could allow Iran to engage in dollar-denominated business transactions, despite no official plans being disclosed. Officials from the U.S. government indicated that the Treasury Department is currently reviewing the matter; however, they clarified that any potential policy modification would not grant Iran extensive access to the U.S. financial system, countering certain media claims. A U.S. official, speaking anonymously, revealed that the administration is contemplating a reduction of some sanctions to allow foreign companies to access the U.S. financial system for dollar transactions involving Iran. This official emphasized that discussions are ongoing and no decisions have been made, nor are any anticipated soon. The rationale behind this consideration stems from the fact that foreign businesses, which can now operate with Iran due to last year’s nuclear agreement, are finding it challenging to do so without eventually interfacing with the U.S. financial system. The official noted that these foreign entities are receiving mixed signals from their own governments, which encourage trade with Iran, while Washington strictly states its intention to enforce sanctions. Republican representatives remain firmly opposed to any moves aimed at loosening restrictions against Iran, particularly in light of the nation’s recent missile launches. Paul Ryan, the Republican Speaker of the House of Representatives, stated, “As Iran continues to undermine the spirit of its nuclear agreement with illicit ballistic missile tests, the Obama administration is going out of its way to help Tehran reopen for business. The president should abandon this idea.” The ongoing debate may hinder the Senate's approval process for Adam Szubin, who has been nominated to lead the Treasury’s sanctions enforcement division, according to Senate aides. President Barack Obama put forth Szubin’s nomination in April 2015; however, he only received committee approval this month. Senate leaders attempted to schedule a full Senate vote on Szubin shortly after, but at least one senator voiced objections, aides revealed. Republicans, who hold the majority in Congress, previously sought to dismantle the international agreement that required Iran to limit its nuclear activities in exchange for alleviating sanctions. Some GOP members indicated their opposition to Szubin stems from his endorsement of the agreement, and aides suggested that discussions about relaxing dollar restrictions might intensify their resistance. Opponents of the deal have highlighted remarks made by U.S. Treasury Secretary Jack Lew as an indication that the administration might be inclined to lift the ban on Iran’s use of the dollar for trade. In a letter addressed to President Obama, Republican Representative Ed Royce pointed out that Lew seemed to leave the possibility open during his testimony before the House last week, hinting that the administration might allow such transactions. Lew remarked that the Treasury was exploring ways to “make sure Iran gets relief” as part of the nuclear deal rather than denying that the topic was under consideration. Currently, U.S. regulations prohibit foreign banks from executing dollar-based transactions with Iran through American banks. Experts in sanctions indicated that the Treasury could potentially issue a license permitting U.S. banks to transfer dollars to an offshore facility, allowing non-Iranian foreign banks to withdraw dollars to support legal trade with Iran. Any such allowance would likely exclude transactions involving Iranian individuals or organizations that are blacklisted. The Associated Press noted that the Obama administration may soon inform foreign governments and banks that they could begin utilizing the dollar in specific situations to facilitate business with Iran, citing sources familiar with the ongoing discussions. Insiders from both the administration and Congress have conveyed to Reuters that this concession is merely one of many options being considered. A spokesperson for the State Department, John Kirby, stated that Washington would persist in analyzing the potential lifting of sanctions under the nuclear accord known as the JCPOA while maintaining pressure on Iran regarding other areas of concern.

text: TOKYO (Reuters) - Ahead of the national election this Sunday, Japanese companies largely desire that Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s ruling coalition maintains its leadership, although approximately two-thirds prefer it to lose some seats, according to a poll by Reuters. The findings indicate that businesses seek political continuity but are apprehensive about granting Abe a sweeping victory, fearing it may lead to complacency regarding economic revitalization. Numerous firms expressed worries that a significant electoral win would motivate Abe to focus on his long-standing goal of amending Japan’s pacifist constitution, potentially neglecting economic strategies. A construction firm manager stated, "We require political stability. However, the foremost priority must be economic measures rather than constitutional revisions," indicating a preference for the ruling coalition of Abe’s Liberal Democratic Party and its ally Komeito to retain a simple majority while losing some seats. On Sunday, voters in Japan will select representatives for the 465-member lower house, which holds more power than the upper chamber of Japan’s national legislature, known as the Diet. Predictions released last week suggested that Abe’s coalition might secure around 300 seats, nearly matching the two-thirds super-majority it previously held before the election was called. The LDP bloc, alongside like-minded parties, also commands a majority in the upper house, which is necessary for constitutional amendments. Conducted between September 28 and October 12, the corporate survey revealed that 94 percent of businesses hoped for a victory for Abe’s coalition. Nonetheless, 48 percent preferred a smaller majority for his bloc, while 20 percent desired that the ruling party maintain the 323 seats it held prior to the lower house dissolution last month. A mere 7 percent wished for the ruling coalition to gain additional seats. "Expectations of unexpected outcomes like Brexit and (Donald) Trump’s presidency often lead to disappointment. This election lacks a single, dominant issue," remarked Masaki Kuwahara, a senior economist at Nomura Securities, who analyzed the survey findings. The fragmentation of votes among opposition parties is anticipated to benefit Abe’s coalition. During the campaign, Tokyo Governor Yuriko Koike’s new Party of Hope emerged, advocating for a halt on a planned sales tax increase scheduled for 2019. According to the Reuters survey, a slight majority favored Abe maintaining a budget-balancing objective, while expressing opposition to his proposal of reallocating funds from a planned increase in the national sales tax towards education and childcare instead of debt repayment. A manager from a metal products machinery company commented in the survey, "Abe must be appealing to the public with such a plan that may attract voters in the election. How can Japan possibly finance the expenses of social security services?" When asked about the policies that should be prioritized post-election, fiscal consolidation - aimed at addressing the industrial world's most considerable public-debt burden - emerged as the leading choice, selected by 35 percent of respondents. This was followed by additional fiscal stimulus, which 14 percent favored. Only 5 percent indicated a preference for further monetary stimulus, highlighting the prevailing market sentiment that easy-money policies have limitations. Merely 3 percent identified constitutional revision as a top priority. Kuwahara noted that many firms are concerned about the potential collapse of public finances, fearing it would destabilize the financial system and the broader economy. There are also apprehensions that amending the pacifist constitution could convey a negative message to Asian nations that suffered from Japan’s wartime aggression. The survey, conducted for Reuters by Nikkei Research, involved 548 large and mid-sized companies that answered anonymously. Approximately 230 businesses provided their insights regarding the election outlook and policies.

text: On Tuesday, Hary Tanoesoedibjo, an influential business figure from Indonesia, announced that he has no intention of competing in the presidential election scheduled for 2019. He expressed his support for the current President, Joko Widodo, should Widodo decide to pursue re-election. Tanoesoedibjo, who is known for his business ties to Donald Trump and whose political aspirations have often drawn comparisons to the U.S. President, previously indicated in January that he would make a decision regarding his candidacy before the end of the following year. text: ADDIS ABABA (Reuters) - In Ethiopia's Oromiya region, a death toll of at least 61 has been reported due to conflicts among various ethnic groups, according to officials, marking another episode of unrest that underscores the escalating instability in a province that experienced severe protests in 2015 and 2016. From Thursday, attacks by ethnic Somali aggressors resulted in the deaths of 29 ethnic Oromos in the districts of Hawi Gudina and Daro Lebu, as stated by regional spokesman Addisu Arega Kitessa. Subsequent to this violence, retaliatory actions were taken by ethnic Oromos in another area, where 32 Somalis, who had been seeking refuge following earlier violence, were killed. The spokesman mentioned that efforts are underway to hold those responsible accountable. While the reasons behind this latest round of violence remain unclear, it occurred after protests erupted in Celenko town within Oromiya, where soldiers reportedly fired upon the crowd, leading to the deaths of 16 ethnic Oromos on Tuesday. "We do not know who ordered the deployment of the military. This illegal act should be punished," remarked Lema Megersa, the president of the region. The ongoing clashes are likely to heighten concerns regarding security in Ethiopia, which holds the status of the largest economy in the region and is considered a key ally of Western nations. Lema's statements also reflect the growing tensions within the ruling EPRDF coalition of Ethiopia, particularly since significant unrest plagued the Oromiya region in 2015 and 2016, resulting in numerous fatalities. The unrest was ignited by a development project in Addis Ababa that opponents claimed amounted to land seizures, leading to widespread anti-government protests focused on political and human rights issues. text: The attempt by Democratic lawmakers to secure nearly $1 billion in funding to fight the opioid crisis was dismissed by Republican members of the U.S. Congress on Wednesday, according to aides. This decision, made during discussions among negotiators from the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate regarding the proposed bipartisan legislation, may jeopardize the support of Democrats for the final bill, which could be put to a vote in the House as soon as Friday. In recent months, both the House and Senate have approved their distinct versions of the legislation. Now, Democratic representatives in both chambers are withholding their endorsement for the final bill, as reported by two aides from the Democratic side. This opposition from the Democrats might create hurdles, particularly in the Senate, where 60 votes are necessary to advance any legislation. The two amendments proposed by House and Senate Democrats aimed to provide $920 million initially to fund grants for state programs. Aides mentioned that these initiatives would otherwise require a lengthy appropriations process, which could be delayed due to the shortened congressional session caused by this year’s election campaigning. Republican aides were not available for immediate feedback. However, House Republicans are looking at an alternative health funding initiative that would allocate over $581 million to tackle opioid misuse. On Wednesday, House Democratic Caucus Chairman Xavier Becerra noted that this is merely the latest example of bipartisan-supported legislation lacking adequate funding. "It’s becoming a bit of a joke to say we’re concerned and want to do something, when the only thing we’ll do is shell of what it actually takes," he remarked.
source_text: U.S. Republicans reject Democratic funding proposals for opioids. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Republican lawmakers in U.S. Congress on Wednesday rejected two Democratic amendments to provide nearly $1 billion in funding for bipartisan legislation intended to combat America’s opioid epidemic, aides said. The rejection, which came during a meeting of U.S. House of Representatives and Senate negotiators on the measure, could undermine Democratic support for final legislation that could come up for a vote in the House of Representatives as early as Friday. The House and Senate each passed its own versions of the legislation in the last few months. House and Senate Democratic lawmakers are now withholding their support for the final version of the bill, according to two Democratic aides. Democratic opposition could prove to be an obstacle, especially in the Senate, where lawmakers need 60 votes to move legislation forward.  Two amendments, from House and Senate Democrats, would have provided $920 million up front to finance program grants for states. Aides said the programs otherwise require completion of a lengthy appropriations process that could stall in a congressional session shortened by this year’s election campaign. Republican aides were not immediately available for comment. But House Republicans are separately considering a health spending measure that would provide more than $581 million to address opioid abuse. House Democratic Caucus Chairman Xavier Becerra said on Wednesday it was only the latest instance in which legislation with bipartisan backing fell short on funding. “It’s becoming a bit of a joke to say we’re concerned and want to do something, when the only thing we’ll do is shell of what it actually takes,” he said.
